## 1. Purpose, ownership and authoring contract

### 1.1 What this document is

This is the **specification for porting MvcMusicStore's MVC 5 edition from ASP.NET MVC 5 on
System.Web to ASP.NET Core**. It is written to be executed: an engineer holding this document, its
sibling deliverables and repository access should be able to carry out the port without making a
design decision this document declined to make.

Deliverable [12](12-migration-blockers.md) enumerated twenty-three blockers and, for each, named the
successor or recorded that there is none. **This document's job is the next step and a different
one: every one of those twenty-three gets a resolution — a decision, with the target construct named,
the affected sites listed, and the test that proves it.** Section [13](#13-resolution-register--all-23-blockers-of-deliverable-12)
walks all twenty-three and is the audit trail for that claim.

The scope is the **migration source only**. Edition triage is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to
sequence and it selected MVC 5; MVC 4 and MVC 3 are retained read-only as **historical and comparative
references**, and appear here only where their code is evidence about a decision this
document makes — which happens once, in section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command).

**MVC 5 is the sole executable behavioural baseline, and that distinction is load-bearing rather than
terminological.** In this document "behavioural baseline" means *the artifact the suite drives and
compares the port against*, and exactly one edition is that artifact: `LegacyBaselineFixture` drives
**MVC 5** over HTTP (section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)), and **neither MVC 4
nor MVC 3 is driven by the suite at all** — no row of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) issues a
request against either. Calling all three "the behavioural baseline" would advertise three executable
references where there is one, and would imply a cross-edition comparison the suite does not perform.
The reason only MVC 5 can hold the role is that the port derives from MVC 5 and is validated against
it: a difference between the port and MVC 4 or MVC 3 would not be a regression at all, because those
editions' behaviour is not what the port promises to preserve. Per-edition build outcomes — including
whether either of the other two editions can be stood up to be driven — are
[10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s and are not restated here. **The other two editions are
read as evidence; MVC 5 is run.**

### 1.2 What this document is not

It is not an inventory. Where a fact about the current system is already established and owned
elsewhere, this document **cites it and moves to the resolution** rather than re-deriving it. It is
not a schedule: **no implementation effort figure, no delivery duration and no sequence position for the
work** appears anywhere below, because those belong to [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) and
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) and a second statement of them would be a second decision.

**That exclusion is about the delivery of the work and not about time as such, which is worth stating
because a blanket "no figures" claim would be plainly false of the pages that follow.** Operational
periods and retention figures are runtime configuration, they are part of the contracts this document
owns, and they appear throughout: the readiness cache's ten seconds (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), the lockout window and the cookie and
security-stamp intervals (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), the submission
token's twenty-four-hour lifetime (section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)), and the length of the legacy-cookie
middleware's retention floor, which this document fixes from the legacy ticket lifetime while the
instant it is measured from is [06 §11.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 3). Two periods that a reader might expect
here are deliberately **not** this document's and appear nowhere in it as values: the genre
aggregate's expiry and the bounds of its fallback, both [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
and both cited rather than set (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)). None of
those is an estimate, none names a date, and none says how long any of this work takes.

And it is not authorization. See section [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible).

### 1.3 Authoring contract, and the absence of user rules

**`review_rules` returns exactly "No user rules provided."** Verified directly during the production
of this document. There is therefore no project rule to name, summarize or cite, and no rule forcing a
file into scope. That absence is **not** licence to lower the bar; enterprise-standard practice applies
instead, and this document holds itself to four explicit contracts:

1. **Citation contract.** Every claim about the **existing** system carries an inline
   `[<path>:<locator>]` citation at the point of the claim, with a repository-relative path that
   resolves in the checkout. A prescription about the target needs no repository citation — but the
   fact that motivates it almost always does, and where it does, it carries one.
   **One citation form is used, and exactly one: the full form, which names both halves at every
   occurrence** — `[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:24]`. There is **no locator-only
   shorthand** and no path inherited from a neighbouring citation, so every citation is resolvable
   **where it stands** without reading backwards to find which file it belongs to — which is what
   `[<repo-relative-path>:<locator>]` has to mean if a reader is to check it. A **path-only** citation
   — a path carrying no locator — is likewise not a form this document uses.
   A locator is a line (`:24`), a line range (`:24-28`), a comma-separated list of either
   (`:16,27,36,44`), or — for the one cited artifact that has no line structure, a committed `.mdf` —
   the database objects the claim reads (`:AspNetUsers,AspNetUserLogins`).
   [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) carries the mechanical check, and it is deliberately
   retained in the shape that can **detect** a locator-only citation rather than reduced to what the
   document now contains: it segments the document into the blocks such a citation would have inherited
   a path within — **one table cell, one list item, or one paragraph** — and reports **1834** full
   citations, **0** locator-only citations, **0** path-only citations, **0** citations with no
   antecedent, **0** locators outside the file they cite, and **68** distinct cited paths, all of which
   resolve in this checkout. Those middle zeroes are the assertion: a reintroduced shorthand becomes a
   non-zero count in that output rather than a judgement somebody has to remember to make.
2. **Repository-wide claims carry their reproducing command.** A count, an absence, or a fact held in a
   **binary** tracked file has no single line to point at, so its evidence is the command or query that
   produces it, stated next to the claim. Every such command in this document was run against this
   checkout; [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) collects them. **A bracketed path with no
   locator is not one of these forms and is not admitted anywhere in this document** — a claim that
   cannot carry a locator carries a command instead, and the locator check in
   [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) counts the path-only form and requires zero of it.
3. **Exact versions only, and version pins are not this document's to state.** Where a version
   matters, [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) and [04 §9.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
   own the pins. This document names the *capability* and cites 04 for the *version*.
4. **One fact, one owner.** Section [1.6](#16-what-this-document-does-not-own) lists what belongs to
   someone else. Where this document needs such a fact, it links to the owner rather than restating
   the value.

Markdown line length follows the corpus convention recorded in [`README.md` § 10 Markdown line-length convention](README.md#10-markdown-line-length-convention).

### 1.4 The no-modification constraint, and the boundary that makes this document possible

The user directed **"Do not make code changes initially"**, and the project's environment setup
instructions independently restate the same gate. **No tracked repository file was created, modified or
deleted in producing this document except the file you are reading** — and that sentence is narrower
than "nothing was written", so the difference is stated rather than glossed.

**Restores and builds were performed against this checkout during the assessment, and they wrote
output into it.** Those runs left **eight gitignored trees** behind — 527 files, 114,310,394 bytes:

```text
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/bin      src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/bin
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/obj      src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/obj
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/bin                              src/MVC4/packages
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/obj                              src/MVC5/packages
```

**All eight were removed and their absence was verified.** None was ever a tracked file and none is in
the checkpoint commit; what they were is ignored output that a status command cannot see. The account
of them belongs to [10 §1.4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md), which owns build hygiene as its
subject and carries the per-tree record; **none of those runs is build evidence**, and MVC 5's build
status remains **blocked pending a Windows verification run**
([10 §3.1](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md),
[10 §5.4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)). This document repeats none of that — what it owes
the reader here is the honest form of its own attestation.

**That is exactly why the acceptance check is four commands rather than one, and why a bare
`git status --porcelain` is not sufficient evidence for it.** All eight trees were ignored on this
checkout, so build and restore output was **invisible** to plain porcelain and to a tracked-file diff
alike: for the whole period they existed, both would have reported a clean tree. An attestation resting
on either was attesting to something it had not looked at.

**Which rule ignored which tree, because the obvious answer is wrong for half of them.** The `bin` and
`obj` trees are matched by `[Bb]in/` [.gitignore:2] and `[Oo]bj/` [.gitignore:1]. The two nested
`packages` trees are matched by **`Packages/` [.gitignore:33]**, not by `packages/*`
[.gitignore:15]: a pattern whose only separator is trailing matches a directory of that name at **any**
depth, whereas a pattern with an interior separator is anchored to the repository root and so cannot
reach `src/MVC4/packages` or `src/MVC5/packages` at all. `Packages/` reaches them only because
`git config core.ignorecase` reports `true` on this checkout, which makes the capitalised pattern match
the lowercase directories — so **on a case-sensitive filesystem nothing in `.gitignore` would ignore
those two trees**, and there they would have been visible to plain porcelain as untracked paths.
[04 §A.6](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns this analysis and states it the same way; the
per-path rule is reproducible with `git check-ignore --no-index -v`, in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility). Neither half of that changes the conclusion for this
checkout: all eight were ignored here, so the two ignore-aware commands are the ones that carry the
claim.

The check therefore runs the two ignore-aware commands beside the two tracked ones, and all four have
to agree:

```bash
git status --porcelain              # -> 0 lines  (no tracked change, no untracked file)
git status --porcelain --ignored    # -> 0 lines  (and no "!!" row: no ignored path exists either)
git clean -ndX                      # -> empty   (nothing ignored is there to be removed)
git diff --name-status ea2552d6eda7c20e9477a512e5c615665618cf35..HEAD
# -> exactly 13 rows, every one an "A", every path under docs/modernization/:
#    01-architecture-overview.md            08-technical-debt-register.md
#    02-dependency-inventory.md             09-security-assessment.md
#    03-modernization-roadmap.md            10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md
#    04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md       11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md
#    05-aspnet-core-migration-approach.md   12-migration-blockers.md
#    06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md    README.md
#    07-effort-risks-sequencing.md
# No M row, no D row, and no path outside docs/modernization/.
```

The first three are read against a clean checkout of the checkpoint commit; the fourth is the one that
survives later commits, which is why it remains the check of record. `git clean -ndX` is listed
because it is the only one of the four that answers the question in the form it is asked — *is any
ignored artifact present* — and it answers it in a dry run that removes nothing.

**Why the fourth command's range is pinned at one end and not the other, since a fully pinned range
would otherwise be the obvious improvement.** The first endpoint is pinned exactly:
`ea2552d6eda7c20e9477a512e5c615665618cf35`, the full forty-character hash of the commit this work
started from, written out rather than abbreviated so that it cannot become ambiguous as the history
grows. The second endpoint cannot be given the same treatment, and the reason is arithmetic rather than
reluctance — **no document can contain the hash of the commit that adds it.** A commit's hash is
computed over its own content, this file included, so the hash does not exist until the commit does, and
the commit cannot be made until all thirteen files are final. Any hash written here in `HEAD`'s place
would therefore name some *earlier* commit, and citing an earlier commit as the endpoint of the range
that adds these files would assert something false about what the range contains. A range that looks
more precise while naming the wrong commit is worse than one that is honest about which end is symbolic.

`HEAD` is consequently the endpoint of record, and a reader who wants the pinned form **produces it
rather than receiving it** — one command, run on the checkout under review while `HEAD` is still the
checkpoint commit:

```bash
git rev-parse HEAD      # -> the checkpoint commit; substitute it for HEAD in the range above
```

From that point the range is fixed at both ends and no later commit can widen it. **The substitution
changes nothing the check asserts**: the four expected values are the same either way — exactly **13**
rows, all **13** of them `A` rows, **0** rows carrying any other status, and **0** rows outside
`docs/modernization/`. `HEAD` and the resolved hash name the same commit at the moment the check is run;
the only difference is that the resolved form keeps naming it afterwards. The same range appears four
more times in this document — once in the roll-up of section
[14.2](#142-what-this-document-creates-nothing-and-what-the-assessment-nonetheless-wrote) and three
times in [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) — and each is the same assertion under the same
convention, which this clause states once rather than repeating at each site.
**Both ends of that fourth command are named rather than assumed, because a range is only evidence if
both of its ends are.** The left side, `ea2552d6eda7c20e9477a512e5c615665618cf35`, is the **immutable
evidence revision**: every citation in this document was read against that commit, and it is the commit a
later reader re-reads them against. Its short form is `ea2552d`, and every later mention in this
document's prose is that same revision. The right side, `HEAD`, is the **delivery commit the reviewer has
checked out**, so the range reads forward from the evidence revision to whatever commit carries these
thirteen files at review time. **It is named `HEAD` rather than a hash for a reason that is not a
convenience and is not an omission: a document cannot cite the commit that creates it.** The commit
carrying these thirteen files does not exist while they are being written, so its hash is unknowable to
the text inside them; writing any literal hash there would be either wrong on the day or a value nobody
could have obtained. `HEAD` is the one form that is correct at the moment the command is run, and the
reader resolves it on the delivered checkout — which is exactly the checkout the review is performed
against. Deliverables [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md),
[10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) and [11](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) state the same
rationale for the same command, and it is stated here rather than cited because each of the four states
it about its own copy of a runnable block. The runnable blocks in this section and in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility) spell the left side out in full because they are meant to be
pasted and run as written. **This is the only commit range this document states**, and it states it only
as this check.

**This document lives closer to that line than any other in the set, so the line is worth stating
precisely: the prohibition is on *mutating*, not on *planning*.**

Every target artifact named below — `Program.cs`, `appsettings.json`, `ErrorViewModel.cs`,
`Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs`, `Binding/AlbumCreateInputModel.cs`, `Binding/AlbumEditInputModel.cs`,
`Binding/CspReportModels.cs`, `Services/ShoppingCartService.cs`,
`Services/CspReportSink.cs`, `Data/MusicStoreEntities.cs`,
`Data/ApplicationDbContext.cs`, `Data/Migrations/Catalog/**`, `Data/Migrations/Identity/**`,
`Data/SeedData.cs`, the three `*ViewComponent.cs` classes and their `Default.cshtml` views,
`Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`, `wwwroot/**`, `libman.json`, `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/**` and
`tools/provision-admin/**` — is **content written into this document, not a file created on disk.**
The list is exhaustive: the four `Binding/` and six `Services/` files are the whole of what this document
adds inside those two folders, and **every one of the ten has its own row in
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map** — that map is one row per physical file with no
delegation and no catch-all, so a file this document declares and that map omits is the unowned target
its §12.1 forbids rather than a file covered by a folder. No artifact
outside AAP §0.4.1's map is introduced anywhere in this document. **An earlier form of this paragraph
counted "the two `Binding/` … files" and named only two of them**, which had been true before section
[8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) resolved the
administration over-post with two input models of its own; it is corrected rather than qualified, because
a count of what this document adds is the one sentence a reader checks the map against.
Likewise, every row below whose fate is "Deleted" describes a target state; nothing was deleted.

**This document therefore fails in both directions.** It fails if it reads as authorization to begin
changing code. It fails equally **if it declines to specify a change because it mistook the
prohibition on mutating for a prohibition on planning** — and that second failure is the more likely
one, because it looks like caution. What follows is written as a specification an engineer executes
after approval.

## 2. The composition root

### 2.1 Disposition of every current startup and configuration file — twelve files, four fates

Composition in MVC 5 is split across twelve files and two entry points. In the target it is one file
plus a handful of Razor and MSBuild conventions. The table below is the **complete** disposition, and
its column headings matter: *Physical fate* is what happens to the file, *Responsibility* is what
happens to what the file did. Those are different questions, and four distinct answers appear in the
second column.

**"No counterpart" is not the same as "no successor."** A responsibility with a successor moves; a
responsibility with no counterpart **ends**, and the target simply does not have the concern. Both
appear below and each row says which it is.

| Current file | Physical fate | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Global.asax.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11-21] | Deleted | **Moves, per registration** — the five registrations do not share one fate; see [2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate) |
| `Startup.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:4-14] | Deleted | **Moves** — attribute-declared host discovery becomes explicit composition in `Program.cs`; see [2.3](#23-owin-startup-the-abstraction-goes-the-responsibilities-do-not) |
| `App_Start/RouteConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:12-21] | Deleted | **Moves** — one conventional route registration in `Program.cs`; the `.axd` ignore route ends |
| `App_Start/FilterConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/FilterConfig.cs:8-11] | Deleted | **Replaced** — exception-handling middleware plus the global anti-forgery filter of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems) |
| `App_Start/Startup.App.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:14-45] | Deleted | **Splits** — the initializer registration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:16] is replaced by migrations; administrator provisioning [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18-45] **leaves the web application entirely** for `tools/provision-admin` (section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command)) |
| `App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:11-36] | Deleted | **Moves and becomes explicit** — cookie authentication is a framework feature; the policy it silently inherited today is stated in section [6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited). The external sign-in cookie [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20] is **retained in substance**: the Katana registration call ends with `IAppBuilder`, the cookie itself becomes the framework's external scheme, because section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (5) retains the surface it serves. The four commented-out providers [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35] **end**, per the same decision |
| `Global.asax` — the markup file [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax:1] | Deleted | **Ends.** The target has no application-declaration file of any kind and nothing reads this one |
| `App_Start/BundleConfig.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/BundleConfig.cs:9-29] | Deleted | **Ends.** No bundler in the target — section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler) |
| `Views/Web.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:1-35] | Deleted | **Splits three ways**, one part with a successor and two with no counterpart. The **namespace registration** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:14-21] moves to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`, carrying six `@using` directives 29 views depend on. The **Razor host and page-base-type registration** — its `configSections` section-group declaration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:4-9] and the `system.web.webPages.razor` element [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:11-23] it configures — **ends**: the target compiles views through its own SDK and has no host factory or page base type to name. The **`BlockViewHandler` handler mapping** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:29-34], whose `remove`/`add` pair is [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:31-32], together with the `webpages:Enabled` app setting [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:25-27], **ends** with the IIS integrated pipeline — section [8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports) |
| `Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs:8-15] | Deleted | **Absorbed** into MSBuild properties — [04 §5.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns it |
| `Web.Debug.config` | Deleted | **Ends.** It carries no active transform at all — verified, section [3.2](#32-the-one-active-transform-and-the-two-halves-it-splits-into) |
| `Web.Release.config` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18] | Deleted | **Re-expressed.** Its one active transform becomes a publish-time Release setting — section [3.2](#32-the-one-active-transform-and-the-two-halves-it-splits-into) |

Two rows in that table are the ones a reader is most likely to compress into the others, so they are
called out. `Startup.App.cs` **splits across a project boundary** — half of it becomes migrations and
half of it leaves the web application to become a separate console tool — which is a stronger statement
than "moves into `Program.cs`". And `Views/Web.config` splits **three ways**, with one part having a
direct successor and two having no counterpart at all; a plan that deletes the file without noticing the
namespace part loses six `@using` directives that 29 views depend on.

### 2.2 The five `Application_Start` registrations do not share one fate

`public class MvcApplication : System.Web.HttpApplication`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11] runs five registrations in `Application_Start`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:13-21]. Treating the method as one unit is the single most
common way to get this port wrong, because **three different outcomes are present in five lines**.

| Registration | Line in `Global.asax.cs` | Resolution | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AreaRegistration.RegisterAllAreas()` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:15] | **Deleted.** There is no `Areas` folder anywhere in the repository — `git ls-files \| grep -c 'Areas/'` returns `0` — so the call has always been dead scaffolding ([08 §9.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt). Nothing replaces it. | Ends |
| `FilterConfig.RegisterGlobalFilters(GlobalFilters.Filters)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:16] | **Replaced.** Its one filter, `new HandleErrorAttribute()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/FilterConfig.cs:10], becomes **exception-handling middleware** — a pipeline registration, not a filter — and the global filter slot it vacates is taken by the **anti-forgery filter** of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems). Design in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). | Replaced |
| `RouteConfig.RegisterRoutes(RouteTable.Routes)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:17] | **Moves.** The `.axd` ignore route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:14] is **dropped** — the target has no `.axd` handler, so there is nothing to exclude. The single conventional route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:16-20] becomes one conventional route registration with the pattern `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}`, which preserves the whole of the application's URL surface: one route, no areas, no attribute routing, no constraints. | Moves |
| `BundleConfig.RegisterBundles(BundleTable.Bundles)` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:18] | **Deleted outright**, under the no-bundler decision of section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler). The five bundle virtual paths cease to exist, which is approved delta `D-04` (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)). | Ends |
| `System.Data.Entity.Database.SetInitializer(new SampleData())` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:20] | **Replaced** by explicit migrations plus the guarded seeding command of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks). Note this call is made a **second** time at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:16] — `SetInitializer<TContext>` *sets* rather than *adds*, so only one initialization ever runs ([08 §5.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns the redundancy). Both call sites disappear into one migration path, which is the point. | Replaced |

### 2.3 OWIN startup: the abstraction goes, the responsibilities do not

MVC 5 has a **second** entry point, declared by assembly attribute:
`[assembly: OwinStartupAttribute(typeof(MvcMusicStore.Startup))]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:4]. Its `Configuration(IAppBuilder app)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:9] calls `ConfigureAuth`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:11] and then `ConfigureApp` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:13].

**`IAppBuilder` has no successor type.** Nothing in the target has that shape, so the three method
signatures that take it — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Startup.cs:9],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:14] and
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:11] — cannot be preserved even in principle, and the
`Owin` and `Microsoft.Owin.*` package family goes with it ([04 §8.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
assigns each package its outcome). Attribute-based host discovery goes too: composition in the target is
explicit in the program entry point, so **there is no attribute and no convention to find it by.**

What survives is every *responsibility*: cookie authentication, the database bootstrap decision, and
administrator provisioning. Each is re-expressed rather than translated.

### 2.4 What `Program.cs` contains, in order

Six files collapse into one composition root. Order matters twice over — service registration must
precede use, and middleware order is behaviour, not style — so this is specified as an ordered
sequence rather than a list of ingredients.

**Stage 1 — service registration (the container).** Nineteen registrations, in this order:

1. **Configuration binding.** Options types bound from `IConfiguration` using the options pattern
   (section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)).
2. **The two `DbContext` registrations**, scoped, **both reading the one connection-string key**
   [06 §6.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names — `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` — and each with
   **its own migrations history table**, with both sets of migrations compiled into **this** assembly
   since neither sets `MigrationsAssembly` (section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables); the project-structural half is
   [04 §12.5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)). **One key, not two**: the two contexts share a single
   database by the decision in section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), and the session cache options and the
   data-protection key context read the same key. **06 owns the string's content** — host, database and
   authentication mode ([06 §6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) — never the key it arrives under.

   **Both registrations use the `(IServiceProvider, DbContextOptionsBuilder)` overload, and each ends with
   `.AddInterceptors(sp.GetServices<IInterceptor>())`.** That one call is the *only* interceptor seam in
   the application, and it is stated here — in the application's own composition — rather than in a test
   fixture, because a seam that exists only in a test host is not a seam the code under test has. In every
   deployed environment `GetServices<IInterceptor>()` resolves to an **empty** sequence, since nothing
   registers an `IInterceptor`, and `AddInterceptors` over an empty sequence changes no behaviour, adds no
   allocation on the query path and produces no configuration difference — so the line is inert in
   production by construction rather than by a flag. What it buys is that the suite's observing interceptor
   (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)) can be **added** as
   one more implementation of a type this composition already enumerates, instead of the fixture having to
   reach into `DbContextOptions<T>` after the fact — which is not a supported operation, for the reason
   that subsection states.

   **This item is also where the retrying execution strategy is registered, and it is the only place in
   this document that a retry count is stated as a registration.** Both registrations call
   `UseSqlServer(connectionString, o => o.EnableRetryOnFailure(maxRetryCount: …, maxRetryDelay: …).CommandTimeout(…))`
   with **every** parameter supplied from the options table of section [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) —
   `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` (**default 5**, and `maxRetryCount` counts *retries*, so that is
   **five retries and six executions in total**), `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryDelaySeconds` and
   `Data:CommandTimeoutSeconds` — together with the provider's own transient error list, unextended.
   **This item owns the registration; section [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) owns the values and the
   envelope arithmetic they produce; no other section states a retry count of its own.** An earlier
   revision of this document carried three different counts — 3, 5 and 2 — in four places, and the two
   that were not five were each attributed to a registration that configures no retrying at all: item 3
   below, which is `AddIdentity`. Every consumer now cites this item for *where* and section
   [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) for *what*.
3. **Identity, in one registration.** `AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, IdentityRole>(options => …)`
   followed by `.AddEntityFrameworkStores<ApplicationDbContext>()` and `.AddDefaultTokenProviders()`.
   Every `IdentityOptions` value — password, lockout, sign-in, user — is set in that setup action with
   the explicit values of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). This one call is what
   supplies `UserManager<ApplicationUser>`, `SignInManager<ApplicationUser>` and
   `RoleManager<IdentityRole>` to the constructors of section
   [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces); `.AddRoles<…>()` is
   **not** called additionally, because the two-type overload already registers the role services.
   Role claims are what keep `[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12] working, so the role store is not
   optional here. **Two additions to the same chain, each written exactly once**, because the composition
   root is this document's and the artifacts they register are consumed elsewhere:
   `.AddUserManager<AuditingUserManager>()`, which is the single registration of the audit seam
   [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns — it substitutes the resolved
   `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` so `SignInManager` and every controller go through its overrides, and no
   second user-manager registration exists anywhere; and, **after** this call, the hasher-decorator seam
   whose artifacts [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns and whose registration this composition
   root writes, in **three lines and in this order**:

   ```csharp
   services.AddScoped<PasswordDerivationObservation>();
   services.AddScoped<PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>();          // the inner hasher, by concrete type
   services.AddScoped<IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>(sp =>
       new RehashObservingPasswordHasher(
           sp.GetRequiredService<PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>>(),
           sp.GetRequiredService<PasswordDerivationObservation>()));
   ```

   **The middle line is the one that makes the seam constructible, and its absence is not a style
   difference — it is a container that cannot build the object.** The shape an earlier form of this
   document specified,
   `services.AddScoped<IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>, RehashObservingPasswordHasher>()` "wrapping the
   previously registered hasher", **cannot work in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection`**: the
   decorator's own constructor parameter is `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`, which is the service type
   it is *itself* registered as, so resolving it resolves the last descriptor for that service — itself —
   and the resolution recurses until it fails. The container has no descriptor-capturing `Decorate`
   primitive; the library that supplies one is a third-party dependency neither the inventory of
   [02](02-dependency-inventory.md) nor the target package set of
   [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) carries, and this port adds no package to obtain one. So the
   inner hasher is
   made **separately resolvable by its concrete type** — `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` is public, its
   constructor takes `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>`, and the container builds it from the options
   Identity has already registered — and the decorator takes that concrete type. It is the same framework
   hasher Identity would have used, reached by a name the decorator's registration cannot collide with.

   **Why the ordering still matters, for a different reason than the withdrawn one.** `AddIdentity`
   registers its hasher with `TryAddScoped`, so it adds the `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` descriptor
   only if none exists; the factory line above then **appends** a descriptor for the same service, and a
   single-service resolution takes the **last** one. So "after `AddIdentity`" is what makes the decorator
   the resolved hasher — not, as the earlier form had it, what lets it capture a descriptor. Registering
   before `AddIdentity` would leave Identity's `TryAdd` a no-op and the decorator resolved anyway on some
   framework versions and not on others, which is exactly the kind of order-dependence this list exists to
   remove.

   **Four registration lines for the seam, and the number to hold onto is one of each artifact rather than
   a total**: one auditing user manager, one observation object, one inner hasher and one decorator. A
   second `PasswordDerivationObservation` registration or a second user manager gives two objects where the
   contract has one, which is the failure [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s registration row
   guards against; the concrete inner-hasher line is not a second hasher **artifact** — it is the
   framework type the decorator delegates to, given a resolvable name.

   **This is asserted rather than reasoned about**, by the coverage assertion, which builds the provider with
   validate-on-build and validate-scopes enabled, resolves `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` from a
   request scope, and exercises the seam concurrently — because a recursive registration of this kind
   throws only when something resolves it, and nothing in a start-up smoke test necessarily does.
4. **The application cookie, configured in exactly one place.** `ConfigureApplicationCookie(options => …)`
   carries the cookie half of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) — name, lifetime,
   sliding expiration, `HttpOnly`, `SecurePolicy`, `SameSite`, `LoginPath`, `LogoutPath`,
   `AccessDeniedPath` and `ReturnUrlParameter` — **and the two `Events` handlers**, which are part of this
   one call rather than a separate registration: `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` **globally** writes `403`
   instead of redirecting, so the denial is one response with no `Location`, and `OnRedirectToLogin`
   writes `401` **for the diagnostic instance route only** and performs the configured 302 everywhere
   else. Section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint)
   carries the code and the reason for the asymmetry.
   **There is no second `AddAuthentication().AddCookie(…)`
   call.** Item 3 has already called `AddAuthentication` internally and registered a cookie handler
   under `IdentityConstants.ApplicationScheme`; adding another one would either register a competing
   scheme or overwrite the first handler's options depending on call order — the class of composition
   defect that compiles and then misbehaves.
5. **Data protection**, decided rather than delegated:
   `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()` with
   `.SetApplicationName(...)` taking the **required** `DataProtection:ApplicationName` configuration value,
   validated at startup and never a literal (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)),
   **and `.DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration()`** — the third call in the chain and not an optional one. It
   sets `KeyManagementOptions.AutoGenerateKeys` to `false`, which is what makes the key-ring custody
   service of section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof)
   the ring's **only** writer; without it the framework's own `DataProtectionHostedService` mints a key in
   its `StartAsync`, before that service's first `await` returns, and every instance mints its own. Section
   4.9.1 states the obligation the call creates — with generation off, that service owns **rotation** too,
   because nothing else will create a replacement key
   — the key-context decision of section
   [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). The **store's location, protection at
   rest, rotation and slot-isolation policy** remain [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and the
   *requirement* remains [11 §3.2](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)'s; what this document supplies is
   the context, the registration and the migration that creates the table.
6. **The distributed cache, then session.** `AddDistributedSqlServerCache(…)` against the one database
   of section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), then `AddSession(…)` with
   the session options of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). Session stays keyed by
   the constant at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19] (section
   [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)). **The cache registration is load-bearing, not a preference
   between two working options.** `AddSession` registers the session middleware's own services and
   *consumes* `IDistributedCache`; it does **not** register an implementation of it, and no in-memory
   default is supplied on its behalf — that would come from `AddDistributedMemoryCache()`, which this
   application does not call. So with the cache registration removed, `IDistributedCache` is simply
   **unresolved**, and the failure is a dependency-resolution exception the first time the session store
   is constructed rather than a quiet fallback to a per-instance cache. The ordering of the two calls is
   immaterial to the container — registration order does not affect resolution — and they are written in
   this order because it reads in dependency order.

   **`AddMemoryCache()` is registered alongside them, and it is a different cache with a different
   subject.** The distributed cache above is session's store and carries session and nothing else (section
   [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)); the memory cache is the in-process store
   [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes for the layout aggregate of section
   [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components), whose view component resolves `IMemoryCache` from the
   container. It is written out for the same reason item 7 below writes out its accessor: the call uses
   `TryAdd` semantics, so it adds nothing where the memory cache has already been supplied and is never a
   duplicate registration, while stating it makes the cache a **declared requirement of application code**
   rather than something inherited from whatever the MVC registration happens to compose. **The key, the
   cached value's lifetime, the cold-miss concurrency control and the failure behaviour are not set here**
   — they are [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, this document neither restates nor
   re-decides them, and section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) states which part of the
   mechanism is this document's.
7. **`AddHttpContextAccessor()`.** Stated **explicitly and idempotently**, not because nothing else
   registers it: `AddIdentity` (item 3) already adds `IHttpContextAccessor` as part of its own
   composition, and the accessor's registration uses `TryAddSingleton`, so this call adds nothing when
   Identity is present and is not a duplicate registration. It is written out anyway because the
   dependency is a **first-class requirement of application code**, not a side effect of an authentication
   choice: `ShoppingCartService` resolves the cart id from `IHttpContextAccessor.HttpContext.Session`,
   which is how the `HttpContextBase` parameter at
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:21] stops being a parameter (section
   [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)). Relying on Identity to
   supply it would make the cart badge depend on the authentication stack's internals, so that a change
   to item 3 breaks an anonymous page — a failure at run time rather than at build time, on the first page
   that renders the badge.
8. **Application services** — `ShoppingCartService` scoped
   (section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)).
9. **MVC** — `AddControllersWithViews(options => options.Filters.Add(new AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute()))`.
   That is the **one** global filter: the anti-forgery filter of section
   [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems). Nothing corresponds to `HandleErrorAttribute`, which
   becomes middleware in stage 2.
10. **Anti-forgery options — the header contract *and* the cookie, because configuring only the header
    leaves the cookie on its framework defaults.** `AddAntiforgery(options => { options.HeaderName =
    "RequestVerificationToken"; options.Cookie.Name = "MvcMusicStore.Antiforgery"; options.Cookie
    .SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always; options.Cookie.HttpOnly = true; options.Cookie.SameSite =
    SameSiteMode.Strict; options.Cookie.IsEssential = true; options.Cookie.Path = "/"; })`. **Every
    literal in that call is owned elsewhere and none of them is chosen here.** The header name and the
    `Name`, `SecurePolicy`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` and `IsEssential` assignments are the antiforgery row of
    the policy table in section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled); `Cookie.Path` is the
    cookie-attribute rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which fixes `Path=/` on
    every cookie in its inventory. The header name is consumed by the scripted transport of section
    [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form), and **`SecurePolicy` is the one that changes
    behaviour**: its default for this cookie is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, so an application that sets
    `Always` on its authentication and session cookies and says nothing here ships one unmarked cookie
    among three. The coverage assertion requires all three cookies together.
11. **Health checks** — `AddHealthChecks()`, whose registration set is the **three tagged registrations**
    section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) specifies and
    owns. This item states one of the three, the only one that reaches a dependency:
    `AddCheck<CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck>(name: "catalog-db", failureStatus: HealthStatus.Unhealthy, tags: new[] { "ready" }, timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3))`,
    an application-owned `IHealthCheck` rather than the framework's `AddDbContextCheck<T>`. It carries the
    `ready` tag only, so the liveness and startup endpoints of stage 2 run no dependency check at all.
    **One
    registration is the whole set**: section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) states what each of
    the two endpoints means and the closed list of what this check may not do, and nothing else is
    registered against either path. **The count of registrations and the
    tag-to-endpoint mapping are stated in section
    [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) and not here**, because
    two places stating a registration set is how one of them comes to disagree. Net-new capability: the repository has no health endpoint of any kind
    ([11 §3.8](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). **`AddHealthChecks()`, `AddCheck<T>()`, the middleware
    and all three endpoint mappings are all shared-framework, so this registration adds no package** — and the
    Entity Framework Core health-check package pinned by
    [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) and explained in
    [04 §10.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) as existing for `AddDbContextCheck<T>` therefore loses
    its only consumer. The manifest is [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, so retiring that pin is
    04's edit and not this document's; what this document owes 04 is the statement that nothing here
    references it any more.

    **Two endpoints, and one direction of dependency work — stated before anything else, because getting
    either wrong is what produced two incompatible health models in earlier forms of this document.** The
    application maps **exactly two** health paths, `/healthz/live` and `/healthz/ready` — the two
    [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) opens by naming and the two stage 2 item 13 maps — and
    **no third**. **The refresh service performs every database operation; the registration performs
    none.** A probe reads the last completed verdict out of memory, so nothing a probe does can open a
    connection and database load is not a function of probe volume. Configuration correctness needs no
    endpoint of its own: it is asserted at start by the validation of section
    [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), so a process configured wrongly **is not listening at
    all**, which every probe consumer and the release gate already read as a failure. Two earlier forms of
    this item are withdrawn together, and they are named because each has a plausible-looking defence. The
    first had the registration open a connection and execute `SELECT 1` **inside the request**, behind a
    healthy-only ten-second result cache with coalescing probes: that puts a dependency call on an
    anonymous path, makes database frequency a function of probe traffic, and makes the first probe after
    every cache expiry pay for a connection. The second added a **third, startup-scoped endpoint**
    reporting configuration assertions that already prevent the process from starting, so its only
    reachable failure was one this document now asserts at start instead (section
    [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)).

    **Which of 06's two descriptions is implemented, said plainly rather than left to inference.** The
    model implemented is [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s — a **background refresh** of
    the five checks `C1`–`C5` whose completed verdict the handler serves, with **no I/O in the request** —
    and every number that goes with it is that section's. [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
    own response-and-cache table additionally describes a probe-triggered result cache with a ten-second
    healthy-only window; the **requirement** in those rows is what this design satisfies structurally —
    the database frequency is a function of the refresh interval rather than of probe volume, the cache is
    in-process and per instance, and a failing verdict is never served as healthy — and where the two
    descriptions differ in **mechanism**, reconciling them is 06's edit and not this document's. What
    matters for application code is that only one mechanism is built, and it is the background one.

    **Why `AddDbContextCheck<T>` is not used: it is a raw-exception channel, and this document promises
    there are none.** `HealthCheckResult` exposes an `Exception` property and an
    `Unhealthy(string description, Exception? exception, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>? data)`
    overload; `AddDbContextCheck<T>` populates the exception on a failed probe, and the framework's
    health-check service then logs that result **with the exception object**, which puts the provider's
    message — server name, database name, login identity, network detail — into a sink under a category
    this document does not own. That is the same defect as the framework exception-handler log described
    in item 13 below, arriving through a component whose purpose looks unrelated to error reporting.
    Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) lists the category among the channels it
    closes, and this registration is what makes closing it sufficient rather than merely quiet.

    **What the replacement does, precisely — and where each half of it runs, because the two halves are
    in different components.** `CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck` is the `ready`-tagged registration's
    `IHealthCheck`; the connectivity checks it reports are **executed outside the request** by
    `ReadinessRefreshService`, the `BackgroundService` of item 15 below and section
    [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment). The registration takes
    `IReadinessVerdictHolder`, `IOptions<HealthProbeOptions>`, `ILogger<CatalogConnectivityHealthCheck>`
    and `IHostEnvironment` — and deliberately **no `DbContext`**, because it opens nothing. Six things are
    required of the pair and nothing else:

    - **The request path performs no I/O at all: the registration reads the published verdict and returns
      it.** `CheckHealthAsync(HealthCheckContext, CancellationToken)` reads the immutable verdict from the
      holder, applies the staleness rule of section
      [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — a verdict older
      than 06's bound, and the absence of any verdict, are both unhealthy — and returns. **This is
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 4's decision, and the mechanism it replaces is
      withdrawn here by name**: an earlier form of this item described a **healthy-only in-process result
      cache with a TTL, three invalidations and concurrent probes coalescing onto an in-flight check**, held
      in a singleton `ReadinessResultCache` that the scoped check consulted **before opening a
      connection**. That mechanism cannot coexist with a background refresh — the two disagree about which
      component executes the check and about whether an unhealthy result costs a round trip per probe — and
      06 keeps the refresh. `ReadinessResultCache`, `HealthProbeOptions.ReadinessCacheTtl` and the
      coalescing rule therefore do not exist in the target. The verdict is **in-process and per instance**,
      never the distributed cache of section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity), which is backed by the
      very dependency being tested.
    - **Each half is bounded, and the two bounds bound different things.** The registration's own bound is
      the readiness **request** budget of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s
      timeout hierarchy, carried as `HealthProbeOptions.ReadinessBudget` and met with room to spare because
      the handler reads memory; `HealthProbeOptions.LivenessBudget` carries that hierarchy's liveness
      request budget and is the value any liveness-tagged registration must be given, so a dependency added
      to that endpoint later cannot inherit no bound. **Both are members of the `HealthProbe` section
      section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) admits, and neither has a default in this
      document** — that section's row enumerates all ten members of the type, every one of them required,
      because a value
      [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) owns and this document is forbidden
      to restate cannot be a constant here, and a silently defaulted member would be this document owning
      that value after all. The registration's `timeout:` argument above is a
      framework-side **backstop** and is deliberately longer than the request budget, so the endpoint still
      answers if a read of the holder is somehow blocked. The refresh's bounds are the per-operation and
      per-evaluation bounds of the same hierarchy, applied in the refresh pass. An unbounded probe does not
      fail; it answers **late**, after the platform has already decided the instance is not answering,
      which is the failure mode this replaces.
    - **The refresh issues [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s two checks on
      one pooled connection, deliberately outside the retrying execution strategy.** It takes
      `Database.GetDbConnection()` from a scope of its own, opens it under its linked token, and executes
      `C1`'s `SELECT 1` and then `C2`'s single-row availability read of `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` on **that
      same connection**, each with its own `CommandTimeout`. Going through `ExecuteSqlRawAsync` would enter
      the `EnableRetryOnFailure` strategy registered in item 2 above — **six executions and up to five
      intervening delays**, at the values section
      [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) supplies — and an evaluation that
      retries inside a check is an evaluation that misses its budget; the one bounded retry a pass may make
      is the refresh loop's own, per section
      [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment). Both statements are
      chosen over any query against application data on purpose: readiness reports connectivity and the
      availability of the one object every authenticated request depends on, never the state of the catalog
      — which is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s requirement that the probe be a
      connectivity check and specifically not the per-request aggregate of that document's §6.4.
    - **It returns a sanitized result, and both of its values come from the verdict rather than from an
      exception the request never saw.** Success is `HealthCheckResult.Healthy()`. Failure is
      `HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(description: $"{category}; trace {traceId}")` — the **single-argument
      description overload**, with **no `exception:` argument and no `data` dictionary** — where `category`
      and `traceId` are the two the published verdict carries, one of each per verdict because
      [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s two checks and its one
      short-circuit leave at most one check failing in a pass (section
      [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)). `category` is one of the
      **four literals of [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
      shape R4**: **`Timeout`**, **`Unreachable`**, **`Rejected`** or **`Unknown`**. **That vocabulary is
      06's and not this document's**, stated in its register as the one failure-category set it owns rather
      than 05 — every *other* path's categories in this document are 05's, which is why this one is worth
      calling out. An earlier form of this bullet used three locally invented strings,
      `catalog-unreachable`, `catalog-timeout` and `catalog-authentication-refused`; they are **withdrawn**,
      and with them the assumption that three categories suffice. **The classification is performed where
      the fault is observed — in the refresh pass, which is the only place a provider exception exists — and
      it is fixed here because 06 owns the literals and this document owns the call site:**

      | Condition in the evaluation's `catch` or budget | R4 literal |
      | --- | --- |
      | The evaluation's **own** linked token cancelling — its bound in 06's timeout hierarchy elapsing with no answer | **`Timeout`**, and a per-statement command timeout expiring maps here too, since both mean the dependency did not answer in time |
      | A connection-level failure: the connection could not be opened, was refused, was reset, or name resolution failed | **`Unreachable`** |
      | The dependency answered and **declined**: an authentication or authorization refusal, including a managed-identity token the server rejected, and a login that failed for a reason the server stated | **`Rejected`** — this is the literal the withdrawn `catalog-authentication-refused` mapped to, and it is deliberately wider than authentication alone |
      | Any other fault reaching the `catch` — a provider exception that matches none of the above, including a shape a future provider version introduces | **`Unknown`** |

      **`Unknown` is the member the withdrawn three-string set lacked, and its absence was the defect
      rather than an omission of tidiness:** a closed set with no residual member forces a classifier either
      to guess one of the three or to let the fault escape, and both are worse than recording that the fault
      did not classify. **`traceId` is `Activity.Current?.Id` as observed **in the refresh pass**, and where
      no activity is current it is a value that pass generates itself** —
      `ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()` — carried on the verdict so that the log record below
      and every result description derived from that verdict correlate. It is deliberately **not** read from
      an `HttpContext`: the evaluation runs in a `BackgroundService` with **no request at all**, and
      `CheckHealthAsync` receives a `HealthCheckContext`, which carries the registration and nothing about a
      request, so a component that reached for `IHttpContextAccessor` would be depending on something that
      need not exist. **The generated fallback is therefore the normal case rather than the exception** —
      nothing starts an activity for a timer tick unless the telemetry pipeline does — which is why the value
      is generated once per evaluation and published, rather than recomputed per probe: a probe-side value
      would differ between two responses reporting the identical verdict. No provider message, no connection
      string fragment, no server or database name, and no exception type name reaches the verdict or the
      result, so nothing raw can reach the response body or the framework's own log of that result.
    - **The evaluation writes the one record the operator needs, and its fields are 06's closed set rather
      than a locally chosen one.** Exactly one `ILogger` record at **`Warning`** under the application's
      own `MvcMusicStore` category, carrying **the six fields
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 6 fixes for a health-check failure — and no
      seventh**:
      1. the **endpoint literal**, `/healthz/ready`, so a record is attributable to a path without the
         response having to name anything;
      2. the **failure category** — one of the four literals classified above;
      3. the caught exception's **type name**, `GetType().FullName`, plus the **type-name chain of its
         inner exceptions**, types only;
      4. the **stack trace as a string field**;
      5. the **elapsed milliseconds** of the attempt;
      6. the **trace identifier**, which correlates the record with the platform's own probe log.

      Never the message, never an inner message, never `ToString()`, never a provider message, never a
      server, database or connection-string fragment, and never the exception object itself — which is
      what keeps this channel inside the closed-record rule of section
      [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). **One record per failing execution, with no
      transition-based suppression**: the record is written every time the check runs and fails, and
      specifically not only on a transition from healthy to unhealthy, because
      [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s alarm evaluates a count within a window and a
      suppressed repeat is indistinguishable from a recovery. **The volume on this path is bounded by
      coalescing alone, not by the result cache**, and an earlier form of this sentence said the opposite —
      *"at most one execution, and therefore at most one such record, per ten-second window per
      instance"* — which cannot hold beside the rule two items above that an unhealthy verdict is never
      cached. It is withdrawn rather than qualified: **the ten-second window governs the healthy path
      only**, so while the instance is failing there is no cached value to serve, **every** probe executes
      its read and **every** failing execution emits its record, and the single-flight rule is the only
      remaining bound — at most one read *in flight*, and therefore at most one record per check duration
      rather than per window. That is a concurrency ceiling, and a consumer sizing record volume against
      the ten-second figure while an instance is unhealthy would be sizing against a number that does not
      apply. It is also the reason `27f` of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) can issue a **second**
      readiness request inside the same denied state and require a **second** record: under the withdrawn
      wording that case would have had to wait out a window that was never there. **The severity, the sink, the collection and the
      retention are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s**; the field list is this
      document's, because row 27 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) holds an implementation to it.
      It is also why `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks` is pinned to **`None`** in the
      category table of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — that is the category
      `DefaultHealthCheckService` writes a failed check's exception under, and closing it is what makes
      this record the *only* signal a failed probe produces. **The volume is bounded by the refresh
      interval rather than by the probe volume**, which is the point of moving the evaluation out of the
      request: at most one such record exists per evaluation, however many probes read the verdict that
      evaluation published, and the ceiling on evaluations and on database round trips per instance is
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 5's.
    - **No dependency failure escapes as an exception from either half, and exactly one exception may
      escape at all.** In the refresh pass every provider fault, timeout and authentication refusal is
      caught, classified into one of the four R4 literals above and **recorded in the verdict** — so no
      fault of the dependency ever reaches the framework as a thrown object, and the registration that
      later reads that verdict has no exception to mishandle. The single exception allowed to propagate out
      of an evaluation is an `OperationCanceledException` carrying the **host's stopping** token, the case
      where the process is shutting down: that is not a statement about the dependency, and the containment
      rules of section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) require
      that such a pass publish no verdict and write no record at all. Cancellation from the evaluation's
      **own** linked token — its bound in 06's hierarchy elapsing — is *not* propagated; it is classified as
      **`Timeout`** and published, which is what distinguishes "the dependency is slow" from "the host is
      going away". The request half throws nothing of its own: it reads an immutable value from a singleton
      and performs no I/O, so the only cancellation it can observe is the caller's, which the framework
      already owns.

      **That one escape cannot reopen a raw-exception channel, and the reason is its content rather than
      its handling.** An `OperationCanceledException` raised from a cancelled token carries the
      framework's fixed cancellation text and no store, server, credential or command detail, so a sink
      that recorded it would learn that a pass was abandoned and nothing more. The channel this
      registration closes is a *provider* exception reaching a log — what `AddDbContextCheck<T>` produced
      by attaching one to its result — and that object never exists outside the refresh pass's `catch`.

    **The response contract is this document's, and one artifact produces the whole of it.** It is a
    fixed pair of opaque literals rather than a document, and it is precise enough that a probe consumer
    and a coverage assertion can both be written against it:

    | Response property | The contract |
    | --- | --- |
    | `/healthz/ready` healthy | **`200`**, body exactly **`ready`** |
    | `/healthz/ready` unhealthy | **`503`**, body exactly **`not-ready`** |
    | `/healthz/live` | **`200`**, body exactly **`live`**. It has no failure body, because a host that cannot answer does not answer |
    | Content type, both paths | **`text/plain; charset=utf-8`** |
    | Cache headers, both paths | **`Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache`**, so no front end, proxy or platform probe ever serves a stale verdict. This is the *response* cache, and it is not the background refresh above — row 3 names both precisely because "cached" applied to a health endpoint reads as the first and is meant as the second, and a verdict already refreshed out of band is exactly the value that must not be re-cached at the edge on top of it |
    | What the body may never contain | **No dependency or check name** — not `catalog-db`, not `"database"`, not the context type name; **no server, database, host or connection-string fragment; no trace identifier; no exception type, message or stack; no failure category.** The literals are the whole body: no JSON, no per-check entries, no aggregate status word, no duration, no timestamp |

    **All four response properties are set by one artifact — the shared `ResponseWriter` both endpoint
    mappings are given** — because a body literal written in one place and a cache header added in another
    is how a health response acquires two owners. It is not the security-header middleware of stage 2
    item 2: that middleware emits the header set [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns and
    counts — **six** emitted names, with three further names asserted absent — and `Cache-Control` is not
    among them, so there is no header both would write and no ordering question between them.

    The framework's default writer is therefore **replaced rather than accepted**: its default emits the
    aggregate status *as text*, which is a status word rather than the fixed literal, and the JSON writers
    that ship for health-check UIs emit per-check entries **by name**, which is precisely what row 2
    forbids. Two earlier forms of this paragraph are withdrawn — one emitted "status and check name", which
    discloses the dependency name; the other emitted **no body at all**, which is not what the coverage assertion requires
    even though it discloses nothing, and a test asserting an empty body would fail an implementation that
    is correct. The failure category, the trace identifier and the elapsed milliseconds live in the
    refresh's records and reach an operator through the sink, behind its access controls, not through a
    body served on an anonymous path. The coverage assertions require the exact body literal on each of the
    three cases, the content type, the no-store headers, the absence of any provider text on both the
    response and every retained sink, and that a probe request performs **no** database operation.
12. **Forwarded-headers options, and the host-integrity pair that goes with them.**
    `Configure<ForwardedHeadersOptions>(options => …)` setting **five** members explicitly, expressing the
    **single** trust mode [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns and
    [06 §10.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requirement 1 hands to this section:
    **`ProvenExclusiveIngress`** — one mode, on both hosting targets and under every topology, with
    `KnownNetworks` **and** `KnownProxies` **cleared**. There is no second branch to compose.
    **Two earlier forms of this item are withdrawn together, and why the second one failed is why this
    mode exists.** The first cleared both lists on the reasoning that the platform front end is not
    loopback and the defaults would otherwise ignore the headers. The second replaced that clearing with
    a list populated from `Ingress:TrustedNetworks` and `Ingress:TrustedProxies`, on the reasoning that an
    empty list is the absence of a restriction rather than a configuration of it. The second reading is
    the more plausible of the two and it is still wrong, because **the list it requires has no correct
    value**: on neither target is the address the platform front end presents to a worker published as a
    stable literal, and neither is covered by any published service tag, so a range written there would be
    an inference dressed as a control — which is the finding
    [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records when it withdraws the enumerated-range mode
    in full. Both key names are therefore **withdrawn rather than merely unused**, and this section's
    options validator **refuses to start if either resolves to a value**
    (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), `Ingress`).

    | Member | Value | Why |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `ForwardedHeaders` | `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor \| ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto` | The scheme and the client address, and **nothing else**. `XForwardedHost` is deliberately **absent**, which is [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) control 2 — `X-Forwarded-Host` is the one header that makes `Request.Host` attacker-controlled from outside the front end, and not enabling it is a stronger control than validating it |
    | `ForwardLimit` | **`1`** | Exactly one hop is trusted, because exactly one proxy sits in front of the application on both hosting targets. The framework's default is also 1, and it is set explicitly here because the value is a security property of the topology rather than a default worth inheriting silently: a limit of `null` walks the whole header right-to-left and lets a client-supplied entry become the resolved address |
    | `KnownNetworks` | **Cleared** — `options.KnownNetworks.Clear()`, with nothing added back, including the framework's own loopback entry | The trust input is a **reachability** property rather than an address: the platform ingress is trusted because it is the only hop that can set these headers, so there is no range to enumerate and an empty list is the accurate expression of that rather than a gap in one. [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the topology and states the same clearing for both targets; the precondition it rests on is stated below rather than left implicit |
    | `KnownProxies` | **Cleared** — `options.KnownProxies.Clear()`, same rule expressed per address | Same reason, and it is cleared **explicitly** rather than left at its default so that the pair reads as one decision. The platform shortcut [06 §10.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records — `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` — is documented as clearing both lists and enabling exactly these two headers, so this composition is that same decision written where a reader can see it |
    | `RequireHeaderSymmetry` | **`false`**, deliberately | The platform front end sends `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` with independent cardinality, so requiring symmetry would discard both on ordinary requests. It is stated rather than left at the default so it reads as a decision and not an oversight |

    **Startup fails closed on a trust configuration it cannot parse, and an empty trust list is legal in
    exactly one mode.** An earlier form of this item required a non-empty list **unconditionally**, which
    would leave the **primary** hosting target unstartable: [06
    §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) decision 2 fixes that target's mode as
    `ProvenExclusiveIngress` precisely because App Service publishes no authoritative range to enumerate.
    What the two states mean to the middleware is what decides the rule. With **either list non-empty** the
    middleware checks the immediate peer against it and drops the headers when the peer is not on it — the
    `EnumeratedRanges` posture, where a range genuinely exists to declare. With **both lists cleared** the
    known-address check is skipped and the immediate peer's forwarded headers are honoured — the
    `ProvenExclusiveIngress` posture, and the same state the platform's own
    `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` shortcut produces, which is why [06
    §10.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records that shortcut as this decision taken implicitly.
    Neither state is safe on its own: the first fails shut if the range is wrong, and the second trusts
    whatever can reach the socket. So the validator asserts the one thing that is wrong in **both** modes —
    **every entry that is present must parse** as a CIDR range or an address, and an unparseable entry
    **refuses to start** — while each mode's own safety is asserted at deployment by §10.1.4's per-mode
    readback and its hostile-forwarded-address assertion rather than by the application. Failing to start on
    an unreadable value converts the one application-detectable error into a deployment failure at the
    moment it can be fixed.

    **Host integrity is the second half, and it is here because it shares the same threat.**
    `AllowedHosts` is set to the application's **real hostnames** — the platform's assigned default
    hostname and any custom domain — **never the template's `*`**, and the default host builder's
    host-filtering middleware then answers **`400`** to a request bearing any other `Host` value. The same
    startup validation rejects a value that is empty or that contains `*` in a non-development environment,
    for the same fail-closed reason. That is [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) control 1, and
    the pair is what closes the class rather than an instance: every absolute URL the application ever
    emits — a redirect, a generated link, a `Location` header — reads `Request.Host`, so the host is
    validated once at the edge of the pipeline instead of at each use.

    **The coverage assertion drives both halves adversarially**: a request carrying a hostile `Host` header,
    and a request from an untrusted peer carrying a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`.
13. **The exception record's writer** — `AddExceptionHandler<ErrorRecordExceptionHandler>()`, one
    implementation of `IExceptionHandler`. It exists because the middleware of stage 2 item 4 renders a
    response and the error action deliberately reads no exception
    (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), so **without this registration nothing
    writes the closed record that section promises.** Its `TryHandleAsync` writes the record and
    **returns `false`**, which is the whole trick: returning `false` means "recorded, not handled", so the
    middleware continues to its configured `/Home/Error` path and the generic response is produced by the
    action exactly as specified. It writes **no** response body, sets **no** status code and swallows
    **no** exception. Its content, and the reason it is a separate component rather than a line in the
    action, are in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). Registration order within
    stage 1 does not matter for this one — it is placed last because it is the only registration whose
    subject is another stage's middleware.
