14. **The two request-policy registrations — rate limiting, then request timeouts.** The first is
    `AddRateLimiter(options => …)`, a **shared-framework** capability reached through
    the ASP.NET Core framework reference, so **no package is added** and
    [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s manifest is unchanged. It exists because per-account lockout
    does not bound the work an anonymous caller can cause, which is set out in the abuse-model paragraph
    of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **Three
    limiters and one named policy**, all with their limits bound from `RateLimiting:*` configuration — the
    defaults below — validated at startup.

    **The composition is one chained global limiter, and the shape is forced rather than chosen.** The
    two credential controls must **both** apply to the same three actions: a per-source bound on the
    derivation cost, and an aggregate bound that a per-source bound cannot see. Expressing them as two
    **named** policies would silently deliver only one, because
    `RequireRateLimiting`/`[EnableRateLimiting]` attaches an `EnableRateLimitingAttribute` whose
    `PolicyName` selects **exactly one** policy for an endpoint — a second attribute replaces the first
    rather than composing with it, so "two named policies on `Login`" is not a configuration the
    framework has. The framework's composition primitive is
    `PartitionedRateLimiter.CreateChained<HttpContext>(params PartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext>[])`,
    which acquires from every limiter in the array and admits only if all of them admit, and
    `RateLimiterOptions.GlobalLimiter` is typed `PartitionedRateLimiter<HttpContext>` — so the chain goes
    there:

    ```csharp
    options.GlobalLimiter = PartitionedRateLimiter.CreateChained(
        perIpCredentialLimiter, aggregateCredentialLimiter, generalLimiter);
    ```

    Each of the three is a `PartitionedRateLimiter.Create<HttpContext, string>` whose partitioner returns
    `RateLimitPartition.GetNoLimiter(...)` for every request it does not govern, so the three compose
    without rationing each other's traffic:

    - **`perIpCredentialLimiter` — the per-source credential bound, keyed on the client address and on
      nothing else.** It governs the three credential-verification endpoints: the `Login` POST, the
      `Register` POST and the change-password POST, selected by a `[CredentialEndpoint]` marker attribute
      read as `context.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<CredentialEndpointAttribute>()` rather than by
      a path string, so a renamed action cannot silently leave the set. For those endpoints it returns
      `RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(clientAddress, …)` with **10 permits per minute per
      partition** and `QueueLimit = 0`, where `clientAddress` is the reconstructed client address defined
      below — **not** the Identity `UserId`, and **not** the submitted user name, for the reasons stated
      with the partition keys. For everything else it returns `GetNoLimiter`. This is the control that
      bounds the fixed derivation cost the service of section
      [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) now spends on **every** attempt, unknown usernames
      included.
    - **`aggregateCredentialLimiter` — the flood bound the per-source limiter cannot see.** Same endpoint
      set, same marker, but **one partition for all of them** — a constant key — with a fixed window of
      **200 permits per minute** and `QueueLimit = 0`. A per-partition limit is blind to a flood spread
      across ten thousand source addresses; this one is not, and its ceiling is set high enough that it
      engages only under an aggregate no real population produces. `GetNoLimiter` everywhere else.
    - **`generalLimiter` — everything the other two do not govern.** A fixed window, **300 permits per
      minute per partition**, `QueueLimit = 0`, so a scripted crawl of the catalog cannot monopolize the
      instance either. It returns `GetNoLimiter` for three sets, each for its own reason: for a
      `[CredentialEndpoint]`, because the 10-per-minute bound already binds and a second budget over the
      same request would only obscure which control refused; for any endpoint already carrying an
      `EnableRateLimitingAttribute`, so an endpoint with a named policy is governed by that policy alone;
      and for the two literals of `HealthPaths`, because rationing a platform health probe reports a
      healthy instance as unhealthy and takes it out of rotation — the same reason item 5 of stage 2
      exempts those paths from HTTPS redirection, and held in the same one place.

    **No named policy is registered, and the branch that would defer to one is kept deliberately.**
    `AddRateLimiter` registers the chained global limiter above and **nothing else**: no
    `AddPolicy(...)` call, and therefore no endpoint carrying `[EnableRateLimiting]`. An earlier form of
    this item registered a named policy for a content-security-policy violation collector at 20
    permits per minute; **that endpoint is withdrawn in full** (item 13 below states the decision and
    [06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns it), so the policy it needed is withdrawn with
    it. The `generalLimiter`'s `GetNoLimiter` branch for an endpoint already carrying
    `EnableRateLimitingAttribute` therefore matches **nothing today**, and it stays: it is the rule that a
    named policy, if one is ever added, governs its endpoint **alone** rather than being rationed twice —
    once against a catalog-sized budget it has no business consuming and once against its own. A rule
    written when the first named policy is added is a rule written under pressure.

    **The global limiter runs on every request, and that is why the no-op branches are part of the contract
    rather than an optimization.** The framework evaluates the global limiter **first** and any
    endpoint-specific limiter afterwards, for **every** request that reaches `UseRateLimiter` — there is no
    path the global limiter skips. That is what makes the health-path branch above necessary rather than
    merely tidy: without it a platform probe is rationed by the catalog's budget, and a rationed probe
    reports a healthy instance as unhealthy.

    **The partition keys differ between the credential limiter and the general limiter, and the difference
    is the point rather than an inconsistency.**

    - **`perIpCredentialLimiter` partitions on the client address, unconditionally — authenticated
      requests included.** The resource it rations is the fixed password-derivation cost of section
      [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), which a request spends whether or not the caller is
      already signed in, and the party driving that cost controls the submitted user name but not the
      address the request arrives from. Keying it on `UserId` for the authenticated case would leave the
      change-password endpoint bounded per session rather than per source, so a caller holding one valid
      session could drive derivations without limit; keying it on the **submitted** user name would be no
      limit at all, because the caller chooses that value, and would additionally make the limiter an
      account oracle. So the credential partition is the address, and the accepted cost is stated rather
      than hidden: a population behind one egress address shares the ten-per-minute credential budget.
      That bound is `RateLimiting:*` configuration, a refusal is a 429 with `Retry-After` rather than an
      account lockout, and the aggregate limiter — not a per-address ceiling — is what a distributed
      flood runs into.
    - **`generalLimiter` partitions on a trusted client identifier, and "trusted" is the load-bearing
      word.** For an **authenticated** request it is the Identity `UserId`, so a signed-in customer
      browsing the catalog is never rationed by whoever shares their egress address; for an **anonymous**
      request it is the client address. The resource here is ordinary throughput rather than a
      cryptographic cost, so the fairness trade goes the other way.

    **Either way the address must be the real one.** It is the client address as reconstructed by
    `UseForwardedHeaders` (stage 2 item 1), under the trust mode **stage 1 item 12** composes: the two
    forwarded headers processed, `ForwardLimit = 1`, and both known-peer lists cleared because the platform
    ingress is the only hop that can set them. Two properties of that mode are what make this partition key
    trustworthy, and both matter more here than anywhere else in the pipeline. The headers are **processed
    at all**, so an anonymous request partitions on the caller's address rather than on the front end's own
    — a configuration that ignored them would collapse the whole fleet's anonymous traffic into one
    partition. And `ForwardLimit = 1` consumes **only the right-most entry**, which on a deployed target is
    the one the front end appended itself: a caller who prepends a fresh chain per request does not get a
    fresh partition per request, because the entry the limiter sees is not the one the caller wrote. A limit
    of `null` would walk the header right-to-left and hand a caller a partition of one each time, which is
    no limit at all — which is why item 12 sets the value explicitly rather than inheriting it. Partitioning
    on anything else the caller supplies — a header, a cookie — fails the same way, for the same reason the
    submitted user name is not used.

    **Every permit figure above is a *per-instance* figure, because the built-in limiter's state is
    process-local — and saying so is the difference between a bound and an estimate.**
    `System.Threading.RateLimiting` holds its windows and permit counts in memory in the process that
    created the limiter. There is no shared store, no coordination between replicas and no distributed
    variant in the framework, so a fleet of *n* replicas behind a load balancer admits **up to *n* times**
    any figure written here. That is tolerable for the **per-partition** figures — the ten credential permits
    per address and the general limiter's 300 — and **not** tolerable
    for the **aggregate** one, whose whole purpose is to bound a flood spread across many source addresses:
    an aggregate stated as a fleet ceiling and implemented per instance is not a ceiling at all.

    | Requirement | Value |
    | --- | --- |
    | **The replica ceiling is configuration, and startup fails without it** | `RateLimiting:MaxReplicas`, a required positive integer equal to the **maximum** replica count the deployment's autoscale rule permits. The application refuses to start if it is absent, non-positive or unparseable. It is a deployment input for the same reason the ingress trust ranges of stage 1 item 12 are: [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the scaling configuration, and a figure this document invented would silently stop matching it |
    | **The aggregate credential bound is derived from a fleet figure, not written as one** | The figure that means something operationally is the **fleet** ceiling — **200 permits per minute across the whole deployment** — so each instance is configured with `ceiling(200 / MaxReplicas)`. At `MaxReplicas = 1` the instance figure is 200 and nothing changes; at 4 it is 50. **Two consequences of the rounding are stated rather than left to be discovered.** Where `MaxReplicas` does not divide 200 the fleet maximum is the derived figure times the replica count, which **exceeds** 200 by at most `MaxReplicas - 1` — at 3 replicas, `3 × 67 = 201`. The bound is therefore **200 plus at most one permit per replica**, not exactly 200, and rounding **up** is chosen deliberately over rounding down so that no single instance is configured below the fleet share it is expected to serve; an overage of under one percent at any plausible replica count is not what this control exists to prevent. And when the fleet is running **below** its maximum the effective aggregate is proportionally lower than 200, which errs toward refusing rather than admitting — the correct direction for a flood control |
    | **The per-source bounds are per-instance by design, and their fleet effect is stated** | Ten credential permits per minute per address per instance means a caller spread across instances by the load balancer can reach up to `10 × MaxReplicas` per minute. That is accepted: this control bounds a **cost**, the aggregate limiter bounds a **flood**, and account lockout (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) bounds guessing against any one account independently of both. The general limiter's 300 per minute needs no fleet arithmetic at all, because it rations instance throughput and that is what it is written against |
    | **A shared limiter is the alternative, and it is rejected with its reason** | A distributed limiter needs a store touched **before** every request is admitted — the SQL cache of section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) or a new Redis instance — which adds a round trip to every request, makes that store's availability a precondition for serving anything at all, and introduces a fresh failure mode on the hottest path: what the limiter does when its own store is unreachable, where failing open removes the control and failing closed takes the site down. For a bound whose purpose is to blunt abuse rather than meter a paid quota, per-instance accounting with a derived aggregate is the proportionate mechanism. **If an exact fleet-wide quota is ever required, that is a scoped addition with its store named at the time it is approved** — not a silent reinterpretation of these figures |

    **The coverage assertion requires the multi-instance property directly**, because no single-instance test
    can observe it.

    **`RejectionStatusCode` is 429** and the `OnRejected` callback sets `Retry-After` from the lease's
    `MetadataName.RetryAfter` — the whole seconds remaining in the window — writes **one** `Information`
    record and returns without invoking the endpoint. The record carries the **limiter identity**, the
    partition kind and the endpoint, and never the submitted user name and never the partition value for
    an anonymous caller beyond a pseudonymous label. **That label's key, its identifier, its rotation and
    its `<keyId>:<HMAC>` grammar are [06 §8.4.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and that section
    is their sole owner** — this document names no key, derives no label and states no rotation period,
    because a pseudonym produced under a second key or a second grammar does not correlate with the records
    every other producer writes, which is the one property a pseudonym exists to have. **The limiter
    identity is
    `context.HttpContext.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<EnableRateLimitingAttribute>()?.PolicyName ?? "global"`**,
    which is exact rather than approximate for one reason: the chain no-ops every endpoint that carries a
    named policy, so a refusal on such an endpoint can only have come from that policy, and a refusal
    anywhere else can only have come from the chain. Which **member** of the chain refused is not
    attributed, because a chained limiter surfaces one lease and the framework does not label it — the
    endpoint plus the retry window is what an operator acts on, and the coverage assertions distinguish
    the per-source bound from the aggregate bound by construction rather than by reading the record.
    Recovery is therefore deterministic and self-service: a fixed window with no queue means a refused
    caller waits out a stated number of seconds rather than being locked out, and nothing an anonymous
    caller does can lock an account it does not own.
15. **The readiness verdict holder and the hosted services** — one
    `AddSingleton<IReadinessVerdictHolder, ReadinessVerdictHolder>()` followed by two
    `AddHostedService` registrations, `ReadinessRefreshService` and `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService`,
    grouped as one item because the
    container is the only place their lifetime is decided. `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService` is the one
    heartbeat loop and runs on every host; `KeyRingBootstrapService` is registered **beside it on the web
    host only** and runs one pass per process start rather than a loop, per section
    [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof).
    All three are specified in full by section
    [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment), whose file table names the
    two long-lived loops and whose roster statement is the one that governs. The readiness answer the
    `ready`-tagged registration of item 11 returns is the verdict this holder publishes — computed
    **outside** the request by `ReadinessRefreshService` and read from the holder in the request path,
    which is what section
    [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) states and why the
    singleton is registered here to carry it.
16. **The report collector's sink** — `AddSingleton<CspReportSink>()`, the normalizer and per-process
    budget holder of section
    [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half). It is a singleton
    because its budgets are per replica per hour, and it is registered here rather than with item 8
    because its subject is an endpoint's collector rather than an application service a controller
    consumes. The collector's **named** rate-limit policy is part of item 14's `AddRateLimiter`
    registration and is not a second registration.
17. **Host filtering — the second half of item 12's host-integrity pair.**
    `services.AddOptions<HostFilteringOptions>().Configure<IOptions<SiteOptions>>((o, site) => o.AllowedHosts = site.Value.HostList)`,
    the dependency-taking overload deliberately, because the list is not available at registration time:
    it is produced by the validated options type of section
    [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which resolves after the container is built. Forwarded
    headers without host filtering trusts a `Host` header the front end never sent, which is why the two
    are a pair rather than two independent choices.
18. **The culture pin, and the reason it is not `UseRequestLocalization()`.** `Localization:DefaultCulture`
    is read here and applied to `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture` and
    `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentUICulture` **once, at composition time**. The application supports
    exactly one culture and negotiates none, so the request-localization middleware could only ever
    resolve the same value on every request — and it would resolve it for **requests only**. The records
    the hosted services of item 15 write, and every number and date they format, run outside the request
    pipeline and would keep the machine's culture, which is the difference between a deterministic
    process and a deterministic response. A missing or unparseable value is a **start-up failure** rather
    than a silent fall back to the machine culture, by the same rule as the trust list of item 12. The
    literal is [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s and is not restated
    here.

19. **The request-timeout policy** — `AddRequestTimeouts(…)` with a single `DefaultPolicy`. The timeout's
    value, its required relationship to the platform's own request timeout and the startup validation
    over both are section
    [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)'s
    and are not restated here. It is registered here and applied by the middleware at stage 2 item 8,
    for the reason this stage exists: service registration precedes use.

    **The request-timeout policy is the second registration in this item, and this is the only place it
    is registered.** `AddRequestTimeouts(options => options.DefaultPolicy = new RequestTimeoutPolicy { … })`,
    whose `Timeout` and whose deliberately unset `WriteTimeoutResponse` are both section
    [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s — that section owns the value,
    the ordering constraints it has to satisfy against the unit-of-work deadline and the platform limit,
    and the status code the middleware sets; this item owns only the fact that the registration exists
    and where it sits. It sits beside the limiter because both are request-admission policies whose
    service-side half is a registration and whose behaviour is a middleware placement, and its pipeline
    half is stage 2 item 8 for the framework reason stated there. **An earlier revision of this section
    registered neither half of the pair** while section
    [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) specified both, so the
    composition root this section publishes did not contain the middleware that section's 504 behaviour,
    its envelope validation and its coverage assertions all rest on. The two registrations are added
    here and at stage 2 item 8 rather than the timeout being deleted there, because a policy no
    composition root registers is not a policy.

**The scheme set this composition produces, stated because it is not visible in the one call that
creates it.** `AddIdentity<TUser, TRole>` registers **four** cookie schemes —
`IdentityConstants.ApplicationScheme`, `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme`,
`IdentityConstants.TwoFactorRememberMeScheme` and `IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme` — and sets
the default authenticate and challenge schemes to the application scheme. Two consequences are
load-bearing:

- **The application scheme carries every session; the other three are scheme entries with no flow.** The
  distinction the next sentences draw is between a **surface**, which is removed, and a **scheme entry**,
  which `AddIdentity` creates and which cannot be declined without replacing that call.
  The external-login **challenge** surface and the external sign-in **cookie** are both **removed** (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), so nothing in the target challenges a provider or
  reads a provider callback: no `ConfigureExternalAuthenticationProperties` call and no
  `GetExternalLoginInfoAsync` call is written anywhere, and `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme` is
  therefore a **registered scheme with no flow** — no cookie is ever issued under it and none is ever
  read. It stays registered for the same reason the two two-factor schemes do, which is the only reason:
  suppressing any of the three means abandoning `AddIdentity` for `AddIdentityCore` and hand-wiring the
  sign-in manager, the role services and the cookie handler in order to remove registrations that never
  execute. What the retained **management** half needs is not a scheme at all — it reads and deletes
  `AspNetUserLogins` rows through `UserManager`, and neither operation authenticates anything.
- **Sign-in and sign-out go through `SignInManager` only, never through `HttpContext.SignInAsync`.**
  `AddIdentity` sets the default *sign-in* scheme to the **external** cookie rather than the application
  cookie, so a direct `HttpContext.SignInAsync(principal)` would write a short-lived external cookie and
  the user would appear signed out on the next request. `SignInManager` names the application scheme
  explicitly, which is why the sequence in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) is
  expressed in terms of it.

**Stage 2 — the middleware pipeline.** Thirteen numbered items, in this order — an **item is a position
in the order**, and two of them carry more than one call: item 4 registers the exception handler and the
status-code pages, and item 8 registers routing and the request timeouts. Order here is behaviour:
every entry is placed where it is because something after it depends on what it does.

1. **`UseForwardedHeaders()`** — **first**, ahead of everything else. The request scheme and the client
   address are read by HTTPS redirection, by HSTS, by secure-cookie emission and by logging, so anything
   registered ahead of it decides on the wrong values. Its options are stage 1 item 12.
2. **The security response headers**, registered here — **before exception handling, before HSTS, before
   HTTPS redirection and before static files** — and applied through `context.Response.OnStarting(...)`
   so the values are written immediately before the first byte, whichever component produced the
   response.
   **Placement is the point, and the intuitive placement is wrong in three separate ways:** after
   `UseStaticFiles()` they would cover controller responses and **not** stylesheets, scripts, fonts or
   images; **after the exception handler they would not cover error responses**, because the handler
   catches the exception below itself and produces the error response from there, so a component
   registered underneath it never sees that response at all; and — the one most easily missed —
   **after `UseHttpsRedirection()` they would not cover the redirect responses that middleware itself
   emits**, which are the very responses an attacker sees first on a plain-HTTP request. A 307 to
   `https://` carrying no `X-Content-Type-Options`, no `Referrer-Policy` and no frame protection is a
   real response to a real client. Registered **first among the response-shaping entries**, the set
   covers **every** response the application emits: controller, static, redirect, status-code page and
   error page alike, which is what [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §10.2 requires and what
   the coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires across all five response kinds.
   **This position is also what makes the callback register exactly once, and the assignment is written
   to be idempotent anyway.** `UseExceptionHandler` and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` **re-execute
   the pipeline below themselves** — they clear the response, rewrite the path and call the remainder of
   the chain again — so a component registered **underneath** them runs a second time for one
   client-visible response and registers a second `OnStarting` callback. That is precisely what the
   earlier below-the-handler placement did, and with an accumulating write it is visible to the client:
   two callbacks each appending `nosniff` produce `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, nosniff`, and a
   duplicated `Content-Security-Policy` is not a stricter policy but two policies the browser
   intersects — the shape that breaks a page nobody changed. Registered **above** the handler this
   middleware is outside the re-executed segment, so it runs once and registers one callback, and the
   response-clearing the handler performs is exactly why the emission is deferred to `OnStarting` rather
   than written eagerly: `Response.Clear()` discards headers already set, and the deferred callback
   re-applies the set to the response the client actually receives.
   Each value is nonetheless written **through the indexer** —
   `context.Response.Headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff"` — which **replaces**, and **never**
   through `Headers.Append(...)` or `Headers.Add(...)`, which **accumulate**. The no-duplicate property
   then holds by construction rather than by ordering: any second invocation, from any cause, overwrites
   instead of appending. **The coverage assertion requires it directly**: no security header appears with a
   duplicated value on any of the five response kinds, the re-executed error page included.
   **[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §10.2 owns the header set, the exact directive values, the
   `AddServerHeader = false` host option and the report-only-then-enforce discipline for the
   content-security policy**; this document owns the position in the pipeline and the emission mechanism
   above. Two application-side consequences of that policy are specified here because they are code
   changes: the `javascript:` sign-out trigger goes (section
   [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)) and the cart page's inline script becomes a file under the web root
   (section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)).
3. **The legacy-cookie expiry middleware** — a pass-through middleware that, when a request presents the
   Katana authentication cookie, emits a `Set-Cookie` for that name with an empty value and an expiry in
   the past, then calls the next middleware. **The cookie name is `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie`**: the
   source sets `AuthenticationType = DefaultAuthenticationTypes.ApplicationCookie`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16] and never sets a cookie name, so Katana's
   default applies — its `.AspNet.` prefix followed by that authentication type. **The name alone does
   not identify the cookie, and an expiry that matches only the name does not remove it.** A browser
   identifies a stored cookie by **name, domain and path**, so a `Set-Cookie` differing in any one of the
   three stores a *second* cookie and leaves the first to be presented again on the next request. What
   Katana wrote is knowable exactly, because the source configures **only** the authentication type and
   the login path [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18]: with `CookiePath` unset the
   path is `/`, and with `CookieDomain` unset the cookie is **host-only**, carrying no `Domain` attribute
   at all. The expiry is therefore emitted with **`Path=/` and no `Domain` attribute**, and both halves
   are stated rather than inherited — the framework's `CookieOptions.Path` happens to default to `/`,
   which makes the path right by accident rather than by decision, while **adding** a `Domain` would be an
   active defect, since a domain-scoped deletion does not remove a host-only cookie. `HttpOnly` and
   `Secure` are emitted alongside for consistency with the original; neither participates in the match.
   **Emitting the header is not the same as the cookie being gone**, which is why section
   [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 99** asserts on a **follow-up request through a real cookie jar**
   rather than on the header: the second request must carry no `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie` at all. That
   row is this item's whole coverage — the deletion on all three response kinds, the no-duplicate
   property, the no-cookie case and the record — and no other row asserts any part of it.

   **Its position is third, and it is above every entry that can end a response early.** The expiry is
   written through `context.Response.OnStarting(...)` on the same basis as item 2, so it lands on
   **whichever** component produced the response — but only if this middleware is actually on the path
   that produced it. Exception handling, `UseHsts()`, `UseHttpsRedirection()`, `UseStaticFiles()` and
   `UseRateLimiter()` each either produce a response themselves or return one without reaching an
   endpoint, so a middleware registered **below** any of them misses exactly the responses a dormant
   client receives first: a stylesheet or script fetched by a cached page, a 307 to `https://`, a
   status-code page. A placement **below** any of them — after item 7, say — is rejected for exactly
   that reason: it leaves every static-file response uncovered and makes the expiry depend on the client
   happening to request a controller action in the same visit. Sitting third also puts it necessarily above
   `UseAuthentication()` (item 10), so the ticket is cleared in the same response in which it is first
   presented and is never handed to a handler that cannot decrypt it.

   **It is idempotent, and the guarantee has three parts because a deletion header can be emitted more
   than once from three different causes.** *Within one request* the middleware body runs **exactly**
   once and registers **at most one** `OnStarting` callback: it is registered third, above item 4, and
   `UseExceptionHandler` and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-execute only the segment **below**
   themselves, so a re-executed request never re-enters this middleware — the same property item 2
   depends on. *Within one response* the callback writes the deletion through
   `Response.Cookies.Delete(name, options)`, which appends one `Set-Cookie`; because the callback is
   registered at most once, the response carries **exactly one** deletion header and never a duplicated
   one. *Across requests* the emission is conditional on the request **presenting** the cookie, so a
   browser that dropped it receives nothing further, and a browser that ignored the deletion — or lost
   the response to a network failure — presents it again and is served an identical header. That repeat
   is safe by construction rather than by a counter: the deletion is a **pure function of the cookie
   name, `Path=/` and no `Domain`**, it carries no nonce and no timestamp, it accumulates no server-side
   state, and applying it twice reaches the same end state as applying it once. **No request is ever
   failed, redirected or short-circuited by it**, which is what makes the retry path uneventful.

   **One further attribute, because the response it rides on may be cacheable.** The middleware sits
   above static files (item 7), so the response carrying the deletion can be a stylesheet or a script,
   and a `Set-Cookie` on a response a shared cache retains would be replayed to a client that never held
   the cookie. The callback therefore also sets **`Cache-Control: no-store`** on **exactly** the
   responses in which it emits the deletion, written through the indexer so it replaces rather than
   accumulates. The scope is the point: the only requests affected are those presenting a legacy ticket,
   which is one browser's stale state rather than general traffic, so the asset-caching policy
   [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns is untouched for every other client.

   **What it records, stated here because the record is this middleware's only observable and nothing
   else in the pipeline can produce it.** One entry per response in which the deletion is emitted,
   written through `ILogger` — no in-process telemetry package, per [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — with
   exactly these six fields and no others: the event name **`LegacyAuthCookieExpired`**, a fixed literal
   rather than a description of one, so [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s sink has a single
   string to filter on and the cutover runbook has a single string to count; an **`outcome`** of the single
   literal **`expired`**; the **request method** and
   the **request path**; the **response status code**; and an **actor** of the literal
   `anonymous`. One event name, one field set, one record per response — there is no second shape and no
   array of names.

   **An earlier form of this paragraph read *five* fields and named no `outcome`, and it is corrected
   rather than qualified.** This is an `R8` record — section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s
   producer table assigns it — and [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R8` row requires
   three members over its envelope: the event name, **the outcome**, and the producer's own permitted
   field set. A field list omitting the outcome therefore described a record that shape could not accept,
   and the domain is this document's to fix because `R8` delegates it by name to the section of this
   document that fixes the producer. One literal is the whole domain here: the record exists **only** on
   a response in which the deletion is emitted, so there is exactly one thing for it to report. **The
   count is six because it counts this record's own fields.** `R1`'s envelope — the category, the level
   and the trace identifier — is attached to every application record and is not re-listed by any
   producer; the actor appears above only because its **value** is fixed to a literal here rather than
   resolved from a principal. The actor is not a choice between two values here: the ticket is undecryptable by
   construction, so no identity exists to name, and inventing one from the cookie's bytes is exactly
   what the *never recorded* list below forbids. **Never recorded**: the cookie's value or any fragment
   of it, the ticket bytes, any other cookie's name or value, the query string, and any user name or
   email — a legacy ticket is credential material, and a record that quotes it hands a log reader a
   replayable one. The **severity, the collection mechanism, the sink and the retention are
   [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s**, as they are for every record this document
   specifies; this row states the content and the writer. **The record is diagnostic evidence and not a
   gate**: it lets an operator see whether the dormant population is still non-zero as 06's dated
   follow-up approaches, and it defines no condition that could defer that date — the retention
   paragraph below is the only removal trigger.

   The target's own cookie has a different name (section
   [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so this middleware cannot delete a live session, and
   **the external sign-in cookie is deliberately not handled**: `UseExternalSignInCookie`
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20] issues `.AspNet.ExternalCookie` only during an
   external-provider handshake, and every provider registration is commented out
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35], so no browser can be holding one.
   **[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) consumes this definition rather than restating it.** Its
   cutover runbook owns the *step* — when the middleware is deployed, what the operator verifies and when
   the removal falls due — and this item is the *mechanism* that step invokes: the name, the three
   matching attributes, the position, the idempotence guarantee, the cache attribute and the record are
   fixed here and nowhere else, and no numbered runbook step is reproduced in this document.

   **Its removal has a retention floor, and the floor is split between this document and the runbook the
   way [06 §11.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) divides it.** The floor's **length is this
   document's**, and it follows from the ticket the middleware exists to clear rather than from an
   operational preference: the legacy cookie's lifetime is the middleware default this document records
   with its evidence, **fourteen days** (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so the
   stage outlives the last cookie that can have been issued only at **fourteen days plus one** — the extra
   day absorbing clock skew between the issuing host and the browser. The **instant that length is measured
   from is 06's**: the legacy application's stop, [06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) step 4,
   which is the last moment a legacy cookie can have been issued, and the two halves together are what
   make the floor computable rather than notional. Three further facts about the removal are that
   runbook's and are read from it rather than restated here — the **unsampled channel** its removal gate's
   absence proof must be read from, the **anchors** at which the test fixture is prepared and the deletion
   observed, and the **dated follow-up** that carries the removal
   ([06 §11.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) together with the outer limit past which the stage
   goes whether or not the observation has gone quiet. **Removal is not conditional on that runbook's
   in-window browser verification**, for a reason 06 gives and this mechanism cannot see: the in-window
   check observes a browser that *visited* during the window, while the population this middleware protects
   is the **dormant** client whose user selected "remember me"
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:350] and presents its legacy cookie on a first
   visit that may fall anywhere inside those fourteen days. So the check proves the middleware **works**;
   it is not a licence to remove it. The follow-up's due date and the outer limit are read from 06 and are
   not restated here.
4. **Exception handling**, branched on the environment:
   `if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage(); } else { app.UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error"); app.UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/Home/Error/{0}"); }`.
   It sits **below the header middleware** for the reason item 2 gives — an error response produced by
   this handler must still carry the header set — and **above everything that can fault**, which is
   everything below it.
   **The condition is `IsDevelopment()`, not "not Production".** Staging, QA, UAT and every other named
   environment get the non-disclosing handler, because a Staging deployment is reachable by people who
   are not developers and the developer exception page renders exception messages, stack frames, source
   snippets, request headers, cookie names and configuration keys to whoever asks. Section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) specifies the error action, the model, the status
   codes, what is logged and what may be disclosed. Status-code pages are registered in the same branch:
   in Development a bare status code is more useful than a rendered page, and in every other environment
   a status-code response must render the generic view **with its own code preserved**.
   **The path form of `UseExceptionHandler` produces a response; it does not produce this document's log
   record.** The framework's own middleware logs the exception itself, under its own category and by
   passing the exception object — so its output carries the provider message, which is a diagnostic rather
   than the actor-enriched closed record section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) specifies, and is **suppressed by that section's
   category and level configuration** rather than left to coexist with it. The error action reads no exception feature,
   so it cannot write the record either. The record is written by the `IExceptionHandler` of stage 1
   item 13, which the middleware invokes before it re-executes the path.
5. **`UseHsts()`, outside Development only, and *configured* rather than merely called** —
   `if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseHsts(); }`. An HSTS header served from a local HTTP
   endpoint pins a developer's browser in a way that is tedious to undo.
   [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the policy **and its numbers** — enabled outside
   development, `max-age` per its **mandatory 1-day → 30-day → 365-day ramp**, `includeSubDomains` set and
   preload not asserted — and this item is its configuration expression, because `UseHsts()` alone silently
   takes the framework's **30-day** default `MaxAge`, which is neither of the ramp's first two values and
   is the one value in this pipeline that would be wrong without anybody writing anything wrong. So stage 1
   also carries `Configure<HstsOptions>(options => …)` setting three members explicitly:
   - **`MaxAge = TimeSpan.FromDays(configuration.GetValue<int>("Hsts:MaxAgeDays"))`** — the value read from
     configuration and **not defaulted in code**. **Whose number this is, stated plainly:**
     [06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes the target as
     **`max-age=31536000`** — 365 days — and requires it to be **reached by a ramp**, `Hsts:MaxAgeDays = 1`
     on the first release that enables HSTS, then `30` once the site has been observed serving HTTPS on
     every hostname, then `365`. So the deployed value is **the ramp step the environment is on**, and this
     document neither hard-codes 365 nor supplies a code default that would silently place a first release
     at the target: `Hsts:MaxAgeDays` is a **required** configuration value outside Development, and a
     missing or non-positive one is a start-up failure by the same rule as the trust mode of item 12,
     rather than a silent fallback to any figure. **An earlier form of this bullet defaulted to 365 and
     asserted that 06 "publishes no numeric value" so the figure was this document's; both halves are
     withdrawn** — 06 publishes the figure and the ramp, this document reads them, and a code default of
     365 would have made a deployment that forgot the setting land straight on the hardest-to-undo value on
     its first release, which is precisely what the ramp exists to prevent.
   - **`IncludeSubDomains = true`** — 06 §10.1.4's value, stated as the option rather than inferred from
     the header text. Its cost to sibling hostnames is that section's to state and is not restated here.
   - **`Preload = false`, set explicitly** — 06 §10.1.4's value, and the explicit form is what makes a
     future `true` a reviewed change rather than a side effect of someone tidying the configuration; that
     section states what a future `true` would require.
   - **`ExcludedHosts` retains its framework default**, which excludes `localhost` and the loopback
     addresses; the middleware is already off in Development, so this is defence in depth rather than the
     mechanism.
   - **The two health paths get no HSTS exemption, and the reason is a property of the middleware rather
     than an oversight.** This document owns the probe-path treatment of **both** transport middlewares —
     `UseHsts` here and `UseHttpsRedirection` in item 6 — as one pipeline-order fact, so
     [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) can cite it instead of restating it, and the two
     answers are deliberately different. `UseHsts` **adds a response header and never short-circuits a
     request**, so it cannot take a replica out of rotation the way a `307` can, and it writes nothing at
     all on a plain-HTTP request — the header is meaningless over an insecure scheme and the middleware
     skips it. A probe is therefore unaffected whichever scheme it uses: over HTTPS it receives the header
     and ignores it, over plain HTTP it receives no header, and in both cases the health checks execute.
     Exempting the paths here would add a `UseWhen` branch that changes no response, which is the kind of
     symmetry that reads as a requirement and is really a no-op. Item 6's exemption, by contrast, is
     mandatory, because that middleware **does** short-circuit.

   Registering HSTS *after* the header middleware is deliberate and is not a conflict: `UseHsts` adds
   `Strict-Transport-Security` and the header middleware sets a disjoint set, so neither overwrites the
   other — and it is why the coverage assertion requires that header's **exact value and a cardinality of one**
   rather than merely its presence. The expected value is **the one
   [06 §10.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) check 4 states for the ramp step the environment is
   on**, read from the same `Hsts:MaxAgeDays` value the middleware is configured from so the assertion
   cannot drift from the deployment, with the `preload` token asserted **absent** in every step. Three
   distinct failures are separated by that: a header set that also emitted `Strict-Transport-Security`
   produces two headers and passes a presence check; a `UseHsts()` left unconfigured produces one header at
   the framework's 30-day default, which is a legal-looking value belonging to no ramp step this
   deployment chose; and a `preload` token passes a presence check while asserting something effectively
   irreversible that nobody approved.
6. **`UseHttpsRedirection()`, with the two health paths exempted** —
   `app.UseWhen(context => !HealthPaths.Matches(context.Request.Path), branch => branch.UseHttpsRedirection())`,
   where `HealthPaths` is the single source of those two literals — `/healthz/live` and `/healthz/ready`,
   **two of the three health endpoints item 13 maps**, and the two a platform probe reaches over plain
   HTTP. **The exemption is not
   optional and `.AllowAnonymous()` does not substitute for it.** Anonymous access is an *authorization*
   decision evaluated at the endpoint; this middleware answers **before** routing has selected one, so a
   probe arriving over plain HTTP receives a `307` to `https://` and the health checks never execute. A
   platform or sidecar probe that follows redirects then reports on a **different** request than the one
   it issued, and one that does not follow them reports the instance unhealthy and takes a healthy
   replica out of rotation — the exact failure the anonymous mapping exists to prevent, arriving one
   middleware earlier. Exempting **exactly** two literal paths and nothing else is what keeps the
   exemption from becoming a hole: no prefix match, no wildcard, and every other plain-HTTP request —
   including any path that merely starts with `/healthz` — is still redirected. **Which consumer probes
   over which scheme is [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to state, and it states it as
   `1 + 2`: one probe over HTTPS — App Service's health check, which is HTTPS *because* `HTTPS Only` is on
   for the site, so it reaches the instance through the front end and the application sees a
   forwarded-HTTPS request — and two over plain HTTP, Container Apps' internal `httpGet` liveness and
   readiness probes, issued inside the environment straight at the container's target port where no front
   end and no TLS is involved.** The release pipeline's pre-traffic gate is a fourth caller, over HTTPS, and
   is not a platform probe. **The consequence is what scopes this exemption: it exists for the two Container
   Apps internal probes, it is inert on App Service — which needs no exemption and must not be cited as a
   reason for one — and it is present in the same build on both targets so the two do not need two
   builds.** For a consumer arriving over HTTPS the exemption changes nothing at all, because that request
   never enters the redirection branch; the branch predicate is therefore written on the **path** and not
   on the scheme, which is also what keeps the exemption's scope auditable as exactly two literals.
7. **`UseStaticFiles()`**, serving `wwwroot` (section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)).
8. **`UseRouting()`, then `UseRequestTimeouts()`** — two calls in one position, and the order between
   them is a framework requirement rather than a preference: the request-timeout middleware reads the
   selected endpoint's timeout metadata, so it must be registered **after** routing. The policy it
   applies is stage 1 item 14's `AddRequestTimeouts`, and the timeout value, the `504` it sets and the
   re-execution that turns that code into the error page are section
   [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s. **An earlier form of this item
   registered `UseRouting()` alone**, which left the pipeline published here without the middleware
   section 4.12's timeout chain depends on; the call is added rather than the chain deleted.
9. **`UseSession()`** — after routing and **before** authentication, because the sign-in path writes the
   cart key into session (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) and the cart badge reads
   it on every page from the layout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26].
10. **`UseAuthentication()`** — the call that establishes a principal, and therefore the one every entry
    below it depends on: item 11 partitions on it, item 12 evaluates against it, and the endpoints of
    item 13 authorize against it — including `RecoverCart`, whose `[Authorize]` and whose reading of the
    pending owner both need an established principal (section
    [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)). It sits **below item 3** for the reason item 3 gives.
11. **`UseRateLimiter()`** — after item 10 and **before** item 12, so the three calls run in the order
    `UseAuthentication()`, `UseRateLimiter()`, `UseAuthorization()`. Both sides of that position are
    requirements rather than taste: it must be **after `UseRouting()`** (item 8) because **both** the
    named policy of stage 1 item 14 **and** the `[CredentialEndpoint]` marker its chained partitioners
    select on are endpoint metadata, invisible before routing has selected an endpoint,
    and **after `UseAuthentication()`** because the partition key for a signed-in caller is their
    Identity `UserId`. Placing it ahead of authorization is the cheaper of the two remaining options: a
    refused request then evaluates no authorization policy either. What the placement concedes is small
    and stated: an anonymous flood still costs one cookie-decrypt attempt per request before it is
    refused, which is cheap and bounded, whereas moving the limiter ahead of authentication would ration
    signed-in users by their shared egress address instead.
12. **`UseAuthorization()`** — after item 10 and never before it. Authorization evaluates a principal;
    authentication is what establishes one. Reversed, every `[Authorize]` in the application sees an
    unauthenticated request, and the whole account, checkout and administration surface challenges users
    who are already signed in.
13. **The endpoints**, in one block:
    - `MapControllerRoute(name: "default", pattern: "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}")` — the
      whole of the URL surface, per section
      [2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate).
    - `MapHealthChecks("/healthz/live", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false })` — no
      dependency check; it answers only whether the process is up.
    - `MapHealthChecks("/healthz/startup", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = registration => registration.Tags.Contains("startup") })`
      — the in-process configuration assertions, which issue no SQL at all.
    - `MapHealthChecks("/healthz/ready", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = registration => registration.Tags.Contains("ready") })`
      — the connectivity probe of stage 1 item 11.

    **Three health mappings, one per tagged registration**, which is the set section
    [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) specifies: a predicate
    per path is what stops an endpoint silently acquiring another's checks, and the liveness predicate is
    `_ => false` rather than a tag precisely so that a dependency registered later cannot reach it.
    - **No content-security-policy violation-report endpoint is registered, and that is a decision rather
      than an omission.** [06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) settles the report-only phase as
      a **manually walked browser gate** — the reviewer reads the browser's own console across the 22
      rendered states deliverable [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) §A.4 enumerates — with **no reporting
      destination of any kind**: no reporting directive inside the policy, no reporting response header, and
      no server-side trace of a violation. An earlier form of this block mapped an anonymous `POST`
      collector here and carried it through the anti-forgery register of section [7.1](#71-the-policy), a
      named rate-limiter partition and a per-replica cap; **all of that is withdrawn**. The reason it is
      withdrawn rather than deferred, in one sentence: a public unauthenticated `POST` collector is a new
      attack surface *and* a new personal-data store — a violation report carries the user agent and full
      document and blocked URLs — built for a one-time layout migration whose validation is manual anyway
      and already bounded to a 22-state list. It remains available as a **separately approved addition**,
      and adding it would mean a second row in section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s register, a named limiter
      partition and an ingestion contract, in that order, rather than a `MapPost` call.
    - **What this document's suite therefore asserts about the policy is its payload and nothing about its
      effect.** A `WebApplicationFactory` client parses no policy, blocks no script and generates no
      violation, so row **45** of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts that the content-security
      header is present exactly once on each of four response kinds, that exactly one of the enforcing and
      report-only names is used and the other absent, and that its value is byte-equal to the policy
      [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes — parameterized by the
      `Security:ContentSecurityPolicy:Mode` key of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract).
      **Enforcement is established by 06's browser gate and nowhere in this suite**: its two runs, one
      under each header name against the deployed non-traffic target, are 06's to run and are counted in
      neither the row nor the case totals of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage). Conflating a header's
      bytes with a header's effect is how a policy ships that an agent ignores.
    - **All three health endpoints are anonymous** — `.AllowAnonymous()` on each — because a probe that
      receives a redirect to a login page is reported as unhealthy, which takes a healthy instance out of
      rotation. **The three paths are exactly `/healthz/live`, `/healthz/startup` and `/healthz/ready`**,
      which are the paths [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) configures as the platform
      health-check path, the swap warm-up ping path and the probe targets; the names are a contract
      between the two documents, not a local choice. **An earlier form of this bullet read "both health
      endpoints" over two literals, and it is deleted rather than reconciled**: it contradicted this
      item's own three mappings, [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s requirement that all
      three be anonymous by requirement, and that section's pinning of `WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH` to
      `/healthz/startup`, which a login redirect would fail. **Anonymity and the redirection exemption
      are two different sets, and they are stated as two**: all three endpoints are anonymous, while
      `HealthPaths` — the two literals item 6 exempts from HTTPS redirection — is the **subset** the two
      Container Apps plain-HTTP probes reach, held in one place so the exemption and its consumers cannot
      drift apart.
    - **The probe contract is an application-side requirement stated over both transports, and which
      consumer issues which request over which scheme is
      [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to state rather than this document's to
      reproduce.** A request to either path **must answer with the health result — the status and the body
      literal of the contract in stage 1 item 11 — and never a `3xx`, over plain HTTP and over HTTPS
      alike.** Anonymous access and the redirection exemption of item 6 are the two halves of the
      plain-HTTP case and neither alone is sufficient: without the exemption the response is a redirect,
      and without the anonymous mapping it is a challenge. The coverage assertion drives both schemes**
      for exactly that reason — an HTTPS-only assertion passes an application whose plain-HTTP probe is a
      `307`, and a plain-HTTP-only assertion would leave the scheme an HTTPS consumer uses untested. The
      two treatments of a stray `307` are wrong in opposite directions, which is why the exact status is
      asserted rather than "a success": one consumer class reads a redirect as unhealthy and rotates a
      healthy instance out, while another counts a `3xx` as success and admits an instance whose readiness
      check never ran.

**There is deliberately no cart-recovery middleware in this pipeline, and its absence is a decision
rather than an omission.** Completing a pending cart reassignment is a **write**, and a write belongs to
an endpoint: pre-endpoint middleware runs on safe methods, runs before MVC's anti-forgery filter, and —
because the exception handler re-executes the pipeline — runs again while the error page is being
rendered, so a middleware that can fail turns one database fault into a fault on **every** authenticated
request including the one trying to render the error. Recovery is therefore an explicit
`POST /ShoppingCart/RecoverCart` action, `[Authorize]` and inside the global anti-forgery filter, reached
by the conventional route of item 13 like every other action and needing no mapping of its own. Section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) specifies it, and the coverage assertions require both that
it recovers and that its repeated failure is bounded.

**No CORS middleware is registered, no CORS policy is defined, and the application is strictly
same-origin.** This is stated rather than left silent because an absent registration and an absent
*decision* read identically in a pipeline listing, and the two have opposite consequences for the next
person to add a caller. Every request this application serves originates from a document it rendered
itself: the one scripted call is the cart removal of section
[7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form), which posts to its own path from the page
that rendered it, and section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)
records that the application exposes **no** API surface for an external consumer to call. So `AddCors` is
absent from stage 1 and `UseCors()` is absent from this pipeline, and the consequences are exact:

- **No response carries any `Access-Control-*` header**, on any of the five response kinds. A
  cross-origin `fetch` from another site is therefore refused **by the browser** on the absent
  `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, which is the correct place for it to fail — the request may still reach
  the server, so the anti-forgery policy of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) and the `SameSite` attributes
  of the cookie inventory in section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) are what make the
  *effect* of such a request nil, and CORS is not a substitute for either.
- **A preflight `OPTIONS` receives no CORS response header either.** With no policy registered nothing
  short-circuits the request, so it reaches routing and answers on the conventional route's own terms —
  a `404` or a `405` — carrying no `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and no `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`.
  The assertion is on the **absence of the headers** rather than on the status, because the status is the
  framework's choice and the fourth excluded class of section
  [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) covers it.
- **What a future consumer would require, so that nobody reaches for the quick form.** A named policy
  listing its origins as literals, registered and applied to **that** endpoint rather than globally, an
  approved-delta row, and a coverage row. `AllowAnyOrigin()` is prohibited outright, and
  `AllowAnyOrigin()` together with `AllowCredentials()` is not merely prohibited but rejected by the
  framework itself — which is worth stating, because discovering that at runtime is how a policy gets
  loosened somewhere else instead.

Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row **45** asserts this: on each of its four responses no
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` or
`Access-Control-Allow-Headers` is present, and the row drives one `Origin`-bearing request and one
preflight `OPTIONS` so that the absence is asserted against the requests a registered policy would have
answered.

**Responses that carry a principal's own data are not cacheable, and that is an explicit policy of this
document rather than a framework default.** The framework sets **no** `Cache-Control` on an MVC response,
and a response with no cache directive is one an intermediary is free to treat by its own heuristics — so
a shared cache holding `/Account/Manage`, an order page or the administration list can serve one
principal's page to another. `Cache-Control` is deliberately **not** a member of the header set
[06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns — that set is **six** emitted names and three names
asserted absent, on 06's count, and this document cites it rather than restating it — so this cache policy
is 05's own, and it is applied by the
same middleware as item 2, in the same `OnStarting` callback, written through the indexer for the same
no-duplicate reason.

- **The two conditions, evaluated in the callback.** A response is sensitive when the request has an
  authenticated principal — `context.User.Identity?.IsAuthenticated == true` — **or** when the selected
  endpoint carries a `[SensitiveResponse]` marker, which covers a response carrying personal data with
  no principal behind it: the checkout form an **anonymous** caller has filled in renders back the
  address, phone and email that caller typed. The marker follows the `[CredentialEndpoint]` pattern of
  stage 1 item 14 rather than inventing a mechanism.
- **Why the callback can read both, given that this middleware is registered above
  `UseAuthentication()`.** `OnStarting` runs immediately before the first byte, which is *after*
  authentication has established the principal and after routing has selected the endpoint — so
  `context.User` and `context.GetEndpoint()` are both populated by then. Reading them in the middleware's
  own body instead would see neither, which is the failure this bullet exists to prevent.
- **The three values, together, and why three rather than one.** `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache,
  must-revalidate`, `Pragma: no-cache` and `Expires: 0`. `no-store` is the directive a current cache
  honours; `Pragma` and `Expires: 0` cost two header writes and cover an HTTP/1.0-era intermediary that
  honours neither.
- **The surfaces, at minimum.** The account surface of section
  [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths); the checkout form,
  its redisplays and the order confirmation; and the whole administration surface. Each is reached by an
  authenticated principal, so condition one covers it; the anonymous checkout redisplay is what condition
  two is for.
- **The negative half, which is what makes this a policy rather than a blanket.** An anonymous catalog
  page and a static asset are **left cacheable**, and no `no-store` is emitted on either. Caching them is
  the point of the version-appended asset URLs of section
  [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler), and a blanket `no-store` would discard that quietly
  while looking stricter.
- **It does not overlap the health writer.** The two health responses get their own
  `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache` from the shared `ResponseWriter` of section
  [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — a different value on
  a different response, produced by a health endpoint rather than an MVC one, so no response is written
  by both and there is no ordering question between them.

Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts the three headers on `/Account/Manage` (row **22**),
`/Checkout/AddressAndPayment` (row **10**) and `/StoreManager` (row **15**), and asserts on row **45**
that the anonymous catalog page and the static asset carry **no** `no-store` — the pair being what
distinguishes the policy from a blanket.

**The four requirements [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) places on the application pipeline are
satisfied in this stage, and are listed here so that the two documents describe one pipeline rather than
two:** forwarded-headers handling ahead of anything scheme-dependent (item 1); the security response
header set applied to every response, static assets and error responses included (item 2); the two health
endpoints at the paths 06 polls (item 13); and the legacy-cookie expiry the cutover runbook requires
(item 3). Nothing in 06's list is left to be added elsewhere, and nothing in this stage restates a value
06 owns.

**Migrations are not applied here.** No migration call, no `EnsureCreated`, no seeding and no
provisioning appears in `Program.cs`. Section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) states why
and what replaces it.

---

### 2.5 The health endpoints — the application half of the readiness contract

**The split.** [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the two paths, which probe consumes
each, what each of the readiness endpoint's **two connectivity checks** asserts, the response-disclosure
rule, the refresh-and-cache rule with all of its numbers, and every platform-side probe value. **The
object-existence, permission-probe, migration-comparison and row-write checks an earlier form of that
contract gave to readiness are not readiness checks at all**: [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)
closes the set at two and relocates those four to its
[deployment gate](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification), run once per release under
the monitoring identity — because the runtime identity this endpoint executes as holds no permission on
either migration-history table and no `VIEW DEFINITION`, so two of the four **would have failed against a
correctly provisioned database**. This document therefore states no permission or grant assertion for
readiness. **This
document owns three things that are properties of application code rather than of the platform**: the
registration and refresh **shape** that makes those numbers enforceable, the *API-level semantics* of the
migration comparison **06's deployment gate performs as its check 2** — the calls, their costs and the
direction of the test, which are properties of EF Core rather than of a probe, and which are stated below
precisely because the comparison no longer runs here — and the single path exemption stage 2 item 6 carries, in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). Each is a decision about code that no probe configuration can
express, and each has a wrong answer a platform-side specification cannot rule out.

**Registration shape — one registration, two endpoints, and a predicate per endpoint rather than a
registration per endpoint.** `AddHealthChecks()` with the **single** `ready`-tagged registration of stage 1
item 11, and `MapHealthChecks(path, new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = … })` per path, so no endpoint can
silently acquire the other's checks. **There is no third registration and no third path**: the
configuration assertions an earlier form of this document reported through a startup endpoint are enforced
at start instead, which the boundary table below states check by check.

| Endpoint | Predicate | What it evaluates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/healthz/live` | `_ => false` | **No registration at all.** It returns healthy, which for this path is the whole contract: the process is answering ([06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids wiring it to any dependency, and a predicate matching nothing is the strongest form of that prohibition — there is no registration to accidentally tag `live`) |
| `/healthz/ready` | `registration.Tags.Contains("ready")` | The one registration, which returns the **last completed verdict** of the two connectivity checks of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) from memory, performing **no I/O in the request** |

**The readiness registration performs no I/O, and that is the property the whole timing model rests on.**
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) makes the check set a **background refresh** whose result
the handler serves, and publishes every number that goes with it — the refresh interval, the per-operation
bounds, the total refresh budget against the sum of its parts, and the staleness rule that turns a stale
verdict into a 503. **None of those values is restated here**, because a security- or availability-shaped
number with two homes acquires two versions. What this document owns is the **code shape that makes 06's
numbers true rather than aspirational**, and it is four statements:

| Property | The application-side mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| The refresh runs outside the request | A `BackgroundService` registered in stage 1 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) evaluates the check set on 06's interval and publishes an immutable verdict record — status, evaluation timestamp, the identifiers of **every** check that failed, and the identifiers of every check the pass did not reach, the last two as ordered read-only collections rather than as a single identifier — into a singleton the readiness registration reads. **The collections are not there to hold two simultaneous failures**: with [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s two checks and its one short-circuit, at most one identifier is ever failing in a single pass, and that document states both emitted shapes itself. They are there because the verdict has to distinguish **three** states per check — passed, failed, and not evaluated — and a single nullable identifier carries only one of the three, which is how a `C1` failure ends up indistinguishable from a `C2` failure whose `C1` was never recorded |
| Every operation is individually bounded | Each of 06's per-operation bounds is applied as an explicit **`CommandTimeout` on that command** and a connection timeout in the probe's own connection string, not as one outer cancellation. An outer-only bound would report "the refresh timed out" where 06's log contract requires **each failed check's identifier** |
| The refresh's own total bound is enforced | The evaluation runs under a linked `CancellationToken` cancelled at the evaluation budget of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s hierarchy — the retry shape below supplies the attempt count and defers every duration to that hierarchy — and a cancelled evaluation is recorded as a **failed** evaluation rather than as a slow one, so a hung refresh cannot leave the previous verdict looking current. A cancelled evaluation's verdict carries the identifiers of the checks that had already failed plus a `budgetExceeded` marker, so cancellation does not erase the diagnosis the pass had reached |
| Staleness is a property of the read, not of the writer | The registration compares the verdict's timestamp against 06's staleness bound on **every call** and returns unhealthy when it is exceeded, and returns unhealthy when **no** verdict exists yet. Both are read-side checks, so a refresh loop that has died — the case a writer-side check cannot cover — still produces an unready instance |

**The failure record is the application's, and it is specified per check — because the response says
nothing and the log is therefore the only diagnosis.**
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) fixes the response disclosure (a status
code and a fixed opaque body, naming nothing) and requires a `Warning` naming the failed check by
identifier, **one record per failing check**. **Both checks need a record, because either can fail, so the
shape of each is fixed here.** **The cardinality is one record per check the pass actually *evaluated* and
found failing** — never one record per pass, and never a record for a check the pass did not reach, which
is what keeps a `C1` failure from being reported as a `C2` failure nobody looked for. Every value below is
a **named log-state property**, never interpolated into the message, for the reason section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) gives:

| Check | What its record names | What it must not contain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C1** | `checkId = "C1"`, the failure category — one of the four [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) R4 literals classified in stage 1 item 11 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), the provider's error number where one was returned, and the elapsed milliseconds | The connection string, the server name, the database name and the identity — the connection-validation rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) applies unchanged here, and C1 is the check most likely to tempt an exception dump |
| **C2** | `checkId = "C2"`, the failure kind as one of the four an **availability read** can actually produce — the object could not be resolved, the read was refused to this identity, the command exceeded its bound, or the provider faulted for another reason — plus the provider's error number where one was returned and the elapsed milliseconds. **The object name is `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` and is a constant, so it is not a property**: the check reads one object and the identifier already says which | Any row value, the `Id` the statement selected, the payload column (which the statement does not select at all), the statement text, and the identity's own name. A record that carried a key row would put key material in a log to report that the key table was readable |

**The four checks [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) relocated have no row
here, and their absence is the point rather than an omission.** Object existence, the permission probe, the
migration comparison and the `dbo.SessionCache` round-trip are now checks 1, 3, 2 and 4 of
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s deployment gate, executed **once per
release by the release pipeline** — the first three under the monitoring identity and the fourth as the
runtime principal. A diagnostic record is a property of the component that performs the check, so their
diagnosis is the gate step's output and its release log, and **this document specifies no log record, no
field list and no failure category for any of them**. Nothing in the application evaluates them, so nothing
in the application could write one.

A **successful** evaluation writes nothing at `Warning`; the recovery transition — a failing verdict
becoming healthy — writes one `Information` record naming **every** check that had been failing in the last
failing verdict, so an incident's end is visible without polling. The record is derived from the verdict's
collection rather than from a hard-coded identifier, which is what makes it correct for whichever check was
failing without a second rule per check. That is the only record readiness produces on a healthy
instance.

**What each endpoint touches, stated as a boundary because the two paths look like they might overlap and
do not.** Two paths, two depths, and the distinction is what keeps a database incident from restarting
healthy processes:

| Endpoint | What it touches | What it never touches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/healthz/live` | Nothing at all. No configuration read, no cached verdict, no dependency | The database, the cache, the key ring, and the readiness verdict — wiring liveness to any of them turns a dependency outage into a restart loop, which [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids |
| `/healthz/ready` | The **cached** verdict of the background refresh, read from memory | Any I/O in the request path, and any application data in the refresh either — `C1` is a `SELECT 1;` and `C2` a single-column availability read of `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` on the same connection, neither of which reads an application row, an object's contents or any catalog metadata |

**Configuration correctness is enforced at start rather than reported by a third endpoint, and this is
where the withdrawn startup endpoint's content went.**
[06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists seven checks, `S1`–`S7`, for a startup endpoint.
