**All seven are assertions this document makes at start**, so none of them can be observed *through* an
endpoint at all: a process that fails one is **not listening**, and the evidence is silence on both probe
paths plus the aggregated `OptionsValidationException` naming the member, written unstructured to the
container's console stream — which is the record [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A8
**arm 1** reads from the raw console table rather than from a log projection. That is not a loss of
coverage and not a redundancy; it is **enforcement in place of report**, and it is strictly earlier than
any probe could be.

| [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) check | Enforced by | Evidence of a failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is this process configured for the intended server, database and environment? | **`/healthz/startup`**, in-process | Parsed configuration values compared against the `Expected:*` members. **No connection, no command, no outbound call of any kind** |
| Does the intended database answer this identity, and is the key table available to it? | **`/healthz/ready`**, from the cached verdict of the background refresh | The two connectivity checks of [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) — live SQL, executed **outside** the request by the refresh service, never by the startup path. **It deliberately does not ask whether the schema owners are present or whether this identity's grants are exactly right**: those are release-time questions, answered once by the row below rather than continuously by a probe |
| Do the schema owners exist, and does each principal hold exactly its intended grants and nothing more? | **The release side**, once per release, under the **monitoring** identity | [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s deployment gate. It is not a readiness check and cannot be one: the runtime identity holds neither `VIEW DEFINITION` nor any permission on the migration-history tables, so asking these questions from the readiness path would fail on a correctly provisioned database |
| Did the *release* reach the intended server, database and principal? | **The release side**, before traffic and before any write | The server on the **control plane** — the expected server name parsed, required to carry the `database.windows.net` suffix, and compared case-insensitively against the `properties.fullyQualifiedDomainName` the resource itself reports — and then `DB_NAME()` and `USER_NAME()` asserted **in session** against their expected values. That is [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s assertion, re-run by every operator invocation as assertion 1 of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract). It runs under the **deployment** principal, which is the only identity for which the answer is meaningful |

Those four rows are the whole of the division, and no row borrows another's mechanism.

**The startup endpoint's boundary against start-time validation, which is the one place the two contracts
could be read as contradicting each other.** [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists seven
checks (`S1`–`S7`) for that endpoint, and six of them are **also** start-time validators in this document —
so they cannot be observed failing *through* the endpoint, because a process that failed one of them is
not listening. That is not a redundancy and not a contradiction; it is a split between **enforcement** and
**report**, and it is stated here so that neither document is read as promising the other's behaviour:

| [06 §9.3.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) check | Enforced by | What the endpoint can report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S1` — the host started and validation passed | The host itself | **The answer is the evidence.** A failed start means no answer at all, which the warm-up reads as a failure and the swap aborts on |
| `S2` — both environment variables present, equal, and equal to the expected name | The environment assertion of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a, applied to the web host as well as to the tools, against `Expected:Environment` | **Nothing it could fail on — a mismatch already prevented the start.** Its observable evidence is therefore a **fail-to-start**, not a 503: the aggregated `OptionsValidationException` naming the member, written unstructured to the container's console stream, which is the record [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A8 **arm 1** reads from the raw console table rather than from a log projection |
| `S3` — the connection's server, database and `User Id` | The connection validator's fourth and third checks of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S4` — no password keyword | The accepted-mode check, over parsed fields rather than a keyword scan | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S5` — the discriminator present and expected | `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator` equality | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S6` — no unresolved `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` value | The standing check on every bound string member | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |
| `S7` — the deployed migration identifiers are readable and non-empty | **A start-time assertion, and the one `S`-check that had to be made into one.** Both contexts' `GetMigrations()` are read during start — an in-memory read of the migrations assembly with no I/O at all, per the API table below — and an **empty** set for either context fails the start | Same, and the same fail-to-start evidence |

**Why `S7` had to become an assertion rather than being dropped with the endpoint, because this is the one
place removing a path could have removed a guarantee.** An assembly with no readable migration set is a
**packaging** defect: the host starts cleanly, every configuration value is valid, and nothing during a
request needs that list — so nothing else catches it. It cannot be left to readiness either, and the
reason is precise rather than cautious: `C4` compares the assembly's expected identifiers against the
history table, so an **empty expectation set is vacuously satisfied** and a build with no readable
migrations would be reported **ready**. Reading `GetMigrations()` at start costs no I/O, cannot fail
because a dependency is slow, and cannot make the start depend on the database — which is exactly what
makes it safe to assert there, and why the failure arrives as a fail-to-start rather than as a 503 that a
platform might retry into rotation.

**One arithmetic property is this document's, because it is about the registrations rather than about the
checks**: registrations are evaluated **concurrently**, not serially —
`DefaultHealthCheckService.CheckHealthAsync` runs each registration in its own task and awaits
`Task.WhenAll` (.NET 8) — so an endpoint's cost is the maximum of the registrations its predicate selects,
never their sum. With each of the three doing an in-memory read, all three endpoints answer in
sub-millisecond time, which is what lets
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) bound the probe path at its request budget
without that bound ever being the thing that decides the verdict.

**How the migration comparison is implemented, and why the API matters — and it is a release-gate
computation, not a readiness check.**
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s deployment gate owns this comparison as
its **check 2**: it runs **once per release**, from the release pipeline, before traffic is admitted, and
its in-database read is the **monitoring** identity's. It is not evaluated by an instance and not evaluated
continuously, for the reason [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) gives — the
runtime identity holds no permission of any kind on either `__EFMigrationsHistory_*` table, so a readiness
check could not have performed this read at all. What this document adds is the **API-level semantics** of
the computation, because the two calls that produce its two sides are easy to choose wrongly and a wrong
choice here is invisible until a release passes a gate it should have failed:

| Side of the comparison | Call | What it costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What this build defines, and therefore which targets a release may legitimately declare for it | `GetMigrations()` — "gets all the migrations that are defined in the configured migrations assembly" | **No I/O at all.** It reads the migrations assembly, so the defined set is a property of the deployed bytes rather than of anything queryable |
| What the database has | `GetAppliedMigrationsAsync()` — "asynchronously gets all migrations that have been applied to the target database" | **One** read of that context's own history table, and the only read the comparison needs |

`RelationalDatabaseFacadeExtensions`, EF Core, for both.

**The expected side is the release definition's, not the assembly's, and conflating the two is the error
this paragraph exists to prevent.** 06's gate compares the applied set against the **declared expected
target** its release definition states for that context — which is deliberately **not always head**, because
the release that also performs the data load leaves both contexts short of head until its post-load stages
have run. The expected set is therefore the assembly's ordered defined list **truncated at the declared
target**, and the role of `GetMigrations()` is to establish that the declared target is a member of that
list at all: a release whose declared target its own build does not define is a release definition and a
build that disagree, and that fails before anything is read.

**The verdict is exact set equality, in both directions.** Subset containment is used nowhere — an
identifier present in the history table and absent from the expected set is as much a failure as the
reverse:

| Difference | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| An expected identifier missing from the history table | **Fail the release.** Something the release authorized did not run, so the schema is not the one this build was verified against |
| A history row the expected set does not contain | **Fail the release** — and this is the direction a subset test would have passed. 06 states the case it exists for: a catalog context already at head *before* the load means the post-load migrations ran early, so the schema diff of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) was compared against a polluted baseline and the history tables were not empty when traffic was admitted |

Once both lists are in hand the comparison is in-memory over two short lists, which is why the **applied**
set is read rather than only the framework's `GetPendingMigrationsAsync()` set — "all migrations that are
defined in the assembly but haven't been applied to the target database" (same reference). The pending set
answers one direction and structurally cannot answer the other.

Each context reads **its own** history table, and the two table names are bound once in section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) — which is where
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s gate takes them from. Two contexts
sharing one history table would put each context's identifiers into the other's applied set, where equality
reports them as rows the expected set does not contain; the separation of section 4.5 is therefore a
precondition of this check rather than an independent preference.

**Why no instance performs this, stated as two independent reasons rather than one.** The permission is the
first and it is decisive on its own. The second is that the expected side does not exist inside the
process: the declared expected target is an input of the **release definition**, so an instance holds its
own assembly and nothing that says which of its migrations this release authorized. An instance could
therefore only compare against its own head — the wrong expectation in exactly the release that matters,
the one that loads data — and a check that is wrong in one release and right in the others is worse than
absent. 06's gate holds both inputs, which is why it holds the check.

#### 2.5.1 The instance-verification route, and why it is not a fourth health endpoint

**Where it comes from, and what is being asked of this document.**
[06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines a route, `/healthz/instance`, whose whole
purpose is to make [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s affinity-retirement check provable:
that check has to send requests somewhere and read a worker identity out of the answer, and without such a
route its gate cannot be evaluated at all. That subsection states plainly that it is requiring **two
additions of this document** rather than citing sections that already carry them — the handler, and one
configuration member. This subsection is the first of the two; the `Diagnostics` section of
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) is the second.

**The ownership split, stated first because it is what keeps the two documents from disagreeing.** 06 owns
the path, the single method, both response shapes and their field names, the identifier source, the
four-condition gate and the lifecycle that opens and closes the route. **This document owns the handler's
code, where it is mapped, how each condition is expressed in that code, and the options member's type,
default and validation.** No value 06 fixes is re-decided here, and nothing about the verification
sequence is restated.

| Property | The application-side mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it is mapped** | One `MapGet` among the endpoint mappings of **stage 2 item 13** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), in `Program.cs`, with the route path, the session key and the role literal declared as constants on the `public partial class Program` declaration [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) already requires for the test host. **No file and no folder is added anywhere**: `Program.cs` and the options type both fall under the catch-all row of [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map, which delegates the file-by-file contents of `src/MvcMusicStore/` to this document, so that map gains no entry and the project, folder set and project graph are untouched |
| **What it is not** | **Not a health check, and not a fourth health endpoint.** `AddHealthChecks()` keeps the **single** `ready`-tagged registration above, this endpoint carries no tag, and no `MapHealthChecks` predicate can select it — so the registration table and the boundary table of this section are unchanged and no platform probe can reach it. It shares the `/healthz/` prefix and nothing else: the two health paths touch no session at all, and this is the only path under that prefix that does ([06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) |
| **How "off" is expressed** | The mapping is **conditional**: the block runs only when the `Diagnostics:InstanceEndpointEnabled` member of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) reads true, so when it is false or absent **the route does not exist** and a request receives **404** rather than a refusal. That is 06's condition 1, and it is also why the endpoint is a `MapGet` rather than an attribute-routed action on a controller: an attribute route is mapped whatever configuration says, so its "off" state could only be a handler returning 404 — a route that exists and confirms its existence on every instance of every environment. [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s V8 asserts the closed state as an authenticated administrator `GET` returning **404 and explicitly not 403**, which only the unmapped form satisfies |
| **The role gate** | `RequireAuthorization` on the endpoint, requiring an authenticated principal in the **`Administrator`** role — the same literal the administration surface's own attribute names [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12], which is 06's condition 3. **No protected diagnostic endpoint exists in this design today**: the two health paths are anonymous by requirement (section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)), and they are the only other endpoints under the `/healthz/` prefix. So this is the first, and it borrows the application's one existing role rather than introducing a policy name nothing else uses |
| **Why the refusal is a status code rather than a redirect** | An unmodified cookie handler answers **both** refusals with a redirect — a **302 to `LoginPath`** when nobody is signed in, a **302 to `AccessDeniedPath`** when the policy fails. [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s V2a asserts **401 or 403** for the anonymous caller and **403** for the authenticated non-administrator, so an unmodified handler would fail assertions it satisfies in substance. **The two refusals are therefore handled at two different scopes, and this row states which is which because an earlier form of it made both path-scoped.** The **access-denied** refusal is **global**: `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` writes **403** on every path, because 403 is the target-wide outcome section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) pins for an authenticated caller who is not permitted, and a redirect there would make that outcome a second hop that a non-redirect-following client never sees. The **login** refusal stays **path-scoped**: `OnRedirectToLogin`, which the framework documents as "[i]nvoked when the client needs to be redirected to the sign in url", writes **401** for this one path and performs the configured 302 for every other request — because the anonymous outcome everywhere else *is* the redirect, and it is preserved from the source |
| **The identifier** | Read from the platform and **never computed, never defaulted**: **`WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID` on App Service** and **`CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME` on Container Apps**, the two variables 06 names, tried in that order because exactly one platform serves at a time and neither sets the other's. **Both absent or empty is the failure shape** — 06's `503` carrying its one `error` field and none of the success fields — and that branch **writes nothing to session**, so a 503 leaves no half-initialized value for a later read to find |
| **Session** | The value lives under a fixed key, `healthz-instance`, which is deliberately **not** the preserved cart key `CartId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so neither writer can overwrite the other's **value**. **That is the whole of the isolation the distinct key buys, and this row says so rather than claiming more.** An earlier form of it ended "so a verification run can neither disturb a cart nor be disturbed by one"; **that is deleted rather than qualified**, because it is not true of the store underneath: `ISession` holds **one entry per session**, and `CommitAsync` writes **all** of it, so two concurrent requests in one session overwrite each other's work whatever keys they touched. Distinct keys give **value** isolation, never **write** isolation. Section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) owns the resulting concurrency rule and the reason its residual cost is acceptable; what this route adds is that it is off by default, `GET`-only and administrator-gated, so the ordinary shopping request it would have to race is one an operator has to arrange deliberately. It reaches session through the same `AddDistributedSqlServerCache` and `AddSession` registrations and the same **stage 2 item 9** `UseSession` placement as every other session access — stage 1 registration item 6 and stage 2 item 9 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), specified in section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) — which is the point of the check: the round trip is evidence about the shared store only because the route uses the ordinary one. `LoadAsync` is awaited before the first read, on the framework's own guidance for avoiding a synchronous load of a distributed session |
| **Serialization** | 06's field names are already camelCase, so they survive the framework's web-default naming policy unchanged and need **no** `[JsonPropertyName]` attribute and **no** policy change — the annotate-one-model decision of section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) is untouched, and the response the verification parses carries exactly the names 06 publishes |
| **Transport and host filtering** | The path is deliberately **absent** from the two-literal `HealthPaths` set of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 6, so HTTPS redirection applies to it exactly as to an ordinary page — and HSTS applies to it for the simpler reason that **no path is exempt from HSTS at all**, item 5 being gated on the environment rather than on the path. An earlier form of this row named a `ProbePaths` closed set, which no section of this document declares; that name is deleted rather than carried — which is why 06's verification issues `https://` requests. Host filtering applies too, above every application stage, so the request must arrive on a name `Site:Hosts` carries: the operator drives the check at the target's own default hostname, one of the names [06 §8.4.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s union requires that setting to include |
| **Filters and anti-forgery** | It is not an MVC action, so it appears in no filter inventory; and only `GET` is mapped, so section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s policy keeps **exactly the two opt-outs it maps today** — the property 06 relies on when it declines to make the session write a `POST`, and the reason its method behaviour is 06's to state rather than a second decision here |
| **What it logs** | **One `Information` record at start, when the route is mapped**, through the application category section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) holds at `Information` — so an instance carrying an open diagnostic route says so once, in a sink the platform retains, and the record is a fact about configuration rather than about a request. **No per-request record**: a verification issues forty reads, and forty application log records for a one-time diagnostic would be noise in the sink every real incident is read from. The per-request evidence the check actually asserts on is the **response body**, and its corroborating log is the platform's own HTTP log rather than anything this handler writes — [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) reads both, and [06 §8.3.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records that the route's request telemetry is dropped by the `/healthz/*` probe filter while the platform HTTP log keeps it |

**The whole of the code, in two excerpts.** Both are verbatim from one file that **builds with no error and
no warning on the pinned 8.0 SDK** — verified on 8.0.424, inside the band
[04 §3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins, and again under `/warnaserror`. The first sits inside
stage 1 item 4's cookie registration; the second among stage 2 item 13's endpoint mappings, with the constants
after the last top-level statement:

```csharp
// Inside stage 1 item 4's AddCookie, after LoginPath and AccessDeniedPath are set:
options.Events.OnRedirectToLogin = context =>
{
    if (context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(InstanceRoutePath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    context.Response.Redirect(context.RedirectUri);
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};

// Global, not path-scoped: 403 is the target-wide outcome for an authenticated caller who is not
// permitted, so this event never redirects. UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute renders the generic view
// by re-executing /Home/Error/403 — the same string AccessDeniedPath holds, reached by re-execution
// rather than by a second round trip the client has to follow.
options.Events.OnRedirectToAccessDenied = context =>
{
    context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden;
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};
```

```csharp
// Among the top-level statements of Program.cs, in stage 2 item 13 beside the endpoint mappings:
if (app.Services.GetRequiredService<IOptions<DiagnosticsOptions>>().Value.InstanceEndpointEnabled == true)
{
    app.Logger.LogInformation("Diagnostic instance endpoint mapped at {Path}.", InstanceRoutePath);

    app.MapGet(InstanceRoutePath, async (HttpContext http) =>
    {
        // WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID on App Service, CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME on Container Apps —
        // read from the platform, never computed and never defaulted.
        var instanceId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("WEBSITE_INSTANCE_ID");
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(instanceId))
        {
            instanceId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CONTAINER_APP_REPLICA_NAME");
        }

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(instanceId))
        {
            // Neither variable is set: the failure shape, and session is not touched at all.
            return Results.Json(
                new { error = "instance-identifier-unavailable" },
                statusCode: StatusCodes.Status503ServiceUnavailable);
        }

        await http.Session.LoadAsync();
        var sessionValue = http.Session.GetString(InstanceSessionKey);
        var sessionCreated = sessionValue is null;
        if (sessionCreated)
        {
            sessionValue = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
            http.Session.SetString(InstanceSessionKey, sessionValue);
            await http.Session.CommitAsync();
        }

        return Results.Json(new { instanceId, sessionValue, sessionCreated });
    })
    .RequireAuthorization(policy => policy
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .RequireRole(AdministratorRole));
}
```

**Coverage.** Row 27's cases assert both paths with the database reachable and unreachable, the anonymity
and disclosure properties, and the failure record; row 82 `82a` and `82b` assert that neither mapping
answers a method other than `GET`; and the three fixed oracles of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) carry the status, body, content type and cache headers, so that no row
restates them.

### 2.6 The two hosted services — files, algorithm, timing and containment

Item 15 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) registers two `BackgroundService`
implementations, and [06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names both as the writers of two
mandatory records. A registration and a name are not an implementation, so this subsection is the rest of
it: where the files sit, what each depends on, the algorithm each runs, the timer, the cancellation and
shutdown behaviour, the retry policy, and the containment rule that applies to both.

**Where they sit.** Three new files plus one existing folder. **They are named by
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map, and this document does not add to it** — that map is
closed, with every file under `src/MvcMusicStore/` carried by an enumerated row and no catch-all
delegation, so the three files below appear there as rows rather than by inheritance. The division of
labour is unchanged by that: **the map fixes the path and the folder; this document fixes each type's
members, its lifetime and its registration**, which is why the rows exist in both places and say
different things. `Services/` is the same folder the collector's sink was placed in by section
[7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half).

**One further `BackgroundService` exists and is specified elsewhere, named here so this subsection is not
read as the complete roster.** `Services/KeyRingBootstrapService.cs` sits in the same folder under the same
delegation, is registered beside item 15 on the **web host only**, and runs one pass per process start
rather than a loop — so its algorithm belongs with the key store it bootstraps, in section
[4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof).
What the bootstrap takes from **this** subsection unchanged is the part that is about being a hosted
service at all: the mandatory `await Task.Yield()` before any synchronous work, the off-thread bounded
call shape, the shutdown rule, and the containment rule below. **Two is the whole roster** — there is no
third `BackgroundService` anywhere in this design, which is a statement the next paragraph makes
load-bearing.

**Where they sit.** Two new files in one existing folder, each with **its own row** in
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map. **An earlier form of this paragraph said no map row was
required because "that map's catch-all delegates unlisted content under `src/MvcMusicStore/**` to this
document", and that map has no catch-all**: it is one row per physical file, and a declared file with no row
is the unowned target its §12.1 forbids. `Services/` is the same folder the collector's sink was placed in
by section [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half), which likewise
carries its own row.

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `Services/ReadinessVerdict.cs` | The immutable verdict record — `Status`, `EvaluatedAtUtc`, `FailedCheckIds` as an `IReadOnlyList<string>` (**empty**, never null, when healthy), `NotEvaluatedCheckIds` for the `C1`-short-circuit case, `BudgetExceeded`, and the two values the health registration's sanitized result is composed from rather than derived independently: `FailureCategory`, one of the four [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) R4 literals and null when healthy, and `TraceId`, the identifier of the evaluation that produced the verdict (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) item 11). **One of each is sufficient rather than one per check**, for the same reason the collections are not: at most one check fails in a pass, and a value generated once per evaluation is what makes two responses reporting the same verdict report the same identifier — and `IReadinessResultCache`, a one-property interface over the record. **Both check-identifier members are collections rather than one nullable identifier**, and the reason is the number of *states* a verdict carries per check rather than a number of simultaneous failures: with [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s two checks and its one short-circuit at most one identifier is ever failing in a pass, but *failed*, *not evaluated* and *passed* are three outcomes and one nullable identifier separates two of them |
| `Services/ReadinessResultCache.cs` | The **singleton** implementation. One `volatile` reference to a `ReadinessVerdict?`, written whole by the refresh service and read whole by the health registration; no lock, because a whole-reference swap of an immutable record needs none and a lock in a health handler is a place a probe can block |
| `Services/ReadinessRefreshService.cs` | The refresh loop below |
| `Services/KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService.cs` | The heartbeat loop below |

**What the heartbeat depends on, taken as constructor parameters so it is testable without a host.**

| Dependency | Why it is taken |
| --- | --- |
| `ReadinessRefreshService` | `IReadinessResultCache`; `IServiceScopeFactory` — **not** a `DbContext` and not `IOptions<T>`-scoped state, because a singleton hosted service must not capture a scoped service and every refresh opens its own scope; `ILogger<ReadinessRefreshService>`; `IOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>`; `TimeProvider`, so the interval is testable without waiting for it |
| `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService` | `IKeyManager`; `IDataProtectionProvider`, for the sentinel probe of the note below and for **no other purpose**; `IOptions<KeyManagementOptions>`, read for the configured `XmlRepository`'s concrete type; `ILogger<KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService>`; `TimeProvider` |

**The readiness refresh algorithm.** One pass is: open a scope; evaluate
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s `C1` and then `C2`, both on the **one**
connection that document requires and each under its own `CommandTimeout` per the bounds table of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract); **evaluate every check the
pass can reach and aggregate their outcomes, with no first-failure short-circuit**; construct a new
`ReadinessVerdict` carrying the identifiers of every check that failed and of every check the pass could not
reach; publish it into the cache; and — **on every failing pass, with no de-duplication** — write **one**
`ReadinessCheckFailed` record **per failed check**, each in the per-check shape section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) fixes.

**"No first-failure short-circuit" has exactly one exception, it is 06's own, and that document states it is
the only one in the set.** `C1` is a **reachability precondition** rather than a peer:
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks) bounds it with "a failure here
short-circuits `C2` — there is nothing to ask", and that is literally true, because `C2` is a statement
issued on the connection `C1` failed to open. With two checks and one short-circuit the emitted cardinality
is small enough to state completely, and what keeps the statement honest is the distinction between
*failed*, *not evaluated* and *passed* — three outcomes per check, not two:

| Pass shape | What the verdict carries | How many records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `C1` fails | `["C1"]` failing, and `C2` recorded as **not evaluated**, which is neither passing nor failing, and the verdict says so | **One** — for `C1`. A record for a check that was never issued would be a fabricated observation, and A2 would count a key-table failure nobody had looked for |
| `C1` succeeds and `C2` fails | `["C2"]` failing, and nothing recorded as not evaluated | **One** — for `C2` |
| Nothing fails | An empty failed-check collection, an empty not-evaluated collection, and a healthy status | **None** at `Warning` |

Those three shapes are 06's own. What this table adds is the **algorithm** that produces them without a case
analysis per check — *evaluate what the pass can reach, record what failed, record separately what it could
not reach* — and the reason it is written as a general rule rather than as the two cases above.

**Why the rule is a rule, rather than a first-failure stop.** The first-failure short-circuit an earlier
form of this subsection applied among the peer checks was justified on the grounds that "a second failing
check adds nothing the first has not already decided": true of the *status*, false of the *diagnosis*, and
the diagnosis is the only thing the response discloses nothing about — the response is a status code and a
fixed opaque literal ([06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), so the record is the whole of what an
operator receives, and a rule that stops early to save a statement decides what the operator is allowed to
know. Under the present set the rule costs nothing to hold: **`C2` is one single-row read on the connection
`C1` has already opened**, so 06's evaluation budget covers both checks with room over the sum of its parts,
which is that document's own arithmetic and is not restated here. Keeping the rule in general form is what
makes the verdict's shape independent of the check set — it is the algorithm that stayed correct when 06
closed the set at two, and the reason nothing in this subsection had to be re-derived per check.

**Emitting on every failing pass rather than only on the transition is a decision, and suppression is
rejected for a specific reason.** Suppressing the repeat looks like the tidier choice — an outage lasting
an hour writes the same record on every interval — and it would break the alert it feeds:
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A2 fires on a **count of ≥ 1 within its evaluation
window**, grouped by instance and check identifier — **the window is that document's number and is not
restated here** — so a suppressed repeat would let the alert
**auto-resolve after the first window while the instance was still failing**, which is worse than
noisy. The volume is bounded and small: one record per **failing check** per failing pass per instance, at
that document's
refresh period, and the grouping is what makes the repetition readable rather than the emitter's
restraint.

**The heartbeat algorithm, using the public key-management surface.** One pass reads
`IKeyManager.GetAllKeys()` — "returns all keys in the keyring" (`IKeyManager.GetAllKeys`, API reference,
ASP.NET Core 8) — and computes from that one collection **every field but one**
[06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires: `keyCount` is its count; the newest key is the
one with the greatest `CreationDate`, and its `CreationDate` and `ExpirationDate` are reported directly
from `IKey`; `newestKeyAgeDays` is the whole days between that creation date and `TimeProvider`'s now;
and `repositoryType` is the **runtime type name** of the `XmlRepository` on the resolved
`KeyManagementOptions`, which is what makes [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s alarm A6 a real
comparison rather than a restatement of the intended configuration. The one remaining field,
`defaultKeyId`, is obtained in the same pass **behaviourally** rather than by query — the paragraph below
states how, and why that is the form taken.

**One read, one probe, one record, and the heartbeat itself writes nothing:** it never calls
`CreateNewKey`, never revokes and never deletes. The only way a row can appear because of it is the
framework's own automatic generation reacting to the sentinel `Protect` on a ring with no usable default —
which is precisely what a single served page would cause, since every authentication cookie and every
antiforgery token protects through the same ring. **So the probe cannot reach a state one page view would
not**, and on an **empty** ring it is not issued at all, leaving the first key to the leader of section
[4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof).

**That read is synchronous, it is database I/O, and where it is issued from decides whether this service
can stop the host from listening. This is a correction: an earlier version of this section had it in the
one place it must not be.** `IKeyManager.GetAllKeys()` is declared
`IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> GetAllKeys()` — no `Task`, no token — and with the EF Core repository of section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) behind it, the call
reads `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` on the calling thread. The framework's own contract for a
`BackgroundService` is explicit about what that costs on the start path: *"No further services are started
until `ExecuteAsync` becomes asynchronous, such as by calling `await`"*, and *"Avoid performing long,
blocking initialization work in `ExecuteAsync`"* (*Background tasks with hosted services in ASP.NET Core*,
ASP.NET Core 8). So an `ExecuteAsync` whose **first** statement is `GetAllKeys()` runs that database read
**inline on the host's start path**, before it has awaited anything — which delays every hosted service
registered after it and, if the key store is slow or unreachable, holds the start open with no cancellation
observed anywhere. That is the exact inversion of the containment rule below, and it is what this shape
prevents:

```text
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    // 1. Yield first, unconditionally, before touching anything.
    await Task.Yield();

    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromHours(6), _timeProvider);
    do
    {
        await EmitOnePassAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false));
}

private async Task EmitOnePassAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    using var bound = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken);
    bound.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
    try
    {
        // 2. The synchronous read and the sentinel probe run inside ONE offload:
        //    both can reach the repository, neither takes a token, so what is
        //    bounded and cancellable is the wait rather than either call.
        KeyRingObservation observed =
            await Task.Run(() =>
                  {
                      IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> keys = _keyManager.GetAllKeys();

                      // 3. defaultKeyId is OBSERVED, never predicted: protect a fixed
                      //    sentinel and read back the key id the framework stamped on
                      //    the payload. Skipped on an empty ring, so this can never be
                      //    what creates the first key. Returns null on any mismatch.
                      Guid? defaultKeyId = keys.Count == 0
                          ? null
                          : TryReadStampedKeyId(keys);

                      return new KeyRingObservation(keys, defaultKeyId);
                  }, bound.Token)
                      .WaitAsync(bound.Token)
                      .ConfigureAwait(false);
        WriteKeyRingStatusRecord(observed);       // one record, per 06 §7.4
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Shutdown. No record, per the shutdown row below.
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning(
            "{eventName}: outcome={outcome} traceId={traceId}",
            "keyRingStatusUnavailable", "timeout",
            Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString()
                ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString());
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // No exception object is passed: the record shape of section 3.3, which every
        // ILogger call in the port is held to. Types and stack as named values; no Message.
        var innerTypes = new List<string>();
        for (var inner = ex.InnerException; inner is not null; inner = inner.InnerException)
        {
            innerTypes.Add(inner.GetType().FullName!);
        }
        _logger.LogWarning(
            "keyRingStatusUnavailable exceptionType={ExceptionType} " +
            "innerExceptionTypes={InnerExceptionTypes} exceptionStack={ExceptionStack}",
            ex.GetType().FullName, innerTypes, ex.StackTrace);
    }
}

// 4. The whole of the internals-free derivation. Public API only:
//    IDataProtectionProvider.CreateProtector(...).Protect(...), then two checks.
private Guid? TryReadStampedKeyId(IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> keys)
{
    byte[] payload = _protectionProvider
        .CreateProtector("MvcMusicStore.KeyRingStatus.Probe")
        .Protect(SentinelPlaintext);         // one constant byte; result discarded

    if (payload.Length < 20) { return null; }
    if (payload[0] != 0x09 || payload[1] != 0xF0 ||
        payload[2] != 0xC9 || payload[3] != 0xF0) { return null; }   // magic header

    Guid stamped = ReadKeyId(payload.AsSpan(4, 16));    // order settled by the gate
    return keys.Any(k => k.KeyId == stamped) ? stamped : null;       // membership gate
}
```

**One property of those two catches is a rule rather than a style, and it is the same rule the whole
document rests on.** Neither call passes the `Exception` to `ILogger`. An earlier form of this block wrote
`_logger.LogWarning(ex, "keyRingStatusUnavailable")`, and that is the one shape this design cannot use: the
built-in JSON console formatter serializes an exception argument through `ToString()`, so the provider
message and the full stack reach the sink whatever the category's level says — the mechanism this section
establishes when it states that the control is on **what is passed to the formatter**. The category is
`MvcMusicStore`, which is at `Information`, so the record is emitted and the leak would be real rather than
theoretical. What is passed instead is the exception's **type name**, which is a permitted field on every
fault-describing record in this document, plus a closed `outcome` literal — `timeout` when the bounded wait
expired, `readFailed` otherwise.

**The trace identifier is written as the expression itself, at both call sites, and an earlier form of
this block called a helper that was never declared.** That form put a **named helper method call** in the
excerpt at both sites and described it here only as "the non-request trace expression fixed in section
3.3" — a name defined by reference and declared nowhere: no type in this document declares such a member
and no file on [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map holds one, so the excerpt as written
would not have compiled, and inventing a file for a single expression would add a target artifact that
map is closed against. **The expression is therefore
stated inline wherever it is used**, here and everywhere else in this document:

```csharp
Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString() ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()
```

The rule it implements is not re-decided here. [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s **`R1`**
row fixes it for every record this document specifies: the identifier is the **ambient activity's trace
id** where one exists and a **producer-generated** one where none does, in the same domain either way —
**32 lowercase hexadecimal characters**. `ToHexString()` is named rather than implied because
`Activity.Current.TraceId` is an `ActivityTraceId` value and only that method renders it in the asserted
domain, while `Activity.Current?.Id` renders the composite `traceparent`-shaped string instead.

**Three properties of that shape, each stated because each is load-bearing rather than idiomatic.**

| Property | Why it is written that way |
| --- | --- |
| **`await Task.Yield()` is the first statement, before the timer and before any read** | It is the one construct guaranteed to suspend: `YieldAwaitable.YieldAwaiter.IsCompleted` is documented as **always `false`**, so the await can never complete synchronously and `StartAsync` for this service always returns at that line. A `PeriodicTimer` first tick or a `Task.Delay` would also yield in practice, but neither is documented as *never* completing synchronously, and this property is the whole point |
| **The read *and the probe* are offloaded in one `Task.Run`, and the wait is bounded with `WaitAsync` on a linked source** | Two different jobs, which is why both appear. `Task.Run(…, token)` moves the synchronous read **and the sentinel `Protect`** — which reaches the repository itself whenever the cached ring is stale — **off** the loop's thread, so the loop and the shutdown path are never the thread sitting in provider I/O. `WaitAsync(token)` bounds the **wait** — 30 seconds, or shutdown, whichever comes first — so a hung read cannot make the service unresponsive to `StopAsync`. The token is a `CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken)` with `CancelAfter`, so shutdown and the bound are one token rather than two racing ones |
| **What the bound does *not* do is stated plainly** | Cancelling the wait does **not** abort either call. Neither `GetAllKeys()` nor `Protect` takes a token, so a thread blocked inside one of them stays blocked until the provider's own connection and command timeouts return — which for the EF Core repository are section [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)'s, and they are what actually terminate it. The bound therefore buys **responsiveness of the service**, not termination of the call, and this document does not claim otherwise. One worker thread may remain occupied for the provider's timeout; at one pass every six hours that is bounded and acceptable, and it is preferable to the alternative of that thread being the host's start path |

**`defaultKeyId` is the one field no public *query* returns, and it is obtained from public API by
*observing* the ring rather than by reaching into the framework's internals.**
[06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires the **default key's identifier** — which key the
ring would actually protect with, given activation dates, expiry and revocations. The framework's
selection rule lives in `IDefaultKeyResolver`, in the
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal` namespace, whose members the API reference
marks as supporting infrastructure and **not** intended to be used directly from application code. Three
options existed and the third is taken:

| Option | Why not / why yes |
| --- | --- |
| Recompute the selection in this application from `GetAllKeys()` | **Rejected.** It would put a second, independently maintained copy of the framework's eligibility rule in this codebase, and a monitoring field that disagrees with the framework's real choice is worse than no field: alarms A6 and A5 would then be reading this document's opinion of the ring rather than the ring |
| Resolve `IDefaultKeyResolver` and call it, accepting the namespace | **Rejected.** The type is public and resolvable, and calling it would compile today on 8.0.30 — which is exactly what makes it the wrong dependency to build monitoring on. A namespace the API reference marks as supporting infrastructure carries no compatibility promise across a **servicing** release, so the failure mode is a heartbeat that stops compiling, or silently changes shape, on a patch upgrade this project takes for security reasons and cannot decline. **And the practical consequence is what settles it:** a monitoring field that breaks the build on a mandatory upgrade gets deleted under time pressure, not repaired, so the internal API is the option most likely to end with no field at all. Its two supporting facts — `DefaultKeyResolution` is a `struct` whose members are fields, and the type needs a second `using` — are recorded here only so that a future reader can see the option was examined rather than overlooked |
| **Derive it behaviourally: protect a sentinel and read the key identifier the framework itself stamped on the result** | **Taken.** The heartbeat depends on the public `IDataProtectionProvider`, calls `CreateProtector("MvcMusicStore.KeyRingStatus.Probe").Protect(…)` on a fixed one-byte sentinel, and reads the identifier out of the returned payload: ASP.NET Core's data-protection payload format is **documented** — *Authenticated encryption details*, ASP.NET Core 8 — as a 32-bit magic header, `09 F0 C9 F0`, followed by the **128-bit key id** and then the encryptor-specific protected data, which is why the sketch reads four bytes and then sixteen. **The one thing this document does not assert is the byte order** in which those sixteen materialize a `Guid`, and it does not need to: the membership check below decides it. A `Guid` built the wrong way round matches no listed key, so the wrong reading yields an omitted field and a warning rather than a wrong identifier — and the implementation settles the order once, against a payload the running application produces, with the membership check standing between a misread and anything published. So the field reports the key the ring **did** protect with, which is strictly stronger than any prediction of which key it would choose — and it needs no package reference and no internal namespace, leaving [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s pin list untouched. **Two checks make the byte-level read safe, and they are the whole of the compatibility gate:** the four magic bytes are compared against the documented constant before the offset is trusted, and the derived identifier must be **one of the identifiers `GetAllKeys()` returned in the same pass**. A format change, a different constant, or a byte order this document read wrongly therefore produces an identifier that matches no listed key, and the field is **omitted** rather than reported — the failure path below. The probe is a `Protect` and never an `Unprotect`, it stores nothing, and it creates no key on a ring that already has one; on an **empty** ring it would cause the framework to create one, which is why the bootstrap of section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof) runs under its lock first and why the heartbeat skips the probe — and omits the field with the same warning — whenever `GetAllKeys()` comes back empty |

**The revalidation obligation stays, and it is now a runtime check rather than a compile-time hope.** The
framework upgrade of [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s support-window risk must re-check the magic
constant and the key-identifier offset against the payload-format documentation for the release being
moved to; but because both checks above run on every pass, a change nobody noticed degrades **one field**
and raises the warning below instead of breaking the service or reporting a wrong identifier. **No
infrastructure namespace is imported anywhere in this application**, so there is no isolation type to
audit and no closed call-site list to keep.

**If the probe, the magic-header check or the membership check fails, the field is omitted and the record is still emitted**, with one
`Warning` naming `defaultKeyIdUnavailable` and the reason. **That `Warning` is this same `KeyRingStatus`
record at the higher level, not a second record and not a second event name** — the literal is the value
of the record's **`outcome`** member, which [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R8` row
requires and whose domain here is exactly two values: **`reported`** on a nominal pass, at `Information`,
and **`defaultKeyIdUnavailable`** on this one, at `Warning`. Reading the sentence as a separate emission
would add an eighth `R8` producer to a list `R8` closes at seven, and would give alarm A4 a second event
name to miss. `R8` reserves `Error` for the request-path exception shape, which is why a monitoring
producer's worst outcome is a `Warning`. That ordering matters:
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s alarm A4 fires on the **absence** of the whole record, so a
heartbeat that suppressed itself over one missing field would raise an availability alarm about a healthy
key ring.

**Timing, cancellation and shutdown, for the loop.**

| Property | `ReadinessRefreshService` | `KeyRingStatusHeartbeatService` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First pass | Immediately on start, before the first wait | Immediately on start, **but after `ExecuteAsync` has already yielded** — the `await Task.Yield()` above comes first, then the first `GetAllKeys()` off-thread read, and the record is written when that read returns. That return is also the point [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s "once the ring has resolved" names, because that call is what resolves it. The yield is what makes "immediately on start" mean *concurrently with* the rest of the start rather than *inside* it |
| Period | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s refresh interval. **Not restated here** | **6 hours**, which is [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s figure and is cited rather than re-decided |
| The timer | A `PeriodicTimer` created from `TimeProvider`, awaited with `WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken)`. Chosen over `Task.Delay` in a loop because it does not drift with the duration of the pass, and over `System.Threading.Timer` because it cannot re-enter: a pass that overran its period delays the next tick instead of running twice | The same |
| Cancellation | The `stoppingToken` is passed into **every awaited call that accepts one** — the scope's database commands and the tick wait — so a shutdown does not wait out a hung database call. **`ILogger` calls are synchronous and take no token**, so the record write is not a cancellation point and is not claimed as one; it is a memory-to-stdout write bounded by the formatter | The same |
| Shutdown | `WaitForNextTickAsync` returns `false` on cancellation and the loop exits. **`OperationCanceledException` raised during a pass while the token is signalled is treated as a clean stop, not an error**, and no verdict or record is written for it — a shutdown must not publish a failing verdict, because on App Service a swap stops instances routinely | The same, and no partial record is emitted |
| What runs at shutdown | Nothing. Neither service holds a resource whose release needs a `StopAsync` override, so neither declares one | The same |

**Retry, with backoff, and it is per pass rather than per loop — but the numbers are [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s
and are cited rather than re-decided here.** The **shape** is this document's, because it is a property of
application code no probe configuration can express: a failing pass makes **at most two attempts** — the
initial attempt, then, only for a transient failure, **one** retry after a single fixed pause. A small
fixed-step pause rather than an unbounded exponential one, because the loop itself is the long retry and a
pass must finish well inside its own period. **Every duration in that shape — the per-operation timeouts,
the evaluation budget, the pause between attempts and the budget for the whole pass — is a number
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s timeout hierarchy publishes**, and this
document restates none of them. That is the same division section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) states for the refresh
interval and the staleness bound, applied to the rest of the hierarchy for the same reason: two documents
that both publish a budget will eventually publish two different ones, and an earlier form of this
sub-section did exactly that — it summed a five-check evaluation that no longer exists, and its pass budget
disagreed with the owner's.

| Quantity | Who supplies it |
| --- | --- |
| The per-operation timeouts, the budget for **one evaluation**, the pause between attempts, and the budget for a **whole pass** | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s timeout hierarchy, which states all four in one place and is the only place any of them is stated |
| Attempts per pass — **at most 2**, the initial attempt plus one transient retry | This document, because it is a property of the refresh loop's code rather than a duration |
| Refresh period and staleness bound | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s figures, **not restated here** |

Every duration this sub-section previously pinned is withdrawn in favour of that division, and the reason
is worth stating rather than leaving as tidiness: those figures were derived by summing a **five-check**
evaluation, and readiness now has [two checks](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks), so
each of them was arithmetic over a check set that no longer exists. They are withdrawn by name, so that a
reader meeting them in an older copy can recognize them: a 9-second attempt ceiling, a 20-second
worst-case pass, a 2-second pause and a 25-second pass budget, together with the reconciliation that
argued a 10-second figure in the owning section bounded one evaluation while the 25 seconds here bounded
the pass. **That reconciliation was true while the owner published one figure, and is false now that it
publishes both** — an evaluation budget and a pass budget — which is exactly why every duration in the
hierarchy belongs to one document.

**What this document requires of those durations, without supplying them**, is the one property the shape
above depends on: the budget for a whole pass must exceed two evaluations at their ceiling plus one pause,
or a transient failure would be reported as a budget-exceeded evaluation rather than retried at all. That
is the defect the withdrawn arithmetic existed to rule out, and the owner's hierarchy rules it out where
the four numbers actually live.

Two rules bound the retry beyond the durations. The whole pass including its retry runs under a linked
token cancelled at the owner's pass budget, so a retry cannot extend
a pass past its bound; and **only transient failures are retried** — for the refresh, the SQL error
numbers the execution strategy of section
[4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)
already treats as transient, and a check that failed **non**-transiently is **not** retried at all,
because no such condition becomes true a pause later — for readiness's two checks, a login the server
rejects on `C1`, and a `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` absent or unreadable by this identity on `C2`;
for the heartbeat, nothing, because reading an in-memory key ring has no
transient failure mode and a retry there would only hide a configuration fault. After the retry, the
refresh publishes a failing verdict naming every failed check and the heartbeat writes its `Warning`, and
both wait for the next
tick.

**Containment is mandatory, and the reason is a framework default rather than a style preference.**
`HostOptions.BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` **defaults to `StopHost`**, so "if any
`BackgroundService` throws an unhandled exception, the host will crash" — the behaviour
`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` documents (API reference, .NET 8), and the reason the framework
changed the earlier ignore-and-continue default. Neither of these services may rely on that:

- **The body of every pass is wrapped**, so no exception leaves `ExecuteAsync`. A pass that throws writes
  one `Warning` naming `keyRingStatusUnavailable` and waits for the next tick, and the bootstrap's single
  pass does the same with its own record, per section
  [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof).
  Row 100 `100b` asserts it on the heartbeat, through a real provider fault rather than a thrown test
  double.
- **The loop itself is wrapped**, so an exception raised by the tick wait rather than by the body of a
  pass cannot escape either. This is the case the per-pass wrapper does not cover and the one that would
  actually take the host down — and it is also the one no case in section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) can reach, which is why it is entry **10** of section
  [12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests) with a code review as its closure rather
  than an unstated gap.
- **`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior` is left at its default.** Setting it to `Ignore` would be a way
  to get containment without writing it, and it is rejected: it would silently swallow a fault in any
  future hosted service as well, and the containment here is deliberate per service rather than
  host-wide.
- **A monitoring service must never be able to stop the thing it monitors.** A key-ring heartbeat that
  crashed the site because the ring was unreadable would convert an alertable condition into an outage —
  the precise inversion this rule exists to prevent.

**Warm-up behaviour, stated because the first few seconds of a new instance are exactly when a probe
arrives.** Neither service blocks the start, and that is a property of how each one is written rather than
a property of `BackgroundService`. `StartAsync` returns at the first `await`
in `ExecuteAsync` **that actually suspends** — the framework's own wording is that no further service is
started "until `ExecuteAsync` becomes asynchronous, such as by calling `await`" — so a first statement that
completes synchronously, and specifically a synchronous database read, holds the start open. Each service
therefore reaches its first suspension before it touches anything: the heartbeat by the mandatory
`await Task.Yield()` above, and the refresh because its first act is to `await` its own bounded, linked
pass. With that, the host finishes starting and begins listening while the first pass is still
running. The consequences are defined rather than incidental. **Before the refresh's first pass
completes, the cache is empty and `/healthz/ready` answers unhealthy** — the no-verdict rule of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — so a new instance is
never advertised as ready on the strength of never having checked. `/healthz/live` answers normally
throughout, which is what lets the platform distinguish "starting" from "broken" — the process is up and
the instance is not yet ready, and the two endpoints express that difference between them with no third
path needed. And **the heartbeat's startup record is emitted once per process start**, so an instance that is
replaced twice in an hour produces three records rather than one — expected, and the reason
[06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s A4 tests for absence rather than for a count.

**The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)** exercises both: the readiness cache is
asserted empty-then-populated across the first pass, a forced failure inside a pass is asserted to publish
a failing verdict **and leave the host running**, a forced exception in the loop is asserted the same way,
cancellation is asserted to stop both loops without a record or a verdict being written for the
shutdown, and **each of the two pass shapes is asserted separately, because the difference between them is
the property that is easy to lose**: a forced `C1` failure produces **one** `ReadinessCheckFailed` record
and a verdict carrying `C1` as failing with `C2` marked **not evaluated**, and a `C1` that succeeds against
a `C2` forced to fail produces **one** record for `C2` and a verdict whose not-evaluated collection is
**empty**. An assertion that only counted records would pass an implementation that fabricated a `C2`
failure whenever `C1` failed.

---

## 3. Configuration and the one active transform

### 3.1 Configuration: `Web.config` becomes `appsettings.json` read through `IConfiguration`

**The configuration surface is seven groups, not two, and the two that are routinely overlooked are
the two that carry runtime behaviour rather than values.** `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config` is 71
lines and every one of its elements needs a disposition:

| Group | Locator | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `configSections` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:7-10] | The `entityFramework` section declaration, naming `EntityFramework, Version=6.0.0.0` |
| `connectionStrings` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:11-14] | Two entries |
| `appSettings` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:15-22] | Six keys |
| `system.web` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:31-35] | `authentication mode="None"`, `compilation`, `httpRuntime` |
| `system.webServer` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:36-40] | One module removal |
| `runtime/assemblyBinding` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:41-60] | **Four binding redirects** |
| `entityFramework` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:61-70] | **`defaultConnectionFactory` and `providers`** |

`Views/Web.config` is a separate file with its own two responsibilities, dispositioned in section
[8.6](#86-view-serving-and-_viewimports). In the target the value-carrying groups become
`appsettings.json` and `appsettings.Development.json`, read through `IConfiguration`, with typed
options classes bound at startup; the behaviour-carrying groups map to code, and the table below gives
each of the seven a target.

**The options pattern is required here rather than merely conventional, and the reason is a specific
line of code.** `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` is read **directly from startup code**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24], via `using System.Configuration;` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:7]. That
is not a configuration *file* problem that a file format solves — it is a startup component reaching
into a static ambient configuration store, which the target has no equivalent of. The two values it
reads are the administrator credential, and section
[10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) removes them from configuration
altogether, so the correct target for [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24] is **nothing at all**: no `appsettings` key, no
options class, no environment variable in the web application.

Per-key disposition. Every row below carries its own citation into
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config` in full, path and locator together — an earlier form of this sentence
declared a shared path so the rows could carry bare locators, and it is deleted rather than kept as a
convenience, because a locator whose path is inherited from a sentence above it is a locator a reader
cannot check where it stands, and the rows below never used the bare form in the first place:

| Current key | Target |
| --- | --- |
| `configSections/entityFramework` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:7-9] | **Deleted.** It exists only so the `entityFramework` element below can be parsed; EF Core has no configuration section and reads no configuration file of its own |
| `connectionStrings/DefaultConnection` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12] | One connection string for one database, supplied by platform configuration — the mechanism and the identity model are [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; the blocker framing is [11 §3.4](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)'s |
| `connectionStrings/MusicStoreEntities` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13] | The **same** connection string; see section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) for why one database and what it trades |
| `DefaultAdminUsername`, `DefaultAdminPassword` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17] | **Removed from source entirely.** Section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command). [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding |
| `webpages:Version`, `webpages:Enabled` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:18-19] | **End.** Web Pages is not part of the target; the same `webpages:Enabled=false` appears redundantly at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:26] and ends with it |
| `ClientValidationEnabled`, `UnobtrusiveJavaScriptEnabled` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:20-21] | **End as configuration keys.** Both behaviours are the target's default and are not switched from `appsettings` |
| `system.web/authentication mode="None"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:32] | **Ends.** The value is an artifact of authentication having been moved to OWIN; the target has no `system.web` |
| `system.webServer/modules remove FormsAuthenticationModule` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:38] | **Ends.** An IIS-integrated-pipeline instruction with no counterpart |
| `compilation targetFramework="4.8"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:33] versus `httpRuntime targetFramework="4.5"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:34] | **Ends — the concept has no target.** The target has no quirks mode, so there is nothing to carry the value into. The consequence is for the *baseline*, not the port: see below |
| `runtime/assemblyBinding` — four `bindingRedirect` elements for `System.Web.Helpers`, `System.Web.Mvc`, `System.Web.WebPages` and `WebGrease` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:43-58] | **Deleted, all four.** See below: they exist to paper over assembly-version drift that the target's dependency model does not produce |
| `entityFramework/defaultConnectionFactory` — `LocalDbConnectionFactory` with parameter `v11.0` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:62-66] | **Deleted, with no successor and no equivalent fallback.** See below |
| `entityFramework/providers` — `invariantName="System.Data.SqlClient"` mapped to `SqlProviderServices` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:67-69] | **Replaced by provider selection in code:** `AddDbContext<T>(o => o.UseSqlServer(...))` for both contexts (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), supplied by the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer` package that [04 §7](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins |

**Why all four binding redirects are deleted rather than translated.** Each one maps a range of old
assembly versions onto the single version the project actually ships — for example
`System.Web.Mvc` `1.0.0.0-5.0.0.0` onto `5.0.0.0`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:48-49]. They exist because `packages.config` restore installs each
package independently and performs no unified version resolution across the graph, so an assembly
compiled against an older version of a dependency has to be redirected at load time. The target's
dependency model removes both halves of that problem: `PackageReference` resolves **one** version of
each package for the whole graph (the conversion is [04 §5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s), and
The target framework has no assembly-binding-redirect mechanism at all — assembly resolution is driven by the
generated `.deps.json` and a `bindingRedirect` element in a configuration file would be ignored even
if one were written. Two of the four also name assemblies the target does not contain
(`System.Web.Helpers`, `System.Web.WebPages`) and one names a package the target removes (`WebGrease`,
retired with bundling in section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)), so there is
nothing left to redirect.

**Why the EF 6 connection factory has no successor, and what changes when it goes.**
`defaultConnectionFactory` is EF 6's *fallback*: it constructs a connection when a context cannot
resolve a named connection string, and the configured parameter `v11.0`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:64] would make that fallback target a `(LocalDb)\v11.0` instance —
an instance name that appears nowhere in either connection string, both of which name `MSSQLLocalDB`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13]. In this application the fallback is **inert**, because both contexts resolve a named string:
`MusicStoreEntities` declares no constructor and EF 6 matches the class name to the entry at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13]
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:5-13], and `ApplicationDbContext` passes
`base("DefaultConnection")` explicitly
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:10-15]. Recording it matters anyway, for one reason:
**EF Core has no ambient fallback of any kind.** A context registered without a configured provider
throws at the first resolution rather than quietly constructing a LocalDB connection, so the class of
misconfiguration this element could mask cannot occur silently in the target — and the explicit
`UseSqlServer` in `AddDbContext` is not an optional convenience but the only thing that configures the
provider.

**The framework-version mismatch is a baseline-integrity problem, and it must be handled before the
baseline is captured rather than diagnosed afterwards.** `httpRuntime targetFramework="4.5"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:34]
holds 4.5-era compatibility behaviour in force even though the project targets 4.8
([12 F-12-18](12-migration-blockers.md) owns the finding). So the behaviour a reviewer records from
the running MVC 5 application **is 4.5 quirks-mode behaviour**, and the ported application has no
quirks mode at all. The resolution is procedural and belongs to the baseline exercise of section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage): the baseline capture must record that the source
runtime was in 4.5 quirks mode, and any behavioural difference the suite surfaces in request
validation, encoding or a related default must be checked against that setting **before** it is
classified — because the error is available in both directions. A pre-existing configuration artifact
can be misfiled as a port regression, and a real regression can be dismissed as "just the quirks
mode".

### 3.2 The one active transform, and the two halves it splits into

Across the six transform files in the repository there are **fifteen** `xdt:Transform` occurrences and
only **three** of them are outside an XML comment — one per `Web.Release.config`, and all three are
the same line at the same line number:

```text
src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
src/MVC3/MvcMusicStore-Completed/MvcMusicStore/Web.Release.config:18:  <compilation xdt:Transform="RemoveAttributes(debug)" />
```

The three `Web.Debug.config` files carry **zero** active transforms. Every other occurrence in all six
files is commented-out template text. The verifying command is in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**This one transform splits into two target concerns, and conflating them is the error this section
exists to prevent.**

**Half one — build and publish.** Removing the `debug` attribute from `<compilation>` is what stops
the release deployment compiling with debug semantics. Its target is the **Release build
configuration's own publish behaviour** — the publish step of
[04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s sequence, which owns that invocation and every option on
it — under which optimization and debug-symbol behaviour are properties of the configuration rather than
of a setting anyone writes. It does **not** map to an `appsettings`
key and it does **not** map to an environment variable. There is nothing to write into a configuration
file for it, which is why a reader looking for its successor in `appsettings.json` will not find one
and may wrongly conclude the behaviour was lost.

**Half two — runtime error behaviour.** What `debug="true"` *also* influenced in practice — how much
detail an error response discloses — is in the target a **runtime** decision made in the middleware
pipeline: the developer exception page is registered **only when the environment is Development**, and
the exception-handler middleware handles **every** other environment, Staging included (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), designed in section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). That is governed by the environment the application
runs in, not by the build configuration it was compiled with. **The two are independently settable in
the target and must be set independently** — a Release build can run in a Development environment and
a Debug build in Production, and neither combination should surprise anyone reading this plan.

**One net-new obligation follows from the same six files.** The commented-out examples include a
connection-string substitution that was **never active**, so the repository has no working mechanism
for supplying a secret at deploy time. Providing one is therefore net-new work rather than a migration
of anything, and its mechanism is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s.

### 3.3 The target configuration contract

Section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) says what
happens to each key the application reads **today**. This section says what the ported application
reads **tomorrow** — every section name, every options type, every member with its type, whether it is
required, its default when absent, and what fails the start when it is wrong. It exists because
"configuration moves to `appsettings.json` and the options pattern" is not implementable: a reader
cannot write the file, and a reviewer cannot approve a value that has no name.

**The ownership split, so neither half is stated twice.** This document owns the **contract** — key
paths, types, defaults, validation and precedence. [06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns
