security attribute is a downgrade that one mistyped application setting can perform, and no legitimate
deployment needs any of them off. The first three carry section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)'s values; **`Path` is `/` and `Domain` is `null`**, and
those two are this contract's, for the reason the next paragraph gives.

**`Path` and `Domain` are stated rather than left to the framework, and the second of the two is the
decision.** `Path=/` is set explicitly on every cookie in the inventory above so that the scope is a
property of this contract rather than of the request path a cookie happened to be issued from — the
application cookie is issued from `/Account/Login`, the anti-forgery cookie from whatever page rendered
the form, and a path-scoped cookie would then be absent on the pages that need it. **`Domain` is left
`null` deliberately, which produces a host-only cookie**: the browser returns it to the exact host that
set it and to no subdomain. Setting a domain would widen every cookie in the inventory to every
subdomain of it, which this application has no use for — it is served at one host per environment
([06 §3.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) and generates no cross-subdomain link (the
`XForwardedHost` row of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) — and widening a session or
authentication cookie's scope for no requirement is the kind of change nobody notices until a
subdomain is delegated. There is a second, concrete reason to fix both values here: the temporary
legacy-cookie stage of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) can only delete a cookie by
matching the `Path` and `Domain` it was issued at, and **that stage's own definition — section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 3, which is where the attributes a deletion must
match are fixed and the only place they are — emits the deletion with `Path=/` and no `Domain`
attribute**, both halves derived there from the legacy configuration's own evidence rather than from a
runbook. So the target's own cookies are issued at exactly the scope the transition stage is written
against, and the two statements agree because one document makes both. The
local development case is handled by the host rather than by a key: the development server binds an HTTPS
endpoint and uses the development certificate — the artifact and the exact ports are
[04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, and the keys' place in this schema is the `Kestrel` entry
below — so an always-secure cookie is delivered locally too. That is a development-environment
requirement, not a configuration knob.

**`Session` — `SessionPolicyOptions`.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IdleTimeout` | `TimeSpan?`, bounded to 5 minutes – 4 hours | **`00:20:00`** | `TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20)` (`SessionOptions.IdleTimeout`) | **Preserved** — it equals both the target default and the source platform's own 20-minute session window, so an anonymous cart survives exactly as long as it does today |
| `CookieName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`MvcMusicStore.Session`** | `.AspNetCore.Session` (`SessionDefaults.CookieName`) | **Deliberate change** — the framework default is overridden, for the reason the application cookie's `Name` row gives, and the value is the one the closed inventory above publishes |

**Why the idle timeout is preserved rather than lengthened.** [06 §8.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
requires a session window "at least as long as a realistic shopping session", and the preserved window of
section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) satisfies it for the reason that is easy to miss:
**the cart rows are not in session.** Only the cart *key* is
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so an expired anonymous session orphans rows rather
than deleting a cart, which is the same outcome the source produces today and the same one section
[11](#11-the-cutover-decision) accepts at cutover. Lengthening the window would change behaviour, extend
the lifetime of a correlatable identifier and grow the cache table, for no preserved outcome.

**`IOTimeout` is left at the framework's `00:01:00`, and what it actually bounds is narrower than its name
suggests.** An earlier version of this paragraph described it as bounding "an individual cache read or
write", which is not what the option does. It is "the maximum amount of time allowed to load a session
from the store, or to commit it to the store", and the reference adds the qualification that matters:
**"this may only apply to asynchronous operations"** (`SessionOptions.IOTimeout`, API reference, ASP.NET
Core 8). So it bounds the session middleware's **asynchronous load and commit**, not each cache round trip
and not a synchronous property access. Three consequences, and the first is a requirement on application
code rather than on configuration:

| Consequence | What this design does about it |
| --- | --- |
| A synchronous `ISession` access loads the session **implicitly and synchronously** on first use, outside `IOTimeout`'s reach | **Every session access in this application is preceded by an explicit `await session.LoadAsync()`**, which the framework's own guidance requires for exactly this reason ("`ISession.LoadAsync` … must be awaited before `TryGetValue`, `Set` or `Remove`" — *Session and state management in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). It is a **single** call site: cart-id resolution belongs to the service of section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted), so the load is awaited there and nothing else in the application touches `ISession` at all — which is what makes "every access" a checkable statement rather than a hope |
| The **commit** is the other operation the bound covers, and the session middleware performs it asynchronously as the request completes | So the write path is bounded without any further requirement on application code. What the design must **not** do is treat that bound as a health signal. A session write carries the cart **key** and nothing else — the cart rows are in the database (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) — so a commit that exceeds the bound costs an anonymous visitor their key and destroys nothing that was paid for. Whether the database is sick is reported by section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)'s readiness checks, which is the one place that question is answered |
| What bounds the underlying **SQL** call is not this option | It is the provider's own connection and command behaviour against the same database the request is already using, under the resilience settings of section [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them). Setting `IOTimeout` to a hand-chosen value would therefore add a second, unrelated timeout to keep in step with those, which is why the framework's minute is kept |

**The test is the coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**: with the cache pointed at a
target that does not answer, a cart request completes with the load failing inside the bound rather than
hanging, and the request does **not** return a cart populated from a half-loaded session. Asserting a
timeout is only meaningful because the load is explicit — with an implicit synchronous load there is no
awaited operation for the option to bound and the test would be characterising the provider instead.

**Its other four attributes are code-set for the same reason**, and their values are section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)'s session-cookie-attributes row rather than this
contract's. One of the four is worth its own sentence here: the session cookie carries the **cart
identity** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], so a consent gate that suppressed it
would empty carts silently rather than degrade a feature — which makes **`IsEssential`** a factual claim
about this application, not a convenience.

**`Antiforgery` — `AntiforgeryPolicyOptions`.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HeaderName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`RequestVerificationToken`** | **Not asserted, and deliberately not relied on** — the value is written by `AddAntiforgery` either way | **Explicitly configured.** Neither preserved nor hardened: the source has no header-based anti-forgery at all, so there is no source value to preserve. What the contract guarantees is that **one literal is set in code and the client uses the same one** — the reason is the next paragraph |
| `CookieName` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`MvcMusicStore.Antiforgery`** | *derived, not fixed*: when no name is set, the framework assigns `".AspNetCore.Antiforgery." + Base64Url(SHA256(applicationName)[0..8])` (`AntiforgeryOptionsSetup`, .NET 8) | **Deliberate hardening** of a different kind — see below |

**The cookie name is set because the framework's default one is a function of a value this contract varies
per environment.** The derived default hashes `DataProtection:ApplicationName`, and that member
exists precisely so production and a slot differ (section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it)). Left derived, the anti-forgery
cookie would therefore be **named differently in every environment**, and any change to the discriminator
— a deliberate one, or a slot swap — would rename it, invalidating every in-flight form for reasons no
log would explain. An explicit literal makes the name a constant of the application, decouples it from a
value that is allowed to move, and leaves the discriminator doing only the job section 4.9 gives it.

**Its other four attributes are code-set, and one of them is the reason this cookie is listed in the
inventory above.** `SameSite=Strict`, `HttpOnly` on, `IsEssential` true — all three equal to the
framework's defaults, stated rather than inherited — and **`Secure` always**, which is *not*: this
cookie's framework default is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, the weakest in the set. `FormFieldName` is left
at the framework's `__RequestVerificationToken`, which is byte-for-byte the field name the source's own
`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` emits [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Login.cshtml:13], so the form
transport is preserved without a key.

**The header key exists to state the name once, not to vary it per environment.** Section
[7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form) sets `AntiforgeryOptions.HeaderName` from it
explicitly rather than leaving it implicit, and the **same literal is fixed on the client**
by section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script). So the two move together or cart removal breaks
in the one way that is hardest to see — a rejected POST whose only symptom is a row that does not
disappear. The key is therefore **not** placed in any environment overlay.

**One anti-forgery behaviour is code-set and belongs here because it collides with a header value this
document does not own.** `SuppressXFrameOptionsHeader` is set to **true**. The framework's anti-forgery
emits its own `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` on responses that carry a token, and
[06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) sets that header centrally, for every response, to a
different value. Suppressing the anti-forgery copy leaves **one** owner of the header and no
per-response divergence between a form page and every other page.

**`DataProtection` — `DataProtectionSettings`.** The discriminator is the one member in this section whose
*value* section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) does not publish either: it differs per
environment and is a platform setting, so [06 §8.4.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes it and
marks it slot-scoped. This contract owns the key, its type, its required-ness and the failure.

| Member | Declared as | Value | Framework default | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ApplicationName` | `string?`, `[Required]`, and validated non-whitespace | **Not stated here, deliberately** — the value differs per environment and is a platform setting, so [06 §8.4.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes it and marks it slot-scoped. This contract owns the key, its type, its required-ness and the failure | *derived*, not fixed: left unset, the framework derives a discriminator from the content-root path ([06 §8.4.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) | **Deliberate hardening**, and the one member in this contract whose absence has no runtime symptom at all |
| `KeyRotationPeriod` | `TimeSpan?`, `[Required]`, and validated by the one `IValidateOptions<DataProtectionSettings>` to be **at least 14 days and at most 365 days** | **Not stated here** — [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the rotation *policy* and publishes the value. This contract owns the key, its type, its bounds and its failure | `KeyManagementOptions.NewKeyLifetime`, 90 days — which is the framework's value for a mechanism this design **disables**, so it is a reference point rather than a fallback | **Deliberate change.** It becomes load-bearing because `DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration` (item 5 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) makes the custody service of section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof) the only writer; this is the `_rotationPeriod` its `CreateNewKey` calls pass. The lower bound exists because a period shorter than the ring's own propagation window would rotate faster than every instance can observe |
| `CustodyPassPeriod` | `TimeSpan?`, `[Required]`, and validated by the same rule to be **at least 1 hour**, **at most 12 hours**, and **strictly less than `KeyRotationPeriod`** | **Not stated here** — same division: the period is operational and [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes it | none; there is no framework analogue, because the framework has no periodic pass | **Net-new**, and required by the same disable. This is the `_passPeriod` of the custody service's `PeriodicTimer`. The two bounds are the ones the property table in section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof) derives: longer than the key-ring cache refresh so a pass observes the previous pass's write, and short enough that at least one pass falls inside the framework resolver's generation lead time |

It is the argument to `SetApplicationName` in section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it), it is what gives each
environment its own ring inside a shared store, and it is **configuration-backed rather than compiled
in** precisely so that a slot can differ from production without a rebuild
([06 §7.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), control 2). A silently absent discriminator is the
worst case in this contract: the application starts, issues cookies against a ring keyed by an inferred
name, and a staging slot may then decrypt production tickets. That is why it is fail-fast rather than
defaulted.

**`SqlIdentity` — `SqlIdentityOptions`. One member, and it is the value mode M1 above compares against.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ClientId` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — a conditionally required member, per the member-class rule above | **Not stated here** — it is one GUID per environment and per slot | **Platform configuration**, `SqlIdentity__ClientId` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), marked slot-scoped so a swap cannot move the staging identity's GUID onto production | All of it in the one `IValidateOptions<SqlIdentityOptions>`, which reads the selected connection mode. **Under M1: required, parseable as a `Guid`, and equal to the connection string's parsed `User Id`.** **Under M2 and M4: required to be absent** — those modes present no identity of their own, so a stray value fails the start rather than being ignored. **Under M3: not required and not compared**, because the identity in play is the *deployment* principal's rather than the site's: its client ID arrives inside the connection string's `User Id`, which the connection validator requires and parses as a `Guid`, and which principal actually connected is then asserted **at the database** by the `USER_NAME()` check of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) assertion 1 — a stronger statement than comparing a GUID against a second locally declared copy of it |

It is not a secret — a client ID names which identity to ask the platform's token endpoint for and
possessing it grants nothing ([06 §6.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) — which is why it may be
named in the failure record of the connection validation above.

**`Expected` — `ExpectedDeploymentOptions`. Four members, every one of them **deployment-supplied
configuration**, and **none of them compiled into the artifact**.**

That last point is the reason this section exists as configuration rather than as constants. The
published output is built once and promoted unchanged ([04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so
an expectation baked into the bytes would make one artifact valid in exactly one environment and destroy
the property the promotion model depends on. Each value below is declared once per environment, in the
same pipeline environment definition that declares [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s
`EXPECTED_*` variables, and delivered as a platform setting — so the release-time assertions and the
in-process assertions compare against one declaration rather than two.

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Environment` | `string?`, `[Required]` | The **deployment's** expected environment name — [06 §8.4.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the value, and it is `Production` on both slots of the production site | Platform setting `Expected__Environment` in every deployed environment; the committed Development overlay carries `Development`, which is the only environment whose expectation is committed and the only one the overlay is ever loaded in. For a tool invocation the same value arrives as `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` (section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a) | Non-whitespace; **equal to both `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` and `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT`**, which must themselves be present and agree — the rule section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 2a states and this key supplies the expected side of |
| `SqlServer` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, per the member-class rule above | The logical server's fully qualified name | Platform setting `Expected__SqlServer`; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_SQL_SERVER` | Non-whitespace, no scheme and no `,`-port suffix; compared against the parsed `DataSource` by the connection check above |
| `SqlDatabase` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, as above | The database name | Platform setting `Expected__SqlDatabase`; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_SQL_DATABASE` | Non-whitespace; compared against the parsed `InitialCatalog` |
| `DataProtectionDiscriminator` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, as above | The discriminator this slot is supposed to be running | Platform setting `Expected__DataProtectionDiscriminator`, supplied **by the release** for the slot being deployed; the same declaration as `EXPECTED_DISCRIMINATOR` | Non-whitespace; **equal to `DataProtection:ApplicationName`**. This comparison is deliberately labelled the **weaker** of the two that exist: both values reach the process as settings on the same site, so it detects a release that supplied one and not the other, and it cannot detect an operator who set both to the same wrong value. [06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s pre-traffic assertion, which compares the site's setting against the pipeline's variable from **outside** the process, is the authority; this is the in-process backstop that also covers the invocations no swap performs |

**`Telemetry` — `TelemetryOptions`. One member, and it is the only secret in this contract.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CartKeyHashSalt` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** — conditionally required, per the member-class rule above | **Not stated anywhere, in any document** — one value per environment | A **platform secret**: a slot-scoped App Service application setting or a Key Vault reference resolved by the site's identity ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). **It is never in `appsettings.json`, never in the Development overlay, and never baked into the artifact**; the Development value comes from user secrets, which is the mechanism source 3 of the precedence list exists for | Present and non-whitespace; decodes from base64 to **at least 32 bytes**, because a short salt is a salt an attacker can exhaust; the standing `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` check; and it is **excluded from every log record and every failure message** — a validation failure names the key and the rule it broke and nothing else |

It is consumed in exactly one place: the salted `cartKeyHash` that every cart-scoped record carries
instead of the cart key itself ([06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the hash's
construction and its truncation). The value is **per environment** so that a pseudonym from one
environment cannot be correlated with the same cart's pseudonym in another, and it is a secret for the
reason any keyed pseudonym's key is a secret: with the salt, the identifiers it protects are recoverable
by exhaustion, because the cart key's domain is small — a GUID or a username.

**`Site` — `SiteOptions`. Two members, each existing because a control in another document needs a value
from this one.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Source | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Hosts` | **`string?`, `[Required]`** — a **comma-separated scalar**, not an array; the validated collection is a separate `IReadOnlyList<string>` accessor | The host names this application is served at, per environment | The platform setting `Site__Hosts` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), slot-scoped, in every deployed environment; the Development overlay carries `localhost` | Splits on `,`, trims each element, discards empties, and requires **at least one** surviving entry; each entry a syntactically valid DNS host name with **no scheme, no port, no path and no wildcard**; duplicates after case-folding fail rather than being de-duplicated silently; compared ordinal case-insensitively where it is used |
| `PermittedImageOrigins` | **`string?`**, a comma-separated scalar, **no `[Required]`** — legal to omit in every environment, and the exception list at the end of this section counts it | The external image origins the administration write path and the content-security policy both permit | The platform setting `Site__PermittedImageOrigins` ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), slot-scoped, **which is its single owner**. It is **not** carried in any committed file: an empty platform value is the fail-closed state and the one [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records today | Splits and trims as above, and an **empty or absent value is legal and reads as the empty list**. Each surviving entry an absolute **`https`** origin — scheme, host and optional port, with no path, query or fragment. `http`, protocol-relative, `data:`, `javascript:` and `file:` entries **fail the start** rather than being filtered at use, so a widened list cannot smuggle a scheme past the write-path validator |

`Hosts` has exactly **one** consumer, and naming it is worth a sentence because an earlier form of this
section claimed two. That form gave the second to a content-security-policy report collector's
foreign-document check; the collector is withdrawn in full ([06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
settles the report-only phase as a manually walked browser gate with no reporting destination, and section
[7.1](#71-the-policy) records the consequence for the anti-forgery register), so no CSP mechanism reads this
member at all. The one consumer is **host filtering**, below. It is also worth stating what `Hosts` is *not*:
it is not an input to the policy text of [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), which is
`self`-based and admits off-origin content only through `PermittedImageOrigins`.

**Both members are comma-separated scalars rather than arrays, and that is a correction rather than a
preference.** The environment-variable provider binds an array only from **indexed** keys — `Site__Hosts__0`,
`Site__Hosts__1` — so a `string[]` member and a platform setting holding `store.example.com,www.example.com`
do not meet: the scalar binds to **no** element of the array, the array stays empty, and a `[Required]`
attribute on a non-null empty array passes. The result is a validated-looking member with nothing in it.
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declares both settings in the **scalar, comma-separated**
form, so this contract takes the value as a scalar and does the splitting itself. Two properties follow.
The delimiter is this document's: it is a `,`, and it is **not** the `;` the framework's own `AllowedHosts`
key uses, because that key is not read at all (below). And the split is **validated rather than tolerant** —
an entry that fails its per-entry rule fails the start, so a mistyped setting is a failed deployment
rather than a silently narrowed policy.

**`Site:PermittedImageOrigins` has exactly one owner, and it is the platform setting.** An earlier version
of this section put the list in the committed `appsettings.json` while
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declared a slot-scoped platform setting of the same name —
two owners for one control, with the committed file losing every time (it sits at precedence layer 1 and
the platform setting at layer 4) and a reviewer reading the wrong one. The platform setting wins on the
merits as well as on precedence: it is slot-scoped, so a staging slot cannot widen production's policy,
which is the property [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) needs and a committed file cannot
provide. The committed files carry no `Site` section at all.

**The validated host list is wired into host filtering, which is the mechanism that makes it enforceable
rather than merely declared.** The default web host **already registers the host-filtering middleware**, at
the very start of the pipeline through an `IStartupFilter`, and fills `HostFilteringOptions.AllowedHosts`
from the `AllowedHosts` configuration key **only when the list is otherwise empty**, falling back to `*` —
allow everything — when that key is absent too (`WebHost.ConfigureWebDefaults`, ASP.NET Core 8 source).
That default is the state this contract must not leave in place, and the wiring is **one** registration
statement, whose contract is the **four** rows below. The lead-in read "three statements", which described
neither the single statement in the first row nor the rows that follow it, so it is corrected here with
the arithmetic in place: 1 statement, 3 rows of contract plus the never-record compatibility row added
later = **4**:

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| How the list gets there | `services.AddOptions<HostFilteringOptions>().Configure<IOptions<SiteOptions>>((o, site) => o.AllowedHosts = site.Value.HostList)` — section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 12, the forwarded-headers and host-integrity registration. The dependency-taking overload is used deliberately: the list is not available at registration time — it is produced by the validated options type, which resolves after the container is built — so a delegate closing over a value read during registration would close over nothing. `Configure` delegates run **before** every `PostConfigure` delegate, and the framework's fallback is a `PostConfigure` that acts only on an empty list, so an explicitly set list is never overwritten and the `*` fallback is unreachable |
| What is **not** used | The `AllowedHosts` configuration key. It is left unset in every file and every environment, so there is exactly one declaration of the host set: `Site__Hosts`. Setting both would be two owners again, with a `;`-delimited spelling beside a `,`-delimited one |
| What a non-matching request gets | The middleware's own response: **400** with no body, and the framework's own record naming the rejected host. The application writes nothing of its own, because the request never reaches any stage of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)'s pipeline — host filtering runs ahead of all of them |
| Whether that record is compatible with the never-record list | **Yes, and it is worth stating rather than assuming.** A `Host` header value is a routing input, not a credential, a session identifier or customer data — none of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s prohibited categories — and the platform's own HTTP log carries the same host on every request anyway ([06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). What the rule does forbid is the application **adding** anything to this path: no record of its own, and specifically nothing carrying the rejected request's cookies, query or body, none of which the application ever sees on it |

**One operational obligation follows and it belongs to the setting's value rather than to this code**: the
list must contain **every** host name that reaches the application, including the platform-assigned default
hostname and whatever host header the platform's own probes present, or a probe is answered with a 400 and
the instance is reported unhealthy. **Two** of the two probe paths are exempted from HTTPS redirection
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 6) and from nothing else — no path is
exempt from HSTS, whose item is gated on the environment rather than on the path — while **no** probe
path is exempt from host filtering, and none can be: the middleware runs before any
application-registered stage. The value is
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; the requirement on it is this document's.

**The test is the coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**: a request carrying a `Host`
header on the list is served normally; a request carrying one that is not gets **400** and no body; and the
two probe paths answer only under a listed host. The negative half is the half that matters — with the
framework's `*` fallback in force every one of those requests succeeds, so a positive-only test passes a
configuration that filters nothing.

`PermittedImageOrigins` is the same list twice over by construction, which is the requirement `D-38` of
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) carries: the administration write path validates
`AlbumArtUrl` against it, and if it is ever non-empty the `img-src` origins of
[06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s policy are composed **from this member** rather than
written out a second time. Validation and policy cannot then drift apart, which is the failure a second
copy would eventually produce. **The allow-list carries no approved-delta row**, and the third excluded
class of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) states why: it is a control closing an
exposure this document identifies, owned by this section rather than by an approver.

**`Seeding` — `SeedingOptions`. Read by the seeding command; validated everywhere.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Absence | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Enabled` | `bool?` | **`false`** in `appsettings.json`, and in no other committed file — the Development overlay carries no such key, per the file scoping at the end of this section | **Legal, and read as `false`** — the only member in this contract where absence is a decision rather than an omission, because `false` is the fail-closed value | **Deliberate hardening** — the source seeds unconditionally at startup [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/SampleData.cs:9] |
| `AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` | `string?` | **Not committed for any environment.** The seeding invocation supplies it, and section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) states the pattern it must match | **Legal only while `Enabled` is `false`.** Absent with `Enabled` true fails validation | **Deliberate hardening** — no such concept exists in the source |

**Why `Enabled` is `bool?` even though absence is legal.** The nullable declaration is not about
rejecting absence here; it is about distinguishing `false` *supplied* from `false` *assumed*, which is
what lets the validator apply the second rule below without guessing. The accessor the guard reads is a
non-nullable `bool` that is `false` when the member is null.

These are checks 2 and 3 of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) expressed
as keys. Two rules make them a guard rather than a switch. **`Enabled` set to true while the environment
is Production fails the start** — in the web application as well as in the command, because a deployed
configuration that authorizes seeding is itself the misconfiguration section 5.4 is defending against,
and refusing to start is the loud version of that discovery. And **`AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` is
required whenever `Enabled` is true**, a cross-member rule rather than an attribute on one property, so
"enabled with no allow-list" cannot exist.

**`Diagnostics` — `DiagnosticsOptions`. One member, and its absence is its production value.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Absence | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `InstanceEndpointEnabled` | `bool?`, **no `[Required]`** | **Not committed in either file** — no entry in `appsettings.json` and none in the Development overlay. The only place it is ever `true` is the platform setting `Diagnostics__InstanceEndpointEnabled`, set on a staging slot or a non-production revision for the duration of [06 §8.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s verification and removed by that procedure's own teardown ([06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) | **Legal, and read as `false`** — the fail-closed value, and with it false the route of section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint) is not mapped at all | **Net-new.** The source has no diagnostic endpoint and no switch of any kind, so there is nothing to preserve or harden |

**One name, and the condition compares against `true` rather than reading the member as a `bool`.** The
bound member and the configuration key carry **the same name** — `Diagnostics:InstanceEndpointEnabled`
binds to `DiagnosticsOptions.InstanceEndpointEnabled`, and there is **no second, differently named
accessor**. An earlier form of this document declared the key one way and had the mapping read a member
whose name differed from it by an inserted `Is`; that spelling is **withdrawn**, and why it mattered is worth one sentence: a
bound name that does not match its key neither fails to build nor fails validation — it simply never
receives the value, so the gate reads its unset default and the route is mapped, or left unmapped,
contrary to the setting an operator actually supplied. As with `Seeding:Enabled` above, the declaration
stays `bool?` so that `false` *supplied* and `false` *assumed* remain distinguishable, and the endpoint
mapping therefore reads `….Value.InstanceEndpointEnabled == true` (section
[2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint)'s excerpt) — an
expression that is `false` for both a supplied `false` and an absent value, which is the fail-closed
reading this member needs. Using the member **directly** as the condition does not compile: the pinned SDK
rejects it with `error CS0266: Cannot implicitly convert type 'bool?' to 'bool'`, which is worth stating
because a mapping condition is exactly the place the shorter form looks correct.

**One validation rule, and it is the standing one rather than a new kind.** The type carries no
`[Required]` and no cross-member rule — there is no second member for one to relate to — but it is bound
with `ValidateDataAnnotations()` and `ValidateOnStart()` like every other type above, so a **malformed**
value fails the **start**: `ValidateOnStart` forces the options instance to be produced during start, which
is when a value that is not a boolean fails to bind. The distinction that matters operationally is that
*absent* is legal and *unparseable* is not, so a setting typed `Ture` stops the host rather than quietly
leaving the route closed and looking as though the switch had been honoured.

**Why nothing is committed here, when `Seeding:Enabled` commits its `false`.** The two differ in who
supplies the true value and where a wrong one does damage. `Seeding:Enabled` is read by an **operator
command** whose configuration a reviewer inspects, so a committed `false` puts the fail-closed value in the
file that command loads. This member is read only by the web host's endpoint mapping, is supplied by exactly
one platform setting on exactly one non-production deployment unit, and is removed again when the
verification closes — and absence and `false` produce the identical unmapped route, so a committed `false`
would add a third place to look and change nothing.
[06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s row records the key as platform-supplied and never set on
production; this is the type side of that same fact.

**`Ingress` — `IngressOptions`. Three members: one required literal, and two that are required to be
absent.**

| Member | Declared as | Value | Absence | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TrustMode` | `string?`, `[Required]` | **`ProvenExclusiveIngress`** — the single recognized literal, committed in `appsettings.json` because it is invariant across environments and across both hosting targets, and therefore needs no platform setting | **Fails the start.** So does an empty value | The single `IValidateOptions<IngressOptions>` compares the value against the one literal with `StringComparison.Ordinal` and fails on anything else, **including a re-introduced `EnumeratedRanges`** — adding a second mode is a change to section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 12, not a value an operator can supply |
| `TrustedNetworks` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** | **Withdrawn. Committed nowhere, and legal in no environment** | **Absence is the only legal state**, and it is what every deployed environment resolves to | The same validator **fails the start when the member is non-null**, empty string included. It is declared rather than simply unread because a key nobody binds is a key nobody can refuse: binding it is what turns a re-introduced value into a failed start instead of a silently ignored setting |
| `TrustedProxies` | `string?`, **no `[Required]`** | **Withdrawn**, on the same terms | Same | Same rule, expressed per address |

**Why two withdrawn keys are members of a type rather than absent from this contract.** The trust list they
belonged to has no correct value on either hosting target, so
[06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) withdraws the enumerated-range mode in full and requires
that **a resolved value for either key stops the application** — its rotation gate then re-reads both names
on every release and fails the release on the same condition. That requirement cannot be met by omitting
the names from this section: an unbound key is inert, and the configuration providers would resolve it
happily while the composition ignored it, which is precisely the state a reviewer would mistake for the
withdrawn model still being honoured. Declaring both as members keeps the enforcement inside this section's
one-validator-per-type rule, and keeps section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 12 free of any direct `IConfiguration` read.

**These three members are the exception to the "absent key fails the start" rule below, and they are
counted there rather than here** — `TrustMode` under the rule itself, and the two withdrawn names in the
class the exception table adds for them.

**`Logging` — the framework's schema for the filtering, and `LoggingPolicyOptions` for the assertion.**
The filtering is the framework's: it reads `Logging:LogLevel:<category>` itself, and nothing this document
adds changes that. What is missing without this table is the thing a reviewer needs — **which categories
are named, and at what level, in which environment**. [06 §9.2.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
owns *why* each level is required, and the release-side expected values it asserts are
[06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; this table is the configuration that satisfies them.

<a id="the-one-category-level-table"></a>
**This is the one category-level table in this document, and it is closed.** Every level for every
category appears here and in no other table: an earlier revision published a **second** level column, in
section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s suppression table, and the two disagreed in
four places — `Default` at `Information` here against `Warning` there, and
`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` at
`Warning`/`Information` here against **`None`** there — while the validator below simultaneously forbade
any key from being `None` and forbade any key that is not in this table, which made every `None` row of
that table doubly illegal. **The suppression table's levels are withdrawn**; it keeps what only it has —
what each channel would otherwise disclose and what carries the diagnostic instead — and reads its levels
from here. Where a value here and a value in [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) controls 1 and
5 ever disagree, **06 governs**, and this table is the `appsettings` expression of those controls rather
than a second authority over them.

| Key | Type | `appsettings.json` — the value every deployed environment gets | `appsettings.Development.json` override | Category it filters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Default` | `LogLevel` | **`Warning`** | none | Everything not matched more specifically. **`Warning`, not `Information`** — 06 control 1's baseline, and the value that makes each specific row below a decision rather than a partial measure |
| `Logging:LogLevel:MvcMusicStore` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | **`Debug`** | The application's own namespace — the root namespace of `src/MvcMusicStore`, so every controller, service and view component. Its records are the closed record of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and the event classes of section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic), all sanitized at the producer |
| `Logging:LogLevel:MvcMusicStore.Security.Events` | `LogLevel` | `Information`, **pinned explicitly** | none | The reserved security-event category. **The spelling is [06 §9.6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) entry 3's and is reproduced literally rather than described**, because a configuration key is not executable as a description — an earlier form of this row carried the placeholder *"the reserved security-event category"* in the key position, which no `appsettings.json` can contain. The pin's whole purpose is that a later tightening of `Default` or of the `MvcMusicStore` parent cannot silently drop an audit record, which is effective only because the longest-prefix rule below makes the more specific rule win |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | **`Information`** | Framework request plumbing, and the floor the two `None` sub-category rows below tighten further |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | none | Model-binding and filter diagnostics. Held at `Warning` rather than closed, because nothing at or above that level carries an exception object |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | none | A rejected token. Below `Warning` it narrates every validation; the 400 the filter returns needs no record of its own |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity` | `LogLevel` | `Information` | none | Identity's own user and password operations. It is **not** closed, and the reason is that it passes no exception object at this level — its records carry outcomes and, in the actor position, a user id, which is one of the exactly two values permitted there |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | none | The parent authentication category. **The row that would report a cookie the application cannot decrypt is the handler's, `…Authentication.Cookies`, and that one is closed below** — an earlier form of this row claimed the undecryptable-cookie record for itself at `Information`, which the closure of the longer category makes false under the longest-prefix rule |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | Cookie decryption and validation failures **with the exception attached**, in bulk at cutover when every legacy ticket is undecryptable (section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)) |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | The unhandled exception object for every 500, `ToString()`-expanded with every inner message — and the developer-exception-page middleware in the same category, which is why the parent is pinned rather than the handler sub-category alone |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.Diagnostics` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | The same exception object on any path where no handler is reached — the case the row above does not cover |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | `ApplicationError` and connection-level failures at `Error`, each carrying the exception object, including faults raised after the response has started |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | Key-ring records carrying key material and key identifiers, and unprotect failures with the exception attached — the channel every protected cart marker, anti-forgery token and authentication cookie failure would surface through |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | Key-ring resolution and default-key selection. It is closed rather than left at `Information` **because leaving it open would reopen its `None` parent for the longest-prefix reason below**, and because its own records carry the exception on a read failure |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` | `LogLevel` | `Warning` | none | The EF parent. The pin is what stops the rest of the EF tree from reaching `Information`; the three sub-categories that carry exceptions or command text are closed individually below |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | **`Information`** | Both of its levels are channels rather than one: `Information` echoes command text with parameter placeholders, and `Error` carries the failing command **and** the exception. **The Development override is legal precisely because this column is scoped to Development** — the deployed value is `None` and nothing may relax it there |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Update` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | `DbUpdateException` and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` objects, whose inner provider text names the constraint and frequently the offending value |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Query` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | Query-execution failures with the provider exception attached. **Beyond 06 control 5's enumeration and deliberately retained**: that control states no list of framework categories is provably complete, so pinning one it does not name is never a conflict with it |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | Provider-level connection, retry and command diagnostics. An earlier form held it at `Warning` on the reasoning that provider text reaches the log only through the EF categories above — not a property the provider guarantees, and 06 control 5 names this category among those closed |
| `Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks` | `LogLevel` | **`None`** | none | The health-check service logs each failed result **with the result's `Exception`** — which is why stage 1 item 11 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) replaces `AddDbContextCheck<T>`, whose result carries one. A probe failure recurs every few seconds, so an open channel here is the highest-volume disclosure in the application |

**Twenty keys: eleven closed at `None`, six at `Warning`, three at `Information`.** 11 + 6 + 3 = 20, and
the three Development overrides are `MvcMusicStore` → `Debug`, `Microsoft.AspNetCore` → `Information` and
`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` → `Information`.

**`None` rather than `Warning` wherever a channel writes its exception-carrying entries at `Error`**, which
no minimum-level threshold short of `None` suppresses. That is the single mechanical reason eleven rows
read `None`, and it is why the validator below cannot forbid `None` outright.

**Several rows only work because of how the framework selects a rule, and the mechanism is worth stating
because the table looks self-contradictory without it.** `Microsoft.AspNetCore` is at `Warning` while two
categories beneath it are at `Information` and five are at `None`; `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` is at
`Warning` while three beneath it are at `None`. None of that is a contradiction: for each provider the
factory "select[s] rules with longest matching category prefix… If multiple rules are selected, take the
last one" (*Logging in .NET*, .NET 8). So `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies` wins over both
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication` and `Microsoft.AspNetCore` for the cookie handler's logger, and
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement` wins over `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection`. The
corollary is the one that decides two rows above: **a sub-category left more verbose than its closed
parent reopens the parent for that logger**, which is why `…DataProtection.KeyManagement` is `None` rather
than `Information` and why the undecryptable-cookie claim moved off the parent authentication row.

**This enumeration is not the closure, and saying so is not a hedge.** 06 control 5 states explicitly
that a list of framework categories cannot be proven complete. The closure is therefore its redaction test
together with the coverage assertion of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — asserted against the **entire** captured stream rather
than against these twenty categories — so a channel missing from this table fails that row rather than
passing unnoticed.

**What the data-protection rows do and do not establish — enumerated rather than assumed, because an
earlier version of this table claimed a record the framework does not emit.** The claim removed from the
first row was "a failure to persist a key", and the correction matters operationally rather than
pedantically: that is precisely the record an operator would search for after a key-ring incident, and
searching for a record nothing writes is how a silently non-durable ring survives a review. Each row below
was established by exercising the case on the pinned 8.0 line — a key repository that throws on store, one
that throws on read, a key file deleted between two hosts, and a cookie replayed after its key was gone —
and reading the category, level and event name of every record produced. **The third column asks one
question: does the record survive the table above?** Every category in this enumeration except the last
sits beneath row 15's `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection`, which is pinned to **`None`**, and no rule
names any of them more specifically — so for those the answer is *no* at any level the record is written
at, which is the register's decision and not a gap in it:

| What happens | The record, and the level it is written at | Reaches the log under section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A key is created | `…KeyManagement.XmlKeyManager` / `CreatingKey`, **`Information`** — written **before** the repository is asked to store anything, so its presence says a key was *minted*, not that it was *saved* | **No.** Its category is `…DataProtection.KeyManagement`, closed at `None` |
| The ring cannot be **read**, the absent-table case of section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) | `…KeyManagement.KeyRingProvider` / `ErrorOccurredWhileReadingKeyRing`, **`Error`**, and `…DataProtection.Internal.DataProtectionHostedService` / `KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup`, **`Information`** — both carrying the exception | **No.** `KeyRingProvider` is `…KeyManagement` and `DataProtectionHostedService` is under `…DataProtection`; both are closed at `None`. **This was the one failure an earlier form of this column called well covered**, and it is not covered at all |
| The repository **fails to store** a new key | **No named persistence event exists.** What appears is the same generic `ErrorOccurredWhileReadingKeyRing` at `Error`, whose text says *reading* although the operation was a write, and only at the moment the ring is first needed rather than at startup | **No**, and doubly so: the record is misleading *and* its category is closed |
| The repository is the **wrong one** — keys landing on instance-local storage because the intended registration was not the one in force | **Nothing.** Whichever repository resolved logs an ordinary *success* record for the write it performed, so the healthy-looking case and the ephemeral-key case are indistinguishable from the log | **No** — nothing is written, so no level could carry it |
| The ring loads successfully at startup | `…DataProtectionHostedService` / `KeyRingWasLoadedOnStartup`, **`Debug`** | **No.** `Debug` is below every floor, and its category is closed above that besides |
| No XML encryptor is configured, so keys are stored without an envelope | `…XmlKeyManager` / `NoXMLEncryptorConfiguredKeyMayBePersistedToStorageInUnencryptedForm`, **`Warning`** | **No.** Closed with its category — which is the right outcome rather than a loss, since section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) records that an explicit repository disables automatic at-rest protection deliberately and [06 §7.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) supplies transparent data encryption instead, so the warning is expected and needs no channel |
| A key **rotates**, or fails to rotate on schedule | **No record of either.** Rotation is a property of key ages, and the framework reports ages nowhere | **No** — nothing is written |
| A cookie cannot be decrypted | `…KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector` / `KeyWasNotFoundInTheKeyRingUnprotectOperationCannotProceed` is **`Trace`**; what actually surfaces is `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies.CookieAuthenticationHandler` / `AuthenticationSchemeNotAuthenticatedWithFailure` at **`Information`**, reading *"Cookies was not authenticated. Failure message: Unprotect ticket failed"* | **No.** The `Trace` record is below every floor, and the record that would otherwise surface belongs to `…Authentication.Cookies`, which is closed at `None`. **The authentication row an earlier form of this column pointed at no longer carries it**, which is why that parent row’s text was corrected in section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) too |

**So the `KeyRingStatus` heartbeat is not the best of several data-protection signals — it is the only one**,
and that is the reason it is a registration in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 15 rather than a remark somewhere. The arithmetic
over the eight rows is exact. **Two** of the eight write nothing at all — a ring persisted to the wrong
place, and rotation that has quietly stopped, which are precisely the two states an alert has to catch. The
other **six** write something, and one of those six writes a record that is actively misleading, reporting a
failed *write* as a failed *read* and only at first use. And all **six** land in
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection`, its `KeyManagement` subcategory or
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies`, every one of which the table in section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) pins to `None` — so under the deployed configuration the third
column above is `No` for all eight, and 2 + 6 = 8 leaves no row reaching a retained sink by another route.

**Raising those three categories is not the remedy, which is why the heartbeat is load-bearing rather than
convenient.** The records they carry are the ones section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)
closes for a CWE-532 reason: key identifiers and key-ring detail on the two `DataProtection` categories, and
an unprotect-failure message on the cookie category that names the failure mode of a security token. Opening
them to recover a rotation alert would readmit that disclosure into a retained sink and still not produce the
two records that do not exist. The heartbeat's fields are instead chosen to make each silent state visible
positively: the repository type actually in use answers the wrong-repository row, and the newest key's age
answers the rotation row. [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the alerting built on it, which
is an alert on the record's **absence** — sound only because the application emits the record
unconditionally, and sound *only* because nothing else in this table could carry the signal.

**The production values live in the base file, not in a `Production` overlay.** `appsettings.json` carries
the deployed levels and `appsettings.Development.json` relaxes exactly one of them — row 2, the
application's own category, to `Debug` — so a staging slot and production get the same levels without a
third file to keep in step, and no environment can end up *more* verbose than production by omission. **No
`None` pin is relaxed in any environment, Development included**, which is why the two overrides an earlier
form of the table declared are gone: `Microsoft.AspNetCore` was never a register key, and
`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` at `Information` is the CWE-532 relaxation
[06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids a consumer from making at all. A developer who
needs command text takes it from the local database's own diagnostics, not by editing a register value. `appsettings.Production.json` is not created — the file set is
the two files this section ends by scoping, and the rule is stated once, in full, where that scoping is.

**It is validated at start, and the validation deliberately does no filtering.** `LoggingPolicyOptions`
binds the same `Logging:LogLevel` section as a `Dictionary<string, LogLevel?>` and asserts six things
under `ValidateOnStart`, then is never read again:

1. **Every one of the twenty keys above is present.** A missing key is not a missing value — it is a
   category that silently falls back to `Default`, which for the three `Information` rows means being
   filtered by the `Warning` baseline instead, and for the eleven closed rows means being **reopened** at
   `Warning`, exception object included.
2. **A key is `None` exactly where the table says `None`, and nowhere else.** This is the check an
   earlier form of this list got backwards: it read "**no key is `None`**", on the reasoning that a
   silenced category is an unobservable failure — which is sound for a category whose records are
   diagnostics and false for one whose records are an exception object the disclosure policy forbids. Both
   directions are therefore errors and both are checked. A category the table closes and configuration
   leaves open is a CWE-532 channel; a category the table leaves open and configuration closes is the
   unobservable failure the earlier reasoning was about, and the two most tempting to silence are the two
   whose failures are otherwise invisible ([06 §9.2.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). **What
   replaces the blanket rule is the diagnostic obligation that made it attractive**: no category may be
   closed without a named replacement signal, and section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s suppression table carries exactly that — **a row for
   every one of the eleven categories this table closes**, stating what it would otherwise disclose and
   **what carries the diagnostic instead**, alongside six rows for categories that stay open and record why
   no closure is needed. That table publishes the arithmetic against this one. It is the half of the blanket
   rule worth keeping, and the reason that table survives with its levels removed rather than being deleted
   outright.
3. **No key is more restrictive than the value above.** The values are *floors* in that direction: a
   category may not be made quieter than the table, and validation says so rather than trusting a review.
4. **Outside Development, no key may be more verbose than the value above either — the table is
   *exact*, not a minimum.** This is stricter than an earlier version of this list, which made every
   value a minimum and permitted a deployment to relax any category upward, and the relaxation it
   permitted was not hypothetical: raising
   `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` from `Warning` to **`Information`** in a deployed
   environment emits command text **and parameter values** — order rows, addresses, email addresses — into
   a store [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) retains for 90 days, which is CWE-532 performed
   by a configuration edit no code review sees. A separate check for `Trace` and `Debug` is redundant and
   is folded in here: outside Development **no** deviation in either direction is legal, at any level, for
   any category.
5. **Development may differ from the table in the override column and nowhere else.** Exactly one key
   carries an override, and Development is legal only if its resolved dictionary is the table with that one
   substitution applied. It may not relax a second key, and above all it may not relax a `None` pin —
   [06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids a consumer from loosening a register entry, and
   a local relaxation of a closed channel is how a `None` pin arrives in a deployed `appsettings` by being
   copied.
6. **`Logging:LogLevel` is a closed set over the table's key list, in every environment including
   Development.** An unlisted category is how a relaxation arrives without touching a listed value:
   `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` at `Information` would raise the command category **by prefix** under
   the longest-match rule above, without the command category's own key changing at all — and the same edit
   with `Microsoft.AspNetCore` would raise every framework category the register does not name
   individually. So adding a category means editing this table, which means raising it against
   [06 §9.6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md).

A failure names the key and the two levels — or, for check 6, the unlisted key — and it echoes no log
content, because none has been written yet.

**The levels decide what is written. They do not decide whether it arrives as a record or as a sentence —
and on one of the two hosting targets that difference decides whether the fields are queryable at all.**
[06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) routes the container path's `stdout` and `stderr` to a
Log Analytics workspace, where each line arrives as a **text field**. The default console formatter writes
`Information: MvcMusicStore.Services.ShoppingCartService[0] Order 1043 placed…` — a human sentence, from
which `orderId` is recoverable only by a regular expression that breaks the next time the message template
is edited. So the emission format is part of this contract:

**`AddJsonConsole` is the console formatter, configured explicitly.** Registered as
`builder.Logging.AddJsonConsole(o => { … })`, replacing the default `simple` formatter rather than
supplementing it, so exactly one representation leaves the process:

| `JsonConsoleFormatterOptions` member | Value | Why this value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `JsonWriterOptions.Indented` | **`false`** | **The one option that cannot be wrong.** The formatter writes the object through a `Utf8JsonWriter` constructed with `FormatterOptions.JsonWriterOptions` and then writes a single `Environment.NewLine` (`JsonConsoleFormatter.Write`, .NET 8 source), so indented output would span many lines and the collector would ingest each **line** as a separate record — turning one event into a dozen unparseable fragments |
| `IncludeScopes` | **`true`** | Scopes are written only when it is set: `WriteScopeInformation` begins `if (FormatterOptions.IncludeScopes && scopeProvider != null)` and then emits a `Scopes` array of objects carrying each scope's key/value pairs (same source). This is what carries the hosting scope's request identifier and path onto every record written during a request, without any call site having to pass them |
| `TimestampFormat` | **`"O"`** — the round-trip format | The formatter writes a `Timestamp` property **only if `TimestampFormat` is non-null**, and its default is null (same source), so the default output has no timestamp of its own and relies entirely on the collector's ingestion time. `"O"` is unambiguous and sorts lexically |
| `UseUtcTimestamp` | **`true`** | The formatter chooses `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` over `.Now` on exactly this flag (same source). A container's local time zone is not a fact worth depending on |

**One member of the provider rather than the formatter, and silence on it would have selected the wrong
value.** `AddJsonConsole`'s options object configures the *formatter*; the console provider's own queue is
configured through **`ConsoleLoggerOptions`**, and its `QueueFullMode` default is **`Wait`** — the writing
thread blocks until the queue drains. Blocking is inadmissible here for a reason this document states
elsewhere as a property: [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s emission contract requires that a
failure to write a record cannot alter, delay or block the returned result, and a blocking queue does
exactly that *inside* the `ILogger` call, on a condition a caller can reach — a burst of authentication
failures, each of which is a required record. So the provider is registered with
**`QueueFullMode = ConsoleLoggerQueueFullMode.DropWrite`** and **`MaxQueueLength` left at its default of
2,500 entries**, which is what gives the loss window a number instead of a hope. **The enum's name is
`ConsoleLoggerQueueFullMode`, and an earlier form of this block wrote it with the `Console` prefix
dropped**: no type of that shorter name exists on the pinned surface, so the earlier form did not compile
— the SDK rejects it with `error CS0103: The name … does not exist in the current context`, verified
against the pinned runtime both ways round. The member set is
`Wait` and `DropWrite`, both under
`Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Console`, which is the namespace `ConsoleLoggerOptions` itself lives in, so
the one `using` the registration already needs covers both names.

| Where it is set | `builder.Logging.AddJsonConsole(…)` configures the formatter; the queue is set on the provider, `builder.Logging.Services.Configure<ConsoleLoggerOptions>(o => { o.QueueFullMode = ConsoleLoggerQueueFullMode.DropWrite; })`, in the same stage |
| --- | --- |
| **What a drop costs** | The dropped line, and nothing else. The drop is silent to the process — which is precisely why it cannot alter a response — so it is **not** detected by the producer. It is detected by the arrival gates and the canary of [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) statement (c) and by [06 §9.2.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s absence rules, and the window is the accepted loss statement (d) already records |
| **What it does not license** | A record whose loss is unacceptable does not get a bigger queue; it gets a second, non-console channel — and this design has none, which is the residual [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) raises rather than absorbs |

**What the record actually contains — stated as the literal payload, because every field this contract
promises has to be reachable from the far end and three of them are not where a reader would expect.**
The record below is a **captured record** from the pinned runtime with exactly the four options above set,
emitted from inside a request; only the identifier values and the request path are substituted for this
document's checkout example. It is shown indented for readability — on the wire it is **one line**, which
is what the `Indented` row above is for.

```json
{
  "Timestamp": "2026-08-29T14:24:00.0391819+00:00",
  "EventId": 0,
  "LogLevel": "Information",
  "Category": "MvcMusicStore.Services.ShoppingCartService",
  "Message": "OrderPlaced: order 1043, trace b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
  "State": {
    "Message": "OrderPlaced: order 1043, trace b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
    "eventName": "OrderPlaced",
    "orderId": 1043,
    "traceId": "b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
    "{OriginalFormat}": "{eventName}: order {orderId}, trace {traceId}"
  },
  "Scopes": [
    {
      "Message": "SpanId:2ce2035e27690aef, TraceId:b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840, ParentId:f5878ff76295d93b",
      "SpanId": "2ce2035e27690aef",
      "TraceId": "b1e0c2992a4f678b298d15039fb53840",
      "ParentId": "f5878ff76295d93b"
    },
    { "Message": "ConnectionId:0HNO5R4LID6IK", "ConnectionId": "0HNO5R4LID6IK" },
    {
      "Message": "RequestPath:/Checkout/AddressAndPayment RequestId:0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001",
      "RequestId": "0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001",
      "RequestPath": "/Checkout/AddressAndPayment"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Property | Where it is | What writes it, and what a query has to do with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Timestamp` | Top level | The formatter, **only because `TimestampFormat` is set** — its default is null and the property is then absent altogether (row 3 above). Read directly |
| `EventId` | Top level, **a number** | The formatter, from `logEntry.EventId.Id`. It is **`0` on every record whose call site passes no event id**, which is every record in this application, so it is **not a discriminator** and nothing may key on it |
| `LogLevel`, `Category`, `Message` | Top level, strings | The formatter. `Message` is the **formatted** text, so it is human-readable and not a field set. Read directly; filter on `Category` and `LogLevel`, never parse `Message` |
| `Exception` | Top level, **a string**, present only where an exception was passed | The formatter, from `exception.ToString()` — type, message, inner exceptions and stack trace in **one escaped string**, not a structured object. A query reading `Exception.Message` or `Exception.Type` finds nothing; and because the whole `ToString()` lands in the sink, the exclusion list of [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) applies to exception **messages** as much as to log messages |
| `State` | **Nested object** | The formatter, from the log state: the formatted `Message`, **one property per named placeholder in the message template**, and `{OriginalFormat}` carrying the template itself. **Every field this application contributes is here and nowhere else** |
| `Scopes` | **Array of objects**, present only because `IncludeScopes` is `true` | The framework, not the application — three of them inside a request: an **activity** scope carrying `TraceId`, `SpanId` and `ParentId` (the logging libraries "implicitly create a scope object with `SpanId`, `TraceId`, and `ParentId`", enabled by default through `ActivityTrackingOptions` — *Logging in .NET Core and ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8); Kestrel's `ConnectionId` scope; and the hosting scope carrying `RequestPath` and `RequestId`. A query reaches these only by indexing into the array |

**Three fields a query will look for at the top level and not find — and each one fails by matching
nothing rather than by erroring, which is why this is stated as a shape rather than left to discovery.**

- **`EventId.Name`.** The formatter writes the numeric id only, so a *named* `EventId` puts the name
  nowhere in the payload — verified by emitting `new EventId(4711, "OrderPlacedNamedEventId")` and reading
  back `"EventId": 4711` with the name absent.
- **A top-level `eventName`.** It is a message-template property, so it is at **`State.eventName`**.
- **A top-level `TraceId` or `SpanId`.** Both exist only **inside a `Scopes` element**, and only under two
  conditions: `IncludeScopes` is on, and an `Activity` exists. **A record written outside a request has
  `"Scopes": []`** — verified from a background service, which is exactly where the key-ring heartbeat of
  section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 writes from, so a heartbeat record carries
  no framework-supplied correlation field at all.

**So the rule is one line, and it is the reason every event in this document is specified the way it is:
every field the application contributes is a named log-state property, and it is read from `State`.** That
covers `eventName`, the correlation identifier, and each record's own properties — the audit record of
section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4, the checkout
failure of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), the residual-failure records of
section [4.10.2](#4102-what-retries-do-not-fix), the readiness failures of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract), the key-ring heartbeat
and the transition record of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). The event **names**
themselves are [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s.

**Every producer above is assigned to one of [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s record
shapes, and the ones that fit none are named rather than quietly emitted.** That register's field lists are
**closed** — "a record carrying a field not listed is a defect, and a record omitting one is incomplete" —
and [06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids a consumer from adding a ninth shape or a
field to an existing one. Those two rules together make the assignment a **statement this document owes**:
a producer whose record matches no shape is not a record with a shape nobody wrote down, it is a defect in
one of the two documents, and leaving the mapping implicit is what lets it stay one.

**The table below is closed at thirteen rows, and closed in a sense a reader can check rather than take on
trust.** Every row states five things and states each of them **as a value rather than as a description**:
the producing section, the **event-name literal**, the **category**, the **level** together with the
outcome that selects it, and the **shape** — plus a fifth column carrying the **outcome literal**, whose
purpose is explained in the paragraph after next.

**The check a reader performs is mechanical: every `ILogger` call this document specifies appears as a row
of this table.** Sweep the document for its emissions and match each to a row; if a section specifies one
that no row names, the table is not closed and the omission is a defect in *this* document. That is not a
hypothetical, and three defects the sweep found are recorded rather than silently repaired. **An earlier
form of this table was short by one and long by one at the same time**: it carried a row for a record
written when a conditional operator route was mapped — a route section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) withdraws, so that row
leaves the table rather than being assigned a shape — and it carried **no row at all for start-up
validation**, on either outcome, although this document specifies both and
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s release gate reads the successful one. **The third defect was
in two columns rather than in the row set**: seven rows named their shape only as prose or left the level
to be inferred from the producing section, and the security-event row named its event as "per class" where
every other row named a literal. Neither omission is reachable by reading a shape register — only the
producer-by-producer sweep this paragraph describes finds them.

**The outcome column exists because [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) puts an `outcome`
field on four of its live shapes and on no others, and a table that added one uniformly would have
violated four closed field lists to make a column look tidy.** `R3`, `R5`, `R7` and `R8` each carry an
`outcome` and each **delegates its domain to the producer**, so those rows name the literals: 09's per
class for `R5` and per operation for `R7`, and **this document's** for `R3` and for all seven `R8`
producers. `R2` and `R4` carry **no** such field — eight and six fields respectively, neither
of them an `outcome` — so those rows name the closed field that stands in its place instead: a failure
category for both. Adding an `outcome` to either would have been a field
[06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids a consumer from inventing.

**Three of the seven `R8` rows already carried their outcome literals** and are only quoted by the table:
start-up validation's `succeeded` and `failed`, fixed by its own row further down this section; the
bootstrap's `notLeader`, `alreadyPresent`, `created` and `failed`, written into the excerpt of section
[4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof);
and the unavailable-read record's `timeout` and `readFailed`, written into the excerpt of section
[2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment). **The remaining five sets are
fixed by this pass and carried back into the section that produces each**, because each of those sections
published a field list or a record description with **no `outcome` member at all** and so described a
record `R8` could not accept: the heartbeat's own `reported` and `defaultKeyIdUnavailable`
(section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)), and the four
single-literal domains `expired` (section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)), `retriesExhausted`
(section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)), `budgetExceeded`
(section [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half)) and
`clientDisconnected` (section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)). A single-literal
domain is not a degenerate one: it is the statement that the producer has exactly one branch, which is a
fact a reader can check against the branch and an implementer cannot widen silently.

**Two consequences reached beyond the table and are recorded where they landed.** Section 8.12's
