duplicate-submission row read *"category `duplicate-submission`"*, putting `R3`'s failure category on a
record that row itself calls not a fault; the value is now that record's `outcome`, `reconciled`. And
row 62 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) expected the cart-migration record at `Error`, a level
`R8` does not admit; it now expects `Warning` with the event name and outcome literal above.

| Producer, and the section that fixes its fields | Event name | Category and level | Outcome literal, or the closed field that stands in place of one | Shape it satisfies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The checkout write's order record, section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) | `OrderPlaced` | `MvcMusicStore` — `Information` on `placed` and `reconciled`, `Error` on `failed`, which is [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R3` rule of `Information` on success and `Error` on failure applied to the three literals beside this cell | **Three, and this document fixes them** because `R3` carries an `outcome` field and delegates its domain to the producer: **`placed`**, an order was written; **`reconciled`**, the duplicate-submission replay section 8.12 classes as *not a user-facing failure*, which redirects to the winning order rather than creating one; and **`failed`**. `failed` is the **only** literal on which the record carries `R3`'s failure category, which is what makes 06's "present only on a failure" true of this producer | **R3** |
| The `IExceptionHandler` and every in-line failure branch this document enumerates, section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) | `CheckoutFailed` and the branch names section 8.3 fixes | `MvcMusicStore`, `Error` | **Not an `outcome` field — `R2` carries no such member**, and adding one would put a ninth field on a shape [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) closes at eight. The closed field standing in its place is the **failure category** from the emitting path's own set, which for the checkout write is section 8.12's `concurrency`, `persistence`, `missing-album` and `database` | **R2**, whose eight fields section 8.3 is the sole producer of |

**What a producer with no request puts in R1's trace-identifier field — the half of R1's rule this document
supplies, because the ambient context cannot.** Four of the producers above — the start-up validation
record, both key-ring records and the bootstrap record — run outside any request: one from the options
validator during the host's start-up validation, two from a
`BackgroundService` and one from a startup hosted service. **An earlier form of this paragraph also
counted four, but not these four**: it counted the three key-ring producers plus a record written from a
top-level statement when a conditional operator route was mapped, and it omitted start-up validation
altogether. That route and its record are withdrawn by section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) and start-up validation is
now a row of the table above, so the membership changed while the count happens to be the same — which is
why the four are named rather than counted. There is no
`HttpContext`, and the framework's activity scope is absent, which is the `"Scopes": []` fact stated above.
The field is nonetheless populated rather than omitted, with **exactly the expression the readiness check
uses**:

```csharp
// A non-request application producer. Same domain as R1 requires: 32 lowercase hex,
// a W3C trace id, never a run identifier.
Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString() ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()
```

That lands a value **inside R1's stated domain** — a 32-lowercase-hex W3C `trace-id`, and specifically not
a run identifier — so no field of R1 changes and no field is added. One record per pass gets one identifier,
which is what makes a heartbeat pass and the `keyRingStatusUnavailable` record of the *same* pass joinable.
R1's **actor** field needs no accommodation at all: [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits
the literal `anonymous` wherever the request carries no authenticated identity, and a record with no request
carries none.

**R1's trace-identifier rule now states this, and an earlier form of this document raised it as an open
request.** R1 had justified its domain with the words *"because R1 envelopes application records and an
application record always has a request"* — a premise these producers falsify, since they are application
`ILogger` records with no request. [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s R1 row carries the
corrected rule: the identifier is the W3C trace id taken from the ambient activity where one exists and
generated by the producer where none does, the same 32-lowercase-hex domain either way, so **no field of R1
changes and the shape stays closed at four**. That is the register's statement and this document does not
restate it; what a non-request producer of this document must not do is leave the field empty or substitute
a run identifier. [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s listing of `traceId` as **nullable**
reaches the same accommodation by a different route, and the two now agree.

The trace field is the smaller of the two problems the assignment table exposes, and the larger one is the
shape set itself.

**The seven producers that matched no shape now have one, and it is the register's row rather than this
document's.** Seven of the producers above — start-up validation failure, the key-ring heartbeat and its
unavailable-read record, the key-ring bootstrap's outcomes, the legacy-cookie expiry record, the
cart-migration exhausted-retry record, the `CspReportSuppressed` budget record and the cancellation record
— matched no shape while [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) ran from R1 to R7, so the
register asserted a closure it did not have. This document raised it as an amendment request rather than
widening a shape locally, which [06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) forbids outright, and the
amendment has landed: **`R8`, the operational record**, is now a row of that register. Its category, level
and closed field list are stated there and are not restated here. What this document owns is the other half
of R8's delegation — the **event-name literal** and the **outcome literal** for each of the seven, and each
producer's own permitted-field set, fixed in the section named in the assignment table above. That is the
same division R5 and R6 already use, where the register fixes the shape and the naming section fixes the
domain. **Every one of the seven is therefore shape-compliant**, and the assignment table's `None` entries
now read `R8`.

**The correlation identifier, defined once, because two different values answer to the name "trace
identifier" and they are not interchangeable.** `traceId` carries
**`Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString()`** — stated as the exact expression because
`Activity.Current.TraceId` is an `ActivityTraceId` value and only `ToHexString()` renders it as the
**W3C 32-lowercase-hex trace id** [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires, whereas
`Activity.Current?.Id` renders the composite `traceparent`-shaped identifier
(`00-<32 hex trace id>-<16 hex span id>-<2 hex flags>`) and is therefore **not** this field, however
similar the two look at a call site. **Where no activity exists the value is generated by the producer in
the same domain** — `ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()` — so the one expression, stated inline
at every use, is:

```csharp
Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString() ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()
```

**`HttpContext.TraceIdentifier` is excluded, in every position, and an earlier form of this paragraph made
it the fallback.** It is a **different shape** entirely — `0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001`, the connection id and
the request number, which is also the value the hosting scope reports as `RequestId` — so it satisfies
neither the 32-character length nor the lowercase-hexadecimal character class the oracles assert, and a
record or a view carrying it would fail the very assertion the domain exists to make checkable. The
exclusion is stated with its shape precisely so a reviewer can check it by looking at a value rather than
by reasoning about an intent. **This is the rule [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R1`
row fixes**, and it is cited rather than re-decided: ambient activity where one exists, producer-generated
where none does, one domain either way. Two consequences are load-bearing. The value section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) renders into the error view is **this same value**, so
the identifier a user quotes is the one that finds their record — a view showing `TraceIdentifier` while
the log carried the W3C id would be a support path that never resolves. And each record carries `traceId`
in its **own state** rather than relying on the activity scope, because the scope is absent from every
background and startup record and depends on `IncludeScopes` remaining on.

**Two fields the application deliberately does not contribute, so that the query reads them from the one
place that cannot drift.** [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires the `environment` and
the **slot or revision** on every record and names their source as platform configuration plus the
platform's own enrichment — and that is where they stay. Neither is emitted as a log-state property:
`Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` has no enricher concept, so a fixed per-instance field can reach `State`
only by every call site passing it, and a value repeated at hundreds of call sites is a value that will
disagree with itself. Both are already carried **beside** the record by the collection path — the resource
and host columns of `AppServiceConsoleLogs`, the container-app and revision columns of
`ContainerAppConsoleLogs` — which is a platform fact rather than an application claim, and is the same in
every record whether the application was involved or not.

**And one field that no operational record carries at all: the customer's identity.** This is a standing
rule rather than a property of one event, because the exposure it prevents accumulates rather than
announcing itself — a login name written into a record is a login name in a general-purpose log store that
[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) retains for **90 days** and that every principal with
workspace access can read, which is CWE-532, *Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File*. So **no
record on the ordinary operational stream carries a customer's login name, email address or any other
direct identifier** — not the checkout records, not the cart records, not the error record of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and not the readiness records of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract). The captured payload above is
the concrete instance: the checkout record carries `orderId` and `traceId` and nothing that names the
person who placed the order.

- **Where a record does have to be attributable to a customer, it carries `cartKeyHash`** — the salted,
  truncated pseudonym [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines, keyed by the
  `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt` entry earlier in this section. For a signed-in visitor the cart key **is**
  the login name, so the hash is a stable per-customer pseudonym that supports the operations an
  investigation actually needs — group one visitor's records together, count how many visitors a fault
  reached — without carrying the name itself. It is also why that entry is a required per-environment
  secret: an unsalted hash over a domain this small is reversible by exhaustion, and one salt shared
  across environments would let a non-production pseudonym identify a production customer.
- **So the checkout record and the cart records are consistent by construction rather than by
  coincidence**, and stating it is the point: they use **one** mechanism, defined once here and once in
  [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), so neither can be hardened without the other
  following. An earlier version of this document interpolated the login name into the checkout record
  while the cart events beside it hashed the same value — the two-authors failure this rule closes.
- **The one exception is a different record on a different path, and naming it is what keeps the rule
  absolute.** The provisioning audit record of section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 carries the
  **target username in clear**, because a record whose entire purpose is to state which account was
  granted an administrator role is useless pseudonymized. It is not an operational record: it is written
  by a one-shot process under its **own** category rather than one of
  [06 §9.6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, so it is separable at the sink from every record the
  web application writes, and its route, destination and retention are
  [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s — cited here rather than restated. An administrator
  account name is an administrative fact carried on a separable channel; a customer name is neither, which
  is why the two are treated differently deliberately. **An earlier form of this bullet named a
  destination** — an append-only container under a time-based immutability policy — and named it wrongly:
  [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) withdraws that container from the design, so the sentence
  pointed at nothing, and a destination is not this document's to state in any case.

**Four prohibitions, because "no PII or secrets in retained telemetry" is a promise and the rules above
are not yet enough to keep it.** [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the exclusion
*list* — what must never reach the sink — and closes with the honest admission that its enforcement is a
review task. A review is not a control, so the four items below are the mechanisms that make the same list
hold without one, and each names the concrete channel it closes.

| # | Prohibition | The channel it closes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **`EnableSensitiveDataLogging` is not called on either `DbContext`, in any environment — including Development.** It is not a Development convenience with a production guard; it is absent from the codebase, so there is no call for an environment condition to get wrong | The option "enable[s] application data to be included in exception messages, and logging" (*DbContextOptionsBuilder.EnableSensitiveDataLogging*, EF Core), which puts parameter values into **both** the command category *and* the message of any provider exception — and an exception message travels on a channel **no log-level setting reaches**. *An earlier form of this cell named that channel as "the framework's own unhandled-exception record", which the table above now closes at `None`; the channel that a level genuinely cannot reach is the platform's auto-collected exception telemetry, retained by [06 §9.2.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) as `Accepted, restricted`, which reads the thrown exception rather than the log.* Development is included because a developer's connection is to a database that, per section [5.1.1](#511-the-extract-is-pii--how-it-is-held-and-how-it-is-destroyed), can be holding a copy of production PII |
| 2 | **`EnableDetailedErrors` is called only when the environment is Development**, on the same `IsDevelopment()` condition the developer exception page uses (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) — never on a negated Production test | It adds field-level detail to data-reading exceptions, which is a disclosure channel of exactly the shape item 1 closes, and it is the option most often reached for as a substitute once item 1 is forbidden |
| 3 | **No category may be relaxed outside Development, and the category set is closed** — checks 4 and 5 of the validator above, enforced at start | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` at `Information` in a deployed environment, which [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) itself calls "the single largest route by which order data would otherwise arrive in a log store" |
| 4 | **No value the application controls is ever placed in a URL's query string** — not a token, not an identifier of a person, not a cart key, not a configuration value. The application's own query parameters are exactly **three**, enumerated so the rule is checkable rather than aspirational: `?ReturnUrl=` (a local path, validated as local), `/Store/Browse?genre=` (a genre name from the catalog's own closed set of fifteen — no person, no secret, and the same value the path of any other route would have carried), and `?page=` on the two list endpoints of section [4.11](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost) (a small positive integer, validated, and `400` when it is anything else). **The census substitutes one entry rather than changing its size, and both halves are stated because each was wrong on its own.** The error path's `?code={0}` is **deleted**: stage 2 item 4 registers `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/Home/Error/{0}")`, which substitutes the code into the **path**, so no status code is ever placed in a query string and this rule has nothing to except. `?page=` is **added**: section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 102 exercises it in all three of its cases, including four malformed values, so a census that omitted it was not checkable. 3 − 1 + 1 = **3** | **The platform's HTTP log, which no application setting filters.** `AppServiceHTTPLogs` retains the request query, the referrer and the client address for the 90 days [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) sets, and the auto-instrumented request telemetry retains the URL. Neither passes through `ILogger`, so the only application-side control over them is what the application puts in a URL in the first place. This is the reason the cart's remove call posts its token in a **header** and its id in a **body** (section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)) rather than in a query string |

**What the exception record carries, which is not `exception.ToString()`.** The field table above records
that the formatter writes the whole of `ToString()` — type, message, inner exceptions and stack — into one
string. That is the formatter's behaviour and this document does not replace the formatter, so the control
is on **what is passed to it**:

- **A record the application writes passes no exception object.** It carries three named log-state
  properties instead, and the names are the **message-template placeholder tokens**, which is what the
  logging pipeline uses as the property name: **`{ExceptionType}`** (the full type name),
  **`{ExceptionStack}`** (`Exception.StackTrace`, which is the frames of the call stack — method
  names — and carries **no argument values**), and **`{InnerExceptionTypes}`** (the chain as an array of
  type names, built by walking `InnerException` to its end). The two writers in this document that had
  been passing `ex` as `ILogger`'s exception argument — the key-ring heartbeat's handler in section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) and the custody path of section
  [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) — were corrected to this shape,
  and they are the shape's only two exception-carrying writers. **No source-file path and no line number
  appears in `{ExceptionStack}`**, and the control is the artifact rather than the string: the deployed
  build carries no debug symbols, which is
  [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) channel 1 control 4's artifact-side condition and is
  asserted from the record side by 06's own sweep. The `Exception` top-level property is therefore
  **absent** from every application-written record — and since every framework category that writes one is
  pinned to `None` in the table above, a query for that property over the application's log stream returns
  nothing at all rather than framework records.
- **`Exception.Message` is deliberately the one part left out.** It is the only component of `ToString()`
  that can embed a value — a provider's constraint or parameter text, a validator's rejected input, a
  formatter's argument — and it is the component with the least diagnostic value once the type and the
  stack are present. Where a specific condition genuinely needs describing, it is described by the
  record's own **message template and named properties**, which the field rules above already govern,
  rather than by quoting an exception.
- **The application never throws or wraps an exception whose message embeds request data, a row value or
  a configuration value.** This is the rule that bounds the one channel the two rules above do not reach,
  and **naming that channel correctly is what keeps the rule load-bearing rather than redundant.** It is
  *not* the framework's own unhandled-exception record — an earlier form of this bullet said so, and the
  category table above closes `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics`, `…Hosting.Diagnostics` and
  `…Server.Kestrel` at `None`, so that record reaches no log at all. The channel that remains is the
  **platform's auto-collected exception telemetry**, which [06 §9.2.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
  retains as `Accepted, restricted` rather than discarding: it reads the thrown exception directly and no
  `Logging:LogLevel` value reaches it, so the *content of the exception the application constructs* is the
  only control available over it. With prohibition 1 in force the provider cannot put values into a
  message either, so what that table can hold is a type, a framework message and a stack. **Whether that record is written at all is not decided here**: the framework categories that
  pass an exception object are pinned by [06 §9.6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s category
  register, which is that document's operational requirement against this contract rather than a second
  definition of it. This bullet bounds the record's *content* wherever the register leaves it enabled,
  which is why the bound is stated as a property of what the application throws rather than as a
  reliance on the category being suppressed.
- **`exception.ToString()` is never interpolated into a log message, a view, a response body or a
  header.** Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) already forbids the response half;
  this states the log half, and it is the reason the record's writer reads the exception it obtains from
  `IExceptionHandlerFeature` for its **type, its inner type-name chain and its stack** rather than for its
  text — the projection section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) fixes.

**The fields the application must never place in a record, stated as a list it can be tested against.**
[06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s list is the authority and is not restated; what belongs
here is the application-side form of it, because a rule expressed as "no PII" cannot be asserted and a
named field can. No log-state property, message template argument, scope value or exception field written
by this application carries: a **password**, its hash, or any credential; **any part of a connection
string**; **any configuration value** from the contract in this section; **any cookie value** — the
authentication, session and anti-forgery cookies are all bearer credentials; an **anti-forgery token**;
the **`Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`**; the **raw** cart key or session id, which reach a record only as
`cartKeyHash`; a customer's **login name, email address, full name, postal address or phone number**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]; a **promo code**; or a **request body** or **query
string** in raw form. The one deliberate exception is the provisioning audit record's target username,
which is not written to this channel at all — section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 owns it and its
destination.

**The canary test, because every rule above is only as good as the evidence that it holds.** Coverage row
47 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) plants **two** distinguishable literals — a known secret
value in a configuration member and a known PII value in a seeded order row — then drives the paths that
have historically leaked them: a failed sign-in, a checkout that throws, an unhandled exception in an
action, a deliberate provider failure that produces an exception carrying command context, a readiness
failure, and a request whose route data is malformed. It then asserts that **neither literal appears
anywhere in the captured `stdout` stream** — not in `Message`, not in any `State` property, not in
`Exception`, and not in any `Scopes` element — by searching the raw captured text rather than by inspecting
parsed fields, so a value that arrives inside an unexpected property still fails the row. It is a **canary
rather than a proof**: it demonstrates that the paths it drives are clean, and prohibitions 1 to 4 are what
make that generalize.

**What this half cannot close, and whose it is.** Three retained channels take nothing from `ILogger` and
are unreachable from application code without the in-process telemetry SDK
[04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s pin list deliberately excludes: the platform **HTTP log**'s
query, cookie, referrer, client-address and user fields; the **auto-instrumented** request, dependency and
exception telemetry's URLs, identities and raw exception detail; and the platform's own audit and platform
logs. Prohibition 4 is the whole of what this document can do about the first of them.
**[06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
own the platform-side half** — whether those columns are dropped, redacted or accepted with their
retention stated — and this document states the requirement it places on them: **a field this section
forbids in a record must not be retained beside the record either**, or the exclusion list holds only for
the channel that was easiest to control.

**Where this meets the other document, stated plainly because the two halves have to agree for a single
alert to fire.** [06 §9.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the workspace-side extraction — the
parse expression, and the **query-time workspace functions** that project these fields into a normalized
shape. It is deliberately not an ingestion-time transformation: a transformation's output has to match the
built-in table's own predefined schema, so it cannot add columns of its own, and a design that assumed it
could would have produced queries against columns that never appear. Separately,
[06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the event names and the required field set. This
document owns the shape above. The consequence for the query is not a preference: a predicate or a
projection keyed on **`EventId.Name`, on a top-level `eventName`, or on a top-level `TraceId` or
`SpanId`** matches **no record this application emits**, and a filter built from two such tests matches
nothing at all. The fields are at `State.eventName`, `State.traceId` and each record's own `State.*`
properties, with `Scopes` as the framework-supplied fallback for the activity identifiers on
request-scoped records only.

**And one consequence for the operator tool — stated per producer, because an earlier form of this
paragraph gave one stream three different first hops.** Every verb of `provision-admin` runs as a
one-shot process outside App Service, so **nothing auto-instruments any of them**: every record any verb
writes leaves the process through **standard output**, and each verb registers the same formatter with
the same options — the one logging decision the console shares with the web application. Three
corrections, each a deletion rather than a qualification:

- **The verb count is ten, not four.** Section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)'s verb table is closed at
  **ten** verbs and section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) owns **eight** of them, so the
  earlier "the four of section 10.2" left the executor's records governed by nothing at all.
- **One record in this console is not produced by this formatter, so the blanket "in exactly the format
  above and nowhere else" is deleted.** The `admin` verb's **four** audit lines are written by the
  **dedicated serialiser** of section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 — **not** by an
  `ILogger` call, because they must survive a failure that happens before a logger exists. They are
  byte-identical to what this formatter would have produced for the same record, which is that
  property's parity requirement, and they reach the same stream — so the shape above remains the shape a
  reader parses, while the producer is named where it actually is.
- **The durable destination is per producer, and neither route is the tool's single one.** Every
  ordinary `ILogger` record the console writes — the executor's operational records and `seed`'s alike —
  travels the captured stream of whatever host ran the verb, which
  [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) collects for the executor's data-load invocations
  exactly as [06 §6.10](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s logging row states and section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) restates from this side. The `admin` verb's four audit lines
  travel [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s capture-and-upload into the immutable
  container instead, and **no workspace table receives them**
  ([06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) says the same from the other side). **The earlier
  sentence routed every verb's output through §9.5.1**; that is deleted, because it would send
  reconciliation diagnostics into a 365-day immutable container while leaving the workspace every gate
  in [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) reads empty of them. The failure behaviours differ
  with the routes and are property 4's: losing an audit line **fails the provisioning step**, and an
  ordinary diagnostic record may be lost without consequence.

**`Kestrel` — Development only, and it is in this contract solely so that its absence from every deployed
environment is a stated fact rather than an accident.**

| Key | Type | Value | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Kestrel:Endpoints:Http:Url` | `string`, an absolute URL | [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s | `appsettings.Development.json` only |
| `Kestrel:Endpoints:Https:Url` | `string`, an absolute URL | [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s | `appsettings.Development.json` only |

Three properties make this safe to state briefly. **The keys exist only in the Development overlay**, so
no deployed environment loads them — a deployed instance's listening address comes from the platform
([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the container port contract), and a `Kestrel`
section in the base file would fight it. **No `Certificates` section accompanies them**: an endpoint that
names no certificate falls back to `Certificates:Default` or, absent that, to the development certificate
(*Configure endpoints for the ASP.NET Core Kestrel web server*, .NET 8) — the certificate's provisioning
is [04 §12.8](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s prerequisite, not a key. And **they are the reason the
always-secure cookie policy above is testable locally**: the HTTPS endpoint is what makes a `Secure`
cookie reach a development browser, which is why the policy needs no development exemption.

**These two keys are also why `launchSettings.json` is not in this contract.** That file is a local
development artifact outside the target file map, and Kestrel reads its own configuration section
regardless of it, so declaring the endpoints here keeps the local HTTPS binding inside a committed file
the map does contain.

**Validation: `AddOptions<T>().Bind(section).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` on every options
type above, plus one `IValidateOptions<T>` per type.** The split between the two halves is not stylistic —
each half can express something the other cannot, and the mechanism paragraph above is why the first half
alone is not sufficient.

| Half | What it checks | Why it cannot be the other half's job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ValidateDataAnnotations()` over the **nullable** members | Presence, via `[Required]` on a member that is genuinely `null` when the key is absent; and a contained value's range, via `[Range]` on the nullable numeric members | It sees one member at a time and knows nothing about the environment or about another member's value |
| `IValidateOptions<T>` | Every rule that needs more than one member, a type `[Range]` does not cover, or the host: the `TimeSpan` bounds; `PersistentExpireTimeSpan <= ExpireTimeSpan`; the `SameSite` allowed-set; a leading `/` on each path; the five connection-string checks and the accepted-mode selection behind the third of them; `SqlIdentity:ClientId` equal to the connection's parsed `User Id`; `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator` equal to `DataProtection:ApplicationName`; `DataProtection:KeyRotationPeriod` within 14 to 365 days and `DataProtection:CustodyPassPeriod` within 1 to 12 hours **and strictly less than** the rotation period — a two-member rule, which is why it cannot be two `[Range]` attributes; the two `Site` members' per-entry host and origin rules; `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`'s decoded length; the members required only outside `Development`; `AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` required when `Enabled` is true; `Enabled` true while the seeding invocation's expected environment is anything other than the non-production name it declares; and the standing `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` check on every string member | An attribute cannot read a sibling property, `IHostEnvironment`, or a parsed form of its own value |

`ValidateOnStart()` is what makes both halves run **before the first request** rather than at first
resolution of the options type ("Options validation runs the first time a `TOptions` instance is created…
To run options validation when the app starts, call `ValidateOnStart`" — *Options pattern in ASP.NET
Core*, .NET 8). Without it, a member that only the checkout path reads would be validated by the first
checkout.

**The rule, stated as a rule rather than as a list of examples: a setting is fail-fast when a wrong or
absent value produces behaviour the application cannot detect at runtime and a user cannot report.**
Every member marked required above meets it. Four consequences are worth naming because each has a
distinct failure signature:

- **`ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` absent** — without `ValidateOnStart` this surfaces as the
  first request to touch a database, which on a deployment with a warm health probe may be a real user's.
- **`DataProtection:ApplicationName` absent** — never surfaces as an error at all. See above.
- **`Seeding:Enabled` true in Production** — surfaces as data loss, once.
- And **any `Identity` member absent** — surfaces as a silently weaker policy than the one section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) had approved.

`ValidateOnStart` is what converts all four from a runtime surprise into a failed start, which the
deployment gate and the health probe of [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) can both see
**before** traffic arrives. A validation failure names the section and the member; it does **not** echo
the value, because the value may be a connection string.

**Safe defaults and conditional requirements — the complete list, counted in one way rather than two.**
The exceptions are sorted by **what the condition is**, because a member qualified by a condition in the
same breath as its class is not a count anybody can check. Each class is separately checkable and the
total is stated once:

| Class | Members | The rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Legal to omit unconditionally** — two members | `Seeding:Enabled`; `Site:PermittedImageOrigins` | Each read as its fail-closed value: `false` for the first, and the **empty** list for the second — no external image origin permitted at all, which is both the safe answer and the state [06 §10.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records today. **An earlier form of this row carried a third member**, the optional boolean gating the operator route section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)'s withdrawal record withdraws; with that route, its configuration section and its options type gone there is no third member to read as `false`, so this class is **two** rather than three. These are the only two members in the contract where absence is a decision rather than an omission |
| **Legal to omit conditionally on another member** — one member | `Seeding:AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` | Legal to omit **only** while `Enabled` is `false`; absent with `Enabled` true fails validation |
| **Required conditionally on the environment** — four members | `Expected:SqlServer`, `Expected:SqlDatabase`, `Expected:DataProtectionDiscriminator`, `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt` | **Required in every environment that is not `Development` and is not the test fixture**, where each is legal to omit: those two have no environment-declared expectation to compare against and no need of a stable per-environment telemetry salt |
| **Required conditionally on the connection mode** — one member | `SqlIdentity:ClientId` | Required under **M1**, required to be **absent** under **M2** and **M4**, and neither required nor compared under **M3** — the mode table above states each case and why |
| **Required to be absent, unconditionally** — two members | `Ingress:TrustedNetworks`, `Ingress:TrustedProxies` | **Withdrawn keys.** Absence is the only legal state in every environment, and a resolved value of either — empty string included — **fails the start**, because it means the withdrawn trust-list model was re-introduced by configuration edit ([06 §10.1.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). They are bound members rather than unread key names for the reason given with the type above |

**Eleven names in total**, and every condition among them is enforced by the type's single
`IValidateOptions<T>` rather than by an attribute, per the member-class rule earlier in this section.
**An earlier form of this paragraph said nine**, and it was right when the first class held three members;
the withdrawal recorded in that row takes the total to eight and nothing else about it moves.
`Antiforgery:HeaderName` is **not** on this list — it is unconditionally required, because a value that
has to match a client literal (section [8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script)) is a value that must
never be left implicit on either side. **A conditional requirement is still fail-fast**: absent where its condition holds, each of
the **six** that carry a condition fails the start, while the **two** that carry none are read as their
fail-closed value instead — which is what makes those two classes worth separating rather than counting
together. **The last class inverts the direction rather than adding a condition**: its **two** withdrawn
names fail the start when they are *present*, so they are fail-fast on the opposite input to every other
name here, which is why they are counted as their own class instead of being filed under the three that are
legal to omit.

**Every other member of every type above has no default, and an absent key fails the start.** Enumerating
the exceptions rather than the rule is deliberate: a reader who wants to know whether a key may be omitted
looks in one place and finds eleven names and the condition attached to each. One member defined **outside**
this section carries a default of its own and is counted where it is defined rather than here: the
operator-only `Load:BatchSize` of section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), which no web host binds.

**Precedence, explicitly and completely, because a secret arriving late is the whole mechanism — and
because an omitted provider is a silent override.** The two hosts do **not** have the same source list, and
the difference is a decision this section makes rather than an accident of how each builder is constructed:
the site is built with **`WebApplication.CreateBuilder()`**, parameterless, and
`tools/provision-admin` with the **defaults-disabled** builder
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) fixes — `Host.CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder` with
`DisableDefaults`, which starts with no configuration source at all and adds only the sources named in
the per-process matrix above. **04 owns the tool's builder and its provider list; this document names
neither a different builder nor a different source order**, and the numbered list below is the **site's**
list. The site adds **four** sources, in this order, and **a later source wins**:

1. `appsettings.json` — committed. Non-secret, environment-independent values only.
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json` — committed. Environment-shaped non-secret values.
3. **User secrets** — added **only when the resolved environment is `Development`**, and therefore
   present on a developer machine and in no deployed environment. It exists in this list because it is
   the mechanism that keeps a local credential *out of* the committed Development file, which the file
   scoping at the end of this section forbids from carrying one.
4. **Environment variables** — the layer the platform injects into, including an App Service application
   setting, a connection-string setting, and a **Key Vault reference** resolved by the site's managed
   identity ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)).
And, for **the operator tool only** and therefore outside the site's four:

5. **Command-line arguments** — added **last** and therefore **outranking
   every other source including the platform's own settings**. The framework documentation is explicit
   about the consequence: "Because the provider is used at the end, it has the highest priority", and
   "configuration values set on the command-line override configuration values set by all of the other
   configuration providers" (*Configuration in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). The tool's own arguments reach it
   through the **closed pre-parse** of section
   [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1b, which runs
   **before** the builder is constructed and rejects every token it does not recognise, so this
   highest-priority provider can contribute only the handful of keys that pre-parse names.

**The site does not have this provider at all, and that is the decision rather than a prohibition on
using it.** An earlier version of this section passed `args` to `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` and relied
on a written rule that nothing would use it. That is not a control: the provider outranks every platform
setting, so anything able to influence the site's command line — a release definition, a container
`command`/`args` override, a start-up script, a debugger profile — could have replaced the
platform-inventoried connection string, the data-protection discriminator, a log level, `Expected:*`, the
environment name or a Key Vault-backed setting, silently and from outside everything that inspects
configuration. The operator tool, which genuinely needs arguments, reads them with a hard allow-list
parser instead and never routes them through configuration at all. Both hosts therefore end without the
channel, by two different mechanisms:

| Host | Builder | Command-line provider | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The site | **`WebApplication.CreateBuilder()`**, no `args` | **Absent** | The builder adds the provider only when it is given a non-empty argument array, so passing nothing removes the provider itself rather than trusting a rule about it. The site needs no arguments: it is started by the platform, not by an operator |
| `tools/provision-admin` | The defaults-disabled builder of [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) — `Host.CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder` with `DisableDefaults`, and **the raw `args` array is never assigned to it** | **Present, behind the pre-parse, and fed only the pre-parse's normalized pairs** | A verb and a switch are the tool's whole interface. The pre-parse of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) is what bounds the provider's reach to the mapped keys, and it runs **before** the builder exists, so the provider never sees a token the parser did not admit |

**What the site gives up by not taking `args`, stated so the trade is checkable rather than asserted.**
Three things, and none of them is load-bearing:

- **`--environment` and `--urls` on the site's command line stop working.** Both have platform-native
  equivalents that this design already uses exclusively: `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` for the first
  ([06 §8.4.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) and the platform's own port contract for the second
  ([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), with the Development endpoints coming from the
  `Kestrel` keys above. No release step, container definition or committed file in this plan passes
  either switch.
- **Ad-hoc local overrides on `dotnet run` stop working.** A developer overrides through user secrets or
  `appsettings.Development.json`, which are sources 2 and 3 — reviewable, and the same two a colleague
  reads.
- **Nothing in the test fixture is affected.** `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>` invokes the
  application's entry point **without supplying arguments of its own** and configures the host through
  `ConfigureWebHost`, which is where the in-memory source named at the end of this list is added
  (*Integration tests in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). So the fixture of section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) neither passes nor needs a switch, and an
  earlier claim here that it relied on `dotnet test` argument plumbing was simply wrong: arguments given
  to `dotnet test` reach the test runner, not the application under test.

**The prohibition that remains is narrower and still necessary, because the tool keeps its provider.**
Two things are forbidden:

- **(a) Any secret on the command line, by any process, in any environment.** An argument is visible in
  process listings and recorded in shell and pipeline history — the separate and stronger argument of
  section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1.
- **(b) Any configuration override to the operator tool on a release invocation** — not the connection
  string, not the discriminator, not a log level, not a seeding flag. Configuration reaches it through
  invocation-scoped environment variables ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), and section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) for its own secret channel) and
  through nothing else. The command's pre-parse enforces this by construction: the only keys its switch
  mapping can produce are the non-configuration ones named there.
- The reason is not that the channel is weaker in principle but that it is **invisible to the platform's
  own record of configuration**: a value overridden on the command line does not appear in the site's
  application settings, so [06 §9.3.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s pre-traffic assertion and
  every audit of "what is this environment configured with" would both read the wrong answer while the
  process used another. An override that no reviewer can see is the failure mode, and its severity is
  exactly the same whether the value is a secret or a log level. Removing the provider from the site is
  the same argument carried to its conclusion.
- **The two pinned release tools take a credential-free target connection as an argument, and that is
  not an exception being tolerated — it is the only channel either of them has.** A migration bundle
  accepts `--connection`, and omitting it makes the connection compiled into the context decide which
  database receives DDL; `dotnet sql-cache create` takes the connection as its **first positional
  argument** and accepts configuration by no other route at all. Neither is an application host and
  neither reads this contract, so clause (b) above does not reach them — and a rule written as "no
  command line, ever" would have been a rule those two commands cannot obey, which is how a policy stops
  being applied to the host it should bind. What makes the argument safe rather than merely unavoidable
  is four properties [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) states and this document does not
  restate: the value is a declared pipeline variable, it carries no credential because it authenticates
  as a managed identity, it is never echoed into a log or a failure message, and the server and database
  it names are asserted against the expected values before it is used. The invocations themselves are
  [06 §6.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, under the artifact contract of
  [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md).
- **The operator command's own switches are exempt because they are not configuration values** — they name
  the account and role to provision, not a key of this contract. Section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) states the closed pre-parse
  that accepts exactly those and rejects everything else; [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns
  the command's argument grammar and its exit statuses. The web application's own guarded seed mode of
  section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) is exempt on the same basis and for
  the same reason: it selects a one-shot mode before the host is built and binds no key.

An **in-memory** source is added after every source above, but only inside the test host — section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) owns it. In the site's list, where there is no
command-line provider, it is the only layer above the environment variables; in the tool's, it is the only
layer that would outrank the command line, and the tool is never run under the test host anyway.

**A nested key arrives from the environment in double-underscore form**: `ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection`,
`DataProtection__ApplicationName`, `Identity__PasswordMinimumLength`. The colon separator is not
a legal environment-variable name character on every platform the application will run on, so the
double underscore is the portable form — and it is how both the platform and a one-shot migration or
provisioning invocation supply a nested value without a file. **This is why a Key Vault reference
surfaced as an application setting outranks the committed JSON**: it arrives at layer 4 and the JSON is
layers 1 and 2.

**Precedence is a safety net here, not the mechanism, and the difference matters.** The committed files
contain **no secret and no connection string for any deployed environment**, so in a deployed
environment there is nothing at a lower layer for the platform's value to override. A design that
relied on ordering to shadow a committed secret would still have committed the secret.

**The administrator credential is not in this contract at all.** Section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) records that the
correct target for the two `appSettings` reads
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24] is *nothing*, and this is where that carries
through: **there is no key, no section, no options member and no member of any type above that holds an
administrator username or password.** The provisioning secret reaches
`tools/provision-admin` through a single-invocation environment variable or an echo-disabled prompt —
section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) owns that channel — and
it appears in no `appsettings` file, in no App Service setting on the web application, and in no options
type. A compromised web process has nothing to read.

**`appsettings.Development.json`, scoped explicitly, because "the developer file" is where secrets
accumulate.**

| May contain | Must never contain |
| --- | --- |
| A **local** connection string carrying no credential — a local instance reached by integrated security, or a container whose credentials arrive through the environment rather than the file | Any secret, any credential, any Key Vault reference value |
| A raised log level for local diagnosis — the **one** `Logging:LogLevel` override stated above, `MvcMusicStore` at `Debug`, and no other key at any value | Any connection string reaching a deployed database. **And any relaxation of a `None` pin**, which is check 3 of the validation above and is forbidden to a consumer by [06 §9.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) |
| Local values for the `Identity`, `Authentication:Cookie` and `Session` members where a developer needs them to differ | `Seeding:Enabled` — seeding authorization is supplied **per invocation** through the environment, which is check 2 of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks); a committed `true` would authorize every process that believes it is in Development, against whatever database it is pointed at |
| The two `Kestrel:Endpoints` URLs stated above, which exist in this file and nowhere else | `DataProtection:ApplicationName` for any deployed environment |
| Nothing else | A `Kestrel` section in `appsettings.json`, which would bind an endpoint in every deployed environment and fight the platform's own port ([06 §4.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) |

The file is **committed**, so its content is reviewed like any other source. A developer value that
cannot be committed is not a Development override — it is a secret, and it belongs in the environment of
that developer's own session.

**The file set is exactly two files, and there is no `appsettings.Production.json`.** This is the closing
rule of the section rather than an aside, because it is a fact another deliverable has to be able to rely
on: [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s third rule states that **no command or release step
may require a `Production` overlay**, and cites this section as the place the absence is decided. So it is
decided here, unambiguously and in one direction:

- **`appsettings.json`** and **`appsettings.Development.json`** are the only two files in the set. No
  `appsettings.Production.json`, no `appsettings.Staging.json`, and no per-slot variant — matching
  [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map, which carries those two names and no third.
- **The deployed levels and defaults live in the base file**, which is what makes the absence safe rather
  than an omission: every deployed environment reads `appsettings.json` and gets the production shape,
  and the Development overlay is the only file that relaxes anything.
- **Deployed *values* arrive from platform configuration** ([06 §8.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md))
  at layer 4 of the precedence list below, which is why no file is needed to carry them and why one would
  be a second place for a reviewer to look.
- **Nothing may be built, promoted, copied or asserted on the assumption that such a file exists.** A
  release step that placed one beside an artifact would be placing a file the map does not contain, and a
  step that read one would be reading a source no environment has. The consequence for a generated
  migration artifact specifically — that none of them carries an `appsettings*.json` beside it — is
  [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, for a different reason, and the two rules agree.

---

## 4. Dependency injection and object lifetime

### 4.1 The ten manual instantiation sites constructor injection replaces

Ten sites in the migration source construct a `DbContext` or an Identity manager by hand. They are
enumerated individually because they are not all the same shape and two of them are not in a
controller at all.

| # | Site | What is constructed | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19] | `new UserManager<ApplicationUser>(new UserStore<ApplicationUser>(new ApplicationDbContext()))` — a chained constructor building the entire Identity graph, three objects deep | The chained constructor is deleted; `UserManager` and `SignInManager` are injected. The second, parameter-taking constructor already at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:23-26] is the shape that survives |
| 2 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32] | `new MusicStoreEntities()` — one ad hoc catalog context **inside a method body**, in `MigrateShoppingCart` | Injected catalog context, or the injected `ShoppingCartService` that supersedes this method's body (section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)) |
| 3 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:15] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 4 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:12] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 5 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:10] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 6 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:11] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 7 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:11] | `MusicStoreEntities` field initializer | Constructor-injected scoped context |
| 8 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27] | `new ApplicationDbContext()` at startup | **Leaves the web application.** Resolved from the console tool's host — section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) |
| 9 | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:28] | `new UserManager<ApplicationUser>(new UserStore<ApplicationUser>(context))` at startup | As above |

**`AccountController` is the exception in this list, and describing it as "the sixth controller with a
field-initialized context" is wrong.** It has **no** field-initialized catalog context. It holds an
`ApplicationDbContext` only *indirectly*, through the `UserManager` its chained constructor builds
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19], and it creates exactly **one** `MusicStoreEntities` on demand, inside `MigrateShoppingCart`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32]. So dependency injection does two different things to this file: it replaces that single ad hoc
catalog context, and it replaces the hand-built Identity graph with injected managers. The Identity
context remains a **separate registration** either way — it is not folded into the catalog context.

The file also already has the constructor injection needs: `public AccountController(UserManager<ApplicationUser> userManager)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:23-26] exists today and is unused by the framework, because MVC 5 resolves the parameterless one.
The port keeps that shape and deletes the parameterless overload.

### 4.2 What scoped registration actually changes — and what it does not

**Scoped registration gives one instance per context type per request, not one instance overall.**
That sentence is the whole of this section, and it is here because the opposite reading produces a plan
that quietly assumes atomicity it will not have.

After the port there are still **two `DbContext` instances per request** and therefore **two change
trackers** — one for `MusicStoreEntities`, one for `ApplicationDbContext` — and **no automatic unit of
work spanning them**. A `SaveChanges` on one does not enlist the other.

What scoped registration removes is narrower and worth having:

- the hand-rolled construction at all ten sites in section [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces);
- the ad hoc mid-method instance at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32],
  which today means a *second* catalog context exists inside a request that already has none of its
  own — the account controller has no field context, so this instance is created, used and abandoned;
- the consumer-side disposal that becomes wrong (section [4.7](#47-the-dispose-overrides-must-be-removed));
- and the inconsistency where one controller's context is disposed and four others' are not
  ([08 §5.8](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns that as debt).

What it does **not** remove is the two-store boundary. That boundary is a design decision, taken
deliberately in section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables), and the
consistency model that makes it safe is section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

### 4.3 The cross-store consistency model

Sign-in writes to the Identity store; cart reassignment writes to the catalog store. And **a database
transaction cannot make an authentication cookie atomic with either of them**, because the cookie is
issued in the HTTP response, outside any transaction and outside the database entirely. So the
ordering has to be designed rather than inherited.

**The current order is the reverse of the safe one, which is the evidence that this needs deciding.**
`SignInAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:346-354] signs out the external
cookie [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:348], creates the identity [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:349], **registers the sign-in grant** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:350], and only **then**
migrates the cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:353]. `MigrateShoppingCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:30-40] creates its own context [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:32], reassigns
ownership through `MigrateCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193], calls
`SaveChanges` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:37] and rewrites the session key [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39]. The action that calls it
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] has no `try`/`catch`, so a failure in the
cart write propagates out of a method that has already granted the sign-in.

**The target sequence, with the API named at each step.** This is the `Login` POST handler in order;
nothing here is optional and the order is the contract.

| Step | Call | What it must and must not do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(model);` | Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:58] |
| 2 | `var user = await userManager.FindByNameAsync(model.UserName);` | A null result takes the **same** failure branch as a wrong password (section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)), so nothing discloses whether the account exists. **A null `user` must not be passed on to step 3** — `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` throws `ArgumentNullException` on a null user, which would make the uniform failure path unreachable for exactly the case it exists for, and answer 500 instead. The null case is handled by step 2a and step 3 is skipped |
| 2a | **Null user only:** `await uniformCost.SpendFullCostAsync(cancellationToken);` — nothing is returned to inspect — then the failure branch of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) | **Fixed work, not an early return.** An early `return View(model)` here is functionally correct and a username-enumeration oracle: it skips the key-derivation function entirely, so an unknown account answers in a fraction of the time a real verification takes and the response time discloses which usernames exist. This step spends **the target derivation cost defined below** so that the unknown-account path costs what the most expensive real path costs. The service is described immediately after this table, because getting it right is not a one-liner: "hash a fixed dummy value" is **not** equivalent work across this application's account population, and the obvious implementation of it does not compile |
| 3 | **Non-null user only:** `var result = await signInManager.CheckPasswordSignInAsync(user, model.Password, lockoutOnFailure: true);` **then, unconditionally, `await uniformCost.TopUpAsync(user.PasswordHash, derivationObservation, cancellationToken);`** — where `derivationObservation` is the scoped observation the hasher decorator below populates, and **never** a flag inferred from `result` | **This is the step that must not issue a cookie, and it is why `PasswordSignInAsync` is not used here.** `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` verifies the password, applies the lockout accounting the policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) enables, and — where the stored hash is in the older format — rehashes and updates the user through `UserManager`. Those are **Identity-store writes, and they are complete when this call returns.** `result.Succeeded == false` takes the failure branch of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **The top-up is what makes this path cost the same as step 2a**: a locked-out account is rejected *before* any derivation and an older-format hash is derived far more cheaply than a current-format one, so both would otherwise answer measurably faster than an ordinary wrong password |
| 4 | `await cartService.MigrateCartAsync(anonymousCartId, user.UserName, cancellationToken)` — **in its own transaction**, in the catalog store, and **only when the session's current cart key passes the three-part provenance test of the isolation rule below** | **Gated, provenance-tested and idempotent — and the idempotence is the ledger's, not the anonymous cart id's.** The anonymous id selects *which* source cart is merged; **this submission's `dbo.CartMutationOperation.OperationId` is what identifies the attempt**, so an unknown commit outcome is settled by reading that row (requirement 4 of section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) rather than by re-merging under the same anonymous id. The withdrawal of the "keyed on the anonymous cart id" reading is stated in full below this table. **The gate itself is a provenance test rather than a shape test.** The value passed as `anonymousCartId` is the session's current key **only if all three of these hold**: it begins with the `anon:` namespace prefix; its remainder is exactly the 32-character lower-case hexadecimal form the issuing service writes; and the session additionally holds the **protected marker** that binds *that* key to *this* session and unprotects to a match. Where **any** of the three fails the step is **skipped, not performed**. **`Guid.TryParse` is explicitly not the gate**, and an earlier form of this row made it one: a shape test is wrong in *both* directions — it rejects every key the target actually issues, because `anon:`-prefixed values do not parse as GUIDs, and it admits the cart of an account whose user name happens to be GUID-shaped. The coverage assertions exist to fail exactly those two mistakes. The write itself is "reassign the rows whose cart id is *this* anonymous id", so a retry finds no rows and cannot double-assign. Retry behaviour is specified in full below rather than as a number. **The merge rule this step performs is section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s sum-and-delete, and nothing here restates or qualifies it**: contributions into an existing line are summed on `(CartId, AlbumId)`, the earliest `DateCreated` is retained, the source rows are deleted, and the whole step is idempotent through its ledger entry |
| 5 | **On success only:** `cartService.AssignSessionCartId(user.UserName)` — an explicit service method that writes the session slot through `IHttpContextAccessor`, so the controller still touches no session directly (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)) | **Omitting this step is a silent, total cart loss, and it is not obvious from reading the migration alone.** `GetCartId` writes the session slot **only when it is empty** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176] and otherwise returns whatever is already there [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] — so an anonymous visitor's GUID stays in session for the life of that session even after they sign in. With the rows now carrying the username and the session still naming the GUID, **every subsequent cart read returns nothing and the cart renders empty.** The source does this write explicitly at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39] and the port must too |
| 6 | `await signInManager.SignInAsync(user, model.RememberMe);` | **Last.** This is the only step that issues the authentication cookie, and it goes through `SignInManager` rather than `HttpContext.SignInAsync` for the scheme reason in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). If it throws, the handler calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` — undoing step 5, and **only** step 5 — and returns the generic failure, so a session can never name a username while unauthenticated. It does **not** reverse step 4's database write, and it is not meant to: see the invariants below |
| 7 | `if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(returnUrl) && Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)) { return Redirect(returnUrl); } return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");` — the one redirect rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) | Preserves the source's `RedirectToLocal` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:382-392] statement for statement: the same `Url.IsLocalUrl` test [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:384] and the same home-page fallback [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:390]. **`LocalRedirect(returnUrl)` is deliberately not used**, for the reason in section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths). **This step also writes the recovery notice** when the recovery cookie of step 4's failure branch is present on the request, which is what re-offers `RecoverCart` to a user who did not take the offer the first time |

**The schema precondition step 4 depends on, stated here because five other sections cite this one for
it.** The merge is well-defined only if a cart holds **at most one line per album**, so the catalog
schema carries a **unique index on `Cart(CartId, AlbumId)`**. It is created by its own migration in the
**post-transform catalog stage** section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) orders — after the
load, never before, because the shipped data can violate it: the `(CartId, AlbumId)` duplicate report of
section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) is the source's own sign-in rename showing through, and
creating a unique index over rows that violate it fails late. Two consequences follow, and both are
requirements rather than notes. **`Cart.CartId` must carry an explicit bounded length in its mapping**,
because an unfaceted `string` maps to the provider's unbounded type, which cannot be an index key column
at all; the entity-mapping table of section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) carries that requirement and cites this
paragraph, and `Order.Username` takes the same treatment on the same evidence gate. And **the
contribution path is an insert that falls back to a relative update on the index violation**, which is
section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 2 — the index
is what makes that fallback reachable, and without it two contributions of one album would insert two
rows and the merge would not be a merge.

**Uniform verification cost — a fixed-work service, not a dummy hash.** The tempting design here is a
`static readonly DummyPasswordHash` field, hashed once at startup, verified against on the unknown-user
path. It fails on two counts, one of them mechanical.

- **It does not compile as described.** A `static readonly` field cannot be initialized from an injected
  instance — `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` is registered per scope by the Identity call of stage 1
  item 3 (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), and a static field initializer has no
  access to any scope. Making the field non-static per controller would recompute a key derivation on
  **every** request that constructs the controller, which is a self-inflicted denial of service on the
  sign-in page.
- **Its constant-work claim is false across this application's population**, which is the more important
  half. This store holds hashes in **two formats at once** after the Identity migration: migrated
  accounts carry the legacy format, whose derivation is roughly a hundredth of the work of the format
  the target hasher produces, and an account is rewritten to the current format only when it next signs
  in successfully (section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)). A lockout, meanwhile,
  short-circuits **before** any derivation at all. So "one dummy derivation" produces three visibly
  different costs — cheap for a migrated account, expensive for a rehashed one, near-zero for a locked
  one — and the response time discloses which of the three a username is.

**The design.** One singleton, `UniformVerificationCost`, with two operations and a stated target:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **The target cost** | **The cost of the most expensive hash format present in the store**, which is the format the configured `PasswordHasherOptions` produces — the migrated legacy format is the cheap one, so the current format is the ceiling and the ceiling is what everything is padded up to. The value is derived from options rather than written down: the service reads `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>` and treats its iteration count as the target |
| **Construction** | A **singleton** taking `IOptions<PasswordHasherOptions>` — both are process-lifetime, so nothing scoped is captured — which constructs its own `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` and computes **one** reference hash over a cryptographically random 32-byte value in its constructor. The reference value is never persisted, never logged and not a literal. It is computed once per process, on first resolution, and never on a request path |
| **`SpendFullCostAsync`** | Performs one derivation at the target cost against the reference hash and discards the result. This is the unknown-account path, and it is also the fallback whenever no real derivation happened |
| **`TopUpAsync(storedHash, observation)`** | Spends **the difference** between the target cost and the work the real path already did, and it takes that fact as an **observation of the hasher** rather than as an inference from the sign-in result. Where the observation says no derivation ran, the difference is the whole target cost. Where it says one ran, the iteration count the decorator recorded is the work already spent — the legacy format is fixed at its own well-known count and the current format encodes its count — and a top-up derivation is performed over the reference salt for the remaining iterations using the same pseudo-random function. Where the difference is zero or negative — a hash already at or above the target — nothing is spent |
| **Where it runs** | Steps 2a and 3 of the sequence above, and the registration path of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) does **not** use it: `Register` resolves no account and reveals nothing by its timing, which is why step R2 replaces steps 2, 2a and 3 outright |

**Where the "a derivation ran" signal comes from — an observed fact, never an inferred one.** The
signal is produced by `RehashObservingPasswordHasher : IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`, a decorator
registered over the hasher Identity registers, and by nothing else:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Registration** | The three lines in stage 1 item 3 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), placed after `AddIdentity`, and **not** the two-type overload: the decorator is registered by a **factory** that takes the inner hasher from a **separate registration of the concrete `PasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>`**, because a decorator registered as the interface it also depends on resolves itself and the resolution recurses. That item states the mechanism and why the ordering matters; this row states only the lifetime, which is **scoped**, because what it records belongs to one request. The decorator wraps the framework hasher rather than subclassing it, which is the form [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) specifies for the artifact |
| **What it records** | On `VerifyHashedPassword(user, hashedPassword, providedPassword)` it writes, into the scoped `PasswordDerivationObservation`, that a derivation **ran** and the format marker and iteration count it read from `hashedPassword`'s encoded header; then it delegates and returns the inner result unchanged. It also sets **`RehashObserved`** where the inner result was `PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded` |
| **What it never does** | It performs no derivation of its own, changes no result, records no password, no hash and no user name, and takes no branch on what it observed. `HashPassword` is delegated untouched. **It emits nothing** — see the row below |
| **Who reads it, and with what semantics** | Two consumers of **one** scoped object. (1) `TopUpAsync` above reads `DerivationRan`, the format marker and the iteration count on the request path, **before** any store write and **without clearing them** — these three members are 05's, and they are deliberately **not** consume-once, because the top-up must be able to read them again in the same request without a second observation. (2) [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam-1 emitter reads `RehashObserved` and `UserInitiatedCredentialChange`, which **are** consume-once and are read in exactly one place. Nothing else reads or writes any member. Because the two sets are disjoint and only one set is cleared, the two consumers cannot interfere |
| **Who emits, and who owns that decision** | **Not this artifact, and not any code on the sign-in path.** The `ACCT-2002` record carrying `RehashedOnSignIn` is emitted by [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam-1 **artifact 2** — the `AuditingUserManager : UserManager<ApplicationUser>` subclass overriding the `protected virtual UpdateUserAsync(ApplicationUser)` — after `base` returns, and **only** where the returned `IdentityResult.Succeeded` is true, `RehashObserved` is set, and `UserInitiatedCredentialChange` is not. That document owns the seam, its emission condition, its failed-write diagnostic and its registration; this section owns only the composition root that registers the hasher and the scoped observation, and the `TopUpAsync` consumer above.
