The single registration of `AuditingUserManager` is stage 1 item 3's `AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, IdentityRole>().AddUserManager<AuditingUserManager>()` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so there is **one** user manager type and **one** hasher registration, not one per consumer |
| **Who sets `UserInitiatedCredentialChange`, which is this document's action to write** | The change-password action of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) sets it **before** it calls `ChangePasswordAsync`, because verifying the *current* password of an account still holding a legacy hash makes the hasher report `SuccessRehashNeeded` on a request that is a user action rather than an opportunistic rehash. Without the flag one credential change would produce two `ACCT-2002` records — the action's own and a spurious rehash one — which is the arithmetic section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) states as one change, one record |
| **Rejected form, recorded so the cheaper one is not reintroduced** | Emitting from this decorator, or from the controller reading the observation after `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` returns. Both were an earlier form of this section and both are wrong for one reason: `SuccessRehashNeeded` is the hasher's **advice, returned before persistence is attempted**, and `UserManager.CheckPasswordAsync` then performs the rehash write and **discards the `IdentityResult` it gets back** — so on a run where the store rejected the write, the observation is still set and either form writes an audit record asserting a credential change that never happened. The coverage assertion is the test that fails for both |

**Inferring the signal from `result.IsLockedOut` is wrong in both directions, and each direction is a
real timing channel.** It is worth stating explicitly because the expression reads as obviously correct:

- **True when no derivation ran.** `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` runs `PreSignInCheck` first, and that check
  short-circuits on more than lockout — an account the sign-in options do not permit to sign in returns
  before any verification, and an account whose `PasswordHash` is null fails inside
  `CheckPasswordAsync` **without invoking the hasher at all**. In each of those the result is not
  `LockedOut`, so `!IsLockedOut` is **true**, so the top-up spends only a "difference" against work that
  never happened — and the request answers measurably faster than an ordinary wrong password. The
  null-hash case is not hypothetical here: it is exactly the shape section
  [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
  rejects for the neutralization set, and rejects partly for this reason.
- **False when a derivation did run.** On the attempt that *crosses* the lockout threshold,
  `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` verifies the password — one full derivation — fails, calls
  `AccessFailedAsync`, finds the account now locked and returns `LockedOut`. So `!IsLockedOut` is
  **false**, and the top-up spends the **whole** target cost on top of the derivation already performed:
  that one request costs roughly double every other failure, which is a signature identifying the
  threshold-crossing attempt from the outside. Since the lockout policy of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) admits five failures before locking, that signature is
  reachable by an attacker who simply counts.

**Two honest limits, stated rather than papered over.** Iteration count is a proxy for cost, not cost
itself: fixed overheads, allocation and the store round trip are not iteration-proportional, so this
equalizes the **dominant** term rather than producing identical wall-clock times. And one asymmetry is
deliberate and irreducible: a wrong password against a real account performs the failed-attempt
accounting write that the lockout policy of section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) requires, and an unknown username has nothing to write.
Both are why the acceptance test is a **distribution comparison per population with a stated
tolerance** — **five** populations, rather than one median pair, which can be passed by an
implementation that leaves two of the five distinguishable:

| Population | Why it is its own population |
| --- | --- |
| **Unknown username** | Takes step 2a and never reaches the hasher; the only path with no store write to accompany the derivation |
| **Migrated legacy-format hash** (`V2`) | Its real derivation is roughly a hundredth of the target cost, so it is the population the top-up does the most work for |
| **Current-format hash** (`V3`) | Its real derivation is already at the target, so its top-up is nothing — the control against which the others are compared |
| **Already-locked account** | `PreSignInCheck` short-circuits, so **no** derivation runs and the whole target cost is spent by the top-up |
| **The threshold-crossing attempt** | A derivation **and** the lockout accounting write both happen on one request; it is the population the inferred flag got backwards, so a suite that omits it cannot detect the defect the observation above fixes |

Two fixture requirements make the comparison mean anything, and both follow from framework defaults
rather than from taste:

- **Every sample runs against a freshly provisioned account, or resets `AccessFailedCount` and
  `LockoutEnd` between samples.** Identity's defaults are `MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5`,
  `DefaultLockoutTimeSpan = 00:05:00` and `AllowedForNewUsers = true`, and the policy of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) keeps lockout enabled — so a run of two hundred
  wrong-password samples against **one** account locks it on the fifth and the remaining
  hundred-and-ninety-five measure the **locked-out** path instead of the password path. That is not a
  failed test; it is a test that passes while measuring the wrong thing, in the one place where the whole
  point is which population a timing belongs to. The threshold-crossing population is the exception that
  proves the rule: it is sampled by driving exactly five failures against a fresh account and timing the
  fifth, which is only possible if the fixture provisions accounts per sample.
- **The fixture raises the credential rate limits from configuration.** Two hundred samples against the
  `Login` POST would otherwise be refused from the eleventh, because the per-source credential bound of
  stage 1 item 14 admits ten per minute per address partition, and a fixture drives all its samples from
  one address. The limits are `RateLimiting:*` configuration
  rather than constants precisely so a fixture can widen them; the fixture does that and asserts the
  widening rather than partitioning its way around the limiter, so the samples measure the handler and
  not the limiter.

**The coverage assertion is that test**, and it is section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 104**,
which carries the per-population distribution comparison with a stated tolerance and a stated sample
size, asserts **both** of this section's two fixture requirements, and replaces the median-pair clause an
earlier revision of this section carried. **Row 96 is its companion and not a duplicate of it**: that row
owns the *response* oracle over the same five populations — status, `Location`, message and event class —
and states no timing, so a failure names which of the two contracts broke. [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md)
requires the timing row by name for finding **F-09-38**, and records there that a pair of matching
response bodies does not satisfy it.

**The cart-key isolation rule, and why step 4 is gated rather than unconditional.** Reassigning "the
rows under the session's current cart key" is not safe, because that key is not always an anonymous one.
`GetCartId` writes the **user name** into the session slot for an authenticated caller
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] and a fresh GUID only for an anonymous one
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172-175], and on any later request it returns whatever the slot already holds [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179]; `MigrateCart`
then reassigns **every** row carrying that value [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193]. And both anonymous entry points stay
reachable while already authenticated: `AccountController` carries a class-level `[Authorize]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:15] with `[AllowAnonymous]` on `Login` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:44],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:54] and on `Register` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:78], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:87], and `[AllowAnonymous]` **permits** an authenticated caller rather
than excluding one. So a caller signed in as A who posts `Login` — or `Register` — for B arrives at step
4 with the slot holding **A's own user name**, and an unconditional reassignment moves **A's cart to
B**. Nothing but A's own session is required for it, and the same shape lets A leave a username-keyed
slot behind for the next anonymous request in that session.

Three rules close it, and all three belong to the cart service rather than to the controller:

- **Migration input must be *proved* to be a server-issued anonymous key, and shape is not a proof.**
  `MigrateCartAsync` is called only when **both** of the tests below pass on the session's current cart
  key. Where either fails, step 4 is **skipped**: no rows are read, none are reassigned, and the sequence
  continues at step 5.

  **Why `Guid.TryParse` alone is insufficient, stated because the opposite is the intuitive reading.** A
  successful parse proves the *shape* of a value, not its *origin* — and a login name of that shape is
  legal in this application. The `AllowedUserNameCharacters` value this design sets — section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s 67-character set, which is also Identity's own default —
  is `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789-._@+`, and it admits every hexadecimal
  digit **and** the hyphen, so **both** `Guid` formats — the 32-character `N` form and the hyphenated `D`
  form — are spellable as user names under it. So "a user name cannot be mistaken for a GUID" is
  false as stated, and an account registered under a GUID-shaped name would have its **own** cart treated
  as an anonymous one and reassigned to whoever signed in next from that session. Two mechanisms close
  it, and both are required:

  - **A namespace no user name can occupy.** Anonymous keys are written as
    `"anon:" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N")` — a fixed prefix, then the 32-character form — and the test
    is the prefix plus a parse of the remainder, never a parse alone. The prefix is chosen for a
    mechanical reason rather than an aesthetic one: **`:` is absent from the framework's default allowed
    set quoted above and from section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)'s narrower set**, so
    no account can ever be created whose name begins `anon:`, and the two value spaces are disjoint by
    construction rather than by convention. `"N"` rather than `"D"` is chosen so the stored value has one
    canonical spelling and no hyphen-form variant to reconcile.
  - **A protected marker binding the key to *this* session.** The session additionally holds a
    data-protection-protected token — `IDataProtector` with a purpose string naming this use — whose
    payload is the anonymous key and the session id, and step 4 verifies it before any row moves. This is
    what makes the rule hold against a value **injected into the session** rather than issued by the
    server: the distributed session store is a database table (section
    [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)), so a session value is not automatically a server-issued one,
    and an unprotectable or mismatched marker fails the test even though the key's shape is perfect.
    The marker is written by the same service method that issues the key, and cleared by
    `ClearSessionCartId()` alongside it, so the two cannot drift apart — and **that holds because they
    travel in one session commit, not because two session entries are independently stored**. A session
    is one whole-blob, last-commit-wins entry (the concurrency rule of section
    [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)), so a concurrent request can lose **the pair together**, which
    leaves no key rather than a key without its marker; a marker that is missing anyway fails this test
    and skips step 4, which is the direction that is safe.

  **Legacy rows carrying the bare form are rewritten, and the rewrite is selected by owner rather than by
  shape — for the same reason the runtime gate is.** The source writes `Guid.NewGuid().ToString()` — the
  hyphenated `"D"` form with no prefix — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172-175] for an
  anonymous cart, and the signed-in user's **name** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167]
  for an owned one, into the same single column. So `Cart.CartId` values arriving from the domain data
  load hold both kinds, and "rewrite every `CartId` that parses as a `Guid`" would rewrite the cart of any
  account whose name is GUID-shaped — the exact collision this rule exists to close, reintroduced as a
  one-off data transformation. The load therefore selects on ownership, using a set the load already has:

  | Class of row | Test | Action |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Anonymous | `CartId` parses as a `Guid` **and** is **not** in the source user-name set, compared upper-invariant as Identity normalizes names | Rewritten to `"anon:" + <32 lower-case hex digits>`: lower-case the value, strip the hyphens, prepend the prefix. Deterministic, so a re-run produces byte-identical output |
  | Owned | `CartId` is in the source user-name set | **Not** rewritten. It is that account's cart, which is what the source writes for a signed-in user, and the prefix belongs to anonymous keys alone |
  | Ambiguous — GUID-shaped **and** in the user-name set | Both tests above are true | Falls under **owned** and is not rewritten, **and** is enumerated in the load report by user name with no cart contents. The ambiguity is pre-existing in the source, which stores both kinds in one column and cannot distinguish them either; the migration inherits it, resolves it in the direction that preserves the account's own items, and reports it rather than silently choosing |

  Three reconciliation assertions close the load, and the third is the one the runtime gate actually
  depends on: the count of rewritten rows equals the count of rows matching the anonymous test; every
  ambiguous row appears in the report; and **every** `CartId` in the loaded table is either in the user-name
  set or begins `anon:` — no third form remains. The rewritten form is **37 characters** — `anon:` at five,
  then the 32-digit `N` form — which is one more than the 36-character hyphenated value it replaces, and
  it is checked against a **bound** rather than against an unconstrained column: the target faces this
  column, and the width, its derivation and its overlength gate are the
  [cart-key width rule](#the-cart-key-width-rule) below. Sequencing the rewrite inside the load — after the user-name set exists and before the
  application reads the table — is [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s to carry as a gated step; the
  transformation, its selection rule and its assertions are stated here because this document owns the
  key format they produce.
- **The slot is cleared before any identity change.** A `Login` or `Register` POST arriving on an
  **already-authenticated** request calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` before step 2, so nothing
  crosses the identity boundary in either direction: the previous identity's key is not migrated, and it
  is not left in place for whoever holds that session next. The previous identity's cart is untouched —
  its rows stay keyed by that user name and reappear when that user signs in again, which is the
  source's own behaviour for a signed-in cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167].
- **Sign-out clears the slot too.** That is section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)'s rule and the third
  side of the same box: without it a username-keyed slot outlives the ticket that justified it.

The first two rules are **`D-40`** of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) and the third is **`D-41`**, because the skipped
migration is observable — an authenticated caller who signs in as somebody else no longer carries a cart
across, and an anonymous request after a sign-out no longer sees the signed-out user's items.
**The coverage assertions require two things of these three rules.** They require the account-switch
isolation on *both* entry points rather than on `Login` alone, and they require the sign-out half. The
provenance half needs its own three rows,
because none of the above would fail if the gate were a bare `Guid.TryParse`: **row 100** registers an
account whose user name is a 32-character hexadecimal string, signs it in from a session holding that
same string, and asserts **no** cart row moves; **row 101** writes a perfectly shaped `anon:` key into
the session store without its marker and asserts the same; and **row 103** posts `RecoverCart` with no
authentication and asserts a challenge with no row moved.

**The merge rule itself — one rule, stated here because two other sections cite this one for it.** Step 4
is a **merge**, not a rewrite of one key over a whole cart. Section
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 5 cites this
sub-section for the rule its locked consumption implements, and section
[5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) cites it for the **sum-and-earliest** rule its one-time duplicate
reconciliation applies over historical rows. One rule serves both, and it is this:

| Element | The rule |
| --- | --- |
| **The unit** | One **line** — one `(CartId, AlbumId)` pair — never the cart as a whole. The merge enumerates the source cart's lines and settles each one, so an over-bound line fails alone (requirement 3 of section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) and every other line still merges |
| **Destination already holds the album** | The destination row's `Count` is **raised by the source line's `Count`**, its `DateCreated` becomes the **earlier** of the two — so the cart shows when the customer first chose the album rather than when they signed in — and the **superseded source row is deleted** |
| **Destination does not hold the album** | That source row's **`CartId` is rewritten** to the destination key. Its `RecordId` and `DateCreated` are unchanged, which is what keeps the moved line's own age intact and is why the merge rewrites rather than inserting a copy and deleting the original |
| **Every statement** | Token-conditional and exact: each carries the row's `RowVersion` witness in its predicate and asserts an **affected count of exactly 1** (requirement 5 of section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)). Anything else rolls the whole merge back |
| **`ModifiedUtc`** | Assigned **explicitly in every statement**, because none of them passes through `SaveChangesAsync` and so none runs the maintenance path the change-tracking group of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) defines; omitting it would leave the column stale on exactly the rows a rollback decision reads ([06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). `nowUtc` is captured **once, outside** the delegate, so the value is attempt-invariant |
| **The transaction** | **One** catalog transaction for the whole merge, opened inside the delegate the execution strategy runs (below), holding the alias-row take or insert, the locked enumeration, the per-line statements, the ledger rows and the deletions. Nothing outside the database is inside it |
| **Provenance and idempotence** | **The ledger row, and nothing else**: `dbo.CartMutationOperation`, keyed by an operation id generated **once per sign-in submission** (requirement 4 of section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)), written inside the same transaction, and read by `verifySucceeded` when a commit's outcome is unknown |
| **Its precondition** | The **unique index on `(CartId, AlbumId)`**, per the paragraph below |

**The key rewrite is not a fourth member of requirement 2's statement table.** That table enumerates the
shapes a **quantity** mutation takes, and the rewrite changes no quantity. It belongs to the merge's own
authored-SQL site — the one requirement 2's census attributes to requirements 5 and 6 — and is held to
that site's rule without exception: every value is a parameter.

**The precondition is a schema object, and its staging is stated once here.** The rule above depends on
the **unique index on `(CartId, AlbumId)`**: the index is what makes "already holds the album" a decision
the database settles rather than a race between a read and a write, and what makes a split line
unrepresentable rather than merely unintended. The index is target-only. It ships in the named
post-baseline migration **`AddCartMergeConstraints`** of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction), **applied before traffic is admitted**,
and there is no pre-load cart migration of any kind. It cannot be applied any earlier, and the obstacle
is the data rather than the sequence: the source declares no such uniqueness, so the load **preserves and
reports** the duplicate pairs it finds (section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)) and the index
would fail to build on the loaded table. The staging is therefore one order and admits no other — **the
load, then the duplicate reconciliation that report is the input to, then `AddCartMergeConstraints`, then
traffic** — and that reconciliation collapses each historical group under **the same sum-and-earliest
rule above**, recording the lineage section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) requires. One rule
applied twice: once over history by a one-time transformation, once per sign-in at runtime.

<a id="the-cart-key-width-rule"></a>
**The bound on the cart key and on the ownership key — the requirement three other sites cite this section
for, stated here in full because it was promised and never written.** The extraction table of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) says of `Cart.CartId` that "this mapping
must give it the explicit bounded length section 4.3 requires before the unique index can exist at all",
and says of `Order.Username` that it takes "the same explicit bounded length … on the same evidence gate";
section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) says the same of both of
`CartAlias`'s id columns. Those three forward references had no destination, and one bullet above them
asserted the opposite — that `CartId` "is an unconstrained string with no length attribute
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:10], so the five added characters need no schema change". **That
sentence is withdrawn.** It is true of the *source* column and false of the target's, and it drew the
wrong conclusion from a true premise: the source's column is unfaceted, which is precisely why the target
has to face it, and an unfaceted `string` property maps to `nvarchar(max)`, which cannot be an index key
column at all. **Four statements replace it, and together they are the requirement.**

- **The width is `nvarchar(256)`, and it is derived rather than picked.** It applies to `Cart.CartId`, to
  `Order.Username`, and to both of `CartAlias`'s `SourceCartId` and `DestinationCartId`. All four hold one
  value space — a login name, or an anonymous key in the disjoint `anon:` namespace above — and the widest
  member of that space is fixed by a column this document does not own: ASP.NET Core Identity's own model
  configuration declares `AspNetUsers.UserName` as `nvarchar(256)`, which is the alignment section
  [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) already applies to the
  account models' `UserName` maximum. A login name that cannot be stored in `AspNetUsers` cannot reach
  either of these columns, so 256 is not a policy choice but the ceiling of the value space, and matching
  it exactly is what keeps `Order.Username`'s ownership comparison
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73] and `Cart.CartId`'s owned form
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] able to hold every value the other can.
- **The key arithmetic, which is the reason the number has to be stated rather than left to a convention.**
  The unique index on `Cart(CartId, AlbumId)` that the block above makes load-bearing has a two-column
  key: `nvarchar(256)` at two bytes per character, plus a four-byte `int`. **2 × 256 + 4 = 516 bytes**,
  against SQL Server's 900-byte limit for a non-clustered index key — inside it with 384 bytes of
  headroom, and no `INCLUDE` restructuring or hash-column substitute needed. The arithmetic also bounds
  any future widening: 2n + 4 ≤ 900 gives **n ≤ 448**, so 448 is the largest width at which this index is
  buildable as specified, and above it the index — not the width — is what has to be re-decided.
- **The evidence gate: the bound is asserted against the extracted data before anything is written, not
  discovered when a migration fails.** The bound ships in `AddCartMergeConstraints`, which the staging
  above applies **after** the load, so an overlength row loaded into the still-unfaceted column would
  surface as an `ALTER` that cannot complete — the same late, opaque failure the duplicate-pair
  reconciliation exists to keep off that step. Step 1's extraction therefore records the source width and
  the **longest stored value** of `Cart.CartId` and of `Order.Username`, and the load's preflight — the
  same pass that runs the user-name character and normalized-collision checks — reports both, together
  with the **longest value the rewrite will produce**. A rewritten anonymous key is exactly **37**
  characters (`anon:` at 5, then the 32-digit `N` form), so the rewrite cannot be what breaches a bound of
  256; the measured maxima can be, and they are what the gate reads.
- **What happens when a value does not fit — refuse, or widen by approval, and never truncate.** Three
  outcomes, and the ordering between them is fixed: every measured and every post-rewrite value at or
  below the width, and the bound applies as specified; a value above it, and the sub-command **exits `2`
  having written nothing**, naming the column, the measured maximum, the offending row count and the
  width, exactly as the character check does; or the width is **raised by the data owner's approval** to a
  value that still satisfies 2n + 4 ≤ 900, at which point the census below carries the approved width and
  this arithmetic is recomputed against it. Truncation is refused outright and the refusal is not a
  preference: `Cart.CartId` and `Order.Username` are compared for **exact string equality** against the
  authenticated principal's name, so a silently shortened value detaches that account from its cart or
  from its order history with no error raised anywhere and nothing to reconcile against later — the same
  irrecoverable loss the no-renaming rule of section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) exists to prevent, arriving by a different route.

**The bulk reassignment is withdrawn, and it is withdrawn because it loses a line rather than because it
is coarse.** An earlier revision of this step specified the write as a single set-based statement over the
whole cart — `db.Carts.Where(c => c.CartId == anonymousCartId).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.CartId, userName), ct)` —
which is the source's own shape [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193] and **preserves
duplicates by construction**: a visitor holding album 12 anonymously who signs in already holding album
12 ends with **two** rows for one album. Under the index above that statement fails outright on a
unique-index violation — which the classification below deliberately does **not** retry — so no merge
happens at all; without the index the two rows split one line, and the add path's own `SingleOrDefault`
resolution [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:37-39] then throws on the next add of that
album. It is not a coarser implementation of this rule but a different rule, and it is gone.

**Withdrawn with it: the reading that made the anonymous cart id the idempotence key.** "Keyed on the
anonymous cart id, so a replay finds no rows" is a property of that statement and not of this one,
because a contribution into an existing line is **relative** — `Count = Count + @n`. Consuming each
source row inside the same transaction as the contribution it feeds does make a replay a no-op, and that
property is retained and relied on; it is nonetheless **the ledger** that settles an unknown commit
outcome, because requirement 4 of section
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) admits no exception and one writer
exempted from it is one writer running a different rule. Section
[4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s retry-safety table states the merge
on that basis.

**This is approved delta D-16** of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — cart migration
becomes a merge — and nothing in this sub-section widens it.

**Step 4's retry behaviour, stated as a mechanism rather than a count.** "Up to three attempts" names no
classifier and no execution model, and the wrong reading of it is a `catch`/`retry` loop wrapped around
an explicit transaction, which either replays a half-applied transaction or throws before it retries
anything. **It was also the wrong count.** This step states **no count of its own**: the strategy is the
one registered in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) item 2, its parameters are the ones section
[4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) supplies, and the arithmetic that follows from them is
stated there — `maxRetryCount` counts **retries after the first execution**, so the default 5 is **six
executions in total**, and `maxRetryDelay` caps **each individual delay** rather than their sum. Six
things are fixed here, and none of them is a number:

- **Who classifies a failure as transient: the provider.** The `EnableRetryOnFailure(…)` call of section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) item 2 — with `errorNumbersToAdd: null` — installs the
  provider's retrying execution strategy, whose transient set is its own list of
  SQL Server and Azure SQL error numbers plus the timeout and broken-connection cases. **No error number
  is added to it**: widening that set by hand is how a constraint violation becomes something the
  application retries. Anything the strategy does not classify as transient — a unique-index violation, a
  login failure, a permission failure — is **not retried** and takes the failure branch below on its
  first occurrence.
- **What is retried: a delegate, not a statement — and the transaction is the strategy's, not this
  step's.** Step 4 needs an explicit transaction, and under a retrying strategy EF Core **refuses** a
  user-initiated one: `BeginTransactionAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException`, for the reason section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) states in full. So the call is
  `await db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteInTransactionAsync(operation: async ct => { … }, verifySucceeded: async ct => { … }, cancellationToken)`
  — the **wrapper** opens the transaction and commits it, and the delegate contains the reassignment
  statements and nothing else. `BeginTransactionAsync` and `CommitAsync` are **not called on this path
  and must not be**; the single shape and the deletion of the two-shape reading are section
  [4.10](#410-azure-sql-connection-resilience--bounded-retries-and-the-transactions-that-must-wrap-them)'s.
- **What the replay boundary implies for the delegate's contents.** A retry re-runs the delegate **from
  the beginning** against a new connection and a new transaction, so its body must be safe to run twice.
  It contains no session write, no cookie write, no `TempData` write, no user-visible outcome and no
  in-memory mutation the caller depends on — steps 5 and 6 are outside it by construction — and a replay
  after a commit whose acknowledgement was lost is **settled by the ledger**: the merge is invoked through
  the `verifySucceeded` overload, that callback finds this submission's operation row present, and the
  strategy reports the recorded result rather than contributing a second time (requirement 4 of section
  [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)).
- **The change tracker is *not* reset between attempts, so this delegate is written to hold no tracked
  state at all.** This is the hazard "safe to run twice" does not close on its own, because it is not
  about side effects — it is about state the replay silently *inherits*. `ExecuteInTransactionAsync`
  re-runs the delegate against a new connection and a new transaction, but the `DbContext` and its change
  tracker are the **same instance** across every attempt, and `SaveChangesAsync` marks the entries it
  accepted `Unchanged` when it returns. So the sequence *load the rows, set `CartId`, `SaveChangesAsync`
  succeeds, the wrapper's commit fails transiently* leaves those entries `Unchanged` while the transaction
  has rolled
  back: the replay's `SaveChangesAsync` finds nothing to send, affects zero rows, commits an empty
  transaction and **reports success having moved nothing.** Step 5 then writes the user name into the
  session, the rows are still under the anonymous key, and the cart renders empty — a silent, total loss
  that raises no exception and that a happy-path test cannot see. Two requirements close it, and both are
  mandatory:
  - **`MigrateCartAsync`'s writes are set-based and track nothing.** Every statement the merge issues is
    one of those the merge rule above defines — the token-conditional contribution, the token-conditional
    key rewrite, and the token-conditional deletion of each consumed source row — issued inside the
    delegate's transaction, with **each statement's affected row count the only outcome the delegate
    reads** and each asserted to be exactly 1. Nothing is materialized, nothing is tracked, and there is
    therefore no accepted state for a replay to inherit; what makes the replay itself safe is the ledger
    read named in the previous bullet rather than the statements happening to match no rows.
  - **The delegate's first statement is an explicit `db.ChangeTracker.Clear();`, asserted by a test
    rather than assumed.** With the statement-based form above there is nothing to clear and the call costs
    nothing — which is the point: it is a **named attempt-state precondition** that survives a later edit
    reintroducing tracked mutation into this delegate, and without it that edit would reintroduce the
    silent loss above with no failing test. Resolving a **fresh `DbContext` per attempt** is the
    equivalent fix and is deliberately **not** chosen: the catalog context is request-scoped and
    constructor-injected (section [4.1](#41-the-ten-manual-instantiation-sites-constructor-injection-replaces)),
    and creating a second one inside a retry delegate would leave two catalog contexts live in one
    request for steps 5 through 7 — and for the cart summary the layout renders — to disagree over.
- **Backoff: the strategy's own exponential backoff with jitter, and the worst case is arithmetic rather
  than an impression — but the arithmetic is not performed here.** Each delay is drawn below the
  `maxRetryDelay` ceiling, the ceiling is **per delay and not aggregate**, and the number of delays is
  one fewer than the number of executions. **The worst-case envelope this produces, and the bound it has
  to fit inside, are section [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s** — that section owns the
  values, multiplies them out, and states which of the two bounds on the interval binds. This bullet
  owns only the two properties a reader of *this* step needs: the wait is bounded rather than open, and
  **the sign-in is not held for it** — the failure branch below signs the user in regardless, so a longer
  wait buys nothing the notice does not already deliver, which is why this step never argues for a larger
  per-delay ceiling.
- **Cancellation is not a transient failure.** The request's token is passed into
  `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` and into
  `SaveChangesAsync`; the strategy observes it between attempts and does not retry a cancelled
  operation. An `OperationCanceledException` carrying that token terminates the sequence under rule 4 of
  section [4.16](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once) — the client
  has gone, so there is nobody to sign in and nobody to show a notice to, and steps 5 through 7 do not
  run. A cancellation exception carrying a **foreign** token is not absorbed.

**The coverage assertion requires the two directions that distinguish this from a loop**: a retriable
failure injected once completes the reassignment and signs the user in with no notice, and a non-retriable
one takes the failure branch on its first occurrence without a second attempt.

**The failure branch of step 4, and the durable state it leaves.** If cart migration still fails after
its retries — or fails on a non-retriable error — the handler **continues to step 6 and signs the user
in**, skipping step 5, and surfaces a non-blocking notice. A failed sign-in is not recoverable by the
user at all, whereas an unreassigned cart is, which is why the sign-in proceeds. Within that session
nothing is even visibly wrong: step 5 was skipped, so the session still names the anonymous cart id whose
rows still exist, **the user keeps their items**, and a checkout bills them correctly because the order
is written against their user name regardless of the cart's key.

**Leaving the session pointing at those rows is not, however, a recovery mechanism.** The session's idle
timeout is twenty minutes, sliding (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so the
moment it lapses the only link between that browser and those rows is gone and the rows are orphaned —
and the fault that most plausibly caused the failure is a database fault, which is also a **session**
fault, because the session store is that same database (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)).
The recovery link therefore has to survive session expiry and a process restart, and it must not live in
the store that just failed.

**The recovery ticket.** On this branch the handler writes one single-purpose cookie,
`MvcMusicStore.CartRecovery`, whose payload is **data-protection protected** and carries exactly four
fields — the anonymous cart id, the user name the reassignment is pending for, an absolute expiry, and an
**exhausted-attempt counter** initialized to zero, which the exhausted-retry branch below increments and
re-protects. It is `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, host-only, `Path=/`, with a fixed lifetime of
**seven days** and no sliding renewal. Five properties follow from that shape:

- **It survives what session does not.** Nothing about it is stored server-side, so session expiry, a
  session-store outage and an instance restart all leave it intact; the persisted key ring of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is what lets a different replica read it.
  **This property has no case in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**, and it is named here rather
  than left to be inferred from the shape: every recovery case in that matrix posts the ticket to the
  same running host inside the same session, so each of them would pass against an implementation that
  had put the ticket in session after all. Reaching it needs a **pre-request state or a second host** —
  an expired session, a session store made to fail, or the same protected cookie presented to a host
  restarted over the same persisted key ring — which is the one shape an extra request inside an existing
  case cannot supply. It is coverage limit **18** of section
  [12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests), with the branches below.
- **It cannot be forged into somebody else's cart.** The payload is protected rather than merely encoded,
  so a caller cannot substitute an anonymous cart id they never held — which an unprotected cookie or a
  client-supplied parameter would allow, an anonymous key being a guessable, unauthenticated string
  whatever its spelling.
- **It is honoured only for the identity it names.** Recovery reassigns only when the authenticated
  principal's user name **equals** the name in the payload; otherwise the ticket is deleted and nothing
  is written.
- **It is the provenance evidence on its own path, and it does not — must not — require a live session
  marker.** This is where the two provenance mechanisms of the isolation rule above divide, and the
  division is deliberate rather than a gap:
  - **In-session migration (step 4)** proves provenance from the session: the `anon:` namespace plus the
    protected session marker bound to *this* session id.
  - **Recovery** proves it from the **ticket**: the payload is protected, so its anonymous cart id was
    written by the server and has not been altered, and it was issued **only** on a branch where the
    session-marker gate had already passed — a ticket cannot exist for a key that never satisfied it.
    Provenance is therefore established once, at issue time, and carried forward cryptographically.

  Requiring the session marker on the recovery path as well would make recovery impossible in exactly the
  cases it exists for: session expiry, a session-store outage and an instance restart all destroy the
  marker, and those are the three conditions the ticket was introduced to survive. So recovery verifies
  the ticket and the caller's identity, and does **not** consult the session marker; the key's namespace
  is still checked, because a ticket naming a non-`anon:` key could only come from a defect and is
  refused rather than trusted.
- **It is single-use and self-clearing.** The cookie is deleted on success, and equally when the payload
  cannot be unprotected, when it has expired, when its user name does not match the caller, when its
  anonymous cart id is not in the `anon:` namespace, and when that id names no rows — so a stale or
  malformed ticket cannot accumulate work.

**Where recovery runs — two places, both of them endpoints, and neither of them middleware.** First, at
the start of the next `Login` or `Register` POST that reaches step 4: the ticket is consumed there, with
the same execution strategy and the same idempotence, before the current session's own migration.
Second, through an **explicit action** — `POST /ShoppingCart/RecoverCart` — reached by the conventional
route of stage 2 item 13 in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order):

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Signature** | `[HttpPost] [Authorize] [RequestSizeLimit(2 * 1024)] public async Task<IActionResult> RecoverCart(CancellationToken cancellationToken)`. It takes no input at all: the anonymous cart id and the pending owner come from the protected cookie, never from the request. Anti-forgery validation arrives from the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) — it is **not** an entry in that section's opt-out register |
| **How it is offered** | A `TempData` notice on the sign-in or registration redirect (the notice mechanism below) renders, in the shared layout, a one-button form posting to this action. The user chooses to recover; nothing recovers on their behalf behind a page they did not submit |
| **Guards, in order** | The cookie must be present; its payload must unprotect; it must be unexpired; its user name must equal the authenticated caller's; its anonymous cart id must be in the `anon:` namespace; and its exhausted-attempt counter must be below three — the ticket's properties above, in the order that fails cheapest first. A failure of any one **deletes the cookie, writes nothing, and redirects to `/ShoppingCart`** with no notice; there is no error page for a stale ticket. The session marker is deliberately **not** among the guards, for the reason the ticket's provenance property gives |
| **The write** | Step 4's merge verbatim — the one merge rule above, over the lines of the cart the ticket names, inside the same execution strategy and the same single transaction, with its own ledger row carrying the operation id this submission generates. On success step 5's `AssignSessionCartId` runs, the cookie is deleted, and the action redirects to `/ShoppingCart` so the user sees the items they came back for |
| **Where it must not be** | **Not pre-endpoint middleware**, and the three reasons are separate. It would run on **safe methods** — an ordinary authenticated `GET`, a health probe, a violation report — which makes a state change reachable by navigation. It would run **before** MVC's anti-forgery filter, so a `POST` whose token is invalid would have mutated before it was rejected (section [7.1](#71-the-policy)). And `UseExceptionHandler` **re-executes the pipeline**, so a middleware that faults faults again while rendering `/Home/Error` — the recursion section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) exists to prevent, arriving from the one place that section does not look. **Not the cart service's read path** either: the cart badge renders from a view component on every page (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)) and a view component must not write (the coverage assertion) |

Either way the write is the same ledger-keyed merge, so a ticket consumed twice contributes once: the
second consumption finds the operation row already present and returns its recorded result.

**Recovery has an exhausted-retry branch, and it is the branch that keeps one database fault from
becoming a fault on every request.** A recovery attempt is classified and bounded exactly as step 4 is:
the provider's retrying execution strategy decides what is transient, and **the same registration and the
same values** — section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) item 2 and section
[4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) — bound the executions and the backoff, and
cancellation is not a transient failure. **The same attempt-state precondition applies unchanged**, and it
is not optional here either: the writes are the same set-based, token-conditional statements the merge
rule defines, the delegate opens with the same `db.ChangeTracker.Clear();`, and the timestamp is captured
once outside it — so a commit that fails after a successful save replays the write rather than replaying
an empty transaction, and a commit whose outcome is unknown is settled by the same ledger read. What is stated here is what happens when that bound is reached:

- **Transient, retries exhausted.** The cookie is **kept** — the pending reassignment is still pending
  and still recoverable — and the action returns its redirect with a `TempData` notice offering the
  button again. Exactly **one** `Warning` record is written under the event name **`CartMigrationRetried`**
  with an **`outcome`** of the single literal **`retriesExhausted`**, carrying the failure category, the trace
  identifier and **`cartKeyHash`**, and no provider message (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). **It carries the pseudonym and not the anonymous cart
  id, and an earlier form of this bullet carried the id itself** — which section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s never-logged list forbids by name: the raw cart key
  reaches a record only as `cartKeyHash`, the salted truncated pseudonym of that section's rule, keyed by
  `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`. The pseudonym is computed over the same anonymous key, so it still groups
  every record of one visitor's recovery attempts together and still counts how many visitors a fault
  reached, which is the whole of what this record is read for; what it stops doing is publishing a live
  cart key into a store [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) retains. Nothing else about the
  request changes: the user stays signed in and every other page still works.

  **The `outcome` member is stated because an earlier form of this sentence omitted it**, and this is an
  `R8` record that section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s producer table assigns:
  [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R8` row requires an outcome literal from the
  producer's own closed set, and this producer's set has exactly one member because the record is written
  on exactly one branch — a transient failure whose bounded retry is spent. The failure category and the
  outcome are two different fields and neither substitutes for the other: the category names *what* the
  provider raised, the outcome names *where in the recovery the request stopped*.

  **An earlier form of that sentence had this record carry "the anonymous cart id", and it is withdrawn
  rather than qualified**, because it named a field the prohibition list of section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) forbids in terms: *"the **raw** cart key or session id,
  which reach a record only as `cartKeyHash`"*. The raw value here is the session GUID the anonymous
  visitor's cart is keyed by [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-179] — session material,
  and the correlation handle for every other record that visitor's session produced — so writing it to a
  log store is the disclosure that list exists to close. The substitute is the one this document already
  uses for every cart-scoped record, including the mutation-retry record of section
  [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity): the salted, truncated
  `cartKeyHash` of [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), keyed by
  `Telemetry:CartKeyHashSalt`. It costs the investigation nothing that the raw id bought — the records of
  one failing recovery still group together and are still countable across visitors — because the
  reassignment is keyed from the **protected ticket** rather than from anything in the log, so no operator
  procedure ever needed to read the id back out of a record.
- **Non-transient.** The failure branch on its first occurrence, with the same single record and the
  same notice, and no second attempt. **This branch has no case either, and it is a different gap from
  the exhausted-retry branch that does**: row 36 `36a` drives the transient failure to exhaustion under
  the every-execution injection, so an implementation that treated a non-transient failure as retriable
  — attempting it again, or recording twice — would still satisfy that case. Separating the two needs an
  injection that raises a **non-transient** error number on the recovery path, which is its own injection
  lifetime rather than an extra request. It is coverage limit **18** of section
  [12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests).
- **The ticket is not retried indefinitely across requests either, and the boundary is stated as a guard
  rather than as a count.** The payload's fourth field — the exhausted-attempt counter named in the
  ticket's inventory above — is incremented and the payload re-protected on **every** exhausted attempt.
  The guard runs **before** any database work: a post arriving with the counter **already at three** —
  which is the fourth post, the first three having each attempted and exhausted — makes **no further
  reassignment attempt at all**, deletes the cookie, and renders the final notice saying the cart could
  not be restored. So three posts attempt and record, and the fourth deletes without attempting, which is
  exactly the sequence **the coverage assertion drives**; stating it as "at three exhausted attempts the
  cookie is deleted" is the ambiguity that lets an implementation delete on the third post and fail that
  row.
  The counter lives inside the protected payload rather than in a separate cookie or in session so that
  it cannot be reset by the caller and cannot be lost by the store whose failure is being counted.
  The rows are then abandoned anonymous rows, which is the pre-existing ceiling stated below rather
  than a new one.
- **No path leaves a persistent per-request fault.** Because recovery is an endpoint the user posts to,
  a failing recovery affects **that** request and no other, and the error page — which posts nothing —
  cannot re-enter it. **The coverage assertion requires exactly this**: recovery made to fail on every
  attempt, with the ordinary pages and `/Home/Error` still answering normally throughout.

Nothing in the failure text names an exception, a store or a connection detail, under the
permitted-content rule of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types).

**The notice mechanism is named, because "a non-blocking notice" does not survive a redirect by itself.**
The branch ends in step 7's redirect, so the message is written to **`TempData`**: read once, on the next
request, and gone afterwards — it survives **exactly one** redirect and no more. It uses the framework's
default **cookie-backed** `TempData` provider rather than a session-backed one, deliberately, because the
failure being reported may be a fault in the very store a session-backed provider would write to, which
would lose the notice for exactly the request that needs it. The text names no exception detail and no
store detail, under the permitted-content rule of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types).

**The notice is also what carries the recovery offer, and the ticket outlives it deliberately.** The
notice renders the one-button form that posts to `RecoverCart`, so the offer is present on exactly the
page the user lands on after the failed sign-in. Because `TempData` survives one redirect and the
protected cookie survives seven days, the two are not the same lifetime and the difference is handled
rather than ignored: **step 7 writes the notice whenever the recovery cookie is present on a successful
sign-in or registration**, not only on the request that created the ticket. So a user who ignored the
offer is offered it again the next time they sign in, and no request outside that path — no `GET`, no
probe, no error page — is asked to do anything about it.

**The durable state on this branch is therefore:** rows under the anonymous id, a protected recovery
ticket naming those rows and their pending owner, the user signed in, one notice shown offering
`RecoverCart`, and a deterministic point at which the reassignment completes. Past the ticket's expiry the rows are
unreachable anonymous rows — indistinguishable from an abandoned anonymous cart, which the source
already leaves behind whenever an anonymous session lapses
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176] — so the ceiling on this failure mode is the
pre-existing one rather than a worse one. The coverage assertion requires recovery **after the session has
expired** and **after a restart**, which is the pair the session-only story failed.

**The invariants this achieves, stated so a reviewer can check them — and the one that does *not* hold,
stated because a looser version of it would be false.**

Two invariants hold, and they are the ones worth having:

- **Cart rows are reassigned only after the credentials have been verified and the Identity-side writes
  committed.** Step 4 cannot run unless step 3 returned `Succeeded`, so a caller who fails
  authentication — wrong password, unknown account, locked out — never causes a catalog write of any
  kind.
- **A session never names a username unless a cookie was issued for that username.** Step 5 is the only
  writer of that session value, it runs only after step 4 succeeds, and step 6's compensation removes it
  if the cookie is not issued. This is the security-relevant one: without the compensation an
  unauthenticated request in that session would resolve `GetCartId` to the username
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] and read and modify that user's cart.

**What does not hold, and is not claimed: "no cart row ever carries a username unless a sign-in
completed."** If step 6 throws, steps 4 and 5 have already run, the rows already carry the username, and
**`ClearSessionCartId()` does not move them back** — nothing in this sequence does. That residual state
is accepted deliberately, for three reasons:

- **It is not readable by anyone else.** The rows are keyed by the username, and the only session value
  that resolves to a username is the one step 5 writes and step 6's compensation removes. An anonymous
  visitor's key is a fresh prefixed anonymous key, issued where the source issues a bare GUID
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-176], and the `anon:` namespace **cannot** be
  occupied by a login name for the character-set reason given with the isolation rule above — so no other
  visitor, and not the same visitor while anonymous, can reach those rows.
- **Nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated.** At the next successful sign-in, step 4 finds no rows
  under the new anonymous id (there are none to move) and step 5 points the session at the username, so
  the same items reappear exactly once. What stops the second run double-assigning is **not** the
  anonymous id: it is that the merge **consumes** each source row in the same transaction as the
  contribution it feeds, so the next run has nothing to move, and that the attempt itself is identified
  by its own `dbo.CartMutationOperation.OperationId` row (requirement 4 of section
  [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)).
- **A compensating reassignment would add a failure mode rather than remove one.** Writing the rows back
  to the anonymous id is itself a database write that can fail, leaving the identical state plus a
  second error to handle; and the realistic cause of a throw at step 6 is a data-protection key-ring
  fault (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), which says nothing
  about the catalog store and would not be repaired by touching it.

The converse case — a signed-in user whose rows did **not** move, from the step 4 failure branch above —
is likewise permitted deliberately, because it is the recoverable direction, and the recovery ticket of
that branch is what makes "recoverable" a mechanism rather than a hope.

A third invariant holds because of the isolation rule, and it is the one the reachability of `Login` and
`Register` while authenticated would otherwise break: **no cart row is ever reassigned from one account
to another.** Every path that moves cart rows requires provenance evidence for the key it is moving, and
there are exactly two admissible forms: step 4 requires the `anon:` namespace **plus** a valid protected
session marker bound to the current session, and recovery requires a valid protected **ticket** whose
payload names both an `anon:` key and the authenticated caller — issued, as the ticket's properties state,
only where the session-marker form had already held. Neither form can be satisfied by a value that names
an account's cart, **including an account whose own name is GUID-shaped**, because an account name cannot
begin `anon:` under either character-set policy. A GUID-shaped user name is therefore no longer a way in
on either path.

**All six failure paths need tests** (the coverage assertions): cart migration failing
after its retries must still produce a successful sign-in **with the notice and with the items still
visible**; an Identity-side failure must produce **no** cart reassignment and **no** cookie; recovery
must complete after the session has expired and after a restart; a non-retriable failure must not be
retried; and recovery failing on **every** attempt must bound itself and leave every other request
working.

**The `Register` POST is the same sequence, and the source is why — not an analogy.** It is easy to read
registration as account creation followed by a redirect, and that reading is wrong here. `Register`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:89-104] calls **the same private helper `Login`
calls** — `await SignInAsync(user, isPersistent: false)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:97] against
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] — and that helper is the whole orchestration:
external-cookie sign-out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:348], identity creation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:349], the sign-in grant [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:350] and **then**
`MigrateShoppingCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:353] with its own context, its `SaveChanges` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:37] and its session-key rewrite
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39]. So registration today issues a cookie, reassigns the anonymous cart and rewrites the session
slot, in exactly the order `Login` does — **including the reversal this section exists to correct.** A
port that gives the safe sequence to `Login` alone reintroduces the original defect on the other
anonymous entry point, and it does so where it is *most* likely to bite: registering is the one moment a
visitor is guaranteed to have been anonymous a request ago, so a pre-registration cart is the normal case
rather than an edge one.

`Register` therefore runs **steps 4 through 7 of the table above, unchanged**, with its own first two
steps in front of them. The differences are only the ones the source's own signature forces:

| Step | Call | How it differs from the `Login` sequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | `if (!ModelState.IsValid) return View(model);` | **No difference.** Step 1, and the registration-path counterpart named by the input-bounds rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) — the bound is enforced here, before `CreateAsync` and before any insert |
| R2 | `var result = await userManager.CreateAsync(user, model.Password);` | **Replaces steps 2, 2a and 3.** There is no account to resolve, so no enumeration-timing problem and no dummy-hash step; there is no stored hash to verify or rehash, and no lockout accounting to apply. Identity hashes the password inside this call. `result.Succeeded == false` redisplays the form with the per-error messages the source's `AddErrors` produces [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:102], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:356-362], and — being an Identity validation outcome rather than a credential outcome — it is the `ACCT-2001` event at its `ValidationFailed` outcome, never an `AUTH-1002` one. **This is the step whose writes must be committed before R3**, exactly as step 3 is |
| R3 | Step 4 verbatim: `await cartService.MigrateCartAsync(anonymousCartId, user.UserName, cancellationToken)`, own transaction, with the anonymous cart id as the **source selector** and this submission's `dbo.CartMutationOperation.OperationId` as the idempotence witness, gated on **step 4's three-part provenance test** — the `anon:` namespace prefix, the 32-character lower-case hexadecimal remainder, and a matching protected session marker — and executed through the retrying execution strategy specified for step 4 | **No difference, and not optional.** The source performs it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:353] and the anonymous cart it moves is the items the visitor added before registering. Both of step 4's guards apply unchanged, and **that provenance gate — not a GUID shape test** — is what stops an **already-authenticated** caller registering a second account and carrying their own cart into it: an authenticated session's cart key is the account's user name, which cannot begin `anon:` under either character-set policy and for which no session marker was ever issued, so the gate fails on two counts rather than relying on the name not looking like a GUID — `Register` is `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:78], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:87] on an otherwise `[Authorize]` controller [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:15], so that request is reachable. Its failure branch is step 4's failure branch verbatim: skip R4, continue to R5, write the `TempData` notice, and leave the rows under the anonymous id with a protected recovery ticket naming them |
| R4 | Step 5 verbatim: `cartService.AssignSessionCartId(user.UserName)` | **No difference.** Omitting it loses the cart silently for the same reason step 5 gives — the ported `GetCartId` equivalent will not overwrite a session slot that already holds the anonymous key, exactly as the source will not overwrite one holding its bare GUID [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163-179] |
| R5 | `await signInManager.SignInAsync(user, isPersistent: false);` | **Last, and always non-persistent.** The source passes `isPersistent: false` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:97] and `RegisterViewModel` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:46-58] carries no remember-me property, so there is no user input to honour and none is introduced. Step 6's compensation applies unchanged: if this throws, `ClearSessionCartId()` undoes R4 and only R4 |
| R6 | `return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");` | **Unconditional, and no `returnUrl` test.** `Register` POST declares no return-URL parameter [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:89] and the source redirects straight to the home page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:98], so the redirect rule of section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) has no input to validate here and `Url.IsLocalUrl` is **not** added — adding a parameter the source does not accept would widen the anonymous surface for no requirement |

Both invariants above hold on this path for the same reasons: R3 cannot run unless R2 succeeded, and R4
is still the only writer of the session's username value with R5's compensation removing it. **Section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 20 case `20a` is where the continuity is required** — an anonymous cart
built before the registration request is still the registrant's cart afterwards, asserted on **both**
fixtures because the source migrates it too [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:353]
— and it is asserted there rather than alluded to here because the failure it guards is silent:
registration succeeds, the user is signed in, and the cart is simply empty.

**Merging the two contexts into one was considered and is not taken.** It would collapse this ordering
problem into a single `SaveChanges` and would be the simpler design on that axis alone. It is rejected
because `ApplicationDbContext : IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser>`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:10-16] is a framework-shaped context whose model the
Identity packages own, and merging the six catalog `DbSet` properties
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] into it entangles the catalog model with
Identity's schema versioning — every future Identity package upgrade would then arrive as a migration
against the catalog. The ordering above is five lines of explicit code; the merge is a permanent
coupling. **The ordering is cheaper than the coupling, so the boundary stays.** Note also that the
merge would not have removed the cookie problem, which is not a database problem at all.

### 4.4 What "the cart" is coupled to — and what it is not

Stated here because sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) both depend on it.

`Order.Username` is a plain string [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18], compared against
`User.Identity.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73]. The cart's
`CartId` is likewise a plain string, holding either the signed-in user's name or a generated GUID
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180] — a single value space shared by two kinds of
identifier, which is the property section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s `anon:` prefix
separates in the target. **Neither references the Identity primary
key, and there is no foreign key between the catalog store and the credential store in either
direction.** The two stores are coupled **only by convention** — a string that happens to match a login
name.

That fact carries three consequences used later: it is why one database is an operational choice rather
than a relational necessity ([4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); it is why
**usernames** rather than user ids are the invariant of the Identity data migration
([5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)); and it is why signed-in
carts survive cutover while anonymous ones do not ([11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)).

### 4.5 Two contexts, two migration sets, two history tables

**Neither context's current configuration convention survives.**

`MusicStoreEntities : DbContext` declares six `DbSet` properties, **no constructor and no
`OnModelCreating`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:5-13]. EF 6 resolves its
connection string by matching the **class name** against a `connectionStrings` entry, and there is one
named `MusicStoreEntities` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:13]. The coupling between the class and
its database is a name, expressed nowhere in the code — which is why this is the dangerous half: the
class compiles in the target, instantiates in the target, and simply does not know where its database
is. There is no line for a reviewer to notice, because the thing that stops meaning something is the
**absence** of a constructor.

`ApplicationDbContext : IdentityDbContext<ApplicationUser>` passes the name explicitly,
`: base("DefaultConnection")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:12-13], matching the
entry at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12]. This half announces itself — the base overload does
not exist in the target, so it fails to compile. ([12 F-12-19](12-migration-blockers.md) owns the
as-is finding and its two opposite failure modes.)

**Resolution.** Both contexts get an **explicit `DbContextOptions<T>` constructor** and an explicit
container registration, scoped, with the connection supplied from configuration. `MusicStoreEntities`
additionally gains an `OnModelCreating` override, because EF 6 inferred its **entire** mapping by
convention and there is no reason to expect two ORM generations' conventions to agree facet by facet.

**All six entities are mapped explicitly, and every facet is settled against the extracted schema of
section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) rather than against a
convention.** Naming a subset would be worse than naming none, because the unnamed entity is the one
nobody checks: `Artist` and `Order` are as convention-mapped as the other four, and `Artist` is the
smallest and therefore the easiest to assume is fine.

| Entity | Facets that must be stated explicitly rather than inferred |
| --- | --- |
| `Album` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:7] | Key `AlbumId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:10]; `Price` **precision and scale** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:24]; `Title` and `AlbumArtUrl` **length**, where the annotated 160 and 1024 [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:17], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:27] are validation attributes and the *column* length is whatever the database holds; **Unicode versus ANSI** on both strings; nullability on every column; the two relationships and their **delete behaviour** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:30-31]; any index on `GenreId` or `ArtistId` |
| `Artist` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:8] | Key `ArtistId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:10]; `Name` length, Unicode and nullability [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:11] — **the file carries no annotation at all**, so every one of its column facets exists only in the database and nowhere in the source |
| `Genre` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:5] | Key `GenreId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:7]; `Name` and `Description` length, Unicode and nullability [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:8-9], again unannotated; the `Albums` collection [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:10], which is **not** `virtual` and therefore never lazy-loaded (section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)) |

**And across all six, uniformly**: table and column names as the database actually spells them, every
column's **nullability**, every **default constraint**, every **check constraint**, every **index** with
its ordered key columns and uniqueness, and every relationship's **referential action** — that is, the
full output of the extraction of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction), facet for facet. **The acceptance
condition is section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3's, unchanged
and unqualified: inside the store's declared comparison scope the DDL generated from this mapping and the
extracted schema differ in nothing at all.** **Zero differences is the bar — not zero *unexplained*
differences**, because there is no annotation under which a difference is admitted: a reported difference
is either corrected in this mapping or shipped as a named post-baseline migration, which are step 3's only
two dispositions. This table is the work that meets that bar — not a convention, and not an assumption
that a `[StringLength]` attribute describes the column it validates.

**One entity-level decision that is not a facet: concurrency on the album update.** The administration
edit marks the whole entity modified — `db.Entry(album).State = EntityState.Modified`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:91] — and **no concurrency token exists on
`Album` in any edition** ([09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md) owns the current-state finding, F-09-27,
including the partial-post and posted-key consequences). The target must therefore *choose*, because
porting the line unchanged into EF Core silently keeps a choice nobody made.

**Decided: last-write-wins is preserved, explicitly and with its consequence stated.** Two
administrators editing the same album concurrently means the later write wins in full and the earlier
one is lost without notice — which is exactly today's behaviour, so this is a **preserved contract**
rather than a new exposure, and the actor set is small and already fully privileged
([09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md) rates the pairing Medium on that basis). Adding a `rowversion`
token would be the better design in a system with concurrent editors; here it would be a schema
addition beyond the extracted baseline, a new column to map, a new failure mode to surface in the view
and a conflict-resolution interaction to design — for a surface with one privileged actor. **If it is
ever wanted**, the shape is fixed here so it is not re-argued: a `rowversion` column added as an
**additive migration in a later release** under the compatibility rule of section
[5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), mapped `IsRowVersion()` on `Album`, with the update path
catching the concurrency exception, re-reading current values and redisplaying the form with a conflict
message — and a test asserting that the second of two concurrent edits is rejected rather than applied.
**Scope note, so the decision is not read as more than it is:** F-09-27's other half — that both
administration actions bind the `Album` entity itself, so a partial post blanks the omitted columns —
is an input-shape question rather than a concurrency one, and [09 §6.3](09-security-assessment.md)
remains its owner. Choosing last-write-wins does not address it and is not offered as doing so.

**The two contexts remain separate.** [12 §7.3](12-migration-blockers.md) records this as 05's
decision; it is taken, for the reason in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

**Both target one database.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the hosting and
provisioning; the *reason* belongs here, and it must be stated accurately because the obvious
justification is false. **It is not a foreign key between them — there is none** (section
[4.4](#44-what-the-cart-is-coupled-to--and-what-it-is-not)). Consolidation therefore removes an
**operational** dependency, not a relational one — and that distinction is this document's contribution,
because it is a property of the context and entity design.

**The trade itself — everything gained and everything given up — is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.5's,
and is not restated here.** It is a hosting consequence, it is enumerated there in full, and a partial
copy in this document would read downstream as a second and smaller assessment of the same decision.
A reader weighing whether to reverse the consolidation reads §6.5; a reader asking *why the reason is
not a foreign key* reads this section.

**Each context owns a separate migrations folder and a distinct migrations history table** —
`Data/Migrations/Catalog/**` and `Data/Migrations/Identity/**`, with two differently-named history
tables, configured per context in its `AddDbContext` registration. **The decision is fixed and is not
reopened here; what follows is why, on grounds that hold.**

**One thing a shared history table does *not* do, stated so it is not offered as the reason.** Pending
migrations are computed **per context, from the migrations discovered for that context** — the ones the
generator attributes to it, which in this design are the ones in its own folder and namespace — so rows
recording identifiers that context does not own are **not reported as pending to it**, and a shared
table would not by itself make either context's tooling report the other's work as outstanding. The
separation rests on the two consequences below instead.

- **Migration identifiers can collide, and a collision is silent in the worse direction.** A migration
  identifier is a timestamp prefix plus the name given at creation, and both sets are generated by the
  same tool by developers working to the same conventions — so two contexts each acquiring an
  `InitialCreate`, or each acquiring a same-named migration created in the same second, produce the
  **same identifier**. In one shared table that identifier is the primary key: the second application
  either fails on the key, or — if the row is already there — leaves the second context believing its
  own migration is **already applied** and skipping it, which is a schema that was never created and no
