  error anywhere. Two tables make the collision impossible rather than unlikely.
- **A row cannot be attributed to a context, and attribution is what release and rollback need.** A
  shared table records identifiers with nothing saying which context applied them, so "what is the
  catalog schema's current state" is not answerable from the table, and neither a per-context rollback
  target nor an audit of who applied what can be reconstructed from it. With one table per context, each
  context's state is **independently and correctly readable**, which is the property the release process
  is built on.

**Verification that each context's bundle targets its own history table, and that each context reports
its own migration state after a release, is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s** — it owns the
release-side mechanism and the two context-specific bundles, so it owns the check that they landed
against the tables this section separates.

**Two folders in the one web project, not two migrations assemblies.** The distinction matters because
the two are easy to conflate and only one of them is true here: both migration sets live in the single
application project the target map fixes ([04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), in separate
folders under separate namespaces, and **no separate migrations assembly and no separate migrations
project exists**. What separates them is the folder, the namespace and the history table — nothing
about assembly boundaries. Every design-time and release invocation is therefore **context-qualified**,
naming the context explicitly rather than relying on a single-context default that does not apply here;
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the release-side mechanism and the fact that there are
**two** context-specific bundles rather than one.

**The data-protection key table belongs to the Identity context, and this is where that is placed.**
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §7.2 fixes the key ring's location, its protect-at-rest
behaviour, its rotation policy and its slot and revision isolation, and explicitly leaves **which
context owns the migration** to this document, because this document owns the context design. The
placement:

- **`ApplicationDbContext` additionally implements `IDataProtectionKeyContext`** and declares a
  `DbSet<DataProtectionKey>` for the key rows. The Identity context rather than the catalog one,
  because the key ring is authentication-adjacent state and because `ApplicationDbContext` is already
  the framework-shaped context whose model framework packages contribute to — the same reasoning that
  keeps the catalog model out of it in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), read in
  the other direction.
- **The table is `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`**, created by the **Identity context's migration set** in a
  dedicated final migration named `AddDataProtectionKeys`, and recorded in the **Identity context's
  history table**. It is therefore step 4 of the ordering in section
  [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and needs no separate DDL artifact, no third context and
  no third migration set — the two-context, two-set, two-history-table shape above is unchanged.
- **Runtime registration is `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()`**, in
  the service registration of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) step 5. The
  application **reads and writes** key rows and does not create the table, which is what keeps it
  inside the grants [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.6 allows it.
- **Why a dedicated final migration rather than folding it into the initial one.** The Identity
  baseline migration is diffed against the extracted source schema (section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)), and the key table
  exists in no source schema at all. Keeping it in the **named** migration `AddDataProtectionKeys`, which
  is applied by its own targeted invocation after the baseline, puts it **outside the Identity store's
  declared comparison scope by construction** — section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3
  names it in the closed list of objects outside both scopes. It is therefore not an exception annotated
  onto a diff that is required to report none; the diff never sees it.

### 4.6 Lazy loading — a resolution per site, not a policy

EF 6 populates navigation properties on demand through proxies. The target does not: an unloaded
reference navigation is `null`. The code that depends on this **compiles identically under both**, so
nothing announces the change.

**The decision is explicit eager loading or projection at each query site — not a lazy-loading proxy
package.** Two reasons: the affected set is small and fully enumerated below, so explicit loading is
*verifiable* in a way a global proxy behaviour is not; and a proxy package would re-create the exact
property that makes this blocker silent — a query whose loading behaviour is invisible at the call
site.

"Use eager loading" is a policy, not a plan. [12 F-12-15](12-migration-blockers.md) enumerated
**nine** sites in **three categories that need opposite treatment**. Each gets its own resolution.

**Why exactly these sites and no others.** EF 6 lazy loading requires the navigation to be `virtual`.
`Album.Genre` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:30], `Album.Artist` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:31],
`Album.OrderDetails` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:32] and `Cart.Album` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:17] are `virtual`;
`Genre.Albums` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:10] is **not**, which is why the genre-browse
page had to eager-load and is therefore unaffected.

**Category (a) — client-side dereference after materialization. Six sites; every one is a definite
break. Resolution: eager-load or project at the query.**

| # | Query | Dereference | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a1 | `storeDB.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:38] | `@Model.Genre.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:16], `@Model.Artist.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:20] | Replace `Find` with a filtered single-result query carrying **`Include(a => a.Genre)` and `Include(a => a.Artist)`**. `Find` cannot take an `Include`, so the method call changes, not just its arguments |
| a2 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:32] | `model.Artist.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Details.cshtml:18], `model.Genre.Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Details.cshtml:26] | Same change as a1. Note the sibling **list** action at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:22] already uses the typed `Include(a => a.Genre).Include(a => a.Artist)` and ports unchanged — which is why the admin list page is absent from this table and the admin detail page is in it |
| a3 | `storeDB.Carts.Single(item => item.RecordId == id).Album.Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:61-62] | `.Album.Title` on the same expression [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:62] | **Project instead of loading**: select the title directly in the query, so no navigation is dereferenced client-side at all. This also fixes the unscoped read that [09 §6.2](09-security-assessment.md) records, because the projection carries the cart-id predicate |
| a4 | `GetCartItems()` — `ToList()` with no `Include` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-101] | `.Select(a => a.Album.Title)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-92] | The cart-summary path gets its **own projection query** returning count and titles, rather than materializing `Cart` entities and walking navigations. This is the highest-reach site: it renders from the shared layout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26], so a failure is **every page**, not one page |
| a5 | `GetCartItems()` via the cart view model [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:17-24] | `item.Album.Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:64], `@item.Album.Price` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:68] | The cart-page query carries **`Include(c => c.Album)`**. This is the one site where the view genuinely needs the entity graph, so `Include` rather than projection |
| a6 | `GetCartItems()` inside order creation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:129] | `orderTotal += (item.Count * item.Album.Price)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:145] | **The financial one.** Resolution: compute the running total from `album.Price` — the album the same loop **already loads explicitly** at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:134] and already uses for `UnitPrice` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:140] — instead of from the lazy navigation at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:145]. One loop, two ways of reaching the same price, and only one of them survives; the surviving one is already in the file. Acceptance is an order-total assertion in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) |

**Category (b) — navigation read inside a server-translated query. One site. Resolution: verify the
translation; do *not* add an `Include`.** `GetTotal` composes
`select (int?)cartItems.Count * cartItems.Album.Price` over the `DbSet` and calls `.Sum()` on the
resulting queryable [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:119-122]. The navigation is read
inside an expression the provider translates to SQL, so **no lazy load ever occurs** and the target
translates it too. Adding an `Include` here would load entities the query does not need and would be a
regression in the name of a fix. The required work is a **test that the query translates and returns
the same total**, not a code change. Listing this alongside category (a) would send the port to the
wrong fix, which is why the category exists.

**Category (c) — collection aggregates inside an `OrderByDescending`. Two sites, and they are two
*different* aggregates, which is why they get two different checks rather than one shared verdict.
Resolution: verify the translation and the result of each, and rewrite to a translatable form if either
fails.** The genre menu orders by a **nested `Sum`** — a `Sum` over each genre's albums of a `Sum` over
each album's order-detail quantities
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] — while the home page orders by a
**single-level `Count`**, `a.OrderDetails.Count()`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:29-32]. Calling both "the nested aggregate" is
what produces the wrong check at one of them, as the table below shows.

**What each runtime actually does with an expression like this, because the usual framing of it is
wrong.** It is often said that EF 6 quietly evaluates in memory whatever it cannot translate, so a
query that "worked" starts throwing on EF Core. That is a **category error**, and a plan built on it
looks for the wrong failure:

- **EF 6 does not partially client-evaluate a translated query.** A LINQ-to-Entities expression it
  cannot translate **fails**, at execution, with `NotSupportedException`. There is no silent fallback
  to substitute for it.
- **Silent partial client evaluation was EF Core's behaviour, in 1.x and 2.x only**, and it was removed
  in **EF Core 3.0** — "LINQ queries are no longer evaluated on the client" is that release's
  highest-impact documented breaking change. From 3.0 onwards, including the target, an untranslatable
  expression outside the final projection **throws `InvalidOperationException`**.
- So **both** runtimes fail loudly rather than falling back, and the migration risk is therefore **not**
  "it used to run in memory". What the source shows statically about the aggregate at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] is its shape: a nested `Sum` over a
  collection navigation inside a collection navigation, composed on the `DbSet` and ordered by — a form
  within EF 6's documented LINQ-to-Entities translation surface, with nothing in it (no local method
  call, no unmapped member) that would put it outside. **Whether it executes is not established by
  reading the source**, and this document asserts no runtime outcome: the source's actual behaviour on
  this page is recorded by the baseline capture of section
  [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage), and the per-edition build and run status is
  [10 §3.1](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md)'s.

**The risk that is real is the SQL and the result, not the fallback — and it is not the same risk at the
two sites.** Both are correlated aggregates the provider evaluates in a subquery beneath an `ORDER BY`,
so both can differ in *shape* between the two providers: subquery versus lateral join, and whether the
aggregate is computed once or recomputed for the projection. What is **not** common to them is the
empty-collection behaviour, and that is the half a single shared verdict gets wrong:

| Site | Aggregate | Empty-collection behaviour | What its check has to establish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Genre menu** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52] | Nested `Sum` — over `Genre.Albums`, of a `Sum` over `Album.OrderDetails` | **Real, at both levels. SQL `SUM` over no rows yields `NULL`, not `0`.** A genre with no albums and an album with no order details each produce a null the provider must turn into the `int` the expression is typed as — both `Sum` overloads here are over non-nullable `int`, so the null has nowhere to go in the CLR type. The outcomes available to a provider are a coalesce in the generated SQL, a substitution on materialization, or a materialization failure, and each provider decides for itself | Whether the query returns a row **at all** for a genre with no albums, and **where such a genre sorts**. SQL Server treats `NULL` as lowest, so it sorts **last** under `OrderByDescending` — the same position a provider that coalesces to `0` puts it in, which is why the two are indistinguishable without the assertion and why a genre silently *missing* from the menu is the failure to look for |
| **Home top six** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:29-32] | Single-level `Count` over `Album.OrderDetails` | **None. SQL `COUNT` over no rows yields `0`.** There is no null to propagate, no coalesce to get wrong and no materialization question, so the behaviour above **does not apply here** and a check written to look for it establishes nothing | Whether the **same six albums come back in the same order** as the baseline. The exposure here is **tie ordering**, not nulls: `OrderByDescending` over a count with **no tie-breaking key**, followed by `Take(count)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:30-31], leaves the relative order of equal-count albums undefined, so a differently shaped subquery may return a different — and equally correct — sixth album whenever the sixth and seventh are tied |

**They also do not run with the same frequency, which is what decides where the caching
[08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) records as separate performance debt is worth adding.** The
genre menu renders from the shared layout
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:25], like site a4, so it executes on **every page
the layout renders**. The top-six query does not: `GetTopSellingAlbums` is a private method whose only
caller is `HomeController.Index` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:18,24], so it
executes on **the home page only**. Both are worth caching; only one of them is a cost on every request.

So the required work is stated as observation rather than repair: **inspect the generated SQL for both
sites once**, and assert the rendered result against the baseline for the case each site is actually
exposed to — the **empty-collection ordering** for the genre menu, with a fixture carrying a genre that
has no albums and an album with no order details, and the **six albums and their order** for the home
page, with a fixture whose order-detail counts are distinct so the expected result is determinate rather
than tie-dependent. The coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) carry the two, one
each, and neither is written as the other's. If a site does not translate, rewrite it as an explicit
grouped projection over `OrderDetails`; that is the contingency, not the expectation.

**One favourable detail that reduces the work.** The **string-based** `Include("Albums")`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:30] **remains valid** in the target, even
though the typed lambda form is the convention. It may be modernized for consistency; it does not have
to be.

### 4.7 The `Dispose` overrides must be removed

Two overrides in the migration source dispose objects the code currently constructs and therefore
currently owns:

| Override | Object disposed | Constructed at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:125-128] | `MusicStoreEntities` | field initializer [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:15] |
| [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:324-331] | `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` | chained constructor [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19] |

([12 F-12-20](12-migration-blockers.md) records four across all three editions; the two above are the
migration source's.)

Today each is correct — the controller creates the object, so the controller disposes it, and the
account controller is even careful about it, null-guarding and nulling the field [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:326-330].

**Resolution: delete both overrides.** There is no replacement construct; container-owned lifetimes
need no disposal from the consumer. **The reason this is a required step rather than a tidy-up is that
leaving them compiles.** `Dispose(bool)` still exists on the target's controller base class, so there
is no signature error and no warning, and the ownership violation is therefore invisible: the
container owns what it created, and a consumer disposing an injected instance is reaching outside its
own lifetime.

**What that violation does not license is a predicted crash, and the plausible version of this claim is
wrong.** The framework releases the controller — and so calls `Dispose` — **after** result execution,
and `DbContext.Dispose` is **idempotent**, so on today's call graph the disposal is a no-op and no
`ObjectDisposedException` follows. The defect is that the code asserts an ownership it does not have,
and whether that is observable is a property of the current call graph rather than of the design: the
moment any second consumer in the same scope holds the same instance — a view component, a service, a
filter, an action executing after the controller is released — the override disposes an object still in
use. [12 F-12-20](12-migration-blockers.md) states the same correction, and it is why the removal is
justified on ownership grounds rather than on a failure nobody has observed.

The account controller carries the sharper version, because its `UserManager` is one of three objects
its chained constructor builds [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:19]. Once the container supplies all three, an override disposing the
middle one reaches an object other consumers may still hold. That override is deleted along with the
constructor, in the wholesale rewrite of section [9.2](#92-the-four-groups).

### 4.8 The service layer, and the two patterns deliberately not adopted

**`ShoppingCart` stops being a model and becomes a service.** Its business logic is real:
`CreateOrder` computes the order total, writes `OrderDetail` rows, sets `order.Total` and empties the
cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:125-158], and `MigrateCart` reassigns cart
ownership on sign-in [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193]. That is the one place in the application where business logic sits in
a model, so it is the one place worth extracting — to `Services/ShoppingCartService.cs`, registered
scoped, taking the catalog context and the HTTP context accessor by injection.

Three changes travel with the move:

1. **`HttpContextBase` becomes the framework's context type.** The class takes it as an explicit
   parameter [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:21] and reads session through it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180]; it never touches a static ambient context.
   That is the favourable finding of [12 P-12-01](12-migration-blockers.md) — `HttpContext.Current`
   appears nowhere in the repository — and it is why this move is a signature change rather than an
   architectural excavation.
2. **The dead `Controller` overload is dropped.**
   `public static ShoppingCart GetCart(MusicStoreEntities db, Controller controller)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:29-32] takes a
   `System.Web.Mvc.Controller`, a type with no target equivalent — and it is **provably unreferenced**.
   All six call sites use the `HttpContextBase` overload [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:21]:
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:35],
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:17], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:41], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:58], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:89] and
   [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:47]. **Deleting it has zero call-site
   impact**, which is materially cheaper than porting it ([12 P-12-02](12-migration-blockers.md)).
3. **The static factory pair collapses.** With the service injected and the cart id resolved from the
   accessor, `GetCart` stops being a static factory taking a context and becomes ordinary instance
   state.

**The order-creation path is rewritten, not relocated — it carries two defects that a move would carry
with it.** `CreateOrder` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:125-158] is the application's
only financial write, and it is the one method where "port it as it stands" is the wrong instruction.

**Defect one: an album lookup per cart line, and a price read that depends on lazy loading.** The loop
at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:132] calls `_db.Albums.Find(item.AlbumId)` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:134] — a lookup per cart line, since
`GetCartItems` returns `Cart` entities with no album data [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-101] — so an *n*-line cart issues **up to
*n*** album lookups on top of the cart read, fewer when a line repeats an album the context is already
tracking. It then reads the price a second time at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:145] through the `item.Album` navigation (site a6
of section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy)).

**What that second read is, precisely, because the difference decides the fix.** `Find` returns a
**tracked** entity, and relationship fixup therefore populates `item.Album` with **that same tracked
instance** — so `UnitPrice` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:140] and the running total at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:145] read **one object in memory**, not
two fresh database reads, and they **cannot** disagree with each other however the underlying row
changes mid-order. **Nor does the access break in the target.** The `Find` for that same item runs at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:134] before the read at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:145] within the same iteration, and relationship fixup is a change-tracker
behaviour rather than a lazy-loading one, so `item.Album` is populated under EF Core as it is under EF 6.
This site is therefore **not** one of the silent-correctness breaks: what is real about it is the
**lookup-per-line query cost** and the **unguarded dereference of the `Find` result** at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:140], and both
are removed by the same resolution:

- **One query for every value the order needs, including its own delete keys**, before the loop: a
  projection over the cart rows, cart-id-scoped, returning **`(RecordId, AlbumId, Count, Price)` and the
  row's concurrency token** per line. The loop then reads from that result and performs **no** further
  database access, so the per-line lookups disappear and no navigation is dereferenced client-side at
  all. `UnitPrice` and the running total continue to be computed from **one value**, which is the
  preserved property rather than a new one.
- **`RecordId` and the token are in the projection because the deletion is keyed on them.** A projection
  of `(AlbumId, Count, Price)` alone carries no key, so the only ways to delete afterwards are to
  re-query the rows — which the round-trip claim below forbids — or to attach constructed stubs, which
  makes the delete a change-tracker operation over entities the projection never materialized. **Neither
  is used.** The deletion is a **set-based delete over exactly the `(RecordId, token)` pairs the
  projection returned**, per requirement 7 of section
  [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity): no attach, no second `SELECT`,
  and no `CartId`-scoped predicate that could take a row this transaction never read.
- **A missing album is validated rather than dereferenced — a defensive check, and stated as one.**
  Today `album.Price` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:140] would throw a null reference if the album row were gone, and the
  administration delete removes an album without consulting the carts that hold it
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116-122]. **Whether that delete can
  actually leave an orphaned cart line is not established from the source code**: it depends on whether
  the real schema carries a foreign key from `Cart` to `Album` and on that constraint's referential
  action, which only the authoritative extraction of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 settles — a `NO ACTION` rule
  would make the delete fail instead, and a cascade would remove the cart lines with it. The validation
  is therefore required as a **defensive** measure pending that extraction, not as the remedy for a
  demonstrated data state: the projected line count must equal the cart line count, and a discrepancy
  fails the checkout with a message naming the unavailable item rather than throwing. **If the extraction
  shows the shortfall is impossible, the check stays** — it costs one comparison and it is the difference
  between a handled message and a null reference in the application's only financial write.
- **Acceptance is a bounded *read* count, a *stated* write-round-trip count, and an unchanged total — and
  the write count is not independent of cart size.** The read side is fixed: **exactly one** query
  resolves the cart lines and every price the order needs, issued **before** the loop, and the loop
  issues **no** database access. One is a reduction from two, not a restatement of today: the source
  reads the cart rows in `GetCartItems` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:129], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:98-101]
  and then reads them **again** in `EmptyCart`, whose deferred `Where` is enumerated by the `foreach`
  that removes them [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:89-91]. The target deletes the rows it already read and **must not re-query them**.
  The write side must not be claimed fixed, because it is not. The unit of work contains **one
  order insert, *n* order-detail inserts and the removal of *n* cart lines** for an *n*-line cart
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:136-152], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:87-96]. Two things shape how many round
  trips that becomes, and **an earlier formulation of this document got the second one wrong**:
  - **The cart removal is one statement, not *n*.** Section
    [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 7 makes it a
    **single set-based delete** over the projected `(RecordId, token)` pairs, which is a command in its
    own right rather than *n* tracked deletions inside `SaveChanges`.
  - **The order insert and its detail inserts cannot share a command batch.** `SaveChanges` batches
    commands into fewer round trips, and the SQL Server provider caps a batch at `MaxBatchSize` — a
    **provider default of 42** unless the registration of section
    [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) sets one. But batching is bounded by **dependency**
    before it is bounded by size: each `OrderDetail` carries the order's **generated** `OrderId` as the
    value that relates it to the order (defect two below), so that value has to come **back** from the
    database before the dependent rows can be sent. The provider therefore splits the batch at that
    dependency regardless of `MaxBatchSize`, and the write is **at least two command batches for every
    cart, including a one-line cart**.
  - **The consequence for acceptance: `ceil((2n + 1) / MaxBatchSize)` is withdrawn.** It is not merely
    imprecise, it is wrong at the smallest input — it predicts one round trip for a one-line cart where
    the dependency forces two — and it counts *n* deletions that no longer exist as tracked commands.
    Nothing replaces it with another formula, because the exact number is a property of **the pinned
    provider's batching implementation**, not of arithmetic this document can perform.

  Acceptance is therefore three assertions, in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage):
  - **One SELECT for the whole write path and zero SELECT statements issued from inside the loop**,
    asserted by **counted statements** rather than by elapsed time — a per-line query is invisible in
    every functional assertion and cheap enough not to show up as latency on a small cart.
  - **A DML round-trip count that is measured against the pinned provider and then asserted as a
    recorded number.** The suite counts the statements the pinned provider version of
    [04](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) actually issues for a given cart size and `MaxBatchSize`, and
    that observed number becomes the assertion — so a later provider change that alters batching **fails
    the test** instead of quietly satisfying a formula. Three cases are required: a **one-line** cart,
    whose count must be **at least two** and is the case the withdrawn formula got wrong; a cart wholly
    inside one batch; and a cart sized **one line past** the boundary `MaxBatchSize` implies, whose count
    must be **strictly greater** than the case below it. That last pair is what distinguishes provider
    batching from a loop that saves per iteration, and the recorded numbers are stated in the test
    rather than here, because this document cannot observe them without running the application — which
    section [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible)
    forbids.
  - **The financial result unchanged**: `order.Total` and every `OrderDetail.UnitPrice` and `Quantity`
    match what the source produces for the same cart, to the cent.

**Defect two: the detail rows depend on key-generation timing that the target does not promise.**
`CheckoutController` adds the order and calls `CreateOrder` **before** any save
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:48], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:51], so `order.OrderId` at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:139]
is still the unsaved default when it is copied into each `OrderDetail` — and because the detail sets
`OrderId` as a **scalar** and never sets the `Order` navigation, the rows are related to their order only
by a value that has not been generated yet. It works today because EF 6 fixes the relationship up during
`SaveChanges`; relying on that is relying on an implementation behaviour rather than on a stated
relationship, and it is silent when it is wrong. **Resolution: make the principal's state transition
explicit before constructing a dependent, then relate each detail through the aggregate.** Call
`db.Orders.Add(order)` first, which moves the principal from `Detached` to `Added`; then construct each
`OrderDetail` with its `Order` navigation set, or add it to the order's `OrderDetails` collection
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:66]. Automatic change detection observes each new dependent
through that tracked navigation as `Added`, and relationship fixup propagates the principal's temporary
and then store-generated key to it. That removes the *ordering* defect; it does **not** by itself make the
unit atomic, which the next paragraph settles.

**The write is one explicit transaction, and the execution strategy owns it. This supersedes an earlier
formulation of this section, which offered the aggregate navigation and an explicit transaction as
alternatives and preferred the implicit one.** That preference cannot hold, and the reason is specific
rather than stylistic: the deletion of the cart lines is a **set-based, token-matched delete** over the
projected `(RecordId, token)` pairs (requirement 7 of section
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)), which executes as **its own
command** and therefore **outside** whatever implicit transaction `SaveChangesAsync` opens for the order
and its details. Two commands in two implicit transactions cannot commit or roll back together, so the
preferred path could not deliver the atomicity the whole paragraph claimed for it. The requirement is
therefore:

- **The algorithm is section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)'s, and it is not restated here.** That section
  fixes the wrapper (`ExecuteInTransactionAsync` with a `verifySucceeded` predicate, and **not**
  `BeginTransactionAsync`, which a retrying execution strategy refuses outright), what runs inside the
  delegate and what runs before it, the submission key that resolves an unknown commit outcome, and the
  ordered body — the order save, then this section's token-matched delete, then its affected-count gate.
  **An earlier form of this bullet list specified a different wrapper** — `strategy.ExecuteAsync` around
  `BeginTransactionAsync` — and it is deleted rather than reconciled: two sections specifying one
  transaction is how a transaction acquires two shapes, and only one of the two can be written.
- **The aggregate navigation is still required**, because it is what makes the generated key reach the
  detail rows without a second `SaveChanges`. The two resolutions are **complementary and both required**,
  not alternatives: the navigation fixes how the detail rows obtain the key, and the transaction fixes
  what commits together.
- **Everything the unit touches commits or rolls back once**: the order row, its detail rows, and the
  cart lines the projection read. Today's single `SaveChanges`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:51] achieves that incidentally for the rows
  it happens to track; the target achieves it deliberately for a set that includes a command
  `SaveChanges` does not carry — which is the whole reason the transaction has to be explicit.
- **The submission key and the `verifySucceeded` callback are mandatory on this path**, not optional as
  they were when the implicit-transaction alternative was preferred. A retried transaction is
  re-executable; that is not the same as correct, because the first attempt may already have committed.

**The token pairs need a transport, and an unbounded one is not a design.** The delete predicate has to
carry *n* `(RecordId, token)` pairs for an *n*-line cart, and neither an interpolated list nor an
unbounded parameter list is acceptable — the first violates the parameterization rule of section
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 2, and the second hits
the provider's parameter limit at a cart size nobody has bounded. So the carrier is specified:

- **Preferred: a table-valued parameter, and it carries two columns because the predicate matches on
  two values.** A single parameter carrying the pair set, joined against `Cart` on **both** columns in
  one statement. It is one round trip regardless of cart size, every value is a parameter, and the type
  it requires is **`dbo.CartRecordIdList`**, a **two-column** table type — `RecordId` of `Cart.RecordId`'s
  extracted type and `RowVersion` of `Cart.RowVersion`'s (`binary(8)`, the value a `rowversion` column
  yields), with `RecordId` as its primary key — created by the named post-baseline migration
  **`AddCartMergeConstraints`** of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) — outside both comparison scopes by
  construction, and therefore invisible to the step 3 gate rather than annotated onto it. **A
  single-column form is withdrawn by name**: a carrier holding only `RecordId` cannot express the token
  half of the predicate, so the statement it produces would delete a row a concurrent request had
  changed — precisely the outcome the token match exists to prevent — and the affected-count gate would
  then pass on a delete that was not safe.
- **Permitted alternative: a chunked parameterized `VALUES` list, at a stated bound.**
  `Checkout:DeleteChunkSize`, **default 200**, owner **Engineering**, options-bound and startup-validated
  with the values of section [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access). The
  projection is chunked at that size and **every chunk is issued inside the one transaction above**, so a
  cart larger than one chunk is still one atomic unit. The bound exists because the provider caps
  parameters per command; 200 pairs is two parameters per pair inside that cap with room to spare, and
  the number is Engineering's to revise against the pinned provider rather than a value this document
  measured.
- **The affected-count gate applies to the chunked carrier exactly as it does to the single-statement
  one**: the **sum** of the affected counts across every chunk is what must equal the projected line
  count. Chunking changes the transport and nothing about the gate, which is section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) step 7's and is stated there once — including what a shortfall and
  an excess each mean and which of them retries.

**Empty and stale submissions are both rejected before anything is committed, and section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) owns both branches** — the empty projection at its step 4 and the
short affected count at its step 7 — **because they are steps of the one write algorithm rather than
properties of the carrier this section specifies.** The two are separated there for the reason that
matters here: an empty projection is an invalid submission and produces no order, while a short count is
contention and is retried from a fresh projection under section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 7,
bounded by `Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries`, because the customer's late addition belongs **in** the
order. Conflating them would either reject a valid purchase or accept a stale one. Coverage is section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row `96b` — the unknown commit outcome, sequential and as two overlapping
submissions — together with row `99b`, the concurrent add between the projection and the delete, and row
`99c`, the concurrent change that produces the shortfall and the fresh outer attempt. Row 10's
`10-cart-emptied` invariant is the non-contended baseline all three are read against.

**This one is verified against a real SQL Server, not an in-memory provider.** Key generation,
identity-value assignment and relationship fixup are precisely the behaviours an in-memory provider
models differently, so a test that passes there proves nothing about the case at hand — which is why the
fixture of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) provisions a real
engine. The assertion is that a multi-line order's detail rows all carry the order's **generated**
`OrderId`, and that the confirmation number the redirect returns
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54] is that same value.

**Two patterns are deliberately not adopted, and the reasons are specific to this application rather
than general.**

**No repository abstraction over EF Core.** `DbContext` is already a unit of work and `DbSet<T>` is
already a queryable collection; the domain has six entities
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] and there is exactly one data source and no
outbound service dependency ([11 §4.3](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). A repository layer would add
indirection with no test seam `DbContext` does not already provide — and the suite of section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) is HTTP-level black-box, so it does not need one.
The one place a genuine seam is wanted is the cart's business logic, and that is what
`ShoppingCartService` is.

**No uniform service layer across the six controllers.** Five of the six are thin: they query, build a
view model and return a view. `HomeController` is 34 physical lines
([08 §3.1](08-technical-debt-register.md)). Wrapping each in a service would produce five pass-through
classes and one real one. The real one is extracted; the pass-throughs are not written.

### 4.9 The data-protection key store — `ApplicationDbContext` owns it

[06 §7.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires a persisted key ring in `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`,
created by a migration under the deployment principal, and says in as many words that **which context
owns that migration is this document's to place**. Section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) defines two contexts and, until this
section, assigned it to neither — which left a platform requirement with no code behind it. It is
assigned here.

**The decision: `ApplicationDbContext` is the key store.**

| Element | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Context | `ApplicationDbContext` — additionally implements `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.EntityFrameworkCore.IDataProtectionKeyContext` |
| The interface member | `DbSet<DataProtectionKey> DataProtectionKeys` — the one property the interface requires, mapped to the table below |
| Table | `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`, the name [06 §7.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes. This document does not choose it and does not vary it |
| Created by | A **migration in `Data/Migrations/Identity/`** — the last migration in that set — recorded in **`__EFMigrationsHistory_Identity`** |
| Applied by | The deployment principal, **during step 3** of [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s order and of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)'s — the same executor invocation that applies the rest of the Identity set, because this migration is that set's tail. **Step 4 verifies the table exists; it does not create it** |
| Registration | `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>().SetApplicationName(...)`, whose argument is the `DataProtection:ApplicationName` value of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) rather than a literal. **`SetApplicationName` is the whole of the isolation mechanism** — there is no second setting to find and no separate discriminator option to set, because that method is what writes the framework's own discriminator value, and this document names no other |
| Read and written by | The runtime identity, with the data-only grants of [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — **`SELECT` and `INSERT` only**, for the reason in the next paragraph |

**The store is append-only, and that fixes the runtime's grants exactly rather than approximately.** The
repository this registration installs has **two** operations and no others:
`EntityFrameworkCoreXmlRepository<TContext>.GetAllElements()` enumerates
`context.DataProtectionKeys.AsNoTracking()` — a read — and `StoreElement(element, friendlyName)` does
`context.DataProtectionKeys.Add(newKey)` followed by `SaveChanges()`, which is an **insert of a new row**
(`EntityFrameworkCoreXmlRepository<TContext>`, ASP.NET Core 8 source). There is no update path and no
delete path in the type at all. **A revocation is an insert too**, not an edit of the row it revokes:
the key manager builds a new `<revocation>` element and persists it through the same `StoreElement`
(`XmlKeyManager.RevokeAllKeys` and `RevokeSingleKey`, ASP.NET Core 8 source), so the ring's history is
accumulated rather than rewritten.

**So the runtime identity needs `SELECT` and `INSERT` on this table and does not need `UPDATE` or
`DELETE`** — a grant this document can state as a consequence of the code rather than as a
least-privilege aspiration.
[06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-inventory) grants exactly those two and denies the
other two, and **check 3** of
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s deployment gate asserts the denial
positively, once per release under the monitoring identity; the two documents agree, and this paragraph is
why.

**What happens if the table is absent, verified — because the intuitive answer is wrong in a way that
would misplace a control.** An **explicitly configured** `PersistKeysToDbContext` does **not** quietly
substitute an in-memory ring: ephemeral keys exist only where an application asks for them explicitly, and
this one asks for the database. What actually happens has two stages, and only the second is a failure the
user sees:

- **Start-up does not fail.** The framework preloads the ring in a hosted service, inside a `try`/`catch`
  whose comment states the intent exactly — "This should be non-fatal, so swallow, log, and allow server
  startup to continue. The `KeyRingProvider` may be able to try again on the first request" — logging
  `KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup` and returning (`DataProtectionHostedService.StartAsync`, ASP.NET Core 8
  source). So the process starts, binds its port and looks healthy.
- **The first request that protects or unprotects anything throws.** The repository read hits a table that
  does not exist and the provider's exception propagates — in practice on the first rendered form, because
  an anti-forgery token is data-protected, and on the first sign-in for the same reason. The visible result
  is a 500, not a subtly non-durable cookie.

**Two consequences follow, and they are why the verification lives where it does.** The good one: a missing
table is loud rather than silent, so there is no state in which the application appears to work and cookies
quietly stop surviving a restart. The one that needs a control: **the application's own start-up will not
catch it**, which is exactly why the table's presence is asserted before traffic — by step 4 of
[06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), and continuously thereafter by readiness check `C2` of
[06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks), whose single-row **availability** read
fails on a table this identity cannot resolve or cannot read — rather than by trusting the process to have
failed. A readiness contract that assumed a start-up crash would let the first customer discover this.

**One property of choosing an explicit repository, stated because it is a trade and not a free
improvement.** "If the developer overrides the rules outlined above and points the Data Protection system
at a specific key repository, automatic encryption of keys at rest is disabled" (*Data Protection key
management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). **What that costs here is less than it sounds, and
saying so precisely matters**: on the App Service default path the same source states keys "aren't
protected at rest" anyway, so this registration forfeits automatic protection that path never provided —
the automatic mechanism applies to the user-profile path, where Windows encrypts with DPAPI. Either way
**at-rest protection becomes an explicit decision rather than an inherited one**, and that decision is
[06 §7.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and is not restated here. The registration in the table
above is what makes it a decision, which is why the consequence is named at the point that causes it.

**Why `ApplicationDbContext` and not `MusicStoreEntities`.** The key ring protects **authentication
cookies and anti-forgery tokens** — the identity and security domain, not the catalog domain. The
Identity context is already that domain's context, so the key table lands beside the tables it protects
tickets for, under one migration set, one history table and one set of grants. Putting it in the catalog
context would give the catalog code path a schema-level stake in cookie key material and would separate
the key table from the credential tables it is operationally paired with — during a restore, during a
slot-scoped repoint, and in the backup that covers both.

**The tension a careful reader will notice, and its reconciliation.** AAP §0.3.2 lists **four schema
owners** — the session cache, the catalog migrations, the Identity migrations and the data-protection key
table — while AAP §0.3.1's and §0.4.1's frozen future map contains exactly **two** contexts and exactly
**two** migration folders. Both are true at once, and conflating them is what would invent a third
context:

- **Conceptually the key table is its own schema owner.** It is not part of either domain model, no
  entity references it, and its lifecycle is the framework's rather than the application's.
- **Physically it is created by the last migration of the Identity set**, so it needs **no third
  `DbContext`, no third migrations folder and no third history table**, and the frozen map stands
  unaltered.
- **So it is a distinct schema owner and not a distinct execution step**, and that is the distinction the
  order in [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) turns on: the table is **created during step
  3**, by the same invocation that applies the rest of the Identity set, and **step 4 asserts that it
  exists** before the data steps proceed. Nothing in steps 1 to 3 needs a key; step 5's Identity data
  migration does, because its acceptance test signs an account in and a sign-in issues a cookie against
  the ring (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)).
- **The consequence is the failure mode a separate creating step would have had, removed:** if a release
  applies the Identity set at all, the key table is created, so there is no state in which steps 1 to 3
  succeeded and the ring's table is absent. Step 4 exists to catch the remaining case — a set applied
  from an assembly that predates this migration — and it catches it by verification rather than by
  creating something the migration set should have.

**Two consequences for the context's own definition**, both of which belong to section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)'s resolution rather than to a separate
design. `ApplicationDbContext` gains the interface and the `DbSet`, so its model contains one framework
entity beyond Identity's own; and its `OnModelCreating` calls the base implementation before any
catalog-independent configuration, exactly as the Identity base type requires.

**Everything operational about the ring is [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and is not
restated here**: the store's location and its rationale (§7.2), protection at rest (§7.3), rotation
(§7.4), and isolation between deployment slots and Container Apps revisions (§7.5), including the
slot-scoped marking of the discriminator setting this section consumes. This document's contribution is
exactly the three lines of code that make those decisions real — the interface, the migration's home, and
the registration call.

**And the reason none of it is optional — stated from what the platform default actually does, not from an
assumption that it does nothing.** The framework "attempts to detect its operational environment and
handle key configuration on its own", and on the primary hosting target it does something quite specific:
"If the app is hosted in Azure Apps, keys are persisted to the `%HOME%\ASP.NET\DataProtection-Keys`
folder. This folder is backed by network storage and is synchronized across all machines hosting the app.
Keys aren't protected at rest. The `DataProtection-Keys` folder supplies the key ring to all instances of
an app in a single deployment slot. Separate deployment slots, such as Staging and Production, don't share
a key ring" (*Data Protection key management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8). Three things follow,
and the first is the one a "keys are per-instance" reading gets wrong:

- **Multi-instance sharing is not what the database store buys on App Service** — the default share
  already synchronizes the ring across instances of one slot. Saying otherwise would justify the right
  control with the wrong reason.
- **What it does buy there is at-rest protection and slot-swap survival.** The default ring is not
  protected at rest, and it is *slot-scoped*: the same source states that after a swap "any app using Data
  Protection won't be able to decrypt stored data using the key ring inside the previous slot", which
  "leads to users being logged out". [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s release model swaps slots,
  so on the default ring every deployment would sign every user out — and it names a SQL store among the
  external providers that make key rings slot-independent.
- **On the container path the default is not durable at all.** The same source directs that "when hosting
  in a Docker container, keys should be persisted in a folder that's a Docker volume ... or in an external
  provider", so under the secondary option of [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) an unconfigured
  ring dies with the replica. The database store is the one choice that is correct on both targets, which
  is why it is not conditional on which one is chosen.

Either way the pairing with session holds: the distributed session of section
[6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) would be undermined by a ring that a swap or a replica replacement
invalidates — the two controls only work together. The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts exactly
that pairing: a cookie issued by one instance accepted by another, and a cookie issued before a restart
accepted after it.

#### 4.9.1 An empty ring needs a leader — the key-ring bootstrap, and why polling readiness is not a proof

**One state is reached deliberately and repeatedly by this design, and the framework's own behaviour in it
is safe but not *single*.** [06 §6.7.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s recovery sequence deletes
every row of `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` at step **K2** and restarts every instance at step **K3**, so every
instance comes up against an **empty** ring. The framework handles that: with automatic generation left at
its default, a system whose default key is missing generates a new one with immediate activation. What it
does not do is nominate one instance to be the one that generates it. There is **no leader** in that
mechanism — each process independently observes a ring with no default key and each independently creates
one — so with *n* instances the honest expectation is *n* keys, arriving in whatever order the restarts
complete. Step **K4** asserts **exactly one row**, and nothing in the platform's contract makes that
assertion true.

**A leader election on top of automatic generation would not have fixed it, and the reason is the ordering
rather than the election.** This is stated before the mechanism because an earlier form of this subsection
added the lock and left automatic generation enabled, which cannot work: the framework registers
`DataProtectionHostedService` inside `AddDataProtection`, and that service resolves the key ring in its
**`StartAsync`** — during host start-up, before any `BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync` body has run past its
first `await`. With `AutoGenerateKeys` at its default of `true`, resolving a ring that has no usable
default key **creates one there and then**. So on every instance the sequence is: framework creates a key,
*then* the bootstrap yields, *then* it takes the lock and finds a default key already present and reports
`alreadyPresent`. The election runs correctly and elects a leader with nothing to do, while *n* keys have
already been minted by *n* processes. The same applies without a restart: the first request that protects
anything resolves the ring and generates a key on whichever instance serves it.

**Therefore automatic key generation is disabled, and this is the decision the rest of the subsection
depends on.** `AddDataProtection()` is followed by **`.DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration()`** — the builder
call that sets `KeyManagementOptions.AutoGenerateKeys` to `false` — registered exactly once, on the web
host, in item 5 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) beside
`PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()` and `SetApplicationName(…)`. With it set, **no framework
code path creates a key**: neither the hosted service at start-up nor the key-ring provider on a
protect operation, and `KeyRingProvider` instead surfaces the empty ring as the load failure section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s log table already allocates
(`KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup` at `Error`, non-fatal because `DataProtectionHostedService.StartAsync`
catches it and returns). The bootstrap below becomes the **sole creator**, and its `sp_getapplock` is then
a real mutual exclusion over the only writer rather than a lock around a race that has already finished.

**What disabling it obliges this document to own, stated immediately because the obligation is easy to
create and easy to forget: with automatic generation off, nothing else will ever create a key — including
a replacement.** The framework's rotation is *implemented by* automatic generation: it is the key-ring
provider noticing that the default key is expiring and minting a successor. Turning generation off turns
rotation off with it. So the bootstrap does not merely create the *first* key; it owns **creation and
rotation both**, and the property table below states the pass that does it. The division with
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is unchanged in substance and sharpened in wording: **§7.4 still
owns the rotation *policy*** — the period, and what a rotation means operationally — and **this document
owns its *execution*, because disabling automatic generation is what moved the execution here.** A reader
who takes "rotation is the framework's" from an earlier form of the table below and also takes
`DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration` from this paragraph would build a system whose keys expire and are never
replaced, which fails closed in the worst possible place: every cookie and every anti-forgery token stops
validating at once, on every instance, with no deployment having occurred.

**And polling readiness cannot supply what is missing, which is stated plainly because the earlier
formulation of K4 opened with exactly that.** One request to `/healthz/ready` establishes nothing about
the ring, for three independent reasons and each one alone is sufficient:

| Why | Where the property comes from |
| --- | --- |
| The endpoint performs **no I/O in the request at all** — it returns the last completed verdict from memory | Section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract)'s no-I/O rule, which is [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s |
| **Neither `C1` nor `C2` reads a key or protects anything, and that is *more* true of the closed two-check set than of the five it replaced.** `C2` now reads `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` directly — and it is an **availability** check: it selects `Id` for at most one row, **does not select the payload column**, treats **zero rows as a pass**, inspects nothing about the row it may get back, unprotects nothing and calls `Protect` nowhere. So a passing `C2` says the table is present and readable by this identity and says nothing whatever about how many keys the ring holds or whether any of them is usable | [06 §9.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#readiness-checks)'s check definitions |
| A probe request is **load-balanced**, so even if it did protect something it would exercise **one** instance's ring and say nothing about the others | The platform's own routing; it is the same property that makes the cross-instance half of the postcondition below necessary rather than redundant |

So a 200 from that path is compatible with an empty ring, with one key, and with five. **Readiness polling
is not a fresh-ring proof and this document does not treat it as one.**

**The application-side mechanism: one leader, one key, by construction.** A third hosted service,
`Services/KeyRingBootstrapService.cs`, sits in the same `Services/` folder as the other three and is
carried by the same enumerated [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) row section
[2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) records, so **no new folder, no
new project and no new operator verb is introduced.** It is registered on the **web host only**,
beside item 15 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) and **not** in the shared
registration half, so `provision-admin` never runs it. It runs **one pass at process start and one pass per
period thereafter**, every pass identical, for the reason the property table below gives — with automatic
generation disabled this service is the only writer the ring has, so it owns rotation as well as the first
key:

```text
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    await Task.Yield();                            // never block the start; see 2.6

    // One pass now, then one per period. Every pass is the same pass under the same
    // lock, so a pass that finds nothing to do is the normal outcome and a pass that
    // is skipped costs only its own interval.
    await RunCustodyPassAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false);

    using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(_passPeriod);
    while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false))
    {
        await RunCustodyPassAsync(stoppingToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
}

private async Task RunCustodyPassAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    using var bound = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(stoppingToken);
    bound.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));

    // Every synchronous key-management body this pass starts is held here, because
    // ownership of the lock may not be given up while one of them is still running.
    // CancellationToken.None is deliberate: Task.Run's token can only prevent a body
    // from starting, never interrupt one that has started, so passing bound.Token
    // there would describe an interruption that does not happen (2.6, third property).
    var started = new List<Task>();
    try
    {
        // Its own session, because sp_getapplock with @LockOwner = 'Session' holds the
        // lock on the connection that took it. Never the context's connection.
        await using var lockSession = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await lockSession.OpenAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);

        int rc = await AcquireAppLockAsync(lockSession, bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
        if (rc != 0 && rc != 1)                    // -1 timeout, or another instance holds it
        {
            _logger.LogInformation("keyRingCustody outcome=notLeader returnCode={Rc}", rc);
            return;
        }
        try
        {
            Task<IReadOnlyCollection<IKey>> read =
                Task.Run(() => _keyManager.GetAllKeys(), CancellationToken.None);
            started.Add(read);
            IReadOnlyCollection<IKey> keys =
                await read.WaitAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);

            DateTimeOffset now = _timeProvider.GetUtcNow();
            DefaultKeyResolution resolution =
                _defaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy(now, keys);

            // Two triggers, one create. No default key at all is the empty-ring and
            // post-K2 case and activates now; ShouldGenerateNewKey is the framework's
            // own "the default key is expiring" signal and activates at that key's
            // expiration, so the ring is never without an active key and never has
            // two active at once. Neither trigger exists in the framework any more:
            // DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration removed both, which is why this service
            // owns rotation as well as bootstrap.
            if (resolution.DefaultKey is null)
            {
                Task<IKey> create = Task.Run(
                    () => _keyManager.CreateNewKey(now, now + _rotationPeriod),
                    CancellationToken.None);
                started.Add(create);
                IKey first = await create.WaitAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
                _logger.LogInformation("keyRingCustody outcome=created keyId={KeyId}",
                                       first.KeyId);
            }
            else if (resolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey)
            {
                DateTimeOffset activation = resolution.DefaultKey.ExpirationDate;
                Task<IKey> rotate = Task.Run(
                    () => _keyManager.CreateNewKey(activation, activation + _rotationPeriod),
                    CancellationToken.None);
                started.Add(rotate);
                IKey successor = await rotate.WaitAsync(bound.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
                _logger.LogInformation(
                    "keyRingCustody outcome=rotated keyId={KeyId} activation={Activation:o}",
                    successor.KeyId, activation);
            }
            else
            {
                _logger.LogInformation("keyRingCustody outcome=alreadyPresent");
            }
        }
        finally
        {
            // The release is gated on the work, not on the wait. A pass that stopped
            // waiting has not stopped working, and releasing here — or merely closing
            // this connection, which returns it to the pool where sp_reset_connection
            // releases session-scoped locks exactly as the procedure would — while a
            // CreateNewKey is still in flight admits a second instance, which re-reads
            // a ring the in-flight insert has not reached and mints a second key. So
            // the procedure call and the disposal both wait for every started body.
            // Completion, not success: a faulted body has finished, which is all the
            // release needs, and rethrowing it here would skip the release it guards.
            await Task.WhenAll(started).ContinueWith(
                    static finishedWork => { _ = finishedWork.Exception; },
                    CancellationToken.None,
                    TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously,
                    TaskScheduler.Default).ConfigureAwait(false);

            await ReleaseAppLockAsync(lockSession, CancellationToken.None)
                .ConfigureAwait(false);
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // The 60-second bound elapsed. Nothing further is started, the lock was held
        // until the started body finished, so no second creator was admitted, and the
        // next pass one period later is the retry.
        _logger.LogWarning("keyRingCustody outcome=waitAbandoned");
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Shutdown during a pass. Nothing further is started; anything already started
        // is waited out under the lock by the finally above, so the next process's
        // first pass observes whatever it committed rather than racing it.
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // Fail-soft, and the loop survives: a failed pass is one interval of delay,
        // not the end of rotation. Rethrowing here would end ExecuteAsync and leave
        // the ring with no writer at all for the life of the process.
        // No exception object is passed, for the same reason as the heartbeat's
        // handler: section 3.3's record shape governs every ILogger call in the port.
        var innerTypes = new List<string>();
        for (var inner = ex.InnerException; inner is not null; inner = inner.InnerException)
        {
            innerTypes.Add(inner.GetType().FullName!);
        }
        _logger.LogWarning(
            "keyRingCustody outcome=failed exceptionType={ExceptionType} " +
            "innerExceptionTypes={InnerExceptionTypes} exceptionStack={ExceptionStack}",
            ex.GetType().FullName, innerTypes, ex.StackTrace);     // see below
    }
}
```

`AcquireAppLockAsync` and `ReleaseAppLockAsync` are two `DbCommand` invocations of
`sp_getapplock` and `sp_releaseapplock` on that same connection, each with a
`ParameterDirection.ReturnValue` parameter, which is how the procedure's return code is read —
`ExecuteNonQueryAsync` returns a row count and not the procedure's value. `_defaultKeyResolver` is the
same `IDefaultKeyResolver` the heartbeat resolves for `defaultKeyId`, whose acceptance terms and
revalidation obligation are stated once in section
[2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) and are not re-argued here:
`DefaultKeyResolution.DefaultKey` being non-null is the framework's **own** answer to "does this ring
already have a key it would protect with", which is exactly the question the bootstrap must not answer for
itself.

**Three type facts are recorded here rather than left implicit, because they are the kind that fails at
the first compile rather than at review, and each was checked against the shipped 8.0 assembly rather than
recalled.** First, `IKeyManager` and `IKey` are in
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement`, with `GetAllKeys()` returning
`IReadOnlyCollection<IKey>` and `CreateNewKey(DateTimeOffset, DateTimeOffset)` returning `IKey` — which is
why the two `Task.Run` results above are typed the way they are. Second, `IDefaultKeyResolver` is **not**
in that namespace: it is public, but it sits one level deeper, in
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal`, so this file carries a **second `using`**
for that namespace and a file that imports only the first will not compile. Third,
`DefaultKeyResolution` is a **struct** in that same namespace whose `DefaultKey`, `FallbackKey` and
`ShouldGenerateNewKey` are **fields rather than properties** — which is why the sketch reads
`.DefaultKey` off the returned value directly and does not null-check the resolution itself.

Whether taking that namespace is acceptable at all, and what re-checking it costs on a framework move, is
section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)'s decision and its
option table; this section adds only the second call site to the closed list that subsection keeps, and
inherits the revalidation obligation unchanged.

**Nine properties of that, each of which is the reason a line is there** — and the count is the table's
own: the lead-in read "six" while the table already carried **eight** rows, a figure left behind when the
rotation and period rows were added, and the ownership-versus-wait rule below adds the **ninth**.

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The lock is the existing one's mechanism on its own resource name** | `sp_getapplock` with `@LockMode = 'Exclusive'`, `@LockOwner = 'Session'` and a **15-second** `@LockTimeout`, released by `sp_releaseapplock` in a `finally` on the same connection — the contract [06 §6.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes for the release lock, including its return-code handling: `0` and `1` are *acquired*, and every negative value is *not acquired*. The **resource name is `MvcMusicStore-KeyRingBootstrap`, deliberately not the release lock's**, so a starting instance can never contend with a release in flight or delay one. The platform requires only membership of the `public` database role to call either procedure, so the runtime identity needs no additional grant for the lock itself |
| **Exactly one key, because the create is inside the lock and is preceded by a re-read** | Every instance takes the same path: acquire, re-read the ring, create only if the framework's own resolver reports no default key, release. The instance that wins creates one key; the instances that queue behind it re-read a ring that now *has* a default and create nothing; instances whose 15 seconds elapse do nothing at all and say so. `n` instances therefore produce **one** row rather than *n*, which is what makes K4's "exactly one row" an assertion instead of a hope |
| **The write is one the runtime identity is already granted** | `CreateNewKey` is an `INSERT` into `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`, and `SELECT` plus `INSERT` on that table are exactly the two verbs [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-inventory)'s grant tables give the runtime identity — while `UPDATE` and `DELETE` stay denied there, and **check 3** of [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#deployment-verification)'s deployment gate asserts that denial once per release. So the bootstrap needs **no privilege this design did not already give it**, and it cannot rotate or rewrite an existing key even if it were wrong |
| **It cannot block the start, and it cannot stop the host** | `await Task.Yield()` first, both synchronous key-management calls offloaded exactly as section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment) requires of the heartbeat, and the whole body wrapped so nothing escapes `ExecuteAsync` into `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior`'s `StopHost` default |
| **The bound governs the wait; ownership is governed by the work — and this is the one place the pass differs from the heartbeat** | Section [2.6](#26-the-two-hosted-services--files-algorithm-timing-and-containment)'s third property already states the general fact: cancelling a `WaitAsync` does **not** abort the offloaded call, because `GetAllKeys()` and `CreateNewKey(…)` take no token and a thread inside them stays there until the provider's own timeouts return. For the heartbeat that is harmless, because it holds nothing. **Here it would be the double-key bug the whole subsection exists to prevent**, so the rule is stated as mechanism rather than as intent: every started body is held in `started`, and **neither `sp_releaseapplock` nor the disposal of the lock session happens until every one of them has finished** — the disposal matters as much as the call, because returning that connection to the pool runs `sp_reset_connection`, which releases session-scoped application locks just as the procedure does. **An earlier form of this design passed `bound.Token` to `Task.Run` and released in a `finally` reached by the cancelled wait; that is deleted**, because it hands the lock to a second instance while the first is still inserting, which is precisely the *n*-keys outcome. A pass whose 60 seconds elapse therefore records `outcome=waitAbandoned` and **keeps the lock until its own body returns**; the cost is that a shutdown can be delayed by one provider timeout, and that cost is accepted because the alternative is two default keys. Process death is not the same case and needs no rule: the connection dies with the process, the engine releases the lock, and the abandoned body dies with it |
| **It is fail-soft, deliberately, and that is consistent with this section rather than a weakening of it** | A failure to acquire the lock, to read or to create writes one record and returns; it never fails the start and never makes the instance unready. This section's failure model for the key store is unchanged: **readiness and the release-side assertions are the controls**, not a refusal to start. What the bootstrap changes is only *how many* keys a recovery produces, and **the worst case is stated rather than softened.** An earlier form of this row ended "the framework's own on-demand generation remains the fallback if the bootstrap did nothing, so the worst case is the behaviour that existed before it, not an outage". **That is deleted, because `DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration` removed the very fallback it names**: with generation off, no framework code path creates a key, so a ring that no pass ever populated stays empty and **the first operation needing key material fails outright** — the same conclusion section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) reaches for the absent key table, and the symptom coverage row 25's `25e` rationale describes. "Fail-soft" therefore scopes to **the pass**, not to the outcome: the pass writes one record and returns, **the next pass one period later is the retry**, `KeyRingFailedToLoadOnStartup` at `Error` (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)) is the signal that the ring is unusable now, and [06 §6.7.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s K4 postcondition with the release-side assertions is what stops a recovery that produced no key from being mistaken for one that did |
| **It is a bootstrap pass and then a periodic custody pass, because disabling automatic generation left no other writer** | An earlier form of this row read "there is no timer and no second pass … rotation is the framework's", and that is withdrawn: `DisableAutomaticKeyGeneration` removes the framework's rotation along with its first-key creation, for the reason the paragraph above gives, so a service that returned after one pass would leave the ring with a key that expires and is never replaced. The service therefore runs its pass **once at start and then on a period**, and every pass is the *same* pass under the *same* lock — acquire, resolve, create only if the resolver says a key is needed, release. **It is not a second rotation mechanism competing with a first**, because after the disable there is exactly one mechanism. The **period** is [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s policy value; the **execution** is this service; the heartbeat still only observes |
| **The rotation trigger is the framework's own resolver, not a date this document invents** | A pass creates a successor when `ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy` reports `ShouldGenerateNewKey` — the field the framework itself sets when the default key is inside its own generation lead time — **or** when it reports no `DefaultKey` at all, which is the empty-ring and post-`K2` case. Using the resolver for both means the trigger cannot drift from the framework's notion of "expiring soon" the way a hand-written lead window would, and it is the same resolver, resolved the same way, that the heartbeat reads for `defaultKeyId`.
