| F5 | `db.Albums.Find(id)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:119] — `DeleteConfirmed` | **Not null-checked.** The result goes straight into `db.Albums.Remove(album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:120], so a POST naming a deleted id throws inside `Remove` and answers **500** — the one write action in the controller with no guard | `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, and **the absent-row outcome is preserved: 500**, with **one log record at `Error`** and **no `SaveChangesAsync`**. **An earlier form of this row specified `NotFound()` before `Remove` is called, and that is withdrawn by name.** The reasoning it gave — that the GET at F4 already answers 404, so the POST answering 500 is an inconsistency — describes the source accurately and still does not authorize a change: the inconsistency is the source's, AAP §0.1.1's preservation baseline covers this outcome, and section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)'s exclusion note names **four** status corrections — S1, S2, the S3/S4 pair and F1 — and **excludes this site from that set by name**. No delta is added for it. What the target *does* add is the record: the source's 500 arrives from inside `Remove` with nothing written anywhere, and this one is logged. The null branch is still written explicitly rather than left to throw inside `Remove` — it logs and then returns a result that produces the same **500**, so the status is preserved while the diagnosis is not left to an `ArgumentNullException` from the framework. [08 §5.4](08-technical-debt-register.md) continues to own the underlying inconsistency as debt, and its remediation is a separately approved change rather than part of this port |
| F6 | `_db.Albums.Find(item.AlbumId)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:134] — inside `CreateOrder` | Null would be dereferenced at `album.Price` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:140], inside the checkout's bare `catch` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62], which discards the exception, redisplays the form with no message and **logs nothing** | A cart row referencing a missing album is a **data-integrity failure**: logged at `Error` with the cart record id and album id, the **explicit transaction of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) rolled back at its step 6**, which is where the album load happens, **no order persisted**, and a generic error surfaced on the checkout form. The relational constraint makes it improbable — which is exactly why it must fail loudly rather than silently produce a short order |

**One site is already correct and is listed so the census is complete rather than selective.**
`_db.Carts.SingleOrDefault(c => c.CartId == ShoppingCartId && c.AlbumId == album.AlbumId)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:37-39] is genuinely guarded at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:41] and its duplicate
case is prevented by the cart's own key discipline. It ports unchanged apart from becoming
`SingleOrDefaultAsync`.

**What every branch above has in common, stated once instead of per row — with the one branch it does not
cover named rather than implied.** A request that a client can issue must never produce an unhandled
exception; a state that only the data can be in may. So client input resolves to **404**, and a broken
invariant resolves to **a log record at `Error` plus a 500**. The **four** status corrections this
produces — the unknown genre name (S1), the absent album on the cart *write* path (S2), the absent cart
record on removal (S3 and S4), and the unknown public album id (F1), each a 500 today — are together
**approved delta `D-49`** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas): one difference on four
sites, carrying a ledger id because a difference the suite can observe is admissible only against a
number. Their *reason* remains the recorded debt [08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns; the
number is the *approval*. **An earlier form of this paragraph recorded them as defect resolutions with no
id at all**, which left four observable differences unapproved, so none of them is now
left as an unannounced improvement.

**Site F5 is the exception, and it is deliberate.** `DeleteConfirmed` with an id in no row is a
client-issuable request that resolves to **500**, not 404, because the source resolves it to 500 and
AAP §0.1.1 authorizes no delta on that action. F5 is therefore the one row where the rule
above yields to preservation: the null branch adds **only** the `ADMIN-4003` record at outcome
`AbsentRow`, the status is the source's, and no delta id is issued — section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) states the same exclusion from the register's side. A reader
who applied the general rule here and returned 404 would be shipping an unapproved contract change on a
destructive administration action. **Every
branch in this section has a test in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)**; a contract with no test
is a comment.

### 4.16 Asynchronous data access and cancellation — the convention, stated once

Every query and write named in this document is asynchronous and cancellable. The convention is stated
here so the individual contracts — sections
[4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census),
[8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) and
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) — can name an `…Async` API without
re-arguing it each time.

**Where the source starts.** The migration source's async surface is real but confined to one file: the
27 C# files under `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/` contain **9** `async` occurrences, **22** `await`
expressions and **7** `Task<…>` signatures, and every one of them except a single `async void`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] is in `AccountController.cs`. The catalog, cart,
checkout and administration paths are **entirely synchronous** — `Single`, `Find`, `ToList` and
`SaveChanges`, with no `Task` anywhere. There is also **no sync-over-async debt to unwind**: `.Result`,
`.Wait()` and `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` do not appear in any of the 27 files. The commands are in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**The convention, in six rules.**

| # | Rule | Why it is a rule rather than a preference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **An action that touches the database is `async` and returns `Task<IActionResult>`.** An action that touches nothing stays synchronous — `HomeController.Error` (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) is the only one | A synchronous EF Core call blocks a thread-pool thread for the duration of the round trip. Under Kestrel that thread is the request's, and blocking it is the mechanism behind thread-pool starvation |
| 2 | **Every EF Core query and write uses the `…Async` API:** `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `SingleOrDefaultAsync`, `AnyAsync`, `CountAsync`, `SumAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`, `ExecuteUpdateAsync`, `ExecuteDeleteAsync`, and the execution strategy's `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` — which is the **only** transaction API this application calls, so `BeginTransactionAsync`, `CommitAsync` and `RollbackAsync` appear in no contract here | The synchronous overloads exist and compile, so a copied query silently keeps blocking. Naming the API in every contract in this document is what makes the omission visible in review |
| 3 | **Every such action declares a `CancellationToken` parameter**, which MVC binds from `HttpContext.RequestAborted` with no attribute and no registration, **and passes it into every EF Core call in the handler** | A token accepted and not passed on is worse than no token: it looks like cancellation is honoured and nothing is cancelled |
| 4 | **`OperationCanceledException` is not an error — and it is not an outcome either.** Where a handler catches it, the catch is **filtered on the request token** and its body has exactly two statements: record the cancellation, then **`throw;`**. `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)` — the filter is part of the rule, because an `OperationCanceledException` carrying *any other* token is a genuine fault and must keep travelling as one. It is not logged at `Error`, not mapped to a 500 and not mapped to a view; the checkout table in section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) states it for the one handler where it matters | A client that closes the tab produces this exception, so treating it as a fault fills the log with noise. But **an `async Task<IActionResult>` action must still terminate**, and the two obvious terminations are both wrong: returning a view or a status code writes a response to a client that has gone and reports success for work that did not finish, and returning nothing does not compile. **Rethrowing is the terminal behaviour**: the framework recognises a cancelled request, abandons the response rather than inventing one, and — because the exception-handler middleware treats a cancelled request as an abort rather than a fault — no 500 and no error page is produced. The record made on the way out is why the catch exists at all |
| 5 | **View components use `InvokeAsync` returning `Task<IViewComponentResult>` and take the token from `HttpContext.RequestAborted`**, because a component receives no bound parameters from model binding | **All three components query** (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), and the rule reaches all three for the same reason at very different frequencies. The two **layout** components — the genre menu and the cart summary — run wherever the shared layout renders, which is every page, so they are the highest-frequency database callers in the application. `RemoveAccountListViewComponent` runs only on the authorized `Manage` view and reads the Identity store, so it is rare rather than exempt |
| 6 | **No `async void` anywhere, and no synchronous EF Core call in any request path.** The one `async void` in the source is the provisioning method [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21], retired by section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) | An unhandled exception in an `async void` method has no caller to propagate to. That is the specific defect that makes today's provisioning failure invisible |

**Cancellation is safe here because the one multi-statement write is transactional — with one honest
exception, which is not a cancellation problem.** A token cancelled **before or during** the checkout
write aborts the in-flight command and disposes the transaction without committing, so the outcome is
the same as any other failure on that path: nothing persisted, per section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract). A token cancelled **during the commit
itself** is the one case where the client's outcome and the database's can differ — the server may have
committed and the acknowledgement may not have arrived — and that is **exactly the indeterminate commit
of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract), which is settled there by the
submission key rather than by anything in this convention.** Cancellation is one way to reach it, a
dropped connection is another, and the resolution is the same for both. No handler in this application
performs two independent *un*transacted writes that a cancellation could split, which is why rule 3 can
be applied without exception rather than case by case.

**How this convention is checked, since it is the one contract in this document with no coverage row of
its own.** It is a **code-shape** rule, not an observable response, so section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) cannot assert it: a synchronous `SaveChanges` and an asynchronous one
return the same bytes to the client. It is enforced at review, against the six rules above, and the
review is mechanical — the prohibited forms are grep-able (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter`,
`async void`, and any EF Core terminal operator without the `Async` suffix), so a reviewer checks a list
rather than forming a judgement. Rule 4 is the one exception with an observable consequence, and it is
**covered directly, by two named cases rather than by the phrase "the coverage assertion"**. Section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 96 case `96c`** cancels the request **around the commit** and then
resubmits the same submission token: the cancelled request produces no response of its own because the
cancellation is rethrown, the commit nonetheless completes, and the resubmission resolves to the
committed order — which is the detached-token half of the rule, and the half a linked token would fail by
aborting the commit. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 31** supplies the other half, requiring
that the redisplayed form with a rendered model error is produced by a **genuine persistence failure** and
by nothing else. **An earlier form of these two sentences claimed a cancellation "at three points — before
the save, during the save and during the commit" and attributed both halves to an unnamed "coverage
assertion"**; no row asserts a three-point cancellation, so the claim named coverage that does not exist,
and it is replaced here by the two cases that do.

**Two places the request token deliberately does not reach.** The Identity data migration and the
domain data load (section [5](#5-schema-lifecycle-and-the-two-data-migrations)) run outside a request
and take their own token from the hosting process. `tools/provision-admin`
(section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)) passes
`CancellationToken.None` to **every** Identity call it makes — the **four** operations of that section's
property 3 in the `admin` verb, and no others: each is a single short call, and an interrupted run is
repaired by the per-operation idempotence that section already requires, so threading a token through it
would add a failure mode rather than remove one. **An earlier form of this sentence added "and the two of
property 3a in revoke mode"**; section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) defines no property 3a and its
verb table carries no revoke verb, so that clause named operations this plan does not have, and section
[6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) records the
consequence for the one event class that depended on it.

---

## 5. Schema lifecycle and the two data migrations

### 5.1 Domain data migration starts with schema extraction

**An EF Core initial migration creates empty tables. It moves no rows.** That sentence needs saying
because "generate the initial migration" reads like the data step and is not it.

Worse, **the generated migration cannot be trusted to match the database the data is actually in.** A
migration generated from the ported model may differ from the real EF 6 schema in column type,
precision and length, nullability, identity and key definition, delete rule, default value and index —
and none of those differences produces a build error or a startup error. They produce wrong data, or a
failed insert, at the first write. **And there is nothing in the repository to compare against:**
MVC 5 ships no schema script at all, and MVC 4's two copies are byte-identical and not runnable as
written ([12 F-12-22](12-migration-blockers.md) owns both facts; [04 §13.1](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
carries the instruction that neither may be used as a baseline).

**Therefore the domain-data workstream begins with extraction, and the diff is a gate.** In order:

1. **Authoritative schema extraction from `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/MvcMusicStore.mdf`.** A
   catalog-view interrogation of the attached database, producing a written schema record —
   `schema.catalog.json` in the run directory of section
   [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) — for all six catalog tables. This can
   only be done on a supported Windows and LocalDB runtime, because that is the only place the file
   attaches ([10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) owns the toolchain). **It must be done against
   a copy outside the checkout** — attaching the tracked `.mdf` and `.ldf` causes the engine to write to
   them, which would dirty the working tree.

   **The interrogation is four root queries, published here with what each one establishes, because
   "interrogate the catalog views" is not something a reader can implement or a reviewer can check.**
   Each root reaches the joined views its own facts live in; the roots are what the record is organized
   by, and there are **four of them and no fifth root**. Any consumer of this contract — in this document,
   in [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) or in [12](12-migration-blockers.md) — cites this table rather
   than restating a count of its own, and **a larger view inventory is not required**: the joined views
   below are reached *through* these four roots, not counted beside them.

   | Root query | Joined views it reaches | What it establishes, exhaustively for the tables in scope |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `sys.columns` | `sys.tables`, `sys.schemas`, `sys.types`, `sys.identity_columns`, `sys.default_constraints`, `sys.computed_columns` | Per column: name, ordinal position, declared type, `max_length`, `precision`, `scale`, `collation_name`, `is_nullable`, `is_identity` with its seed and increment, `is_computed` with its definition, and the **name and definition of any default constraint** bound to it. This is the root that decides seven of the nine divergence dimensions step 3 enumerates |
   | `sys.indexes` | `sys.index_columns`, `sys.columns` | Per index: name, `is_unique`, `is_primary_key`, `is_unique_constraint`, `type_desc` (clustered or not), the **ordered key column list** with each column's ordinal and `is_descending_key`, the included-column list, and `has_filter` with `filter_definition`. This is the root that decides the index dimension, and the filter predicate is why it cannot be inferred from a key list |
   | `sys.key_constraints` | `sys.indexes`, `sys.check_constraints` | Per primary-key and unique constraint: name and the backing index it is enforced by — so a constraint and its index are recorded as one fact rather than two guesses — and, through `sys.check_constraints`, **every named `CHECK` constraint with its `definition`**. This is the root that decides the key dimension |
   | `sys.foreign_keys` | `sys.foreign_key_columns`, `sys.columns`, `sys.tables` | Per foreign key: name, the referencing and referenced tables, the **ordered** referencing and referenced column pairs, `delete_referential_action_desc` and `update_referential_action_desc`, and `is_disabled` and `is_not_trusted`. This is the root that decides the delete-rule dimension |

   Two properties of the record follow and are stated so the diff has something total to compare
   against. **The record is complete for the tables in scope or the extraction fails** — a root that
   returns no rows for a table the scope names is a precondition failure (exit `2`), not an empty
   section, because "no indexes recorded" and "no indexes exist" are the two readings a gate cannot
   distinguish afterwards. And **the record carries no value the four roots did not return**: no default
   supplied by convention, no width inferred from a CLR type, and no delete rule assumed from a
   relationship's optionality. Where a fact is genuinely absent from the source, the record says so, and
   step 3 compares against that absence rather than against a guess.
2. **Map every extracted object to the EF Core model**, and express the result in
   `MusicStoreEntities.OnModelCreating` (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)).
3. **Generate each store's baseline migration and diff its DDL against that store's extracted record,
   inside that store's declared comparison scope. The diff must report zero differences — not zero
   *unexplained* differences — before any data is loaded.** The rule
   is absolute and it is one rule, because the alternative is the one this step cannot survive: **there
   is no annotation under which a difference is admitted.** "Expected difference, see section X" is
   precisely the label a genuine discrepancy is waved through under, and a single sanctioned exception
   converts the gate from a comparison into a judgement call for every later reader. A reported
   difference therefore has exactly **two** dispositions and no third: it is **corrected in the model**,
   so that the baseline reproduces the source; or — where it is an intended target-state change rather
   than a modelling error — the model is written to the **source's** shape for the baseline and the
   intended change **ships as a named subsequent migration** in the post-baseline group below, never
   inside the baseline. This is the gate; a data load against an unverified schema is the failure this
   whole section exists to prevent.

   **The comparison scope is declared per store, and declaring it is what makes an absolute rule
   achievable rather than aspirational.** "Zero differences" is only a rule if both sides of the
   comparison are the same set of objects; a comparison whose right-hand side is "the target database"
   can never reach zero, because the target database also holds objects the source never had. So the
   scope is fixed, per `--store`, before the diff runs:

   | `--store` | The baseline migration | The comparison scope — the objects on both sides |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `catalog` | **`InitialCatalog`** | The **six catalog tables** the extracted record covers [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12], and every column, default, `CHECK`, key, index and foreign key **on those six tables**. `InitialCatalog` contains nothing that is not in `schema.catalog.json`, so this side is a pure source-equivalent reproduction and the comparison is total |
   | `identity` | **`InitialIdentity`** | The **Identity tables the extracted record covers** — the ASP.NET Identity 1.0 tables the source store carries — and, on those tables, **the columns the extracted record names**. `InitialIdentity` creates the target ASP.NET Core Identity schema **fresh**, which is the decision section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) takes and AAP §0.3.2 requires, so the target framework's added columns — the stamps, the two-factor, lockout, phone and confirmation columns, and the normalized columns — exist on the target side and in no source. **They are outside this scope by construction, and section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) declares them as a closed set with a defined origin per column.** They are therefore not annotated exceptions on a diff report; the diff never sees them, and inside the scope it must still report zero |

   **Everything outside both scopes is outside by construction, not by exception**, and it is a closed
   list: the tool's four `dbo.__DataMigration*` run tables (section
   [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)), `dbo.SessionCache`,
   `dbo.SecurityAuditLog`, `dbo.DataProtectionKeys`, the cart-merge objects and the table type of the
   post-baseline group below, and every `history` schema object of the change-tracking group. Each of
   those is created by a **named** migration or a **named** non-context artifact that the manifest
   [06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes orders — which is what "held back" means
   concretely, and why no target-only object ever has to be waved through a diff.
4. **Back up the source, then extract the data.** The backup copy is preserved as the rollback
   position, and the source itself moves through the **source-disposition lifecycle** section
   [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
   owns — this extraction is that lifecycle's stage **X**, between the neutralization at **M1** and the
   read-only freeze at **M2**. "Preserved unmodified" was an earlier form's wording and is withdrawn: the
   source receives exactly the writes that lifecycle's `Writes?` column enumerates, and after **M2** the
   engine refuses any further one. **The backup is taken after `M1`, never before it**, and that ordering
   is a security requirement rather than a convenience: a copy taken before the neutralization still
   carries the repository-published administrator hash, so restoring it during a rollback would put the
   published credential back into service — the exposure [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) criterion 6
   exists to close. A pre-`M1` copy, if one is taken for any other reason, is not a rollback position and
   is destroyed rather than retained.
5. **Apply the baseline migration to the target database**, then **load in dependency order**:
   **genres and artists** (no dependencies), then **albums** (referencing both), then **carts**
   (referencing albums), then **orders**, then **order details** (referencing orders and albums).
   Identity-column behaviour must be handled explicitly at load time so that existing key values are
   preserved — `Cart.RecordId`, `Order.OrderId` and `OrderDetail.OrderDetailId` are referenced by
   other rows and by nothing else, but `Order.OrderId` is also the **confirmation number** the
   application shows the customer [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:53-54],
   so renumbering orders would change a value users have already been given.
   **The load converts timestamps as it goes**: `Order.OrderDate` and `Cart.DateCreated` are rewritten
   from the required `LegacySourceTimeZone` parameter into UTC, and the load **fails closed** if that
   parameter is absent or unresolvable — section
   [8.13](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) owns the rule, and the
   coverage of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts both halves of it — the conversion the load
   performs and the refusal it returns when the parameter is absent or unresolvable.
6. **Reconcile.** Row count **per table**, before and after. And **financial totals per order** —
   `Order.Total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] compared against the sum of its
   `OrderDetail.UnitPrice * Quantity` rows, computed on the source and on the target and required to
   match to the cent. Reconciliation failure blocks cutover.
7. **Protect the data in transit and at rest.** The order tables carry name, postal address, phone
   number and email address [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61], so the extract is PII: it
   travels only over an encrypted connection, is held only in an encrypted location, is access-logged,
   and is destroyed on a stated schedule after reconciliation passes. [09 §6.8](09-security-assessment.md)
   owns the standing PII finding.
8. **Define how rows written between extraction and cutover are handled.** Under the single-cutover
   decision of section [11](#11-the-cutover-decision) the answer is a **drain**: the legacy
   application is drained before the final extract, so the window is closed rather than
   reconciled. Any trickle-load design is therefore explicitly **not** built; if the cutover approach
   were ever revisited, this step would have to be re-answered.
9. **State the rollback position and the closing acceptance criteria.** Rollback is: the source
   database is **at its frozen state — stage `M2` of the source-disposition lifecycle of section
   [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)**,
   which is read-only and whose content equality is established by that section's two mechanisms — the
   legacy application is redeployable, and the target database is
   discarded. Acceptance is: the schema diff passed, every per-table row count matches, every order
   total matches, and the coverage of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) passes against the loaded
   data.

**Four groups of schema changes are deliberately held back until after that acceptance, and they are the
only ones.** Each is a **named** migration, applied in the post-load deployment step in the order below:

| # | The named catalog migration | What it carries | Specified in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **`AddCheckoutSubmissionId`** | The nullable `Orders.SubmissionId` column and its unique index filtered to `WHERE [SubmissionId] IS NOT NULL` | Immediately below, and section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) for what consumes it |
| 2 | **`AddCartMergeConstraints`** | Every target-only object the cart's one concurrency domain needs: the **bounded length** on `Cart.CartId` and `CartAlias`'s two id columns, the **unique index on `(CartId, AlbumId)`**, the named `CK_Cart_Count_Positive` constraint, the `dbo.CartMutationOperation` ledger, the `dbo.CartAlias` table, and the `dbo.CartRecordIdList` table type where section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)'s preferred table-valued carrier is chosen | Sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity), which state what each object is for; this table states **when it ships** |
| 3 | **`AlterTimestampColumnTypes`** — conditional | `Order.OrderDate` and `Cart.DateCreated` from the source's type to `datetime2` | The end of this sub-section |
| 4 | **`AddChangeTracking`** — one per context | The `rowversion` and `ModifiedUtc` column pair and system versioning on every tracked table, including **`Cart.RowVersion`** | The end of this sub-section |

<a id="the-two-ordered-manifests"></a>
**The Identity context's post-baseline set, and the two heads — stated literally here because a set with
one member still has an order, and because a rollback target and a bundle's terminal argument are the same
string.** The Identity context takes **two** post-baseline migrations, in this order: **`AddChangeTracking`**
— the same name as the catalog migration above and a different migration, per
[06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s note on the shared name — then
**`AddDataProtectionKeys`**, the key-repository table of section
[4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it). That is the order
[06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `M8` publishes.

| Context | Its migrations, in applied order | Its head | Held constant across the conditional branch? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Catalog** (`Data/Migrations/Catalog/`) | `InitialCatalog`, `AddCheckoutSubmissionId`, `AddCartMergeConstraints`, `AlterTimestampColumnTypes` (**only where section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)'s extraction branch generates it**), `AddChangeTracking` | **`AddChangeTracking`** | **Yes.** The conditional migration is *third* when it exists and absent when it does not, so it never displaces the head. Every consumer that names the catalog head — a rollback target, a bundle's terminal argument, and the post-`M7` history-table comparison — reads this one string in either branch |
| **Identity** (`Data/Migrations/Identity/`) | `InitialIdentity`, `AddChangeTracking`, `AddDataProtectionKeys` | **`AddDataProtectionKeys`** | **Yes.** No conditional migration exists in this context |

**These two rows are the manifest every other statement in this document consumes verbatim.** No other
site states either order or either head; where one is needed it is cited from here. That rule exists
because the alternative was already tried and failed: an earlier form of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) placed `AlterTimestampColumnTypes` **after**
`AddChangeTracking` and made the catalog head branch-dependent, section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 84 applied the set in that reversed order, and
[06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s cutover row still carries the same reversal — which is
a defect in that document and is reported rather than restated here. All three disagreed with
[06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `M7`, which is the ordering above, and a release that
followed any of them would have altered a live system-versioned column pair for no reason.

<a id="cart-merge-object-census"></a>
**`AddCartMergeConstraints`'s object census, once and exactly — six items unconditionally and a seventh on
one recorded decision.** Three enumerations disagreed: one counted five *including* the bounded lengths and
made the table type a sixth, another named five *excluding* them, the withdrawn pre-load stage spoke of
"the cart's five target-only objects" while listing a different five, and **none** of the three carried
`Order.Username`'s alteration at all. This table is the census; every other site cites it.

| # | Item | Kind | Specified in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `Cart.CartId` altered to a **bounded** `nvarchar(n)`, `n` fixed by section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s width rule from step 1's extraction | **Alteration** of an existing column — the reason this migration must precede `AddChangeTracking` | Sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) |
| 2 | The **unique index on `Cart(CartId, AlbumId)`** | New object | Section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) |
| 3 | **`CK_Cart_Count_Positive`**, `CHECK (Count >= 1)` | New object | Section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) |
| 4 | **`dbo.CartMutationOperation`**, the mutation ledger | New table | Section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) |
| 5 | **`dbo.CartAlias`**, whose two id columns are declared bounded **at creation** at the same width, which is why bounding them is not a separate item | New table | Section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) |
| 6 | **`Order.Username` altered to the same bounded `nvarchar(n)`** — the ownership key, which the same width rule and the same evidence gate govern, and which must therefore land in this migration rather than a later one for the ordering reason below | **Alteration** of an existing column | The [cart-key width rule](#the-cart-key-width-rule) |
| 7 | **`dbo.CartRecordIdList`** table type — **conditional**, shipping only where section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)'s preferred table-valued carrier is chosen over its chunked alternative | New type | Section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) |

**Six plus one conditional, and two of the six are alterations rather than objects** — which is the
distinction the two disagreeing enumerations lost, and `Order.Username` is the item both of them dropped
entirely even though section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)'s extraction
table has always required it. 6 + 1 = 7 at most; **4 new objects, 2 alterations, and 1 conditional new
type**, and 4 + 2 = 6 unconditional items. Both alterations are on existing columns, which is what places
this migration before `AddChangeTracking` in the [ordered manifest](#the-two-ordered-manifests) above.
None of the seven is recorded in the step 3 diff: all seven are outside the catalog store's comparison
scope by construction, so none is annotated onto a diff required to report none.

**All four are held back for the same reason — step 3's rule admits no annotated exception — and stating
them as a closed set of four is what makes that rule enforceable**: a fifth intended difference is not
permitted to appear as an annotation on the diff, it has to appear here. **There is no pre-load catalog
migration other than `InitialCatalog`.** An earlier revision of sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) placed
the cart's five target-only objects in a "pre-load catalog migration stage" and had step 3 record each of
them as a *deliberate net-new object in the diff* — which is precisely the annotated exception step 3
refuses, five times over. They ship in `AddCartMergeConstraints` instead, and because that migration is
applied before traffic is admitted, nothing that consumes those objects at runtime is affected by the
move. **Ordering inside the step matters, and the rule is one rule rather than a special case**: every
migration that alters an existing column must precede `AddChangeTracking`, which is why `AddChangeTracking`
is **last** of the four. Both of the others alter columns — `AddCartMergeConstraints` puts a bounded length
on **two** of them, `Cart.CartId` and `Order.Username`, and `AlterTimestampColumnTypes` changes two datetime columns outright — and from `AddChangeTracking` onward
the tables are system-versioned, at which point an alteration has to land on the history table too. The
order above is therefore `AddCheckoutSubmissionId`, `AddCartMergeConstraints`, `AlterTimestampColumnTypes`,
`AddChangeTracking`, which is the order [06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s canonical manifest
publishes for this step; this document states which object each migration carries and why the relative
order is forced, and 06 remains the sole numbering of the release sequence. Both of
`AddCartMergeConstraints`'s alterations are the single
[cart-key width rule](#the-cart-key-width-rule), and the second of them — `Order.Username`, which three
earlier enumerations dropped — is why that migration's own object
[census](#cart-merge-object-census) carries six unconditional items rather than five.

**One clarification the closed set needs, because it is the way a fourth member gets in by accident: a
bound on an input model is not a schema difference.** The checkout input model's `[StringLength(254)]` on
`Email` and `[StringLength(16)]` on `PromoCode` (section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)) and the administration models' copied
attributes (section [8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target))
constrain what the application **accepts**; they are not `HasMaxLength` calls on an entity and they change
no column. So they are absent from this set by construction rather than by omission — and the corollary
binds: a validation bound may **not** be paired with a narrower column "for alignment" in the baseline
model, because that pairing is exactly a fourth intended difference wearing an annotation. Section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) records that `Order.Email` therefore keeps
**whatever width step 1's extraction records for it, whatever that turns out to be** — the width is a
property of the source database and is not derived here from an EF 6 convention — and that narrowing it
would require a **fifth** named post-baseline migration with an overlength precheck rather than a note on
the diff. The checkout submission key of section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) needs a nullable `SubmissionId` column on
`Orders` and a unique index over it filtered to `WHERE [SubmissionId] IS NOT NULL`. Neither is in the
initial migration, and the reason is step 3: the value of the diff gate comes entirely from the initial
migration being a **pure reproduction** of the extracted schema, so that every difference it reports is a
real one. Introducing the column there would put a known, intended difference into the one comparison
whose whole job is to surface unintended ones — and "expected difference" is exactly the annotation under
which a genuine discrepancy gets waved through. It therefore ships as a **second catalog migration**,
applied after the load and after reconciliation, against which the diff has nothing to say. Every
migrated order carries `NULL` in the new column, which is what the index filter accommodates.

**The change-tracking pair — `AddChangeTracking`, the last of the four — exists so that a rollback
decision rests on evidence rather than on a probe.** [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) decides whether a
rollback is still available by detecting whether any customer write has been accepted since traffic was
admitted, and it establishes that counting rows cannot answer that question: a successful password change
leaves the account count unchanged, and a quantity-only cart update leaves both the row count and the key
set unchanged. Detection therefore needs per-row evidence, and this document owns the schema, so the
columns are specified here rather than assumed there. Every tracked table gains a database-maintained
`rowversion` column and a `ModifiedUtc` `datetime2` column, **and is made system-versioned** — the third
mechanism, without which the first two cannot see a deletion at all. **Which tables those are is
[06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to state and it states them**: the catalog context's six
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/MusicStoreEntities.cs:7-12] and the tables the Identity context owns, with
the session cache table and `dbo.DataProtectionKeys` **excluded** as platform state. **No audit table
appears in that list, because there is none** — [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) withdrew it,
and [06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states the same from the tracking side. That list is
06's and this document does not widen it. This document owns what the requirement takes of the schema and
the model, and there are **four** parts to it.

**It is two migrations, one per context, and it cannot be one.** The columns span both contexts, and each
context owns a separate migrations folder and a distinct history table (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)) — so a single *catalog* migration carrying
`ALTER TABLE` statements against `AspNetUsers` would place Identity DDL in the catalog history, leave the
Identity model's snapshot disagreeing with the database, and make the next Identity migration generate
those same columns a second time. What ships is therefore **`AddChangeTracking` in
`Data/Migrations/Catalog/`** covering the six catalog tables and **`AddChangeTracking` in
`Data/Migrations/Identity/`** covering the Identity tables, each generated from and validated against its
own model snapshot. Both are applied in the same post-load deployment step as `AddCheckoutSubmissionId`
and after it — after the load and after reconciliation, for the same diff-gate reason
`AddCheckoutSubmissionId` is held back — in the sequence [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns.

**The mapping is authored per context, in each context's `OnModelCreating`, and the `rowversion` half takes
three explicit calls rather than one convenient one.** There is no shared base class and no cross-context
convention to lean on, so each context configures its own entities: `ModifiedUtc` as a required
`datetime2`, and a `byte[] RowVersion` property configured with **`.HasColumnType("rowversion")`,
`.ValueGeneratedOnAddOrUpdate()` and `.IsConcurrencyToken(false)`** — the call pair
[06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) names, plus the column type that pair leaves
undetermined.

**The third call is why the first is necessary, and this is the one place the shorthand's absence has a
consequence worth writing down.** `.IsRowVersion()` sets store generation *and* concurrency-token
semantics together, and 06 wants only the first half — but SQL Server's provider convention selects the
`rowversion` store type for a `byte[]` property *because* that property is a concurrency token generated on
add or update. Turning the token off therefore also turns off the convention that chose the type, and a
property left with `.ValueGeneratedOnAddOrUpdate()` alone maps to `varbinary(max)`: a column with no engine
maintenance behind it, which never moves, and whose failure mode is that every detection query reports **no
writes** — the one failure this evidence cannot tolerate, because it is silent and it reads as good news.
The type is therefore stated rather than inferred. Two further properties follow from the configuration and
need no extra calls: EF Core's before-save and after-save behaviour for a store-generated,
non-concurrency-token property is `Ignore`, so no insert or update ever sends a value the engine owns; and
because the property is not a concurrency token it never enters an `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause, which is what
keeps last-write-wins intact. The property is declared with a private setter so no application code can
assign it even by mistake.

The two contexts' configurations are deliberately parallel rather than shared, because the alternative — a
common `DbContext` base type introduced solely to hold two property configurations — couples the catalog and
Identity models for the rest of the port's life to save eight lines.

**The maintenance path is per context too, and `ModifiedUtc` is where that matters.** `rowversion` needs
no application involvement at all; `ModifiedUtc` does, and a save path that maintains it in one context
and not the other yields exactly the half-complete evidence [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
says the determination cannot rest on. **Both** contexts therefore override `SaveChangesAsync` — and
`SaveChanges`, so a synchronous call cannot bypass it — to stamp `ModifiedUtc = DateTime.UtcNow` on every
entry whose state is `Added` or `Modified` and whose entity type declares the property. Two consequences
are stated rather than left to be discovered: a write issued through `ExecuteUpdateAsync` **does not pass
through this path** and must set the column in its own statement, which is why every statement the cart's
merge and quantity paths issue (sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) assigns it explicitly; and the checkout write path's
single save (section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) step 8) picks the column up
for the order, its details and nothing else, because the cart rows it touches are `Deleted` rather than
`Modified`.

Two properties of the column pair are decisions rather than details. The first is the one the mapping above
implements: `rowversion` is **deliberately not** a concurrency token, because `IsRowVersion()`'s token half
would make every one of these tables optimistically concurrent, turning a second concurrent edit into a
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` — a behaviour change in a port whose baseline is last-write-wins, and one no
approved delta covers. And applying the migration *after* the load is sound
rather than merely convenient, because `ALTER TABLE … ADD rowversion` stamps every existing row at alter
time: every migrated row therefore carries a value strictly below the `MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION()` watermark
[06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records when traffic is admitted, which is exactly the
comparison the rollback regimes make. `ModifiedUtc` is written by the application on every update under
the rule of section [8.13](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display), and
corroborates `rowversion` rather than replacing it — a row version moves on any write, including one a
trigger or a tool made, while `ModifiedUtc` says when the application last wrote.

**The fourth part is system versioning, and it exists because the column pair is blind to exactly one class
of write — the one that removes the row it would have been recorded on.** A `rowversion` and a
`ModifiedUtc` live *on* a row, so a `DELETE` takes both away with it. A signed-in customer who removes the
last line from their cart therefore leaves **no current row, no advanced version and no timestamp**; the
cart surface emits no audit class either — [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) defines none for it and
this document does not extend that catalog — so on the columns alone that removal is indistinguishable from
a cart nobody touched. [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s determination is required to see
it, so the schema carries the mechanism that makes it visible: **each tracked table is a SQL Server
temporal table**, and the engine retains the prior state of every updated row and the **full final state of
every deleted row** in a bound history table. Five parts of that are this document's to state.

| Part | What ships |
| --- | --- |
| **Authoring** | `ToTable(tb => tb.IsTemporal(…))` on every tracked entity in that context's `OnModelCreating`, and the resulting DDL is carried **inside the same `AddChangeTracking` migration** in that context's set. So versioning adds **no migration target and no invocation**: the census of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) is unchanged at four or five post-load targets and 06's three invocations. It is authored as a migration rather than as operator DDL for the reason [06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s first operational consequence gives |
| **Naming — 06 defers this to "05's convention", so here it is** | History table `<EntityTable>History` in a dedicated **`history`** schema, one per tracked table; period columns named `PeriodStart` and `PeriodEnd`, mapped as **shadow properties** so they never appear on an entity type and no view or projection can pick them up by accident. The schema is the only departure from EF Core's default, which would put `<EntityTable>History` beside the current table in `dbo`: a separate schema keeps `dbo` legible next to the session cache, key-ring and audit tables that are **not** versioned, and it turns the grant rule below into one schema-level statement instead of one per table |
| **Retention** | An explicit `HISTORY_RETENTION_PERIOD`, set to the PITR retention window [06 §6.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns — **the value is not restated here**, because it is the data owner's at approval and 06 is where it is read. It is applied by a raw-SQL statement **inside the same migration**, because EF Core's temporal mapping models the versioning and the history table but not the retention period, and a migration that calls only `IsTemporal()` leaves retention infinite. One implementation precondition rides with it: retention cleanup requires the history table to carry a clustered index whose leading column is the period-end column, which is what the engine creates when the migration materializes the bound history table — the migration must not replace that index with one of its own |
| **Grants** | **No grant is issued to the runtime principal on the `history` schema.** [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s runtime-identity grants name the current tables only, and ordinary DML on a system-versioned table needs no permission on its history table — so the application keeps working and cannot read the history it is generating. The history rows carry the same fields the current rows do, which makes them personal data on the Identity side; [06 §11.5.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records that consequence and its retention and access treatment, and this document does not restate it |
| **Ordering** | Versioning is enabled in the **same post-load step as the columns**, and that is a precondition of the determination rather than a convenience: [06 §11.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) step 8 asserts **zero rows in every history table** at the moment the watermark is taken, and enabling versioning before the load would have filled them with the load's own writes and the Identity data migration's own — so the emptiness assertion, which is what makes any later history row evidence on its own, would simply not be available |

**How the removal of a final cart line is detected, stated as the query rather than as a property.** Two
facts turn it into an existence check with no clock and no arithmetic in it: the history tables are empty
when the watermark is taken, and the engine writes a history row for **every** update and **every** delete
on a tracked table. So "has any tracked row been written since traffic was admitted" is answered per table
by `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM history.<T>History)`, and the removal of a customer's last cart line is caught by
the `history.CartsHistory` row carrying that row's full final state — its `RecordId`, `CartId`, `AlbumId`,
`Count` and `DateCreated` — at a moment when the current `Carts` table holds nothing for that cart at all.

**Why the watermark alone cannot do it, stated because it is the trap an implementer walks into.** The
`rowversion` value retained in a history row is the value the row carried **before** it was deleted. A cart
row written by the domain load and deleted after admission therefore retains a value **strictly below**
`MIN_ACTIVE_ROWVERSION()`, so a scan that applied the watermark comparison to history rows would classify
that deletion as pre-admission and report no write — the same silent false negative the pair produces on
its own. The determination therefore rests on history **existence**, not on the retained version value;
`PeriodEnd`, which the engine sets to the deleting transaction's UTC start, is available where a
*classification* is wanted — a history row whose key has no matching current row is a delete rather than an
update — but the classification table in [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is where each
class is assigned, and this document owns only that the mechanism exists and answers that query.

**One property the pair does not have, which closes a gap this document flags elsewhere.** System
versioning is engine-maintained, so it captures writes that never pass through a `SaveChanges` override at
all: the set-based and authored statements of sections [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) and
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) — which is why each of them
assigns `ModifiedUtc` explicitly — any future `ExecuteDeleteAsync`, and any write a tool
or an operator makes. `ModifiedUtc` can be forgotten by a code path; a history row cannot.

**`AlterTimestampColumnTypes` carries the timestamp column type, and it is held back for exactly the
reason step 3 admits no annotation.** `Order.OrderDate` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:15] and `Cart.DateCreated`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:14-15] are declared bare — no `HasColumnType`, no fluent
configuration, and the source context declares no `OnModelCreating` at all (section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); `Cart.DateCreated`'s
`[DataType(DataType.DateTime)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:14] is a *display* annotation and
maps nothing — so EF 6's default mapping for a non-nullable `DateTime` on SQL Server governs and the
extracted schema is **expected to show `datetime`**. EF Core's default for the same property is
`datetime2`, which is the type section
[8.13](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) requires. Both cannot be true
of the baseline, and letting the difference through the gate as an annotated deliberate change is the
one disposition step 3 refuses. So:

- **The baseline maps the source's type.** Both properties carry an explicit `.HasColumnType("datetime")`
  in the baseline model, so the initial migration reproduces the extracted type and the diff reports
  nothing at all.
- **The move to `datetime2` ships as a named catalog migration, `AlterTimestampColumnTypes`**, applied
  in the same post-load deployment step as the two groups above and **third** within it — after
  `AddCheckoutSubmissionId` and `AddCartMergeConstraints` and **before `AddChangeTracking`** — once
  reconciliation has passed.
  The `.HasColumnType("datetime")` calls are removed from the model in the same change, so the final
  model is the target model and the alteration is the diff between two migrations rather than an
  exception to one.
- **Being third rather than last is the whole point, and an earlier form of this bullet had it backwards.**
  Because `AddChangeTracking` follows this migration, neither `Orders` nor `Carts` is system-versioned yet
  when the `ALTER COLUMN` arrives: there is no bound history table to keep union-compatible, no
  suspend-and-re-enable pair around the alteration, and no history rows in existence to preserve across it.
  The history tables are created afterwards, by `AddChangeTracking`, from columns that are **already**
  `datetime2`, so both sides carry the target type by construction rather than by a propagation this
  document would otherwise have to assert. That is exactly the ordering rule section
  [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) states — every migration that alters an existing column
  precedes `AddChangeTracking`, which is why `AddChangeTracking` is last of the four — and it is the order
  [06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `M7` publishes. **An earlier form of this bullet placed
  this migration after `AddChangeTracking` and then specified the two-sided alteration, the
  suspend-and-re-enable pair and the pre-alteration history rows that ordering would have required. All of
  it is withdrawn**, so that a reader meeting it in an older copy recognises it as the superseded
  generation rather than as a second requirement: the pass criterion is now that both types are equal on
  both sides and versioning reads back `ON`, which the correct order makes true without an alteration of a
  versioned table ever occurring.
- **Nothing is lost by loading before altering.** `datetime`'s resolution is what the source rows already
  carry, and step 5 writes converted values of exactly that provenance, so the alteration widens a column
  over rows no wider than it. Every value the *target* writes arrives after the alteration, because this
  step precedes traffic admission.
- **The conditional is resolved by extraction, not left open.** If step 1 shows the columns are already
  `datetime2` — which nothing in the source suggests — the baseline maps them as `datetime2`, this
  migration is **not generated**, and the **catalog** post-load set is three migrations rather than four:
  the census of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) then stands at **four** post-load
  targets across the two contexts rather than five. **The catalog head is `AddChangeTracking` on both
  branches, and the head is not branch-dependent** — that migration is last of the set whether the set has
  three members or four, because this one is third when it exists and absent when it does not. What the
  branch moves is the *count*, never the head: a rollback target, a bundle's terminal argument and the
  post-`M7` history-table comparison of [06 §6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) therefore all read the
  same single name in either branch. Either way the decision is made by step
  1's output before the baseline is generated, and neither branch puts a difference through the gate.

#### 5.1.1 The extract is PII — how it is held, and how it is destroyed

**"Encrypted and access-logged" is a property, not a procedure, and an extract with no procedure is the
copy nobody deletes.** Step 4 produces a file — or a set of files — containing every customer's name,
street address, city, state, postal code, country, phone number and email address, joined to what they
bought and what they paid [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]. It is the most sensitive
artifact this entire migration creates, it exists for hours or days, and it is created by a workstream
rather than by a system with a retention policy. So the handling is specified here.

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it is held** | In **one** location: a dedicated container in the migration workstream's own storage account, created for this migration and used for nothing else, with **no public access**, and **not** on an operator's workstation, not in the repository, not in a pipeline artifact, and not in the checkout — AAP §0.11.5 makes a dirty working tree a release failure, and a PII file inside it would be one of the worst forms of that |
| **Encrypted at rest** | Service-side encryption is not optional and is not the control: 256-bit AES "is enabled for all storage accounts and can't be disabled" (*Azure Storage encryption for data at rest*), and it is transparent to any principal holding data-plane read access — which is exactly the failure this handling has to survive. The controls are therefore the ones section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read) sets on a **dedicated account**: **infrastructure encryption** for a second, independently keyed layer; a **customer-managed key**, which is the **residual** destruction control rather than the erasure itself — it is destroyed *after* the deletion has been performed and proven, and what it adds there is coverage of what a delete cannot be **proven** to have reached, such as a soft-deleted blob, a retained version or a copy the enumeration missed, none of which it has to find first (the order and its reason are the destruction row's, in that same subsection); **no shared-key access**, so every access is an attributable identity; and a **private-only network path**, which is what makes "not on an operator's workstation" a route that does not exist rather than an instruction |
| **Encrypted in transit** | Every hop: the extraction connection to the source, the upload, the download, and the load's connection to the target, all TLS — the two database connections carrying `Encrypt=True` with `TrustServerCertificate=False`, per the mode table of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), and the storage account configured **HTTPS-only with a minimum TLS version of 1.2**. No hop copies through an unencrypted intermediate, which specifically rules out an SMB share and an emailed archive. The private-endpoint path of section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read) is what keeps every one of those hops off the public internet in the first place, so a TLS misconfiguration on one of them is a defect rather than a disclosure |
| **Under whose identity** | Written by the **extraction principal** and read by the **load principal** — **two distinct user-assigned managed identities**, named, attached and scoped in the identity block of section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read), and **neither of them the deployment principal** that executes the load's SQL. The application's runtime managed identity has **no** access to this container and is never granted any: the running application has no reason to read a copy of its own database, and a grant that exists is a grant that gets used |
| **Who may read it** | A **named** set of people, recorded before the extract is taken, each with the reason they are on it, and no group membership standing in for a name. The set is scoped to the migration and is removed when the extract is destroyed, not when the migration ends |
| **How access is audited** | Storage read-access logging enabled on the container **before** the first write, and reviewed as part of the closing acceptance of step 9 — so "who read this" is answerable rather than asserted. An extract whose container has no logging enabled is not taken. **The log is retained 365 days**, outliving the extract by a wide margin: it is an audit record rather than operational exhaust, which is the class [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) gives that number to, and its whole value is being producible months after the container is gone |
| **Cleanup on success** | The extract and every derived file — the step reports of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), any intermediate transform output, any local copy made during troubleshooting — are deleted **within 7 days of reconciliation passing**, and **both containers** and the account are deleted with them |
| **Cleanup on failure** | The **same deadline, from the same clock**. This is the row that matters: a failed or abandoned migration is exactly the case where an extract survives, because nobody is left running the procedure that would delete it. The deadline therefore runs from **extraction**, not from success — 7 days from reconciliation passing **or 30 days from extraction, whichever comes first** — and a migration still in flight at 30 days re-extracts rather than extending |
| **Proof of deletion** | A recorded artifact, not an assertion: the deletion operation's own log entries for the container and the account, plus a post-deletion listing showing both absent, captured into the migration's run record with the date and the person who performed it — **and the key-destruction record, the vault deletion and purge records, and the immutable copy of the access log** that section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read)'s destruction rows fix. The **key destruction** is the piece that does not depend on having found every copy inside the account, and it is immediate — and it **follows** the verified deletion rather than preceding it, because a destroyed key answers `403` to the very data-plane delete and listing this row requires, which is the ordering that row fixes and the reason it is fixed; the **vault purge** is the piece that cannot be immediate, because purge protection is mandatory on a vault holding a Storage customer-managed key and it blocks a purge until the retention interval expires. The immutable log copy is the piece that outlives the account it describes. Step 9's acceptance criteria do not close without the same-day items, and the run record does not close without the purge record |

**What this section deliberately does not decide.** It bounds the **temporary extract** and nothing else.
The **standing** retention decision — how long the application itself keeps order PII, which is a policy
question about live data — belongs to the **data owner** through
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s approval gate, and [09 §6.8](09-security-assessment.md) carries the
finding that no such policy exists today. This document does not invent a legal retention period,
because inventing one would let a reader believe the question had been answered.

##### 5.1.1.1 The protection, named — the account, the key, the network path, and the grants that gate a read

**"Password-protected or key-encrypted" is two options, and an option is not a specification.** A
protection that names no mechanism has no access rule, no audit record and no way of being destroyed on
purpose, which is the property the cleanup rows above actually rest on. So the whole of it is fixed here,
once, for **every file this migration puts in that account** — the extract, the
checkpoint file of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), any
row-level extract a troubleshooting step produces, and the verified source backups
[06 §6.7.2.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) takes, which hold the same PII and come under this
handling from the moment they leave the legacy host.

**And one reason the protection cannot be applied by the database engine, which is where a reader would
look for it first.** `BACKUP … WITH ENCRYPTION` and transparent data encryption are both listed as
**Enterprise and Standard only** — "Encryption for backups" and "Transparent data encryption (TDE)" are
**No** for Web, Express with Advanced Services and Express (*Editions and supported features of SQL
Server 2022*) — and LocalDB "is a lightweight version of Express edition". The legacy source is LocalDB,
so the engine cannot encrypt its own backup, and every artifact it produces is plaintext at the moment it
is written. That is not a gap to be closed inside SQL Server; it is the reason the protection is applied
at the moment the file leaves the host.

**The mechanism is entirely platform-side, and the in-process alternative is rejected on a constraint this
plan already fixed.** An earlier version of this subsection specified **Azure Storage client-side
encryption v2** — envelope encryption performed by the operator utility, with a Key Vault-held wrapping
key — and closed by noting that its package references "belong to [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s
table as an approval-time addition". That closing note is the defect. AAP §0.5.2 fixes the pin list and
states the principle in its own words: secrets arrive as **App Service Key Vault references**, "so no Key
Vault client is referenced". Client-side encryption cannot be implemented without exactly that — a blob
client and a key-resolver client in process — so specifying it is specifying an extension of a frozen list,
and the correct resolution is to obtain the same properties from the platform, which can supply every one
of them and needs **no package at all**. The consequence is stronger than a cheaper dependency graph:
**the operator utility gains no storage client either**, so the tool's dependency set is exactly
[04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s with nothing added, and file movement is a release-step
command rather than application code.

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **The account** | A **dedicated storage account** created for this migration, holding this migration's containers and nothing else, deleted with them. Three containers, all under the properties below: the **extract** container; `migration-reports`, whose separation is the identity table's reason and not a naming preference; and `legacy-source-backup`, which [06 §6.7.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) places in this same account so that one key and one destruction sequence cover every PII artifact the migration creates. Not a shared account with a private container in it: the account is the boundary that the next rows are set on, and several of them cannot be set per container |
| **Encryption at rest — the platform's, doubled** | **Infrastructure encryption enabled on the account**, which encrypts data "twice — once at the service level, and once at the infrastructure level — with two different encryption algorithms and two different keys" (*Enable infrastructure encryption for double encryption of data*, Azure Storage). One rule follows and it is a creation-time rule, not a hardening step: infrastructure encryption **can only be enabled when the account is created** (same source), so an account created without it is replaced rather than amended, and this is the one property of this design that cannot be repaired after the fact |
| **The key** | A **customer-managed key** configured on that account — an RSA key in a Key Vault created for this migration and used for nothing else, **non-exportable**, with the account's own managed identity granted `Get`, `Wrap Key` and `Unwrap Key` on that one key through Key Vault RBAC and nothing else. The reason it is customer-managed rather than the platform's own is a single property: **the key is a destruction control this migration holds itself**, destroyed on this migration's own schedule as the **residual** stage of the destruction row below — after the verified deletion, never instead of it, for the reason that row states. Rotation is not scheduled and is not needed — the key outlives nothing, and the rule is non-reuse: one key per migration, destroyed with it and its vault purged after the vault's retention interval. The key must also satisfy the platform's own requirements for this use: it is **RSA or RSA-HSM**, at 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits (*Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption*, key-vault requirements) |
| **The network path** | **`publicNetworkAccess` disabled** on the account, reached through a **private endpoint** in the migration workstream's own network. Every principal that reads or writes the extract — the extraction host, the load host, and a named person performing a troubleshooting read — does so from inside that network, through the release agent or a jump host. This is what enforces the "not on an operator's workstation" rule of the table above **mechanically** rather than by instruction: a workstation outside that network has no route to the account, so a local copy cannot be made by accident |
| **No Shared Key access — and the one bearer credential that survives it, named rather than assumed away** | **`allowSharedKeyAccess` set to `false`.** What that actually denies is **Shared Key authorization**: the account keys themselves, the **service SAS** and the **account SAS**, all three of which are signed with an account key and are refused once the property is false. **It does not deny every SAS, and an earlier version of this row said it did.** Microsoft's own behaviour table for the disabled state lists **user delegation SAS (Blob only), authorized with Microsoft Entra ID — "Request is permitted"** (*Prevent authorization with Shared Key*, Azure Storage), because a user-delegation SAS is signed with a key the service issues to an **Entra** caller rather than with the account key. So the true statement is narrower and is the one this design relies on: **every credential that can reach this container is derived from an Entra identity**, and the remaining bearer credential is derived from one **specific data action**, which the next row excludes and the audit rows alarm on. The point of the property is unchanged — a shared key is a bearer credential that names nobody, and an audit recording "the account key was used" answers no question worth asking — but the property alone does not close the bearer-credential question, and the grants row is where it is actually closed |
| **Who may read or write it — one role assignment per principal per container, and no account-scoped data grant** | Four principals on the **extract** container and no fifth. **The extraction principal**: blob write-and-read on that container. **The load principal**: blob **read** on that container — plus, on the separate `migration-reports` container of the identity table below, blob write, which is the whole reason that container exists. **The named readers** of the table above: blob read on the extract container, individually and never through a group. **The destruction performer**: a role permitting container and account deletion, assigned at the account for the destruction operation and removed with the account. The **application's runtime managed identity holds none of these and is never granted one** — the same rule the table above states, restated here because this is where the assignments are made. One residual is stated rather than glossed: there is **no write-without-read blob capability**, so the extraction principal can read what it wrote; the control on that is that it is a pipeline principal with no interactive sign-in, and every read it performs is in the log below |
| **Those four grants are custom role definitions, not the built-in blob roles — and the reason is one specific action** | `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey/action` is the action that mints the one SAS the row above cannot deny. It is **not** confined to the delegation-specific role: the built-in role catalogue lists it inside the `actions` array of **`Storage Blob Data Contributor`** (`ba92f5b4-2d11-453d-a403-e96b0029c9fe`), **`Storage Blob Data Reader`** (`2a2b9908-6ea1-4ae2-8e65-a410df84e7d1`) and `Storage Blob Data Owner`, as well as of `Storage Blob Delegator` (*Azure built-in roles for Storage*). So assigning the built-in reader and contributor roles — which an earlier version of this row did — hands every one of those four principals the ability to mint a user-delegation SAS over the extract, and a SAS URL is a bearer credential that leaves the private network in a chat message. The contract is therefore: **two custom role definitions, cloned from those two built-ins with `generateUserDelegationKey/action` removed from `actions`** — **`MvcMusicStore Migration Blob Writer`** from the contributor and **`MvcMusicStore Migration Blob Reader`** from the reader — assigned at container scope in their place; **`Storage Blob Delegator` assigned to nobody, at any scope, on this account**; and the exclusion asserted as a provisioning check — the effective permissions of each of the four principals enumerated and the action confirmed absent — because a role definition edited later is a silent regression. Where another deliverable names `Storage Blob Data Contributor` or `Storage Blob Data Reader` for a principal on **this** account — [06 §6.7.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) does, for the legacy-source backup container that shares it — it is naming the **capability**; the definition actually assigned is the narrowed one here, and the grant is made once for the account rather than twice with two different definitions. Custom definitions are the right instrument rather than a workaround: role definitions carry `actions`, `notActions`, `dataActions` and `notDataActions` precisely so a built-in can be narrowed (*Azure custom roles*), and `notActions` subtracts **within a definition** rather than across assignments, which is why the requirement is *excluded from every role granted* rather than *subtracted once* |
| **And its use is alarmed on, because exclusion is a control that can be undone** | A **diagnostic alert on `generateUserDelegationKey`** against this account, standing for the life of the migration: any successful occurrence of that action is an **immediate** notification to the migration owner and to the security owner, treated as a suspected credential extraction rather than as an anomaly to review later. It has no legitimate occurrence — no step in section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) mints a SAS, and the transfer commands of that section authenticate as the principal itself — so the expected count is **zero** and any non-zero count is an incident. This is the row that makes the exclusion above verifiable in operation rather than only at provisioning time: the definition check catches a wrong grant, and the alert catches a right grant that someone widened |
| **How every access is audited** | The account's **blob-service diagnostic setting**, enabled **before the first write**, with the `StorageRead`, `StorageWrite` and `StorageDelete` log categories all on. It goes to **two** destinations, which is the point: the workspace of [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) for investigation, at the audit retention set on the workspace table ([06 §9.5.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), **and** — as the copy that survives this account — the **change record for the migration, lodged through the recovery-record channel of [06 §6.7.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)**, so the record of who read a copy of every customer's address cannot be edited or deleted by a principal that later holds full rights over this account, and does not vanish as a side effect of destroying the account itself.
