  an absent `--report-dir` and an absent connection variable alike; **`3`** the target could not be
  reached; and **`4`** the whole-seed transaction of section
  [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access) rolled back after starting, leaving
  the six catalog tables byte-unchanged. **A gate refusal and a malformed pattern are the same code and
  different named checks**, per the paragraph above, and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 24
  asserts the named check rather than a per-check integer.
- **A third artifact is deliberately not created.** A seeding routine invoked one way by a developer,
  another way by a release and a third way by a test is three behaviours wearing one name; making it a
  verb of the console that already owns fail-closed gating, machine-readable reports and an exit-code
  contract is what makes the gates enforceable rather than documentary.

**The guard itself is a test.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires that a seeding attempt
against a production-shaped configuration fails and leaves the database byte-unchanged — asserted by
row counts before and after, not merely by an exit code.

### 5.5 The Identity transition — a schema decision plus a data migration

**The schema decision: create the target's Identity tables fresh and populate them, rather than
altering the 1.0 tables in place.** Two reasons. It leaves the source tables intact as a rollback
position, so a failed migration is reversible by pointing at the old store rather than by restoring a
backup. And it lets reconciliation compare **two live datasets** rather than a dataset against a log.

**Extraction is a gate here too, and it is the same gate with the same completeness requirement.** The
**complete catalog-view set of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)
step 1** is run against the attached Identity database — not a `sys.columns` query, which is what a
column-shaped question invites and which would answer none of the four questions this migration
actually turns on: **which Identity tables exist at all**, which of their columns are identities or
computed, which unique indexes constrain the insert (the normalized-username index is the one that
decides whether step-by-step collision handling is required), and which foreign keys tie the child
tables to `AspNetUsers`. Every discovered object is dispositioned before any Identity data is
migrated, on the same rule as the catalog extraction — mapped, deliberately retired with a reason, or
recorded as a deliberate change — and **any EF 6 `__MigrationHistory` table found in the credential
store is recorded and not migrated**, for the reason section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) gives.

**The extraction must complete and be reconciled against the target Identity model before any Identity
data is migrated.** [12 F-12-21](12-migration-blockers.md) owns the evidence and — importantly — owns
its **qualification**: a printable-string probe of the committed credential store finds the early
Identity column names and none of the six later ones, but **string-probing a binary is evidence, not
proof**, and a negative result cannot distinguish an absent column from one the probe does not
surface. The converse holds too and is the easier mistake: a **positive** hit — a column name, or a
`__MigrationHistory` string — is equally not proof that the object exists in the shape the name
suggests. This document does not re-derive the probe, does not treat its negative results as proof,
and does not promote its positive results to schema facts. It requires the authoritative query.

Note the sequencing collision [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md) records and
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) must place: **the committed credential stores are simultaneously the
only authoritative schema evidence and a Critical security finding**, so removing them and extracting
from them are the same artifact's two futures and have to be ordered.

**The data migration, specified.**

**User names, not user ids, are the invariant — and the two must not be conflated.**
`Order.Username` stores the **login name** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] and is
compared against `User.Identity.Name`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73]. The cart's `CartId` likewise holds a
login name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167]. **Neither references the Identity
primary key.** So:

- **Preserving usernames exactly is a hard requirement.** A changed username orphans that user's order
  history and their cart, silently — the query returns no rows rather than failing.
- **Preserving the original id values is a separate and optional choice.** It **is** taken here, for
  **convenience rather than referential necessity**: keeping the ids makes role assignments and
  external-login rows trivially re-linkable during the load, and makes a row-by-row comparison between
  source and target possible. Nothing in the application would break if ids changed. The distinction
  matters because a plan that treats id preservation as a correctness requirement will spend effort
  defending it, and a plan that treats username preservation as optional will lose order history.

**Normalization is a new column and a new collision risk — and the username and the email do not get
the same treatment, because they are not the same kind of value.** `NormalizedUserName` and
`NormalizedEmail` do not exist in the 1.0 schema. Normalization is typically an upper-casing, so **two
accounts differing only in case normalize to the same value**. The two columns diverge from there:

- **Normalized username collisions abort the migration, and the collision test is performed by the
  target database rather than by the loader's own string comparison.** The username is **the** invariant:
  it is what `Order.Username` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] holds and what the ownership
  check compares [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73], and it is uniquely
  indexed in the target store. **The migration enumerates the source usernames, computes their normalized
  forms, and aborts before writing anything on any duplicate**, reporting the colliding accounts — each
  by its alias, per the artifact rule of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) — for a
  human decision. It does **not** de-duplicate, rename or drop an account automatically: silently
  losing an account — and with it that account's entire order history, since the history is joined by
  the very string being collapsed — is precisely the outcome this check exists to prevent. **Where the
  test runs is a correctness requirement and not an implementation detail** — see the preflight
  requirement below, which applies identically to usernames and role names.
- **Duplicate normalized emails do not abort, because unique email is not required.** Section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) selects `RequireUniqueEmail = false` and preserves it
  as the source's behaviour, so the target's email index is **not** unique and two accounts sharing an
  email address are a legitimate state that inserts cleanly. Aborting on them would fail the load on
  data the policy explicitly permits. **They are reported, not rejected**: the migration emits the
  duplicate-email set as an informational artifact, under the controls of section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) — which means the set names each account by its alias and the
  shared address by `e_<hash>`, so the data owner can see the duplication without the artifact carrying
  either value. A duplicate email is worth knowing about even where it is allowed, because it becomes a
  real constraint the moment anyone proposes a password-reset-by-email flow, which the source has none
  of.
- **The two are stated together because the inconsistent pair is the easy mistake**: aborting on
  duplicate emails while declining to require unique email asserts an index the target does not have,
  and would reject a load the policy permits. If unique email is ever wanted it is an **explicitly
  approved hardening delta** with **Security** as its owner — `RequireUniqueEmail = true`, a unique
  email index, a remediation path for every existing duplicate decided before the flag is set, and a
  row in the table of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) relabelled from preserved
  to hardening. It is not that today, and this document does not smuggle it in through a migration
  check.

**Fields with no source value get a defined origin.** Each is stated rather than left to whatever the
insert happens to produce:

| Target column | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| `Id` | Carried from the source, per the optional-but-taken choice above |
| `UserName` | Carried exactly. Invariant |
| `NormalizedUserName` | Computed from `UserName` by the target's normalizer, after the collision check |
| `Email` | Carried where present. The 1.0 store may hold none |
| `NormalizedEmail` | Computed where `Email` is present; **null** where it is not — nullable, not empty string, so "no email" stays distinguishable from "empty email" |
| `EmailConfirmed` | **`false`**, documented. Not `true`: no confirmation ever occurred, and asserting otherwise would be inventing a security fact |
| `PasswordHash` | Carried verbatim. See below |
| `SecurityStamp` | **Generated fresh for every account.** A new stamp invalidates nothing that survives cutover, since every session ends anyway (section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)) |
| `ConcurrencyStamp` | **Generated fresh for every account** |
| `PhoneNumber`, `PhoneNumberConfirmed` | **null** and **`false`** — the 1.0 schema holds no such value. **Conditional on the extraction**: if it finds a phone or two-factor table with rows, the non-empty branch of the disposition table below governs and a carried value supersedes this default |
| `TwoFactorEnabled` | **`false`** — the source has no two-factor concept. **Conditional on the extraction**, on the same rule as the row above: retiring an enabled second factor is an approval decision, not a default |
| `LockoutEnabled` | **`true`** — this is a **deliberate hardening**, labelled as such in section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), because there is no lockout today at all ([09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md), finding F-09-03) |
| `LockoutEnd` | **null** — no account starts locked out |
| `AccessFailedCount` | **`0`** |

**The user table is not the Identity store, and a plan that migrates only users is incomplete in a way
that is invisible until someone is locked out.** The 1.0 store carries **roles, role assignments,
external logins and claims** alongside the users, so **every table the extraction discovers gets a
disposition** — carried, or deliberately retired with a reason — and none is left to be noticed after
cutover.

**Two rules govern the table below, and they are what make it a disposition rather than a survey.**
First, **"empty" is a query result and never an expectation**: `load-identity` counts every
discovered table's rows before it writes anything, and a zero is recorded as the evidence for the
retirement rather than assumed from the absence of a feature. Second, **a non-empty table has exactly
two permitted dispositions — a target mapping, or a retirement approved by the named owner — and until
one of them is recorded for that table the migration is blocked**: the verb exits `3` with
nothing written (section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)). **Reporting a non-empty table is not
handling it.** A report with no recorded disposition leaves a table nobody decided about, and the
decision then gets made by whichever behaviour the target happens to have after cutover.

| Source table class | If the row count is zero | If the row count is non-zero: mapping or approval-owned retirement, with its keyed reconciliation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Users** | **Blocking.** A zero user count means the extraction targeted the wrong database, not that the store has no accounts. Exit `3`, nothing written | **Carried**, per the column-origin table above. Reconciled by the **keyed username set** |
| **Roles** | **Blocking, and resolved by approval rather than by proceeding.** The administration surface is reachable only through a role membership [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12], so a store with no roles cannot satisfy section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 15. The recorded resolution is to provision the role and its membership through the operator command of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — an **approval decision by Security and operations**, recorded before the migration proceeds | **Carried.** Role names are preserved exactly, because `[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]` compares the name as a literal [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12] — a renamed role does not fail, it silently denies every administrator. Ids are carried on the same optional-but-taken basis as user ids. Reconciled by the **keyed role-name set** |
| **User-to-role assignments** | **Blocking**, on the same rule and with the same resolution as roles: an unreachable administration surface is a functional regression, not an empty table | **Carried**, as a keyed set of `(user, role)` pairs resolved by **name on both sides** rather than by id, so the pairing survives even if an id decision is later revisited. Reconciled by the **keyed `(username, role name)` pair set**, with the administrator's membership asserted by name |
| **External logins** | **Retired, with the zero recorded as its evidence.** The provider registrations are commented out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35] and section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) removes the provider-driven half of the surface — but **a disabled registration is not evidence that the table is empty**, since the registrations may have been enabled earlier in the store's life, which is why the count is taken rather than inferred | **Two permitted dispositions, and neither is silence.** *Mapping*: the rows are carried into the target's user-login table, keyed by `(username, login provider, provider key)`. This needs no reinstatement of anything, because the **management** half of the surface is retained (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) — a carried row is **listed and removable** by its account holder from the first request after cutover. What a carried row cannot do until a provider is registered as a separately approved addition is **sign anyone in**, which is exactly what the `PasswordHash` halt below exists to catch. *Retirement*: approved by **Product and security**, with the affected accounts named and each one's remedy recorded, since retirement removes those users' only sign-in method; the remedy is the password-reset path this section defines for hash-verification failure. Whichever is chosen, reconciliation is the **owner-bound multiset of `(username, login provider, provider key)` with multiplicity** — compared against the target on mapping, and against the named affected-account list on retirement — and an unrecorded disposition is exit `3`. **The username is part of the key rather than context**: a `(provider, provider key)` pair reassigned from one account to another is the same set on both sides, and it is a sign-in that lands in the wrong account |
| **User claims** | **Retired, with the zero recorded.** The application reads no claim beyond the name and role Identity itself issues, so zero is the expected result — and it is still queried rather than assumed | **Two permitted dispositions.** *Mapping*: carried into the target's user-claims table, keyed by `(username, claim type, claim value)`. *Retirement*: approved by **Security**, with every distinct claim type and its row count named in the approval record, because a claim the source issued may be load-bearing for something outside this application. Reconciliation is the **owner-bound multiset of `(username, claim type, claim value)` with multiplicity**; an unrecorded disposition is exit `3`. **The value is in the key and multiplicity is carried**, because a claim of the same type whose *value* changed is a different authorization fact, and two rows of one type collapsed to one is a lost claim that a set comparison on `(username, claim type)` reports as equal |
| **Tokens, phone and two-factor state, if the extraction finds such tables** | **Retired, with the zero recorded.** The source implements none of these flows, which is the expectation the count confirms rather than replaces | **Handled per class, and each still blocking until recorded.** *Token rows*: the expected disposition is **retirement approved by Security**, with the row count and the token purposes named — they are short-lived by construction and the target's token providers are not the source's, so carrying them would carry values the target cannot validate. *Phone and two-factor state*: either **carried** into `PhoneNumber`, `PhoneNumberConfirmed` and `TwoFactorEnabled`, in which case the carried value **supersedes** that column's default in the origin table above for those accounts, or **retired with Security's approval** and the affected accounts named — retiring an enabled second factor is a **reduction in an account's protection** and cannot be a silent default. **Reconciliation differs by class**: token rows are reconciled as the **owner-bound multiset of `(username, login provider, token name)` with multiplicity**, on the same reasoning as claims; phone and two-factor state are per-account **columns** rather than child rows, so they are reconciled as the **keyed set of affected usernames with the carried or retired value stated per account**. An unrecorded disposition is exit `3` |
| **An EF 6 `__MigrationHistory` table, if present** | **Recorded and not migrated**, per section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) | **Recorded and not migrated**, identically — its rows are EF 6 history, and loading them would make the target believe migrations were applied that were not. Recording the count is the whole of the handling |

**The carried classes, enumerated once here so that the Identity migration's exit gate can cite one
place rather than re-deriving the set.** That gate is satisfied only when **every class below** has both
its disposition recorded and its keyed reconciliation passed — [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) places
the gate and enumerates these classes in it, and this list is what it enumerates:

1. **Users** — carried; keyed username set; per-row digests (section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)).
2. **Roles** — carried; keyed role-name set; per-row digests.
3. **User-to-role assignments** — carried; keyed `(username, role name)` pair set; the administrator's
   membership asserted by name.
4. **External logins** — carried; the owner-bound multiset of `(username, login provider, provider key)`
   with multiplicity. Retirement is not a permitted disposition, because section
   [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) retains the surface those rows are for.
5. **User claims** — carried **or** retired under Security approval; the owner-bound multiset of
   `(username, claim type, claim value)` with multiplicity, or the named claim-type list with counts.
6. **Token rows** — retired under Security approval; count and token purposes named, and where any row is
   carried, the owner-bound multiset of `(username, login provider, token name)` with multiplicity.
7. **Phone and two-factor state** — carried **or** retired under Security approval; keyed affected-username
   set with the value stated per account. **This one is a keyed set and not a multiset**, deliberately:
   these are columns on the user row, so one account has exactly one value and multiplicity would be
   meaningless.
8. **An EF 6 `__MigrationHistory` table** — recorded, not migrated; count recorded.

**A class with no recorded disposition, or with a recorded disposition whose reconciliation has not
passed, fails the gate.** There is no partial pass and no "reported, therefore handled".

**Role metadata has the same new-column problem as users, and it is stated the same way.** The 1.0 role
table has no normalized name and no concurrency stamp:

| Target role column | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| `Id` | Carried from the source, on the same optional-but-taken basis as user ids |
| `Name` | **Carried exactly. Invariant** — for the literal-comparison reason above |
| `NormalizedName` | Computed from `Name` by the target's normalizer, **after** the collision check below |
| `ConcurrencyStamp` | **Generated fresh for every role** |

**Role-name collisions abort, on the same rule as usernames and for a sharper reason.** The target's
role index on `NormalizedName` is unique, and **two roles differing only in case collapse to one**
normalized value. **The migration enumerates the source role names, computes their normalized forms,
and aborts before writing on any duplicate**, reporting the colliding roles. It does not merge them
automatically: merging two roles silently unions their memberships, which is a privilege change, and
`Administrator` is one of the names involved
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12].

**The collation of the normalized columns is *configured explicitly*, never inherited — and an earlier
statement of this section got this wrong twice, in opposite directions.** That earlier text first
described the loader upper-casing each name and comparing the results itself, concluding that surrounding
whitespace produced two distinct roles that "collide with nothing"; it then corrected that by asserting
what "the default collation" is. **Both are wrong, and the second is wrong as a matter of fact.**

- **There is no such thing as "the default collation" to reason from.** A column's collation comes from
  its own `COLLATE` clause, or failing that from the database, or failing that from the instance — and the
  database's is whatever the database was created with. Nothing in this repository fixes any of them:
  MVC 5's connection strings attach a file [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13] and declare no
  collation, and the target database's collation is a provisioning decision
  [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns. **A migration contract that reasons from an assumed
  default is reasoning from a value nobody set.**
- **The specific claim that the default is accent-insensitive is false.**
  `SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS` — the collation most commonly encountered as a SQL Server default — is
  **case-insensitive and accent-*sensitive*.** `CI` and `AS` are exactly what its name says. So the
  earlier bullet asserting that two names differing only in a diacritic collide under the default was
  backwards, and the conclusion drawn from it — that this is a collision class **no ordinal comparison in
  the loader can detect** — had nothing under it. **That claim is withdrawn, and it is not re-attached to
  any other case.**

**The requirement is therefore to configure, not to discover.** `NormalizedUserName` and
`NormalizedEmail`, and every index over them, are configured with an explicit collation in the EF
Core model — **`Latin1_General_100_CS_AS`** — on the context section
[4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables) registers, so the Identity migration set
emits the `COLLATE` clause and the column's semantics are a property of this repository rather than of
whatever database the release is pointed at. `IdentityRole.NormalizedName` and its unique index are
configured identically, for the same reason. **The uniqueness of those indexes is not uniform and is not
changed here**: `NormalizedUserName` and `NormalizedName` are **uniquely** indexed, and
`NormalizedEmail`'s index is **not** unique, because section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) selects `RequireUniqueEmail = false` and preserves it as
the source's behaviour. Collation is configured on all three; uniqueness follows the policy.
**Why case- and accent-*sensitive* is the right choice rather than an oversight:**

- **Uniqueness is supplied by the normalizer, and the collation must not silently add to it.** The
  normalizer already upper-cases, so `admin` and `ADMIN` produce the **same** normalized value and collide
  on that value under any collation. A case-*insensitive* collation would add a second, invisible folding
  on top of it, and a deployment whose database happened to carry a different collation would then enforce
  a **different** uniqueness rule from the one this document specifies — the same class of silent-default
  failure section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) exists to prevent for the cookie and
  lockout policy.
- **Accent sensitivity is a behaviour decision and is now taken deliberately.** Under `AS`, two accounts
  differing only in a diacritic are **distinct**, which preserves both accounts and matches the source's
  behaviour, where the stored string is what `Order.Username`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] and the cart's `CartId`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] match. An accent-insensitive collation would collapse
  them and force one of them to be resolved away — a data-losing outcome chosen by a provisioning default
  rather than by anybody.
- **`Latin1_General_100_CS_AS` is deterministic and indexable**, which a collation carrying
  `UTF8` or supplementary-character variations may make more surprising; nothing in the application
  depends on linguistic ordering of a normalized identifier, so the simplest deterministic choice is the
  right one. The collation is a **configured value in this document's scope**, so changing it is a review
  of this section rather than a redeployment surprise.

**Verification is post-migration introspection of the *target*, and source extraction is explicitly not
the authority for it.** This is the second half of the correction: an earlier statement made the collation
"recorded by the extraction of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1", which cannot be right —
`NormalizedUserName`, `NormalizedEmail` and `NormalizedName` are **net-new target columns that do not
exist in the source at all**, so no interrogation of the source can report a collation for them, and the
diff gate has no source-side facet to compare against. **The authority is the target, after the Identity
migrations have been applied:**

- **`sys.columns.collation_name`** for each of `NormalizedUserName`, `NormalizedEmail` and
  `NormalizedName`, asserted to equal the configured collation exactly.
- **`sys.indexes` and `sys.index_columns`** for each of their indexes, asserted to exist, to be defined
  over the intended column, and to carry **the uniqueness the policy above states** — unique on
  `NormalizedUserName` and `NormalizedName`, **not** unique on `NormalizedEmail`. So a migration that
  emitted the column but not the index, or the index over the wrong column, or a *unique* index on
  `NormalizedEmail` that would reject the shared-email accounts section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) explicitly permits, is a caught failure rather than a
  latent one.
- **Run as a step of the release, after the Identity migration set is applied and before
  `load-identity` writes anything**, and a mismatch on any assertion **blocks the load** — exit `3`,
  nothing written. Source extraction remains the authority for every **carried** column's facets, exactly
  as section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 states; it is not the
  authority for a column the source never had.

**Trailing-blank insensitivity survives all of this, because it is not a collation property — and the
loader is now required to detect it itself.** Under SQL Server's comparison semantics `'ADMINISTRATOR'`
and `'ADMINISTRATOR '` are **equal** regardless of collation: ANSI padding governs trailing-blank
handling in `=` comparisons for these types, and no `CS`/`AS`/`CI`/`AI` combination changes it. So a
unique index on `NormalizedName` **rejects the second row**, the trailing-space variant does not load as a
distinct role, and a loader that decided the two were distinct because their normalized strings differ
ordinally would produce a release step that dies on a duplicate-key error at the worst possible moment —
part-way through the Identity load, after the catalog load has already committed. **This case is
detectable in the loader, and the earlier "no ordinal comparison can detect it" claim is withdrawn for
it**: the preflight compares each candidate **together with its length** — the value paired with
`DATALENGTH(value)`, equivalently an ordinal comparison of the right-trimmed values — which reproduces
`=`'s trailing-blank semantics exactly and additionally lets the report say *why* two members collided.

**The preflight, therefore.** Before any Identity row is written, the migration groups the computed
normalized names — usernames and role names, each in its own pass — **with an explicit `COLLATE` clause
naming the configured collation above**, carrying each candidate's `DATALENGTH` alongside it, and reports
every duplicate group with the reason it grouped: same normalized value, or trailing-blank equality. It
may equivalently insert the candidates into a table in the **target database** whose column carries that
collation under **a unique index of the same definition as the target's** and report the rejections.
**What is not acceptable is a comparison performed in the loader's own runtime using plain ordinal string
equality**, which reproduces neither the configured collation nor the trailing-blank rule. **Owner:
Engineering builds the preflight and configures the collation; the post-migration introspection above is
what establishes that the configuration took effect.**

**Every collision the preflight reports is blocking, and its resolution is an approval rather than a
transformation.** The loader neither trims, merges, renames nor drops. The resolution is recorded by the
named owner before the migration is re-run, and for role names the reason is specific rather than
procedural: today a role named with a trailing space or a differing case matches no
`[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]` check
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12], so **resolving such a collision in
favour of that name grants its members administrative access they do not currently have**, and resolving
it by merge silently unions two memberships. Both are privilege changes, so **Security owns the
resolution of any role-name collision**, and the data owner owns the resolution of any username
collision — where the consequence is order-history ownership, since `Order.Username`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] matches the stored string. The colliding sets are emitted
as artifacts under the controls of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor), and the names that do
load, load **exactly as found**.

**`IdentityOptions.User.AllowedUserNameCharacters` is set explicitly and every source username is
preflighted against it, because a username the target's validator rejects is an account that migrates and
then cannot be maintained.** The option carries a documented default character set in the target
framework, and leaving it at that default is the same silent-default failure section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) exists to prevent for the cookie and lockout policy. Three
requirements:

- **The set is stated in configuration and labelled in the policy table** of section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), the same way every other Identity policy value is. This
  document does **not** assert what the source's registration validator accepted — the source configures
  no validator, so whatever Identity 1.0's default enforced is inherited rather than declared, and an
  inherited default is not evidence. **What is stated instead is measured**: the preflight below reports
  the characters actually present in the stored usernames, and the chosen set is approved against that
  report.
- **Every source username is checked against the chosen set before any row is written**, in the same
  preflight pass as the collision check above. A username containing a character outside the set is
  **blocking**: the step stops with nothing written, and the affected accounts are reported as
  an artifact under section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)'s controls.
- **An incompatible username is never renamed to make it compatible — resolution is an approval, and the
  reason is not stylistic.** `Order.Username` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] and the
  cart's `CartId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] match the **exact string**, and the
  ownership predicate is evaluated in the database
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73], so renaming an account detaches its
  order history and its cart with no error anywhere. The permitted resolutions are to **widen the allowed
  set to admit the characters actually present** — the expected outcome, since the accounts predate the
  policy — or, if a character is to be excluded deliberately, to have the **data owner** approve the
  account-level remedy, with the affected usernames named in the approval record. **Owner: Security owns
  the character policy; the data owner owns any account-level resolution.**

**Where the two differ, registration changes and the change is declared.** If the approved set is
narrower than what the source's inherited validator accepted, then a username registerable before is
rejected at registration afterwards. That is a **user-visible policy change** and is carried as an
approved delta `D-18` in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), with **Security** as its owner,
not left to be discovered by the first person it rejects. It is asserted by section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) rows 20 `20a` — a registration using a character **inside** the set succeeds — and 20 `20e`, where a
registration using one **outside** it is rejected with a validation message rather than an exception; and row 18 `18a` carries the third property, that
**every migrated account still signs in**, which is what the preflight exists to guarantee.

**Password hashes are verified, not assumed.** The target's default password hasher can validate the
older hash format and rehash on a successful sign-in — but that is a property to **confirm against the
hashes this repository actually ships**, not to assert. The verification is concrete: after the load,
a sign-in as a pre-existing account must succeed, and the stored hash must be observed to have been
rewritten in the target's current format. **The acceptance test is a successful sign-in by a
pre-existing account** (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)). If verification fails, the fallback is
a forced password reset for all migrated accounts — which is a materially different user-facing
outcome and therefore an approval decision, not an implementation detail, so it is surfaced rather than
absorbed. **The comparison itself is digest-based and never handles raw hashes**, per section
[5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor).

**Reconciliation and rollback — keyed sets, not counts.** Counts are retained as the cheap first check
and are explicitly not the acceptance criterion, for the reason section
[5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) gives: a redistribution of the same number of role assignments
among the same number of users passes every count in this list.

- **Counts, before and after**: accounts, roles, role assignments, and **every child class the
  enumerated list above names** — including the classes whose disposition is retirement, whose "after"
  count is asserted to be zero rather than left unstated.
- **Every carried child class gets its own comparison, and for the three row-shaped classes that
  comparison is an owner-bound multiset rather than a set**, per that list: external logins as
  `(username, login provider, provider key)`, user claims as `(username, claim type, claim value)`, and
  token rows as `(username, login provider, token name)` — each **with multiplicity**, and each with the
  **username inside the key**. Phone and two-factor state remain a keyed **affected-username** set with
  the carried value per account, because they are columns rather than rows. **Two failure modes are the
  reason for the shape, and a plain set on a partial key reports neither**: a child row reassigned from
  one account to another leaves the unkeyed pair set identical while moving an authorization fact between
  people, and two identical rows collapsing to one leaves a set comparison equal while losing a claim or a
  login. Both are caught by comparing multisets whose key includes the owner. **A class whose disposition
  is retirement is reconciled against its named affected-account list**, not against an empty target
  table, so that "retired" is evidenced by the same kind of artifact as "carried" and an approval can be
  checked against what was actually dropped.
- **Every multiset above is serialized and digested under the multiset rule of section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)** — declared as a multiset, carrying `(member, count)` pairs
  ordered by the member's canonical bytes — so that a multiset's digest can never be produced by the set
  path, and a duplicate inside a declared *set* is still rejected rather than silently collapsed.
- **The keyed set of usernames**, compared as a set between source and target — equal, with any missing
  or extra member named. This is the invariant of this whole section, so it is asserted as a set rather
  than inferred from a count.
- **The keyed set of `(username, role name)` assignment pairs**, likewise compared as a set. This is the
  check that catches a redistribution, and it is resolved by name on both sides so it does not depend on
  the id decision.
- **The keyed set of role names**, and **per-row digests** for the user and role rows (section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)), so that a changed email, a changed role name or a swapped
  hash changes the comparison.
- **The administrator's role membership asserted specifically**, by name, not merely present in the set
  — it is the one assignment whose loss makes the entire administration surface unreachable, which is
  exactly the failure MVC 3 ships as a shipped state ([09 §5.2](09-security-assessment.md)).
- **Every keyed set must match before any source table is removed.** Source tables are the rollback
  position, they are retained until reconciliation passes in full, and they are dropped only as a
  separate, later step under the security remediation that
  [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md) sequences.
- **Every artifact this reconciliation produces is personal data, not merely sensitive**, because every
  keyed set above is keyed on a **username** and a keyed comparison exists in order to name its missing
  and extra members. The controls — encrypted, access-logged, digest-based for hashes and stamps,
  destroyed on a named schedule — are the ones tabulated in section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor), which also records why pseudonymous references are not
  substituted for the names. They are the same controls the domain extract gets, which is the point: the
  credential side must not end up with the weaker half.

#### 5.5.1 Published-credential accounts are neutralized before the load, not after the cutover

**Carrying every hash verbatim is right for every account but one class, and for that class it is a
credential compromise the migration would perform on purpose.** The seeded administrator's password is
**committed to this repository in cleartext** at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17] and restated
in the tracked per-edition documentation ([09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding). Its
hash sits in the committed credential store
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/aspnet-MvcMusicStore-20131025034205.mdf:first UTF-16LE byte offset at any alignment 0x732E9, in a 3,211,264-byte file].
That locator is the binary evidence form of [README §8](README.md#8-standards-and-conventions)
rather than a line, because the artifact is a binary and the `AspNetUsers.PasswordHash` column it holds
is established by the printable-string probe qualified above — whose method and limits
[09 §1.4](09-security-assessment.md) owns — and the file's presence in the index is reproduced by
`git ls-files 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/*'`. That account holds the
`Administrator` role — the only thing standing between an anonymous caller
and album create, edit and delete
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12]. So a migration that carries the hash
faithfully produces, in a hosted environment, **an administrator account whose password anyone with
read access to this repository already has**. Removing the two `appSettings` keys (section
[10.3](#103-what-this-retires)) does not touch it: the keys were only the *source* of the credential, and
the credential itself now lives in the store.

**The mechanism: replace the hash, keep the shape.** For each account in the neutralization set the
load writes a `PasswordHash` computed by the target's `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` over a
**32-byte cryptographically random value generated in the migration process, never persisted, never
logged and discarded when the row is written**. Nobody — including the operator running the migration —
holds a value that satisfies it, and the account is repaired by the operator command of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — run **with
`--rotate-credential`** — before the environment is opened. That run is the **first** of the three
rotation events section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)
property 1b rule 5 defines and coverage row 75 exercises: the account exists, its stored hash satisfies
nothing, and the flag is what makes the *already present* branch write a usable credential instead of
reporting `already-present` and leaving the account unusable. **"One of the exactly two runs that pass
that switch" was an earlier form of this sentence and it is withdrawn**: the switch is not budgeted, it is
the ordinary mechanism for every subsequent credential rotation as well, and a numeric claim about how
many times an environment will ever rotate a credential is not a fact this document can hold.

**Why a random-value hash and not the two more obvious alternatives**, both of which look stronger and
are worse here:

- **Not a null `PasswordHash`.** It works — `UserManager.CheckPasswordAsync` returns failure for a null
  stored hash without invoking the hasher — and it breaks two things this document has already
  committed to. It makes the account's real work *cheaper* than a real verification, leaning on the
  fixed-work service of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) to pad every attempt
  against it, and doing so pointlessly: the padding exists for populations the port cannot avoid, not as
  licence to create another one. And it would **manufacture the one account shape this migration is
  specified to refuse**: a null or empty `PasswordHash` is the external-only condition on which section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) **halts the load
  and writes nothing**, so the neutralization step would produce exactly the row the same migration
  rejects. It would also flip `HasPasswordAsync` to false for an account that is not external-only,
  contradicting the guarantee the retained account surface now rests on: section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) **removes** the set-password branch, and what makes
  that safe is precisely that no migrated account lacks a local password — so manufacturing one would
  leave an account whose `Manage` view offers only a change-password form it cannot satisfy, with no
  branch left to catch it and the migration's own halt condition no longer identifying what it is for.
- **Not a permanent lockout** (`LockoutEnd` far in the future). `SignInManager` evaluates lockout
  **before** verifying the password, so a locked account performs no derivation at all and depends
  entirely on the fixed-work top-up of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) to look like
  anything else; and its `AccountLockedOut` outcome is a distinct value in the `AUTH-1002` event of
  [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md), which would let anyone watching the log stream identify the
  account by name. Lockout is for runtime accounting, not for retiring a credential.

A random-value hash costs exactly what every other verification costs, produces the ordinary
`InvalidCredentials` outcome, and leaves `HasPasswordAsync` true, so nothing else in this document
changes.

**Who is in the set, determined by rule rather than by a name.** The set is *every source account whose
password is derivable from tracked repository content*, and the migration's pre-load census must
enumerate it rather than assume it is a single row. It provably contains the seeded administrator
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17].

**Exactly one account is *named* by tracked repository content, and an earlier form of this paragraph
claimed a second.** That form carried "the second seeded account named in the repository's own
documentation" as a standing candidate. **No such account exists**, and the claim is withdrawn rather
than softened, because a candidate nobody can locate is not evidence — it is an instruction to look for
something that is not there. The repository tracks three README files, and only one of them names a
credential at all:

```text
git grep -l -iE 'DefaultAdminPassword|Password' -- README.md src/MVC4/README.md src/MVC5/README.md
# -> src/MVC5/README.md          (the only tracked README naming a credential at all)
git grep -c -iE 'password'       -- README.md src/MVC4/README.md src/MVC5/README.md
# -> src/MVC5/README.md:2        (two lines, both the same single account)
```

Both matching lines name **the same single account's** password — the bullet under that file's *Default
Administrator Account* heading, and the `DefaultAdminPassword` configuration key the same section quotes
immediately below it — and the user name bullet alongside them names `Administrator`
[src/MVC5/README.md:75-84]. One account, named twice; not two accounts.

**The rule still governs, and it is not discharged by that census**, because documentation is not the
only derivation path: a source account whose stored hash happens to verify a published value is a member
whether or not any file names it. So membership is decided by **testing**, not by reading: for every
source account, the pre-load census verifies each published value against that account's stored hash
using the configured `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` — an offline, read-only check against the
extracted source rows that issues no sign-in, touches no lockout counter and writes nothing — and every
account for which any published value verifies is a member. Where a hash cannot be evaluated at all, the
account is neutralized anyway, because a needless password reset costs one user one reset and a missed one
leaves a live published credential. The census is a step of the migration, its output is recorded with the
reconciliation report, and **the published values themselves appear in no deliverable** — they are cited
by location, here and everywhere else in this set, which is also why the two commands above are written
in their `-l` and `-c` forms rather than printing the matching lines.

**Ordering: neutralization happens in the load, before the store is reachable.** It is not a
post-cutover clean-up task and not a runbook item to be caught up on later. The row is written already
neutralized, so **no window exists in which the hosted store holds the published hash** — which is the
property a "reset it after go-live" step cannot offer, and the reason this is specified in the migration
rather than in [06 §11](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s runbook.

**Reconciliation and rollback.**

- Account count, role count and role-assignment count compared **before and after**.
- **The administrator's role membership asserted specifically**, by name, not merely counted — it is
  the one assignment whose loss makes the entire administration surface unreachable, which is exactly
  the failure MVC 3 ships as a shipped state ([09 §5.2](09-security-assessment.md)).
- A per-account comparison of username and hash between source and target — **with the neutralization
  set carrying the inverse assertion**. For an ordinary account, source hash equals target hash; for a
  neutralized account, the target hash must **differ** from the source hash and must not equal the hash
  of any published value. Stating this explicitly matters because the general form of the rule, applied
  uniformly, would make a correct migration **fail** reconciliation and invite someone to "fix" it by
  restoring the compromised hash.
- **A negative verification assertion, per environment, before it is reachable — and it is deliberately
  *not* a failed sign-in.** For every account in the neutralization set the gate reads that account's
  stored `PasswordHash` with a read-only query and calls
  `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>.VerifyHashedPassword(user, storedHash, publishedValue)`, requiring
  **`PasswordVerificationResult.Failed`** for every published value. It is the same hasher the
  application verifies with, so a `Failed` result is the same fact a refused sign-in would establish —
  and it establishes it **without issuing a request, without a lockout counter and without writing
  anything**: the gate additionally records `AccessFailedCount` and `LockoutEnd` for each account
  **before and after** and asserts both **unchanged**.

  **A repeated failed `POST /Account/Login` must not be used as this gate**, and an earlier form of this
  bullet made it one. The policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) sets
  `Lockout.MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5` with a fifteen-minute window and the sign-in path of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) step 3 passes `lockoutOnFailure: true`, so a probe that
  posts a wrong password **increments the counter on the one account that holds the `Administrator`
  role**. Five of them lock it out — and this gate is specified to run *per environment*, so the
  arithmetic is not hypothetical: a re-run, a retried pipeline stage or an operator repeating the check
  by hand locks the only administrator out of a freshly cut-over environment, at the moment the runbook
  most needs to sign in. There is also nothing to reset it: a standing probe has no owner and no
  post-condition, which is exactly why it is replaced rather than merely paired with a reset.

  **If an environment's own policy insists on an end-to-end attempt** — because a refused HTTP request
  is what an auditor will accept — it is permitted under three conditions and no fewer, all recorded in
  the runbook log: **exactly one** attempt per account, never a series and never a timing sample;
  immediately followed by `await userManager.ResetAccessFailedCountAsync(user)` and
  `await userManager.SetLockoutEndDateAsync(user, null)`; and both **asserted afterwards** —
  `AccessFailedCount == 0` and `LockoutEnd == null` — so a reset that silently failed is a gate failure
  rather than a latent lockout. The end-to-end assertion in its unrestricted form, including its timing
  companion, belongs to the suite's **disposable fixture database**, where the accounts are fixture
  accounts and the reset discipline of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) already governs sampling.

  This is still the check that tests the property people actually care about — the others test that a
  field changed — and it is the gate condition [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) attaches to the Identity
  migration and [06 §11](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) repeats per environment. The published
  value is supplied to it by reading the legacy `Web.config` in the build source, so satisfying the gate
  never requires writing the value into a document, a test file or a pipeline variable. **Coverage row
  75** asserts it.
- **The source is frozen after two named mutations — it is never described as untouched, and the
  difference is the whole of this bullet.** "Untouched" was an earlier revision's word for it and it was
  wrong in both directions: it overstated the guarantee, because two mutations are required and specified
  below, and it understated the exposure, because an untouched credential store is one whose published
  password still works. The contract is therefore stated as a lifecycle rather than as a property, and it
  is the one this document and [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s runbook both hold to.

  **The lifecycle has a name and five stages, published here as the single owner so that no other
  section states a stage of it.** It is the **source-disposition lifecycle**, and every consumer — section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)'s rollback paragraph, section
  [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure), step 4 and step 9 of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction), row 58 of section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) and [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s runbook — cites the stage
  by name rather than re-deriving it. **Stages run in this order and no stage may be skipped or
  reordered**, and the `Writes?` column below is **exhaustive**: the source receives the two mutations
  `M1` and `M2`, plus — contingently, and only inside the interval the table names — the single-column
  write `Rh`. There is no fourth, and a write that is none of those three is a gate failure.

  | Stage | What happens | Writes? | Actor | Gate on leaving it |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | **M1 — neutralize** | The published credential is neutralized **in the legacy store**, by the same random-value-hash mechanism this sub-section specifies for the target | **Yes** — one `PasswordHash` write per account in the neutralization set, and nothing else | For a **file-attached** source, the **LocalDB instance owner on the Windows verification host**; for an **Azure-hosted copy**, the **deployment identity** inside a named change window | The negative-verification check of the bullet above returns `Failed` for every published value, run against the **legacy** host too |
  | **X — extract** | The authoritative schema and data extraction is taken and verified. This stage is between the mutations deliberately: extracting **before** M1 would capture the published hash into an artifact, and extracting **after** the freeze is impossible for the shapes whose extraction needs an attach | **No** — the source is opened read-only, by this artifact's `extract` verb | This artifact, under the migration principal | The extract's digest is computed and recorded (see the mechanism note below) |
  | **`Rh` — contingent legacy rehash** | **Not a stage anybody performs — a write the design must admit.** Between **X** and **M2** the legacy application is still in service, so a successful sign-in may re-derive and store that one account's password hash. It is enumerated here so it is never discovered as an unexplained third write | **Possibly** — confined to `AspNetUsers.PasswordHash`, one row per signing-in account, and nothing else. It adds, removes and re-keys nothing | The legacy application's own runtime, under its own connection identity. No operator issues it | Closed by **M2**: once the store is read-only the engine refuses it, so the contingency exists only inside the X-to-M2 interval |
  | **M2 — freeze** | The store is set **read-only**, which is what "frozen" names. From here the source takes no schema change, no row write and no further mutation of any kind — `Rh` included | **Yes** — the read-only switch itself, a state change and not a data write | The same per-shape actor as **M1** | The read-only state is **read back and asserted**, and the engine's refusal of a probe write is observed (see below) |
  | **R — retain** | The frozen source is kept for **14 days after cutover** — the rollback window. Nothing destroys it inside the window, whatever `reconcile` reports, and `close-run` **may not run** before the window closes | **No** — and now the engine enforces that rather than the design asserting it | Nobody: the stage is a wait, and its only rule is a prohibition | The window has elapsed **and** [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s list has passed |
  | **C — close** | `close-run` destroys the manifest, the lineage and the verification key. The source's own **removal** is a further, separate step, sequenced by [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) under [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md) item 2's collision, and this document states its precondition rather than its schedule | **No** | `close-run`: this artifact. The removal: [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s named actor | Every keyed set of the reconciliation matched — a **necessary and not sufficient** condition, since the source is also the rollback position |

  **What proves the source did not change, stated as a mechanism because a claim of equality needs one.**
  An earlier form of the retention and coverage text asserted the source was "byte-identical" at two
  inspection points, which is a conclusion and not a check: nothing in the design computed anything that
  could have established it, and a page-level or `CHECKSUM`-style comparison would not have established it
  either. **`CHECKSUM` and `BINARY_CHECKSUM` are explicitly not used**: both are non-cryptographic
  32-bit functions with trivially constructible collisions, and neither is order-stable across a
  re-organized heap, so a matching value is not evidence of equal content. Two mechanisms carry the claim
  instead, and each covers a different stage:

  - **From M2 onwards the barrier is engine-enforced, and that is the primary mechanism.** The store is
    read-only, so a write is refused by the engine rather than avoided by convention — the guarantee does
    not depend on every future actor's discipline. It is verified two ways at each inspection point: the
    read-only state is read back from the engine's own catalog, and a **probe write is attempted and its
    refusal observed**, because a state flag that nothing has tested is an assumption about a flag.
  - **Between X and M2, where the store is still writable, the mechanism is a deterministic cryptographic
    digest over a declared scope.** A **SHA-256** is computed over a **canonical projection** of every
    source table: rows ordered by primary key, a fixed column order, and a fixed invariant literal
    rendering for every value, so the digest is a function of content alone and not of storage layout, and
    two runs over unchanged data agree. It is computed at the end of **X** and recomputed at **M2**, and
    the two are required **equal, with zero differences, inside the declared scope**.

    **The declared scope is every source table and every column except `AspNetUsers.PasswordHash`, and
    that one exclusion is what makes the requirement achievable rather than aspirational.** Two writes to
    that column are authorized between the two inspection points, and both are named in the table above:
    stage **`Rh`**, a legacy sign-in's rehash. The row set is emphatically *inside* scope — the primary
    keys and the row count of every table, `AspNetUsers` included — so an account, role, assignment, cart
    row or order added, removed or re-keyed is still caught, and so is any other column of an account,
    `UserName` and `Email` among them. What the exclusion gives up is exactly one column's value on
    accounts that signed in, and nothing else.

    **This corrects an earlier form of this bullet, whose chronology did not work.** That form said the
    digest was computed "across M1 and X", excluded `PasswordHash` because "M1 changed it on purpose", and
    required a second whole-projection digest as well. But **M1 precedes X** in the very table above, so
    both inspection points are already after it and M1's write cannot appear in the comparison at all;
    the exclusion it offered was therefore for the wrong reason, and the whole-projection digest it also
    required would have been failed by any `Rh` write — a failure the design would have had no answer for.
    One digest, one scope, one exclusion with the right justification. A difference **inside** the scope
    means an unrecorded write, which is a gate failure and not a discrepancy to explain.

  **Mutation 1 — the published credential is neutralized in the legacy store.** The same neutralization
  this sub-section specifies for the target is applied to the source, **before** the interim Windows
  option of [06 §5.8](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is ever exposed and **before** any rollback
  returns the legacy application to service, with the negative-authentication check run against the legacy
  host too, per [06 §11.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and
  [06 §11.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md). [09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) criterion 6 owns
  the requirement and states why an earlier reading was wrong: criterion 2 requires the committed value to
  authenticate in **no** environment, and the legacy application during a rollback is an environment.
  Without this mutation, **rolling back to the source store would restore a working published
  credential** — and accepting that exposure for the rollback's duration is not an available response.
  Neutralizing it does not weaken the rollback position: the rows, the orders and the account all remain,
  and only the published password stops working.

  **Mutation 2 — the store is switched read-only, and that switch is what "frozen" names.** After the
  extraction is taken and verified, the legacy store is set read-only so that the rollback position cannot
  drift from the record every reconciliation artifact was computed against. From that point the source is
  **frozen**: no schema change, no row written, no further mutation of any kind. The complete enumeration
  of the writes it ever received — `M1`, this one, and the contingent `Rh` — is the `Writes?` column of the
  lifecycle table above, which owns it; this paragraph does not restate it as a second list.

  **The actor is named per source shape, and it is always an actor capable of the statement it issues.**
  For the **file-attached** source under `App_Data` the switch is performed by the **LocalDB instance
  owner on the Windows verification host** — the only principal that can attach, detach or alter that
  instance's databases. For an **Azure-hosted copy** it is performed by the **deployment identity**,
  inside the named change window of [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s identity inventory. It is
  never an identity that cannot authenticate to the store it is switching, which is the failure mode the
  per-shape split exists to exclude, and the switch is **read back and asserted** rather than assumed.

  **Retention: the source outlives cutover by a fixed window, and closure is gated on it.** The window is
  **14 days after cutover** — the rollback window — and nothing destroys the source inside it, whatever
  reconciliation reports. `close-run` (section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)) **may not run
  before the window closes**, because it destroys the manifest, the lineage and the verification key that
  make a rollback's own reconciliation answerable. The source's eventual **removal** is a separate step
  again, sequenced by [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) under
  [09 §8.2](09-security-assessment.md) item 2's collision — the committed store is at once the only
  authoritative schema evidence and a Critical finding — and this document states the precondition rather
  than the schedule.

### 5.6 The data-migration executor

Sections [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) and
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) describe two data
migrations and a schema gate. **This section names the thing that performs them**, because
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.3 places the data movement as step 5 of the provisioning
order and delegates the tooling — and step 5's idempotence — to this document. A plan that specifies
the data migration without specifying its executable produces a release step nobody can run.

**The scope of this contract is the *target* migration, and one adjacent operation is deliberately
outside it.** Everything in this section moves source rows into **target-shaped** schemas — the EF Core
catalog schema of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and the ASP.NET Core Identity
schema of section
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration). The interim hosting branch
of [06 §5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) needs a **different** operation: a copy that preserves
the *legacy* EF 6 and Identity 1.0 schemas unchanged, because the un-ported application cannot read a
target-shaped store. **This tool does not perform it and this section is not its contract.**
[06 §5.8](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) holds that branch **conditional and not executable** until
a contract of its own is authored and approved, and enumerates what that contract must contain. Nothing
here is reusable for it beyond the `extract-schema` sub-command's schema interrogation.

**The artifact: no new artifact at all — these are eight verbs of the one operator console project.**
They are verbs of `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj` and its `Program.cs`, the project AAP
§0.4.1's future application map already carries and the only operator console project in the target
(section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties),
[04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)). There is **no separate data-migration project and no second
operator executable**: a required operator capability becomes another verb of the mapped project rather
than a project beside it, for the structural reason section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) gives — one lockfile, one publish
output, one checksum and one promotion path for every operator action the target needs. The project is on
the target framework that [04 §2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) fixes and takes a `ProjectReference`
on the web project for its model and context types. **It is not deployed with the web application**: not
referenced by the web project, not in its publish output, and nothing a compromised web process can
invoke. It is run from the release pipeline or an operator session by the **deployment principal**, whose
identity and grants are [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §6.2 and §6.6 — the same principal that
applies the migrations, because the load writes rows and creates the tool's own run tables.

**Eight verbs, one per gated action across the two migrations, the verb that seals them and the two
lifecycle transitions that close them.** They are eight of the ten section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) enumerates; the other two are
`admin` (section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)) and `seed`
(section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)), which move no source rows and are
not part of this contract. An earlier revision listed six and left acceptance and closure as prose
describing "the acceptance step" and "the run-closure step" with no executable — which is the same defect
as specifying a data migration with no tool, one level down: a release step nobody can run, whose
preconditions nobody can enforce and whose writes nobody can audit. The last two rows below are those
steps given contracts of the same shape as the other six.

| Verb | Performs | Specified by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extract-schema` | The complete catalog-view interrogation of **the one store its mandatory `--store` names**, emitting the written schema record. **With `--begin-run` it additionally creates the run descriptor**, and with or without `--begin-run` it creates **that store's** run-source row; it is the only invocation in the whole tool permitted to do either — see the run-identity sub-section below | [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1, [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) |
| `diff-schema` | The generated-DDL-versus-extracted-schema comparison for the store its mandatory `--store` names, which **must report zero differences inside that store's declared comparison scope** | [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 |
| `load-catalog` | The dependency-ordered catalog and order load, with the per-table identity mechanics. `--store catalog` is mandatory and is its only permitted value | [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 |
| `load-identity` | The Identity load: collision detection, user and role rows, child rows, column origins. `--store identity` is mandatory and is its only permitted value | [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) |
| `reconcile` | The keyed-set and digest comparison for the store its mandatory `--store` names, and — for the catalog — the per-order financial comparison. **`--store both` is a distinct, explicit invocation** that reconciles the two stores against their own run-source rows in one pass and is the form `seal-manifest` requires | below, and [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 6 |
| `seal-manifest` | Binds the imported `Cart.RecordId` set — **read from the run's member rows below rather than accumulated in the sealing process** — and the many-to-one merge lineage to **the exact run named by its mandatory `--run-id`**, each store's own source fingerprint and extraction cutoff taken from that run's run-source rows, and **the committed table unit each member came from**, computes the integrity digest over the canonical serialization below, and writes the result to the store whose immutability guarantee [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) specifies. It takes **no `--store`**: it seals the run, not a store. It **fails with exit `2`** rather than sealing if the run descriptor is absent, if either store's run-source row is absent, if a fingerprint recorded on a run-source row does not match the one this invocation computes for that store, or if any member of the set has no committed checkpoint row in that run. **It runs only after `reconcile --store both` has passed**, because a manifest bound to an unreconciled load — or to a load only one of whose stores was reconciled — would attest to a set nobody has verified | [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) §11.4, which owns the manifest's storage, content, integrity and the gates it must satisfy before any cleanup runs |
| `accept-run` | **Records the data owner's acceptance of the migration, and nothing else.** Mandatory `--run-id`; no `--store`. **Preconditions, all checked before the single write and each producing exit `2` with nothing written**: the parent row exists and its `State` is `Sealed`; a `reconcile --store both` pass is recorded for the run and returned `0`; `seal-manifest` succeeded for the run and the sealed manifest verifies against the parent, both run-source rows and the run's checkpoint rows on the gates [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists. **Writes**: `AcceptedUtc` and `State = Accepted` on the parent row, in one transaction, and an `ILogger` acceptance record on the output channel this section fixes below — **not** an `AdminProvisioned` record and not on [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s route — naming the authorizing principal, the run id and both stores' fingerprints. **It destroys nothing and drops nothing** — that is `close-run`'s job, and separating them is what lets the post-load cleanup run between the two. **Idempotent**: a second invocation against an already-`Accepted` run re-verifies the preconditions and exits `0` without writing; against a `Closed` run it exits `2`. **Authorizing principal**: the data owner authorizes, and the deployment principal [06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) executes — the tool records both, and refuses to run under a principal that is not the one that opened the run unless `--authorized-by` names the data owner explicitly | [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9, and the lifecycle sub-section below |
| `close-run` | **Retires the run: destroys its evidence in a fixed order and stamps its closure.** Mandatory `--run-id`; no `--store`. **Preconditions, each exit `2` with nothing written**: the parent row exists and its `State` is `Accepted`; the post-load cleanup of [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) has completed and every manifest gate that document lists passed; and the reconciliation artifacts' retention has expired under the schedule in the controls table below. **Writes and deletes, in the order the lifecycle sub-section fixes**, ending with the verification key so that every earlier destruction is still authenticable while it happens. **It deletes only this run's rows** — its checkpoint rows, its member rows, its manifest and its lineage records — and **drops no table**: the four run tables are permanent objects, for the reason the lifecycle sub-section states. **Idempotent**: each step is skipped when its own evidence is already absent, and a second invocation against a `Closed` run re-verifies and exits `0`. **Authorizing principal**: operations executes on the data owner's schedule; the data owner approves the retention period | The lifecycle sub-section below, and [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) for the cleanup gates it confirms |

**Invocation, secrets and output.** Connection strings and every secret arrive **only through
environment variables scoped to the single invocation** — never as command-line arguments, for the
reason section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) gives for the
provisioning command: an argument is visible in process listings and is recorded by shell and pipeline
history. The command refuses to accept a connection string as an argument at all. Output is
**structured `ILogger` records** written through the JSON console formatter of section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) to **standard output**, whose captured stream
[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) collects —
[06 §6.10](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s logging row owns that route and section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) states this side of it — carrying the sub-command, the
target database name, the table, the batch boundary, row counts and outcomes, and **no PII, no password
hash and no security stamp**, per the controls below.

**That is not [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s route, and saying so is what keeps one
first hop per producer.** §9.5.1 carries the `admin` verb's `AdminProvisioned` set alone — four lines
from a dedicated serialiser, captured and uploaded into an immutable container, section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 — so **no record
any verb in this section writes travels it, and none of them is an `AdminProvisioned` record**. The
audited privilege grants this executor does emit, one `AUTHZ-3001` per role assignment (section
[5.8](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)), are ordinary
records on the channel above, and their loss is a lost diagnostic rather than a failed step — which is
the opposite of the audit lines' rule and the reason the two routes are not interchangeable.

**The two output channels are separate, deliberately**: a mismatch's *named* members — the usernames, the
role names, the colliding pairs — go **only** to the controlled reconciliation artifact, never to the log
channel above, because the artifact is the thing held to the personal-data controls below and a log sink
has a different retention, a different access model and a different audience.

**Exit codes are the tool-wide allocation of section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation), not a second table.**
Every verb in this section returns one of that allocation's five codes and defines none of its own. What
belongs here is the mapping from **this section's** conditions onto those classes, stated once:

- **`0`** — the verb completed and its own verification passed. The pipeline proceeds.
- **`2`** — a precondition was rejected and **nothing was written**: a missing parent run row; a run
  already `Accepted` or `Closed`; an absent `--run-id` on a verb that requires one; an absent or invalid
  `--store` on a verb that requires one; a missing run-source row for `(RunId, --store)`; a source
  fingerprint that does not match **that store's** run-source row (the run-identity sub-section below); a
  second `--begin-run` against a target carrying an **unclosed** run; a non-empty target with no matching
  checkpoint; a `--resume` invocation whose checkpoint table holds no row for this run and store or whose
  recorded durable run id or per-store source fingerprint does not match; a `seal-manifest` invocation
  whose `reconcile --store both` has not passed; an `accept-run` or `close-run` whose own preconditions
  are unmet (the lifecycle sub-section below); or a **non-empty Identity child table with no recorded
  disposition** (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)).
  The pipeline stops, and there is nothing to clean up.
- **`3`** — could not connect, a grant was refused, or the target's schema does not match the extracted
  record. The pipeline stops, and there is nothing to clean up.
- **`4`** — partial work, rolled back to the last committed table boundary; the checkpoint rows record
  what completed. The pipeline stops, then **re-runs the same verb with `--resume` and the same
  `--run-id`**.
- **`5`** — a verification failed: `diff-schema` found a difference inside the declared comparison scope, or `reconcile` found a
  mismatch. The pipeline stops and **cutover is blocked** until it is explained or corrected.

**One condition is deliberately absent from code `3`: an absent checkpoint table on a run that is not
resuming.** That is the expected first-run state, not a rejection, and the next sub-section separates the
two operations so that the same condition cannot be both. **And two refusals that used to carry different
codes now carry `3` together** — "could not connect" and "the schema is not in the expected state" — which
is the allocation's point: both are refusals before a write, both leave nothing behind, and the specific
check is named by its `PROV-xxxx` message code rather than by a numeric code of its own.

#### One run, two sources — the run identity, and what makes the invocations provably one migration

**A durable run id carried on checkpoint rows is not the same thing as a run.** The verbs are
separate processes, invoked at different times by different release steps, and a run id that exists only
