as a column on rows those processes write cannot answer the question the cutover gate actually asks:
**were these results produced by one migration of one pair of sources?** Without a parent record, a
`reconcile` pass can be handed a run id that no load ever opened, an operator can resume one run's tables
under another run's id, and a manifest can be sealed over a set assembled from two. So the run is a
**first-class object**.

**One run reads *two* sources, and an earlier revision of this sub-section modelled it as reading one.
That is corrected here, because the conflation was structural rather than cosmetic.** The catalog store
and the credential store are **separate databases** — section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) extracts from
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/MvcMusicStore.mdf` and section
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) from the Identity store
declared beside it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13] — with **their own schema records, their own
per-table row counts and their own extraction cutoffs**. A single scalar `SourceFingerprint` on the run
therefore had to be either one store's, in which case the other store's load validated against a
fingerprint that does not describe it, or a blend of both, in which case neither store could be extracted
before the other and no invocation could validate a fingerprint it had not already computed for a source
it was not reading. Both readings are broken, and the columns marked "per store" in the old descriptor
table were the symptom: **a single row cannot carry two values of one column.** The run therefore has a
parent row and **one child row per store**.

**The parent: `dbo.__DataMigrationRun`, one row per run, created under the deployment principal. It
carries the run's identity and lifecycle and no source facts at all.**

| Column | Content | Why it is on the parent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RunId` | The durable run id, generated once — the primary key | It is the identity every child row and every artifact points at |
| `OpenedByPrincipal` | The principal that opened the run | Accountability, and it is the same value the audit record of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) carries |
| `OpenedUtc`, `Environment`, `TargetDatabase` | When it opened, and what it was pointed at | A rehearsal run and a production run are distinguishable in the parent itself, not only by inference from a fingerprint |
| `VerificationKeyId` | The label under which the logical-run digest key is held in the approved secret store | The key authenticates **every** store's evidence, so it belongs to the run and not to a source. Recording its label here is what makes "which key verifies this run's artifacts" a query |
| `State` | `Open`, `Sealed`, `Accepted` or `Closed` | A single state column is what the open-run and acceptance gates test, so a gate cannot be written against a combination of nullable timestamps and get the combination wrong |
| `SealedUtc`, `AcceptedUtc`, `KeyDestroyedUtc`, `ClosedUtc` | Stamped by steps 6, 7 and 8, the last stamping the final two together | These four are the run's lifecycle, and each is a separately recorded fact rather than an inference from a missing row — which is why the parent row outlives the run rather than being deleted with its children |

**The child: `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource`, one row per store per run, keyed `(RunId, Store)` with
`RunId` a foreign key to the parent.** `Store` takes exactly two values, `catalog` and `identity`.

| Column | Content | Why it is per store |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RunId`, `Store` | The composite primary key; `RunId` references the parent | Two stores, two rows, one run |
| `SourceName` | That store's source logical server and database name | An operator reading the row can see what was read without recomputing a digest, **for the store they are asking about** |
| `SourceFingerprint` | The fingerprint defined below, computed over **that store's** identity and state | Each store's load, reconciliation and sealing validate against **their own** source, so a rehearsal catalog copy can never satisfy a production Identity gate or the reverse |
| `SchemaRecordDigest` | The digest of that store's extracted schema record (section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1) | Each store has its own extraction and therefore its own record |
| `ExtractionCutoffUtc` | That store's extraction cutoff | The two extractions do not happen at the same instant, and pretending they did would make one store's cutoff a claim about the other |
| `ExtractedUtc` | When that store's `extract-schema` completed | Distinguishes "this store has been extracted" from "the run is open", which are different facts and were previously one |

**Opening a run and registering a source are two operations, and the second happens twice.**
`extract-schema --begin-run --store <s>` creates the parent row **and** the run-source row for store `s`
in **one transaction**, so a run never exists without at least one registered source.
`extract-schema --run-id <id> --store <t>` then registers the second store's row against the existing
parent. `extract-schema` is the **only** invocation in the tool that creates either kind of row. It
refuses to open a second run against a target that already carries an **unclosed** one — exit `3`,
nothing written, on the gate the lifecycle sub-section below defines — so two concurrent releases cannot
interleave, and it emits the generated `RunId` on its structured output so the release definition can
carry it forward. `extract-schema` invoked with **neither** `--begin-run` nor `--run-id` is exit `2`, and
invoked without `--store` is exit `2`: there is no unattributed invocation and no invocation that leaves
which source it read to be inferred.

**`--run-id` is mandatory on every later sub-command, `--store` is mandatory on every sub-command that
touches one store, and both are validated rather than trusted.** `--run-id`'s *form* is checked earlier
still — in the closed pre-parse, against the one grammar of section
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure), before a path is composed from it or a
connection opened — and the four checks below are what a **well-formed** identifier is then checked
against: **none of them is lexical**, so they are the second half of that contract and not the whole of it.
`diff-schema`, `load-catalog`,
`load-identity`, `reconcile`, `seal-manifest`, `accept-run`, `close-run` and every `--resume` all
require `--run-id`; every one of them except `seal-manifest`, `accept-run` and `close-run` also requires
`--store`. Each performs these checks **before its first write**:

1. **The parent row exists** for that `RunId`. If it does not, the run was never opened — exit `2`,
   nothing written.
2. **The run-source row exists** for `(RunId, --store)`. If it does not, that store was never extracted
   in this run, so nothing about it has been established — exit `3`, nothing written. This check has no
   counterpart in the old single-fingerprint design, and it is the one that stops a load running against
   a store whose schema this run never looked at.
3. **The source fingerprint the invocation computes for that store equals `SourceFingerprint` on that
   store's run-source row.** This is the check that stops a rehearsal's evidence satisfying a production
   gate and stops a `reconcile` being run against a source the load never read — exit `3`, nothing
   written. **It is per store**: a catalog invocation compares against the catalog row and is indifferent
   to the Identity row's value, which is precisely what the single scalar could not express.
4. **The run is not already accepted or closed** — `State` is `Open` or `Sealed`. A run past acceptance
   does not acquire new children.

Step 5 run over both stores performs checks 2 and 3 **for each store in turn** and halts on the first that
does not hold, naming the store. Step 6, which is not per store, performs checks 2 and 3 for **both**
stores, which is what makes a manifest unsealable while either store's evidence is missing or mismatched.

**Checkpoints, members and the manifest are children of the parent, declared as such.** Every
`dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` and `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` row carries the `RunId` as a **foreign key
to the parent** and the `Store` value as part of its own key, so a row for a run that does not exist is
unrepresentable rather than merely unexpected; and the manifest
[06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) specifies carries the same `RunId` and is verified against
the parent and both run-source rows by the gates that document lists. **The consequence is the property
the cutover gate needs**: the results are one migration exactly when they all bind to **one** parent row
and each validated its own store's fingerprint against that store's own run-source row before writing
anything — and that is checkable with a query rather than by trusting a release log.

**Why the four bookkeeping objects are not a fifth schema owner.** [06 §6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
enumerates four schema owners in the target — the two contexts, the session cache table and the
data-protection key table — and a helper table created beside them invites the objection that this is a
fifth. It is not, on three stated grounds: the objects are **absent from both models and both migration
sets** (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), so they never appear in a
migration diff and no migration can drop them without being written to; they are **created and read only
by this procedure under the deployment principal**, and the runtime identity is granted nothing on them
([06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)); and they hold **no application data the application
reads**, so no request path depends on them. What a model-tracked helper table would have risked — being
dropped by a later migration that had no idea what it was for — is precisely what excluding them from the
model prevents.

**The member table: `dbo.__DataMigrationMember`, the durable, cross-process carrier of the exact key sets
the run produced.** This table did not exist in an earlier revision of this contract, and its absence was
a real gap rather than a missing convenience. `seal-manifest` is required to seal **the exact imported
`Cart.RecordId` set**, and `reconcile` is required to compare **named** members of keyed sets — but
`seal-manifest` and `reconcile` are **separate processes** from `load-catalog`, so any set the loading
process held in memory is gone by the time either of them runs. Re-deriving the set by re-querying the
target would seal whatever the target happens to contain at sealing time rather than what this run
imported, which is the difference between provenance and a snapshot. So the set is written durably, by
the process that produced it, in the transaction that produced it.

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `RunId`, `Store` | Foreign key to the parent, and which store this member came from |
| `TableUnit` | The table whose committed unit produced the row — the same value the checkpoint row for that unit carries, so a member and its provenance join on `(RunId, Store, TableUnit)` |
| `SourceNaturalKey` | The member's natural key in the source, canonicalized on the serialization rule below. This is what a human resolving a mismatch reads. **For an Identity member the natural key is a user name, so the column carries that value's alias — `u_<hash>` — and never the name itself**, under the deterministic-pseudonym rule of the reconciliation sub-section below; for a catalog or order member it is a key value and is carried verbatim. The column takes the personal-data controls tabulated below without exception either way, because an alias is pseudonymized rather than anonymized data |
| `SourceKey` | The member's primary-key value in the source |
| `TargetKey` | The member's primary-key value in the target. Equal to `SourceKey` under the preserve-all-keys decision of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction), and recorded separately anyway so that the one place the decision is ever revised does not require this table to change shape |
| `LineageRole` | `Imported`, `MergeSurvivor` or `MergeRemoved` — which side of a many-to-one transformation this member is on, or neither |

- **A member row is written inside the same transaction as the rows it describes and their checkpoint
  row**, so "imported", "recorded as imported" and "recorded as loaded" are one fact rather than three
  that can disagree. A table that rolls back leaves no member rows, exactly as it leaves no checkpoint
  row, which is what makes the tentative-key rule below hold without a second mechanism.
- **Step 5 reads this table rather than accumulating anything.** The keyed set comparison below takes the
  run's member rows for the store as the **target-side** set for each table, joins them to the source by
  `SourceKey`, and names the missing and extra members from `SourceNaturalKey`. A member row with no
  corresponding target row, or a target row with no member row, is a mismatch — and the second of those is
  the failure no comparison against a re-queried target could ever see.
- **Step 6 reads this table rather than accumulating anything.** The `Cart.RecordId` set it seals **is**
  the `TargetKey` values of the run's `Cart` member rows whose `LineageRole` is `Imported` or
  `MergeSurvivor`, plus the `MergeRemoved` values the merge lineage records; it is enumerated from the
  table and canonicalized on the set rule below. **Nothing in the sealing derives the set from the
  target's current contents**, which is what makes the sealed set the set this run imported rather than
  the set the target holds today.
- **Row volume is stated rather than left as a surprise.** One member row per imported row is the largest
  object this procedure creates — for the catalog store one row per genre, artist, album, cart line, order
  and order detail. It is bounded by the per-table source row counts the data owner states before the run,
  it is written in the same batches as the rows it describes so it adds no round trips of its own, and its
  rows are deleted by step 8 with the run's other lineage. The alternative — sealing a set nobody recorded
  — is not cheaper, it is unverifiable.

**Commit granularity is one transaction per table unit — the eight-unit definition of section
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure), used here without variation — and the
checkpoint row commits inside it.** A
checkpoint written in a *second* transaction would be exactly as unreliable as no checkpoint at all — the
table could commit and the checkpoint fail, or the reverse:

- **The unit's rows, its checkpoint row and its member rows commit or roll back together**, in the one
  transaction. There
  is no window in which a unit is loaded and unrecorded, or recorded and unloaded.
- **The committed table unit is therefore the unit of provenance.** The manifest binds each member of its set
  to **the committed table unit** it came from — the `(RunId, table)` pair of a checkpoint row that exists
  — rather than to a batch, a wall-clock time or an in-flight boundary.
- **Tentative key values produced inside a rolled-back table are discarded, not carried.** A table that
  rolls back has produced no committed rows, so any `RecordId` or other generated value observed during
  its attempt is **not** a member of any set, does not enter the manifest, and is not written to any
  artifact. A rerun re-loads that table from its source and the values it produces the second time are the
  only ones that exist. This is stated because the opposite — collecting identifiers as rows are inserted
  and sealing them later — is the natural implementation and it would seal identifiers that no longer
  exist.
- **Batching therefore has no provenance role whatsoever.** It bounds round-trip size and the memory the
  executing session holds, and nothing else; the checkpoint's `BatchId` column identifies the committed
  unit's final batch for operator diagnostics and is never a resume point. Any statement that a batch
  "commits and is resumable" contradicts this contract, and
  [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is written to this rule.

**Every unordered set that contributes to a digest is canonicalized before it is hashed, and the framing
is part of the requirement.** A digest over a set has to be independent of enumeration order, and the
obvious implementation — sort, concatenate, hash — is not sufficient. So:

- **Count-framed.** The serialization begins with the **member count** as a typed, length-prefixed value,
  before any member. Without it a set of *n* members and a set of *n* + 1 whose extra member is empty can
  produce the same bytes under some framings, and — more importantly — a truncated artifact hashes as a
  smaller set rather than failing.
- **Ascending order by the canonical byte serialization of the member**, not by a culture-sensitive string
  comparison. Ordering by a collation would make the digest depend on the machine's locale, so two correct
  implementations could disagree.
- **Duplicates are rejected, not deduplicated.** A duplicate member in what is declared a set means the
  producing query is wrong, and silently collapsing it makes a real defect — a `RecordId` counted twice,
  a role assignment enumerated twice — indistinguishable from a correct set. The verb exits `5`.
- **A multiset is declared as one and carries multiplicity explicitly**, as `(member, count)` pairs
  ordered by the member's canonical bytes, so that a multiset's digest cannot be produced by the set path
  and vice versa. The Identity child-class comparisons of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) are multisets on this rule.
- **The same convention applies wherever a set is hashed** — the keyed set comparisons below, the manifest
  `RecordId` set, and the merge lineage — so that [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s HMAC over the
  manifest is computed over the identical bytes this document defines.

#### Idempotence and rerun mechanics

**"Run it again" has to be a defined operation, not a hope.** The load is the one release step whose
failure mid-way leaves durable state behind, so its rerun behaviour is specified rather than inferred:

- **Idempotence is per table unit and keyed**, not global. Each unit's load is complete or absent; there is
  no half-loaded unit after any exit.
- **One transaction per table unit — and what batching bounds is stated precisely, because the two bounds are
  not the same bound.** A unit's rows are inserted in **batches** inside a single transaction that
  commits at the unit boundary. **Batching bounds the client's memory** — how many rows the process
  holds at once, and how large each round trip is. **It does not bound transaction-log growth**: log
  records become reclaimable only when the transaction that produced them commits or rolls back, so a
  table loaded inside one transaction holds log for the **whole table** however small its batches are.
  **The trade is taken deliberately, in favour of atomicity**: a failure anywhere in a table rolls that
  whole table back, so the partial-load cleanup rule is "there is nothing to clean up", which is the only
  cleanup rule that survives an operator under pressure. That choice carries three **requirements**, not
  caveats: the target database's transaction log is **pre-sized for the largest single table's load**,
  against a per-table source row count the **data owner states before the run** rather than one
  discovered during it; log space is **monitored during the load**, with a stated threshold at which the
  verb aborts and rolls back rather than filling the log; and the run is sized against the service
  objective's log limits, which [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns. **The alternative was
  considered and is not taken**: committing each batch separately would bound log growth, but it would
  leave a table **partially loaded** after a failure, which turns the resume contract from "restart this
  table" into "reconcile a partial table against its source" and would require every duplicate-detection
  and reconciliation rule below to be restated for that case. If a table is ever too large for its log,
  changing the commit granularity is an **explicitly approved revision of this contract** — data owner
  and Engineering — and never a silent switch.
- **The checkpoint is a table the tool owns**: `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint`, created under the
  deployment principal, with one row per completed table carrying the **durable run id — a foreign key to
  the parent run row** — the **`Store` value**, **that store's source fingerprint** as recorded on its
  run-source row, the verb, the table name, the **batch id** of
  the committed unit, the row count, the digest and the commit timestamp. **The row is inserted inside the
  same transaction as the table's rows** and therefore commits or rolls back with them, which is what
  makes "loaded" and "recorded as loaded" the same fact rather than two facts that can disagree. **It is
  deliberately not part of either context's migration set
  and not present in either model** (section
  [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)) — a model-tracked helper table would
  appear in the next migration diff and eventually be dropped by a migration that had no idea what it
  was for. **The table itself is a permanent database object that no step ever drops**; `close-run`
  deletes **only the closing run's own rows** from it, on the rule the lifecycle sub-section below states.
  Because the transaction boundary is the
  table, the batch id is a **provenance marker rather than a resume point**: it identifies the committed
  unit whose rows an artifact describes, which is what lets the manifest of
  [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s post-load cleanup manifest bind its `RecordId` set to a run and a committed unit
  instead of to a wall-clock time.
- **`dbo.__DataMigrationMember` is owned on exactly the same terms**: created by the tool under the
  deployment principal, absent from both models and both migration sets for the same reason, written
  inside the table unit's own transaction, a **permanent object no step drops**, and cleared of a run's
  rows only by that run's `close-run`.
- **Creation and validation are two operations with two outcomes, and the same condition may not be
  both.** A missing checkpoint object is the expected state of a first run and a rejection of a resume,
  so the tool is specified as two paths:
  - **Without `--resume` — atomic first-run creation.** The tool **creates
    `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` if it is absent** and proceeds; creation is atomic and idempotent, so
    two concurrent invocations cannot both create it and neither fails on finding it already there. An
    absent object here is **not** an error and **not** exit `3`; establishing it is the tool's job.
  - **With `--resume` — validation only, and it never creates.** The object **must exist**, and it must
    carry at least one row whose **durable run id and source fingerprint both match the invocation's**.
    An absent object, no matching row, or a row whose run id or fingerprint differs is **exit `3` with
    nothing written**. This is the only place a missing checkpoint object is an error, which is what
    keeps the two meanings apart.
- **The two identity inputs are defined rather than assumed, because a checkpoint that cannot be tied to
  a run and a source is a checkpoint that can be resumed against the wrong database.**
  - **The durable run id** is generated **once, by `extract-schema --begin-run`**, written to the run
    descriptor and then into every checkpoint row of that run. No other invocation generates one: every
    other verb, and every `--resume`, takes it as a **required argument** and validates it against
    the descriptor, so a resume extends its own run rather than opening a second. It survives a process
    restart because it lives in the descriptor, and it is the identifier
    [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s cleanup manifest carries as its durable run id.
  - **The source fingerprint** identifies **which source** the run read, and is computed over the
    source's identity and state rather than its contents: the source logical server and database name,
    the **digest of the extracted schema record** (section
    [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1), and the **per-table source
    row counts as of the extraction cutoff**. That combination is what distinguishes a rehearsal run
    against a restored copy from the production run against the real source — the property
    [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s manifest provenance check depends on, and the reason a rehearsal's evidence can
    never satisfy a production gate.
- **A rerun resumes at the first table without a committed checkpoint row** and re-verifies the rows of
  every table that does have one, by count and digest, before continuing. It does **not** re-insert a
  committed table, and it does not trust the checkpoint without checking it against the data.
- **The clean-target precondition.** Before the first write of a run the tool requires the target tables
  to be **empty**, and **refuses to run against a non-empty target unless it is resuming a validated
  checkpoint — the same durable run id and the same source fingerprint** — exit `3`, nothing written.
  This is the check that stops the accident this whole design exists to prevent: a second load appended
  to a first one, producing duplicated catalog rows and doubled orders that every row count reports as a
  successful load of twice as much data.
- **The digest key is a logical-run key held in the approved secret store, and never process-scoped.** A
  digest whose key dies with the process cannot verify a checkpoint row written before a restart, and
  being read by a *later* process is the checkpoint's entire purpose. So the key is generated **once per
  logical run**, **stored in the approved secret store** — [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)
  owns secret delivery and the store — **labelled with the durable run id and the source fingerprint**,
  and **retrieved by every subsequent invocation of that run**, including a `--resume` after a machine
  restart and the `reconcile` pass that runs later. Two failure modes are named because both are silent: a
  **process-scoped** key makes every persisted digest unverifiable the moment the process ends, and a key
  **shared across runs** makes a rehearsal's digest verify against a production checkpoint.
- **The key is retained until the last evidence it verifies has itself been destroyed, and its
  destruction is a step in its own right.** This corrects an earlier reading of this document, in which
  the key was destroyed "with the run's other artifacts" at acceptance. That is too early, and the
  consequence is specific: the manifest [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) requires is
  authenticated by an HMAC computed under **this** key, and the cleanup that consumes the manifest runs
  **after** acceptance ([06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md),
  [06 §6.11](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). A key destroyed at acceptance would leave that manifest
  — and every retained checkpoint digest and reconciliation artifact — **unverifiable at exactly the moment
  something needs to verify it**, converting a controlled cleanup into an unauthenticated delete. The rule
  is therefore:
  - **The key's retention is the maximum of the retentions of everything it authenticates** — the manifest,
    the checkpoint rows and the reconciliation artifacts — so it outlives acceptance, outlives the post-load
    cleanup, and expires only when the last of those has been destroyed under the schedule in the controls
    table below.
  - **Destruction is a final, separately recorded, verified action**: the key is destroyed from the secret
    store, the destruction is verified by attempting a retrieval and confirming it fails, and
    `KeyDestroyedUtc` is stamped on the parent row. A run whose parent row carries no `KeyDestroyedUtc` is
    a run whose key is still live, which is a query rather than a recollection.
  - **The asymmetric alternative is rejected**: destroying the key early and accepting that the retained
    artifacts become unverifiable would shorten the key's exposure, and it would mean the cleanup gate
    could no longer establish that the set it is about to delete is the set that was reconciled — the
    single most consequential check in the whole data migration.
- **The canonical serialization is typed and length-prefixed, with its encoding stated — because an
  unframed concatenation collides.** Every value that contributes to any digest in this document — a
  checkpoint row's fields and a migrated row's field values alike — is serialized as an ordered sequence of
  `(type tag, byte length, value bytes)` triples, in a **stated field order**, with **UTF-8** as the
  encoding of every textual value, a **distinct type tag with zero length for null** so that a null is not
  the empty string, invariant decimal formatting with the scale carried, and ISO-8601 UTC for every date
  and time. **Length prefixing is the part that matters**: over a plain concatenation the field sets
  `("ab", "c")` and `("a", "bc")` produce identical bytes, so two different rows can produce one digest and
  the comparison reports a match that is not one. Type tagging closes the same hole between a string and a
  number that render alike. [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) computes its cleanup manifest's
  HMAC over **this same** serialization, so the target carries one convention rather than two.
- **Duplicate detection rejects only what the extracted schema establishes as unique, and reports the
  rest.** A row violating an **extracted primary key, unique constraint or unique index** — from
  `sys.key_constraints`, `sys.indexes` and `sys.index_columns` in section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 — is a **failure**: the table rolls
  back, because the target cannot hold the row and because its presence means the source disagrees with the
  schema the diff gate passed. **Four candidate "natural keys" are explicitly not in that set, and
  rejecting on them would reject legitimate historical rows:** `Genre.Name`, `Artist.Name`,
  `(CartId, AlbumId)` and `(OrderId, AlbumId)`. Nothing in the source model declares any of them unique
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:5-11], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:8-13],
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:7-18], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/OrderDetail.cs:5-12], and
  `(CartId, AlbumId)` duplicates are a documented **consequence** of the source's sign-in rename
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:184-193] rather than a corruption. For these four,
  duplicates are therefore **preserved and reported** — counted, enumerated by key in an artifact under
  the controls below, and carried into the target as they stand — and the **`(CartId, AlbumId)` report is
  the input to the duplicate reconciliation that section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) makes the precondition of catalog stage 2's unique
  index** (section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)). If step 1's extraction **does** find a
  unique constraint or unique index on one of the four, that one moves into the rejecting set — on the
  strength of the extracted evidence and on nothing else. **What the browse path does about the
  `Genre.Name` duplicates this rule preserves is section
  [4.14](#414-the-duplicate-genre-browse-contract)'s contract**, which consumes the enumerated report as
  the input that selects its branch; this rule decides only that the rows are carried rather than
  rejected.
- **The merge transformation is many-to-one, so it records lineage, and every downstream comparison is
  written to be many-to-one aware.** Resolving the reported `(CartId, AlbumId)` duplicates collapses two or
  more loaded rows into one under the sum-and-earliest rule of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model). A one-to-one key comparison cannot express that: the
  target's `Cart` key set is legitimately **smaller** than the source's after the transformation, so a
  plain set equality on `RecordId` reports a failure for a correct migration — and, worse, would report a
  pass for a transformation that dropped a row it should have summed. Three requirements follow:
  - **A lineage record per merge, written as part of the transformation's own transaction**: the
    **surviving `RecordId`**, the **complete set of removed `RecordId` values**, the **summed `Count`**, the
    **earliest `DateCreated`** carried, and the `(CartId, AlbumId)` pair the group shared. The removed set
    is canonicalized on the set rule above, so its digest is order-independent and a duplicate inside it is
    rejected rather than collapsed.
  - **Reconciliation compares against the lineage rather than against a bare set — and that is the generic
    rule below, not a `Cart`-specific override of it.** The keyed-set rule in the reconciliation
    sub-section is stated in the union form for **every** table, so `Cart` needs no exception: the removed
    set is simply non-empty here and empty everywhere else. **Two checks are additional and specific to the
    transformation**: each surviving row's `Count` equals its lineage record's summed `Count`, and each
    surviving row's `DateCreated` equals the recorded earliest value. A row that vanished without a lineage
    record therefore fails, which is the failure a one-to-one comparison would have to be many-to-one aware
    to see.
  - **The cleanup set is exact because of the lineage, not in spite of it.** The set
    [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s manifest seals, and therefore the set its cleanup is
    permitted to delete, is the **surviving** `RecordId` values plus the recorded removed values —
    enumerated, not derived by re-running the transformation, so a cleanup can never widen itself by
    recomputing a group differently. The lineage record is an artifact of the same class as the duplicate
    report and carries the controls tabulated below.

#### Reconciliation: counts and totals are necessary and not sufficient

**Row counts and per-order totals cannot detect the failures that matter most**, and treating them as
the acceptance criterion is the quiet way to sign off a corrupted migration. Each of the following
passes a count-and-total check: two orders' `Username` values swapped, so both customers see the
other's history; a `Genre` renamed or two genres' ids exchanged during a keyed load; an address or
email altered anywhere in the PII columns [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]; a set of
role assignments redistributed among the same number of users. So the acceptance evidence is stronger:

- **Deterministic keyed set comparison, stated so that it is true of every table including `Cart`.** For
  every migrated table:

  > the **source primary-key set** equals the **union of the target primary-key set and the removed-key
  > set recorded in this run's lineage**, and those two sets are **disjoint** — with the missing and extra
  > members named when it does not hold.

  **The union form is the rule and not an exception to it.** A plain source-to-target set equality would
  **fail a correct `Cart` migration** — the target's key set is legitimately smaller after the merge — and
  the natural fix for that failure is to relax the `Cart` comparison, which would then **pass a
  transformation that dropped a row it should have summed**. So the rule carries the lineage term for every
  table. **For every table other than `Cart` the lineage removed set is empty** and the rule reduces to
  plain set equality; for `Cart` after the merge transformation it is not empty, and the same single rule
  still holds. The lineage-specific `Count` and `DateCreated` checks the merge rules above state are
  **additional** to this rule, not a substitute for it. Under the preserve-all-keys decision of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) both sides are compared directly; had a key
  map been used it would run over the mapped values, which is one of the reasons the map is an artifact
  rather than a scratch variable.
- **Per-field digests, over a declared projection rather than over "the row".** For every migrated row, an
  **HMAC-SHA256 digest over its canonicalized field values**, using the **typed, length-prefixed, UTF-8
  canonical serialization** and the **logical-run key held in the approved secret store** that the rerun
  mechanics above define — the same serialization and
  the same key, so a digest written by step 3 or step 4 verifies in step 5, which runs later and after
  any restart between them. Rows are compared by key and digest. A field that changed value changes the
  digest; a row that moved to another owner changes the digest.
- **The projection is declared per class, because "the row" is not the same set of fields on both sides.**
  A digest computed over every target column and compared against a digest computed over every source
  column **cannot match for any class that gains a column**, and the target gains columns in six places.
  Left undeclared, the implementer resolves that by whichever expedient comes first — dropping the new
  columns from the comparison silently, or comparing digests that can never be equal — and the first of
  those leaves a net-new column asserted by nothing at all. So every migrated class declares its fields in
  three buckets, and the digest is computed over the **carried** and **transformed** buckets only, with the
  **target-only** bucket asserted separately against its defined origin:

| Class | Carried unchanged — in the digest | Transformed — in the digest, with the transform named | Target-only — **not** in the digest, asserted against its defined origin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Genre` | `GenreId`, `Name`, `Description` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Genre.cs:7-9] | None | None |
| `Artist` | `ArtistId`, `Name` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Artist.cs:10-11] | None | None |
| `Album` | `AlbumId`, `GenreId`, `ArtistId`, `Title`, `Price`, `AlbumArtUrl` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:10-19] | None | None |
| `Cart` | `RecordId`, `CartId`, `AlbumId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:8-11] | **`Count` and `DateCreated` for merge survivors only** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Cart.cs:12-13]: the summed `Count` and the earliest `DateCreated` of the group, both taken from the lineage record. For every non-survivor row both are carried unchanged | **The `rowversion` change-detection witness** (section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)'s post-baseline change-tracking group; section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 1 consumes it). **Origin: the column does not exist while the load runs.** It is added post-load by `AddChangeTracking`, and `ALTER TABLE … ADD rowversion` stamps every row present at alter time — so it is asserted as **present and non-null on every loaded row after that migration**, never during the load, and never compared to a source value: there is no source value, and its bytes are meaningless outside the target database |
| `Order` | `OrderId`, `OrderDate`, `Username`, `Total` and every PII column [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:12-64] — the PII columns **by digest only**, per the artifact rule below | None | **`SubmissionId`** — the checkout submission key of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract), and the only target-only field this class has. **Origin: the column does not exist while the load runs.** It is added post-load by `AddCheckoutSubmissionId` (section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)'s post-baseline manifest), which adds it **nullable**, so every row present at alter time — that is, every migrated historical order — receives `null`, and that is why its unique index is filtered to exclude nulls. Asserted as **null on every loaded row after that migration**, never during the load: a non-null value on a migrated order would mean the load invented a submission identity |
| `OrderDetail` | `OrderDetailId`, `OrderId`, `AlbumId`, `Quantity`, `UnitPrice` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/OrderDetail.cs:5-9] | None | None |
| Identity user | The user id and `UserName`, and `PasswordHash`, `Email` and `PhoneNumber` where the source holds them — the hash **by digest only** | None | **`NormalizedUserName`** and **`NormalizedEmail`** — **origin: the normalizer applied to the carried value**, asserted by recomputing the normalizer over the carried value and comparing, which is a *derivation* check rather than a source comparison. **`ConcurrencyStamp`** and **`SecurityStamp`** — **origin: generated per account by the load**, asserted as present, non-null and **distinct across accounts**. **`EmailConfirmed`, `PhoneNumberConfirmed`, `TwoFactorEnabled`, `LockoutEnabled`, `LockoutEnd`, `AccessFailedCount`** — **origin: the documented defaults section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) fixes**, asserted as **equal to those defaults on every loaded account**, which is what makes a default a checked fact rather than an assumption |
| Identity role, and each carried child class | The keys and names the class carries, per section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) | None | **`ConcurrencyStamp`** on the role, on the same terms as the user's |

  **Two properties make this table a specification rather than a list.** Every target-only field has a
  **named origin and a stated assertion**, so none is left merely absent from the comparison; and the
  buckets are **exhaustive per class** — a column that appears in neither the source nor any bucket is a
  column the diff gate of section
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 has not accounted for, which is a
  failure of that gate rather than something reconciliation should paper over. **The facets of every
  target-only column remain gated on the extraction of step 1 and the Identity extraction of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)**; this table fixes what is
  compared and what is asserted, not what type or length anything is.

- **Why a keyed digest rather than a plain hash.** A key **scoped to one logical run** means the
  artifacts are useless outside that run, so a digest file that leaks cannot be used to confirm a guessed
  value in a PII or hash column — which a plain hash of a low-entropy field, an email address or a
  password hash, would permit. The key is scoped to the run and **not** to the process: those are
  different properties, and only the first is a confidentiality control.
- **The financial comparison stays**, as the one domain-specific invariant worth asserting twice:
  `Order.Total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] against the sum of its
  `OrderDetail.UnitPrice * Quantity` rows, on source and target, matching to the cent.
- **Every personal identifier these artifacts carry is a deterministic pseudonym, and none of them is a
  cleartext value.** The keyed sets this section requires are keyed **on the username** — the username
  set, the `(username, role name)` pair set, the child-class affected-username sets and owner-bound
  multisets of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) — and the whole point of a
  keyed comparison is that it **names the missing or extra member**. A reconciliation artifact that named
  nobody would not be a reconciliation artifact. What it names is the **alias**: `u_<hash>` for a user
  name and `e_<hash>` for an email address, in the exact grammar section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) specifies — `HMAC-SHA256` over the
  canonicalized UTF-8 bytes of the value, the result rendered as lowercase hexadecimal and truncated to
  16 characters, prefixed — computed with **the same function, the same key and the same `aliasKeyId` as
  the suite**, so that a tool report and a test failure concerning one account carry the same token. That
  section owns the grammar, the canonicalization, the key custody in the platform secret store, the
  rotation rule and the destruction; here the operative property is that **the `aliasKeyId` travels with
  every record that carries an alias and the key never does**.
- **One interpretive rule, so that every key specification in this section and in section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) is covered without being
  restated: wherever a set member, a multiset member, a pair, a tuple component or a report column is
  described as a *user name* or an *email address*, the artifact carries that value's alias.** Two
  properties make the reconciliation work on aliases, and both are properties of the grammar rather than
  hopes about it. **Determinism**: the same source value produces the same token in every artifact of the
  run and on both sides of every comparison, which is what lets a username set, a `(username, role name)`
  pair set and a per-account digest be compared and joined at all. **Reference semantics**: an alias
  identifies a member without disclosing it, so a set comparison still reports *which* member is missing
  or extra, and an owner-bound multiset still detects a child row that moved between two accounts.
- **Role names are carried as themselves, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** A role name
  names an authorization group rather than a person — `Administrator` identifies nobody — so aliasing it
  would make every mismatch report unreadable in exchange for no reduction in personal data. The
  `(username, role name)` pair therefore aliases its first component and carries its second verbatim.
- **The prohibition is total, and it is a prohibition rather than a preference.** No artifact, no report,
  no run table and no log sink written by either migration carries a **cleartext user name, email
  address, postal address, phone number, password hash or security stamp** — the order tables' PII
  columns [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] included — in any log, report or file. Values in
  the hash and stamp categories are compared by **digest only**, which is what the per-field digest above
  is for; values in the identifier categories are carried as the alias above. The one place cleartext
  personal data exists at all is the **extract itself**, under the controls tabulated below, and it is
  destroyed on the named schedule.
- **Resolving an alias to an identity is a separate, authorized, audited lookup performed by the data
  owner against the retained source.** It is not an operation the artifact enables, and this migration
  creates **no** reverse-lookup mapping of any kind: the source extract it already holds *is* the lookup,
  so there is no second store, no token table and no new custody question. Each resolution is authorized
  per occasion, names the actor, and lands in the actor-attributable PII read trail
  [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) defines — which exists for exactly this kind of read, and is
  why the source's retention window matters to reconciliation as well as to rollback.
- **The rejection an earlier revision recorded is withdrawn, and its two arguments are answered rather
  than dropped** — a withdrawal that leaves them standing invites the next reader to re-take the rejected
  position. It argued that a reverse-lookup store merely **relocates** the personal data: answered,
  because no such store is created; the retained extract is the lookup, already classified and already
  controlled. It argued that a human resolving a mismatch would **dereference every alias** and reassemble
  the data the pseudonymisation avoided: answered by scope, because the comparison itself dereferences
  nothing and a human dereferences one account on the one occasion an account has to be acted on, under
  the audited lookup above rather than by reading a file. What the earlier reading got right and what
  survives intact is the classification: an alias is **pseudonymized, not anonymized**, so these
  artifacts remain **personal data** and take the controls tabulated below in full — encrypted in transit
  and at rest, least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only for the run, destroyed on the named
  schedule with an owner. [09](09-security-assessment.md) owns the standing PII finding.
- **Any mismatch blocks cutover.** The reconciliation verdict is `fail`. It is explained and corrected, or the migration is rolled
  back to the position section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9
  states. It is not waived.

#### Controls on the sensitive artifacts, applied to both migrations equally

Section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 7 states the controls on
the domain extract because the order tables are PII. **The Identity side's artifacts are at least as
sensitive and get the same controls or stronger** — an asymmetry here would be the most consequential
kind of oversight, since the credential store is the one dataset whose compromise is not recoverable by
re-running anything.

| Artifact | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| The Identity extract and schema record | Encrypted transport and encrypted storage; least-privileged access, **access-logged**; held only for the run; destroyed on the stated schedule after acceptance |
| The normalized-username and role-name collision reports | The same, **plus redaction — and this artifact needs one property the others do not, because the alias canonicalizes before it hashes.** Section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) computes the alias over the value **`ILookupNormalizer` has already normalized**, so two user names differing only in case produce the **same** alias: the very collision being reported collapses the two members into one token. The report therefore carries **the shared alias as the collision group's identity and each member's source primary-key value as its discriminator** — an opaque Identity `Id`, which is neither a name nor an address — plus the count of colliding members. That is enough for the data owner to act: the group is located by alias, its members are distinguished by id, and the names themselves are obtained through the audited lookup below rather than from the file. It carries no cleartext identifier, no normalized form, no hash, no stamp and no email body content. **Role-name collisions are reported verbatim**, because a role name is not personal data |
| Per-account hash verification | **Digest comparison, never raw values.** The comparison establishes that source and target hold the same hash without either side's artifact containing one; the successful sign-in of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 18 is the functional proof |
| The reconciliation artifacts — keyed sets, mismatch reports, duplicate reports | The same controls as the extract, **and for a stronger reason than digest sensitivity: they identify people**, by alias rather than by name, because a keyed comparison that names no member cannot be resolved by a human. An alias is **pseudonymized, not anonymized**, so they are classified and handled as **personal data**: encrypted in transit and at rest, least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only for the run, destroyed on the named schedule. They carry **no cleartext user name or email address**, no password hash, no security stamp and none of the order tables' PII columns [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61]; each record carries the `aliasKeyId` and never the key |
| The checkpoint table `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` | The same controls; it holds run ids, store names, source fingerprints, table names, counts and digests rather than row values. **It is retained past acceptance**, because the post-load cleanup of [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) verifies the manifest against it. **The table is permanent**; `close-run` deletes only the closing run's rows |
| The run-source table `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource` | **Retained after closure with the parent row**, and on the same basis: it holds a store name, a source server and database name, a fingerprint, a schema digest and two timestamps — **no data row values, no usernames and no hashes** — so it is operational metadata under the log-retention policy [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes rather than under this schedule. Retaining it is what keeps a closed run's per-store provenance answerable |
| The member table `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` | **The strongest controls in this table, because it is the one tool-owned table that holds source-side identifiers.** Its `SourceNaturalKey` column carries the **alias** `u_<hash>` for every Identity member — never the user name — and a key value for every catalog or order member; because an alias is pseudonymized rather than anonymized, the table is still classified and handled as **personal data**: encrypted in transit and at rest, least-privileged and **access-logged**, retained only until `close-run`, which **deletes the closing run's rows** from this permanent table and verifies the deletion. It carries **no cleartext user name or email address, no password hash, no security stamp and none of the order tables' PII columns** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] |
| The run descriptor `dbo.__DataMigrationRun` | **Retained after closure, deliberately** — it carries run ids, fingerprints, digests, server and database names, the operator name and the lifecycle timestamps, and **no data row values, usernames or hashes**, so it is operational metadata held under the log-retention policy [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes rather than under this schedule. It is the record that makes closure checkable; see the run-lifecycle sub-section below |
| The `(CartId, AlbumId)` merge lineage records | The same controls as the duplicate report they resolve. They are retained until the post-load cleanup has completed, because the cleanup's permitted delete set is enumerated from them, and they are destroyed with the manifest at run closure |
| The logical-run digest key | Held in the approved secret store, labelled with the run id and source fingerprint, **retained until the last artifact it authenticates has been destroyed** and then destroyed as the final step of the run — verified by a failed retrieval and stamped as `KeyDestroyedUtc` on the descriptor |
| Every artifact, at the end | **A named destruction schedule with an owner**, and destruction verified rather than assumed — an extract that outlives the migration is a credential store nobody is watching ([09 §6.9](09-security-assessment.md) records what happens when one is left in place) |

#### The run lifecycle: opening, acceptance and closure

**Four classes of evidence deliberately outlive acceptance, and an earlier revision of this section said
three. The count was wrong and the omitted class was the consequential one.** Acceptance (section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9, executed by `accept-run`) closes
the *migration*; the *run* closes later, once the post-load cleanup of
[06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) has completed and the retention of the reconciliation
artifacts has expired. What survives acceptance until then is:

| # | Retained class | Why it must survive acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The sealed manifest** | The post-load cleanup runs **after** acceptance and consumes it. A manifest destroyed at acceptance leaves the cleanup with no authenticated statement of what it is permitted to delete |
| 2 | **The lineage** — the run's `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` rows **and** the `(CartId, AlbumId)` merge lineage records | **This is the class the earlier count omitted.** The cleanup's permitted delete set is *enumerated* from the lineage rather than re-derived (the merge sub-section above), so destroying it at acceptance would leave the cleanup either unable to run or forced to recompute a set — which is the one thing the exactness requirement forbids. It is also what makes a post-acceptance question about a specific migrated row answerable at all |
| 3 | **The run's `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` rows** | The manifest gates [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists verify the manifest **against** them, so they are an input to the same cleanup |
| 4 | **The logical-run verification key** | It authenticates all three of the above. Destroying it first would convert the controlled cleanup into an unauthenticated delete, which is the correction the rerun mechanics above already record |

**One owner and one schedule for all four, so they cannot drift apart.** The **data owner** approves the
retention period for the whole set and **operations** performs the destruction on that schedule; the four
are destroyed by **one** invocation of `close-run` in the order below rather than by four independently
scheduled jobs. The reason is the same reason the cart cleanup of section
[4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 6 is one job over three
tables: four schedules of one shape are four things to get wrong, and here getting one wrong destroys the
evidence that authenticates another.

**`close-run` does five things in this order, and the order is the requirement:**

1. **Confirm** that the cleanup completed, that every manifest gate
   [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) lists passed, **and that the 14-day rollback window of
   section
   [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover) has
   closed** — the last of the three because everything steps 2 to 5 destroy is evidence a rollback's own
   reconciliation would need. Closure is not permitted before all three — exit `3`, nothing written or
   destroyed.
2. **Destroy the sealed manifest**, verifying the destruction.
3. **Delete this run's lineage** — its `dbo.__DataMigrationMember` rows and its merge lineage records —
   verifying the deletion by re-reading for rows with this `RunId` and finding none.
4. **Delete this run's `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` rows**, verified the same way.
5. **Destroy the logical-run verification key last**, verify the destruction by a retrieval that fails,
   and **stamp `KeyDestroyedUtc`, `ClosedUtc` and `State = Closed` on the parent row**. The key is last so
   that every destruction in steps 2 to 4 happens while the evidence being destroyed is still
   authenticable, which is what makes each of those verifications meaningful rather than a delete followed
   by a hope.

**The four run tables are permanent database objects, and no step in this contract ever drops one. This
corrects an earlier statement of step 3, which dropped `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` outright.**
`dbo.__DataMigrationRun`, `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource`, `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` and
`dbo.__DataMigrationMember` are created once, by the first `extract-schema --begin-run` that finds them
absent, and thereafter persist. Dropping a table would have destroyed **every** run's state rather than
the closing run's: the retained parent and run-source rows of previously closed runs, and — for a table a
later run recreates — the object identity a resume validates against. **`close-run` deletes rows scoped by
`RunId` and nothing else**, which is why steps 3 and 4 are deletions with verification rather than drops.
The two tables whose rows are *not* deleted at closure — the parent and its run-source rows — are retained
for the reason the controls table gives: they hold no data row values, no usernames from the migrated data
and no hashes, so they are operational metadata under the log-retention policy
[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes. Retaining them is what makes closure **checkable**:
a parent row with no `ClosedUtc` is an unclosed run and is reported as one, whereas a deleted parent row
would make an unclosed run and a closed one look identical — which is precisely the failure this
sub-section exists to prevent.

**Opening a run blocks on any *unclosed* run, not on any unaccepted one, and the difference is a real
window.** `extract-schema --begin-run` refuses — exit `3`, nothing written — when the target carries a
parent row whose `ClosedUtc` is null, whatever its `State`. An earlier revision gated on acceptance
instead, which left the whole interval between `accept-run` and `close-run` open: a second run could be
begun while the first run's manifest, lineage, checkpoint rows and verification key were all still live,
and both runs would then be writing member and checkpoint rows into the same tables while one of them was
mid-cleanup against a set enumerated from lineage the other was adding to. **Overlapping runs are
deliberately unsupported**, and the reason is not that they are hard to implement: the clean-target
precondition, the exact-set seal and the enumerate-don't-recompute cleanup rule are all statements about
**the** load of **a** target, and every one of them would need re-deriving per run against a target two
runs were writing. A release that needs a second run runs `close-run` on the first, which is a step with a
contract rather than a judgement call.

**These controls are gate conditions, not advice.** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) places the
workstream gates, and this document's requirement is that the data-movement gates it places cannot be
passed without them — the extract encrypted and access-logged, the reports redacted, the comparison
digest-based, **every user name and email address in every artifact carried as its deterministic alias
and the artifacts still classified and handled as personal data**, and the destruction scheduled with an
owner named.

---

### 5.7 The data migration is an artifact, not a procedure

**Everything sections [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) and
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) specify is stated as a
sequence of steps, and a sequence of steps has nothing a test can invoke.** That is the defect this
subsection closes. Read the two sections back as an implementer would: extract the schema, diff it,
back up, load in dependency order, reconcile per table, reconcile order totals to the cent, scan for
duplicate normalized user names before the first write, retain the source, roll back on failure. Nine
obligations, every one of them checkable — and **no named thing that performs them**. The consequences are
three, and they compound:

- **The gates are unenforceable.** "The diff must pass before any data is loaded" is a rule about the
  *order of two operations*. With no artifact owning both, nothing can refuse the second because the
  first did not pass; the rule reduces to a person remembering it.
- **The suite cannot exercise them.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is required to prove the
  nine obligations above, and a test can only invoke something that exists. A fixture that *pre-populates*
  the target database proves the assertions run — it proves nothing whatever about the migration,
  because the migration was not what put the rows there.
- **The thing that runs in production is not the thing that was tested.** A migration performed by hand,
  or by a script written on the day, is a different artifact from whatever the tests exercised. That is
  the failure this document has already rejected twice — for administrator provisioning (section
  [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command)) and for seeding (section
  [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)) — and the reasoning is identical here.

**Resolution: one production artifact — the mapped operator console — and the tests invoke that same
artifact.** The eight data and lifecycle verbs of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) are verbs
of `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj` and its `Program.cs`, carrying their own committed
lockfile and restored in locked mode like every other project ([04 §6.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
owns the mechanism and the pins). **There is no second tool project**: the alternative — a
a separate data-migration console beside it — was considered and rejected in section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) for a structural reason, and nothing in
this subsection needs it. The project is **not deployed with the web application**: an executable that can
rewrite the whole dataset has no business inside a process that serves anonymous requests. It is **run by
the deployment principal from the release pipeline**; [06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns
that principal and the identity model, and this document does not restate them.

**What this subsection owns, and what it does not.** Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) owns
the verbs and what each one performs, the run identity, the idempotence and rerun mechanics, the
reconciliation contract, the controls on the artifacts and the run lifecycle. Section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) owns the canonical invocation
literal, the closed pre-parse, the per-verb accepted switch sets and **the one exit-code allocation**.
What this subsection owns is the property that makes all of that an *artifact* rather than a procedure:
**the immutable, identified run record the verbs hand between themselves, the transaction boundary the
load commits on, the rollback position, and the machine-readability that lets a test assert on any of it.**

**The handoff between verbs is a named immutable run, not "the same extract".** This is the mechanism the
gates rest on, and without it they are unenforceable in a way that is easy to miss: `load-catalog` refuses
without a `pass` from `diff-schema`, but if the schema record were a location anything may overwrite, then
a `pass` computed over one schema would authorize a load over another and **the gate would pass while
proving nothing**. Nothing errors; the diff was genuinely green, over inputs that are no longer there. So
the run is addressed by identity and its every artifact is verified by digest.

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The run identifier** | **`--run-id`**, and it is the only handoff token in the tool. `extract-schema --begin-run` generates it in **exactly one closed form** — `^[0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6}Z-[0-9a-f]{8}$`, 25 ASCII characters, the single grammar the paragraph below this table fixes and the only form any verb accepts — **echoes it to standard output on its own line** and records it in the run descriptor, which is how a caller learns the value every later verb must be given. There is deliberately **no separate extract identifier**: one token identifies the run, its per-store extractions, its diffs, its loads, its reconciliations and its manifest, so no invocation can pair one run's verdict with another run's rows |
| **The directory** | Each verb writes under **`<report-dir>/run/<run-id>/`** and nowhere else, in a per-store subdirectory where the verb takes `--store`. The directory is created by `extract-schema --begin-run`; a pre-existing `<run-id>` directory is a precondition failure (exit `2`), not an overwrite. An extraction is created once and never amended |
| **Its contents** | Three things, fixed: **`schema.<store>.json`** — the schema record of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 1 for that store, every column, index, key and foreign key within that store's declared comparison scope; **`data/`** — the extracted rows, one file per table unit in the dependency order step 5 fixes; and **`manifest.json`** |
| **The manifest** | Carries the `run-id`; the UTC extraction time per store; the source-copy identification (server, database name, and the copy's own provenance, never a credential); the culture, time zone and collation literals of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split), including the **observed** collation of the source database, which that section requires to equal the pinned literal; and, for **every** other file in the directory including each `schema.<store>.json`, its **relative path, byte length and `SHA-256` digest as lowercase hexadecimal**. The manifest is the last file written, so a manifest that exists describes a complete extraction |
| **Verification, before any work** | Every verb that consumes the run **recomputes the `SHA-256` of every file the manifest lists, and compares byte length and digest, before it opens a connection to the target.** A missing file, an extra file in `data/`, a length mismatch or a digest mismatch is a precondition failure: the verb exits **`2`**, names the offending relative path and both digests — the recorded one and the recomputed one — and **does nothing else**. It does not repair, re-extract or continue with a warning. This is the property that makes "the same extraction" checkable rather than assumed |
| **What a load leaves behind** | Its **checkpoint rows** in `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` and its **member rows** in `dbo.__DataMigrationMember`, written transactionally per table unit as the boundary contract below specifies, and the local checkpoint **evidence** file of section [5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read) beside them. The rows are the record of what was committed; the file is a projection of it for readers without a connection, and **is never read to decide anything** |
| **`seed` and `admin` are deliberately outside the handoff** | Neither consumes a run: `seed` writes catalog reference data from `Data/SeedData.cs` behind the three gates of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks), and `admin` creates one account and one role membership. Neither is part of the source-to-target handoff at all (section [5.2](#52-the-seed-is-not-the-data-migration) is the reason), and passing `--run-id` to either is rejected by the closed accepted set of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) |

**The run identifier has one closed grammar, stated here and nowhere else, because every use of it — a
directory name, a JSON string value, a resource-name component, a `case` label in a runbook — is only safe
if the form is exact rather than nearly exact.** The grammar is:

```text
run-id  ::=  stamp "-" nonce
stamp   ::=  [0-9]{8} "T" [0-9]{6} "Z"      -- YYYYMMDD "T" HHMMSS "Z", UTC, separator-free
nonce   ::=  [0-9a-f]{8}                    -- 32 bits from a cryptographic RNG, lowercase hex

anchored form: ^[0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6}Z-[0-9a-f]{8}$        length: exactly 25 characters
```

- **Both halves are load-bearing, and neither is decoration.** The fixed-width UTC stamp makes
  lexicographic order chronological order, which is what a human scanning a report directory or a run
  table needs; the nonce is what makes two runs opened in the same second distinct, which a stamp alone
  does not, at a collision probability of `2^-32` per same-second pair.
- **Two earlier descriptions of this form are deleted rather than tightened, because a value used as a
  path segment cannot be governed by two rules.** This row previously read "a UTC timestamp to the second
  plus a random suffix", and this document's own to-the-second form is `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` — three
  colons. A value carrying `:` is not a directory name on Windows at all: it names an *alternate data
  stream* on the segment before it, so `run/2026-08-27T09:12:44Z-a1b2c3d4/` would not be the directory the
  next row of this table requires it to be, and the manifest verification would look for files under a
  path that was never created. Section
  [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) separately described "a sortable,
  punctuation-free form plus a short random component" — a second rule for one job, admitting values this
  one rejects. Both descriptions are gone; that section now cites this grammar.
- **One grammar, two values, never the same value.** Section
  [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)'s identifier is **caller**-generated and
  identifies a *test run*; this one is **tool**-generated by `extract-schema --begin-run` and identifies a
  *migration run*. They share the grammar because they share the hazards — each becomes a directory name,
  a resource-name component and a JSON string — and they are never interchangeable as values, which is why
  no runbook variable holds both.
- **It is validated before use, in three stages, in this order.** (1) **The grammar**, in the closed
  pre-parse of section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1b — before the host
  is built, before any path is composed from it and before a connection is opened. (2) **The filesystem**:
  the containment test below and the manifest digest re-computation the row above requires, still with no
  connection open. (3) **The database**: the run-row, run-source-row and per-store fingerprint checks of
  section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor), after connecting and before the first write. Stage 1 is
  the one that did not exist: section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)'s "validated rather than
  trusted" is four row-existence checks and **none of them is lexical**, and the row above requires the run
  directory to be read *before* a connection exists — so without stage 1 the value reached the filesystem
  having been checked by nothing at all.
- **The rejection never echoes the value.** Exit `2`, naming the switch, this grammar, and the zero-based
  index and Unicode code point of the first character that fails it. Rule 7 of property 1b names the
  rejected *token*, which is safe for a switch name drawn from a closed set and is not safe here: a value
  that failed this grammar may carry a newline or a control character, and writing it verbatim into the run
  record, a report or a log line is precisely the injection an exact grammar exists to foreclose.
- **Canonical containment, and the one thing the grammar cannot do for itself.** The run directory is
  `Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(reportDir, "run", runId))`, and a verb proceeds only if that string
  starts with `Path.GetFullPath(reportDir)` followed by `Path.DirectorySeparatorChar`, compared
  ordinally; otherwise exit `2`. `<report-dir>` and its `run` child are each additionally rejected, exit
  `2`, if `File.GetAttributes` reports `FileAttributes.ReparsePoint`. The grammar makes the `<run-id>`
  segment provably incapable of escaping; it says nothing about `--report-dir`, which is operator-supplied
  and legitimately absolute, and nothing about a `run` directory a previous release left behind that
  something has since replaced with a junction — containment is a test on a string, and a junction is
  resolved underneath it by the filesystem. The `<run-id>` segment needs no reparse test of its own,
  because a pre-existing `<run-id>` directory is already the precondition failure the next row states.
- **JSON escaping is a no-op by construction, and that is a property rather than a convenience.** Every
  character admitted is in `[0-9A-Za-z-]`: no `"`, no `\`, no character below `U+0020`. The value is still
  written through whatever serializer the writing site uses, and the consequence of the grammar is that it
  cannot malform any of the places it lands — each checkpoint `JSONL` line, the manifest's `run-id`, the
  run descriptor, and the hand-built ownership record of section
  [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety), which is what makes that record's heredoc legitimate rather
  than a latent injection.
- **What the grammar forecloses, provably rather than by policy.** No `/` or `\`, so no separator and no
  traversal segment; no `:`, so no drive-relative or rooted form and no alternate data stream; no leading
  `\\`, so no UNC path; no `.`, so the value is never `.` or `..` and never ends in a dot; no space, so it
  never ends in one; no control character and no non-ASCII character; no shell metacharacter, so it is one
  word unquoted; no `]`, so a bracket-quoted SQL identifier built from it cannot be closed early. It can
  never equal a Windows reserved device name either — every one of those is at most four characters and
  begins with a letter, and this value is 25 characters and begins with a digit.

**The run bookkeeping is four permanent tables, and the reason is atomicity.** "Each table unit's
transaction writes its own progress record" is only true if the record is written **by that transaction**,
and a file cannot be: a process that commits a unit and then dies before writing a file has committed rows
no file describes, and a process that writes the file first and dies before the commit has a file
describing rows that do not exist. Neither state is recoverable by inspection, because a target row count
is equally explainable by a prior load, by a seed or by a partially applied unit. So the record lives **in
the target database, written in the same transaction as the unit it describes**. The four objects are
`dbo.__DataMigrationRun`, `dbo.__DataMigrationRunSource`, `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` and
`dbo.__DataMigrationMember`; section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) defines what each row carries
and which verb writes it, and this subsection states only the four properties that make them an artifact's
bookkeeping rather than a script's scratch space.

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **They are the tool's own objects, and they are permanent** | Created by the tool when absent — not by either context's migration set, because they are the migration workstream's bookkeeping and not part of the application's schema — and **never dropped**: `close-run` deletes *this run's rows* and drops no table, for the reason section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)'s lifecycle sub-section states. They are **not** a migrations-history table, which records applied migrations rather than committed data units |
| **Atomicity holds by construction** | A checkpoint row is inserted **inside its table unit's own transaction**, so the row and the rows it describes commit together or roll back together. A checkpoint that names a unit is a checkpoint whose unit is present, and there is no window in which either exists without the other. This is the property a filesystem receipt cannot have at any ordering |
| **The resume reads them, not the file and not the shape of the target** | A re-run of a load verb reads `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` filtered to `(RunId, --store)` and resumes after the last unit it names. If the recorded durable run id or the per-store source fingerprint disagrees with this invocation's, it exits **`2`** and writes nothing, rather than mixing two runs' rows into one target |
