| **Their scope of visibility is the database** | The tables are in the target database, so their scope **is** the target database: two runs against two databases cannot see each other's progress, and no run can be confused by another's. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s crash cases each acquire their own database under section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s acquisition gate for exactly that reason — shared bookkeeping would make one case's committed units another case's starting state |

**One invocation form, used identically by the tests and by the release pipeline — because two forms
are two artifacts again.** The form is section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)'s canonical literal, and every
site in this document that invokes one of these nine verbs writes it verbatim.

**Two properties of the literal, because a usage line read as a contract is read wrongly in exactly two
ways.** First, it is **the form for the nine verbs other than `admin`**: that verb takes `--username` and
`--role`, which appear nowhere below, so its own canonical form is property 1's
`provision-admin admin --username <name> --role Administrator [--report-dir <dir>] [--rotate-credential]`
and the two forms together cover all ten verbs. Second, **a bracket here means "not accepted by every one
of the nine", never "optional"** — `--store` is mandatory on five of them and rejected on the rest,
`--run-id` is mandatory on seven, and `--model-overrides` is legal on one. **Requiredness per verb is
section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1b rule 2's
switch table and is stated in no other place**, including here; this literal fixes token spelling and
order and nothing more.

```text
dotnet <published-tool>/ProvisionAdmin.dll <verb> [--store catalog|identity|both]
    [--begin-run | --run-id <run-id>] [--batch <n>] [--resume]
    [--model-overrides <file>] [--authorized-by <principal>]
    --report-dir <dir>
```

Four properties of that form are requirements, not conventions:

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **`<published-tool>` is a path the caller produced and captured** | The caller publishes `tools/provision-admin` and holds the resulting output directory path; the invocation names `ProvisionAdmin.dll` inside it. There is no globally installed tool, no `PATH` entry and no shell wrapper, so **the artifact the tests run and the artifact the pipeline runs are the same published output** — which is the whole claim of this subsection. The form is also **cross-platform by construction**: the same command line runs on the Windows agent that captures the baseline and the Linux agent that runs the target half (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)) |
| **`<verb>` is exactly one of the ten**, as a single positional argument | An unrecognised verb exits **`2`** — it could not run — rather than defaulting to anything. There is no default verb: an invocation with none exits `2`. The legality of every remaining token is the per-verb accepted set of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 1b, which is the single place a switch's legality is stated — so no reader has to reconcile a grammar table with prose beside a verb |
| **No connection string and no secret is ever an argument** | Both datasets' connections arrive through **named environment variables scoped to the single invocation**: `MIGRATE_SOURCE_CONNECTION` and `MIGRATE_TARGET_CONNECTION`, channels 2 and 3 of the closed set in section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract). An argument is visible in a process listing and is recorded by shell and pipeline history, which is the same reasoning section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) applies to the administrator password. A connection supplied as an argument is **refused** rather than accepted-and-warned |
| **The report destination is a caller-supplied directory switch**, `--report-dir <dir>` | Absent, the tool exits **`2`** and writes nothing: there is no default location, because a default is how a PII-bearing report ends up somewhere nobody is looking. The caller owns the directory, its access restriction and its retention — for the suite, that is the per-run artifact directory of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) |

**`--model-overrides` is legal on `diff-schema` alone**, per the accepted sets of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — which is what makes section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s "no override can ever influence a write" bound mechanical rather than a
promise. Where it **is** supplied, the report records the file's path and its `SHA-256`, so a `pass`
obtained under an override can never be mistaken for a `pass` obtained without one.

**`dotnet run --project tools/provision-admin -- <verb>` is a developer convenience and nothing more.** It
is stated so that a developer is not left inventing a form, and it is explicitly **not** the form the
tests or the pipeline use: it builds, it resolves the project rather than a published output, and a
build in the middle of a migration invocation is the failure-classification problem section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) keeps out of the runbook.

**Why the reports are machine-readable, stated because it is the property that makes section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s migration rows possible at all.** A human-readable log can only be
asserted against by string matching, which breaks on wording. A structured report — verdict, per-object
differences, per-table counts, per-order totals, per-provider counts — is something a test asserts on by
**field**, which is what every other row in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) does. The report is
also the release record: it is the evidence the acceptance criteria of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9 were met, and it passes the
redactor of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) before it is retained,
because per-order totals and per-account comparisons are computed over PII.

**Two failure classes, distinguished, because the guarantees below would otherwise read as a
contradiction.** A **verification** failure is a check the artifact completed and refused on — the exit
**`5`** class of section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — and it has **written nothing**: every target
table's row count and column values are exactly as they were before the invocation, no migration-history
row was added, no checkpoint row and no member row was written, and **the source is unchanged by the
mechanism section
[5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
names for its stage** — the engine-enforced read-only barrier from **M2** onwards, and the canonical
SHA-256 projection before it. That is stated as a mechanism rather than as "byte-identical", which was an
earlier form's word for a conclusion nothing computed.
That is what makes a failed gate safe to retry. An **interruption** is the artifact ceasing to run
mid-write: a crash, a cancellation, a lost connection, a retry envelope exhausted — the exit **`4`**
class. An interruption **can** leave a partially loaded target, and that is the case idempotence exists
for: the checkpoint rows name the units that committed, and the re-run inserts only what is absent. So
"a failed verb wrote nothing" and "a re-run repairs a partial load" are statements about **different
events**, and the two exit classes are what tell them apart without inspecting anything.

**The table unit is defined here, once, and every other section in this document uses this definition
without variation.** It is the atomic checkpoint-and-provenance unit: the thing that commits, the thing a
checkpoint row names, the thing member rows are attributed to, the thing resume restarts at, and the thing
exit **`4`**'s "last committed table boundary" means. There are **eight units**, fixed, in this order:

| # | Verb | Table unit | Why it is one unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `load-catalog` | `Genres` | One whole table, no dependency inside it |
| 2 | `load-catalog` | `Artists` | One whole table, independent of `Genres` |
| 3 | `load-catalog` | `Albums` | One whole table; depends on units 1 and 2 |
| 4 | `load-catalog` | `Carts` | One whole table; depends on unit 3 |
| 5 | `load-catalog` | `Orders` **and** `OrderDetails` **together** | The one combined catalog unit, for the reason the first consequence below gives: an order separated from its details is a wrong financial figure, not a partial load. Step 5's "then orders, then order details" is the **insert ordering inside this unit**, not two commits |
| 6 | `load-identity` | `AspNetUsers` | One whole table |
| 7 | `load-identity` | `AspNetRoles` | One whole table, independent of unit 6 |
| 8 | `load-identity` | `AspNetUserRoles` **and** `AspNetUserLogins` **together** | The second combined unit: both are child tables of units 6 and 7 with no order between them, and an account whose role assignment committed without its linked logins is a half-migrated principal rather than a resumable prefix |

**`AspNetUserClaims` is deliberately not a unit.** It is not loaded at all: the rule in section
[5.8](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables), which owns that
table's disposition, counts the source rows and **stops if the count is not zero** rather than carrying
or dropping them, so
there is nothing for a transaction to commit and nothing for a checkpoint row to name. A ninth unit for it
would assert a load that does not happen.

**A load verb commits one transaction per table unit, in that order**, which is the dependency order
section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 5 fixes. Each unit's
transaction writes its own **checkpoint row** and its own **member rows** in that same transaction, so
they and the rows they describe commit or roll back together and the bookkeeping can never claim a unit
that is not there. **The local evidence file is appended after the commit**, outside that transaction,
which is why it is a projection rather than the record.

**Two granularities are rejected by name, so no reader has to infer which one this document means.**
**Per batch** is rejected: `--batch` bounds statement size and process memory inside a unit's transaction
and never commits, because a committed batch would make a table half-loaded and would give resume a
boundary that no checkpoint row can describe. **Per order** is rejected for unit 5 and **per account** for
unit 8: they would multiply checkpoint rows by the row count, turn resume into a key scan rather than a
unit lookup, and — for unit 5 — separate an order from the detail rows its `Total` is reconciled against.

Three consequences, and they are what the crash cases of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) assert:

- **An order and its details are never separated.** They share one transaction because
  [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 6 reconciles each order's `Total`
  against the sum of its detail rows: an order committed without its details is not a partial load, it is
  a wrong financial figure that reconciliation would report as a mismatch rather than as an interruption.
- **An interruption leaves whole units, never half a unit.** The committed units are complete, the
  interrupted unit is wholly absent, and the checkpoint rows name the last unit that completed. That is
  the state a re-run reads, and it is why the re-run's repair is a resumption rather than a diff of the
  entire dataset. **The local evidence file may be one unit behind the checkpoint rows** — that is the
  ordinary consequence of appending it after the commit, and it changes nothing, because nothing reads it
  to decide.
- **A single whole-run transaction is deliberately rejected.** It would hold locks across the whole load
  and, more importantly, would make partial progress *unrecoverable* rather than *repairable* — every
  interruption would restart from nothing. Run-level safety does not need it: the rollback position below
  is that the target is discarded, so all-or-nothing at the run level is already guaranteed by a means
  that costs nothing. **The seed is the one deliberate exception** — one transaction across the three
  catalog tables, for the reason section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) gives:
  it is bounded, it is non-production by construction, and a partial catalog is worse than none.

**Rollback is a verb's absence, not a verb.** Section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 9 and section
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) define rollback as: the
source is **at its frozen state**, the legacy application is redeployable, the target database is
discarded. The
artifact's contribution is to **make that position true at every point** — **no verb of this artifact
writes to the source**, the source Identity tables are frozen rather than altered until `reconcile`
returns `0`, and the exit
classes guarantee that a verification failure left no partial state to reverse. So there is deliberately
**no `rollback` verb**: a rollback command implies the artifact could undo a write, and the design's whole
safety argument is that the write it would undo cannot have happened.

**"No verb writes to the source" is scoped to this artifact's verbs, and it is *not* the categorical claim
an earlier form of this paragraph made.** That form said the source is "unmodified" and that nothing
writes to it, full stop — which contradicts section
[5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
directly, because the source receives **two named mutations** before it is frozen, one of them a
`PasswordHash` write. Both statements cannot be true, and a reader who believed the categorical one would
conclude either that the neutralization does not happen or that the rollback position is unsound. The
accurate statement has two halves and both matter:

- **None of this artifact's eight verbs writes to the source.** `extract`, the two `load` verbs,
  `diff-schema`, `reconcile`, `seed`, `admin` and `close-run` open the source **read-only** and issue no
  `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or DDL against it. This is the property row 58 of section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts, and it is why there is no `rollback` verb to undo.
- **The source's only writes are the lifecycle's, and they are performed by named actors outside the verb
  set.** Section
  [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover)
  publishes that lifecycle in full — mutation, freeze, retention, closure — with an actor per stage and
  per source shape. It is the single owner of the source's disposition, and nothing in this section
  restates a stage of it.

**And the tests invoke this artifact.** Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s migration rows drive
`tools/provision-admin` in the same verbs the release drives it, against the disposable database of
section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two, and assert on the
machine-readable verdicts and on the database state afterwards. That is the point of specifying it as an
artifact: the migration the pipeline runs, the migration CI runs and the migration the tests exercise are
**one versioned, source-controlled thing**, so a green suite is evidence about the release rather than
about a rehearsal of it.

**Why no plan-correction record is needed here, stated because an earlier revision filed one.** That
revision proposed a second console project and then recorded the plan's §0.4.1 map as *omitting* it. The
omission was an artifact of the proposal: the map names **exactly one** operator console project, and the
eight verbs above live in it, so there is nothing absent from the map to notify. What the map does need is
the reference direction stated for the one project it carries — `tools/provision-admin` takes a
`ProjectReference` on `src/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj`, because it must compile against the two
contexts, `ApplicationUser`, both migration sets and the composition that registers them, and it is not
included in the web application's publish output. The direction is one-way: **the web application
references no tool**, so nothing a tool contains can reach a deployed request path.
[04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns that map row and states it; this document states only the
constraint the row must satisfy.

### 5.8 Roles, role assignments, claims and external logins — the other four tables

Section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) specifies the user
table. **The user table is not the whole migration**, and the omission that matters most is the role
one: the entire administration surface is reachable only through
`[Authorize(Roles = "Administrator")]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12],
so a role row or an assignment row that does not arrive takes administration with it — and it does so
**silently**, as a 403 rather than an error.

**`AspNetRoles` — four target columns, two source columns.**

| Target column | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| `Id` | Carried from the source, on the same convenience grounds as the user id in section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) |
| `Name` | **Carried exactly. This is an invariant, for the same reason usernames are:** the authorization attribute compares a **string** — `"Administrator"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12] — so a renamed role denies every administrator without failing anywhere |
| `NormalizedName` | Computed by the target's normalizer, **after** the collision check below |
| `ConcurrencyStamp` | Generated fresh per row |

**Role-name collisions stop the migration; they are never merged.** Two role names differing only in
case normalize to one value and violate the unique index — the same mechanism as the username collision
of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration), and the same
resolution: enumerate, compute, **abort and report**. Merging is specifically forbidden here rather than
merely undesirable, because merging two roles grants every member of each the access of the other,
which is a privilege escalation performed by a data-migration script.

**`AspNetUserRoles` — carried row for row.** The pair (`UserId`, `RoleId`) is the whole row in both
schemas, so the mapping is an identity mapping once the two id sets are carried. The reconciliation is
in section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration): counts before
and after, **plus the administrator's membership asserted by name** rather than counted.

**Each assignment this table loads is an audited privilege grant, not a silent row copy.** The migration
emits **one `AUTHZ-3001` per assignment**, which makes it the **second** of that class's two producers
([09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)) — the provisioning command of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) being the first. The outcome
value, the actor rule and the field list are 09's; section
[6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) states the
arithmetic and why no HTTP request produces this class. Without those records the target's audit trail
would begin with every existing administrator's access already granted and nothing recording when or by
what.

**`AspNetUserClaims` — expected empty, and "expected" is verified rather than assumed.** No application
code writes a claim: `git grep -n 'AddClaim' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore'` returns **no matches**. The
migration therefore **counts the source rows and stops if the count is not zero**, reporting them. It
does not carry them silently and it does not drop them silently — a claim row that exists without any
code to create it is an authorization fact placed there by something outside the application, and both
"keep" and "discard" are decisions a person must take.

**`AspNetUserLogins` — the one table whose disposition is a product decision, because of what it
implies about passwords.** The external-login **management** surface is retained while the **challenge**
surface is removed (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), and the source can
genuinely hold rows here: `UserManager.AddLoginAsync` is called at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:252] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:284]. **The rows are migrated
regardless of the removal**, and the rule is three-part:

- **The rows are carried, and the one column with no source value gets a defined origin.** The target's
  login table adds `ProviderDisplayName` to the 1.0 shape; it is **carried as the provider name** where
  a row exists, which is what the removal list renders today
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:11] and what its view component
  renders after the port. `LoginProvider`, `ProviderKey` and `UserId` are carried verbatim, the last of
  them re-linked by the preserved id of section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration). Carrying them is what
  makes the retained management surface's own behaviour preserved rather than merely present: a migrated
  account's registered logins are listed and removable after cutover exactly as before it. **The
  authoritative extraction's row count for this table is reported to the data owner** with the rest of
  the reconciliation record, because it is the number that decides whether the retained surface has
  anything to show.
- **The runtime's grants on this table follow the split exactly: SELECT and DELETE, and no INSERT.**
  SELECT because the component lists rows, DELETE because `Disassociate` removes one, and no INSERT
  because the only code that ever inserted here was the removed challenge surface — so the absence of
  the grant and the absence of the code are the same fact stated twice, which is what makes the negative
  assertion worth making. [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes the grant inventory.
- **The migration still stops before writing anything if any source account has a null or empty
  `PasswordHash`.** Such an account is external-only: it has never had a local password, and **no
  external provider is registered in the target** (section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), exactly as none is registered today, so it would be
  **unable to sign in** until one is. **The challenge surface's removal makes this halt stricter rather
  than looser**: with no provider handshake **and** no set-password branch (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), such an account has no route into the application at
  all and no way to acquire a local password from inside it. That is a user-facing loss, not a migration
  detail, so the migration reports the affected accounts and halts. The available responses — an
  operator-driven password reset, or registering a provider under its own scoped decision — are both
  approval decisions and belong to [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s risk register once the count is
  known. The halt is also what lets every surviving account use the one `Manage` branch that remains:
  there is no migrated account without a local password to change.

**`AspNetRoleClaims` and `AspNetUserTokens` are net-new tables in the target schema.** They have no
source counterpart, are created empty by the Identity migration set, and nothing is loaded into them.
Stated so that a reviewer comparing table lists does not read their emptiness as a lost dataset.

**Acceptance for this section**, as the coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage):
after the load, `RoleManager.RoleExistsAsync("Administrator")` is true, the migrated administrator is in
that role by `UserManager.IsInRoleAsync`, a **non**-administrator is not, and the role and assignment
counts match the source.

---

## 6. Authentication policy is decided, not inherited

Cookie authentication is configured today with **exactly two values** — an authentication type
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16] and a login path [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:17], inside the options object
at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18] — plus the external sign-in cookie [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20]. Nothing else is set anywhere. **The policy is
therefore not absent: it is in force on every request and it is whatever the framework's defaults
happen to be.** [09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md) owns that finding (F-09-02) and assigns this
document the duty of setting each value explicitly.

**The principle: hardening is welcome; hardening that arrives as an unannounced framework default is a
change nobody approved.** The target's defaults are mostly better than the source's. That is not a
licence to leave them implicit — an unstated value cannot be reviewed, cannot be approved, and
silently changes again on the next framework upgrade. **Every row below is set explicitly in
`Program.cs`, and every row is labelled.**

**What the table covers.** The authentication cookie and the Identity policy around it — the rows
naming an unqualified `Cookie.*` property are that cookie's — plus the `Secure` policy of the
**session** and **anti-forgery** cookies, which belong here because they are the same class of
decision, are set in the same composition root, and are asserted together by the deployment checks of
section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order). Those two are the values most easily left
implicit: unlike the authentication cookie, neither has a counterpart setting in the source to prompt a
decision, and both of their framework defaults are `CookieSecurePolicy.None`. This section is the
contract [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and
[11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) cite for all three cookies.

### 6.1 The policy table, every row labelled

Every value below is the value written into `Program.cs`. **No row says "set explicitly" in place of a
value**; where a value is the same as the framework's, it is written out anyway, because an unstated
value cannot be reviewed and changes silently on the next upgrade. Options-object names are given so
each row maps to one assignment.

**This table is the single owner of every value in it.** Section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) fixes each configuration member, its declared type, its
validation and the framework default the value replaces, and cites this table for the value rather than
carrying a second copy of the decision — which is why its tables have a framework-default column and no
value column. No other section of this document *decides* one of these values: where a section quotes a
number in order to make an argument, it is quoting this table and has to agree with it, and where a value
moves this table is the only place it is edited. Where a row's value is **code-set with no configuration
key**, the row says so, and this table is then its only home.

| Policy | Today | Target value | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password minimum length | `UserManager` default; no `PasswordValidator` assigned anywhere in the edition | `IdentityOptions.Password.RequiredLength` = the `PasswordMinimumLength` value of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is **12**. **That table is the only place the number appears**, per its own rule, and this row does not restate it as a second value | **Deliberate hardening** — above every Identity default, source or target |
| Password complexity | `UserManager` defaults | `RequireDigit = true`, `RequireLowercase = true`, `RequireUppercase = true`, `RequireNonAlphanumeric = true` — all four classes required — and `RequiredUniqueChars` = the `PasswordRequiredUniqueChars` value of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is **4**. Same rule: 3.3 carries the numbers, this row carries the label | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Allowed user-name characters | **Letters and digits only.** Identity 1.0 validates user names through `UserValidator<TUser>`, whose `AllowOnlyAlphanumericUserNames` defaults to `true`, and **no `UserValidator` and no `PasswordValidator` is assigned anywhere in the edition** (command in [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility)) — so that default is the effective policy | `User.AllowedUserNameCharacters` = the `UserAllowedUserNameCharacters` value of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is the **67**-character set `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789-._@+` — the 62 alphanumerics **plus** `-`, `.`, `_`, `@` and `+`. **This corrects an earlier form of this row**, which named the 62-character subset and thereby contradicted section 3.3's value: two different strings for one assignment, and the narrower one would have rejected the fixture administrator's own user name `fixture-admin@musicstore.test` (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)) as illegal. **And** the Identity data migration reports any source user name containing a character outside the set before the load (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)) | **Deliberate change — an approved widening.** The target value is the 67-character set in the column beside this one, which is **wider** than the source's effective alphanumeric-only policy in the Today column: `-`, `.`, `_`, `@` and `+` become registerable where today they are refused. That is a change carrying **Security's** approval as `D-18` (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)), and no reading of this row makes it a preservation. **The earlier label is deleted rather than reconciled.** It read "**Preserved** … Widening the set is available as a separate decision with its own owner; this port does not take it", which contradicted four things at once: this row's own target value; section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s single value for the assignment; section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)'s provenance argument, which needs the hyphen to be legal in a user name for the two `Guid` spellings to be a real hazard; and the fixture administrator `fixture-admin@musicstore.test` of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), whose own name the narrower set refuses. **Setting the option explicitly remains mandatory** — by this table's no-unstated-values rule, and because the provisioning command validates `--username` against **this configured set** rather than against the framework default (section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)), so the option and that check move together in one change. **The boundary is covered by existing cases rather than by a new one**: `20g` of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) refuses a name carrying a character outside the set, `20f` submits a name whose every character is inside it, and `75` exercises the command's own pre-store check |
| Account lockout enabled | **No lockout exists** — sign-in is a single `FindAsync` call with no attempt counter, no delay and no lockout [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:60], and the failure path only adds a message and redisplays [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:68] | `Lockout.AllowedForNewUsers = true`, and password verification goes through `SignInManager.CheckPasswordSignInAsync(user, password, lockoutOnFailure: true)` — step 3 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — so failures are actually counted | **Deliberate hardening** — the highest-value row in the table. [09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md) F-09-03 rates it High. The `lockoutOnFailure` argument is part of the row: enabling lockout without it counts nothing |
| Lockout threshold and duration | n/a | `Lockout.MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5`, `Lockout.DefaultLockoutTimeSpan = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15)` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Account confirmation required for sign-in | Identity 1.0 default; **no confirmation flow is implemented** and no email is sent | `SignIn.RequireConfirmedAccount = false`, bound as `Identity:SignInRequireConfirmedAccount` (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)), and `SignIn.RequireConfirmedEmail = false`, which is **code-set with no configuration key** — a second confirmation gate nobody may switch on by editing a setting, since no confirmation flow exists to satisfy it | **Preserved** — deliberately, with the reason recorded: requiring it would lock out every migrated account, since `EmailConfirmed` is `false` for all of them (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)) and many hold no email at all. The one row where the hardening is the wrong call |
| Unique email required | Identity 1.0 default | `User.RequireUniqueEmail = false` | **Preserved.** The source may hold accounts with no email; enforcing uniqueness at migration time would fail the load |
| Authentication cookie name | Katana's default: its `.AspNet.` prefix plus the authentication type at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:16], giving `.AspNet.ApplicationCookie`; no name is set anywhere | `Cookie.Name = "MvcMusicStore.Auth"` | **Deliberate change.** A name distinct from the legacy one means a legacy ticket is never even offered to the new handler, which is what makes the expiry middleware of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) safe |
| Cookie lifetime | `CookieAuthenticationOptions` default, unset [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:14-18] | `ExpireTimeSpan = TimeSpan.FromDays(14)` | **Preserved** — the same fourteen days the unset source option gave, now written down |
| Sliding expiration | Middleware default, unset | `SlidingExpiration = true` | **Preserved**, stated |
| Persistent cookie ("remember me") | The flag is honoured at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:63] with the middleware's own duration | The capability is **preserved**: the checkbox value is passed as `isPersistent` to `SignInManager.SignInAsync(user, isPersistent)` — step 6 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) — and a persistent cookie's lifetime is the same `ExpireTimeSpan` of fourteen days | **Preserved**, with the duration now stated |
| Cookie `Secure` attribute | Katana default `SameAsRequest`, which over plain HTTP means **not secure** ([09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md), [11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)) | `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always` | **Deliberate hardening** |
| Cookie `HttpOnly` | Middleware default (on) | `Cookie.HttpOnly = true` | **Preserved**, stated |
| Cookie `SameSite` | **Not an option in the source middleware at all** | `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax` — preserves top-level navigation to the site while blocking cross-site sub-requests | **Deliberate hardening**. `Strict` is not chosen: it would break inbound links from external pages into authenticated views |
| Login path | `/Account/Login` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:17] | `LoginPath = "/Account/Login"` | **Preserved** |
| Logout path | No such option in the source middleware; sign-out is the `LogOff` POST at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:302] | `LogoutPath = "/Account/LogOff"` | **Preserved** — the same path, now declared to the handler |
| Access-denied path | Not configured — the source redirects to login for both the unauthenticated and the forbidden case | `AccessDeniedPath = "/Home/Error/403"`, the status-code error action of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), **and** the global `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), which writes **403** rather than redirecting — so a forbidden request ends as a **403 in one response with no `Location`**, and the view is rendered by re-executing this same path. Stating both halves matters: the path alone would make 403 a second hop that a client not following redirects never reaches | **Deliberate hardening**, minor: an authenticated non-administrator gets a denial rather than a login form. The path is not a net-new view — it reuses the error action the pipeline already requires |
| Return-URL parameter | Katana default; the login view round-trips it through `ViewBag.ReturnUrl` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:47] | `ReturnUrlParameter = "ReturnUrl"` | **Preserved.** The name is part of the URL surface: changing it would silently drop every return URL |
| Security-stamp validation | **None.** The source sets no cookie `Provider`, so no stamp is revalidated after sign-in and a password change or a role change does not invalidate an issued ticket | `SecurityStampValidatorOptions.ValidationInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)` — the framework wires the validator through `AddIdentity`; this row is its interval | **Deliberate hardening (net-new).** It is also why section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) requires a stamp for every migrated account: a null stamp with validation on signs the user straight back out |
| Session cookie name | No `<sessionState>` element is declared in any edition ([11 §3.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the absence and its command), so the platform default `ASP.NET_SessionId` applies | `SessionOptions.Cookie.Name = "MvcMusicStore.Session"` | **Deliberate change** — a different mechanism with a different name; nothing reads the old name |
| Session idle timeout | Platform default, in force by that same absence | `SessionOptions.IdleTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20)` | **Preserved** — twenty minutes, which is what the undeclared default gives today |
| Session cookie attributes | n/a | `Cookie.HttpOnly = true`, `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always`, `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax`, `Cookie.IsEssential = true` | **Deliberate hardening.** `IsEssential` is the load-bearing one: the cart identity lives in this cookie (section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity)), so a future consent policy must not be able to suppress it |
| Antiforgery cookie attributes | Ten views emit `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` — `git grep -c 'AntiForgeryToken' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views'` lists ten files at one occurrence each — and each emission pairs the field with the `System.Web` anti-forgery **cookie**, whose `secure` attribute in that framework comes from `<httpCookies requireSSL="true"/>`. **No `<httpCookies>` element is declared in any application configuration file** — `git grep -l -i 'httpCookies' -- 'src/**/*.config' 'src/**/*.Config'` returns nothing — so the source cookie is offered over plain HTTP | `AntiforgeryOptions.Cookie.Name = ".MvcMusicStore.Antiforgery"`, `Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always`, `Cookie.HttpOnly = true`, `Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.Strict`, `Cookie.IsEssential = true`, `Cookie.Path = "/"`, and `HeaderName = "RequestVerificationToken"` for the scripted transport of section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form) | **Deliberate hardening**, and **`SecurePolicy` is the row's reason for existing**: the framework's default for *this* cookie is `CookieSecurePolicy.None`, not `Always` — it is the one cookie in this table whose default would leave it marked non-secure while the authentication and session cookies are marked `Always`, so leaving it unstated produces a mixed cookie posture that no review would notice. `SameSite = Strict` is stated rather than inherited and is safe for this cookie specifically: a cross-site top-level navigation that does not carry it simply causes a fresh cookie-and-token pair to be issued with the rendered form, and every request that must *validate* a token is a same-site `POST` from that form. `IsEssential = true` keeps a consent policy from suppressing the cookie and thereby refusing every write in the application. `Path = "/"` is written out because the framework's builder derives the path from the request path base, which is not a value this document leaves implicit |
| External-login surface | Scaffolded and **entirely disabled** — all four provider registrations commented out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35] — plus the external sign-in cookie [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:20] | **Split: the management half is retained, the challenge half is removed**, per section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). Retained: the `RemoveAccountList` rendering as a view component and the `Disassociate` POST, so an account's migrated `AspNetUserLogins` rows can be listed and removed. Removed: the six challenge and link actions, `ChallengeResult` and its `ExecuteResult` override, the `XsrfKey` constant, the provider-tied set-password branch, and four views. **`AuthenticationOptions` gains no provider registration** — the four commented-out ones are not re-created — and `IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme`, registered by `AddIdentity`, has no flow behind it (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)). Section [13](#13-resolution-register--all-23-blockers-of-deliverable-12) records the resolution of `ChallengeResult` | **Management: preserved. Challenge: approved delta `D-11`** (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)). Reachability of an external handshake is unchanged in both directions — none was possible before and none is possible after — so no user-visible capability is lost, while the deployed dead scaffolding that [09 §6.11](09-security-assessment.md) and [08 §9.3](08-technical-debt-register.md) record is **reduced** rather than carried. **Registering a provider remains a separate decision owned by Security**, and is now additive work rather than a switch |
| Data-protection key store | **None declared** — no `machineKey` in any edition, so key identity is a property of the host rather than of the deployment: it cannot be assumed shared across hosts, inventoried, rotated deliberately or isolated per environment ([11 §3.2.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the per-host detail) | `AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>().SetApplicationName(<the required DataProtection:ApplicationName value>)`, with the key table created by the `AddDataProtectionKeys` migration — the decision and its four parts are in section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). **Location, protection at rest, rotation and slot isolation remain [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s** | **Deliberate hardening** |

Two rows deserve a sentence beyond the table. **The confirmation and unique-email rows are the two
places where this document declines a hardening**, and both declines are consequences of the Identity
data migration rather than of taste — which is why they are recorded here with their reason instead of
being quietly omitted. And **the `SameSite` row has no "today" value at all** to be preserved or
hardened relative to, because the source middleware has no such option; it is stated as hardening
because the resulting behaviour is stricter than the absence.

**The labels have an owner, and it is the reason they are labels rather than prose.** Every row marked
**deliberate hardening** or **deliberate change** — **fourteen** of the twenty-five — requires
**Security's** approval before implementation, and the two rows marked *preserved by decision* rather
than by inheritance (confirmation and unique email) require it too, because declining a hardening is as
much a security decision as taking one. The remaining **nine** ordinary **preserved** rows need no
approval: they state, rather than change, today's effective behaviour — `14 + 2 + 9 = 25`. **The split
was `13 + 2 + 10` until the allowed-user-name row's label was corrected**: that row sets a set wider than
today's effective policy, so it moved out of the preserved bucket and into the approval-bearing one —
one row across the boundary, thirteen becoming fourteen and ten becoming nine, with the total of
twenty-five rows unchanged because no row was added or removed. Section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) carries the whole set as `D-10` with the same
owner, so the approver sees one entry rather than twenty-five, and
[09](09-security-assessment.md) — which owns the finding this table answers — is the reviewer of record
for it. **Where a target value differs from the framework default it is marked as such in the row**
rather than left to inference; the **six** rows where that matters most are the two password rows, the two
lockout rows, the security-stamp interval and the antiforgery cookie's `SecurePolicy`, all of which are
stricter than the framework's own default for the same setting and none of which it will produce on its
own.

### 6.2 The sign-out surface

Sign-out today is a POST with anti-forgery validation
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:300-306], posted by a form in the shared login
partial [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:4-14]. **That is preserved
exactly** — a POST, token-validated, from a form. It is called out because MVC 3 ships a `GET`
sign-out ([09 §5.4](09-security-assessment.md)) and a reader comparing editions could conclude the
verb needs changing here. It does not.

One change is mechanical: the link at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:12] invokes
`javascript:document.getElementById('logoutForm').submit()`, which an inline-script Content Security
Policy would block. Since the port adds security response headers where the source has none
([11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)), the trigger becomes an ordinary submit button styled as
a link, and the `javascript:` URL is removed.

**The other change is not cosmetic: sign-out clears the session's cart key.** `LogOff` today signs the
identity out and redirects [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:302-306] and
**touches the session slot not at all**, so the value the sign-in path wrote there — the user's own name
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39] — outlives the ticket. `GetCartId` returns whatever the slot already holds
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] without re-checking who is asking, so every
subsequent **anonymous** request in that session still resolves to the signed-out user's cart and can
read it, add to it and remove from it. On a shared browser that is the next person.

The target's sign-out therefore calls `cartService.ClearSessionCartId()` **before** the redirect, as the
third rule of the isolation set in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model). Two properties
matter and are worth stating so the change is not read as data loss:

- **Nothing is deleted.** The rows keep the user name as their cart id, so the same cart reappears the
  next time that account signs in — which is the source's own behaviour for a signed-in cart
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167].
- **The next anonymous read starts a new anonymous cart.** With the slot empty, the target's anonymous
  branch issues a fresh `anon:`-prefixed key and its protected session marker together, where the source
  issues a bare GUID [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172-175], so the following visitor gets their own empty cart rather than somebody
  else's full one.

It is `D-41` of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), because an anonymous
visitor who used to see the previous user's cart items no longer does, and the coverage assertion requires
exactly that.

### 6.3 Session and cart identity

The cart key lives in session, keyed by a constant
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19], and is reached two different ways: through
`HttpContextBase.Session` inside `GetCartId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180] — read at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:163], written at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167] for a
signed-in user and at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:175] for an anonymous one, read again at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:179] — and through the MVC
`Controller.Session` property [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:39].

**Session in the target is opt-in and in-memory by default.** So two registrations are required
rather than optional: `AddSession` over a **distributed cache**, and `UseSession` in the pipeline
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)). Omitting them does not fail to compile — it
produces a cart that empties itself unpredictably.

**Five specifics**, and the count is the list's own: the lead-in read "three" while the list already
carried **four** bullets — the cache, the registration order, the key constant and the cookie attributes
— and the concurrency rule below is the **fifth**.

- **The cache is SQL-backed, and the registration is named rather than implied.** The call is
  **`AddDistributedSqlServerCache`** (item 6 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)),
  which registers the SQL Server implementation of `IDistributedCache` (*Distributed caching in ASP.NET
  Core*, .NET 8), sharing the one database of section
  [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables). Its **table is provisioned by
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)** — `dbo.SessionCache`, created by
  `dotnet sql-cache create` — and created **first** in the ordering of section
  [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order), because a cache whose table does not exist fails on the
  first session write rather than at start.

  | Option | Value here | Note |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `ConnectionString` | The validated `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` | Read from the validated options type of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), so the cache cannot reach a database the five connection checks never saw |
  | `SchemaName`, `TableName` | **`dbo`**, **`SessionCache`** | Literals. [06 §8.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states that these two are deliberately not configuration-supplied |
  | `ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval` | **Left at its default of 30 minutes** | The minimum the provider accepts is 5 minutes (`SqlServerCacheOptions.ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval`, API reference, .NET 8). Lowering it buys nothing here: it changes only how promptly dead rows are *removed*, not whether a dead entry can be *read* |
  | `DefaultSlidingExpiration` | **Not relied on.** Session's own `IdleTimeout` of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is what governs a session's lifetime, and the session middleware sets each entry's sliding expiration from it | Stated so that two timeouts are not read as one, and so nobody tunes the cache option expecting the session to follow |

  **Expiry is enforced on read and cleaned up opportunistically, and those are two different things.** An
  entry past its expiry is **never returned** — the provider's read path filters on the expiry column, so
  correctness does not depend on the deletion pass having run. The deletion pass itself is triggered **by
  cache operations** rather than by a background timer of its own, and runs at most once per
  `ExpiredItemsDeletionInterval`. Two consequences follow and both are stated because they surface as
  puzzling observations rather than as failures: a replica taking **no** traffic performs no cleanup at
  all, and expired rows are therefore expected to be present in `dbo.SessionCache` between passes. That is
  the normal state of a healthy table, not evidence of a leak — and it is a further reason
  [06 §6.7.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s restore step empties the table outright instead of
  trying to age its contents.

- **The order is written down because the dependency is invisible at the call site.** `AddSession`'s store
  resolves `IDistributedCache`, so the cache must be the one registered — and **when a service type is
  registered more than once, resolving a single instance yields the last registration** (*Dependency
  injection in .NET*, .NET 8). So the rule is absolute rather than stylistic: **`AddDistributedSqlServerCache`
  is the only `IDistributedCache` registration in the composition**, and neither
  `AddDistributedMemoryCache` nor any other cache registration appears anywhere — not in a Development
  branch, and not in the test fixture, whose substitution rule (section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)) overrides configuration rather than
  re-registering services precisely so that this cannot happen. A memory-backed cache would pass every
  single-replica test and lose carts the moment a second replica existed, which is the failure this
  ordering makes unavailable. The coverage assertion of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) resolves
  `IDistributedCache` and asserts the implementation type, then round-trips a session value through a
  second host sharing the same table.
- **The session key constant is preserved** and both access paths converge on one: the service of
  section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) owns cart-id
  resolution, and `AccountController` stops writing session directly — it calls the service, which is
  also what makes the cross-store sequence of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)
  expressible in one place.
- **Session cookie attributes are set explicitly** rather than inherited, and their values are the
  session-cookie-attributes row of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). The reason
  `IsEssential` is one of them belongs here: the cookie carries the cart identity, so a consent gate that
  suppressed it would empty carts rather than degrade a feature.
- **Concurrent writes to one session are whole-blob and last-commit-wins, so the policy is that no
  session entry may be load-bearing — not that two writes to two keys are somehow isolated.** `ISession`
  reads the **entire** entry for a session, mutates it in memory, and `CommitAsync` writes the **entire**
  entry back; the store behind it is `IDistributedCache`, which exposes **no conditional and no
  compare-and-swap write**; and the session middleware takes **no lock** over the row. Two requests in
  one session that set two *different* keys therefore do not merge — the later commit replaces the
  earlier one wholesale — so **a distinct key isolates the value and never the write**. That is why the
  `Session` row of section
  [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint) no longer
  claims its separate key keeps a verification run and a cart out of each other's way, and why "written
  by one method, so the two entries cannot drift apart" (section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) is a statement about the **pair travelling in one
  commit**, not a statement that the pair cannot be lost.

  **The requests are not serialized, and the two mechanisms that would serialize them are rejected here
  rather than left unmentioned.** A browser legitimately issues a page load and the cart's `POST` at the
  same time and neither may wait on the other. A compare-and-swap over the session row cannot be
  expressed against `IDistributedCache` and would mean a bespoke store; taking the application lock of
  section
  [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof)
  per request would put a global serialization point and a database round trip in front of every page.
  Both are disproportionate for state whose worst case is one empty anonymous cart, and recording the
  rejection is what stops a later reader treating the absence as an oversight.

  **What makes it acceptable is the bound on what session is allowed to hold. These are all of the
  entries this application writes, each with the authority behind it and the cost of losing it:**

  | Entry | Written by | What a lost write costs |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | The preserved cart-key slot [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:19] holding an **anonymous** `anon:`-prefixed key | The cart service, when it issues a key for a caller who has none (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) | The `Cart` rows already written under the lost key are **stranded, not deleted**, and the next request issues a fresh key, so the visitor sees an empty anonymous cart. It is exactly the outcome an `IdleTimeout` expiry already produces for an anonymous cart, which this design accepts; no order and no signed-in cart is reachable from it |
  | The same slot holding a **user name** | Step 5 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), `AssignSessionCartId(user.UserName)` | **Nothing durable, because the value is re-derivable rather than stored-only**: resolution writes the authenticated caller's own name into an empty slot on the next request, and the rows keep that name as their cart id (section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)) |
  | The protected provenance marker bound to the key and the session | The same service call that issues the key, cleared by `ClearSessionCartId()` with it | Nothing, and the direction is **fail-closed**: the marker rides in the same commit as the key, so a lost update loses the pair together and never leaves a key whose marker is missing — and if one ever were, step 4's provenance test fails and the merge is skipped |
  | `CartHandoffSourceId` | The handoff path, cleared only after the merge's own verification passes (section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)) | The session-side pointer to an unverified merge. **Recovery does not depend on it**: fix (b) of requirement 4 of section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) enumerates the alias rows for an authenticated principal from the `(DestinationCartId, CreatedUtc)` index with no session entry at all |
  | `healthz-instance` | The diagnostic route of section [2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint), which is off by default and administrator-gated | The next verification request reports `sessionCreated: true` and a new value — a re-run, not a wrong answer. Losing it at all requires two simultaneous requests inside one operator's session, which the verification does not issue |

  **`TempData` is deliberately absent from that list**: the notice mechanism uses the **cookie-backed**
  provider (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)), so a notice neither occupies the
  session blob nor can be lost by a concurrent session commit.

[11 §3.1](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the statefulness assessment, including the precise
point that instance affinity permits multiple instances **today** while foreclosing *resilient*
scale-out. This document's contribution is the mechanism: distributed session plus the persisted key
ring of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), after which affinity is no longer
load-bearing.

---

### 6.4 The account surface — authorization map, redirect safety and error paths

`AccountController` is the one file with no line-for-line successor (section
[9](#9-a-namespace-substitution-table-is-not-a-transformation-plan)), so three things it currently gets
right or nearly right have to be **re-established deliberately** rather than assumed to survive a
rewrite: who may reach each action, where a return URL may point, and what the user is told when
something fails.

**The authorization map, action by action.** The source protects the whole controller and opens
individual actions: `[Authorize]` on the class
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:15] with eight `[AllowAnonymous]` attributes
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:44], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:54], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:78], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:87], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:198], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:208], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:263], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:310]. **The class-level `[Authorize]` is
preserved, so the target remains deny-by-default**, and **four of the eight opt-outs survive** — the two
`Login` and the two `Register`. The other four are attributes on the four external-login **challenge**
actions, which section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) removes, so they disappear with
the actions rather than being dropped from actions that remain. Two actions leave the routable surface
without becoming anonymous, and the table states why:

| Source action | Source attributes | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Login` GET [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:45] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:44] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`** |
| `Login` POST [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:56] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:54], `[HttpPost]`, `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:55] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`.** The token attribute is redundant under the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) and is dropped rather than duplicated |
| `Register` GET [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:79] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:78] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`** |
| `Register` POST [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:89] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:87], `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:88] | **Kept, `[AllowAnonymous]`**, token from the global filter |
| `Manage` GET [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:131] and POST [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:148] | Class-level `[Authorize]` only | **Kept, authorized**, and the POST keeps **one** branch: change-password [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:153-166]. The set-password branch [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:168-189] is **removed with the external-login challenge surface** (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), approved delta `D-11`), because an account with no local password is reachable only through a provider and none is registered. The `ModelState["OldPassword"]` error-clearing that branch performs [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:170-175] goes with it, and the load-time halt of section [5.8](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables) is what guarantees every migrated account has a local password for the surviving branch to change |
| `LogOff` POST [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:302] | Class-level `[Authorize]` | **Kept, authorized**, and it stays a POST (section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface)) |
| `ExternalLogin` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:200], `ExternalLoginCallback` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:209], `ExternalLoginConfirmation` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:265], `ExternalLoginFailure` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:311] | `[AllowAnonymous]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:198], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:208], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:263], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:310] | **Removed**, with the external-login challenge surface of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types). All four routes answer **404**, authenticated or not, and their `[AllowAnonymous]` attributes are not written anywhere in the target — the anonymous surface narrows to the four `Login` and `Register` actions, which is the strongest form this row can take |
| `Disassociate` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:114] | Class-level `[Authorize]` | **Kept, authorized.** It is the retained management half's only action, and its verb and token posture are stated in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| `LinkLogin` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:237], `LinkLoginCallback` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:245] | Class-level `[Authorize]` | **Removed**, with the challenge surface. The source's XSRF binding — `ChallengeResult`'s `XsrfKey` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:336] threaded into `GetExternalLoginInfoAsync(XsrfKey, User.Identity.GetUserId())` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:247] — is what made this pair the most delicate rows in the port: authorization on them means only "some authenticated caller", and the binding is what made it mean "**this** caller". Removing them removes both the pair and the obligation to reproduce that binding correctly in code no request could reach |
| `RemoveAccountList` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:317] | Class-level `[Authorize]`, plus `[ChildActionOnly]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:316] | **Kept as rendering, removed as a route.** It becomes `RemoveAccountListViewComponent` (section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components)), and a view component is not routable at all, so it carries no authorization attribute of its own and cannot be reached by URL; its protection is the authorized `Manage` view that invokes it. `/Account/RemoveAccountList` therefore must not resolve, and coverage row 97 asserts that it does not |

**The rule that makes this checkable rather than a list to trust: the target controller carries
`[Authorize]` at the class and `[AllowAnonymous]` on exactly four actions — the two `Login` and the two
`Register`.** Anything else anonymous is a defect; so is any route resolving to `RemoveAccountList`, which
is a view component rather than an action; and so is any route resolving to one of the six removed
challenge actions. **Coverage row 97** asserts all four properties of that rule — the four anonymous
actions reachable without authentication, every other account action challenging, the six removed
challenge routes answering 404 whether the caller is authenticated or not, and `/Account/RemoveAccountList`
answering 404 — by probing every account route the source declared, authenticated and unauthenticated.
An earlier form of this paragraph cited **row 51** for the same assertion; row 51 is remember-me
persistence and asserts nothing about the authorization map, so the citation is corrected rather than
softened: a rule whose only evidence is a row about something else has no evidence at all.

**Input bounds — every account input carries a schema-aligned maximum, and rejection happens before any
Identity call and before any database round trip.**

The source's account models are bounded inconsistently, and the gap is on the unauthenticated surface.
`LoginViewModel.UserName` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:33-35] and
`RegisterViewModel.UserName` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:48-50] carry `[Required]` and **no length constraint of any kind**;
`RegisterViewModel.Password` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:52-53] is bounded at 100 characters while `LoginViewModel.Password`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:37-40] and `ManageUserViewModel.OldPassword` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:14-17] are **unbounded**. So a syntactically valid
username of arbitrary length binds, passes validation, and travels all the way to
`UserManager.CreateAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:94] and the store
insert behind it — where the only thing that stops it is the column. In the target that surfaces as a raw
`DbUpdateException` from an insert, **on a path an anonymous caller can reach at will** (CWE-20), which
means a 500, a stack trace in the log per attempt, and a provider message that has no business being
anywhere near a response. The same input is also what step 2a of section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) hands to a key-derivation function, whose cost scales with
the candidate's length. Kestrel's request-size limit is not a substitute: a megabyte-long username is
comfortably inside it.

**The maxima, with the column each one matches.** They are added to the adapted
`Models/AccountViewModels.cs` (section [9.2](#92-the-four-groups), Group D) as ordinary `[StringLength]`
annotations, so a violation is a **field validation message on a redisplayed form** — the same outcome as
any other invalid model — and never an error page.

| Member | Maximum | What it is aligned to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UserName` on the login model and on the registration model | **256** | `AspNetUsers.UserName` and `AspNetUsers.NormalizedUserName`, which ASP.NET Core Identity's own model configuration declares as `nvarchar(256)`. Both sides of the surface carry the same bound: a longer value cannot match a stored row on the login path and cannot be stored on the registration path, so accepting it buys nothing |
| `Password` and `ConfirmPassword` on the registration model, and `NewPassword`/`ConfirmPassword` on the change-password model | **100** | **Preserved** from the source's own annotations [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:52-53] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:19-20]. The minimum is not set here — length policy is the `RequiredLength` row of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) |
| `Password` on the login model, and `OldPassword` on the change-password model | **100** | The **consistency fix**: the source leaves both unbounded [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:37-40], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:14-17]. Bounding a *verification* input at the *creation* maximum is safe here because every password that can exist was created either through the registration form, bounded at 100 [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/AccountViewModels.cs:52-53], or by the operator command of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties), which applies the same credential policy (the coverage assertion) — the shipped seeded credential [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:17] is 27 characters. No reachable account can hold a password this bound would refuse |

**Two properties this has to have, and both follow from where the check runs.** DataAnnotations
validation completes during model binding, before the action body runs, so an overlength submission is
refused by the `ModelState` gate — step 1 of section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) on the login path, and its counterpart on the registration
path — **before `FindByNameAsync`, before step 2a's key derivation, before `CreateAsync`, and before any
query or insert**. And the redisplayed form encodes what it echoes, as Razor does by default, so the
submitted value cannot be reflected as markup. **And nothing about the attempt is logged raw**, on either
path. A rejected **registration** is the `ACCT-2001` event of
[09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) at its `ValidationFailed` outcome, which permits a
`ValidationFailureCategory` code and explicitly not the submitted values. A rejected **login** never
reaches a credential check, so it is **not** an `AUTH-1002` event at all — that event's outcome values
cover resolved, unresolved and locked-out credential attempts and none of them describes a request that
failed binding — and it is recorded, if at all, as an ordinary request-level diagnostic under
[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) carrying no submitted value. In neither case is a store or
provider exception recorded, because neither path reaches one. **Section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 20 case `20f` requires all four parts in one case** — no write,
bounded work, encoded output, no raw record — because the four are only meaningful together: a case
asserting the field message alone would pass an implementation that queried the store first.

**And the change is recorded rather than slipped in.** Today an overlength username passes validation and
fails at the store; in the target it is refused with a field message on a redisplayed form. Nobody is
worse off, but the outcome of a request an anonymous caller can issue is **observably different**, and a
difference of that kind is an approved delta in this document or it is nothing. It is carried by
**`D-10`** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), whose subject is precisely
the account policy this document sets explicitly instead of inheriting, and whose owner is **Security** —
the same constituency that owns the maxima themselves.

**Abuse limits — because lockout bounds one account and nothing else.** The lockout policy of section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is real hardening over a source that has neither lockout
nor throttling ([09 §3.3](09-security-assessment.md)), and it is **per account**: it constrains attempts
against a *named* account and says nothing about attempts against names that do not exist. That gap is
wider in the target than in the source, and the reason is this document's own doing:

- **Every attempt now costs a full key derivation, by design.** Step 2a of section
  [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) spends the target cost on an unknown username precisely so
  that the response time discloses nothing. A caller cycling fabricated user names therefore buys the
  most expensive operation the application performs, at one request each, and no lockout counter is even
  incremented — there is no account to increment. Uniform cost is the right decision and it makes an
  explicit request limit a **precondition** rather than an extra.
- **Every attempt also writes a record.** The `AUTH-1002`/`AccountNotFound` record is emitted at
  `Warning` ([09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)), so the same cycle is a log-volume amplifier: it
  costs the attacker one request and costs the platform an ingested, retained, alert-evaluated record.
- **Neither cost is bounded by anything else in this document.** Request-size limits bound one request's
  bytes, the model maxima above bound one request's fields, and the anti-forgery policy of section
  [7.1](#71-the-policy) bounds cross-site submission — none of the three bounds *how many* requests one
  caller may make.

The response is the rate-limiting composition of **stage 1 item 14 and stage 2 item 11** in section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order): a per-partition limiter on the three credential endpoints, an
aggregate limiter over the same endpoints that a distributed flood cannot evade by spreading, and a
general limiter for everything else — **all three chained into one global limiter**, because two named
endpoint policies cannot both apply to one action and the per-source and aggregate credential bounds must
both apply to all three. Three properties belong here rather than there, because they are about behaviour
rather than composition:

- **A refused request is refused *before* the work.** The limiter runs at stage 2 item 11, ahead of the
  endpoint, so a rejected attempt performs **no** `FindByNameAsync`, **no** key derivation and **no**
  credential check — and consequently emits **no** `AUTH-1002` record of any outcome, because no
  credential attempt happened. It emits the single `Information` record stage 1 item 14 specifies. That is the
  amplification closed in both directions at once.
- **Refusal is not lockout, and cannot be used as one.** The partition for an anonymous caller is their
  own client address, never the submitted user name, so nothing an anonymous caller does can ration or
  lock an account belonging to somebody else. A signed-in caller is partitioned by their Identity
  `UserId`, so they are not rationed by whoever shares their egress address either.
- **The residual trade is stated and owned.** Many customers behind one address share an anonymous
  partition, so a large shared-egress population could see 429s on the sign-in form under genuine load.
  It is bounded deliberately: the limits are configuration, not constants; the window is fixed with no
  queue, so `Retry-After` is an accurate, short, self-service wait rather than an opaque failure; and the
  aggregate limiter's ceiling is set high enough that it never engages on real traffic. **429 on these
  endpoints is `D-48`** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), owned by
  **Security and product** — Security because it is a control, Product because a refused sign-in is a
  user-visible outcome the source never produces. **The coverage assertions require both halves of the
  chain.** They require the aggregate bound against a flood arranged so that no per-source bound can fire
  first, and the per-source bound from a single address partition — the two together are what prove the
  chain composes rather than one limiter masking the other.

**Redirect safety — a preserved control that must not be lost in the rewrite.** The source is already
careful: `RedirectToLocal` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:382-392] tests `Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:384] and falls back to the
home page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:390]. The target preserves the control and states it per site, because an open redirect
(CWE-601) is exactly the kind of protection a wholesale rewrite drops without noticing:

- **`Login` POST** tests the value itself and falls back:
  `if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(returnUrl) && Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl)) { return Redirect(returnUrl); }`
  followed by `return RedirectToAction("Index", "Home");`. **A non-local, empty or missing return URL
  therefore ends at the home page with a `302`, which is exactly what the source does** — `Url.IsLocalUrl`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:384] with the home-page fallback [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:390].
- **`LocalRedirect(returnUrl)` is rejected for this site, and the reason is not stylistic.**
  `LocalRedirect` **throws** on a non-local URL. The throw is not caught in the handler, so it reaches the
  exception-handling middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and the
  response to an attacker-supplied return URL is a **500 with a logged server fault** — a behaviour
  change from the source's `302` to Home, a self-inflicted error-rate signal on a public unauthenticated
  path, and a test hazard: "does not redirect off-site" is satisfied by a 500, so a suite asserting only
  that would pass an implementation that turns a hostile link into an unhandled exception. The explicit
