  test plus fallback keeps the source's behaviour and leaves nothing for a `catch` to interpret.
- **`Login` GET** validates the incoming `returnUrl` with the same `Url.IsLocalUrl` test **before putting
  it in the model**, and drops it — rendering the form with no return URL — when it fails. The POST
  validates again, so this is belt-and-braces — but an unvalidated value rendered into the form is an
  attacker-controlled link on a page the user trusts, which is worth preventing on the way in as well as
  on the way out.
- **The cookie handler's own round-trip** uses `ReturnUrlParameter` and `LoginPath` from section
  [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) and is validated by the framework.
- **No other target action takes a return URL at all**, and that is a narrowing this port performs
  rather than a gap. The source's three other return-URL surfaces are `ExternalLogin`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:200], `ExternalLoginCallback` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:209] and
  `ExternalLoginConfirmation` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:265], all three **removed** with the external-login challenge surface
  (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). That deletes the hardest of the four cases:
  the callback's return URL survived a round trip through `AuthenticationProperties` and came back from
  **outside** the application, which is the one place an unvalidated value would be most tempting to
  trust. `LinkLogin` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:237] and `LinkLoginCallback` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:245] took no return URL and are removed as well.
  The **retained** `Disassociate` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:114] takes none either — it redirects to `Manage` unconditionally,
  with or without a message [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:126], which is preserved. So the whole return-URL surface of the target is
  the two `Login` actions plus the cookie handler's own round trip, and any third is a defect.

**Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 72** is where that is asserted, and it is named rather than
alluded to. Case **`72b`** posts a **scheme-absolute external return URL** and requires the exact outcome
— `302` with `Location` **exactly `/`**, which is a statement a 500 fails — rather than the weaker "does
not redirect off-site". The row carries seven more shapes for the same reason the bullet above rejects
`LocalRedirect`: `72c` protocol-relative, `72e` a literal backslash pair, `72f` the same pair
percent-encoded, `72g` and `72h` the two mixed slash orders, all asserting `Location` exactly `/`, and
`72a` and `72d` the local and absent values.

**Error paths, one per flow, with the disclosure rule stated.**

| Flow | Failure | Target behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Login` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay with the field errors. Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:58], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:73] |
| `Login` POST | Unknown user, wrong password, or `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` returning not-succeeded for any reason **including lockout** | **One generic message — `"Invalid username or password."`, the source's own wording [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:68] — for every one of those cases**, with the same status, the same view and the same model state. Preserved deliberately: a distinct "account locked" or "no such user" message is friendlier and **discloses whether an account exists**. Two things make the uniformity real rather than nominal. **(a) The unknown-user case reaches this branch through step 2a of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)**, and the locked-out and legacy-hash cases through step 3's top-up — the fixed-work service specified there — so all four populations cost what the most expensive real verification costs and the *response time* discloses nothing either. A bare early return would leave an enumeration oracle behind an identical page, and so would a single dummy derivation, because this store holds two hash formats at once and a lockout derives nothing. **(b) The distinction goes to the log and nowhere else**, as the `AUTH-1002` event of [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) at one of its three outcome values — **`AccountNotFound`, `InvalidCredentials` or `AccountLockedOut`, emitted at `Warning`**, named here exactly as that catalog names them because a paraphrase is not an identifier and an implementation cannot be checked against one. Its actor rule — the Identity `UserId` where the account resolves and the bounded literal plus keyed pseudonym where it does not — severity and permitted field list are **09's and are not restated here**. The submitted username is never written, per [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) |
| `Login` POST | Cart migration failed after retries | Sign-in **succeeds** with a non-blocking notice (section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)) |
| `Register` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay with field errors. Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:91] |
| `Register` POST | `CreateAsync` returns a failed `IdentityResult` — a duplicate username, or a password failing the policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) | **Each `IdentityError` is added to `ModelState` and rendered in the validation summary**, which is what `AddErrors` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:356-362] does today and is preserved. Identity's own duplicate-username error text is user-facing here, and that is accepted: a registration form must say the name is taken, and it discloses nothing the form does not already reveal by refusing the name |
| `Manage` POST | Invalid `ModelState` | Redisplay. Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:155] |
| `Manage` POST | `ChangePasswordAsync` returns a failed `IdentityResult` — wrong current password, or a new password failing the policy | Errors mapped into `ModelState` as above, form redisplayed, **nothing changed**. Preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:157-165] |
| `Manage` POST | Success | `RedirectToAction("Manage", new { Message = ManageMessageId.ChangePasswordSuccess })`, rendering *"Your password has been changed."* — preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:160] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:134] |
| `Manage` GET | Status-message surface | **Three of the four `ManageMessageId` members are kept** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:374-380] — `ChangePasswordSuccess`, `RemoveLoginSuccess` and `Error` — with their exact source wording [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:134], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:136], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:137]. `SetPasswordSuccess` and its message arm [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:135] are **removed with the set-password branch** (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), approved delta `D-11`); an enum member no code can produce is not a preserved message but an unreachable one. `RemoveLoginSuccess` is retained precisely because the **management** half is, and `Disassociate` still produces it. **`ViewBag.HasLocalPassword` is removed at both of its sites** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:139], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:151]: the view renders the change-password partial unconditionally, and what makes that safe is not an assumption but the halt in section [5.8](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables), which refuses the load if any migrated account has no local password. **The `HasPassword()` helper [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:364] is a different matter and is not removed as a predicate** — it has a **third** call site, `RemoveAccountList`'s `ShowRemoveButton` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:320], which the retained management surface keeps — so two of its three call sites go and the predicate itself is re-expressed as `UserManager.HasPasswordAsync(user)` inside the view component of section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components), where it is the surviving consumer |

**The account surface's event emission, stated with the catalog's own vocabulary — because two of these
classes are one call apart and an implementation that emits only the obvious one loses the signal that
matters.** [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns the identifiers, actors, outcomes, severities and
field lists; what this document owns is **where in the flow each one is emitted**, and that is the part
no catalog can supply.

| Event | Emitted where | The precision that matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH-1001`, `Success` | Immediately after step 6 of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) issues the cookie | After, not before: an event recording a sign-in that then failed to issue a cookie is a false record of an authenticated session |
| `AUTH-1002`, `AccountNotFound` | The step 2a branch — a null result from `FindByNameAsync`, **after** the fixed-cost derivation has been spent | Actor is the literal **`anonymous`** — one of the exactly two actor values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits, the other being the Identity `UserId` — plus a `SubjectPseudonym` **built under [06 §8.4.7](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s key and label grammar, which that section solely owns**, never the submitted name and never a pseudonym in the actor position. Emitting before the derivation would move the record earlier in the request for this population only, which is a timing signal in the log stream even when the response is uniform |
| `AUTH-1002`, `InvalidCredentials` | Step 3 returning not-succeeded with `IsLockedOut` false | |
| `AUTH-1002`, `AccountLockedOut` | Step 3 returning `IsLockedOut` true | This records **an attempt against a locked account**, which is a different fact from the account becoming locked |
| `AUTH-1003`, `LockedOut` | **Additionally**, on the one attempt that *causes* the lockout | This is the class an implementation drops. `CheckPasswordSignInAsync(..., lockoutOnFailure: true)` returns `IsLockedOut` **both** when the account was already locked and when this very failure crossed the threshold, so the two are indistinguishable from the result alone. **The emission point is therefore not the controller at all**: the transition happens inside Identity's own `AccessFailedAsync`, which increments the failure count and sets `LockoutEnd` in one call, and a before-and-after read either side of step 3 is **not atomic** — two failures arriving together can each observe "not locked before, locked after" and emit two records for one transition, or both observe "already locked" and emit none. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is an override of the virtual `UserManager<ApplicationUser>.AccessFailedAsync` that captures the state, calls `base`, and emits only where the returned `IdentityResult` succeeded *and* the account was unlocked before and locked after. That document owns the artifact, its registration and its at-least-once delivery semantics — the override narrows the window but does not close it, so the contract is **at least one** physical record per transition, each carrying the state-derived de-duplication key `{UserId}\|{LockoutEndUtc:o}` and collapsing to exactly one **logical** event at the reader, and **exactly-once physical delivery is not claimed anywhere**. What belongs here is that the record accompanies the same attempt's `AUTH-1002`/`AccountLockedOut`, that its cardinality is the one the coverage assertion requires, and that **no controller-side reading of lockout state is part of this flow**. Emitting only `AUTH-1002` loses the moment a threshold was crossed, which is the one event a brute-force alert is built on; emitting `AUTH-1003` on every subsequent attempt inflates it into noise and makes the alert useless in the other direction |
| `AUTH-1004`, `Success` | The sign-out action of section [6.2](#62-the-sign-out-surface), after the cookie is expired | |
| `ACCT-2001` at `Success`, `DuplicateUserName` and `ValidationFailed` | R2 of the registration sequence, at each `IdentityResult` branch, and at the `ModelState` gate for a bound-length rejection | The two failure outcomes carry the `anonymous` actor and `none` target sentinels [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) names, because no account exists to identify |
| `ACCT-2002`, `ACCT-2003` | The change-password action's success and its two failure branches | `ACCT-2002` also carries `RehashedOnSignIn` where the write was step 3's migration rehash rather than a user action — and **that case has a different emission point**, because the rehash happens *inside* `CheckPasswordSignInAsync` and the caller sees only a sign-in result. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is **two artifacts, not one**, and that distinction is load-bearing. The first is a decorating `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` — `RehashObservingPasswordHasher` — recording the framework's rehash verdict into a **scoped, per-request signal**, scoped rather than static precisely so two concurrent sign-ins cannot see each other's. That artifact **observes and never emits**, because `PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded` is *advice returned before persistence is attempted*, and `CheckPasswordAsync` then performs the update and **discards its `IdentityResult`** — so a store write that fails leaves the signal set, and a hasher-driven emission would assert a rehash that never persisted. The second artifact is the emitter: the `AuditingUserManager` subclass overriding the protected virtual `UpdateUserAsync(ApplicationUser)`, emitting `ACCT-2002` at `Success` with `RehashedOnSignIn = true` **only** where the returned `IdentityResult.Succeeded` is true, **and** the scoped signal is set, **and** the request is not a user-initiated credential change. Where the update fails, **no `ACCT-2002` is written at all** and a distinct `credential-rehash` diagnostic goes to the ordinary channel instead — deliberately not a seventeenth event class. Where the signal is not set, no `ACCT-2002` is emitted, because a sign-in is not a password change. **Row 19 case `19c` forces the failed update** — it is the case that drives a migrated account's rehash with `UPDATE` on the Identity account table revoked, so the signal is set and the store write fails, and it asserts that no `ACCT-2002` is written; **row 104 case `104c`** asserts the other side, a user-initiated change emitting `ACCT-2002` with `RehashedOnSignIn` absent or false |

**A negative test per flow, and each one is a named case rather than an appeal to "the coverage
assertions".** The rows are section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s.

| The negative test | The case that is it | What makes it that test and not a weaker one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A bad-credentials login**, asserting the generic message, that an unknown user name is indistinguishable from a wrong password, and that the right class and outcome reached the log for each | **Row 18 case `18c`** | One case and two requests, deliberately: the indistinguishability is a statement *about the pair*, so it cannot be asserted by two cases that never compare their responses. `18c` requires the summary text byte-equal across both, **exactly one key derivation on each** — the decidable form of step 2a's fixed-cost rule — and `AUTH-1002` at `InvalidCredentials` and at `AccountNotFound` respectively. Wall-clock timing is explicitly **not** asserted, and `18c` says so: a timing distribution measured inside the test host is not a decidable oracle |
| **A registration whose password fails the policy**, asserting the error is rendered and no account is created | **Rows 48 and 49** | Row 48 takes the length bound from both sides — `48a` one below, `48b` at it — and row 49 omits **one complexity class at a time** across `49a`-`49d` with `49e` satisfying all four. Both assert the account count is identical on every refusal, so "the error is rendered" cannot pass on an implementation that renders a message and writes the row anyway |
| **A registration refused for a reason that is not the password**, so `ACCT-2001`'s other two outcomes are covered | **Row 20 cases `20e`, `20f` and `20g`** | `20e` a user name already held, at `DuplicateUserName`; `20f` a user name one character past its maximum, at `ValidationFailed`, additionally asserting all four parts of the bound-length rule stated earlier in this section — no write, bounded work, encoded output, no raw record; `20g` a character outside the allowed set, at `ValidationFailed`, from Identity's validator rather than from a DataAnnotations bound |
| **A change-password with the wrong current password**, asserting the stored hash is unchanged | **Row 104 case `104a`** | The hash is captured through the read-only observer immediately before the request and required **byte-identical** afterwards, with `SecurityStamp` unchanged. `104b` does the same for a new password that fails the policy, and `104c` is the success that proves the refusals are not vacuous — the hash differs, the stamp rotates, and the new password authenticates while the old one does not |
| **A lockout**, so `AUTH-1002`'s third outcome and `AUTH-1003` are covered | **Row 50, with row 71 for the release** | Named here because the generic message hides it: a locked account and a wrong password produce the *same* response, so the classes are the only thing that distinguishes them, and `50b` is the attempt that *causes* the lockout while `50c` is an attempt against an already-locked one |

**The two input contracts of this section are established by their own cases too**, and neither of them by
the rows an earlier form of this paragraph named — **an earlier revision claimed "Rows 65 and 66 cover the
two input contracts above", which is false**: row 65 is the fixture administrator's survival of the
Identity migration and row 66 is the cart write path's absent album, and neither touches an account input
model. The maxima of the table earlier in this section are asserted by **row 20 `20f`**, at the one boundary that
distinguishes a bound that exists from one that does not, and the allowed user-name character set of
section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) is asserted by **row 20 `20g`**.

### 6.5 The remaining event classes — where each is emitted, and the producer arithmetic

[09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) defines **sixteen** event classes and
[09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) assigns each one a producer. **Thirteen are produced by the
ported web application and three are not**, and both halves of that arithmetic have consequences this
document has to carry: section [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)'s
table places only **seven** of the thirteen — the four `AUTH-` classes and the three `ACCT-` classes, all
of them on the account surface — and the remaining six sit in sections that specify a *contract* rather
than an event. An emission requirement that no section states is an emission requirement that ships
missing, and it ships missing invisibly, because a contract with no record still returns the right status
code.

| Event | Emitted where | The precision that matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTHZ-3003`, `Denied` | **Inside pipeline item 12** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) — `UseAuthorization()` — and nowhere else | **The one class with no site in application code.** A denial is decided by the authorization middleware and **never reaches the action**, so no controller body and no action filter observes it, and the `[Authorize]` attributes of sections [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths) and [8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) have nothing to hook. [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s seam is a custom `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` that **holds the framework's own handler and always delegates to it, on every path**. That delegation is the whole safety property: a handler that emits its record and then produces the response itself has silently redefined every denial's status, its redirect to the login path and its access-denied behaviour, while intending only to add a log line |
| `ADMIN-4001` at `Success` and `ValidationFailed` | The **create contract** of section [8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target) — at step 5's redirect, and at both refusals: step 1's `ModelState` redisplay and step 2's foreign-key redisplay | The target on `ValidationFailed` is 09's `none` sentinel, not an `AlbumId`: nothing was inserted, so no key was allocated to name. A posted `AlbumId` is **not** a target either — it was never bound (`D-23`) |
| `ADMIN-4002` at `Success`, `NotFound` and `ValidationFailed` | The **edit contract** of the same section — step 5's redirect; step 3's `NotFound`; and **three** refusals under `ValidationFailed`: step 1's `ModelState` redisplay, step 2's foreign-key redisplay, and **step 0's route/body id mismatch** | Step 0 is the branch an implementation forgets, because it answers `400` before the action has loaded anything — and an unlogged `400` is indistinguishable from a client that never called. The record names **which properties changed and never their values** ([09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) row 12), which is load-bearing here rather than generic: one of the five is `Price` |
| `ADMIN-4003` at `Success` and `AbsentRow` | The `DeleteConfirmed` action — **census site F5** in section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census): `Success` once the removal is saved, and `AbsentRow` on the null branch. **The second outcome is named `AbsentRow` and not `NotFound`**, because the response is a preserved **500** rather than a 404 — an outcome word borrowed from a status the site does not return would make the record contradict the response beside it | **Per outcome, and the split is deliberate.** `Success` is emitted at **`Warning`**, not `Information`, per [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s security-event catalog — deletion is the one administration operation with no undo, and that severity is not this document's to soften. `AbsentRow` is emitted at **`Error`**, one level above, because it is the *only* record accompanying a **500** response: section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census)'s standing rule is that a 500 carries a record at `Error`, and a record at `Warning` would leave a served 500 invisible to every error-severity alert. **The ownership split is the resolution, and it is settled rather than held open.** The *behaviour* is this document's — the preserved 500, the single record, and the severity pair above — and the *vocabulary* is [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s, whose domain for this record id is `Success` and `AbsentRow`, at `Warning` and `Error` respectively. **`NotFound` is a retired spelling for this record id**, recorded as retired so that a citation of it resolves instead of reading as a live alternative; it stays live elsewhere in that catalog, including `ADMIN-4002` in the row above, where it names a genuine 404 — so the retirement is scoped to this id and not to the word. An earlier form of this cell framed the same facts as a **deviation** from 09 and asked the reader to hold the two documents apart "until that edit lands"; that framing is **deleted** rather than qualified, because it reads as two live vocabularies for one record id, and a coverage row cannot be written against a vocabulary still being decided — row 41 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is written against these values. The `AbsentRow` record is what section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) F5 means by preserving the status while adding the diagnosis |
| `ORDER-5001`, `Success` | Section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) **step 9**, after the step 3 wrapper's commit has returned and `AcceptAllChanges()` has run — the commit is the execution strategy's, not step 8's | After the commit, never before it, for the same reason `AUTH-1001` follows the cookie: an order event emitted inside the transaction records a placement that a rollback then unmakes, and the record cannot be withdrawn |
| `ORDER-5002` at `ValidationFailed`, `EmptyCart` and `PersistenceFailed` | The same section's refusals and its failure table — `ValidationFailed` for step 0's submission-token rejection, step 1's `ModelState` redisplay and step 2's promo-code no-match; `EmptyCart` for step 4; `PersistenceFailed` for every classifier row that redisplays or renders the generic error page | **Two rows of that table deliberately emit nothing.** `Cancelled` is a client disconnect rather than a failed placement, and `DuplicateSubmission` is a reconciled replay that redirects to an order which already exists and was already recorded at `ORDER-5001`. Both already write their own diagnostic record, and counting either as a failed placement puts a false failure in front of whoever reads this class. The record carries a failure **category**, never the provider text — the same rule as section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s sanitized record, because this is the request whose body is a name, an address, a telephone number and an email address |

**The three the ported application cannot produce — and why a gate demanding sixteen from it fails.**

- **`PROV-6001`** — the provisioning command, **four records per invocation, invariantly**, section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4: one per
  `State.operation` literal — the three operations — and then the run record, on every path, including
  the paths that fail and the rejection that happens before a host exists. **An earlier form of this
  bullet read "one record per operation", and it is deleted rather than reconciled**: that is the
  cardinality of the operation records alone, it leaves the run record uncounted, and a consumer written
  against it would expect three lines where four always arrive. **Verified at that command** by section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 75, which drives the three operation outcomes a completing
  invocation can produce — `created`, `already-present` and `rotated` — case by case, and by rows **O5 to
  O9** of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes), which assert the four-record envelope
  itself — its cardinality, its nested `State.eventName`, its operation sequence and its shared
  invocation identifier — on all four paths, and so cover the two outcomes no completing invocation
  produces, `failed` and `not-attempted`.
- **`AUTHZ-3001`** — **two producers.** The command's membership operation, at `Success` and only where
  the membership was actually added; and the Identity data migration of section
  [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor), one record per
  role assignment it loads — at `Success` for an assignment it creates and at `AlreadyHeld` for one the
  target already held, which is the outcome value 09 reserves for that producer. **Verified at both**:
  row **75 `75c`** is the membership operation that actually adds, and row **65 `65a` and `65b`** are the
  migration's own — the fixture administrator's role assignment and the reconciliation report that
  accounts for it.
- **`AUTHZ-3002`** — **no producer among this document's artifacts, and that is stated rather than
  papered over.** Nothing in the ported web application withdraws a role, and neither does
  `tools/provision-admin`: section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)'s verb table is closed at
  **ten verbs** with no revoke among them, that section's property 3 states as its **unconditional** first
  boundary that the command never deletes or demotes any account, role or role membership, and its `admin`
  verb accepts exactly four switches — none of which withdraws anything, `--rotate-credential` included,
  since it replaces a password and touches neither role nor membership. So this plan builds nothing
  that can emit the class. **An earlier revision of this bullet read "that command's revoke mode only,
  property 3a"**, citing a property §10.2 does not define and a mode no verb provides; that citation is
  withdrawn here, and the same withdrawal is recorded at its other site in section
  [4.16](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once).

**The arithmetic, restated so that the sixteen still add up.** Thirteen are produced by the ported web
application, **two** — `PROV-6001` and `AUTHZ-3001` — by this document's non-web artifacts, and **one**,
`AUTHZ-3002`, by nothing this plan builds. 13 + 2 + 1 = 16.

**What that costs a release gate, and who owns closing it.** A gate demanding all sixteen classes from
the application's HTTP surface is failed by a correct implementation, because no request grants or revokes
a membership. A gate demanding fifteen across the application **and** the operator tool passes. A gate
demanding sixteen anywhere in this plan's artifacts **cannot** pass, and that is a real gap rather than a
formality — though it is no longer a *disagreement* between two documents, which is what an earlier form of
this paragraph described when it offered 09 and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) a choice between
reclassifying the class and scheduling a revoke capability.
[09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md) has taken the first: its row for `AUTHZ-3002` carries **no
producer and no interception point**, its first-exists column reads **"Nowhere yet"** where every other
class names a workstream, and it withdraws by name both the revoke-mode attribution and the "property 3a"
citation that attribution rested on — the same withdrawal the bullet above records from this side. What
survives the withdrawal is the finding underneath it, which that section states and this document does not
soften: an operator who must remove someone's administrative access has no audited way to do it, so the gap
is **open**, its owner is **security engineering**, and **no workstream carries it**, because a workstream
needs a specified artifact and there is none. This document specifies none, because doing so would break
two decisions already taken here — the **four-record envelope cardinality** of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4, which is a constant
precisely so a consumer can count records without branching, and the **closed four-switch grammar** of
the `admin` verb. Both are this document's to reopen and neither is reopened by a gate: reopening them
takes the decision that closes the gap, which belongs to the owner named above and arrives as an approved
capability rather than as a demand that sixteen classes be produced.

**The thirteen the application does produce are asserted class by class, at the surface that produces
each.** The mapping is exhaustive, and it is a mapping rather than a promise so that a reader can check
it: `AUTH-1001` row 18 `18a`; `AUTH-1002` at all three outcomes — `InvalidCredentials` and
`AccountNotFound` both in row 18 `18c`, `AccountLockedOut` in row 50 `50c`; `AUTH-1003` row 50 `50b`,
with row 71 for the release; `AUTH-1004` row 20 `20b`; `ACCT-2001` at all three outcomes — `Success` row
20 `20a`, `DuplicateUserName` row 20 `20e`, `ValidationFailed` rows 20 `20f`, 20 `20g`, 48 and 49;
`ACCT-2002` row 104 `104c` for a user-initiated change and row 19 `19c` for the rehash seam's negative
half; `ACCT-2003` row 104 `104a` and `104b`; `AUTHZ-3003` rows 15 `15b`, 32 `32a`, 33 `33a`, 34 `34a` and
97 `97b`; `ADMIN-4001` row 16 `16a` and rows 69 and 92 `92a`; `ADMIN-4002` row 16 `16c`, row 17 `17b` and
rows 90 and 91; `ADMIN-4003` row 16 `16e` and row 41; `ORDER-5001` row 10; `ORDER-5002` rows 11, 12, 31
and 67. **Thirteen classes, every outcome value 09 defines for each, and no class left to an unrooted
appeal to coverage.**

## 7. Anti-forgery — three separate problems

### 7.1 The policy

**Global automatic validation.** `AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` is registered as a global
filter, so **every MVC action reached by a request whose method is not `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` or
`TRACE` is validated by default** — those four are the exact set the attribute exempts, and it "works
identically to the `ValidateAntiForgeryToken` attribute, except that it doesn't require tokens for
requests" using them (*Prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF/CSRF) attacks in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8),
which is why the application's `GET` endpoints appear on no list below. **"Every MVC action" is the exact
scope rather than a hedge**: a global MVC filter does not run for an endpoint that is no action at all, so
the **three** non-action endpoints in this application are accounted for separately below — three rather
than four since the withdrawal that paragraph records. Opt-outs are
explicit, individually justified and reviewable. This is the slot vacated by
`FilterConfig.RegisterGlobalFilters` (section
[2.2](#22-the-five-application_start-registrations-do-not-share-one-fate)).

Opt-in-per-action is rejected for a reason visible in the repository: the source uses opt-in, and it
covers **one controller of the four that need it**. A policy whose failure mode is "someone forgot an
attribute" has already failed here once.

**The opt-out list has exactly one endpoint, it is published here, and it is closed.** "Explicit and
individually justified" is a list or it is nothing, so the list is the contract: one endpoint, with the
property that justifies it, and a second requires editing this table.

| Endpoint | Metadata that opts it out | Why the global filter cannot govern it | Why exempting it is safe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /Home/Error` — and the same action under every verb | `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]` on the action | Stage 3 of the pipeline re-executes a failed request **preserving its method** (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so a missing page requested by `POST` re-enters as a **tokenless `POST`**. Validated, it would answer 400 where the caller asked a question whose answer is 404 | It is **rendering-only and changes no state** — the contract in section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) makes that a requirement of the endpoint rather than an observation about it. A CSRF attack on an endpoint that writes nothing achieves nothing |
| `POST /csp-report` — the CSP violation collector of [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) | **`.DisableAntiforgery()` on the route-handler endpoint**, as registered in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 13. **An earlier form of this cell named `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]` on an action, and it is deleted rather than kept alongside**: the collector is a `MapPost` handler — [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s host-mechanism row fixes that and assigns the registration to section 2.4 — so an action attribute here would decorate nothing, and the audit below would look for it on a surface the application does not have | **Two reasons, and the first is the mechanism rather than the caller.** The global filter is an **MVC** filter: it governs actions, so it does not reach a route-handler endpoint at all. The exemption is declared with the metadata modifier **anyway**, because an exemption that exists only as a consequence of where an endpoint was registered cannot be found by anyone auditing the opt-outs — which is what makes this list a contract instead of an inventory of coincidences. The second reason is the caller: it is **the browser's reporting machinery, not a page of this application**, posting with no anti-forgery token and no form, ignoring the response entirely, and arriving possibly with no session at all. Validated — as it would be if it were ever moved onto an action — **every violation report would be rejected with a 400** and the report-only phase would collect nothing while appearing to work | It **writes nothing to the application database** and returns `204` with no body ([06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), so there is no state for a forged request to change. Its abuse surface is bounded by checks that are all 06's and are not restated here: the media types, the size and batch bounds and the rate bound are [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, the field, cardinality and origin rules [06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s |

**The two exemptions live on two different hosting shapes, and that is the fact the audit below is built
around.** `/Home/Error` is an **MVC action**; `/csp-report` is a **route-handler endpoint**
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 13, on
[06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s host-mechanism decision). **An earlier form of this
paragraph claimed both were declared as actions and argued the choice**, on the ground that a route
handler is exempt "by construction rather than by declaration" and is therefore indistinguishable from an
endpoint someone forgot to protect. **The claim is deleted, and the concern it was reaching for is met a
different way**: the collector *is* a route handler, its exemption *is* declared — `.DisableAntiforgery()`
is written on the registration, not inferred from it — and the enumeration below reads **both** surfaces,
so an endpoint nobody protected is still visible. What the earlier argument got wrong was not the risk but
the remedy: it proposed moving the endpoint onto a controller to suit a one-surface audit, when the audit
is the cheaper of the two to widen.

**Both exemptions are declared, and each is declared in the form its own hosting shape understands, which
is why this list is auditable rather than aspirational.** On the action, `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]`
overrides the global filter for the action it decorates (*Prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF/CSRF)
attacks in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8); the mechanism is a **filter**, since
`IgnoreAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` implements `IFilterMetadata`, `IOrderedFilter` and
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ViewFeatures.IAntiforgeryPolicy` (API reference, ASP.NET Core 8), and the
attribute declared on the action is the more specific of the two policies in play. On the route handler,
`.DisableAntiforgery()` attaches **endpoint metadata** —
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery.IAntiforgeryMetadata` with `RequiresValidation` set to `false` (API
reference, ASP.NET Core 8) — and there is no filter involved at all, because there is no filter pipeline
on that endpoint.

**So the enumeration reads two surfaces, and reading only one of them is the near-miss worth naming: it
would report the wrong fact about a correctly configured application, in either direction.**
`IgnoreAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` does **not** implement `IAntiforgeryMetadata`, so an audit that looks
only for that interface finds the collector and **misses `/Home/Error` entirely**; and an audit that
enumerates only filter descriptors finds `/Home/Error` and **misses the collector**. Either audit reports
one exemption where there are two, and a reviewer reading a green result learns nothing about the surface
it did not visit. The assertion therefore has two halves and a total:

- **The action surface.** `IActionDescriptorCollectionProvider.ActionDescriptors` returns every action and
  each descriptor's `FilterDescriptors` is "the set of filters associated with this action" (API
  reference, ASP.NET Core 8), so the test enumerates them and asserts that **exactly one** action —
  `Home/Error` — carries the attribute.
- **The endpoint surface.** The host's `EndpointDataSource` yields every endpoint, and
  `Endpoint.Metadata.GetMetadata<IAntiforgeryMetadata>()` is where the modifier's metadata lands, so the
  test asserts that **exactly one** endpoint — `POST /csp-report` — carries metadata whose
  `RequiresValidation` is `false`. It does **not** read `ActionDescriptor.EndpointMetadata`, which the
  same reference marks as "meant for infrastructure and should not be used by application code".
- **The total is two, and it is asserted as a total** rather than as two independent counts, so a third
  exemption cannot be added quietly on either surface: adding one means a declaration *and* a row in this
  table, and the enumeration fails on the declaration alone.

**Where that assertion is carried, stated precisely because an earlier form of this paragraph cited a row
that asserts something else.** It is a **host-resolved registration assertion** — the same kind as case
`52b` of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage), which resolves options objects from the host's own
service provider rather than issuing a request — and it is **this section's own requirement on the
suite**, carried **outside** the numbered parity rows. That placement is deliberate and it is section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 13's reasoning applied to a second case: a
numbered row would move section 12.4's declared totals, which other documents consume, and the property
being asserted is one of the composition rather than of a request-and-response pair. **The earlier form
read "coverage row 38 of section 12.4 is that assertion"; that citation is deleted, not repaired**, because
row 38 asserts cross-cart record confidentiality and has nothing to do with anti-forgery opt-outs — and a
closed list whose auditability rests on a mis-cited row is a list with the same hole this table exists to
close.

**No other endpoint opts out**, including the health endpoints of section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) — they are `GET`, which
the global filter does not validate in the first place, so they need no exemption and are not on this
list. The pipeline exemption **two of** those two paths *do* carry is a different mechanism about a
different middleware (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), stage 2 item 6), and conflating the two
is how an anti-forgery hole gets justified by a transport decision.

**The emission/validation asymmetry is why the filter is required and not merely tidy.**
`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` appears **10** times across MVC 5's views
(`git grep -o -E '@Html\.AntiForgeryToken\(\)' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml' | wc -l` → `10`). In the target,
**emission becomes automatic** — form tag helpers emit the field without a helper call, so all ten
calls simply disappear. **Validation does not become automatic.** Removing the ten emission calls while
assuming validation came along is the exact shape of a silent regression: every form still carries a
token and nothing checks it.

Adopting the global policy exposes three problems a namespace-level port would miss. Each gets a named
resolution.

### 7.2 Problem one — coverage today is partial

There are **13** POST actions in the migration source and **8** of them validate.

| Controller | POST actions | Validated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AccountController` | 8 — attributes at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:53], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:86], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:112], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:146], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:197], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:235], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:262], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:300] | **8** — `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:55], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:88], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:113], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:147], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:199], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:236], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:264], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:301] |
| `StoreManagerController` | **3** — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:53] Create, [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:86] Edit, [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116] `DeleteConfirmed` | **0** |
| `ShoppingCartController` | 1 — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:54] `RemoveFromCart` | **0** |
| `CheckoutController` | 1 — [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:25] `AddressAndPayment` | **0** |

**Five state-changing POST actions are unprotected**: three administration writes, cart removal, and
the checkout write — the one that creates an order.

**A census trap, stated because getting it wrong understates the work.** `grep -c '\[HttpPost\]'`
against `StoreManagerController.cs` returns **2**, not 3, because its third POST is declared
`[HttpPost, ActionName("Delete")]` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:116]
— a combined attribute list the literal pattern misses.
**The real count is 3.** The correct census matches on the attribute *prefix*, and it must also
tolerate the UTF-8 byte-order mark that all 27 source files carry (section
[9.1](#91-the-census-and-how-to-count-it)). The reproducing commands for both the naive and the correct
form are in [Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility).

**Resolution: the global filter covers all five, plus every future non-`GET` endpoint, with no
per-action attribute.** Adopting it needs no code change at four of the five sites — only at the
fifth, which is the AJAX post of section [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form).
The eight existing `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` attributes are removed as redundant, which is safe
**only because** the global filter is registered; the two changes are one change and must not be split
across commits.

### 7.3 Problem two — one state-changing action is a `GET`, which no policy can cover

`AddToCart` is declared with **no verb attribute**
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:33] and it **mutates**: it loads the
album [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:37-38], resolves the cart [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:41], adds the item [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:43], calls `SaveChanges` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:45] and redirects
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:48]. The comment above it even documents it as `GET: /ShoppingCart/AddToCart/5` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:31].

**No anti-forgery policy can protect a state-changing `GET`**, because a `GET` is issued by any image
tag, link or prefetch without a token and without the user's intent. This is not a coverage gap to
close with a filter; it is a verb that is wrong. [09 §6.1](09-security-assessment.md) owns it as a
finding across all three editions.

**Resolution: convert it to a token-protected `POST`.**

- The action gains an explicit `[HttpPost]`, and the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy)
  validates it with no further attribute.
- **Its call site changes from a link to a posting form**, and the exact markup is published below rather
  than described: `@Html.ActionLink("Add to cart", "AddToCart", "ShoppingCart", new { id = Model.AlbumId }, "")`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:28-29] and the `<p class="btn btn-default">` that
  wraps it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:26] are replaced **together** by one form.
- **The response behaviour is preserved**: a redirect to the cart index
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:48], so the post-redirect-get
  pattern the page already follows is unchanged.

**The exact target markup, published once here because the route and the token both depend on it.** The
form replaces the paragraph and the link together — the paragraph is a styled wrapper rather than a
control, which is why replacing it adds a real control rather than restyling one (section
[8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump)) — and it is the whole of the change at
this call site:

```html
<form asp-controller="ShoppingCart" asp-action="AddToCart" asp-route-id="@Model.AlbumId" method="post">
    <button type="submit" class="btn btn-secondary">Add to cart</button>
</form>
```

Four properties of that markup are load-bearing, and each is what one assertion of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 4 reads:

- **`asp-route-id` and not a hidden `id` field**, so the identifier travels in the **path**. The
  conventional route registered in stage 2 item 13 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) ends in
  `{id?}`, so the value is consumed by that segment and the generated `action` is exactly
  `/ShoppingCart/AddToCart/{AlbumId}` — no query string and no request body. That is the string row 4
  `4a` asserts the rendered `action` equals, and it is why the **path** half of approved delta `D-01` is
  literally unchanged while the verb half is not. A hidden field would also bind, because the parameter
  is a simple type, but it would generate `action="/ShoppingCart/AddToCart"` and make the assertion — and
  the delta's "the path is unchanged" claim — false.
- **`asp-controller` and `asp-action` rather than `asp-page` or a bare `action` attribute**, so the
  `action` attribute is produced by **routing** rather than written as a literal, and the one route pattern
  registered in stage 2 item 13 is what decides the shape of the emitted URL. The same reason the view
  components of section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) name their controller and action
  explicitly.
  **What that does *not* buy is compile-time validation of the names, and an earlier form of this bullet
  claimed it did.** It read that "a renamed action breaks the build's link generation"; both attribute
  values are **strings resolved at request time** by `IUrlHelper` link generation, so a controller or
  action name that no longer exists is not a build error of any kind — it produces a **bad or empty
  `action` attribute** on a page that still renders and still returns 200, and the form then posts to the
  wrong path or to the current one. **The guard is therefore a test rather than the compiler**: row 4 `4a`
  of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts the rendered `action` **equals the exact string**
  `/ShoppingCart/AddToCart/{AlbumId}`, which is the assertion a renamed action fails and the only place
  that rename is caught before a user meets it.
- **`method="post"` is written out**, even though it is the form tag helper's behaviour for a form with
  route attributes, because it is what makes the token emission automatic: the tag helper emits the
  hidden `__RequestVerificationToken` field for any method other than `get`, and this is the one call
  site whose entire purpose is that the verb changed. Row 4 `4a` asserts **exactly one**
  `input[name=__RequestVerificationToken]` with a non-empty value **within that form element**, scoped
  there rather than over the document for the reason section
  [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form) gives — the layout emits a second field of
  the same name on every signed-in page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:4-6],
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:28], so a document-wide count is not a property of
  this form. `4c` asserts its removal yields
  **400** from the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy). **No `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` call is
  added**: a second emission would render two fields and fail `4a`'s exactly-one assertion.
- **A `button` element of `type="submit"`, carrying the class mapping and nothing else.** It is a real
  control rather than a link, which is what makes the surface keyboard-operable and focusable without any
  script; `btn-secondary` is the `btn-default` successor section
  [8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump) maps and **approved delta `D-34`** owns,
  so the fill and label colour change here is that delta's and is not a second one. The label text is
  `Add to cart`, byte-for-byte the source link's text
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:28-29], so nothing user-visible changes but the
  chrome `D-34` already carries.

**This is a deliberate, approval-owned interface delta. The path is unchanged; the verb is not.** Any
external bookmark, link or automation targeting `/ShoppingCart/AddToCart/5` **stops working** — it
will render the cart page or a 405 rather than adding an item. There is no way to have both: a
bookmarkable URL that adds to a cart *is* the vulnerability. It is listed among the approved deltas of
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) with **Security** as its approval owner, and
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires the new verb to be tested and the old one to be
asserted **not** to mutate.

### 7.4 Problem three — cart removal posts without a form

The cart page removes an item with
`$.post(PostToUrl, { "id": recordToDelete }, ...)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17]. The trigger is a plain anchor carrying
`data-id` and `data-url` attributes [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:74-75], read at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:12-13]. **There is no surrounding form.**

So the global policy of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) would **reject every cart removal**: no form
means no tag helper, no tag helper means no emitted token, and no token means a rejected POST. This is
the one site where adopting the policy requires client-side work, and it is the reason the policy has
to be adopted deliberately rather than switched on.

**The transport is form-urlencoded, not JSON.** No `contentType` and no `JSON.stringify` is specified,
so jQuery serializes the object as a form body — jQuery's default. That matters because it means a
hidden form field **would** work; the transport does not force the answer, so the answer is a choice
and is recorded as one.

**The selected contract is the `RequestVerificationToken` request header.**

- **Server side, one call:** `builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(...)` — stage 1 item 10 of section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), which carries the full option set. Of it, `HeaderName =
  "RequestVerificationToken"` is what this sub-section needs: the string is **stated once, in code**,
  rather than assumed. **This document asserts nothing about what the framework's default for that
  property is, and depends on nothing about it**: what the contract requires is that the server's literal
  and the client's literal are the **same one** and that both are written down, which an explicit
  assignment guarantees whatever any default happens to be. **The same call configures the
  antiforgery cookie**, and that is not incidental to this transport: the header carries the *token*, the
  cookie carries its other half, and a `HeaderName`-only configuration leaves that cookie on
  `CookieSecurePolicy.None` while every other cookie in the application is `Always` — so the scripted
  removal path would be the one surface transmitting a non-secure cookie. The values are the antiforgery
  row of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled).
- **Emission, named API:** **`@Html.AntiForgeryToken()`**, called once in
  `Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml` **outside any form**. The helper exists in the target and does two
  things independent of any form: it issues the antiforgery **cookie** on the response and renders
  `<input name="__RequestVerificationToken" type="hidden" value="…">` into the document. That default
  field name is `AntiforgeryOptions.FormFieldName` and is **not** overridden. The field is never posted
  as a field — it is a carrier the script reads.
- **The selector the script reads, exactly:**
  `document.querySelector('#cart-antiforgery input[name="__RequestVerificationToken"]').value`,
  evaluated **at post time** rather than captured at page load, so a token re-rendered by any other
  interaction on the page is still the one sent.
- **Why the selector is scoped to that carrier, and why an unscoped one is wrong.** The cart page is not
  the only emitter of that field name on its own document. The layout renders the sign-out form
  `Html.BeginForm("LogOff", "Account", FormMethod.Post, new { id = "logoutForm", … })` with
  `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` inside it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:4-6],
  in the navbar, rendered by `@Html.Partial("_LoginPartial")` at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:28] — five lines **above** `@RenderBody()` at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:33] — so on every **signed-in** cart page there
  are **two** matching inputs and the layout's is first in document order. A document-wide
  `input[name="__RequestVerificationToken"]` therefore resolves to the sign-out form's token, not the
  cart page's, on exactly the state where a customer actually removes items. Two consequences, and the
  second is why this is a contract problem rather than a tidiness one. Functionally the request would
  still validate, because both tokens are issued against the same antiforgery cookie by the same
  service — so the defect is silent. But **the assertion loses its power**: a port that dropped the cart
  page's `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()` call altogether would still find a token, still post successfully,
  and still pass an unscoped check, so the emission point this sub-section exists to establish would be
  unproven. Scoping the selector to `#cart-antiforgery` makes the match unique on both states and makes
  finding it proof that the cart page's own emission survived. **The scoped selector is asserted in both
  states**, signed out and signed in — section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row **28** cases `28a` and
  `28b` — because the single-token state is the one that hides this defect.
- **How an external script file obtains it.** The removal script moves out of the view and into
  `wwwroot/js/shopping-cart.js`, because the security response headers of section
  [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 2 make an inline `<script>` block a policy
  violation. Being external changes nothing about token access: the file is loaded by a `<script src>`
  in the same document, so the same `querySelector` above reaches the same hidden input. **No token is
  baked into the script file, and no token endpoint is added** — a script served with a token in it
  would be cacheable with one user's token in it.
- **The request, both halves matching:**
  `$.ajax({ url: postToUrl, method: 'POST', data: { id: recordToDelete }, headers: { 'RequestVerificationToken': token } })`.
  The `headers` key is the same literal as `AntiforgeryOptions.HeaderName`; a mismatch between the two
  is a 400 on every removal and is exactly why both sides are written out here. The body stays
  form-urlencoded `id=…`, preserving the source's transport [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17].
- **Why this composes correctly with a form-urlencoded body.** The token store reads the **header
  first** when `HeaderName` is set and falls back to the form field only when the header is absent, so a
  body that carries `id` and no `__RequestVerificationToken` field validates on the header alone. No
  ordering assumption or duplicate emission is required.
- **Why the header rather than a body field:** it keeps the token out of the request body, so it
  applies uniformly to **any** future scripted endpoint regardless of that endpoint's content type. A
  body field only works for form-urlencoded and multipart bodies, and would have to be reinvented the
  first time an endpoint posts JSON.

**Three tests, not one — rows 5, 6 and 7 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage).** **Row 5**: a token
**freshly rendered by the cart page and sent in the header** removes the item and returns the expected
payload — the case that proves the emission point, the selector and the two header names all agree.
**Row 6**: the identical request with the header **omitted entirely** is rejected and the caller's rows
are **unchanged**. **Row 7**: the identical request with **one character of the header token value
altered** is rejected the same way. The last two assert on the data as well as on the status code — a
rejection that had already mutated would pass a status-only assertion, which is why row 7 states its
database expectation as row 6's rather than as a bare 400. **Row 73** gives the checkout write's
form-field token the same three-way treatment, so both token transports are proved by the same shape of
evidence.

The response side of this same endpoint has its own, independent problem; it is section
[8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy).

---

### 7.5 The second opt-out, mapped — the report collector's application half

**Section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s opt-out list is closed at two endpoints, and only one of them was
specified anywhere in this document.** `POST /Home/Error` is section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s. `POST /csp-report` has a registration, its three
modifiers and its position in the pipeline — section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2
item 13 — and a named rate-limit policy with its limits, stage 1 item 14 of the same section. **What it
does not yet have is the code that registration points at: no handler body, no request model, no parser,
no sink and no policy type.** An endpoint whose registration names a delegate nothing defines is a hole of
the same kind as an unregistered one, so this section closes it.

**An earlier form of this paragraph said the endpoint "had a filter attribute, a justification and a
coverage row — and no action, no request model, no parser, no limiter registration and no position in the
pipeline". Every clause of that is now wrong and it is deleted rather than trimmed.** The opt-out is a
metadata modifier and not a filter attribute (section [7.1](#71-the-policy)); the registration, the
limiter and the pipeline position all exist in section 2.4; and the coverage row it claimed **does not
exist** — the endpoint's tests are [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s numbered set, placed
in this document's suite by section 2.4 stage 2 item 13 and counted there rather than as a parity row of
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage).

**The division of labour is unchanged, and it has three parts rather than two.**
[06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns what the endpoint must *be*: the route and verb, the
**host mechanism** — a route-handler endpoint and explicitly not a controller action — the two accepted
content types, the payload and batch bounds, the response statuses, the parser settings and the record.
[06 §10.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the phase and what it measures: the two report
shapes' field naming, the per-field allow-lists, re-serialization, length and character bounds, the hourly
caps, the origin check, the promotion criteria and the daily review. Section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) owns the **registration and the pipeline position**. None of
that is restated here. What this section owns is what is left: **where the code sits, what shape the
handler takes, and the order in which it evaluates 06's gates**.
The endpoint is **permanent**, not part of the report-only phase: that subsection retires the report-only
*disposition* on day 14 and keeps the endpoint, its caps and its review.

**What is added, and what is not.**

| Element | Where it sits | Why there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The handler | The **delegate of the route-handler endpoint** section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 13 registers, written as a forwarding lambda that lets the container supply the sink: `(HttpContext http, CspReportSink sink, CancellationToken ct) => sink.HandleAsync(http, ct)`. **No controller action, and therefore no seventh controller** | The shape is [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s host-mechanism row, and it is also what the AAP's own map wants: §0.4.1 names exactly **six** controllers and a route handler adds none. The body sits in the sink rather than in `Program.cs` because the state it consults is the sink's (row below), and a lambda that only forwards keeps the composition root readable. **An earlier form of this row declared a `CspReport()` action on `HomeController` "so section 7.1's closed list becomes two actions in one file", checkable against "row 40 of section 12.4". Both halves are deleted rather than reconciled**: the list is two endpoints on **two** hosting shapes, which section [7.1](#71-the-policy)'s enumeration now reads as such, and row 40 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts album input integrity on the administration writes — it was never this endpoint's oracle |
| The request models | **`Binding/CspReportModels.cs`** — a new file in the folder `Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs` (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)) already occupies | [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s map delegates the file-by-file contents of `Binding/` and `Services/` to this document, so a file here changes no project, no folder set and no project graph. They are deserialization targets carrying `[JsonPropertyName]` attributes, which is what `Binding/` is for; nesting them privately inside the controller was rejected because the two shapes are a wire contract and a wire contract belongs beside the other one |
| The handler body, the normalizer, the budgets and the emission | **`Services/CspReportSink.cs`**, registered as a **singleton**, exposing the `HandleAsync(HttpContext, CancellationToken)` the lambda above forwards to | The two hourly budgets are **process-wide mutable state** (below), so they cannot live in a per-request controller or a scoped service. Registered as the concrete type with no interface, on section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted)'s stance: an abstraction with one implementation and one consumer buys a seam this suite does not use, because section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) tests through the endpoint |
| The rate-limit policy | `internal sealed class CspReportRateLimitPolicy : IRateLimiterPolicy<string>`, declared in **`Program.cs` after the last top-level statement**, on the same `public partial class Program` declaration section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) puts there for the test host. It implements **`GetPartition` only**, and leaves **`OnRejected` null** | `AddPolicy<TPartitionKey, TPolicy>` needs a **named type**, and the partition rule this endpoint needs — the reconstructed client address, never the `UserId` — is a method rather than a value. `OnRejected` is deliberately not supplied: the rejection behaviour is the options-level one section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 14 already sets for every limiter, a **`429` carrying `Retry-After`**, which is exactly what [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s rate-limiting row requires this endpoint to inherit. **An earlier form of this row declared `OnRejected` in order to answer `204` instead; that is deleted** — see the window paragraph below, which records why |
