  one registered in section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity), against the one database. The objection an earlier
  revision raised against it — that routing a database round trip through the cache to avoid a database
  round trip is self-defeating — does not survive comparing the two reads: the cached read is **one
  point lookup by primary key** on a single narrow row, and the read it replaces is a **nested aggregate**
  that sums order-detail quantities across three joined tables, orders the result and takes nine
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreController.cs:46-52]. Those are not the same cost, and the
  second is the one [11 §3.8.2](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) records as the workload that reaches the
  database first. **The consequence for the cache table is exactly two keys**, stated here so 06 can size
  it: the stamp and the current value. A rotation leaves the superseded value row behind until the
  provider's own expiration sweep removes it, bounded by the absolute lifetime below, so two is the
  steady-state figure and the order of magnitude 06 plans against.

  **The four triggers are all accounted for, and the register that supplies them says so.**
  [08 §5.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) is the source of the fact that changes the shape of this
  mechanism — that **four** distinct writes move the aggregate's ranking key, not one: a checkout, an album
  **create**, an album **delete**, and an album **edit that reassigns `GenreId`**, which moves an album's
  entire accumulated quantity between genres **with no order written at all**. The table below is that
  accounting, and **the maximum staleness is stated once**, in its fourth row.

  | Element | Contract |
  | --- | --- |
  | **The value, and what is cached** | The cached value is the **`GenreMenuViewComponent` view model** — the nine genres in ranked order, projected to the fields the view reads — serialized, and **never a tracked entity**, so nothing `DbContext`-attached outlives its request scope inside a shared cache. A cold read computes the aggregate once and stores it; a warm read issues no aggregate at all. **Stampede control is required rather than optional**: a cold instance under load must compute it **once**, so population is guarded by a per-key single-flight (`SemaphoreSlim` keyed on the versioned key) and concurrent renders await that computation — otherwise the first seconds after every scale-out event run one nested aggregate per in-flight request, which is the load this cache exists to remove. Single-flight is **per instance**, which is correct and is not the defect above: two replicas computing once each is bounded by the replica count, whereas *n* concurrent renders computing each is not |
  | **The key, versioned rather than fixed** | Two keys, and the indirection is the mechanism. The value lives under **`genre-menu:{stamp}`** and the stamp lives under **`genre-menu:stamp`**. A read fetches the stamp, then fetches the value for it; a stamp that is absent is minted, stored and used. **Invalidation is a rotation of the stamp, not a delete of the value** — one small write, after which every replica's next read computes a key that has no entry and repopulates. That is what makes eviction global without any replica having to be told: there is no fan-out, no cache-invalidation message and no distributed lock, and a replica that was not running when the write happened behaves identically to one that was |
  | **The lifetime** | **`Caching:GenreMenuCacheTtl`** — the one member of the `Caching` section of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), referred to by its member name `GenreMenuCacheTtl` in prose here and elsewhere and admitted under that fully qualified name — **60 seconds** by default, configuration-bound with that default, expressed as an **absolute** expiration and never a sliding one: a sliding window on a key touched by every page render never expires, which would turn bounded staleness into staleness measured in the deployment's lifetime. It is an ordinary option and not one of the five channels of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which are the connection and secret channels |
  | **Invalidation, and the one staleness statement** | The three administration writes — **create**, **edit** and **delete** in `StoreManagerController` — **rotate the stamp after a successful `SaveChangesAsync`**, in the same request, so an administrator's change is reflected on **the next page render on every replica** rather than after an expiry. **The edit case rotates unconditionally rather than only when `GenreId` changed**: the reassignment trigger is the subtle one, an edit is rare, and a conditional rotation would depend on comparing the loaded and posted keys correctly on a path whose failure is invisible. Rotation is **after** the save and never before, so "the cache follows the committed state" holds without a second case. **The fourth trigger, the order write, deliberately does *not* rotate** — and this is the document's one staleness statement: a checkout adds `OrderDetails.Quantity` and so can reorder the menu, but rotating on every order would make the cache useless on exactly the traffic it exists for. **So the maximum staleness of the ranking is `GenreMenuCacheTtl` — 60 seconds at the default — and it is reached only by the order-write trigger.** All four triggers are accounted for: three by rotation, one by a bounded window with a named bound |
  | **The degraded contract — three cases, because the cache is now a network dependency of every page** | **(1) The cache is unreachable on read.** The component **computes the aggregate directly and renders normally**; the page does not fail and no error is surfaced. One record at `Warning` in this application's own category per occurrence-window, never per request, so a cache outage cannot itself become a log flood. **(2) The cache is unreachable when storing a computed value.** The computed value is rendered and the store failure is swallowed to the same single record: the next request recomputes, which is the pre-cache behaviour and is correct rather than degraded-unsafe. **(3) The stamp rotation fails after a *committed* administration write.** The write **is not rolled back and no error is shown to the administrator** — the album change is durable and correct, and only the menu's ranking is stale. The failure is recorded at `Warning` with the trigger named, and the staleness falls back to the absolute lifetime above, so even this path is bounded by 60 seconds. **The ordering is what makes case 3 the only possibility**: rotation after the save means a failed rotation can never be mistaken for a failed write, and a failed write never rotates |
  | **`CartSummaryViewComponent`** — the badge | **Not cached at all, and scoped instead.** It is per-user, it changes on every add and removal, and a cache keyed per cart would be a per-user entry invalidated by the same writes it is meant to spare — cost without benefit. What changes is the **query**: the source materializes the cart's rows and reads `a.Album.Title` per row [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-93], which is lazy-loading site a4 of section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy) and one round trip per line under EF Core's explicit-loading rules; the target issues **one projection query** filtered on the cart key selecting `Album.Title` only, materializing no `Cart` and no `Album` entity. **What that projection must return is section [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract)'s, and this row does not restate it in its own words.** It returns the **sum of the cart rows' quantities** — the `D-32` definition 8.2.1 names and coverage row 8 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts as the literal `Cart (5)` over rows of `Count` 2 and 3 — computed **server-side in the same statement** as the capped title list, never by materializing rows and counting them. **An earlier form of this row read "the count is a count of lines and not a sum of quantities", attributed to a \"two-cart-counts rule of section 4.8\"; both halves are deleted** — the claim is the opposite of the definition its own owner and the delta register carry, and section [4.8](#48-the-service-layer-and-the-two-patterns-deliberately-not-adopted) states no such rule to appeal to. What this row does own is the *shape* of the query: `Distinct()` applies to the tooltip text only and never to the count, the titles are ordered by title and capped per `D-29` (section [4.11](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost)), and a zero count renders **no badge element** rather than a badge reading `0` |

  **The cache table now carries session **and** these two keys, and that is the only boundary this bullet
  moves.** Section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) registers the table; nothing else is written to it by this
  mechanism, the two `genre-menu:` keys cannot collide with a session key, and the sizing consequence is
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s to publish. If a distributed home other than the
  application's own database is ever wanted — a fleet large enough that the point lookup itself matters —
  that is a separate decision with its own sizing, and 06 §6.4 is where it would be taken. **The coverage
  of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts the whole mechanism**: one execution of the nested
  aggregate on a cold miss and **zero** on a warm hit — the unit section
  [4.11](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost) fixes, and not a count of all database
  reads, since the cache's own store is a table in this same database — the stamp rotation on each of the
  three administration writes with the effect
  observed **on a second replica**, the non-rotation on an order, the absolute bound, the single-flight
  property under concurrency, all three degraded cases, and the scoped badge query's round-trip count.

#### 8.2.1 The `CartSummary` component DOM contract

**Why this component alone gets a specified DOM contract.** It is the only rendered surface in the
application that **two** code paths address: the server renders it into every page from the shared layout
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26], and the cart page's script attempts to rewrite
it after a removal [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29]. **Today those two paths
do not agree on anything** — not the element, not the format and not even the quantity — and the
disagreement is invisible only because the script's write lands nowhere. Three separate defects,
established before the target is stated — and the contract below resolves all three by leaving the
**server as the only writer**:

| Defect | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **The script's target element does not exist.** `$('#cart-status').text(…)` addresses an id **no view in the application emits**, so the header badge never updates after a removal | `git grep -n cart-status -- src/MVC5` returns exactly one line, the write itself [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29]. The component renders an unadorned `<li>` and `<a>` with no `id` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:3-4] |
| **The two paths compute different quantities under the same name.** The component renders the number of **cart line rows**; the removal response's `CartCount` is the **sum of quantities** | Component: `ViewBag.CartCount = cartItems.Count()` over `GetCartItems().Select(a => a.Album.Title)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-95]. Response: `CartCount = cart.GetCount()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:78], which sums `cartItems.Count` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:103-112]. **One album with five copies renders as `1` and would be written back as `5`** |
| **Removing the Glyphicon leaves an unlabelled digit.** The rendered content is a pictogram plus a bare number, and `D-06` removes the pictogram | `<span class="glyphicon glyphicon glyphicon-shopping-cart"></span>` — note the token is **duplicated** in the source — followed by `@ViewBag.CartCount` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:5-6] |

**The target contract, stated once and consumed by section
[8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script) and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage):**

- **Element and structure.** The component renders `<li class="nav-item">` containing
  `<a class="nav-link" href="@Url.Action("Index", "ShoppingCart")">`, which emits **`/ShoppingCart`** —
  `Index` is the conventional route's default action and is elided from the generated path, so that is
  the literal section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 8 asserts. The badge renders into the navbar
  list [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:23], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:26] and section
  [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) requires those two classes on a navbar
  item and link.
- **The stable identifier is `id="cart-status"`, on the anchor.** That is **the id the existing script
  already expects** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29], so the contract is
  satisfied by making the server emit what the client was always written against, rather than by
  changing the client. The `id` — not a class and not a data attribute — is the authoritative selector,
  and the externalized script selects on it; `RemoveLink` stays a class because it identifies **many**
  controls, one per row, while this identifies exactly one element.
- **Content is a visible textual label and the count together, rendered as `Cart (n)`.** That is exactly
  the string the script writes [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29], so after the port the server-rendered and script-updated states
  are **the same string produced two ways** — which is the property that makes the disagreement above
  impossible rather than merely unlikely.
- **`n` is the total quantity**, the definition the response's `CartCount` already carries
  ([8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) preserves that property's name and
  meaning), so **the component is aligned to `GetCount()`**. Two alternatives were considered and
  rejected: adding a line-count property to the response widens a wire contract this port deliberately
  keeps byte-identical, and leaving the two definitions disagreeing would convert today's invisible
  inconsistency into a visible one the moment the script's target exists.
- **Zero-count behaviour, on both paths, and what "the element" means is stated exactly.** The
  server-rendered path already gets this right and is preserved: `@if (ViewBag.CartCount > 0)`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:1] wraps the **entire `<li>`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:3-8], so
  at zero count the component renders **nothing at all** — no empty badge and **no empty list item**.
  **The script must match that, which means it operates on the list item and not on the anchor.** The
  stable identifier `cart-status` is on the *anchor*, so a script that removed or hid only the element it
  selected would leave `<li class="nav-item">` behind — empty, still occupying its box in the navbar, and
  still announced as a list item by a screen reader. The requirement is therefore explicit: on a response
  reporting a count of zero the script resolves **`.closest('.nav-item')` from the identified anchor** and
  removes or hides **that** ancestor, so the two paths produce the same DOM at the boundary rather than
  two DOMs that merely look alike. The traversal is named rather than left as "the element" because that
  phrasing is exactly what produces the surviving empty parent. The script never has to *create* the
  element: a removal cannot increase the count, so if the anchor is absent the count was already zero and
  no update is due.
- **`ViewBag.CartCount` and `ViewBag.CartSummary`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:95-96] become typed view-model
  properties**, for the reason section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) gives for all
  three components.
- **The `title` attribute is preserved in form and bounded in length, and the two are stated together
  because an earlier form of this bullet said "carried across unchanged", which `D-29` contradicts.** It
  carries the **newline-joined** list of distinct album titles —
  `string.Join("\n", cartItems.Distinct())`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:96], rendered at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:4] — and that **form** is what carries
  across: same attribute, same element, same distinct titles, same newline join, same ascending order.
  **What does not carry across is its unboundedness**: the list is capped at **ten** titles with an
  indication that more exist when the cap is reached, which is `D-29` of section
  [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), owned by section
  [4.11](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost) because the reason is the per-page payload
  and the round trip rather than the DOM. "Unchanged" is therefore **deleted** rather than reconciled: a
  cart of eleven distinct titles renders ten and the indication, and no reading of this section
  authorizes the eleventh.
  **The response carries no summary field**, so the tooltip is **not refreshed** after a removal; it
  becomes accurate again on the next page render. That staleness exists today and the port preserves it.
  Adding a summary field to the response is **out of scope**: it is a wire-contract change for a tooltip,
  and section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy)'s whole argument is that
  this endpoint's payload stays as it is.
- **The count change is announced**, through the live region of section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) item **c1** — a silently mutating number in
  the page header is exactly the update a screen-reader user would otherwise never learn about.

**These are `D-31` and `D-32`** (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)), owner **Product**,
and they are two rows rather than one because they are two visible consequences with two failure modes: the
pictogram gives way to the word `Cart` (`D-31`), and the number changes meaning from line count to total
quantity (`D-32`) — visible only
for a cart holding more than one copy of some album. The rendered comparison is on section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual)'s checklist.

### 8.3 The five views that name legacy types

**A plan that treats all 29 views as a bulk copy breaks in exactly these places — the five the plan
enumerates, and a sixth it does not.**
(`git ls-files 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml' | wc -l` → `29`.) Each is listed with its line-level problem and its
resolution.

**(1) `Views/Shared/Error.cshtml` — a removed model type, and the application's first real error
policy.**

`@model System.Web.Mvc.HandleErrorInfo` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:1]. The type
does not exist in the target and the exception-handling middleware supplies **no Razor equivalent**, so
there is nothing to substitute into the directive. The rest of the file is two static headings [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:7-8]
and it renders **no property of the model at all**.

**Resolution: define `ErrorViewModel.cs` and specify the whole policy, because the source has none to
preserve.** `HandleErrorAttribute` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/FilterConfig.cs:10] engages when custom errors
are in effect, and **no edition declares `<customErrors>`** — there is no live element in any
configuration file in the repository (verified; command in
[Appendix A](#appendix-a--reproducibility); [09 §6.10](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding).

**That absence does not make the attribute inert, and the plausible reading of it is wrong.** With
`<customErrors>` undeclared, classic ASP.NET applies its default of **`RemoteOnly`**, which means custom
errors are *on* for every non-local client and off only for a browser on the server itself. So as
shipped the filter does engage for a remote visitor: it returns the shared `Error.cshtml` with a
**500**, while a developer browsing from the machine hosting the site sees the framework's own
exception page instead. The behaviour is therefore not absent but **split by caller location, and
stated nowhere** — which is exactly why [09 §6.10](09-security-assessment.md) records it as a framework
default nobody chose.

**The target's error behaviour is consequently being chosen, not preserved** — not because nothing
happens today, but because what happens today depends on where the client is and is not a policy anyone
wrote down. Two things follow for the delta table in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas): the **uniformity** of the target's behaviour is the
change (one generic response for every caller, local or remote), and the status code for an unhandled
exception is **preserved** at 500 rather than altered. It is therefore stated in full:

**The action that produces the model.** One action serves both paths, because both render the same
view and differ only in the status they carry:

```csharp
// Controllers/HomeController.cs
[AllowAnonymous]
[ResponseCache(NoStore = true, Location = ResponseCacheLocation.None)]
public IActionResult Error(int? id)
{
    // The route segment is public input. Only a real error status may be echoed back
    // as the response status; anything else — including a success code, a negative
    // number and a value no HTTP status can be — is normalised to 500.
    var statusCode = id is int code && code >= 400 && code <= 599
        ? code
        : StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError;

    Response.StatusCode = statusCode;
    return View(new ErrorViewModel
    {
        StatusCode = statusCode,
        // The 32-lowercase-hex W3C trace id, not the composite Activity.Current?.Id,
        // so this value equals the traceId on the log record (section 3.3). Where no
        // activity exists the value is generated in the SAME domain, deliberately not
        // HttpContext.TraceIdentifier, whose shape (0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001) is not it.
        TraceIdentifier = Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString()
            ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()
    });
}
```

**Why the range test is not defensive decoration.** `/Home/Error/{id}` is a route on the public URL
surface — it has to be, because `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` reaches the action through it, and
because it resolves under the single conventional route like any other action — so **any client can
choose the value**. Writing it to `Response.StatusCode`
unfiltered has three distinct consequences, and the first is a contradiction of this section's own
contract:

- **`/Home/Error/200` would answer `200 OK` with an error page in it** — precisely the defect the
  "neither error path ever returns 200" rule below exists to close, reachable by typing a URL. The same
  goes for `/Home/Error/302` and any other non-error code.
- **A negative or oversized value is not a status code at all.** `Response.StatusCode` accepts a bounded
  range, so `/Home/Error/-1` or `/Home/Error/99999` throws inside the response pipeline — an unhandled
  exception raised *by the error handler*, on an anonymous route, which is both a 500 whose cause is the
  error path itself and a trivially repeatable log-noise generator.
- **A non-numeric segment** — `/Home/Error/abc` — fails to bind, leaves `id` null, and normalises to 500
  with no error of its own. That is already the desired behaviour and the test asserts it.

**The clamp cannot alter a genuine error response**, which is what makes it free.
`UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-executes only for responses already in the 400-599 range, and the
**four** codes this application produces through it — 404, 405, 403 via `AccessDeniedPath`, and the **504**
the request-timeout middleware sets in section
[4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s step 1 — are all
inside it, as is the 500 the exception handler sets. **This census read three and the fourth was already
stated elsewhere in the document, so it is added here rather than left to a reader to notice**: 3 + 1 = 4,
nothing leaves the set, and the clamp claim below is unchanged because 504 is inside the same range. So every value the framework supplies passes the
test unchanged, and only a client-chosen value is replaced. The coverage assertion requires both directions.

Four further details in that signature are contractual rather than stylistic:

- **The parameter is named `id`, deliberately.** `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/Home/Error/{0}")`
  (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)) substitutes the status code into the path, so
  the request re-executes as `/Home/Error/404` — and under the single conventional route
  `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}` that third segment binds to a parameter called **`id`**.
  Naming it `code` would leave it null on every request and every status-code response would render as
  500. **No other configured path binds through this segment**: `AccessDeniedPath` is
  `/Account/AccessDenied` (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) and reaches its own
  action, and `UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error")` supplies no route value at all, so `id` is null there
  and the action normalises to 500.
- **`[AllowAnonymous]` is explicit.** `HomeController` carries no `[Authorize]` today, so the attribute
  is not strictly required — but an anonymous request that 404s, 405s or faults re-executes *here* while
  still anonymous, and an error page that can itself be refused produces a redirect loop. Stating it
  means a later `[Authorize]` on the controller cannot create one.
- **The action sets the response status itself.** On either re-executed path the middleware has already
  set the code, so the assignment writes the same value and is a no-op. On a **direct** request to
  `/Home/Error/{id}` — which is a fresh 200-status request, not a re-execution — the assignment is the
  only thing that makes the response an error status rather than a 200 with an error page in it, which is
  also why the clamp above has to bound the value it writes.
- **No caching.** An error response cached by a proxy or the browser outlives the condition that caused
  it.

**What populates `ErrorViewModel`, exhaustively.** Two properties, both safe in every environment:

| Property | Value | Rendered? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `StatusCode` | `id` when the route supplied a value **in 400-599**, otherwise `500` — the clamp above | Not rendered as a number in the view; it is available so a later refinement can vary the heading by code without changing the contract |
| `TraceIdentifier` | `Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToHexString() ?? ActivityTraceId.CreateRandom().ToHexString()` — the **32-lowercase-hex W3C trace id** when an activity exists, and a value generated **in that same domain** when none does. The expression is the one section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) fixes for the log record's `traceId`, which is what makes the two values equal, and it implements [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R1` rule rather than restating a decision. **Two values are excluded and both are named** so the exclusion is checkable: `Activity.Current?.Id`, which renders the composite `traceparent`-shaped string; and **`HttpContext.TraceIdentifier`**, whose shape is `0HNO5R4LID6IK:00000001` — the connection id and request number — and which an earlier form of this row used as the fallback, putting a value outside the asserted domain in front of a user on exactly the requests that have no activity | **Yes**, so a user can quote a value that correlates to the log record |

**The error view renders without the shared layout, and this is a correctness requirement rather than a
styling choice.** `Views/Shared/Error.cshtml` declares no `Layout`, so `_ViewStart.cshtml` supplies
`~/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/_ViewStart.cshtml:2] — and in the target
that layout hosts the two **layout** view components of section
[8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) — the third renders only on the account-management page —
**both of which query the catalog
database on every render**: the genre navigation runs the nested aggregate and the cart summary reads the
cart. Inherit the layout and the error page becomes a page that cannot render when the database is
unavailable, which is one of the conditions most likely to have produced the error in the first place.
The failure that follows is worse than the original: an exception thrown *while* the exception handler is
re-executing the error path cannot be handled by that same handler, so the client receives a bare 500
with no body, or a reset connection, and the log records a rendering failure whose cause is the error
page rather than the fault.

| Requirement | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Layout** | `@{ Layout = null; }` declared **in the error view itself**, so no `_ViewStart` can reintroduce one, or a dedicated `_ErrorLayout.cshtml` containing only static markup — **no view component, no tag helper that queries, no partial that reads the database, and no injected service** |
| **What the page may contain** | The two static headings, preserved verbatim [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:7-8], the trace identifier, and static assets. It may render before any database call succeeds |
| **Navigation** | A plain link to `/`, not the layout's genre menu — the menu is exactly the component that cannot run |
| **The same rule for status-code pages** | `/Home/Error/{code}` renders the same layout-free view, because a 404 is served under the same conditions and by the same action |

**The persistence-failure classifier — one classifier, owned here, consumed by every handler whose
failure response is a redisplay.** Any write path that answers a failure by redisplaying its own view
inherits the hazard above, because a redisplayed view *does* use the shared layout and the layout's two
view components query the catalog on every render. So the outcome cannot be chosen per `catch` clause in
each handler: two handlers stating it independently is how one of them ends up redisplaying a failure
whose cause is that the database cannot be reached. There is therefore **one** classifier, stated once
here, and section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)'s failure table and section
[8.11](#811-the-administration-input-models--the-entity-stops-being-a-binding-target)'s write paths consume
it rather than restating it.

**Its input is the exception *chain*, not the exception.** This is the half a per-handler rule gets
wrong: a connectivity failure raised inside `SaveChangesAsync` does not arrive as a bare `SqlException` —
EF Core wraps it in a `DbUpdateException` — so a rule written against `SqlException` never fires on the
path where it matters, while a rule written against `DbUpdateException` alone catches the wrapper and
redisplays a page that cannot render. The classifier therefore walks the whole `InnerException` chain and
classifies on the innermost provider exception; **the wrapper never changes the class**, and a bare
provider exception and a wrapped one classify identically.

| Class | Recognized by | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DuplicateSubmission` | A unique-constraint violation naming the `SubmissionId` index, bare or wrapped | **Neither a redisplay nor an error page.** The other submission won; the handler re-reads by key and username and redirects to the winning order, per step 1a of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |
| `Concurrency` | `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate below |
| `Rejected` | Any error the **server itself produced** having accepted the command — a foreign-key, check or unique violation other than the one above, a permission refusal, a deadlock victim | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate. The store demonstrably answered, so the layout's queries can run |
| `DataIntegrity` | An inconsistency the **application** detected with no provider exception at all — the missing-album case of census site F6, section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **Redisplay**, subject to the render gate |
| `Unavailable` | The store could not be reached, or did not answer: a provider exception raised **while opening the connection** (no command was ever sent), a connection-level failure, or a timeout with no server response — again, bare or wrapped | **Never redisplayed.** Rethrown to the exception-handling middleware and answered by the layout-free generic page above. Redisplaying here is the recursion this section exists to prevent |
| `Cancelled` | `OperationCanceledException` whose token is the request's | Recorded and rethrown; **no response is composed at all**, per the cancellation row of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |

**Anything the classifier does not recognize is not caught.** It reaches the middleware and is answered
by the generic page, which is the correct default: an unclassified fault is one nobody has reasoned
about, and inventing a redisplay for it is how an unrenderable page gets served.

**The render gate, and why it is a probe rather than an error-number list.** Every redisplay-eligible
class is gated on one bounded question — *can the redisplay actually render?* — answered by a single
`await db.Database.CanConnectAsync(ct)` on a fresh connection under a **two-second** linked timeout — long
enough to answer on a healthy store, short enough that a customer waiting on a failed submission is not
made to wait twice — and it runs on the failure path only. **False, or the probe itself timing out or
throwing, re-classifies the failure as `Unavailable`** and it is rethrown. Two reasons this is the
criterion rather than matching provider error numbers: a number list is precisely the hand-maintained
transient-set that section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) refuses for retry classification,
and it fails silently when the provider adds a code; and the provider's own `IsTransient` flag conflates a
deadlock, where the server answered and a redisplay is fine, with a connection failure, where it is not.
The gate is skipped as unnecessary for a provider exception raised before any connection was established,
which is `Unavailable` with certainty and needs no round trip to confirm.

**And the gate is allowed to be wrong in one direction, because the fallback is safe.** If the probe
succeeds and the redisplay then faults anyway, that exception reaches the middleware and the **layout-free**
error view answers it. The cost is one wasted render, not a loop — which holds only because the error view
declares `Layout = null` in the view itself, as the table above requires.

**Two coverage rows hold this contract, and they hold different halves of it.** Row **86** of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires the recursion properties from both ends: with the database
stopped, a request to any page yields **exactly one** generic 500 with no recursion and no second
exception in the log, and the same holds with a view component made to throw while the database is up.
Row **85** requires the classifier itself, on the pair that distinguishes it from a per-handler rule — a
server-rejected write redisplays, and a connectivity failure **wrapped in `DbUpdateException`** does not.

**The action reads no exception feature — neither `IExceptionHandlerFeature` nor the `IExceptionHandlerPathFeature` derived from it — and never the exception.** It does not need to,
because the recording happened before it ran — in the `IExceptionHandler` of stage 1 item 13 (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), specified below — and nothing about the exception may reach
the response. Not reading it is what makes it impossible to leak by accident: there is no exception
object in scope in the action or the view. **It is also why the recording cannot live in the action**, and
that is the whole reason the handler component exists rather than being an implementation detail.

**The status codes, per path.**

| Path | Response status | How it gets there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unhandled exception, outside Development | **500** | `UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error")` sets 500 and re-executes with no route value, so `id` is null and the action confirms 500 |
| Unhandled exception, Development | 500 with the developer exception page | The other branch of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 4; this action is not involved |
| `NotFound()` from any of the six census sites of section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **404**, with the generic view | `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-executes `/Home/Error/404` |
| A wrong verb against a mapped action | **405**, with the generic view | Same mechanism |
| An authenticated non-administrator reaching `/StoreManager/**` | **403**, with the generic view, **in one response and with no `Location`** | The global `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) writes 403 instead of redirecting, and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-executes `/Home/Error/403` — the same string `AccessDeniedPath` holds, so the rendered view is the one that path names |
| An unauthenticated request to an authorized action | **302** to `/Account/Login` | Unchanged from the source; the error view is not involved |

**Those last two rows are the whole denial contract, and the reason there is no third is a property of
this application rather than an omission.** A browser request is refused in exactly two shapes — **302 to
`/Account/Login`** when there is no authenticated principal, and **302 to `/Account/AccessDenied`, whose
target answers 403** when there is one and it does not satisfy the policy. **The rendered surface has no
`401` branch and there is no separate API exception policy, because the application exposes no API
surface**: every endpoint is either an MVC action rendering HTML, one of the two health paths of section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), or the single guarded diagnostic route of section
[2.5.1](#251-the-instance-verification-route-and-why-it-is-not-a-fourth-health-endpoint), and the last
is the **one** place a status code replaces a redirect — path-scoped in the cookie handler's events,
for the reason that section states, and asserted by its owner rather than here. The cart-removal endpoint
that answers JSON is an MVC action on the same cookie scheme (section
[8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy)), so it is refused the same way a page
is; it is not an API in the sense that would need a challenge scheme, a bearer token or a problem-details
response. Stating this closes the question rather than leaving a reader to infer that an API policy was
forgotten: if an API surface is ever added, its refusal shapes and its exception policy are a scoped
addition decided at that time.

**Both mechanisms re-execute with the *original* request method, and that has consequences beyond the
status code.** `UseExceptionHandler` and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` re-run the pipeline against
the configured path while preserving the method, so a **`POST`** that faults — a checkout submission, an
administration write, a sign-in — arrives at this action as a **`POST` to `/Home/Error`**. Three
requirements follow, and the first is the one an otherwise-correct implementation misses:

- **The action is exempt from the global anti-forgery filter**, `[IgnoreAntiforgeryToken]`, recorded with
  its justification as the **only entry** in the opt-out register of section
  [7.1](#71-the-policy).
  Without it the filter validates the re-executed `POST`, and a fault page becomes a bare `400` — either
  because the original request body has already been consumed, or, where the original fault *was* an
  anti-forgery failure, because the re-executed request carries the same invalid token and fails again.
- **The action must not require `[HttpGet]`, and must not be reached by a route that does.** One action,
  no verb constraint, both paths.
- **It reads no form value and no body**, which is what makes the exemption safe rather than merely
  convenient: the only input it accepts is the `int?` route segment, clamped above.

**When each mechanism acts, and the responses they deliberately do not touch.** The two branches qualify
a response differently, and the difference is not a detail: only one of them is a status-code rule at all.

- **`UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` is the status-code rule.** It inspects a response the pipeline has
  **already produced** and acts only when that response's status is in the **400-599** range, the
  response has not started, and neither a body nor a `Content-Type` has been set. A response carrying
  either is passed through untouched, and a status outside the range is never its business — which is
  what the two *No* rows of the table below record.
- **`UseExceptionHandler` is not a status-code rule.** It begins from an **unhandled exception**
  propagating out of the pipeline, so there is no produced 400-599 response for it to qualify: the fault
  reached it before a status code was chosen, and it is the branch that assigns one. Its own precondition
  is different and narrower — the response must not have **started**, because a response already on the
  wire cannot be replaced — and when that holds it clears the response, assigns **500**, re-executes its
  configured path, and the status-code rule above never sees the fault at all.

Every error status this application produces is stated below against whichever of the two claims it, which
is what makes the table complete rather than illustrative:

| Response | Rendered by this action? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The `NotFound()` results of the census of section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census), the ownership 404 of (1b) below, the **405** from a verb that no action on a matched route accepts, and the **400** the global anti-forgery filter returns | **Yes** | Each is an empty-bodied status result, so the status-code branch re-executes the path with the code preserved. This is why the coverage rows for a rejected write assert the generic error view and **not** a redisplayed form |
| The **500** an unhandled exception produces | **Yes** | Through the exception branch rather than the status-code branch: the exception reaches that branch before any status is chosen, and the record is already written by the handler of stage 1 item 13 before the re-execution begins. The status-code rule never sees it, because the 500 the exception branch assigns is set on a response it has already taken over |
| The **403** at the access-denied path | **Yes, but not by re-execution** | The cookie handler answers a failed policy with a **redirect** to `/Home/Error/403` (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)), so the browser issues a fresh request that the route serves directly and the action sets the status itself — which is the third of the four signature details above |
| `/healthz/ready`'s **503** | **No** | The status is in range, but the health-check response writer has already written a `text/plain` body, so the status-code rule passes it through — which is why the fixed oracle for that path in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts a body of exactly `Unhealthy` rather than a rendered page, and why those endpoints need no exemption to keep it |
| The report collector's **204** and the platform's plaintext-to-HTTPS redirect | **No** | Neither status is in the range the status-code rule covers, and neither arises from an exception, so no branch claims either; the collector's silence is section [7.5](#75-the-second-opt-out-mapped--the-report-collectors-application-half)'s decision and the redirect is not this application's response |

**No error response in this application carries a JSON body**, and that is a decision rather than an
omission: the only JSON the application writes is the cart-removal success payload of section
[8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy), so a script that receives anything other
than a 200 receives an opaque failure and treats it as one (section
[8.1.2](#812-the-externalized-cart-script)). A JSON error shape would be a second error contract — its own
field names, its own naming policy and its own disclosure surface — for one endpoint.

**Whether the original query string survives the re-execution, stated once because the two mechanisms
treat it differently and the answer must not matter.** The status code travels in a **path segment**,
`/Home/Error/{0}`, so neither mechanism needs a query parameter of its own — which is also what section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s rule 4 requires of every URL this application controls.
Concretely: the status-code branch is registered with **no query-format argument**, so the re-executed
request runs with an empty query string and the original is restored once the re-execution unwinds,
remaining readable through `IStatusCodeReExecuteFeature` for anything that wants it; the exception branch
assigns the **path** and clears the selected endpoint and the route values — the fact the record writer's
table below depends on — and does not assign the query string, so the original is still on the request
while this action runs. **This action reads neither**, in either case: its only input is the `int?` route
segment clamped above, and it reads no feature at all. So the difference between the two mechanisms cannot
produce two different responses, **no caller-supplied query text reaches the view** — the fixed oracle for
the 500 shape asserts exactly that — and the *never recorded* row of the record contract below keeps it out
of the log as well. Where an operator needs the failing URL it comes from the record's path field, never
from the page.

**Neither of the two paths this action serves — the exception path and the status-code path — ever returns
200.** The one surface that really did return one and now does not is the **access-denied path**, where the
source redirects a forbidden caller to the login page and the target answers **403** — written by the
global `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` and rendered by re-executing `AccessDeniedPath`'s own
`/Home/Error/403`; there a 200 would let a crawler index the page, a monitor record it as success and a
client script fail to distinguish it from content. That status change belongs to the explicit
authentication-and-cookie policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) and is owned by
that policy's row in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) (`D-10`); for an **unhandled
exception** the 500 is *preserved* rather than introduced, since `RemoteOnly` already produces one for a
remote caller, and `D-12` owns the change that is real there — the generic page and its trace identifier.

**`Checkout.Complete`'s ownership refusal is deliberately *not* in that set, and an earlier form of this
paragraph put it there.** It named the ownership check alongside the access-denied path as a surface
"being fixed". It is not being fixed: it answers **200** with a generic page in the target exactly as it
does in the source, for the reasons item (1b) of section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) states in full — chiefly that the class-level
`[Authorize]` means no unauthenticated agent can reach the response at all, so the crawler and monitor
arguments above do not apply to it. The rule in this paragraph is therefore scoped to the paths **this
action** serves and to the access-denied path, and it is not a general prohibition on any 200 that
renders generic text.

**The statement holds for a directly requested error URL too, and only because of the clamp above** —
without it `/Home/Error/200` is a 200 with an error page in it, which would make this rule false by the
shortest possible route.

**What is logged, and by what — under the policy [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns.**

**The writer is a named component, because the mechanism chosen for the response cannot produce this
record.** `app.UseExceptionHandler("/Home/Error")` re-executes a path; it renders a response and writes
the framework's own diagnostic, and it enriches nothing. The action it re-executes deliberately reads no
exception feature (above). **So with those two alone, the record specified below is written by
nobody** — which is a promise a document can make and an implementation can quietly fail to keep, since
the response looks correct either way. The record is therefore written by
`ErrorRecordExceptionHandler : IExceptionHandler`, registered as stage 1 item 13 of section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order):

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **When it runs** | Inside `UseExceptionHandler`'s middleware, on the unhandled-exception path only, **before** the `/Home/Error` re-execution. That is the second reason it is not in the action: the action runs *after* re-execution, and it deliberately reads no exception feature, so by then it has nothing to record from. Running early is necessary but **not** sufficient to recover the failing request's identity, for the reason in the next row |
| **Where the original request's identity comes from** | Running before the re-execution does **not** mean the `HttpContext` still describes the failing request. `ExceptionHandlerOptions.ExceptionHandlingPath` is "the path used when executing the exception handler", and the middleware **assigns it to `HttpContext.Request.Path` and clears the selected endpoint and the route values before it invokes any `IExceptionHandler`** — so a handler that reads `context.Request.Path` records `/Home/Error` for every fault, and reads a null endpoint and an empty route-value dictionary. Three sources, therefore, and each is chosen because it is the only correct one: the **path** and the **endpoint** come from `IExceptionHandlerFeature` (`Path`, `Endpoint`), whose own summary describes it as carrying "the error of the original request"; the **method** comes from `HttpContext.Request.Method`, which the middleware does not rewrite and which **no feature exposes** — neither exception-handling feature has a method member, so a design that expected one would have nowhere to read it from; and the **user** comes from `HttpContext.User`, likewise untouched. The feature's fourth member, `RouteValues`, is the request's other lost value and is deliberately **not** recorded, for the reason the *Never recorded* row gives. **The feature is requested as `IExceptionHandlerFeature`, and the reason is not that the other one is weaker.** That interface declares `Error` alongside `Path`, `Endpoint` and `RouteValues` — every member this row reads. `IExceptionHandlerPathFeature` **derives from** it, adding its own `Path` declaration and inheriting the rest, and the middleware registers **one object** under both feature keys, so which key a handler asks for changes nothing about the values available to it. The base interface is named because it is the minimal request that reaches all four members, and naming it that way keeps all. **On an in-line failure branch the sources are different, and that difference is part of the contract rather than an implementation detail**: nothing has been re-executed there, so the `HttpContext` still describes the request that failed, and this row from resting on a capability difference that does not exist four request-identity fields are read from it live — the method and the path from `HttpContext.Request`, the status code from `HttpContext.Response`, and the endpoint from **`HttpContext.GetEndpoint()`**, which is the accessor that exists outside the exception-handling middleware. Same eight fields, same prohibitions, two source sets — one per emission path, and neither borrows the other's |
| **What it returns** | **`false`**, always. `false` means *recorded, not handled*: the middleware proceeds to its configured path and the generic response is produced by the action, unchanged. It never writes a body, never sets a status code and never suppresses the exception |
| **Permitted content** | The **original** request method and path, each from the source named in the row above — the method from `Request.Method`, the path from the feature; the failing **endpoint's display name**, also from the feature, which names code — the controller and action — in the same sense the stack trace does; the response status code; the **trace identifier the response shows** — `Activity.Current?.Id ?? HttpContext.TraceIdentifier`, the same expression the model uses, so the record and the user's screenshot join up; the exception **type name** as `exception.GetType().FullName` **together with the type-name chain of its inner exceptions, types only** — required by the shape this record is, and an earlier form of this row named only the outermost type; the **stack trace as its own string field**, `exception.StackTrace`; a **failure category** from the closed set of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract); and a **pseudonymous actor**. Those fields are assembled by the handler and passed as **values**; the `Exception` **object itself is never handed to the logger**, for the mechanical reason below the table. **The exception *message* is not in this set** |
| **Which record shape this is, and the disagreement that is now closed** | It is [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s record shape **`R2`**, and **all eight of its fields are the eight above**: four describing the fault — the type name with its inner type-name chain, the stack trace as a string field, the failure category, and `R1`'s trace identifier — and four identifying the request that faulted: the original request **method**, the original request **path**, the failing **endpoint's display name** and the **response status code**. **An earlier form of this row recorded an open disagreement and it is withdrawn as resolved.** That form said the second four were "not in that list", stated them as a *consumer requirement on `R2`*, and closed by conceding that until the register carried them "this row and that register disagree". The register now carries them: it amended `R2` from four fields to eight, added the four **as members of `R2`** rather than as a separate shape, and gives the mechanical reason for that choice — every emission of `R2` is an error-path emission, so a distinct error-path shape would have left `R2` with no producer. **Nothing here widens a list this document does not own**; the owner widened it, and this row now agrees with it field for field. Two further alignments come with that: `R2` is **the only exception record the application produces**, which is narrower than an earlier "the sole exception signal in the system" — the platform's auto-collected exception table is a second, platform-produced signal disposed of by [06 §9.2.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) — and the per-member sources this document states two rows above are the sources the register mandates rather than a local choice |
| **The actor** | The Identity `UserId` — `User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)` — where the request was authenticated, and the literal **`anonymous`** for a request carrying no authenticated identity. **Those are the exactly two values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits in an application record's actor position**, and that table is the owner of the pair rather than this row. **Never the login name**, never an email, never a client address, never a submitted form value — and **never a `SubjectPseudonym`**, which that table classes as a *subject* field and not an actor. The target-side `none` and `rejected` sentinels and the pseudonym mechanism itself are [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s and are not redefined here |
| **Never recorded** | The request body, any query-string value, **the route values** — offered by the feature as `RouteValues`, and excluded because a route value is caller-supplied text arriving on the same footing as a query-string value, so admitting it would carve an exception into the rule immediately above it — cookie values, anti-forgery tokens, the session id, and the address and contact fields of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract). A 500 raised inside the checkout write path is the case that rule exists for |
| **Severity, sink, retention** | The severity, the collection mechanism, the sink and the retention are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. This document states the **content and the writer**, not the plumbing |

**The exception message is excluded, and the reason is that a provider message is not the
application's text.** [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s log-privacy policy forbids the nine
address and contact fields, the raw login name and the promo-code value from reaching the sink at all —
and it forbids them **wherever** they appear, including inside a message the application did not compose.
A `SqlException` names the constraint and frequently the offending value; `DbUpdateException` wraps it and
its `InnerException.Message` carries the provider text verbatim; a `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` names
the entity and key. So "log the exception message" and "never log an order's address" are not two
independent rules that happen to coexist — the first defeats the second, silently, on exactly the write
paths where personal data is present. Four consequences, and the first three apply to every `ILogger`
call in the port rather than only to this handler:

- **Log the exception `GetType().FullName`, not `Message`.** The type plus the failure category plus the
  trace identifier identifies the fault for an operator; the message adds provider text nobody has
  reviewed.
- **The application logs a sanitized record and never passes the `Exception` object to the logger.** This
  is the rule that is easiest to state incorrectly, and stating it incorrectly reopens the whole channel:
  `ILogger`'s exception parameter is **not** a stack-trace field. Every logger provider renders that
  argument by calling `ToString()` on it, and `Exception.ToString()` is the type name, **the `Message`**,
  the stack trace and the same three for **every** `InnerException` in the chain. So
  `logger.LogError(exception, "…")` writes the provider text this rule exists to keep out, whatever the
  message template omits — and it does so as one opaque blob a sink-side redaction rule cannot act on
  field by field. **The stack trace is permitted** because it names code rather than data, and it is
  therefore captured **explicitly, as a string field**: the handler reads `exception.StackTrace`,
  `exception.GetType().FullName`, **the type-name chain of its inner exceptions** and the mapped failure
  category, and passes those four plus the trace identifier as named values — which is the same projection
  the *permitted content* row above fixes, and this bullet is not a second, shorter version of it. Nothing
  else about the exception object crosses into the record.
- **`InnerException.Message` is never recorded**, and section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)'s failure table states the same rule at the
  same field: what a `DbUpdateException` contributes to a record is the inner exception's **type** and the
  mapped failure category, never the entity values that caused it. A message worth an operator's attention
  that genuinely needs provider text is obtained from the platform's own SQL diagnostics, which live under
  database access control rather than in the application log.
- **The channels that log exceptions on the application's behalf are suppressed, not trusted, and the
  list is closed rather than illustrative.** The rule above governs what *this application's* code
  writes, and it is not sufficient on its own: several framework components log unhandled and store
  exceptions **themselves**, and each of them passes the exception object — which is the `ToString()`
  expansion above, provider message included. So the port's logging configuration closes them explicitly,
  in `appsettings` per environment, by **category and minimum level**.

  **The levels are not here, and they are not this document's to choose either.** Every category's level
  sits in section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s
  [one category-level table](#the-one-category-level-table) — twenty keys, their deployed values, their
  three Development overrides, the longest-prefix mechanics that make the sub-category pins effective, and
  the validator that asserts all of it at start — and that table is the `appsettings` expression of
  [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s controls 1 and 5. **This table carried a second level
  column until it was withdrawn**, and the two disagreed on `Default`,
  `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` while the
  validator over there simultaneously forbade the `None` values over here. What only this table has is
  what it now carries alone: **per channel, what it would otherwise disclose and what carries the
  diagnostic instead** — which is the obligation that makes closing a category legal at all, since a
  category may not be silenced without a named replacement signal.

  **This enumeration is not the closure**, and neither is that table's. 06 control 5 states explicitly
  that a list of framework categories cannot be proven complete, so the closure is its redaction test and
  the coverage assertion here — asserted against the **entire** captured stream rather than against these
  categories — and a channel missing from both tables fails that row rather than passing unnoticed.

  **What this table's rows are, counted against that one, because the two are not the same length and the
  difference is the point.** Seventeen rows here against twenty keys there. **Eleven** are the eleven
  categories section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) pins to `None`, and every one of them
  appears — which is what discharges the replacement-signal obligation completely rather than for a
  selection. **Six** are categories that stay open, kept because each records a disclosure that was
  considered and the reason no closure is needed, and their third cell says so in those words rather than
  naming a replacement that would have nothing to replace. `11 + 6 = 17`. **Three** of that table's keys
  have no row here — `Microsoft.AspNetCore`, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication` and
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity` — and their absence is deliberate on one shared ground: each is a floor
  or a parent whose own records carry no exception object, so there is nothing for a disclosure cell to
  state that its pinned children do not already state. `17 + 3 = 20`, which is the whole of that table.
  An earlier form of this table omitted `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement`, leaving one
  closed category with no replacement signal on record; that row is now present.

  | Category | What it would otherwise disclose | What carries the diagnostic instead |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `Default` | — | The baseline 06 control 1 sets, stated here because leaving it at the framework default is what makes every row below a partial measure |
  | The application's own `MvcMusicStore` category | — | Its records are the closed record of this section and the event classes of section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic), all sanitized at the producer |
  | `MvcMusicStore.Security.Events` — the reserved security-event category, spelled by [06 §9.6.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) entry 3 | — | **Open, and nothing replaces it because nothing is closed.** This is the one pin whose purpose is that a later tightening of `Default` or of its `MvcMusicStore` parent cannot silently drop an audit record |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` — the parent | At `Information` its command sub-category records the executed SQL for **every** query, which is the largest single source of application data in a log | The three sub-categories that carry command text or an exception object are closed individually; what the parent's own pin buys is that the **rest** of the EF tree cannot reach `Information`, and both values are section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery` | Token-validation diagnostics; at `Information` and below it narrates each validation | The closed record for a genuine failure; the 400 the filter returns for a rejected token needs no log line of its own |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics` | The unhandled exception object for every 500, `ToString()`-expanded with every inner exception's message — **and** the developer-exception-page middleware in the same category, which is why 06 pins the parent rather than the handler sub-category alone | This section's closed record, written by `ErrorRecordExceptionHandler` before the re-execution |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.Diagnostics` | The same exception object on any path where no handler is reached — the case the entry above does **not** cover | The same closed record; the request-level timing and status it also emits are [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s platform telemetry |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel` | `ApplicationError` and connection-level failures at `Error`, each carrying the exception object, including faults raised after the response has started — which the exception handler cannot intercept | The closed record for application faults, and the platform front end's own connection telemetry ([06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) for transport failures |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Update` | `DbUpdateException` and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` objects, whose inner provider text names the constraint and frequently the offending value | The closed record's failure category, drawn from the closed set of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Query` | Query-execution failures with the provider exception attached | The same closed record. **This row is beyond 06 control 5's enumeration and is deliberately retained**: control 5 states that no enumeration of framework categories is provably complete, so pinning one it does not name is never a conflict with it |
  | `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` | Both of its levels are channels, not one: `Information` echoes command text with parameter placeholders, and `Error` carries the failing command **and** the exception | The closed record, plus the platform's SQL diagnostics, which live under database access control rather than in the application log |
  | `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks` | The health-check service logs each failed result **with the result's `Exception`** — which is why stage 1 item 11 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) replaces `AddDbContextCheck<T>`, whose result carries one. A probe failure is the one fault that recurs every few seconds, so an open channel here is the highest-volume disclosure in the application | The one sanitized `Warning` the custom check writes itself, carrying [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) row 6's six fields — the endpoint literal, the failure category, the exception type name and inner type-name chain, the stack trace as a string, the elapsed milliseconds, and the trace identifier — and never the exception object. That is control 4's four-field general fault shape plus the two a probe record has and an arbitrary fault does not |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc` | Model-binding and filter diagnostics; it writes no application fault the closed record does not already own | **Not closed, and the reason is the criterion the whole table turns on**: nothing this category emits at or above its configured floor carries an exception object, so there is nothing here for a replacement signal to replace. Its value is section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s |
  | `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` | Provider-level connection, retry and command diagnostics, exception object attached. **An earlier reading left this channel open** on the reasoning that the provider's exception text reaches the log only through the EF categories above — not a property the provider guarantees, and 06 control 5 names this category among those closed. That reasoning is withdrawn and section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) closes it | The closed record for application faults; connection-level and pool behaviour is read from the platform's own SQL diagnostics, under database access control |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection` | Key-ring records carrying key material and key identifiers, and unprotect failures with the exception attached — which is the channel every protected cart marker, antiforgery token and authentication cookie failure would surface through | **The `KeyRingStatus` heartbeat**, and it is a genuine replacement rather than a gesture: section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s eight-state analysis of this channel shows two of those states write nothing at all even with the category open, so the heartbeat covers strictly more than the channel did. [06 §7.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the alerting on it. *An earlier form of this cell said "nothing from this channel is needed", which was true of the six states the channel reports and false of the two it does not* |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement` | Key-ring resolution, default-key selection and the read-failure record, the last of which carries the exception object. **Its own row exists because closing the parent does not close it**: under the longest-prefix rule an explicit level on this longer category would win over the parent's `None`, so leaving it unpinned is the one way the parent's closure could be reopened by a later edit that looked local | The same heartbeat as the parent row, for the same reason. The one signal that is genuinely lost — the record naming which key the ring selected — is available on demand from [06 §7.4.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s key-row query, which reads the persisted rows rather than the log |
  | `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies` | Cookie decryption and validation failures with the exception attached, which occur in bulk at cutover when every legacy ticket is undecryptable (section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)) | The sign-in and sign-out event classes of section [6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic), which record the outcome without the ticket |

  `EnableSensitiveDataLogging` and `EnableDetailedErrors` are **never** enabled outside Development, since
  either one reintroduces parameter values into whatever channels remain open.

  With those closed, the record of this section is the **only** application-scoped record of a fault,
  which is what makes the coverage assertion's "appears nowhere in the captured output" assertion satisfiable
  rather than aspirational — it is asserted against the whole captured stream, so a framework channel left
  open fails it. **That is why the one deliberately open row costs nothing here rather than being an
  exception to the rule:** the assertion is over the stream and not over a category list, so
  `…Authentication.Cookies` at `Information` is held to precisely the same standard as every closed row,
  and a record of its writing an exception argument is a test failure exactly where a record from a closed
  category would be. An open category is a signal retained under an unchanged obligation, not a channel
  exempted from one. **The scope of that assertion is the `ILogger` stream, and stating it precisely is what
  keeps it true of the deployed estate** — the harness captures what the application's logging pipeline
  emits, at `Trace`, with no platform collector present, so "nowhere in the captured output" is a claim
  about the channels this table governs and about nothing else.

  **[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the sinks, and it does not draw the boundary where
  an earlier form of this paragraph drew it.** That form said a retained sink collecting exception detail
  automatically "reopens exactly what this table closes, so **no retained sink may carry framework-supplied
  exception detail**", verified "by injecting a uniquely marked provider fault and requiring the marker in
  **no** retained sink. **Both halves are withdrawn, because 06's deployed estate contradicts them and the
  assertion would fail every release.** [06 §9.2.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) disposes of the
  platform's auto-collected `AppExceptions` table as **`Accepted, restricted`** — stored, under a
  table-scoped reader role and 06 §9.5's retention, rather than discarded — and 06's own sentinel sweep
  asserts the marker **present** there, as the expected-present control proving the table is collected and
  restricted rather than silently missing, while asserting it **absent** from `AppTraces`, where this
  document's record lands. A blanket "in no retained sink" would contradict that expected-present
  assertion on its own subject.

  **So the boundary is a producer boundary, not a sink boundary, and it is the one this table can actually
  hold.** What this table closes is what *the application's logging pipeline* writes: no framework category
  that passes an exception object reaches the log, and the application itself never passes one — which is
  [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) channel 1 control 4's subject, stated by 06 as governing
  "what the **application** writes". Platform auto-collection is a second producer this document does not
  operate, and its disposition is 06's. The two assertions are therefore split by producer: this document's
  coverage assertions inject a uniquely marked provider fault and require the marker absent from the
  **application's captured `ILogger` output**, and 06's release sweep carries the sink-side case over the
  Application Insights tables.

**The coverage assertion requires the record field by field**, including the fields that must be absent:
row 46 asserts the single entry at `Error`, its correlation with the rendered trace identifier, the type
name and stack trace present, **all four attribution fields present and carrying the failing request's
own method, path, endpoint and status** rather than the re-executed path's, and no exception message, no
query text and no credential; row 97 `97c` asserts the same projection against the record's required and
forbidden fields.

it **injects a forbidden value into a real provider fault** — a unique-index violation whose
message contains a customer's email — and asserts that value appears nowhere in the captured output,
with **every category captured at `Trace`** so the framework channels above are in scope of the
assertion rather than outside it. Row 97 additionally asserts the two mechanisms: that the application's
record carries no `ToString()`-shaped expansion of the exception, and that the suppressed categories emit
nothing. That test is the one that distinguishes a stated policy from an enforced one, because every
other redaction test exercises text the application itself composed. **The coverage assertion runs the same
injection against the other exception-producing surface** — a marked provider fault raised by the
readiness check rather than by a write path — because that check composes its own record, under its own
category and outside this section's exception path, so no case driving a user action reaches it.

**What the response may disclose.** The two generic headings [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:7-8], preserved verbatim, plus the trace
identifier. **No exception type, no message, no stack trace, no query text and no configuration value**
in any environment other than Development, where the developer exception page handles it instead
(section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)).

**The view's own user-facing text is preserved.** Only its model and its plumbing change.

**The coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)** assert this contract:
the response shape on the exception path, status preservation through re-execution, the 403 at the
access-denied path, the status clamp on a client-supplied code, and the closed record itself.

**(1b) The other caller of the error view — `Checkout.Complete`, which stops *sharing* the view and
keeps its *response* exactly as the source produces it.**

`Complete` renders the error view **directly** as the answer to a failed ownership check:
`storeDB.Orders.Any(o => o.OrderId == id && o.Username == User.Identity.Name)`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:71-73], and on false
`return View("Error")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:81]. That is an **HTTP 200** whose body is the two generic headings
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:7-8] inside the shared layout — the view declares no
`Layout`, so `_ViewStart.cshtml` supplies one [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/_ViewStart.cshtml:2].

**Only one thing about that is a portability problem, and it is not the status code.** It is a
controller rendering the *middleware's* view as content: in the target that view is layout-free and
renders a trace identifier (the requirement table above), neither of which the source's response has, so
continuing to share the file would change the rendered page while changing no line of the action.

**Resolution: the response is preserved exactly — status `200`, the same two headings, the same shared
layout — and the refusal branch renders its own view rather than the middleware's.** The action returns
a `ViewResult` naming a dedicated **`Views/Checkout/OrderUnavailable.cshtml`**, which carries those two
headings verbatim and inherits the layout exactly as the source's response does. It is net-new, it is the
only net-new view this section adds, and it changes no figure in section
[8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role): that table dispositions the **29 source views**, and a
net-new target view is outside its arithmetic in the same way `ErrorViewModel.cs` and the three view
components' `Default.cshtml` files are. The name asserts nothing about existence, which is the property
the merged branch needs. `Views/Shared/Error.cshtml` is then reached by the middleware and by nothing
else, so the error contract above has exactly one caller and the trace identifier appears only on
responses that have a log record to correlate with. No error record is written for this branch, matching
the source: a request for an order the caller may not see is a normal answer rather than a fault, and
nothing about it reaches the exception path. Whether a refused order read additionally warrants an
**audit** event is [09](09-security-assessment.md)'s to require, and either answer leaves this response
byte-identical.
