**The complete set of preserving declarations.** This is the whole of what section 8.5 adds to
`wwwroot/css/site.css` beyond the rules section
[8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list) carries across, and it is written out in full so that
no part of it is left to interpretation:

```css
/* Group 1 — base typography, preserving the source's body metrics. */
body {
  font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #333333;
}

/* Group 1a — grid geometry: the 30px gutter, the container's 15px side padding, the
   three container caps at the source's own three boundaries, and the two successor
   steps that have no source counterpart. The custom property is set on both
   .container and .row because the browse-page album grid has no row ancestor and
   inherits it from the `container` class on each <li> instead. */
.container,
.row {
  --bs-gutter-x: 30px;
}

.container {
  padding-right: 15px;
  padding-left: 15px;
  margin-right: auto;
  margin-left: auto;
}

/* The source has no cap below 768px; the successor introduces one at 576px. */
@media (min-width: 576px) {
  .container {
    max-width: none;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 750px;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 992px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 970px;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 1200px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 1170px;
  }
}

/* The successor's fifth step. Source order alone would already win here; the rule is
   written so that the step is visibly accounted for rather than silently outranked. */
@media (min-width: 1400px) {
  .container {
    max-width: 1170px;
  }
}

/* The source wraps a bare <img> in `.row.text-center` (Views/Home/Index.cshtml:6-8), so
   text-align centres it as inline content. Under the successor that row is a flex
   container and the image one flex item, which text-align no longer places, so
   justify-content restates the same centring. Scoped to the jumbotron because it is the
   only source row that centres its children: Account/Login.cshtml:8,
   Account/Manage.cshtml:10 and the album grid at Home/Index.cshtml:10 do not. */
.jumbotron .row {
  justify-content: center;
}

/* No rule is written for the album grid's line behaviour, and the reason is a measured
   fact rather than a judgement: a wrapped flex line starts below the tallest tile of
   the line above, which can only differ from float behaviour when tile heights differ,
   and Site.css:47-49 fixes every tile at height: 160px. Equal-height items wrap
   identically under both models. The tiles also carry no background and no border, so a
   stretched flex item is indistinguishable from a floated one. */

/* Vertical rhythm between form groups: 15px, retained under the source's own class
   name because the successor dropped it. `mb-3` is 1rem — 16px against the pinned
   14px body — and carries !important, so it is not used. */
.form-group {
  margin-bottom: 15px;
}

/* Group 1b — the heading scale, on the elements and on the six type utilities. The
   utilities are pinned because section 8.9 item a4 holds the catalog's rendered sizes
   with class="h3" and class="h5" while correcting the heading outline. */
h1,
h2,
h3,
h4,
h5,
h6,
.h1,
.h2,
.h3,
.h4,
.h5,
.h6 {
  font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  line-height: 1.1;
}

h1,
h2,
h3 {
  margin-top: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h4,
h5,
h6 {
  margin-top: 10px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h1,
.h1 {
  font-size: 36px;
}

h2,
.h2 {
  font-size: 30px;
}

h3,
.h3 {
  font-size: 24px;
}

h4,
.h4 {
  font-size: 18px;
}

h5,
.h5 {
  font-size: 14px;
}

h6,
.h6 {
  font-size: 12px;
}

/* Group 1c — the two contextual colour utilities with a ported site.
   !important matches the successor's own utilities, which carry it; without it
   the override loses. text-info is deliberately absent: both of its source
   sites are in views removed with the external-login challenge surface. */
.text-danger {
  color: #b94a48 !important;
}

.text-success {
  color: #468847 !important;
}

/* Group 1d — block-level text metrics: 24 paragraphs, 7 lists, 10 rules, 2 address
   blocks and 1 small element. The hr rule draws the hairline above the footer on
   every page. */
p {
  margin: 0 0 10px;
}

ul,
ol {
  margin-top: 0;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

ul ul,
ol ul,
ul ol,
ol ol {
  margin-bottom: 0;
}

.list-unstyled {
  padding-left: 0;
  list-style: none;
}

hr {
  margin-top: 20px;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-top: 1px solid #eeeeee;
}

small {
  font-size: 85%;
}

address {
  display: block;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  font-style: normal;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

/* Group 1e — the two form elements around a control. `float: none` is written because
   the successor floats its legend and the source does not; the bottom border is the
   hairline under each of the checkout's two legends. The label weight reaches the
   checkout's labels, which are not col-form-label. */
legend {
  display: block;
  float: none;
  width: 100%;
  padding: 0;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
  font-size: 21px;
  line-height: inherit;
  color: #333333;
  border: 0;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #e5e5e5;
}

label {
  display: inline-block;
  margin-bottom: 5px;
  font-weight: bold;
}

/* The source declares this colour through four vendor-prefixed selectors; one standard
   selector covers every browser in the target matrix. The successor's accompanying
   `opacity: 1` is left in place, which is what makes the colour render as declared. */
.form-control::placeholder {
  color: #999999;
}

/* Group 2 — link colour, resting decoration and the focus ring. Both decoration halves are required: the
   successor underlines links at rest and drops the underline on hover, which is the
   inverse of the source, on every link in the application. */
a {
  color: #428bca;
  text-decoration: none;
}

a:hover,
a:focus {
  color: #2a6496;
  text-decoration: underline;
}

/* The source's own focus ring, preserved rather than dropped: this is the indication
   every link in the application has today (bootstrap.css:348-352). Both `outline`
   declarations are kept in the source's order — the keyword form wins in the engines
   that recognise it, the `thin dotted #333` form is the fallback for the rest. */
a:focus {
  outline: thin dotted #333;
  outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color;
  outline-offset: -2px;
}

/* Approved delta D-35 (section 11.5): the ring is narrowed to keyboard focus. `:focus`
   matches a pointer click as well, so the source draws the ring after a mouse click
   too; suppressing it for pointer interaction is a visible change to an existing
   behaviour and is owned as such. This is the one rule in this stylesheet permitted
   to remove a focus ring, and section 8.9 item d2 states the exception explicitly. */
a:focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 0;
}

/* Group 3 — control geometry, type scale and all three input states, so the button
   and input boxes neither move nor change appearance on focus or when disabled. */
.btn {
  padding: 6px 12px;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

.form-control {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: 34px;
  padding: 6px 12px;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #555555;
  vertical-align: middle;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid #cccccc;
  border-radius: 4px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.075);
  transition: border-color ease-in-out 0.15s, box-shadow ease-in-out 0.15s;
}

.form-control:focus {
  border-color: #66afe9;
  outline: 0;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.075), 0 0 8px rgba(102, 175, 233, 0.6);
}

.form-control[disabled],
.form-control[readonly],
fieldset[disabled] .form-control {
  cursor: not-allowed;
  background-color: #eeeeee;
}

/* Not optional: with height pinned at 34px above and no exception here, the
   checkout's address textarea collapses to a single line. */
textarea.form-control {
  height: auto;
}

/* The `input, select, textarea { max-width: 280px }` cap of Content/Site.css:13-17 is
   carried across unchanged by 8.5.5 and is deliberately not restated here. It composes
   with `width: 100%` above: the control fills its column until 280px and then stops,
   which is exactly today's rendering. */

/* Group 4 — table metrics, border structure and palette, for all three tables. The
   source rules the TOP edge of every cell and the successor rules the bottom, so the
   edges are set explicitly rather than only recoloured. */
.table {
  --bs-table-bg: transparent;
  --bs-table-striped-bg: #f9f9f9;
  --bs-table-border-color: #dddddd;
  width: 100%;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.table > :not(caption) > * > * {
  padding: 8px;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  vertical-align: top;
  border-top: 1px solid #dddddd;
  border-bottom-width: 0;
}

.table > thead > tr > th {
  vertical-align: bottom;
  border-bottom: 2px solid #dddddd;
}

.table > thead:first-child > tr:first-child > th {
  border-top-width: 0;
}

/* The stripe is left to the successor's own mechanism, driven by the custom property
   set above, rather than fought with a competing background rule. */

/* Group 5 — the genre list on the store index. The -1px bottom margin is the
   mechanism that collapses adjacent 1px borders into one rule; without it every
   adjacent pair of genres shows a doubled 2px line. */
.list-group {
  padding-left: 0;
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.list-group-item {
  position: relative;
  display: block;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  margin-bottom: -1px;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid #dddddd;
  border-radius: 0;
}

.list-group-item:first-child {
  border-top-left-radius: 4px;
  border-top-right-radius: 4px;
}

.list-group-item:last-child {
  margin-bottom: 0;
  border-bottom-right-radius: 4px;
  border-bottom-left-radius: 4px;
}

/* The successor collapses adjacent borders by removing the top one, through a
   two-class selector that outranks the single-class `border` above. Left alone, every
   genre after the first loses its top rule and the -1px margin pulls its opaque
   background over the rule above it, so no line renders between rows at all. No state
   rule is written: the source's own hover, focus and active rules match nothing here
   (the anchor is inside the <li>, and no item is active), and `list-group-item-action`
   is deliberately not applied. */
.list-group-item + .list-group-item {
  border-top-width: 1px;
}

/* Group 6 — navbar height arithmetic (15 + 20 + 15 = 50) and both backgrounds.
   The !important matches the successor's background utilities, which carry it. */
.navbar {
  min-height: 50px;
  padding-top: 0;
  padding-bottom: 0;
}

.navbar-brand {
  padding: 15px 15px;
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 20px;
}

.navbar-nav .nav-link {
  padding: 10px 15px;
  line-height: 20px;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-nav .nav-link {
    padding-top: 15px;
    padding-bottom: 15px;
  }
}

.navbar.bg-dark {
  background-color: #222222 !important;
}

/* Scoped to the footer element rather than to .navbar, because the footer no longer
   carries that class — see group 13. It is the only bg-light consumer in the
   application. */
footer.bg-light {
  background-color: #f8f8f8 !important;
}

/* Navbar states. The resting #ddd comes from the rewritten Site.css selectors of
   section 8.5.5; everything below is the library's, and is lost with the class the
   library keyed it on. The hover underline is group 2's `a:hover` and needs no rule
   here — it is the successor's `.nav-link { text-decoration: none }` that loses, on
   specificity. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-brand:hover,
.navbar-dark .navbar-brand:focus,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link:hover,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link:focus {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* The genre toggle while its menu is open: the successor whitens the text and drops
   the panel behind it, so the darkened toggle disappears. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .show > .nav-link,
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.show {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #080808;
}

/* No MVC 5 view applies the active or disabled nav-link states; pin both so any
   runtime-applied state retains source styling. */
.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.active {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #080808;
}

.navbar-dark .navbar-nav .nav-link.disabled {
  color: #444444;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* The collapsed panel's divider and inset highlight, visible only below 768px. The
   media query reproduces the source's own neutralization above that width. */
.navbar-collapse {
  border-top: 1px solid #101010;
  box-shadow: inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-collapse {
    border-top: 0;
    box-shadow: none;
  }
}

/* The toggler's box. Its glyph is D-05's, not this group's. */
.navbar-toggler {
  padding: 9px 10px;
  margin-top: 8px;
  margin-right: 15px;
  margin-bottom: 8px;
  background-color: transparent;
  border: 1px solid #333333;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

.navbar-toggler:hover,
.navbar-toggler:focus {
  background-color: #333333;
}

/* Group 7 — the horizontal form layout `form-horizontal` used to supply. The ported
   markup carries `col-form-label` on each of the 21 labels inside the seven horizontal
   shapes; the alignment stays inside the source's own breakpoint so the narrow
   viewport keeps its stacked, left-aligned labels. */
.col-form-label {
  padding-top: 7px;
  padding-bottom: 0;
  margin-top: 0;
  margin-bottom: 0;
  font-weight: bold;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .col-form-label {
    text-align: right;
  }
}

/* Group 8 — the showcase band. `jumbotron` is gone from the library and retained as an
   application-owned class with the markup unchanged. Content/Site.css's transparent
   background folds in here as the background-color declaration. */
.jumbotron {
  padding: 30px;
  margin-bottom: 30px;
  font-size: 21px;
  font-weight: 200;
  line-height: 2.1428571435;
  color: inherit;
  background-color: transparent;
}

.jumbotron h1 {
  line-height: 1;
  color: inherit;
}

.jumbotron p {
  line-height: 1.4;
}

.container .jumbotron {
  border-radius: 6px;
}

@media screen and (min-width: 768px) {
  .jumbotron {
    padding-top: 48px;
    padding-bottom: 48px;
  }

  .container .jumbotron {
    padding-right: 60px;
    padding-left: 60px;
  }

  .jumbotron h1 {
    font-size: 63px;
  }
}

/* Group 9 — the horizontal description list on the administration detail page,
   retained as an application-owned class with the markup unchanged. The geometry stays
   inside the source's own breakpoint so the narrow viewport keeps term-above-definition.
   `margin-bottom: 0` on the definitions cancels a bottom margin the successor's base
   `dd` carries and the source's does not. */
.dl-horizontal {
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}

.dl-horizontal dt,
.dl-horizontal dd {
  line-height: 1.428571429;
}

.dl-horizontal dt {
  font-weight: bold;
}

.dl-horizontal dd {
  margin-bottom: 0;
  margin-left: 0;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .dl-horizontal dt {
    float: left;
    width: 160px;
    overflow: hidden;
    clear: left;
    text-align: right;
    text-overflow: ellipsis;
    white-space: nowrap;
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd {
    margin-left: 180px;
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd::before,
  .dl-horizontal dd::after {
    display: table;
    content: " ";
  }

  .dl-horizontal dd::after {
    clear: both;
  }
}

/* Group 10 — the two controls that become <button> elements under items a6 and a7 of
   section 8.9 but must keep rendering as the inline links they are today. The
   appearance reset is required because `background: none` alone does not remove the
   platform button chrome on every engine. Applied as
   `<button type="button" class="RemoveLink link-button">` on cart removal, keeping
   RemoveLink for the script's selector, and `<button type="submit" class="link-button">`
   on sign-out. */
.link-button {
  padding: 0;
  font: inherit;
  line-height: inherit;
  color: #428bca;
  text-align: inherit;
  text-decoration: none;
  cursor: pointer;
  background: none;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 0;
  -webkit-appearance: none;
  appearance: none;
}

.link-button:hover,
.link-button:focus {
  color: #2a6496;
  text-decoration: underline;
  background: none;
}

/* One generic rule cannot serve both consumers. The rule above is the cart-removal
   control's, in a table cell, where the body link colour is correct. The sign-out
   control sits between #ddd nav links, so it takes their colour and their box instead;
   only the properties that differ are restated, so the appearance reset, the pointer
   cursor and the hover underline still come from the base rule. Scoped by ancestry
   rather than by an extra class, so it holds whether or not the button also carries
   nav-link. */
.navbar-nav .link-button {
  display: block;
  padding: 10px 15px;
  line-height: 20px;
  color: #ddd;
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .navbar-nav .link-button {
    padding-top: 15px;
    padding-bottom: 15px;
  }
}

.navbar-nav .link-button:hover,
.navbar-nav .link-button:focus {
  color: #ffffff;
}

/* Group 11 — the genre dropdown. Hover is white on the link blue rather than the
   successor's pale grey, and item padding differs on both axes. The library's own two
   focus suppressions — `outline: 0` on the active item and on .dropdown-toggle:focus —
   are deliberately not reproduced; section 8.9 item d2 exists to remove them. */
.dropdown-menu {
  padding: 5px 0;
  margin: 2px 0 0;
  font-size: 14px;
  background-color: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15);
  border-radius: 4px;
  box-shadow: 0 6px 12px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.175);
}

/* Flattened against the navbar it hangs from, as the source flattens it. */
.navbar-nav .dropdown-menu {
  margin-top: 0;
  border-top-left-radius: 0;
  border-top-right-radius: 0;
}

.dropdown-item {
  display: block;
  padding: 3px 20px;
  font-weight: normal;
  line-height: 1.428571429;
  color: #333333;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

.dropdown-item:hover,
.dropdown-item:focus,
.dropdown-item.active,
.dropdown-item:active {
  color: #ffffff;
  background-color: #428bca;
}

.dropdown-item.disabled,
.dropdown-item:disabled {
  color: #999999;
  cursor: not-allowed;
  background-color: transparent;
}

/* Group 12 — the Remember-me control's wrapper and label. The control's own rendering
   is `D-36` and is not pinned here. The label's weight is the declaration
   that would otherwise be silently wrong: group 1e pins `label { font-weight: bold }`
   from the source's base rule, and the source overrides it to normal for this label. */
.form-check {
  display: block;
  min-height: 20px;
  padding-left: 20px;
  margin-top: 10px;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
  vertical-align: middle;
}

.form-check-input {
  float: left;
  margin-left: -20px;
}

.form-check-label {
  display: inline;
  margin-bottom: 0;
  font-weight: normal;
  cursor: pointer;
}

/* Group 13 — the footer, which drops the `navbar` class because the successor's navbar
   is a flex container and this element's two children are blocks. `fixed-bottom`
   supplies the positioning and `bg-light` the background (group 6); the declarations
   below are the ones `.navbar` and `.navbar-fixed-bottom` used to supply. */
footer.fixed-bottom {
  min-height: 50px;
  margin-bottom: 0;
  border-width: 0 0 1px;
  border-style: solid;
  border-color: #e7e7e7;
}
```

**One acceptance rule governs all twenty-five preserved rows — the twenty-seven rows above less the two
approved changes, the withdrawn `text-error` entry and `D-34` — and it is about the criterion rather than
the mechanism.**
Two of the twenty-five carry a **partial** exception rather than being wholly preserved, and each is split
in a stated place. The resting-link-decoration row preserves the focus ring's three values and narrows
only its selector, which is **`D-35`**. The checkbox row preserves the wrapper's and the
label's every metric and hands only the control's own rendering to **`D-36`**. In both cases
the preserved values are held to the criterion below while the named change is held to section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) instead. A successor may apply a property through a mechanism a plain declaration does not override
— a per-component custom property, or a utility carrying `!important`, as `bg-dark` and `bg-light` do.
Where that happens, the **same value** is set through whichever mechanism the pinned build honours. What
does not move is the acceptance criterion: **the measured rendered value against the Bootstrap 3 value
cited in the row**, sampled at both viewports of
[8.5.1](#851-the-breakpoint-and-the-two-viewports) and recorded on the sign-off artifact of section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual). A row is satisfied by the measurement
matching, never by the declaration having been written.

### 8.6 View serving and `_ViewImports`

`Views/Web.config` carries two unrelated constructs and they have opposite fates.

**The `BlockViewHandler` mapping ends, and needs no replacement.**
`<remove name="BlockViewHandler"/>` followed by
`<add name="BlockViewHandler" path="*" verb="*" preCondition="integratedMode" type="System.Web.HttpNotFoundHandler" />`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:31-32] exists to stop `.cshtml` files under `Views/` being
requested directly. **The target does not serve content-root `.cshtml` files at all**, so the behaviour
the handler enforces is the default rather than something to configure. `preCondition="integratedMode"`
is meaningless outside IIS in any case.

**The namespace registration has a direct successor: `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`.** Six namespaces are
imported into every view today [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:14-21]. **Three survive and
three are dead:**

| Namespace | Line | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `System.Web.Mvc` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:15] | **Survives, remapped** to the target's MVC namespace |
| `System.Web.Mvc.Ajax` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:16] | **Dead.** The unobtrusive-Ajax helper family does not exist in the target, and **no view uses it** — there is no `@Ajax.` call anywhere in MVC 5's views |
| `System.Web.Mvc.Html` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:17] | **Dead** as a namespace. The `Html` helpers it contained are reached through the view's own `Html` property in the target and need no import |
| `System.Web.Optimization` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:18] | **Dead entirely** — the package has no successor (section [8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler)) |
| `System.Web.Routing` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:19] | **Survives, remapped** to the target's routing namespace — retained only if a ported view actually references a routing type; **verify during the port and drop it if none does**, rather than carrying an unused import forward |
| `MvcMusicStore` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:20] | **Survives** as the application root namespace, and `MvcMusicStore.Models` is added alongside it, since every strongly-typed view names a model under it — for example [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:1] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:1] |

`_ViewImports.cshtml` additionally registers the framework's tag helpers, which the source has no
equivalent of and which sections [7.1](#71-the-policy) and
[8.1](#81-bundling-and-static-assets--no-bundler) both depend on. The Razor host and page-base-type
registration [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:12-13] and the `configSections` group that declares them [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:4-9] **end**: the
configuration section does not exist in the target and the base type is a framework concern rather
than an application one. `Views/_ViewStart.cshtml` ports unchanged.

The redundant `webpages:Enabled` key [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Web.config:26] ends with the rest of the Web Pages surface (section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)).

### 8.7 The JSON contract — annotate one model, not the policy

The cart-removal endpoint returns a view model with five **PascalCase** properties — `Message`,
`CartTotal`, `CartCount`, `ItemCount`, `DeleteId`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/ViewModels/ShoppingCartRemoveViewModel.cs:5-9] — populated at
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:73-81] and returned as
`return Json(results)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:83].

The page's JavaScript reads **exactly those PascalCase names** — **five distinct properties across seven
reads**: `data.ItemCount` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:21], `data.DeleteId`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:22], `data.DeleteId` and `data.ItemCount` again on the same line [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:24], `data.CartTotal` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:27],
`data.Message` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:28] and `data.CartCount` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29]. Line 24 carries **two** of the seven, which is why the
read count exceeds the property count by two rather than by one:
`$('#item-count-' + data.DeleteId).text(data.ItemCount);` selects by one property and writes the other.
[12 F-12-16](12-migration-blockers.md) states the same five and seven.

**The target's default web serializer camel-cases property names, and the failure is silent.** After
the port the request still succeeds, the response is still 200, the JSON is still well-formed — and
every one of those reads evaluates to `undefined`. The row does not fade out [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:22], the count does not
update [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:24], the total does not change [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:27], the message stays empty [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:28] and the header badge stops
tracking [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29]. **No error occurs, so nothing is logged.**

**One of those seven reads has a second problem this section does not own.** `data.CartCount` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29] is
written to an element **no view emits**, and the quantity it carries is not the quantity the server
renders — so fixing the property name alone leaves that read working and still landing nowhere. The
element, the rendered format and the single count definition are specified in section
[8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract), and the **payload is unchanged by that
decision**: its five property names and their meanings are preserved exactly as this section requires,
and the alignment happens on the component's side. Nothing is added to the response.

**Get the attribution right, because the wrong attribution produces the wrong fix.** The serializer
producing PascalCase today is `JavaScriptSerializer`, by way of MVC 5's `JsonResult` — **not**
Newtonsoft.Json, which is pinned as a package but never called from application source.
[12 F-12-16](12-migration-blockers.md) establishes both facts with its command; this document does not
re-derive them. The consequence is that **removing Newtonsoft.Json is the removal of an unused
dependency, not a serializer replacement** ([04 §8.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns that
outcome).

**Resolution: annotate that one response model with explicit JSON property names. Do not change the
application-wide serializer policy.** [12 §7.3](12-migration-blockers.md) records the choice as 05's;
it is taken this way for three reasons:

1. **The affected surface is exactly one endpoint and one model.** There is one `Json(...)` return in
   the entire migration source, at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:83].
2. **A global PascalCase policy would be a decision about every future endpoint**, taken to
   accommodate one 2013-era script — precisely the kind of application-wide default that section
   [6](#6-authentication-policy-is-decided-not-inherited) argues against inheriting silently.
3. **The annotation is local, visible and self-documenting**: a reader of the model sees why the names
   are pinned, whereas a serializer option in `Program.cs` is invisible from the model and from the
   script.

The alternative of changing the JavaScript to read camelCase was considered and **not** taken: it
would work, but it changes the client and the server contract at once for no gain, and the annotation
keeps the wire format byte-identical to the baseline — which is what lets the same assertion run
against both runtimes in section [12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage).

**The test asserts on property names and values, not merely on a 200** (section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)) — a status-only assertion is exactly what this failure passes.

### 8.8 The checkout input model — ten properties, not nine

`TryUpdateModel(order)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:29] is applied to an
`Order` constructed one line earlier [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:28], inside a POST action whose parameter is a raw
`FormCollection` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:26]. What makes the call safe today is a **separate** construct: a class-level
attribute on the entity,
`[Bind(Include = "FirstName,LastName,Address,City,State,PostalCode,Country,Phone,Email")]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8]. That include list is the **entire** over-posting control at
checkout ([09 §6.4](09-security-assessment.md) owns the consequence), and both halves have to move
together.

**Both halves fail to compile in the target.** Only the asynchronous overload,
`TryUpdateModelAsync`, exists — so [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:29] does not compile — and `[Bind(Include = ...)]` is superseded
by explicit binding models, so the attribute at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] has no target either.

**Resolution: `Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs`, carrying TEN properties.** Nine is the number written
down in the repository and **ten is the number the action actually reads**:

- **Nine** from the `[Bind]` include list [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8]: `FirstName`,
  `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`, `Phone`, `Email`. Each carries its
  existing DataAnnotations attributes across verbatim — `[Required]`, `[StringLength]`,
  `[DisplayName]`, `[DataType]` and the email `[RegularExpression]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-61] — so client and server
  validation messages are preserved.
- **The tenth is `PromoCode`**, which the action reads **separately, straight out of the raw form**:
  `values["PromoCode"]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33], compared
  case-insensitively [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-34] against `const string PromoCode = "FREE"` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:12]. It is not on the
  `[Bind]` list because it is not bound at all.

**Two of the ten are unbounded in the source, and the input model closes both** — because "copied across
verbatim" is only safe where an attribute exists to copy. Eight of the nine address properties carry a
`[StringLength]`; **`Email` does not** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61], carrying only
`[Required]`, `[DisplayName]`, `[RegularExpression]` and `[DataType]`, and `PromoCode` carries nothing at
all because it is never a bound property. So today an arbitrarily long email address and an arbitrarily
long promo code both reach the action, the email reaches the insert, and the only ceiling on either is
the request-body limit — which is the framework's 30 MB default (section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract)).

| Property | Bound on the input model | Why that value, and what it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Email` | `[StringLength(254)]`, alongside the existing `[Required]`, `[RegularExpression]` and `[DataType]` copied from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61] | 254 is the longest address an SMTP path can carry, so it rejects nothing a real customer can own. **The bound is on the input model and the column keeps whatever width the source database has** — and that width is **not asserted here**. The source declares no `MaxLength` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61] and the source context declares no `OnModelCreating` at all (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)), so nothing in tracked repository content states the physical width; EF 6's unfaceted-`string` convention makes `nvarchar(max)` the **expected** result, and no MVC 5 DDL exists to confirm it ([12 F-12-22](12-migration-blockers.md) owns that absence). **Step 1's `sys.columns` root decides it**, and the baseline model is written to whatever it returns — no `HasMaxLength` where the extracted width is `max`, and an explicit `HasMaxLength(n)` where it is a bounded `n`. Either way the initial migration reproduces the extracted type and the diff gate of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 reports nothing at all, which is the property that does not depend on which branch the extraction takes. **An earlier form of this row narrowed the column to `nvarchar(256)` and recorded the narrowing as a "deliberate schema difference" annotated on that gate; both halves of that are withdrawn**, because step 3 admits **no** annotated exception — an intended target-state change has to ship as a named post-load migration, as the `datetime2` change of section [8.13](#813-timestamp-semantics--utc-in-the-database-converted-for-display) does — and no such migration is warranted here: the enforced ceiling is the validation attribute, which refuses an overlength value at step 1 of section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) **before** any read or write, so a narrower column would add a second ceiling behind the one that already stops the request and would buy nothing. **Two consequences, stated because they are what the narrowing would have changed:** the load carries the pre-existing population through unaltered, so a source `Order.Email` longer than 254 characters is **neither truncated nor a load failure** — it is historical order data the target displays and never rewrites; and the 254 bound governs every address the *target* accepts, which is the population a stored-width limit could have protected. Narrowing the column is available as a separate decision with its own named post-load migration and an overlength precheck over the loaded rows; this port does not take it, and the closed post-load set of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) therefore stays at three groups |
| `PromoCode` | `[StringLength(16)]` and `[RegularExpression("^[A-Za-z0-9]*$")]`, optional | The only value with any meaning is the four-character constant at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:12], so the bound is generous by an order of magnitude and still refuses everything a promo field is abused for — long payloads, control characters, markup and injection probes. The pattern is stated as a **whitelist** rather than as an escape rule. **Nothing changes about the outcome a customer sees:** a value that fails either attribute redisplays the form with a field message, which is the same branch a no-match promo code already takes in the source [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-36], and the value is **still never persisted** — see the paragraph below. `D-46` part (b) records the one thing that does change here, which is the **status and the timing** of that refusal and not whether an order is placed |

Both bounds are enforced at step 1 of section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract), before the cart is read and before the
transaction opens, so an oversized value produces **no** read, **no** write and — under the
permitted-content rule of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — **no** log record
carrying it. Together with the per-endpoint request and form limits of section
[8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) they are recorded as `D-46` in
section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), because an overlength email that used to place an
order now does not. **The coverage assertion requires the pair.**

**`PromoCode` belongs on the input model and NOT on the `Order` entity.** `Order` has no such property
and must not gain one: its surface is fourteen properties — the nine bound ones, four suppressed with
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` (`OrderId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:11-12], `OrderDate` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:14-15], `Username` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18], `Total`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64]) and the `OrderDetails` navigation [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:66]. Persisting `PromoCode` would store a **transient form
value** as a column, and would appear in the schema diff of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) as a difference — which that section's
step 3 admits under no annotation at all, so it would fail the gate rather than be explained away.

**Ten remains ten: the submission key is neither a bound property of this model nor a transient value.**
Section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) adds a server-generated
`submissionToken` hidden field and a `SubmissionId` column on `Orders`, and neither belongs here:

- **It is not on `CheckoutInputModel`**, but is a separate `[FromForm] string?` action parameter carrying
  the protected token that section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) specifies. This model
  exists to carry exactly what the source action read, which is what makes "ten, not nine" a checkable
  claim against [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] and
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33]; folding a net-new mechanism into it would
  make the count a coincidence. It travels the same way the anti-forgery token does — a hidden field the
  server emits and the handler reads, outside the domain input. **Outbound, the value reaches the view
  through `ViewData` under one `const string` key**, and that `const` is declared **on this type** —
  `SubmissionTokenViewDataKey`, the carrier row of section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) — because this type is the one both the
  action and the strongly-typed view already reference. **A `const` is not a property**, so the count
  above is untouched: ten bound properties, and one compile-time constant that exists so neither end of
  the carrier writes a bare string literal.
- **It *is* persisted on `Order`, and that does not contradict the paragraph above.** The objection to
  persisting `PromoCode` is that it is transient — its value has no meaning once the promo branch has been
  evaluated. The submission key is the opposite: **durability is its entire function**, because the thing
  it protects against is the loss of a commit acknowledgement, and only a committed row can answer that
  question. Its arrival is sequenced so the schema diff still holds — a second migration after the
  baseline, per section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract).

**Why a nine-property model is the dangerous near-miss.** It compiles, binds and persists correctly —
and **silently loses promo-code handling**. The order-completion branch [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:38-55] is guarded by the
promo-code comparison [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-34], so with the value never bound the comparison always fails and **every
checkout returns to the form** at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:36] with no error message and no log entry. **Test valid, invalid
and missing promo-code values** (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)).

Two further changes in the same action:

- **`Order.cs` loses `using System.Web.Mvc`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:4], which exists
  purely to reference that attribute, along with the attribute itself. A model-layer file with an MVC
  dependency is why this port is not confined to `Controllers/`.
- **The bare `catch` is replaced**, and the whole write path around it is specified as one ordered
  contract in section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) — including the
  per-exception-type branches, what may and may not appear in a log record, and the assertion that no
  row is written on any failure path. `catch { return View(order); }`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62] has **no exception variable**: it
  discards the exception, redisplays the view and records nothing, wrapping the entire order
  transaction [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:31-62] ([08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt).

**The checkout path is the one most exposed to the lifetime change, and must be re-verified
explicitly.** It adds the order, resolves the cart, writes order details, empties the cart and calls
`SaveChanges` in one sequence [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44-51] — and it already passes **its own** context into `GetCart` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:47],
so it is *not* an instance of the multi-context problem. What it is exposed to is the change from a
controller-lifetime context to a request-scoped one across a five-step write: the required verification
is that all of order, order details and cart-emptying commit together, and that a failure part-way
leaves **none** of them. The **account cart-migration path** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:30-40] must be re-verified for the same
reason, against the sequence of section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model).

#### 8.8.1 The view rewrite — why changing only `@model` renders `PromoCode` twice

**Designing the input model is half of this change. The view that posts to it is the other half, and it
is the half where a duplicate control appears silently.**
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml` is declared
`@model MvcMusicStore.Models.Order` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:1] and renders the whole Shipping fieldset [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:14-18] with a
**single** call — `@Html.EditorForModel()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:17]. The tenth field is written by hand in the Payment
fieldset [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:19-29]: `@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:24] and `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27], each inside
a `div` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:23], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:26].

**What that single call renders today is nine editors, and the reason is an attribute rather than
anything in the view.** `Order` exposes fourteen members. Four are suppressed with
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` — `OrderId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:11-12], `OrderDate`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:14-15], `Username` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:17-18] and `Total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:63-64] — and `OrderDetails` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:66] is a collection the object
template skips. Nine remain, which is why one untyped call happens to render exactly the nine that
`[Bind]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] also permits. Two independent attribute-driven mechanisms agree by coincidence, and
neither is visible in the view.

**Point `@model` at the ten-property input model and leave `EditorForModel()` in place, and `PromoCode`
renders twice.** It is an ordinary string with no `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]`, so the object template emits
an editor for it — `name="PromoCode"`, `id="PromoCode"` — **inside the Shipping fieldset**, while the
hand-written control [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27] emits a second
input with the same name and the same id. Three consequences, none of which produces an error at build
time:

- **A duplicate `id`.** Invalid HTML, and a `for` attribute can no longer identify one control — so the
  label association this rewrite is supposed to fix (section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b2) cannot be established at all.
- **Two form entries under one key.** The form value provider surfaces both and a simple string target
  receives them combined rather than either one alone. Whatever the exact combining rule, the bound
  value is not `FREE`, so the comparison
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-34] fails and **every checkout returns to
  the form** — the same end state as the nine-property near-miss above, reached by the opposite mistake.
- **One concept labelled twice, in two fieldsets**, one of them headed "Shipping Information"
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:15].

**Decision: `EditorForModel()` is replaced by the nine shipping fields rendered explicitly, and
`PromoCode` is rendered exactly once, in the Payment fieldset.** Element by element — every bare
locator in the table below is a line of
`src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml`:

| Current element | Target |
| --- | --- |
| `@model MvcMusicStore.Models.Order` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:1] | `@model MvcMusicStore.Binding.CheckoutInputModel` |
| `@Html.EditorForModel()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:17] | **Nine explicit fields** in the `[Bind]`-list order [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] — `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`, `Phone`, `Email` — each a `<label asp-for>`, an `<input asp-for>` and a `<span asp-validation-for>` |
| `@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:24] | `<label asp-for="PromoCode">`, whose `for` is derived from the same expression as the input's `id`, fixing the association defect of section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b2 |
| `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27] | `<input asp-for="PromoCode">` plus a `<span asp-validation-for="PromoCode">` the field has never had, rendered **only here** |
| `<div class="editor-label">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:23], `<div class="editor-field">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:26] | **Retained, and repeated around each of the nine explicit fields**, because that is the wrapper shape `@Html.EditorForModel()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:17] puts around every field today. **No stylesheet in the application defines either** — `git grep -n 'editor-label\|editor-field' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content'` returns no match — so the class names carry no appearance and are kept for continuity with the generated markup they replace; what carries the appearance is the `<div>` block formatting, which is exactly what must not change ([8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)) |
| No validation summary at all | `<div asp-validation-summary="ModelOnly">` — see below |
| `@Scripts.Render("~/bundles/jqueryval")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:8] | The two validation `<script>` elements of section [8.1.3](#813-the-rendered-tags-and-every-bundle-path-they-replace), in the required order |
| `@using (Html.BeginForm())` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:11], `<input type="submit">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:31] | Unchanged in shape. The form tag helper emits the anti-forgery token automatically, replacing nothing the view declares today — this view has no `@Html.AntiForgeryToken()`, which is why the checkout write is one of the five unprotected POST actions section [7.2](#72-problem-one--coverage-today-is-partial) counts |

**The rejected alternative, and why.** An editor template for `CheckoutInputModel` that excludes
`PromoCode` — or `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` on the property — would also render nine fields, and it is
rejected: it would leave the view's rendered field set governed by an invisible attribute on a class in
another file, which is precisely the arrangement that makes the current view fragile. Explicit fields
put the nine, their order and their per-field markup where a reviewer of the port can see them, and they
are what section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) b1-b5 attach to.
`EditorForModel()` over the new type is rejected outright, for the duplicate above.

**The field structure is stacked, not horizontal, because that is what this form is today.** This is the
one form in the application that carries no form class —
`Html.BeginForm()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:11] with no
attributes, against the seven `form-horizontal` shapes section
[8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) inventories — and the object template
stacks the label above the field inside two block wrappers. **The target reproduces that shape rather
than re-expressing it in the successor's form utilities**, and the three utilities a Bootstrap 5 port
reaches for by reflex are each rejected for a measured reason: `mb-3` would insert `1rem` between
groups that have **no** vertical gap today, `form-label` would add `0.5rem` under each label where the
source adds none, and `form-control` would replace an unstyled browser control with the library's
`34px`, bordered, rounded box — a visible change on nine fields plus the promo code. The wrappers are
kept, no field class is added, and the fields therefore keep the one constraint that *does* shape them
today, `input, select, textarea { max-width: 280px }`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:13-17], retained by section
[8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list):

```razor
<div class="editor-label">
    <label asp-for="FirstName"></label>
</div>
<div class="editor-field">
    <input asp-for="FirstName" />
    <span asp-validation-for="FirstName"></span>
</div>
```

**The validation span carries no colour class either, and does not need one.** The validation tag
helper emits the same `field-validation-valid` and `field-validation-error` class names the current
markup relies on, and section [8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list) retains the six
`Content/Site.css` rules that style them — including the `#b94a48` the error message renders in
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:20-22], with the valid state hidden outright by
`.field-validation-valid { display: none }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:24-26]. Adding `text-danger` would set the same colour a
second time through a utility carrying `!important`, so the retained rule would no longer be what
governs the message — and the reviewer's colour check in section
[8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) would be measuring the wrong
declaration. The submit control likewise stays unclassed, exactly as it
is today [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:31].

The nine `[Required]`, `[StringLength]`, `[DisplayName]`, `[DataType]` and `[RegularExpression]`
annotations move to the input model verbatim (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)), so each label renders the same text it
renders today — `First Name`, `Last Name`, `Postal Code` and `Email Address` come from `[DisplayName]`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:21], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:26], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:43], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:57] and the other five from the property
names — and each field keeps its current client-side rules. The email message's existing wording,
`"Email is is not valid."` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:59], is carried across **as written**: correcting the doubled word is a
user-visible content change, which belongs to Product rather than to the port.

**The validation summary is `ModelOnly`, chosen from the application's own convention.** The view has
none today — `git grep -n ValidationSummary -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'` matches seven views and **not this
one**, so a model-level failure currently renders no message anywhere on the checkout page. Of those
seven, five use the model-level-only overload and two the all-errors overload, so `ModelOnly` is the
majority convention and it avoids duplicating messages that already render beside their field. It is
also where the model-level error lands: the message the replaced
`catch` adds (section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine)).

**An earlier form of that sentence said *two* model-level errors land here and named the promo-code
rejection as the second. That was wrong, and it is withdrawn rather than qualified**, because it
contradicted an assertion this document also makes. The source's promo-code branch returns the view
**without adding any model error** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-36], the
target adds none either, and **no entry on either register authorizes one** — so on that path the summary
element renders with no error content, and section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 11 asserts exactly
that absence, requiring no `.validation-summary-errors` element on the promo-code redisplay and recording
the silence as a preserved contract. A message there would be a numbered delta, not a consequence of
adding the summary.

**Both redisplay paths return the input model.** `View(order)` appears twice — the promo-code rejection
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:36] and the bare `catch` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:61] — and both must
pass the **input model** instance in the target, not an `Order`. The type has to match `@model`, and
`Order` has no `PromoCode` property to redisplay. One consequence is worth naming because it is an
**addition rather than a change**, registered as **A15** in section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions): today the nine shipping values do repopulate on redisplay, because they
are bound onto the `Order` the view is handed, while the promo-code box re-renders **empty** — nothing
binds `PromoCode`, so neither model state nor the model can supply it to
`@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27]. After
the rewrite it is a bound property and repopulates with the rest. Nothing that works today stops
working.

**In the action, explicit mapping replaces `TryUpdateModel`.** The nine input-model properties are
assigned onto a new `Order`; `Username` and `OrderDate` stay server-set
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:40-41]; `Total` continues to be written by
`cart.CreateOrder(order)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:48]; and `PromoCode` is read from the input model instead of
`values["PromoCode"]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33] and **never persisted**. That mapping — not an attribute — is the
over-posting control in the target, which is the point section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) makes about both halves moving
together.

Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) carries the assertions this rewrite has to satisfy: one control
named `PromoCode` and one only, a label whose `for` resolves to it, the nine fields with their display
names and validation messages, valid / invalid / missing promo-code behaviour, and a redisplay that
retains what the user typed.

### 8.9 Accessibility and interaction-state requirements

**Scope, stated before the list, because the boundary matters.** Every item below is a **static,
checkable requirement on the ported markup**, derived from a named defect or gap in the source. Two
things this section deliberately does **not** do:

- **It does not claim conformance to any accessibility standard.** Conformance cannot be established
  from source: it needs a running application, assistive technology and a contrast tool. The claim this
  section supports is "these requirements are met", and conformance is asserted — if at all — only after
  the **manual accessibility review** that [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries as a task,
  which is separate from the appearance review of section
  [12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) because screenshots cannot verify
  keyboard operation, focus order, announcement or contrast.
- **It does not authorize a redesign.** Where a requirement would change appearance, the change is
  named and bounded: a heading's semantic level changes while its rendered size is held with a type
  utility, a link becomes a button styled to look the same. The no-redesign boundary of section
  [1.2](#12-what-this-document-is-not) holds.

Most of these are **net-new**, because the source has essentially none of them. That is the finding, not
a criticism of the requirement list — and because they are net-new they are **approval-owned rather than
free**: they are rows in the additions register of section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions), with a named owner, and none of them is described in this document
as an improvement that needs no decision.

**Which register each item lands on, stated exhaustively so that "most" is not doing work a count should
do.** There are **23** numbered requirements below — `a1`-`a7` plus `a5b` and `a5c` (9), `b1`-`b5` (5), `c1`-`c5`
(5) and `d1`-`d4` (4) — and each one lands in exactly one of three places:

- **Sixteen are net-new and carried by the additions register** — `a1`, `a2`, `a3`, `a4`, `a5`, `a5b`,
  `a6`, `b2`, `b3`, `b4`, `b5`, `c1`, `c2`, `c3`, `c4`, `c5`. They resolve to **thirteen** rows of
  section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions), because three of those rows each cover a pair:
  `a1`+`a2`, `a5`+`a5b` and `b3`+`b4`.
- **Two change an existing behaviour and are therefore approved deltas, not additions** — `a7` is
  **`D-13`** (the sign-out control), and `d1` is **`D-35`** (the focus ring's presentation preserved
  and its selector narrowed), both in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).
- **Five are on neither register, by kind rather than by omission** — `b1` records a behaviour the source
  **already has** and the port preserves; `d2` is a **prohibition** on the port's own stylesheet; and
  `d3` and `d4` are **measurements** that record ratios against stated thresholds; and `a5c` is a **verification** of markup that `a5b` and addition **A16** already own. None of the five is a
  change, so none needs an approver.

**16 + 2 + 5 = 23**, so every requirement is accounted for exactly once and no item is left as an
unowned improvement.

**Structure and semantics.**

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a1 | **The navbar toggle gets an accessible name and announces its state.** `aria-controls` naming the collapse element's id (the id introduced in section [8.5.3](#853-non-class-markup-that-changes-with-the-library)), `aria-expanded` maintained by the collapse plugin, and an explicit `aria-label` — "Toggle navigation" | `<button type="button" class="navbar-toggle" data-toggle="collapse" data-target=".navbar-collapse">` with three unlabelled `<span>` bars and **no accessible name and no state attribute at all** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15-18] |

With scripting unavailable the anchor reaches a 404, not the catalog, so the element's only real function is disclosure and `role="button"` is what describes it. **The `href` value is nonetheless preserved byte-for-byte**: repairing it is a behaviour change no entry on either register authorizes, section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s note under the matrix records it as a source defect preserved deliberately, and row 9 asserts the literal on **both** fixtures. So the role is added and the destination is not touched — an announced-only change, carried by addition **A7** rather than by a new identifier. The misapplied form class is **dropped** rather than translated (section [8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens)) | `<h3>` page heading [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:6] with **no `<h1>` anywhere on the page**, jumping to `<h5 class="control-label">` per album [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:19] |
| a5 | **All three data tables get an accessible name and explicit structure**, and **two different defects are being fixed**, so the treatment differs by table. For the two tables that *have* header cells: a `<caption>` or `aria-label`, `<thead>` around the header row, `<tbody>` around the data rows, `scope="col"` on every header cell, and a name for the empty action-column header rather than a blank. For the third — see the row below, because it has no header cells at all and its treatment is deliberately narrower | The cart table is `<table id="cart-summary" class="table table-striped">` with a bare `<tr>` of `<th>` elements, **no `<thead>`, no `<tbody>`, no `scope`, no caption**, and an empty `<th></th>` for the remove column [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:47-59]. | # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| b1 | **Every field's label is programmatically associated with its control.** In the ported forms this follows from `<label asp-for>` plus `asp-for` on the input, which derive the same name | 22 `control-label` sites, all of which do associate today via the typed helpers |
| b2 | **The promo-code label association is fixed.** `<label asp-for="PromoCode">` and `<input asp-for="PromoCode">` in section [8.8.1](#881-the-view-rewrite--why-changing-only-model-renders-promocode-twice)'s rewrite derive the same identifier, so the association exists for the first time | **`@Html.Label("Promo Code")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:24] emits a `for` derived from the string `"Promo Code"`, while `@Html.TextBox("PromoCode")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:27] emits `id="PromoCode"`.** The space guarantees the two values differ, so **there is no label association on this field today.** It is therefore an **addition rather than a change** — nothing that works today stops working, because nothing works today — and it is registered as **A10** in section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) rather than left as an unowned improvement |
