**The cart interaction — announcement, pending, failure and focus.** This is the one interactive surface
in the application, and it currently has none of the four.

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| c1 | **The status message is announced.** `role="status" aria-live="polite"` on the message container, with the cart count either updated inside that region or itself announced | `<div id="update-message"></div>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44-45] is written by script [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:28] with **nothing announced**; the cart count is written to `#cart-status` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29] — an element **no view emits**, which section [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract) supplies |
| c2 | **A pending state exists.** The control is disabled and carries `aria-busy="true"` while the request is in flight, and is re-enabled on completion — success or failure. **Net-new**: the source's handler has no pending state, so a double-click posts twice | `$.post(…)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17-31] with a success callback and nothing else |
| c3 | **Failure is handled and announced.** A visible error message in the live region of c1 on a failed or rejected request, and the row left unchanged. **Net-new, and the most consequential item in this table**: the source handler has **no failure path at all** — no `.fail`, no `error` callback, no status check — so a rejected removal (including one rejected by the anti-forgery validation of section [7](#7-anti-forgery--three-separate-problems)) is **completely silent** and the user believes the item was removed | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:17-31] |
| c4 | **Focus is managed across the removal, to one deterministic destination.** The removed row is faded out while focus sits on the control inside it, so focus is destroyed with the row and lands on `<body>`. **The destination is the status container of c1, and it is made focusable to be one**: `<div id="update-message">` gains `tabindex="-1"` alongside c1's `role="status" aria-live="polite"`, and the script moves focus to it **in the `fadeOut` completion callback**, after the row is gone. `tabindex="-1"` is not optional decoration — **without it a `.focus()` call on a `<div>` does nothing at all**, focus stays on `<body>`, and the code reads as if it managed focus while doing nothing, which is the same silent failure the source already has. **There is no branch for the last row**: the container sits outside the table [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44-45] and is present whether or not any row remains, which is exactly why it is chosen over "the next actionable element" — that alternative needs a fallback for the emptied table and moves focus to a control whose position shifts under the user. One interaction between c1 and c4 is resolved rather than left open: if the interaction-state pass finds the message announced **twice** — once by the live region and once as the newly focused element's name — the remedy is to move focus **before** writing the message text, so the live region announces the change once; the pass records which ordering was used | `$('#row-' + data.DeleteId).fadeOut('slow')` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:22], with no focus handling of any kind, and `<div id="update-message">` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44-45] carrying **no `tabindex`**, so it cannot receive focus even if a port called `.focus()` on it |
| c5 | **Animation respects a reduced-motion preference.** The fade is suppressed under `prefers-reduced-motion` | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:22] |

**Focus visibility and colour — checked, never asserted.**

| # | Requirement | Source position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| d1 | **The focus indication on album links is restated and narrowed — it is not created.** Three things together: the source's own ring is **preserved** by group 2 of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses); its selector is **narrowed** to keyboard focus, which is **`D-35`** (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)); and album links additionally get an explicit `:focus-visible` rule carrying the same shadow the source gives on `:hover`, so the focused state on those anchors reads the way the hovered state does. The underline-suppressing rule is **retained**, not deleted (section [8.5.5](#855-contentsitecss--the-named-change-list)). **Because this changes an existing behaviour rather than adding one, it sits on the deltas register and not on the additions register** — an earlier reading of this item had it the other way round | `ul#album-list li a, ul#album-details li a { text-decoration: none }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:61-63] removes the underline, and the shadow appears on `:hover` only [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:65-70]. **A focused album link is nonetheless indicated today**: the library's global `a:focus { outline: thin dotted #333; outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color; outline-offset: -2px }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:348-352] applies to it, and neither of the two application rules above declares an `outline` property, so nothing cancels it |
| d2 | **No rule removes the framework focus ring for keyboard focus, and the single pointer-only exception is named.** Stated as a prohibition because it is the most common way a port loses keyboard visibility, and the application stylesheet is small enough to verify by reading. **The one permitted rule is `a:focus:not(:focus-visible) { outline: 0 }`** — group 2 of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses), owned as **`D-35`** — which suppresses the ring for a pointer click only and leaves keyboard focus indicated. A rule that removes the ring for `:focus-visible`, or one that removes it unconditionally, fails this item | 86 lines [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:1-86], none of which does this today. The **library** does, on two selectors — `.dropdown-toggle:focus { outline: 0 }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:3231-3233] and `.open > a { outline: 0 }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:3313-3315] — which is why the prohibition is written against the port's own stylesheet rather than against "the source" as a whole |
| d3 | **Three colour pairs are measured with a contrast tool at implementation time, against a stated numeric threshold, and the measured ratios are recorded in the review artifact.** The pairs: **(i)** `#ddd` navbar text and brand on the navbar background [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:72-82], the background being the `#222222` preserved by section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses); **(ii)** `#b94a48` validation text on the page background [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:20-22], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/Site.css:36-38]; **(iii)** the button label against its fill, which is new to this list because **`D-34`** changes that fill from white-with-dark-text to a solid secondary — the one pair whose value the port itself moves. **The thresholds are the pass criteria: 4.5:1 for normal-size text, and 3:1 for large-scale text — 24px, or 18.66px when bold — and for the visual boundaries of user-interface components.** All three pairs above are normal-size text at their rendered sizes, including the 18px navbar brand [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:4194-4199], so all three are measured against **4.5:1**; the button's own border against the page background is measured against **3:1** as a component boundary. **A threshold on named pairs is an objective acceptance check and is not a conformance claim** — this section still asserts nothing about any standard as a whole (see the scope note above), and the artifact records ratios, not a verdict on the application | as cited |
| d4 | **One further pair is measured and reported without blocking**: the `#cccccc` input border [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:1719-1733] against the white page background, a component boundary whose threshold is 3:1. It is separated from d3 because it is **preserved source appearance** — section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) pins that border deliberately — so a failure here is an **inherited** defect the measurement surfaces, recorded with a named owner and a proposed replacement value, and it does **not** fail the port. This distinction exists so the review can separate a contrast defect the port *introduced* from one it faithfully preserved, and so neither gets hidden by the other | as cited |

**Acceptance is split by what kind of fact each item is**, because half of this list is checkable by a
machine and half is not, and conflating the two is how an accessibility requirement ends up unverified.

| Kind of fact | Items | Where it is established |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Attributes and structure in the rendered response** | **a1**, **a3**, **a4**, **a5**, **a5b**, **a6**, **b2**, **b3**, **c1** | **Per item, and an earlier form of this cell put all nine on row 28 alone.** Row 28 is the **cart page**, so it establishes the three that render there: **a1** the navbar toggle, which the layout renders on that page as on every other, **a6** the removal control, and **c1** the status region. The other six render elsewhere and are asserted where they render, all in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage): **a3** the showcase image, **row 30**, the home page; **a4** the catalog heading sequence, **row 1** cases `1a` and `1b`; **a5** the two *headed* data tables, **row 87** `87a` for the cart table and **row 15** `15a` for the administration album list; **a5b** the Registered Logins table, **row 22** `22h` — the *populated* case, since the table exists only when the account has a linked login, and **not row 32**, which is an administration-authorization case on which that table does not appear at all; **b2** the promo-code label, **row 88**, the checkout form as rendered; and **b3** the `aria-describedby` association, **row 67**, whose 41 invalid cases are the only place a field error is rendered |
| **Attributes on a *conditional* render** | **a2** (the dropdown's `role` and menu-item classes), **b4** (`aria-invalid` on a failed field), **b5** (the validation summary) | Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage), and two of the three targets are corrections: **a2** within **row 9**, the genre menu as the layout renders it; **b4** within **row 67**, whose invalid cases are the only ones that produce a failed field for the attribute to appear on — and **not row 31**, which injects a persistence failure and renders no field error at all; and **b5** in two halves, the summary *element* on **row 88** and the summary *populated* on **row 67** — and **not row 30**, which is the home page and carries no form |
| **Already covered by an owned decision** | **a7** (the sign-out control, `D-13`), **b1** (label association through the typed helpers) | Row 20 and the form rows of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) |
| **Runtime behaviour** | **c2**, **c3**, **c4**, **c5** | The **interaction-state pass** of the manual review, [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md). A response-level suite cannot observe a disabled state, an announcement, a focus move or a suppressed animation |
| **Rendered appearance and measurement** | **d1**, **d2**, **d3**, **d4** | The same manual review. **d3**'s three ratios and **d4**'s one are recorded **as measured values against their stated thresholds** — 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for component boundaries — so a failure is a defect with a named owner rather than a silent pass, and d4's failure is reported as inherited rather than as a port regression |

**No row of that table asserts conformance to a standard**, and
[07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) is explicit that its artifact records **requirements met**, not
conformance.

### 8.10 Absent album art — the rendering rule

**This section exists because the write path keeps a field optional and the read path has never defined
what an empty one looks like.** `Album.AlbumArtUrl` carries `[DisplayName("Album Art URL")]` and
`[StringLength(1024)]` and **no `[Required]`** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:26-28], and
[06 §3.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) preserves that optionality explicitly rather than letting
a security validator turn it into a mandatory field. Preserving the write side raises the read side as a
question this document owns: **three views render the value, and today they do not agree with each other
about an album that has none.**

| Render site | What the source does with an absent value |
| --- | --- |
| `<img alt="@album.Title" src="@Url.Content( @album.AlbumArtUrl)" />` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Index.cshtml:15] | **Unguarded.** An `<img>` element is emitted whatever the value is, with its `src` being whatever `Url.Content` returns for a null, empty or whitespace-only path — which cannot be a resolvable image path, so the element resolves to no image |
| `@if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(album.AlbumArtUrl)) { <img … /> }` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:15-18] | **Guarded, and the guard omits the element entirely** — the anchor renders with the title heading [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Browse.cshtml:19] and no image at all. The guard is `String.IsNullOrEmpty`, so a **whitespace-only** value takes the unguarded branch and behaves like the two sites above |
| `<img alt="@Model.Title" src="@Url.Content(@Model.AlbumArtUrl)" />` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Store/Details.cshtml:10] | **Unguarded**, exactly as the home page is |

So the source has **no defined absent-image presentation**: one site omits the image, two emit an image
element that cannot resolve, and the guard that exists misses one of the three forms of absence. That is
a gap rather than a contract, which is why the target states a rule instead of preserving a behaviour.

**The target rule, applied identically at all three sites.** The condition is
`String.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(album.AlbumArtUrl)` — the same test
[06 §3.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s validator applies, so the write side and the read side
classify absence the same way and a value the validator accepted as absent renders as absent. When the
condition holds, the view renders the placeholder asset already in the served inventory —
`wwwroot/images/placeholder.png`, relocated by section
[8.1.1](#811-the-per-file-disposition-of-the-27-source-assets) — and keeps the album title as its `alt`,
so the image alternative stays meaningful and requirement **a3** of section
[8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) is not undermined by a second unlabelled
image. When the condition does not hold, the stored value is rendered exactly as it is today. **No new
artifact is added**: the placeholder is one of the five images section 8.1.1 already relocates, so the
served total of 13 files is unchanged.

**It is an approved delta, not a silent improvement**, and it is `D-37` of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas). Two of the three sites change what they render for an album
with no image path — from an image element that resolves to nothing into a placeholder image — and the
third changes from rendering nothing into rendering the placeholder. Every one of those is visible on the
page, which is precisely the class of change that needs an owner rather than an implementer's judgement.
**Product** owns it, and the alternative the owner can choose instead is stated so the decision is real:
omit the element at all three sites, matching the catalog view's current guard, which preserves one of
the three source behaviours and leaves a ragged grid where an album has no art.

**How much of the committed data this touches: none.** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) W5's measured
baseline is **one distinct value** across the catalog and it is the local placeholder path, so no album in
the committed database renders through this rule on day one. It governs future administrator input and
any non-committed source database the migration is pointed at — the same scope
[06 §3.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) gives its `http://` branch, and for the same reason.

Coverage is section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 33, which asserts the blank-save-then-render path
end to end rather than only the validator.

### 8.11 The administration input models — the entity stops being a binding target

Checkout is not the only place an entity is bound from the request. **Administration binds the `Album`
entity directly, with no include list at all**, and that is the one over-posting exposure in the
repository with no control whatsoever:
`public ActionResult Create(Album album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:54]
and `public ActionResult Edit(Album album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:87].
[09](09-security-assessment.md) F-09-27 records the finding and **hands the resolution to this
document**; this section is that resolution.

**What the binder will accept today, property by property.** `Album` declares six scalars and three
navigations [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:7-33]:

| Property | Intended to be posted? | What the source does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AlbumId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:10] | **No** on create | `[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:8] suppresses it in *scaffolded views*; it does **not** stop the model binder. A create post naming `AlbumId` sets it |
| `Title` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:18], `Price` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:24], `AlbumArtUrl` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:28] | Yes | Bound, with their validation attributes [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:16-17], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:20-23], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:26-27] |
| `GenreId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:12], `ArtistId` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:14] | Yes | Bound, and **not validated against existing rows** — the referential check is left to the database |
| `Genre` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:30], `Artist` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:31] | **No** | Bound as object graphs. A post carrying `Genre.Name` yields a populated `Genre` instance hanging off the album, and `db.Albums.Add(album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:58] cascades that instance into the change tracker as a **new genre row** |
| `OrderDetails` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:32] | **No** | A collection of order-detail rows, bindable by index and cascaded on `Add` the same way |

**And `Edit` is worse than `Create` in a way that is easy to miss.** `db.Entry(album).State = EntityState.Modified`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:91] applied to a **detached** instance
marks **every scalar** as modified, so any scalar the post omits is written as its CLR default — an
omitted `AlbumArtUrl` becomes `NULL`, an omitted `Price` becomes `0`. The POST action also takes **no
`id` parameter**: the identity of the row being edited comes entirely from the request body, so the
route id displayed in the URL is decorative.

**Resolution: two input models, and the `Album` entity is never a binding target again.** Both live in
`Binding/`, beside `Binding/CheckoutInputModel.cs` — the same pattern, applied to the one other action
pair that binds an entity. No new folder, no new project and no new package.

| Type | Properties | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Binding/AlbumCreateInputModel.cs` | `Title`, `Price`, `AlbumArtUrl`, `GenreId`, `ArtistId` | **Five properties, and no `AlbumId`** — the store assigns the key. The validation attributes are copied across from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:16-27] verbatim, so client-side and server-side messages are preserved exactly |
| `Binding/AlbumEditInputModel.cs` | **`int? AlbumId`**, plus the same five | `AlbumId` is present **deliberately**, not by oversight: the edit form round-trips it in a hidden field [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Edit.cshtml:17], so on this model it is the request's **identity** rather than an over-post. What the action does with it is step 0 of the edit contract below — require it to be present and equal to the route id, and refuse anything else. Two sources of identity that can disagree is a defect whether or not it is exploitable. **It is declared `int?` rather than `int`, and that is a contract rather than a style choice** — the reason is below the edit table, because step 0 cannot otherwise mean what it says |

**Create and edit are not one contract, and treating them as one is how this resolution goes wrong.**
They differ in exactly the property that matters. On **create** the key is **absent from the model and
assigned by the store**, so a posted `AlbumId` must have no effect. On **edit** the key is **required**,
and it arrives from two places that have to agree. A single "the models reject `AlbumId`" rule would be
wrong on the edit side — it would reject the form the application itself renders — and a single "the
models carry `AlbumId`" rule would be wrong on the create side. So each action is specified as its own
ordered contract, and the two shared rules are stated once as **R3** and **R4** below.

**`POST /StoreManager/Create`** —
`[HttpPost] public async Task<IActionResult> Create(AlbumCreateInputModel input, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`:

| Step | What happens | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The `ModelState` gate, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:56] | Both select lists repopulated (R4) and the form redisplayed, as at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:63-65]. Nothing written |
| 2 | `GenreId` and `ArtistId` validated against existing rows (R3) | Model error against that field, select lists repopulated, form redisplayed. Nothing written |
| 3 | A **new** `Album` is constructed and exactly the five permitted properties are assigned to it. `Genre`, `Artist` and `OrderDetails` are never assigned; `AlbumId` is never assigned | — |
| 4 | `Albums.Add(...)`, then `SaveChangesAsync` | The persistence-failure classifier of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| 5 | Redirect to `Index`, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:60] | — |

**A posted `AlbumId` on create is not rejected — it is never bound**, because the model has no such
property and an unmatched form key is ignored without a model error. The observable consequence, which is
what the coverage assertion requires, is that the created row's key is the one **the store** assigned rather than
the one posted. That is what the source *intends* and the opposite of what it does:
`[ScaffoldColumn(false)]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:8] suppresses the field in the
scaffolded view, and `Create.cshtml` accordingly renders only the five
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Create.cshtml:51-54] — but the binder is not governed by the
view, so today a hand-crafted post sets the key.

**`POST /StoreManager/Edit/{id}`** —
`[HttpPost] public async Task<IActionResult> Edit([FromRoute] int id, AlbumEditInputModel input, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`:

| Step | What happens | On failure |
| The two reads are **not** additions to the failure census of section
[4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census): that census is of queries that can fail
on ordinary user input, and a table projection takes no input and cannot fail on one. Its empty-table
behaviour is the fourth preserved property below. | --- | --- |
| 0 | **The two identities are compared before anything else**, as `input.AlbumId.HasValue && input.AlbumId.Value == id` — one expression, evaluated on the nullable property, with presence tested before value | **`BadRequest()`** for anything else — absent, unparseable, or a different value — with **no album loaded, no select list built and no column written** in any table. The empty 400 is re-executed into the generic error page by the status-code middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), so the caller gets a page rather than a blank body, and it is **not** the form |
| 1 | The `ModelState` gate, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:89] | Select lists repopulated (R4) and the form redisplayed, as at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:95-97]. The stored album is unchanged **in every column** |
| 2 | `GenreId` and `ArtistId` validated against existing rows (R3) | As create's step 2 |
| 3 | The row is loaded **tracked**: `FirstOrDefaultAsync(a => a.AlbumId == id)` — census site F3 in section [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census) | **`NotFound()`**, nothing written |
| 4 | The five permitted fields are applied **presence-aware** — the table below. **`Entry(...).State = Modified` is not used** | — |
| 5 | `SaveChangesAsync`, then redirect to `Index`, preserved from [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:93] | The classifier of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |

**Step 0 runs ahead of the `ModelState` gate, and that order is part of the contract.** Behind the gate,
a body whose `AlbumId` is absent or unparseable has already failed validation, so the same request would
be answered with a **200 and a redisplayed form** — reporting a tampered identity as a field message on a
page that invites a retry. Ahead of it, that request is a flat 400 that never reads or writes the store.
The route id is the authority either way: it is the value the administrator sees and the value the URL's
own semantics imply. **The source has no such check at all** — its POST takes no `id` parameter
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:87], so the row it edits is whichever one
the **body** names and the id in the URL is decorative.

**Why the property is `int?`, and why an `int` would make step 0 unable to keep its own promise.** Step 0
says `input.AlbumId` "must be present", and **presence is not representable on a non-nullable `int`**. The
model binder gives an `int` property the type's default for both of the cases step 0 is supposed to refuse:
a key absent from the body binds `0`, and a key present but unparseable — `AlbumId=abc` — also binds `0`,
adding a `ModelState` error the gate at step 1 would see and step 0 runs ahead of. So on an `int`, three
different requests arrive at step 0 as the identical value `0`: the absent one, the unparseable one, and a
body that genuinely posted the literal `0`. The comparison then answers correctly only by accident — it
refuses them because a stored `AlbumId` is never `0`, so `0 != id` for every real route id — and the
accident fails in one specific case: `POST /StoreManager/Edit/0` with an absent or unparseable body
compares `0 == 0`, **passes step 0**, and reaches step 3, which is the one place this contract promised
nothing would be loaded. Nothing is written even then, because step 3's lookup returns `null` and answers
`NotFound()` — so the consequence is a `404` where the contract specifies a `400`, and a store read where
it specifies none. That is a small effect with a specific cause, and the cause is a type that cannot
express absence.

`int?` removes the conflation instead of compensating for it. Absent binds `null`; unparseable binds
`null` with a `ModelState` error nobody consults, because step 0 has already refused it; and a posted
literal `0` binds `0`, which is a **value** and is refused by the comparison rather than by the presence
test — the two failures stay distinct even though both answer `400`. The route id needs no lower-bound
check of its own: with presence handled, a route id of `0` and a body of `0` agree at step 0 and are
refused at step 3 as an album that does not exist, which is the correct answer for that URL. Coverage row
90 asserts all four cases, the literal `0` included, for exactly this reason.

**Presence-aware application (step 4), and why the obvious version of it is wrong.** "Load the row and
assign the five properties" is the natural way to state step 4 and it silently reintroduces the defect
the step exists to close. Four of the five fields are guarded by validation and so can never reach step 4
absent: `Title` and `Price` carry `[Required]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:16,20], and
`GenreId` and `ArtistId` are non-nullable value types, whose absence the framework reports as a missing
required value — all four fail step 1 and redisplay. **`AlbumArtUrl` is the exception, and it is the only
one:** it carries `[StringLength(1024)]` and no `[Required]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Album.cs:26-27], so an absent key binds to `null`,
passes validation, and an unconditional assignment writes `NULL` over a stored value nobody asked to
remove. That is the same erasure as `Entry(...).State = Modified`, reached from the other direction.

| Case | What the request carries | What is applied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Omission** | the key `AlbumArtUrl` is **absent** from the form | **Nothing.** The stored column keeps the value it has |
| **Explicit clear** | the key is **present and empty** — what the rendered form posts when an administrator empties the box | **`NULL`.** `ConvertEmptyStringToNull` is the framework default in the source and in the target alike, so an empty text input binds to `null` and the clear is honoured |
| **New value** | the key is present and non-empty | The bound value, after `[StringLength(1024)]` |

**Presence is read from the request, never inferred from the bound value**, because the first two cases
produce the identical CLR `null` and only the request distinguishes them: the action tests
`Request.Form.ContainsKey(nameof(AlbumEditInputModel.AlbumArtUrl))`. **The ordinary path is untouched by
this rule** — `Edit.cshtml` renders the field on every load
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/StoreManager/Edit.cshtml:52-55], so a browser post always carries the key
and always lands in one of the two lower rows. The rule exists for the hand-crafted post, which is the
only thing that can produce the top row.

**The two shared rules.**

- **R3 — `GenreId` and `ArtistId` are validated against existing rows before the write:**
  `AnyAsync(g => g.GenreId == input.GenreId)` and the artist equivalent. A value with no matching row adds
  a model error **against that field** and redisplays the form. The source defers this to the database,
  where it surfaces as a `DbUpdateException` — classified as `Rejected` by section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) — rather than as a validation message next to the
  offending dropdown.
- **R4 — the select lists are repopulated on every failure path**, preserving the source's behaviour at
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:63-64] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:95-96]. In the target they
  are properties on a view model rather than `ViewBag` entries, for the reason in section
  [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) — a typed member cannot be misspelled at
  the call site — but **the rendered form and its messages are unchanged**.

**Nested over-post graphs are a separate case with a separate test, because they fail for a different
reason from a scalar over-post.** `Genre`, `Artist` and `OrderDetails` are absent from **both** models, so
`Genre.Name` and `OrderDetails[0].Quantity` bind to nothing — and, independently, neither action ever
calls `Add` on a graph: create constructs the entity and assigns scalars, edit mutates a tracked row. Both
halves are load-bearing, because binding is not the mechanism the source's exposure actually runs through:
it is `db.Albums.Add(album)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:58] cascading
whatever the binder attached into the change tracker as **new rows**. The assertion is therefore on **row
counts in `Genres`, `Artists` and `OrderDetails`** before and after, not on the response — a rejected
graph and a silently inserted one answer with the same redirect.

**Nothing changes for an administrator using the form**: the same fields, the same validation messages,
the same redirect. **Five things change for a hand-crafted post**, and each is recorded as its own
approved delta in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — with its own reason and its own
approval owner — rather than presented as an internal fix: the key can no longer be set on create
(**`D-23`**); a route/body id mismatch answers 400 where the source edits whichever row the body named
(**`D-24`**); a nonexistent `GenreId` or `ArtistId` redisplays the form where the source reaches the
database (**`D-25`**); an omitted `AlbumArtUrl` leaves the column alone where the source blanks it
(**`D-26`**); and a posted `Genre`, `Artist` or `OrderDetails` graph inserts nothing where the source
cascades new rows (**`D-27`**). **The coverage assertions in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) assert each of these, one row per delta**: `D-23` is row 40 `40a`, the
create-side key; `D-24` is row 90 over its four refusals, with row 40 `40c` the tampered-key case the
rendered form itself can produce; `D-25` is row 91 `91b`, the two unresolvable foreign keys; `D-26` is
row 40 `40b`, the omitted field; and `D-27` is row 92, the nested graphs on both write paths. Row 91
`91a` carries the presence table's explicit-clear row, which pairs with row 40 `40b`'s omission.

### 8.12 The checkout write path — one ordered contract

Section [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) settles what the checkout action
*binds*. This section settles what it *does*, step by step, because the source's write path spans two
files, has no validation gate, computes a total from two different reads of the same price, copies a
foreign key that does not exist yet, and wraps the whole of it in a `catch` with no exception variable.
**Every branch below is stated; an omitted branch here is an order that either fails silently or
persists something wrong.**

**Target signature.**
`[HttpPost] [RequestSizeLimit(16 * 1024)] [RequestFormLimits(ValueCountLimit = 32, KeyLengthLimit = 128, ValueLengthLimit = 4096, MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0)] public async Task<IActionResult> AddressAndPayment(CheckoutInputModel input, [FromForm(Name = "submissionToken")] string? submissionToken, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`.
The class-level `[Authorize]` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:8] is preserved
as-is; anti-forgery validation arrives from the global filter of section
[7.1](#71-the-policy) rather than from an attribute on the action. The `FormCollection` parameter
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:26] and the `TryUpdateModel` call [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:29]
both disappear. `submissionToken` carries the **submission key** specified immediately below; it is a
separate parameter rather than a property of the input model, for the reason section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) gives.

**The two size limits are part of the signature rather than a footnote — and they are two different
limits, with two different failure statuses, which a single "oversized input is refused" sentence gets
wrong.** The framework's defaults are a 30 MB request body and a form body sized for file upload; the
verified `FormOptions` defaults are `ValueCountLimit` **1,024**, `KeyLengthLimit` **2,048** and
`ValueLengthLimit` **4,194,304**. This endpoint's whole payload is ten short fields, an anti-forgery token
and a submission token — under 2 KB in practice — so both are tightened, and the two tightenings behave
differently:

| Limit | Set here by | Framework default | What a violation produces |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Request body size**, bytes on the wire | `[RequestSizeLimit(16 * 1024)]` | 30 MB | The server refuses the body and the request answers **413**, before form parsing and before model binding. This is the only limit on this endpoint that produces 413 |
| **Form shape** — `ValueCountLimit = 32`, `KeyLengthLimit = 128`, `ValueLengthLimit = 4096`, `MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0` | `[RequestFormLimits(...)]` | 1,024 / 2,048 / 4,194,304 / 128 MB | The **form parser** throws `InvalidDataException` the first time the body is read. That read happens inside the **global anti-forgery filter**, which touches `Request.Form` before model binding, so the request answers **400** — not 413, and **not** a field-level validation message, because no model was ever bound |

The form limits bound the shape as well as the total, because a single 4 MB field and thirty thousand
empty ones are both accepted under a byte ceiling alone, and both cost model binding, validation and — if
the values were echoed or recorded — logging. `MultipartBodyLengthLimit = 0` refuses multipart bodies
outright: this form posts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and has no file input, so multipart is only
ever a probe.

**`ValueLengthLimit = 4096` is a deliberate tightening by three orders of magnitude, and it draws a second
boundary that acceptance tests have to respect.** It sits far above every legitimate field — the longest
is the 254-character `Email` bound of section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) — and far below anything worth calling a
payload. So a field of, say, five thousand characters is a **parser**-boundary case that answers 400 with
no field message, while a field of three hundred characters is a **model**-boundary case that answers 200
with a field message from its `[StringLength]`. Both behaviours are correct and neither substitutes for
the other: a suite that submits five thousand characters and expects a validation message is asserting an
outcome the parser precludes, and one that only ever submits five thousand characters never exercises the
DataAnnotations bounds at all. The coverage assertion requires the two boundaries separately for that reason.

Either refusal is a change from the source, which accepts such a request and answers 200; both are
covered by **`D-46`** in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — 413 for the
byte ceiling, 400 for the form shape — and in both cases no bound value, no cart read and no log record
carrying a payload exists. The same discipline is **not** applied to the account POSTs: they carry no
`[RequestFormLimits]`, so the framework's 4,194,304-character default applies and even a
hundred-thousand-character user name parses and reaches model validation, which is exactly why their
bounds are model-level by design (section
[6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)) and why coverage of
those posts is stated differently: the coverage assertion requires a validation message and a 200 on an
over-long account input, rather than the flat refusal the checkout's byte ceiling produces.

**The submission key, and the reason this path needs one: a throwing commit does not mean nothing was
committed.** The obvious reading of step 8 below — the transaction threw, therefore nothing persisted —
is true of a failed `SaveChangesAsync` and **false of a failure in the commit
`ExecuteInTransactionAsync` performs**. A commit that reached
the server, succeeded there, and whose acknowledgement was then lost to a dropped connection, a
cancelled token or a request timeout raises an exception that is **indistinguishable** from one raised by
a commit that never happened. The client sees the redisplayed form of the failure table, does the only
thing a customer does with a redisplayed checkout form, and **submits again — creating a second real
order for one purchase.** Nothing in the transaction, the retry policy or the catch list can tell the two
apart, because the information needed to tell them apart never arrived. So the write is made
**idempotent** instead, keyed on something durable:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **Generation** | The **server** generates the key — `Guid.NewGuid()` — in the `GET` action, which today returns a bare `View()` with no model [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:17-20] and in the target passes it to the view for a hidden field. It is never taken from a client-supplied value, on a fresh render or on any other |
| **Binding — the key travels as a protected token, not as a bare GUID** | A bare `Guid?` on the wire is **client-chosen state**, and a mechanism keyed on client-chosen state is not a control: a caller can mint one, omit one, or post one that was issued to somebody else. So the hidden field carries a **data-protection protected token** whose payload is the GUID, the **user name it was issued to** and its issue time; the handler unprotects it to obtain the GUID. A token that cannot be unprotected has been tampered with or was produced by a different key ring; a token whose user name is not the authenticated caller's was issued to somebody else; a token older than **24 hours** (absolute, no sliding renewal) belongs to a form nobody is still filling in. **None of the three is accepted**, and none of them requires server-side state to detect — which is what lets the check run on a replica that never rendered the form |
| **Stability across redisplays** | Every redisplay of the form — the `ModelState` failure of step 1, the promo-code no-match of step 2, the empty-cart rejection of step 4 and every row of the failure table — re-renders **the same token that arrived**, so the idempotency window is not closed at the exact moment a customer is most likely to resubmit. A **fresh** token is minted only where there was no valid one to re-render: the `GET` action, and the step-0 rejection below |
| **Persistence** | A nullable `SubmissionId` column on `Orders`, set in step 5 from the unprotected key. **`NULL` is permitted for exactly one reason and one population: rows loaded from the legacy store, which have no key because the source has no such concept.** It is **not** a permitted state for an order the target creates — step 0 rejects a submission with no valid key before any cart work, so there is no path on which the target inserts a `NULL` here. Stating it the other way round is what makes the mechanism bypassable: "a submission that arrives without a key still has to be able to place an order" is precisely the sentence an attacker, and an ordinary double-click, both rely on |
| **The constraint** | A **unique index on `SubmissionId`, filtered to `WHERE [SubmissionId] IS NOT NULL`.** The filter is not optional: SQL Server's unique index treats two `NULL`s as equal, so an unfiltered one would reject the second migrated order. This index is what makes the guarantee a database guarantee rather than an application convention, and it is the only thing that holds under two concurrent submissions of the same key |
| **Schema sequencing** | The column and its index are **net-new target state and therefore arrive in a second catalog migration**, applied after the baseline migration and after the domain data load. They are deliberately **not** in the initial migration, because that migration must match the extracted source schema exactly or the generated-schema diff of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) fails — and it should fail on a real discrepancy, not on this one |
| **Reconciliation on retry** | Step 1a below. A submission whose key already names an order belonging to this caller is **not written again**: it is redirected to that order's confirmation, which is the outcome the customer was owed by the attempt that was lost |
| **The concurrent race** | Two submissions of the same key that overlap cannot both be reconciled by a lookup, because neither has committed when the other reads. One insert wins and the other violates the unique index. That branch is in the failure table below, and it resolves the same way step 1a does — look the key up, redirect to the order that won — rather than as a user-facing error |
| **Rejection, and where it happens** | **Step 0**, ahead of everything: a submission with no token, an unprotectable one, one issued to another user name, or one past its 24-hour lifetime **re-renders the checkout form with a fresh token and one generic model error** — *"Your checkout form has expired. Please review your details and submit again."* — and **reads no cart row, opens no transaction and writes nothing**. The status is 200 and the submitted address values are re-rendered so the customer does not retype them. Two things this is **not**: it is not an anti-forgery control — the global filter of section [7.1](#71-the-policy) has already validated that token, and this one answers a different question — and it is not a security boundary around the order itself, which is `[Authorize]` plus the username predicate of step 1a. It is the guarantee that **every** order the target writes carries a server-issued key, which is what the unique index then makes enforceable |

This is an addition to the source's behaviour with no source analogue: the source has no retry path at
all, since its bare `catch` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62] redisplays
the form and records nothing. Its observable half is recorded as **`D-42`** in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) — a checkout that cannot be persisted, or whose submission
is refused, redisplays the form **with a visible message** and the failure is **recorded**, where the
source redisplays silently and logs nothing — and the retry envelope itself is a mechanism, not a delta.
**An earlier form of this sentence cited `D-20`, and that was the wrong register row**: `D-20` is the
**cart** delta, governing a cart mutation that cannot be applied after `Cart:MaxMutationRetries` on one
line (section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)). The two are
different triggers on different
surfaces with different configured bounds, so a reader approving `D-20` would have been approving a cart
behaviour while believing they had approved a checkout one. Nothing else on this path cites `D-20`.
**The coverage assertion requires it against the exact failure it exists for** — a commit that succeeds on the
server with the acknowledgement lost — and the coverage assertion requires the cancellation route into the same
condition.

**Why the transaction is the execution strategy's and not the caller's — this is a throw, not a
preference.** The catalog context is registered with `EnableRetryOnFailure` (section
[4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model)), and under a retrying execution strategy EF Core
**refuses** a user-initiated transaction: `BeginTransactionAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException`,
because the strategy cannot replay an operation whose transaction boundary it does not own — a retry
would re-run part of the work inside a transaction the caller had already begun or disposed. So the
`await using var transaction = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(...)` shape is not merely
suboptimal here; it fails on the first checkout submission, in every environment, at run time. The
cart-migration path in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model) already wraps its transaction
in the strategy for the same reason, and this path now matches it rather than contradicting it.

**Two retry layers, and the construction rule differs between them — which is the whole of this
sub-section.** The path has an **outer attempt loop the application owns**, bounded by
`Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries` (section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)
requirement 7), and an **inner replay the execution strategy owns** for transient faults. They are not
the same retry and they do not have the same rule:

| Layer | What starts it | What it rebuilds | Bound |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Outer attempt** (application) | The stale-projection condition of step 7 — a short affected count — and nothing else | **Everything**: the attempt opens with the explicit reset `db.ChangeTracker.Clear()`, then re-runs step 4's projection, step 5's and step 6's entity graph and step 7's `(RecordId, RowVersion)` payload against the cart **as it now stands** | `1 + Checkout:MaxConcurrencyRetries` attempts; exhaustion is the handled failure of `D-42` |
| **Inner replay** (`ExecuteInTransactionAsync`) | A transient provider fault, or a commit whose outcome `verifySucceeded` reports as uncommitted | **Nothing.** It re-sends the attempt's already-built graph and the attempt's already-built payload | `1 + Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` executions of the delegate |

**So "rebuilt on every attempt" and "constructed nothing inside the delegate" are both true, and neither
is a caveat on the other.** The reprojection the stale-row branch requires is not a special case bolted
onto one branch: it is what every outer attempt does, because an outer attempt begins by discarding the
previous attempt's tracked state and reading the cart again. The delegate the strategy replays sits
**inside** one attempt and therefore constructs nothing, for the reason the next paragraph gives.

**Where the replay boundary falls, and why the order graph is built outside the delegate.**
`ExecuteInTransactionAsync` replays its `operation` delegate on a transient failure, and it replays it
against the **same `DbContext` and the same change tracker** — the strategy resets the connection and the
transaction, never the tracker. Step 8's `acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false` is what makes a replay able to
re-send the work, and it is also what makes the delegate's *contents* consequential: whatever the first
attempt added is **still `Added`** when the second attempt begins. So a delegate that **constructs** the
order graph accumulates rather than repeats. After a failed attempt the tracker already holds one `Added`
`Order` with its `OrderDetail` children; a replay running steps 5 and 6 again would build a **second**
graph, and the replay's single `SaveChangesAsync` would then send **two** order inserts. Both carry the
same `SubmissionId`, so the filtered
unique index of the submission-key table above refuses the second — turning a recoverable transient
failure into a **non-transient unique-index violation** that the strategy does not retry, that the
failure branch answers as a persistence error, and that costs the customer the order it was trying to
save. Were that index ever absent, the same replay would commit **two orders for one submission**, which
is the exact outcome the submission key was introduced to make impossible.

The rule therefore has two parts, and both are asserted rather than trusted:

- **Construction happens once per outer attempt, outside the replayable region, and the attempt opens
  with an explicit context reset.** `db.ChangeTracker.Clear()` is the **first** statement of every outer
  attempt — including the first, where it is a no-op that costs nothing and removes a precondition
  nobody would otherwise assert — and steps 4 through 6 then run before `ExecuteInTransactionAsync` is
  called for that attempt. Step 7's statement is **built** there too: its `(RecordId, RowVersion)` pair
  set is that attempt's own step-4 projection, and a second attempt carries a different pair set because
  it read the cart again. Clearing at the head of the attempt is what makes the rebuild safe — without
  it the previous attempt's `Added` `Order` would still be tracked and the rebuilt graph would be the
  **second** one, which is precisely the accumulation this sub-section exists to prevent. The operation
  delegate contains **only**
  the in-operation submission-key guard of step 3 and step 8's ordered body: it creates no entity,
  mutates no entity, re-projects no cart row and computes no total, so its body is identical on every
  attempt of that delegate **by construction** rather than by care. **Re-running the cart statement on a replay is
  therefore safe, and it is safe for a stated reason rather than by luck**: a replay only happens after a
  failed attempt, a failed attempt's transaction rolled back, and a rolled-back transaction restored the
  rows the statement had deleted — so the same statement matches the same set and the count gate is
  satisfied again. The one case in which the rows would be **gone** is a first attempt that in fact
  committed, and the guard at the head of the delegate catches that before the statement runs.
- **The tracker state at the head of every delegate execution is a named invariant, established rather
  than assumed.** Step 5's explicit `db.Orders.Add(order)` immediately establishes the one `Added`
  principal. The entry-state observation enumerates `ChangeTracker.Entries()` after step 6 — invoking
  automatic change detection — so on entering the wrapper it observes exactly one `Added` `Order`,
  exactly one `Added` `OrderDetail` per billed cart row and
  **no `Cart` entity in any state at all** — the cart emptying is step 7's statement, not tracked state,
  which is itself part of the invariant and is asserted: a `Deleted` `Cart` entry here would mean the
  tracked deletion this path deleted had been reintroduced, and section [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity)
  requirement 2's witness comparison would be silently gone. It holds **that same set** at the head of every
  replay of that delegate, because nothing between replays adds to it and `acceptAllChangesOnSuccess: false`
  prevents a successful-but-uncommitted save from emptying it — and it holds **the next attempt's own set**
  at the head of the next outer attempt, because that attempt cleared the tracker and rebuilt it.
  `db.ChangeTracker.AcceptAllChanges()` is called once,
  after the wrapper returns successfully, and that is the only point at which the invariant is permitted
  to change. **`db.ChangeTracker.Clear()` must not be called inside this delegate** — it would discard
  precisely the work the replay exists to re-send; it is called **only** at the head of an outer attempt,
  where the work it discards is a superseded attempt's. That is the mirror image of the cart-migration
  delegate's requirement in section [4.3](#43-the-cross-store-consistency-model), where the delegate owns
  **no** tracked state and clearing is the safeguard; the two rules differ because the two delegates hold
  opposite kinds of state, and confusing them breaks whichever one borrows the other's rule.

**The coverage assertion's fourth companion assertion is what enforces this**, by observing the tracker's
contents at the head of every attempt and observing that the delegate constructs nothing. It reuses the
existing matrix rather than adding a case: row 10 requires the one persisted order, its generated-key
detail rows, the reconciled total and the emptied cart, while row 99's `DbCommandInterceptor` must observe
the `Orders` and `OrderDetails` inserts before the token-matched cart delete and its
`DbTransactionInterceptor` must observe the commit that encloses all three. A detached graph produces no
inserts and therefore cannot satisfy either witness.

**What `verifySucceeded` is for, and why this path has something to give it.** After a **retriable**
failure, the strategy cannot tell whether the transaction committed: the failure may have arrived before
the commit, or after a commit whose acknowledgement was lost. `verifySucceeded` is the application's
answer to that question, and it must be a read the application can trust:

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **The check** | `await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(o => o.SubmissionId == submissionKey && o.Username == userName, ct)`. `AsNoTracking` is required: the failed attempt's entities are still tracked, and a tracking query could answer from the change tracker rather than from the store |
| **Why it is sound** | The submission key is unique per submission and carried on the order row under a filtered unique index, so the presence of a row bearing this key **is** the fact that this submission committed. Nothing else in the write has that property — the order id is generated by the insert, so it is unknown to a caller whose commit outcome is unknown, and a match on customer, total and timestamp would misidentify a genuine second order |
| **Outcome true** | The strategy stops retrying and returns as a success. The handler proceeds to step 9's redirect, which re-reads the order by key exactly as step 1a does |
| **Outcome false** | The strategy replays the whole operation — including, at its head, the in-operation submission-key re-read of step 3, which runs inside the fresh transaction and abandons the attempt if a row with this key has appeared meanwhile. Because step 8 deferred accepting the tracked changes, a replay that passes that guard re-sends the same inserts and the same deletions in the fresh transaction |
| **Non-transient failures** | Are not the strategy's business at all: it does not classify them as retriable, so it does not call `verifySucceeded` and does not replay. They propagate to the failure table below and are answered there. **The coverage assertion requires that a unique-index violation is answered once rather than attempted six times** — one execution, not the `1 + Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 item 2, which is what a misclassification would produce |
| **Cancellation** | Not a transient failure. The request token is passed to `ExecuteInTransactionAsync`, to the operation and to `verifySucceeded`, and a cancelled operation is not replayed — the convention of section [4.16](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once) |

The coverage assertion drives a transient provider error at three points — inside `SaveChangesAsync`, during
the commit with the commit having failed, and during the commit with the commit having **succeeded** — and
asserts exactly one order in all three, which is the assertion that fails if `verifySucceeded` is omitted
or reads through the change tracker.

**The failure branches, replacing `catch { return View(order); }`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:58-62].** The source's bare `catch` has no
exception variable: it discards the exception, redisplays an empty-looking form and records nothing
([08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns it as debt). The target catches by type:

The **classes are the persistence-failure classifier's**, defined once in section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) and not re-derived here: the exception chain is walked to
its innermost provider exception, so a bare `SqlException` and one wrapped in `DbUpdateException` reach the
same row, and every redisplay row is subject to that section's render gate — which re-classifies the
failure as `Unavailable` where the store cannot be reached, so **no row in this table redisplays a page
that cannot render**.

| Class (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) | Caught here as | Response | Log | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `DuplicateSubmission` | A unique-constraint violation naming the `SubmissionId` index, bare or wrapped | **Not a user-facing failure.** The other submission of this key won the race and its order exists, so this one re-reads by key and username exactly as step 1a does and returns `RedirectToAction("Complete", new { id = … })`. If — and only if — that re-read finds nothing, the case falls through to `Rejected` rather than looping | `Information`, category `duplicate-submission`, with the winning `OrderId`. A concurrent double-submit is a customer double-clicking, not a fault | Row 96 `96a` and `96b` |
| `Concurrency` | `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` | The form is redisplayed with one generic model error — *"We could not complete your order. Please try again."* — and nothing is persisted | `Error`, failure category `concurrency` | Row 85 `85c`, and row 99 `99c` for the re-projection |
| `Rejected` | A server-produced rejection of the command — foreign-key, check or other unique violation, permission refusal, deadlock victim — bare or wrapped | Same user-facing outcome as `Concurrency` | `Error`, failure category `persistence`. The innermost exception's **type** and the failure category are recorded — **not its message**, and the exception object is **not** passed to the logger, per section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types); nothing is surfaced in the response | Row 85 |
| `DataIntegrity` | The missing-album case of census site F6 | Same user-facing outcome | `Error`, failure category `missing-album`, with the cart record id and album id | Row 85 `85c` |
| `Unavailable` | A provider exception raised while opening the connection, a connection-level failure or an unanswered timeout — bare or wrapped — **or** any of the three rows above whose render gate found the store unreachable | **Not redisplayed.** Rethrown, so the exception-handling middleware answers with the layout-free generic 500 and a trace identifier | `Error`, failure category `database`, written by the `IExceptionHandler` of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) rather than twice | Row 85 `85b`, and row 86 for the recursion properties |
| `Cancelled` | `OperationCanceledException`, **caught only under the filter `when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)`** | **Not an error, and not an outcome.** No model error, no view, no status code — the catch body records the cancellation and then **`throw;`**, which is the only terminal behaviour available to it. Returning `View(input)` would write a response to a client that has gone and would report a *validation* shape for work that never completed; returning a status code would report an outcome nobody is listening for; and returning nothing does not compile in an `async Task<IActionResult>` method. Rethrowing hands the request back to the framework, which abandons the response for a cancelled request rather than inventing one, so **no 500 and no error page is produced**. The `await using` transaction is disposed on the way out, uncommitted — see the state note below, which is where the commit-time case is settled. An `OperationCanceledException` whose token is *not* the request token fails the filter, is **not** caught here, and travels on as the genuine fault it is | `Information`, category `cancelled`. Recorded before the rethrow, with the permitted fields below and nothing else | Row 96 `96c` |
| Unclassified | Anything the classifier does not recognize | **Not caught.** It reaches the exception-handling middleware of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), which answers 500 with the generic view and a trace identifier | The closed record of section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), written by its `IExceptionHandler` | Row 46 |

**The state each failure leaves behind, cancellation included — three cases, not one.** The coverage assertion
asserts all three.

- **Cancelled or failed before `SaveChangesAsync` completes** — steps 4 to 7. The in-flight command is
  aborted and the transaction is disposed without committing: **nothing persisted**, and the cart still
  holds every row it held.
- **Cancelled or failed after `SaveChangesAsync` but before the wrapper's commit completes.** The same
  outcome: an uncommitted transaction is rolled back by the server when the connection is released, so
  the order, the order details and the cart deletions all disappear together. This is the property step
  3's transaction wrapper exists to make stated rather than incidental.
- **Cancelled or failed *during* the wrapper's commit** — the one case where the client's outcome and the
  database's can differ, and it is not specific to cancellation: a dropped connection produces it too.
  A commit that reached the server and succeeded there, but whose acknowledgement never arrived, leaves
  **an order that exists** behind an exception that looks identical to one that changed nothing. Nothing
  in the transaction, the cancellation convention or the catch list can distinguish the two, so this path
  does not try to. It is settled by the **submission key** specified at the head of this section, in two
  places that do not overlap: **inside** the request, by step 3's `verifySucceeded`, where the failure was
  retriable and the strategy is deciding whether to replay; and **across** requests, by step 1a, where the
  customer resubmits. The honest statement is that a failing commit means *indeterminate*, never *nothing
  persisted* — and the two mechanisms above are what make *indeterminate* actionable rather than merely
  admitted.

**What the log record may contain, and what it may not.**
[06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the log-privacy policy and this path is its most
sensitive consumer, because the request body is a name, a postal address, a phone number and an email
address. Applying that policy here:

- **Permitted, and the list is 06's and closed — it is that document's record shape `R3` and nothing
  else.** [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes the order record at **six** fields over
  its envelope `R1`: the `OrderId` once assigned, the **line-item count**, the **order total**, the
  **outcome**, a failure **category** rather than a message and present only on a failure, and
  **`PromoCodeApplied`, a boolean**. This document emits exactly those six and **adds none** — a seventh
  field is a defect by that register's own rule, and an omitted one is an incomplete record, which is why
  the boolean is emitted on every order record rather than only when a code was supplied. The boolean's
  form is not a choice here either: [06 §9.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s never-logged table
  forbids the promo code's *value*, so a recorded fact of *application* has exactly one admissible shape.
  The **trace identifier** is present because it is an `R1` envelope field attached to every application
  record, including the failed-rehash diagnostic of [09 §6.8.1.1](09-security-assessment.md); it is not an
  order-specific field, it is not counted among the six, and it is not this document's to add or withhold.
  The **submission key is deliberately not logged**: the duplicate-submission case is identified by the
  `OrderId` of the order the reconciliation of step 1a matched, which is already permitted, so nothing is
  lost by keeping the closed list closed.
- **The level is `R1`'s and follows the outcome** — `Information` on success and `Error` on failure, per
  [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `R3` row, under the application's own
  `MvcMusicStore` category. It is stated because a single fixed level would make a failed checkout
  indistinguishable from a successful one at the sink's filter.
- **The actor is the Identity `UserId`** — the GUID, `User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)` —
  **never the login name**, even though `User.Identity.Name` is what the order row itself stores. That is
  one of the **exactly two** actor values [06 §9.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) permits an
  application record to carry; the other, the literal **`anonymous`**, cannot arise here because the
  checkout write path is reachable only by an authenticated principal (section
  [6.4](#64-the-account-surface--authorization-map-redirect-safety-and-error-paths)), and a
  `SubjectPseudonym` is a *subject* field rather than an actor and never appears in this position.
- **Never logged:** `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`,
  `Phone`, `Email`, the promo-code value, the session id, any cookie value and any anti-forgery token.
  This is why the `DbUpdateException` row above logs the inner exception's type rather than the entity values
  that caused it: a constraint-violation message can carry a column value.

### 8.13 Timestamp semantics — UTC in the database, converted for display

The migration source writes **local server time** in both places it writes a timestamp:
`order.OrderDate = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:41] and
`DateCreated = DateTime.Now` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:49]. Neither value carries
an offset, and `DateTime.Kind` is not persisted, so **the stored rows record a wall-clock reading whose
zone is a property of the machine that wrote them** and is documented nowhere.

**This is a decision the port cannot avoid, because the meaning of the identical line of code changes
underneath it.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) selects a Linux App Service host, whose
process time zone is UTC unless configured otherwise. Porting `DateTime.Now` verbatim therefore yields
UTC values in the same column that already holds local ones, with no marker distinguishing them — a
silent, permanent mixed-zone column. **The decision:**

| Part | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| **Storage** | **UTC.** Both writes become `DateTime.UtcNow`, and both columns end as `datetime2` — EF Core's default mapping for `DateTime` on SQL Server. **The type change does not reach the schema baseline, and it is not annotated onto the diff.** Section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 admits **zero** differences and no annotation, so where extraction (step 1) shows `datetime`, the baseline model maps `datetime` explicitly and the widening ships afterwards as the named `AlterTimestampColumnTypes` migration in that section's third held-back group — after the load and after reconciliation, before traffic admission. Where extraction shows the columns are already `datetime2`, the baseline maps `datetime2` and no alteration migration exists. Either way the diff gate compares a baseline that reproduces the source exactly |
| **Migration** | The domain-data load takes a **required `LegacySourceTimeZone` parameter** — a time-zone identifier resolvable by `TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById` — and converts every legacy `Order.OrderDate` and `Cart.DateCreated` from that zone to UTC as it loads. **It fails closed**: if the parameter is absent, unresolvable, or if any source value is an *invalid* local time in that zone (a reading inside a spring-forward gap, which indicates the wrong zone was supplied), the load **stops before writing any row**. An *ambiguous* value (inside a fall-back overlap) is resolved with the **standard-time** offset and recorded per row in the migration log, because one hour of ambiguity on an order timestamp is tolerable and a silent guess is not |
| **Display** | UTC is converted to a configured presentation zone at render time, `Display:TimeZone` in configuration, **defaulting to `UTC`**. Stated for completeness and for the acceptance test below: **no view in the migration source renders either value** — `git grep -n 'OrderDate\|DateCreated' -- 'src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore'` returns four matches, all of them the two writes and the two property declarations, and none of them a `.cshtml` file. So this rule governs the migration equivalence check and any later display, not an existing page |
| **New writes after cutover** | Are UTC by construction, so the column is single-zoned from the first row written by the target |

**Acceptance**, as the coverage assertions in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage): a newly created
order's `OrderDate` and a newly created cart row's `DateCreated` are both UTC within a tolerance of the
test clock; a migration run with no `LegacySourceTimeZone` writes **nothing**; and for a migrated legacy
order, the stored UTC value converted back to the supplied source zone equals the wall-clock value the
source row held. `D-39` in section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) records the
change, with **Data owner and Product** as approval owner — the data owner because it rewrites stored
values, Product because the zone a timestamp is understood in is a user-facing decision.

### 8.14 The two absolute external links — one decision each

**The views carry exactly two links whose scheme is `http` or `https`, and both are `http://`.** The
count is a measurement rather than an impression — `git grep -n 'https\?://' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'`
returns exactly two lines — and it is a count of **HTTP-scheme** links specifically, because that is what
the command matches. Neither link has a disposition anywhere else in this document, so both are decided
here, and they are decided **separately**, because they leave the port for entirely different reasons and
a single rule applied to both would misstate one of them.

| Site | As shipped | Decision | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The footer, on **every page** | `<a href="http://mvcmusicstore.codeplex.com">mvcmusicstore.codeplex.com</a>` inside a `<p>` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:36] | **Removed** — the `<p>` and its anchor go together, leaving the footer's `@Html.ActionLink("admin", …)` line [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:37] as the footer's only content | CodePlex was shut down in **2017** and the destination is gone, so the anchor cannot resolve for any visitor under any scheme. Upgrading the scheme would only move the failure from cleartext to TLS, which is not an improvement, and **substituting a destination is not available to this document**: nothing in the repository names a current project home, so any replacement would be invented. Removal is the only option that leaves nothing false on the page |
| The external-login help paragraph, in the **empty-provider branch** | `<a href="http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=313242">this article</a>` inside the paragraph at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml:7-13] | **Removed with its view, so it is never decided on its own terms** | `Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml` is one of the four views section [8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) removes with the external-login challenge surface, so the paragraph carrying this anchor [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml:10] does not exist in the target and there is no `href` left to upgrade. It is recorded rather than omitted because a scheme upgrade is the obvious disposition for it and would be wasted work: the correct action is to delete the view, which section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s removal decision and section 8.4's disposition already require |

**The consequence for validation is the opposite of what a reader would expect, so it is stated rather
than left to be inferred: no absolute external link survives the port.** The ported application therefore
has no destination whose correctness lives outside the repository, and nothing in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) or section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) has an external destination to resolve.
What the footer removal does leave is a **visible** difference on every page, which section 12.5 carries
as an enumerated expected difference across the whole capture set rather than as a new capture. **It
carries no approved delta**, and that is a deliberate classification rather than an omission: the
destination is gone, so the anchor cannot function for any visitor, and removing a link that leads nowhere
resolves a defect rather than changing behaviour a visitor could rely on. Section 12.5 names it among the
differences that sit on neither approval register, so the reviewer accepts it on sight instead of filing
it as a regression.

**Two `mailto:` links exist as well, they are outside that census by construction, and they are decided
here so that "exactly two" cannot be read as "exactly two links of any kind".** `Home/Contact.cshtml`
renders `<a href="mailto:Support@example.com">` and `<a href="mailto:Marketing@example.com">`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Home/Contact.cshtml:15-16]; a second measurement finds them and finds
nothing else — `git grep -n 'mailto:' -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'` returns exactly those two lines. They do
not appear in the `https\?://` census because a `mailto:` URI has no HTTP scheme, and neither the scheme
upgrade nor the dead-destination removal above has any meaning for a mail URI. **Their disposition: both
are preserved byte-for-byte, `href` and visible text alike**, on three facts rather than a preference.
The addresses are at the reserved example domain, so neither is a real mailbox, there is no live contact
surface to protect and no correct value to update them to. The view carrying them is **orphaned** —
`HomeController` declares only `Index` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:15], so no
action returns it and the single conventional route cannot reach it — and section
[8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) ports it with the shared mechanical transformations
rather than deleting it, which is the disposition these two anchors inherit. And because the page never
renders, changing or removing a visible address on it would be a user-visible edit with no user to see it.
**One consequence is flagged rather than absorbed**: if a product decision ever gives `Home/Contact` a
route, the placeholder addresses must be replaced with real ones **before** that route exists, which is a
product action with a product owner and not a migration step. It carries **no delta**, because nothing
about either anchor changes in this port.

**Neither of the two absolute links is turned into a generated URL, and neither is among the
application-relative ones.** Both are absolute and external, so `@Url.Action`, `@Url.Content` and the tag
helpers have nothing to contribute — the four `@Url.Content` sites of section
[8.1.4](#814-the-four-urlcontent-call-sites-mapped) are all application-relative, and these two are not
among them.
