## 10. Administrator provisioning becomes an operator command

### 10.1 What it is today

`private async void CreateAdminUser()` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] runs at
application startup, called from `ConfigureApp` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18]. It reads two app settings [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24], hard-codes
the role name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:25], hand-builds a context, a user manager and a role manager [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29], creates the
role if absent [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:32-36], and creates the user if absent [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:38-44]. MVC 4 does the equivalent through
SimpleMembership [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:21-37].

Three properties of that make it the wrong shape rather than merely the wrong place:

- **`async void`.** An unhandled exception in an `async void` method has nowhere to propagate, so a
  provisioning failure at startup is **unobservable** — the application starts, appears healthy, and has
  no administrator ([09 §3.6](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding).
- **A plaintext credential in source control** [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17], read on every
  start ([09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns it; [08 §5.7](08-technical-debt-register.md) rates
  it).
- **Partial idempotence.** See property 3 below.

### 10.2 The target: `tools/provision-admin`, and five required properties

A separate console project, `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj` and its `Program.cs`. Five
properties are **required**, not implied — each is a design constraint whose absence would reproduce a
defect the source has.

**One project, ten verbs — and this subsection is where the invocation is *defined*, because it is where
a reader arrives looking for the tool.** The mapped project is the **only** operator console project in
the target ([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)): `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj`
and its `Program.cs`, the project AAP §0.4.1's future application map carries. There is no second operator
project, and no section of this document may name one — a required operator capability becomes **another
verb of this project** rather than a project beside it, for the structural reason section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) gives.

**The canonical invocation literal, defined once and used verbatim everywhere.** `provision-admin <verb>
[switches]`, where `provision-admin` **is** the published operator tool — concretely
`dotnet <published-tool>/ProvisionAdmin.dll`, with `<published-tool>` the output directory the caller
published and captured. There is no globally installed tool, no `PATH` entry and no shell wrapper, so the
bytes the suite runs and the bytes the release runs are the same bytes; and `ProvisionAdmin.dll` is the
only assembly name any invocation in this corpus writes. The form is cross-platform by construction, so
the Windows agent that captures the baseline and the Linux agent that runs the target half (section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)) issue the identical command line.
**Both spellings are this definition and neither is a second form**: a prose citation writes the short
`provision-admin <verb>`, and a row that has to be executed as written — the migration rows of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) and the runbook of section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) — writes the expansion, because a step
an operator or a fixture runs cannot contain a name that does not resolve on the command line.

**The ten verbs, and no others.** Each verb's own contract — its switches, its guards, its assertions, its
secret channel, its idempotence — is owned by the section named beside it; this table owns only the fact
that the verb exists and belongs to this executable.

| Verb | Operation | Its contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `admin` | Administrator provisioning | This section |
| `seed` | Guarded non-production catalog seeding | Section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) |
| `extract-schema` | Authoritative catalog-view interrogation of one store, and the run descriptor | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) |
| `diff-schema` | Generated-DDL-versus-extracted-record comparison for one store | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor), gating section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) step 3 |
| `load-catalog` | The dependency-ordered catalog and order load | Section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) |
| `load-identity` | The Identity load | Section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) for how it runs, section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) for what it transforms |
| `reconcile` | The keyed-set, count and financial comparison for one store, or for both in one pass | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) |
| `seal-manifest` | Binds the imported record set and merge lineage to one run and seals it | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor); [06 §11.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the manifest's storage |
| `accept-run` | Records the data owner's acceptance | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) |
| `close-run` | Retires the run and destroys its evidence in a fixed order | Section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) |

**The switch grammar, one form for the whole tool.** `--store catalog|identity` selects the store, and
`--store both` is admitted on `reconcile` alone. `--run-id` selects the run; `--begin-run` on
`extract-schema` opens one. `--resume` resumes a checkpointed run. `--batch` bounds a load batch, default
`1000`. `--report-dir` names the artifact directory. `--model-overrides` names one override file.
`--authorized-by` names the data owner on `accept-run`. `--username` and `--role` are the `admin` verb's.
**There is no checkpoint switch**: a load verb appends its checkpoint **evidence** to
`<report-dir>/run/<run-id>/<store>/checkpoint.jsonl`, derived from the two switches it already takes —
evidence, not authority, for the reason section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) gives.
**No other switch spelling exists** — in particular there is no scope selector and no extract selector: a
run is identified by `--run-id` and a store by `--store`, and an invocation naming anything else is
rejected by the closed pre-parse of property 1b below.

**The division of labour inside this section follows from the single project.** **Properties 1, 1b, 3, 4
and 5 below are the `admin` verb's**, while **properties 1a, 2 and 2a are the machinery all ten verbs
share** — the host they build, the registration surface they reach across the `ProjectReference`, the
principal and connection channel they use, and the environment assertion every one of them makes before
doing any work. The exit-code allocation below is likewise **tool-wide**: it governs every verb, and no
verb defines a code outside it. Where a data or seeding verb differs, the difference is stated in its own
section and not here.

**1. The secret does not arrive on the command line.** A password passed as an argument is visible in
process listings to any user on the host and is recorded by shell history and by pipeline logs, which
would move the credential from one durable store to three. It is supplied either through an
**environment variable scoped to the single invocation**, or by **interactive prompt with terminal echo
disabled**. **The release process uses the environment-variable channel**, injected by the pipeline from
the platform secret store for that one step and not persisted to any file; the interactive prompt is
the path for an operator running the command by hand outside a pipeline. Both are implemented; the
command refuses to read a password from an argument at all, so the unsafe channel is not merely
discouraged.

**The three inputs and where each one's name is fixed, because "supplied through the environment" is not an input contract.**

| Input | Channel | Where its name is fixed | Validated, before anything is written |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password | Environment variable scoped to the single invocation, **or** an echo-disabled prompt when the variable is absent and a terminal is attached | [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md), which owns this tool's admitted configuration sources | Present and non-empty; then by **Identity's own password validators**, which is property 2's consequence rather than a second rule — so the policy of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) applies without being restated here |
| Target username | Command-line switch | [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md), which owns the switch's spelling and the configuration key it maps to | Present, non-whitespace, at most 256 characters, and **every character present in the allowed set of section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)**, bound as `Identity:UserAllowedUserNameCharacters` (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). A username that violates the set can be created and then never updated, which is the defect section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) refuses to create during the load and this command refuses to create by hand |
| Role name | Command-line switch, **no default** | [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md), on the same terms | Present, non-whitespace, and **equal to `Administrator`** — the literal the authorization attribute names [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:12]. Any other value provisions a role that authorizes nothing, which is [09 §5.2](09-security-assessment.md)'s MVC 3 failure reached by a different route |

**Why the username and role travel on the command line while the password cannot.** The two arguments
are *not* secrets, and their appearing in the pipeline's own record of the step is the point: the audit
record of property 4 and the pipeline log then agree on who was provisioned, without the tool having to
be trusted to report it. The password's channel is chosen by the opposite reasoning in the paragraph
above. **The absence of a default on the role switch is deliberate**: the source hard-codes the role name
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:25], and a default here would recreate that
invisibility — an operator who has to type the role is an operator who has read what they are granting.

**The command-line inputs are mapped, not accepted raw.** This tool is the **only** host in the plan that
registers the command-line provider at all — the site is built parameterless precisely so that it does not
(section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)) — and here the provider is registered last and
outranks every other source, so a bare
switch would add a top-level configuration key named after itself. The tool therefore supplies an
explicit switch mapping — one entry per admitted switch, on [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s spellings —
and binds the mapped keys to a validated options type of its own under the same `ValidateOnStart` mechanism as
every other options type. One property follows: the switches land in a section **no other part of this
contract defines**, so no argument can shadow a real key.

**1b. A switch mapping does not reject anything, so the tool rejects before the host is built.** This is
the property a mapping is most often assumed to provide and provably does not, which is why it is a
numbered requirement rather than a remark. **Verified against the provider on the pinned band, with the
mapping above in place — the tokens below are example forms chosen to exercise the provider, the canonical set being [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s:**

| What is passed | What the command-line provider does with it |
| --- | --- |
| Every admitted switch, each followed by its value | Binds the mapped keys. The intended case |
| `--rolel Administrator` — one character wrong | Binds a **top-level key named `rolel`**. No error, no warning. The **mapped** role key is simply absent, and the only reason the run stops at all is that `[Required]` on that member happens to catch it |
| `--phase catalog` — a switch that used to exist | Binds a top-level key named `phase`. Nothing reads it, nothing reports it, and the run proceeds as though the argument had not been typed |
| `/role Administrator` | Maps to the **same** key as `--role` — the forward-slash form goes through the same mapping, so one switch has two accepted spellings unless something forbids the second |
| `-x 1` | **Silently dropped.** No key, no exception |
| A bare positional token | **Ignored entirely** — no key of any kind. A positional argument therefore cannot be read from configuration at all |
| `--role` with no value after it | **Ignored entirely.** The missing value is not an error; the key simply does not appear |
| `--flag --role Administrator` — a valueless flag before another switch | Binds **`flag`** = `--role`, and `--role` is consumed as that value, so the role is **never set**. A flag taking no value is not expressible in this provider at all |
| `--role A --role B` | Binds **`B`**. Last wins, and the first value is discarded silently |

So the failure mode is precise: **an unknown switch enters configuration outside every bound section**,
where `ValidateOnStart` cannot see it — it validates the members of the options types this contract
defines, and a stray top-level key is a member of none of them. A typo in an operator invocation then
looks like success, and the switch it was meant to be is missing.

**The rule: `args` is pre-parsed against a closed table before the builder is constructed, and the raw
array is never handed to the builder at all** — [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the
builder and states the same prohibition. The pre-parse is the tool's own code, not a configuration feature, and it is the same code for
every verb:

1. **`args[0]` must be one of the ten verbs of the table above** — `admin`, `seed`, `extract-schema`,
   `diff-schema`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity`, `reconcile`, `seal-manifest`, `accept-run`,
   `close-run`. Absent or unrecognised is a failure — and it has to be checked here rather than in options
   validation, because the bare-positional row above establishes that a positional argument never reaches
   configuration.
2. **Every remaining token must appear in that verb's exact accepted set**, and the sets are closed:

   | Verb | Its closed accepted set |
   | --- | --- |
   | `admin` | `--username`, `--role`, `--rotate-credential`, `--report-dir` |
   | `seed` | `--report-dir` |
   | `extract-schema` | `--store`, `--begin-run`, `--run-id`, `--report-dir` |
   | `diff-schema` | `--store`, `--run-id`, `--model-overrides`, `--report-dir` |
   | `load-catalog` | `--store`, `--run-id`, `--batch`, `--resume`, `--report-dir` |
   | `load-identity` | `--store`, `--run-id`, `--batch`, `--resume`, `--report-dir` |
   | `reconcile` | `--store`, `--run-id`, `--report-dir` |
   | `seal-manifest` | `--run-id`, `--report-dir` |
   | `accept-run` | `--run-id`, `--authorized-by`, `--report-dir` |
   | `close-run` | `--run-id`, `--report-dir` |

   **Admission is not requiredness, and neither is binding — so the three are settled in one table, and
   in no other place.** The sets above answer only "may this token appear on this verb". Every other
   property of every switch — whether it takes a value, whether the verbs that accept it *require* it,
   and what it binds to — is the table below, which is **the sole owner of all three**. An earlier form of
   this section left requiredness to the invocation literals and binding to section
   [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s prose, and the two disagreed in three places: the
   literal of section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) presented one
   requiredness for all ten verbs, property 1's `admin` form bracketed `--report-dir` while that literal
   did not, and section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) described **nine** switches as
   arriving through `AddCommandLine` when three of them bind to nothing at all. All three statements are
   withdrawn in favour of this table.

   | Switch | Takes a value | Required on | Accepted but optional on | Binds to |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | `--username <name>` | Yes | `admin` | — | `ProvisionAdmin:Username` |
   | `--role <role>` | Yes | `admin` | — | `ProvisionAdmin:Role` |
   | `--rotate-credential` | **No — a flag** | — | `admin` | **Nothing.** Invocation intent on the parsed-invocation record, per rule 5 |
   | `--report-dir <dir>` | Yes | `seed`, `extract-schema`, `diff-schema`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity`, `reconcile`, `seal-manifest`, `accept-run`, `close-run` — **nine verbs, and absent it each exits `2` having written nothing**, per section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) | `admin` **only**, and that single exception is deliberate: `admin`'s audit envelope goes to standard output through property 4's serialiser, so the directory is an *additional* destination rather than the only one, whereas on the other nine the directory **is** the artifact. [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s dispatcher depends on exactly this split | `ProvisionAdmin:ReportDir` |
   | `--store catalog\|identity\|both` | Yes | `extract-schema`, `diff-schema`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity`, `reconcile` — **no default**, and `both` is admitted on `reconcile` alone | — | **Nothing.** Invocation intent; its two literals are decided by this pre-parse and by nothing later |
   | `--run-id <run-id>` | Yes | `diff-schema`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity`, `reconcile`, `seal-manifest`, `accept-run`, `close-run`; and on `extract-schema` **exactly one of `--run-id` or `--begin-run`** is required — neither is exit `2`, both is exit `2` under rule 6. **Forbidden on `admin` and `seed`** by the sets above | — | **Nothing.** Invocation intent, matched here against section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)'s closed grammar before it is composed into a path |
   | `--begin-run` | **No — a flag** | — | `extract-schema`, under the exactly-one rule in the row above | **Nothing.** Invocation intent, stripped by rule 5 |
   | `--resume` | **No — a flag** | — | `load-catalog`, `load-identity` | **Nothing.** Invocation intent, stripped by rule 5 |
   | `--batch <n>` | Yes | — | `load-catalog`, `load-identity`; default `1000`, bounds `100`–`10 000` asserted by **`O6`** of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes) | `Load:BatchSize` |
   | `--model-overrides <file>` | Yes | — | `diff-schema` **only**, so no override can influence a write | **Nothing.** Invocation intent, read by `diff-schema` as a file path |
   | `--authorized-by <principal>` | Yes | `accept-run` | — | **Nothing.** Invocation intent, written verbatim into the acceptance record section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) owns |

   **Eleven switches, four of them binding to configuration and seven to nothing, and three of the eleven
   taking no value.** 4 + 7 = 11 and 3 + 8 = 11. The four configuration-bound ones are the only names
   `AddCommandLine` ever sees, which is what keeps section
   [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s key set closed; the seven others are recorded on the
   tool's own parsed-invocation record and are unreachable from an environment variable or a file by
   construction, for the reason rule 5's binding paragraph gives about `--rotate-credential`.

   A token outside the set fails, whether it is a near-miss of an accepted switch, a switch belonging to
   a different verb, or a switch this document has never defined. **`--store` on `load-catalog` and
   `load-identity` accepts exactly one value each** — `catalog` and `identity` respectively — so the
   switch is a redundancy the pre-parse checks rather than a choice the operator makes, and an invocation
   pairing a load verb with the other store is rejected here.

   **`--run-id`'s value is matched here against the closed grammar of section
   [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure), for the same reason and at the
   same moment**: this is the last point before the value is composed into a filesystem path, and it is
   before the host exists, so nothing has been read and no directory has been touched. A value outside the
   grammar is rule 7's exit `2`, with the one difference that section
   [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) fixes — the message names the
   switch, the grammar and the offending character's index and code point, and **not** the token, because
   an operator-supplied value that failed the grammar may carry a control character. Those two are the
   whole of the pre-parse's lexical competence: `--store`'s two literals and `--run-id`'s form are the only
   switch values whose legality is decidable from the token alone, and every other value — `--username`,
   `--authorized-by`, `--report-dir`, `--model-overrides`, `--batch` — is decided by the options validation
   and by the checks the sections owning those inputs define, not here.
3. **Only the `--switch` spelling is accepted.** The `/switch` form is rejected even where it would map
   correctly, because two spellings of one input make an audit of what was actually run harder for no
   gain; and no single-dash short form is defined at all, so every `-x` is rejected rather than dropped.
4. **Every value-taking switch must be followed by a value**, and one given none fails. The provider
   ignores it instead, so without this rule a value-taking switch with nothing after it produces the same outcome as
   not passing it at all.
5. **There are exactly three valueless flags — `--resume`, `--rotate-credential` and `--begin-run` — and
   the pre-parse is the only thing that may see any of them.** The count is three rather than two because
   `--begin-run` is bare: the invocation literals write it as `[--begin-run | --run-id <run-id>]`, with a
   value on the second alternative and none on the first, and an earlier form of this rule said "exactly
   two" while rule 2's table admitted the third — which would have left the one flag the whole
   data-migration run identifier is opened by travelling through the provider and eating whatever token
   followed it. The
   `--resume --batch 500` row above is
   why: a valueless flag cannot be expressed by this provider, and passed through it would eat the next
   switch as its value. So the pre-parse recognises the flag, records the intent, and **removes it from
   the tokens handed on** — none of the three is ever a configuration key, and section
   [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) already treats `--resume` as a
   statement of intent rather than a bound value. **`--rotate-credential` is governed by the same three
   semantics, stated here because a flag that changes what the command writes cannot be left to
   inference:**

   - **Stripping.** The pre-parse removes the token before the command-line provider is constructed. A
     `--rotate-credential --role Administrator` invocation therefore binds `Role` to `Administrator`
     rather than binding `rotate-credential` to `--role` and losing the role entirely, which is the
     failure rule 4 exists to prevent and which a value-taking provider would produce silently.
   - **Binding.** It binds to **nothing**. It is recorded as **invocation intent** on the tool's own
     parsed-invocation record — the same place `--resume` is recorded — and not into `IConfiguration`, so
     no options type gains a member for it, section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s closed
     key set stays closed, and the operator console's admitted-key row is unchanged. The distinction is
     load-bearing rather than tidy: a bound key would be settable from the environment or a file, and a
     credential rotation that could be triggered by an environment variable nobody passed on the command
     line is exactly the accident this tool's audit record exists to make impossible.
   - **Constraint.** It is accepted on **`admin` only** — rule 2's closed sets make it a rejection on the
     other nine verbs — it **requires `--username`**, and passing it a value (`--rotate-credential true`)
     fails under rule 2, because the value is a token outside the accepted set. Repeating it fails under
     rule 6.

   **What it does when present** is one change to one operation, and nothing else: the user operation's
   *already present* branch additionally issues `UserManager.RemovePasswordAsync` followed by
   `UserManager.AddPasswordAsync` with the value from `MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, through Identity's
   hasher exactly as the create path does, and reports `outcome` = **`rotated`**. Absent the flag, that
   branch is unchanged and reports `already-present` — so **the default invocation never overwrites a
   working credential**, which is why rotation is opt-in rather than implied by re-running the command.
   The role and membership operations are untouched by the flag, keeping the per-operation independence
   of property 3 intact. `rotated` is one of the **five** operation-record `outcome` literals section
   [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4 closes, and it
   appears in the audit envelope and in the `--report-dir` report identically, under the one vocabulary
   that property shares between the two destinations.
6. **A repeated switch fails.** The provider's own behaviour is last-wins, which silently discards the
   first value; for an argument that names the account being granted an administrator role, that is not a
   behaviour to inherit.
7. **The failure is exit 2 — the precondition-rejection class of section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — naming
   the rejected token and listing the accepted set for that verb**, and it happens **before the host is built** — so nothing is read, no connection is opened and
   nothing is written. The non-zero exit contract of section [10.3](#103-what-this-retires) is the same
   one; this is an additional way to reach it, not a second convention.

Only the surviving tokens are handed to the host builder together with the command's switch mapping — so
the mapped keys are the only keys the command line can contribute, and the mapping's real job is naming,
not filtering.

**The variable carrying the password is deliberately not a key in this contract, and the reason is worth being
precise about.** Every environment variable is visible to `IConfiguration` — that is what the
environment-variable provider does — so the honest claim is not that the value is unreachable but that
**it belongs to no bound options type and no section this document defines**. Nothing enumerates
configuration into a log, the value is read once into a local, and it is passed straight to
`UserManager.CreateAsync`. Its name — [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s — also carries no `__` separator, so it cannot be mistaken for a member of
any section above.

**Where the pipeline is concerned, one obligation is not the tool's to enforce and is stated as a
requirement on the release rather than as a hope.** The variable carrying the password **is registered as
a secret in the CI provider**, so the provider masks it in every log line the step produces, and it is
**scoped to that single step** rather than defined for the job. Whichever provider is selected —
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) owns that gate — the masking and the scoping are entry conditions for
the provisioning step, and the identity the step runs under is
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. A pipeline that emits the password once has published it to
whatever retains that log, and no property of the tool can undo it.

**1a. The invocation, the principal and the connection channel — because a command whose execution is
undescribed is a design, not an operation.**

| Element | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| The invocation | `provision-admin admin --actor <declared> --username <name> --role Administrator [--report-dir <dir>] [--rotate-credential]`, with `MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `MIGRATE_TARGET_CONNECTION` set for that one invocation and **nothing on the command line outside that verb's accepted set** — the four switches property 1b's table closes for `admin`, and no others. **An earlier form of this row read "and nothing else on the command line" while the accepted set held only `--username` and `--role`**, which made two things this document requires elsewhere unrunnable: coverage row 75 invokes `admin ... --report-dir <run artifacts>` and asserts exit `0`, and section [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover) requires a repair run with `--rotate-credential` — both of which the pre-parse would have rejected with exit `2` under rule 2. Both switches are now in the set, `--report-dir` carrying the same directory contract it carries on the other nine verbs and `--rotate-credential` carrying rule 5's flag semantics. It runs **once per environment** in its non-rotating form, after step 3 of the order in section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) and after the Identity data migration of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) where one is being performed — an administrator created before the load would be an account the load then has to reconcile against a source that never contained it |
| The principal | **Never the application's runtime managed identity.** The runtime identity belongs to the site and is reachable only from inside it, so an invocation outside the site cannot present it and should not want to: the write is being made by a pipeline step or a person, and the audit record of property 4 is only worth keeping if the principal in it is the one that acted. The release-step identity and its grants are [06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s and [06 §6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; this document requires only that the principal is **not** the runtime one and that it holds write access to the Identity tables and nothing wider |
| The connection channel | Through the **same** configuration contract as the site's — `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection`, supplied by the pipeline's configuration channel for the release-job invocation that [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) makes the normal path, or by an invocation-scoped environment variable in the operator session that section records as the exception, and **never as a command-line argument** (properties 1 and the precedence rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). Because property 2 reaches the application's own registration surface, section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s connection-string validation applies unchanged: a string carrying an inline credential, or an unresolved `@Microsoft.KeyVault(` literal, fails the command before it opens a connection |
| How it authenticates | Token-based Microsoft Entra authentication, not a SQL login — and in **exactly one** mode rather than whichever one the host can satisfy. The connection carries `Authentication="Active Directory Managed Identity"` (equivalently `Active Directory MSI`) with the **deployment** principal's client ID in `User Id`, and `Authentication="Active Directory Workload Identity"` as the single permitted fallback where the pipeline's identity is federated — the one flow [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) selects for every release-side operation, and mode **M3** of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), which is what validates it here. **`Active Directory Default` is not used**, and an earlier version of this row specified it: it "acquire[s] a token by passing `DefaultAzureCredential`" (*Using Microsoft Entra authentication with Microsoft.Data.SqlClient*), which resolves whichever of several credential sources the host happens to offer — so the identity that wrote an administrator account would be decided by the agent's ambient state rather than declared, and [06 §6.1.1.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) prohibits it on the release path for that reason. Which principal actually connected is then asserted at the database by `USER_NAME()`, assertion 3 below, so the mode is named *and* confirmed. One version-sensitive fact, stated so a package bump does not quietly break it: from **Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 7.0** the Entra modes require the separate `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.Extensions.Azure` package (same source), so a provider move past the pin [04 §5](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) carries has to re-check this row |

**Assertions before the first write, and there are four.** The command is short, which is exactly why it
is worth refusing to run it against the wrong database:

1. **The environment assertion of property 2a** — both variables pinned and the resolved name checked.
2. **The options validation of property 2, run explicitly, because building the host does not run it.**
   `ValidateOnStart` does not validate during `Build()`: it registers an `IStartupValidator` that the
   **host's start** invokes — "`ValidateOnStart` … validation is performed when the host starts"
   (*Options pattern in ASP.NET Core*, .NET 8; `OptionsBuilderExtensions.ValidateOnStart`), and the
   validator is resolved and called inside `Host.StartAsync`. A console command that calls `Build()` and
   then goes straight to work therefore resolves and uses operational services **before any validation has
   happened** — which is precisely the failure mode this assertion list exists to prevent, and an earlier
   version of this row asserted the opposite. The command therefore does one of two things and states
   which: it **resolves `IStartupValidator` from the built host and calls `Validate()` itself**, as the
   very first statement after `Build()` and before any scope is created, any `DbContext` is resolved or
   any connection is opened. `Validate()` throws an aggregated `OptionsValidationException` on failure,
   which becomes the non-zero exit below. **`RunAsync` is deliberately not used**: this is a one-shot
   command, not a service, and starting a host would also start any hosted service registered in the
   shared half — which today is none, and which a future addition to section
   [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) could silently make one. Calling the validator directly
   keeps the tool's container a strict subset in behaviour as well as in registration.
3. **The target is the intended database, asserted the same way.** The server on the **control plane** —
   `properties.fullyQualifiedDomainName` read from the resource and compared case-insensitively against the
   expected server, which must carry the `database.windows.net` suffix — and then `DB_NAME()` and
   `USER_NAME()` asserted **in session** against their expected values. That is section
   [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) assertion 1, which is in turn
   [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, rather than a third copy of the same idea. An
   administrator provisioned into a neighbouring environment's database is a real credential in a place
   nobody is looking. `@@SERVERNAME` is recorded in the evidence line and gates nothing, for the reason
   [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) gives.
4. **The Identity migration set in `__EFMigrationsHistory_Identity` is compared for exact set equality,
   in both directions, against the set the deployed Identity assembly defines** — truncated at the
   declared target exactly as section
   [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) truncates it. An
   expected identifier missing from the history table fails, **and so does a history row the expected set
   does not contain**. Without the first direction a run against a half-applied Identity schema fails
   inside `CreateAsync` with a provider-level column error, which is a diagnostic message about the wrong
   subject; without the second, a database carrying a migration this build does not define is loaded as
   though it were the schema this build was verified against.

   **`Containment, not equality` was an earlier form of this assertion and it is withdrawn.** It cited
   section [2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) as fixing the
   containment semantics, and that section fixes the **opposite** — exact equality in both directions,
   with "subset containment is used nowhere" as its own words — so the two halves of this document
   asserted different verdicts on the same comparison while each claimed the other as its authority.
   [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the rule and states it for the release, the restore, the
   preview and this tool alike; every location in this document now reads the same way, and there is no
   remaining subset test anywhere in it.

Each failure in items 1 to 3 is an exit **2** (section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation)) naming the assertion
and the two compared values, **before** the first write. **Item 4 is the one exception, and it is exit
`5`** — the verification class, cutover blocked — because [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) pins a
**single** failure code for the migration-set comparison wherever it is performed, so the release gate and
this tool cannot answer the same mismatch with two different classes. The distinction is real rather than
bookkeeping: a `2` tells a pipeline to fix the invocation or the state and try again, while a migration-set
mismatch means the database is not the one this build was verified against and **nothing may proceed until
a human decides which of the two is wrong**. It is still detected **before the first write**.

**2. Identity hashes the password — the command builds a host and resolves the managers from the
container.** "The same Identity configuration as the web application" is not a resemblance to be
maintained by hand; it is **the same method call**. The command:

1. builds a **plain host** — the defaults-disabled generic-host builder
   [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) fixes, not a web host: no server, no
   middleware pipeline and no endpoint, because it serves no request. **04 owns its construction**, and
   the two properties this section relies on are that it adds no configuration source the per-process
   matrix of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) does not name, and that the raw `args` array is never assigned to it;
2. calls **`Program.AddMusicStoreServices(builder.Services, builder.Configuration)`** — the single
   registration surface specified in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), reached across
   the `ProjectReference` edge and the `public partial class Program` declaration that
   [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns;
2a. registers **`IHostRoleSignal` as `HostRole.Operator`** — one `AddSingleton`, immediately after step 2
   and before step 3, because step 3 is what consumes it. It is deliberately **not** inside
   `AddMvcMusicStoreServices` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), so each root declares
   what it is; and it is what makes the validator apply **M3** rather than the web host's **M1** to this
   invocation's connection string (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). Omitting it does
   not fall back to a default — step 3 fails, naming `Configuration:HostRole`;
3. builds the host and, **as the very next statement**, resolves `IStartupValidator` and calls
   `Validate()` — assertion 2 above, and a numbered step of its own precisely because it is **not** a side
   effect of `Build()`;
4. opens a scope, and resolves `UserManager<ApplicationUser>` and the role manager from it;
5. calls their create methods, and returns the failure's allocated exit code — **3** where the store
   refused the identity, **5** where an operation reported an unusable result (the allocation of section
   [10.2](#exit-code-allocation), whose observability rationale is section
   [10.3](#103-what-this-retires)'s).

**Three properties follow from step 2 rather than being separately promised.** The command gets the
**same password hasher**, so the hash it writes is the one the application validates. It gets the **same
validated options** (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)), so a missing or invalid
required key fails the command **before** it touches the database — by way of step 3's explicit
`Validate()` call rather than by way of `Build()`, which is the distinction assertion 2 turns on — and the
password is checked against the
**same** policy the web application enforces (section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) — a provisioned administrator cannot bypass the complexity
rules. And there is **exactly one registration implementation**: a second copy inside the tool is what
would let its password policy, its context configuration or its hasher drift from the application's,
silently, in the direction nobody tests.

**2a. The environment is pinned on *both* variables and then asserted, because the tool is a generic
host and the generic host does not read the variable everyone reaches for.** This is a correctness
property of every non-web invocation in this document, not a nicety, and it is stated here once because
`tools/provision-admin` is the invocation that makes the distinction unavoidable.

Three verified facts force the shape:

- **The two host families read two different variables, which is why this tool cannot inherit the site's
  pin.** A generic host built by `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(String[])` builds its host configuration
  from **`DOTNET_`-prefixed** environment variables (API reference, .NET 8); `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`
  reads the `ASPNETCORE_`-prefixed set. So a release step that pins only `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` pins the
  site and **not** a generic host. **This tool does not rely on either prefix scan**, and that is the
  resolution rather than a complication: its builder has defaults disabled
  ([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so **no prefix-scanning host-configuration source exists
  in it at all**. The tool instead reads **both variables by name**, asserts they are present and equal
  under property 2a below, and passes the agreed value to **`HostApplicationBuilderSettings.EnvironmentName`**
  — which is not a configuration key. The assertion is therefore doing the work the prefix scan would
  otherwise do implicitly, and it fails closed where a scan would silently pick one variable.
- **For a host built by either of the two builders above, an unset environment is `Production`, not
  Development.** "If the `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT` and `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` environment variables aren't
  set, the Production environment is the default environment" (*Use multiple environments in ASP.NET
  Core*, .NET 8), and an unsupplied `EnvironmentName` on the empty builder lands in the same place. So the
  risk for this tool is not an accidental Development default, it is an accidental
  *Production* one — which is why the guard of section
  [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) cannot rest on an environment name and why
  this assertion exists at all. **The design-time `dotnet ef` path is a different host with a different
  default**, which is why it is not covered by this rule and why it pins the environment explicitly
  instead — either on the two variables or through the argument-forwarding form EF Core's design-time
  documentation describes (*Design-time DbContext Creation*, EF Core). **The invocation itself is not
  restated here**: every design-time command and every option on it is
  [04 §13.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, its environment pin is
  [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, and the release-time execution is
  [06 §6.2.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. Between the two rules **no invocation in this plan
  relies on a default at all**, which is the property that matters and is why neither default needs to be
  argued about.
- **The documented precedence between the two variables is not something to rely on.** The same
  Microsoft page states it in both directions in different paragraphs. A contract that depends on which
  paragraph is current is a contract that changes meaning on a doc revision, so this one **does not
  depend on precedence at all**.

**The rule, for every invocation this document specifies that is not the running site — and it is an
equality against a third value, not a pin to a literal.** The three names below are all read from the
environment; none of them is written into a step, and none of them is `Production` by default:

1. **Both `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` and `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT` are set, and neither is left to a default.**
   Both, because one of them governs whichever host type the invocation happens to build, and setting both
   removes the need to know which. Never neither, because the default is `Production` and a defaulted
   `Production` is indistinguishable from an intended one.
2. **They hold the same value**, and a disagreement fails rather than being resolved by precedence.
   Disagreement means the operator believed one thing and one of the two hosts believed another, and there
   is no safe way to guess which.
3. **That value equals the invocation's own `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT`** — the name of the environment being
   acted on, declared once per pipeline environment and **read rather than written** by the step. The
   variable and its per-environment value set are
   [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s; [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)
   states the same comparison for the design-time invocations, so the build side, the release side and the
   in-process assertion are one rule rather than three similar ones. **`EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` being absent
   is itself a failure**: a comparison against nothing is not a check, and defaulting it to `Production`
   would recreate exactly the blanket pin the next paragraph rejects.
4. **The invocation then reads the resolved `IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName` and fails, before any other
   work, if it is not that value.** This is the assertion that survives a doc revision, a platform default
   and a mistyped variable name alike: it checks the value the framework actually resolved rather than the
   input that was supposed to produce it.
5. **Every one of those failures is an exit 2 — the precondition-rejection class of section
   [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — naming the two variable values, `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT`
   and the resolved name**, and nothing is written. Four values in one line are what make the diagnosis
   immediate, and none of them is a configuration value, so the message echoes nothing sensitive.

**Why the rule is an equality and not "always `Production`", stated because the blanket version is the
tempting one and it is wrong in both directions.** A rule pinned to the literal `Production` would be
**unusable** for every operation against a non-production deployment — those invocations resolve to that
deployment's own name — and it would be **actively wrong** for seeding, which has no legitimate production
execution at all. A rule an invocation cannot obey is a rule that stops being applied anywhere, which is
how a guard becomes decoration. So the expected value is per invocation:

| Invocation | Its `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Eight of the nine verbs** — `admin`; both data-load verbs (sections [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) and [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)); and `extract-schema`, `reconcile`, `seal-manifest`, `accept-run` and `close-run` (section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor)) — together with the migration and bundle generation [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns and the bundle run in the release step | **The name of the environment being acted on** — `Production` when the target is the production deployment, and that deployment's own name otherwise. Never inferred, never defaulted, and never a literal written into the step | These run **against** the environment they name, including production, so the equality is how the invocation and the target are made to agree. [06 §12.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) declares which value each environment carries, including the fact that the production site's staging slot carries `Production` like the slot it swaps into |
| The `seed` verb (section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)) | **The target's explicit non-production environment name — and it can never be `Production`.** The invocation additionally fails if the resolved name **is** `Production`, whatever `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` says | Seeding writes ~780 catalog rows and has no legitimate production execution. It **never appears in a production release path**, so no invocation of it has a production expected value — and the extra check exists so that a mis-declared variable cannot create one |

**That is a distinction of expected value, not of mechanism.** Every invocation in both rows pins both
variables, reads `EXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT` and asserts the resolved name; what differs is what it asserts
*to*. And the seeding row's
assertion is the **first** of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s three
checks, not a fourth one — which is why that section says in its own words that check 1 is necessary and
not sufficient: an environment name pinned by the same operator who mistyped the connection string proves
nothing on its own, and checks 2 and 3 are what bind the decision to the database.

**Where the other halves live.** [04 §13.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the same pinning for
the **design-time** invocations — migration generation and bundle generation — and
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns it for the **release step** that runs the bundles, the
seeding command and this command. This document owns the in-process assertion, which is the half that
holds even when a release definition forgets a variable.

**Direct SQL is explicitly not an acceptable substitute**, because it cannot produce a valid Identity
password hash: the hash format, iteration count and salt handling are the hasher's, and a hand-written
`INSERT` produces a row that exists and cannot sign in. That is also the reason the tool resolves the
managers from a container rather than constructing them — the hasher, the validators and the normalizer
are what the container supplies, and hand-building them is how the source arrived at three objects
assembled by hand [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29].

**2b. The content root is set explicitly, and the published console carries no configuration file at
all.** These two go together: a host that reads optional JSON files needs a defined place to look for
them, and the cleanest way to make that place irrelevant is to ship nothing there.

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Content root | Set **explicitly** to `AppContext.BaseDirectory` through `HostApplicationBuilderSettings.ContentRootPath` (API reference, .NET 8), on the settings object [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s defaults-disabled builder is constructed from. It is not left to a default and it is **never** the process's current directory: a release step's working directory is whatever the agent chose, so an implicit content root is the one input to this command that varies between two invocations that look identical in the pipeline definition |
| Configuration files | **No file source is registered, and none ships — two independent facts, and the first is the one that carries the weight.** [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s builder is `Host.CreateEmptyApplicationBuilder` with `DisableDefaults`, which registers **no** configuration provider at all: no `AddJsonFile` call is made, for `appsettings.json`, for `appsettings.{Environment}.json` or for any other path, so there is no optional file layer whose absence has to be tolerated and no path a file can be placed on to be read. The published output additionally contains neither file. An earlier form of this row said the builder registered both **as optional sources** and leaned on the content root being the deployed folder to keep a stray working-directory file from being picked up — which was self-defeating in exactly the case that matters: the deployed folder **is** where a file planted beside the published assembly sits, so that arrangement made the one file it most needed to ignore the one file it would certainly have read. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 83 `83b` plants that file and requires the run to be unaffected; the registered-provider form could not satisfy that assertion and this form satisfies it by construction |
| Why no file | Every value the tool needs is declared **once per environment** in the pipeline's environment definition (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)), and a committed file inside the tool would be a second home for values that document says have one. It would also be the obvious place for somebody to put a connection string |
| How configuration arrives | **Invocation-scoped environment variables in the double-underscore form**, rendered into the step by that same environment definition. The tool's container is a strict subset of the web host's, but the *options* it binds are not a subset: step 1 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) binds **every** options type of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), so the invocation must supply **every unconditionally required member of every one of them** — not merely the connection string, the `Identity` policy and `DataProtection__ApplicationName`, but the `Expected:*`, `Antiforgery`, `Session` and `Site` members too |
| Why that cost is accepted | It is the price of the single registration surface above, and the alternative is worse: a tool-only options subset would mean two definitions of "the required configuration", and the one no deployment runs is the one that drifts. The cost is also **bounded and loud** — the values are the same declaration the site's platform settings come from, and a missing one fails at step 3's `Validate()` with the member named, before any connection is opened |
| What must not be supplied | `Site__*` values that differ from the site's, and anything resembling a *second* environment's declaration. The tool reads these members and acts on none of them; supplying a divergent value would make the environment definition self-inconsistent for no gain |

**3. Idempotence is per operation, not overall.** **Four** checks, evaluated **independently**: create the
role only if absent, create the user only if absent, set the credential only where property 4's credential
row admits it, and add the membership only if absent.

**The count is four rather than three, and an earlier form of this property counted three by folding the
credential into the user's creation.** It is corrected rather than qualified, for a reason that is
behavioural rather than presentational: the credential's three outcomes — `Created`,
`AlreadyPresent_NotRotated` and `Rotated` — are what let a reviewer tell a deliberate no-change from a
rotation, and a record set that folds the credential into "user" cannot express any of them.
[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s execution-path block counts four operations and four
records on a provisioning run for exactly that reason, and section
[4.16](#416-asynchronous-data-access-and-cancellation--the-convention-stated-once) already cites "the
**four** operations of that section's property 3" — so three was this property disagreeing with two of its
own consumers, one of them inside this document.

**The evidence that this matters is a difference between the two editions.** MVC 4 checks all three
independently — `WebSecurity.UserExists` [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:29],
`Roles.RoleExists` [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:32] and `Roles.IsUserInRole` [src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/AppConfig.cs:35] — whereas **MVC 5 adds the membership only
inside the user-creation branch**: `AddToRoleAsync` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:43]
sits inside `if (user == null)` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:39-44]. So if a prior MVC 5 run created the user and then failed
before the membership was added, **every subsequent run skips it** — the user exists, so the branch is
not entered, and the account never gets the role. The administration surface is then permanently
unreachable and nothing reports why. The target repairs such a run rather than skipping it, which is
the whole point of checking the three independently.

**Restart after a partial failure is therefore the same command again, with two boundaries stated so
"idempotent" is not read as "does whatever is needed".** A run interrupted at any point leaves each of
the three operations either done or not done — none of them is partial in itself — so re-running with the
same three inputs completes exactly the ones outstanding and exits zero with an audit record saying which
(property 4).

**Boundary one is unconditional. The command never deletes or demotes any account, role or role
membership**, and nothing in the grammar could: the verb table above is closed at ten verbs with no revoke
among them, and the `admin` verb accepts exactly four switches, none of which withdraws anything. Section
[6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) relies on exactly
this when it records that `AUTHZ-3002` has no producer among this document's artifacts.

**Boundary two is scoped to an ordinary invocation, and an earlier form of this paragraph stated it
unscoped and was therefore false.** That form read: the command "never modifies an existing account — in
particular it does not reset the password of a user that already exists, so a re-run cannot silently rotate
a credential and a forgotten administrator password is a different operation than this one". The last
clause is the one that cannot stand: a forgotten administrator password is **this** operation, under this
command, through the `--rotate-credential` flag that rule 5 of the grammar above defines — and that flag's
whole function is to reset the password of a user that already exists. The boundary is real but it is a
property of the **default** invocation, so it is stated that way:

| Invocation | What it may write to an account that already exists | Reported outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`admin` without `--rotate-credential`** — every ordinary invocation, including every restart after a partial failure | **Nothing.** The user operation's *already present* branch reads and reports; it issues no write against the existing row, so no password, stamp, lockout state or claim is touched | `already-present` |
| **`admin --rotate-credential`** — the one switch in the entire grammar that writes to an existing account, opt-in, valueless, and required to accompany `--username` | **Exactly one change**: `RemovePasswordAsync` then `AddPasswordAsync` with the value from `MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, through Identity's hasher on the same path the create branch uses. The role and membership operations are untouched, so property 3's per-operation independence holds under the flag as well | `rotated` |

**Three consequences follow, and they are what make the scoped boundary as safe as the unscoped one
claimed to be.** First, **no re-run can rotate by accident**: the flag has to be typed, it is refused if
given a value (grammar rule 2) and refused if repeated (rule 6), so an operator re-running the recorded
command line gets `already-present` and not `rotated`. Second, **rotation is idempotent in its end state
but is not a no-op**: whatever the account's hash was, afterwards it is the hash of the supplied value, so
running it twice leaves the same end state — but each run performs the write and emits `rotated`, which is
why the audit vocabulary distinguishes the two literals rather than collapsing them. Third, the worst
outcome of an unnecessary re-run is therefore stated per invocation rather than once: **without** the flag
it is that nothing happens; **with** it, that the credential is replaced by the one the invocation
supplied, which is precisely what was asked for.

**Both boundaries are assertions rather than claims, and they are asserted in one row.** Section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 75 covers the default and the flagged invocation against each other:
`75d` re-runs with identical arguments and asserts the row keys are unchanged, no duplicate exists **and
the credential the first run established still authenticates**, which is boundary two for an ordinary
invocation; and `75f`, `75g` and `75h` add the flag over three different pre-states and assert the password
changed, the keys did not, and the `SecurityStamp` did — which is the rotation branch. Neither half
establishes "rotation is opt-in" alone; the pair does.

**4. The audit record has exactly one destination, exactly one envelope shape, exactly four records
per invocation, and no secret in any of them.** Content first: **actor, timestamp, target username, role
name, and the outcome of each of the three operations separately**, so "role already existed, membership
added" is distinguishable from "nothing to do". **The password is never serialised, never echoed, and never included in an exception message** — the
rule of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s never-record list, applied here to the one
process that holds the secret. This is net-new: the repository has no audit logging of any kind
([09 §3.13](09-security-assessment.md)).

**The envelope is one nested shape and the cardinality is four, and both are fixed here because a
consumer cannot write a selector against a shape that is described twice.** An earlier form of this
property emitted **one** record carrying the three operations' outcomes as three fields of a single
object, and [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) alternated between reading one record and reading
four or more. Neither half of that is left standing. The pinned contract:

| Property | Value, fixed |
| --- | --- |
| **The event name, and where it lives** | **`AdminProvisioned`**, at the **nested** path **`State.eventName`** — never a top-level `.eventName`, for the reason the shape-parity row below gives. **All four records carry the same event name**, which is what keeps a consumer's selector a single equality test and is why the decomposition below uses a discriminator field rather than four event names. A consumer that matched on four distinct names would have to be edited every time the decomposition changed |
| **The discriminator** | **`State.operation`**, taking exactly one of four literals — **`create-user`**, **`create-role`**, **`add-membership`**, **`run`** — and **no others**. The set is closed: a fifth value is a finding, not an extension. **The first three literals are deliberately the ones the `--report-dir` report already uses** (row 75 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)), so this design has **one** operation vocabulary rather than two spellings of the same three operations that a reader would have to map between; `run` is the fourth because the report has no run-level row |
| **The cardinality** | **Exactly four records per invocation, invariantly, on every path including the paths that fail.** One record per `operation` literal, in that order: the user operation, the role operation, the membership operation, then the **run outcome**. Four is a **constant**, not a maximum and not a function of how far the run got — which is the single property that makes the count assertable with no branching by the consumer |
| **What the three operation records carry** | `outcome` taking one of **`created`**, **`already-present`**, **`rotated`**, **`failed`** or **`not-attempted`** — **five** literals, closed — matching the per-operation independence of property 3: each of the three is decided by its own check, so each reports its own result. The first three literals are again the report's own, for the same one-vocabulary reason; the last two are the ones the report has no occasion to emit, because a report is only written on a path that got far enough to have one. **`rotated` is emitted only by the user operation and only when `--rotate-credential` was passed** — the flag whose stripping, binding and constraint semantics are rule 5 of property 1b — so it distinguishes "the account already existed and its credential was replaced" from `already-present`, which is the same discovery with no write. `failed` additionally carries the failing step's name; `not-attempted` carries nothing further, because there is nothing to report |
| **What the run-outcome record carries** | `outcome` taking one of **`succeeded`**, **`failed`** or **`rejected`**; on `rejected`, the `rejectedCheck` field naming the check, and on `failed`, the failing step. It is the **last** of the four lines, so a truncated capture is detectable by its absence rather than by a length comparison |
| **The `outcome` vocabulary, counted, because the two sets above overlap** | **Seven distinct literals across the two closed sets**, with the derivation published rather than left to a consumer to infer: `5 + 3 = 8` declarations, less the one literal declared in both sets, gives **seven**. `failed` is that literal — the only value a record of either kind may carry — so a consumer validating `outcome` **without** first reading `State.operation` admits exactly those seven, `created`, `already-present`, `rotated`, `failed`, `not-attempted`, `succeeded` and `rejected`, while one that reads the discriminator first admits **five** on each of the three operation records and **three** on the run record. The second is the stricter reading and the intended one: `succeeded` on an operation record and `created` on the run record are both malformed, and only the discriminator separates them. **Neither six nor eight is a count of this vocabulary** — eight counts declarations rather than values, and six counts nothing this property defines — so a consumer or a summary publishing either is describing a set this document does not close |
| **What every one of the four carries** | The run-identifying fields — `invocationId`, `actor`, `timestamp`, `targetUserName`, `roleName` — so **any single line is self-describing** and a line separated from its siblings is still an audit record rather than a fragment. This is deliberate duplication: the alternative is a header record the other three depend on, and a consumer that lost the header would hold three unattributable lines |
| **A rejected invocation still emits four** | The three operation records carry `outcome = not-attempted` and the run record carries `outcome = rejected` with its `rejectedCheck`. This is not padding: "this run did not attempt the user operation" is a true and auditable statement, and emitting it keeps the cardinality a constant so the pre-host rejection path — the path the dedicated serialiser exists for — is counted by the same rule as every other path. A serialiser that can write one line before a host exists can write four |
| **The order is fixed and asserted** | `create-user`, `create-role`, `add-membership`, `run`. The consumer asserts the **sequence** of the four `State.operation` values, not merely the set, so a reordering that would confuse a reader of the container is caught |
| **How it relates to the `--report-dir` report, so the two are not mistaken for one artifact** | They are **two artifacts with one vocabulary and two destinations**, and both are required. The **report** is a file in the run's artifact directory, written only on a path that reached the operations, and it is what row 75 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) reads. The **audit record set** is four lines on standard output, written on **every** path, and it is what the immutable container receives. Where both exist, the three operation records' `operation` and `outcome` values are the **same literals** the report's three rows carry for the same invocation — asserted, not assumed, by row **O7** — which is the whole point of not inventing a second vocabulary |

**The four records as literal bytes, because a consumer writing a selector needs the shape and not a
description of it.** Below is one successful invocation's complete audit set, shown indented for
readability — on the wire each object is **one line** and the set is **four lines in this order**, which
is exactly what `$AUDIT_LINES` holds and what the container receives. `Scopes` is `[]` on every one of
them, because the tool is a console process with no request and no ambient `Activity`, which is the
same property the formatter subsection establishes for a background service:

