Three properties of those bytes are worth naming because each is a rule rather than an incidental of the
example. **`targetUserName` is the alias, not the user name** — `a3f1c9d0` above — under the aliasing
contract this document applies to every personal-data field that leaves a process, which is why an audit
record is safe to place in a 365-day immutable container. **No field carries the password, the connection
string or an exception message**, so the never-record list is satisfied by the shape itself rather than by
a filter over it. And **`invocationId` is identical across all four lines and is the value in the blob
name**, which is what lets a reader of the container tie a set back to one invocation without trusting
file ordering.

**Its owner is the immutable blob container, and the workspace is not a destination.** An earlier version
of this property said the record was "written through `ILogger` to the application's configured sink and
retained under the platform's log-retention policy", and that is wrong twice over.
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) is the authority and states both corrections: this command
runs on a build agent, so **no console-log collection applies to it at all** — there is no captured
container stream and no agent — and its record's **single owner is that document's append-only container
under a 365-day time-based immutability policy**, reached by the pipeline capturing the command's output
and uploading it. [06 §9.2.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) draws the same conclusion from the
other side: `AdminProvisioned` is the one mandatory record that "does not travel this channel at all", and
no alert, gate or audit query is written against a workspace table for it. So **an operator querying the
workspace for this event finds nothing, by design**, and this document must not describe a sink that would
imply otherwise.

**The serialisation is deterministic and separate from diagnostic logging, and the reason is a hard one
rather than a stylistic one.**

| Property | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| **What fields the record carries**, and their names | **`R7` of [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)** — thirteen field names, checkable one by one against [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md)'s `PROV-6001` row. Not restated here in any form |
| **Where the record goes, by what mechanism, and how long it survives** | **[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)**, hop by hop: standard output through `ILogger` with the framework's JSON console formatter, captured into the invoking job's run record, the selected lines kept there, with change-record attachment as the named fallback and run-record retention as a provider gate item |
| **How many records a run emits, per mode and per revoke branch** | **[06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s execution-path block**, which is also where the four operations below are enumerated as a record set rather than as behaviour |
| **What each operation may conclude** | [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) row 16's closed outcome set, quoted by operation below because the partition is this command's behaviour even though the vocabulary is 09's |
| **That no credential appears on any path** | This property, below. It is a behavioural requirement on the process that holds the secret and belongs with the process |

**Two claims an earlier form of this property made are withdrawn, and both were load-bearing enough to
name.** The first was arithmetic: it read *"exactly one destination, exactly one instance per
invocation"*, and the per-invocation count is wrong — `R7` is a **per-operation** record, so a correct run
emits one per operation and [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) hop 2 records the withdrawal
of the "exactly one" rule on its own side, noting that it *"would have failed every correct provisioning
run"*. The second was a whole rival record: this property specified a **bespoke deterministic serialiser
over a dedicated record type**, wrote its own field list, and named an **append-only blob container under
a time-based immutability policy** as the record's single owner, with an upload, a byte-for-byte read-back
and a name carrying the invocation id. All of it is withdrawn. The container is infrastructure outside the
AAP's artifact set and [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) withdraws it from the design
entirely, so a destination this document named would have pointed at nothing; and the serialiser's own
justification — that the pre-host rejection paths have no logger — is removed by
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) hop 1's requirement that **the logging pipeline is
constructed before argument validation**, which a `LoggerFactory` with the console provider permits
because it needs no host. One producer, on every path, is both simpler and the thing `R7` describes.

**The operations a run performs — four, not three.** The credential is an operation in its own right, and
an earlier form of this section counted three by folding it into the user's creation. Each is checked
**independently**, and each concludes with one literal from [09 §6.8.1](09-security-assessment.md) row
16's closed set:

| Operation | What the run does | What it may conclude |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Role** | Create the `Administrator` role only if absent | `RoleCreated`, `RoleAlreadyExisted` |
| **User** | Create the target account only if absent | `UserCreated`, `UserAlreadyExisted` |
| **Credential** | Set the password **only** when the account is created by this run, or when the invocation explicitly passes `--rotate-credential` | `Created`, `AlreadyPresent_NotRotated`, `Rotated` |
| **Membership** | Add the account to the role only if it does not already hold it | `MembershipAdded`, `MembershipAlreadyPresent` |

The revoke mode's **operations and their order** are property 3a above — two, `user` then `membership` —
and its **per-branch record set** is [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s execution-path
block's; its two membership outcomes, `MembershipRevoked` and `MembershipNotHeld`, come from the same
closed set. **Six failure outcomes are
shared by every operation** rather than being per-operation: `Failed_ArgumentRejected`,
`Failed_UserNotFound`, `Failed_PolicyRejected`, `Failed_PublishedCredentialRefused`,
`Failed_IdentityError` and `Failed_StoreUnavailable`. Naming them here is what makes the credential's
`AlreadyPresent_NotRotated` legible as a *deliberate no-change* rather than as a silent skip: the
distinction between "the password was left alone because nobody asked for a rotation" and "the password
could not be set" is the whole reason the vocabulary is a closed set of named values rather than the
phrase *"already present"*.

**The password is never serialised, never echoed, and never written to any field, at any level, on any
path — including every failure path.** That is section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s
never-record list applied to the one process in this design that holds the secret, and
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states the same requirement from the channel's side
rather than leaving it to be inferred. Nothing derived from a value that failed validation is recorded
either, which is why a refused credential concludes at `Failed_PublishedCredentialRefused` — a named
outcome — rather than by reporting what the policy objected to. This is net-new: the repository has no
audit logging of any kind ([09 §3.13](09-security-assessment.md)).

**How the actor reaches the record — transported, not asserted.** A process cannot vouch for who invoked
it, so the field is not something the tool determines:

- The actor arrives as **`MUSICSTORE_AUDIT_ACTOR`, an invocation-scoped environment variable rendered by
  the pipeline from its own authenticated trigger** — the channel of property 2b, and the same declaration
  mechanism as every other value the tool reads. **The variable is named here rather than described**,
  because a pipeline cannot set a channel that has no name and a reviewer cannot check that the right one
  was set; it is read directly by name into a typed field on the parsed invocation, exactly as
  `MUSICSTORE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is, and it is admitted by the operator console's row in section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) and by no other process. It is **not** a switch: the
  `admin` verb's accepted switch set is closed at four and none of them is an actor, so an invocation that
  passed the actor on the command line is rejected by the closed pre-parse of property 1b. It is
  **never** read from the operating-system user, never defaulted, and never typed into a prompt on the
  pipeline path.
- **An absent, empty or whitespace-only actor value fails the invocation before any work**, alongside the
  assertions of property 2 — because a provisioning record whose actor is blank is not an audit record, and
  filling it in with whatever the process can see about itself is worse than failing. The check is a
  presence-and-shape check only: non-empty after trimming, and **not equal to the sentinel below**, so the
  channel cannot be used to forge the one value that means "there was none".
- **What the record carries when the actor itself is what is missing**, because the rejection still owes an
  audit record and an empty field would contradict the rule immediately above. The `actor` field carries
  the **reserved literal `(unavailable)`** — parenthesised precisely so it cannot collide with any identity
  the pipeline renders — and `rejectedCheck` carries `actor-missing`. Two consequences make the sentinel
  safe rather than a hole: it is legal **only** in a record whose `outcome` is `rejected` **and** whose
  `rejectedCheck` is `actor-missing`, so a record carrying it in any other combination is itself a finding;
  and no work was attempted, so the record documents an invocation that changed nothing rather than an
  unattributed change.
- **The field is a copy for readability; the authority is elsewhere.** The blob is written into the
  immutable container **by the pipeline's deployment identity**, and the pipeline's own run record carries
  the authenticated trigger independently
  ([06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) hops 2 to 4). So the record is **corroborated by two
  artifacts the command cannot write**, and a tampered or mis-set actor field is detectable by comparing
  them rather than being taken on trust.

**Every path emits exactly four records, and that includes the paths that fail.**

The four rows are ordered by **how far the invocation got**, and the boundary that matters is drawn where
the host is *built* rather than where it is *started* — an earlier version of this table put startup
validation on the pre-host side, which is wrong: validation is the explicit `IStartupValidator.Validate()`
call of assertion 2, and that call happens **after** `Build()` returns.

| Path | What is emitted |
| --- | --- |
| Success | **Four records.** Each operation record carries its own `created` or `already-present`, and the run record carries `succeeded` |
| Failure **after work has begun** — a create that fails, a database error, an assertion of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) that a live target contradicts | **Four records.** The operations that completed carry their own result, the one that failed carries `failed` with the failing step named, any operation not reached carries `not-attempted`, and the run record carries `failed`. No exception text, no connection string, no password: the sanitised fields of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) |
| Failure **after the host is built but before any work** — the environment assertion of property 2a, and the configuration validation of assertion 2, both of which run between `Build()` and the first scope | **Four records.** All three operation records carry `not-attempted`; the run record carries `outcome = rejected`, naming the check and — for a validation failure — each member the aggregated result named. A logger **is** resolvable on this path, and all four records are emitted by the serialiser regardless, because one producer for the audit record is the property being kept and a second producer chosen by how far the process got would be indistinguishable from a missing record when one of the two is broken |
| Failure **before any host is built** — an unrecognised, duplicated or valueless switch, a missing verb, two verbs, a missing actor | **Four records**, on the same rule: three `not-attempted` operation records and a run record carrying `outcome = rejected` and the check that rejected it. This is the path the serialiser **exists** for: there is no container, no configuration binding and no logger, so a logging call could not emit here at all — and it is also why the cardinality is a constant, because a path with no host is exactly the path where a consumer must not be asked to work out how many lines to expect |
| The **manual** path — an operator session, which [06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) records as the exception rather than an equal alternative | The **same four records** on standard output, and the operator is responsible for capturing them, running the **same `jq` selection** as the pipeline and uploading the selected lines with the same `az storage blob upload --auth-mode login --overwrite false` invocation the row below specifies, supplying their own identity as the actor. Stated with its weakness rather than as an equivalent: a human-supplied actor value is not corroborated by a pipeline trigger, so this path's records are weaker evidence and the invocation is recorded as an exception in the run record |

**How the four lines are found, because they share standard output with ordinary diagnostic records.** The
tool's progress and error records go to the same stream, so "capture the output and upload it" is not
specific enough to be implementable. The rule is a selection with a count and an order check:

- The pipeline reads the captured standard output **line by line**, parses each line that is a complete
  JSON object, and selects those whose **`State.eventName` is exactly `AdminProvisioned`** — the **nested**
  path, for the reason the parity row above gives, and expressed once so no consumer has to reconstruct it:

  ```bash
  # $CAPTURE is the command's captured standard output, which also carries the
  # tool's diagnostic records. -R reads each line as raw text and 'fromjson?'
  # drops the lines that are not JSON instead of aborting on them; 'objects'
  # drops any JSON value that is not an object, so the path is only applied to
  # something it can be applied to. --exit-status makes an empty result non-zero.
  jq -Rc --exit-status \
    'fromjson? | objects | select(.State.eventName == "AdminProvisioned")' \
    "$CAPTURE" > "$AUDIT_LINES"
  test "$(wc -l < "$AUDIT_LINES")" -eq 4

  # The four State.operation values, in emission order, must be exactly this
  # sequence. -s slurps the already-selected lines into one array, so this
  # reads the SELECTED set and never re-runs the predicate.
  test "$(jq -Rc -s 'map(fromjson | .State.operation) | join(",")' \
            "$AUDIT_LINES")" = '"create-user,create-role,add-membership,run"'
  ```

  `jq` is not a new dependency: [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) pins it on the release
  agent image and asserts `jq --version` at provisioning, precisely so a readback that captures JSON has
  something to assert with. The serialiser writes **each** of its four objects on a single line, and
  `AdminProvisioned` is
  one named event in [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s closed schema which **no other
  record in this tool may carry** — so the predicate is exact rather than heuristic. A selector written
  against a top-level
  `eventName` matches **nothing**, for the reason the parity row states; that is the one mistake this
  subsection is written to prevent.
- **Exactly four matches are required, and the discriminator sequence is checked too.** Fewer than four
  and more than four are **both** failures of the
  provisioning step, reported distinctly: fewer means the tool exited without discharging its audit
  obligation in full, and more means something emits the event name that should not, which invalidates
  "four records per invocation" more quietly than an absence would. Neither is resolved by picking lines.
  The cases are distinguishable in the block above without any extra reporting code, which is why it is
  written that way: **zero fails at the `jq` line**, because `--exit-status` returns non-zero when the
  filter produced no output; **any other count fails at the first `test` line**, because the count is not
  4; and **four lines carrying the wrong operations, the wrong order or a duplicated operation fail at the
  second `test` line**, which is the case a count alone would pass. So the failing line names which of the
  three happened.
- **The four selected lines are uploaded verbatim** — the exact bytes in emission order, not a
  re-serialisation and not a re-ordering — which is what makes
  the byte-for-byte read-back below a meaningful comparison rather than a comparison of two renderings.
- Lines that are not JSON, and JSON objects carrying any other event name, are **left in the diagnostic
  capture and never uploaded to the audit container**, so the container holds provisioning records and
  nothing else.

**Uploaded and verified, because an audit copy nobody checked is an assumption.** The selected lines — the
exact bytes in emission order, `$AUDIT_LINES` above — are uploaded to the immutable container **as one
blob**, then **read back and compared
byte-for-byte with what the command emitted**, and the read-back copy is re-tested against the **same**
`State.eventName` predicate **and the same four-line count and operation sequence**, so the artifact in
the container is verified to be the whole record set rather than
merely to be a file of the right length. **One blob rather than four** is deliberate: the four lines are
one invocation's audit record, the immutable container's `--overwrite false` guarantee then covers the set
indivisibly, and four separately named blobs would make a partial upload look like a complete one:

```bash
set -euo pipefail

AUDIT_BLOB="adminprovisioned-$INVOCATION_ID.json"

az storage blob upload \
  --account-name "$AUDIT_ACCOUNT" \
  --container-name "$AUDIT_CONTAINER" \
  --name "$AUDIT_BLOB" \
  --file "$AUDIT_LINES" \
  --auth-mode login \
  --overwrite false

az storage blob download \
  --account-name "$AUDIT_ACCOUNT" \
  --container-name "$AUDIT_CONTAINER" \
  --name "$AUDIT_BLOB" \
  --file "$AUDIT_READBACK" \
  --auth-mode login

cmp -- "$AUDIT_LINES" "$AUDIT_READBACK"
jq -Rc --exit-status \
  'fromjson? | objects | select(.State.eventName == "AdminProvisioned")' \
  "$AUDIT_READBACK" > /dev/null
test "$(wc -l < "$AUDIT_READBACK")" -eq 4
test "$(jq -Rc -s 'map(fromjson | .State.operation) | join(",")' \
          "$AUDIT_READBACK")" = '"create-user,create-role,add-membership,run"'
```

A missing or mismatched blob is a **failed provisioning step** even where the
provisioning itself succeeded — the account exists and the audit obligation does not, which is a state that
must be visible immediately rather than discovered at a review. **An invocation whose four records are not
all verified is itself a finding**, which is the property that makes "four records per invocation"
checkable. `--overwrite
false` on the upload is what makes the immutable container's own guarantee assertable from this side too:
a second invocation cannot reuse the name, because the name carries the invocation id.

**Coverage rows O5 to O9 of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes)** exercise this: **four**
records on each of the four paths, exactly four and in the pinned operation order, the actor carried
through **every one** of them, the rejected path emitting all four
without a host, and the secret absent from every one of them.

#### Exit-code allocation

**The exit codes, allocated here — once, tool-wide, for all ten verbs — because "distinct numeric codes"
is not a contract anybody can implement, test or branch on.** Every failure path in this section, in
section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), in section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) and in sections
[5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) and
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) is specified as "a non-zero exit", and
coverage row **O9** required those codes to be "documented, distinct" while no document allocated a single
value. Three consumers need the actual numbers: the implementation, which has to return one; the tests,
which assert on one; and the release pipeline, which branches on one. So the allocation is made **once,
here**, this is **the only exit-code table in this document**, and every verb and every other section
cites it rather than choosing. **Five codes, and no verb defines a sixth.**

| Code | Class | What returns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | **Completed, and its own verification passed** | The verb completed. For `admin`, all three operations reached a terminal state — created or already present. For a load verb, the phase completed and its reconciliation passed. For `diff-schema` and `reconcile`, the comparison found nothing to report. For `seed`, all three guard checks passed and the whole-seed transaction committed. For the three lifecycle verbs, the transition was written — or was already recorded, which is their idempotent re-verification path |
| **2** | **A precondition was rejected and nothing was written** | The closed pre-parse of property 1b — an unrecognised switch, a switch spelled for another verb, a value-taking switch with nothing after it, a repeated switch, a missing verb, two verbs, a `--store` value outside the closed set, an absent `--store` or `--run-id` on a verb that requires one. The startup validation of assertion 2 — any of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s five connection checks, a missing required member, or the absent `IHostRoleSignal` registration. The expected-value refusals — property 2a's environment assertion, the `EXPECTED_*` comparisons, and the control-plane server, `DB_NAME()` and `USER_NAME()` assertions of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract). The three-check seeding guard of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks), including a pattern that cannot narrow anything. The run-state refusals of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) — a missing parent run row, a run already `Accepted` or `Closed`, a missing run-source row for `(RunId, --store)`, a fingerprint that does not match that store's run-source row, a second `--begin-run` against a target carrying an unclosed run, a non-empty target with no matching checkpoint, a `--resume` whose checkpoint holds no row for this run and store, a `seal-manifest` whose `reconcile --store both` has not passed, an `accept-run` or `close-run` whose own preconditions are unmet, a non-empty Identity child table with no recorded disposition, and `sp_getapplock` not granted within its wait. **Every one of these happens before any write**, and a pipeline's response to all of them is the same: fix the invocation or the state, do not retry it blindly |
| **3** | **Could not connect, or the schema is not in the expected state** | Token acquisition for the deployment identity failed, the login was refused, the database was unreachable, or a statement was refused for want of a grant — the `SET IDENTITY_INSERT` and DDL rights of section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) among them. Also the structural preconditions: a migrations-history table or the session cache table absent when a step requires it, and a target whose schema does not match the extracted record. Separated from **2** because the invocation was *right* and the environment was not, which is a different fix and often a different owner |
| **4** | **Partial work, rolled back to the last committed table boundary** | The run committed one or more table units and then stopped — a lost connection, a cancellation, a retry envelope exhausted, or the seed's whole-seed transaction rolling back. The checkpoint rows of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) record exactly what completed, and the interrupted unit is **wholly absent**. The response is mechanical: **re-run the same verb with `--resume` and the same `--run-id`** — except for `seed`, which accepts neither switch and has no intermediate committed boundary, so a `4` from it means the pre-state exactly and the response is to re-run `seed`, safe by its idempotence rule (section [4.12](#412-resiliency-timeouts-cancellation-and-async-data-access)'s seed write contract) |
| **5** | **A verification failed — cutover is blocked** | The **migration-set comparison** of assertion 4 in section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) found the deployed history table and the assembly's declared-target set unequal **in either direction** — the one member of that assertion list that is not a `2`, because [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) pins one code for that comparison wherever it runs; `diff-schema` found a difference the extracted record does not explain; `reconcile` found a mismatch — a per-table row count, a per-order financial total, an Identity account, role, assignment or per-provider linked-login count, a missing administrator membership, a member row with no corresponding target row or a target row with no member row; a duplicate normalized **user name** found by the pre-write collision scan (a duplicate normalized **email** is a notice and exits `0`); or rows in the target whose keys are **not** in the source, so the target is not a partially loaded copy of this source. The operation ran and its result is **not trustworthy**, which is the one class that must never be retried blindly. **The shell steps' verifications are not this code** — the transfer block's `sha256sum --check` and the audit read-back's `cmp` return **their own** statuses per the third property below; they belong to the same *class* for the pipeline's branching, and the pipeline classifies them by **which step failed** rather than by translating a status |

Three properties of the allocation, stated because each one is a decision:

- **`1` is deliberately unallocated.** It is what a runtime-terminated process and most shell built-ins
  produce, so giving it a meaning of its own would make an unhandled failure indistinguishable from a
  classified one. A `1` from this tool means "it fell over", and that is worth being able to tell apart.
  **`6` and `7` are likewise unallocated**: an earlier revision of this table defined them, and every
  condition they carried is folded above — a data or verification failure is **5**, and a partial run
  whose next action is a decision is **5** where the target holds keys the source does not and **4**
  where committed units are simply to be resumed. Two codes fewer is two fewer things a pipeline branch
  can get wrong.
- **The allocation is by *class*, not by individual check** — which is why the pre-parse, the startup
  validation, the expected-value assertions and the seeding guard all share **2**. A pipeline branches on
  the class; the **specific** check is named in the output and in the audit record's `rejectedCheck`,
  where a human reads it. Coverage row **O9** asserts the class per path and the named check in the
  output, rather than a unique integer per check, which is the form that is actually stable across future
  checks being added.
- **Exit statuses from other commands are passed through unchanged and are not part of this allocation.**
  The `az`, `sha256sum`, `cmp` and `jq` invocations in this document's shell blocks return their own
  statuses; the blocks re-raise them rather than translating them, because a translated status loses the
  tool's own diagnosis. This allocation governs `provision-admin` and nothing else — in particular it does
  **not** govern `dotnet sql-cache`, whose own `0`/`1`/`2` contract and the release actions for each are
  [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s, and whose `1` deliberately carries two meanings that
  that section resolves with a post-condition rather than with a code.

**5. It is not deployed with the web application.** A separate project, not referenced by the web
project and not included in its publish output, run from the release pipeline or an operator session.
**The `ProjectReference` of property 2 points from the tool to the web application and never the
reverse**, so sharing the registration surface does not put the tool into the deployed site — the
structural consequence is [04 §12.3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s and is not restated here.
**The credential leaves configuration entirely** — no `appsettings` key, no environment variable on the
web application, and nothing for a compromised web process to read.

#### 10.2.1 Exit statuses and where the allocation lives

**The allocation is [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s, and it is not restated here.** Every
failure path in this section is specified behaviourally — what was refused, at what point, and with nothing
written — and the numeric status each one returns belongs to the command's argument-grammar contract, which
this section's own lead already assigns to that document. Three consumers need the number: the
implementation, which returns one; coverage row **O9** of section
[12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes), which asserts one; and the release step, which branches on
one. All three read it from the one place that allocates it, and this subsection exists so that a reader
who arrives at a "non-zero exit" in this document knows where the number is.

**What this document requires of that allocation, as distinct from what it chooses.** Two requirements,
and neither names a value:

- **The allocation is by *class*, and the specific check is named in the output rather than encoded in the
  status.** Several checks legitimately share a class — the pre-parse refusals of property 1b share one,
  and the expected-value refusals of property 2a share another — so coverage row **O9** asserts the class
  per path *and* that the named check in the captured output differs where the status does not. A unique
  integer per check is the form that stops being true the first time a check is added; the specific check
  is where a human reads it — in the output, and in the audit record's `RejectedField` and `RejectionRule`,
  the two members `R7` of [06 §9.6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) carries for exactly this purpose.
  **An earlier form of this bullet named a `rejectedCheck` field**, which property 4 withdraws: it was this
  document's invention and duplicated those two members under a third name.
- **A refusal has no side effect**, which is what makes a status safe to branch on at all: every path this
  section specifies as a refusal is asserted to have written nothing, so a release step that retries one
  class and stops on another cannot compound a partial write.

**Exit statuses from other commands are passed through unchanged and are no part of the allocation.** The
`az`, `sha256sum`, `cmp` and `jq` invocations in this document's shell blocks return their own statuses and
the blocks re-raise them rather than translating them, because a translated status loses the tool's own
diagnosis; the pipeline classifies those failures by **which step failed** rather than by reading a number.
In particular the allocation does not govern `dotnet sql-cache`, whose own contract and the release action
for each of its statuses are [06 §6.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s.

### 10.3 What this retires

The `async void` method [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:21] and its call [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:18]; the
three hand-built objects [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:27-29]; the two `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` reads [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:23-24] and the
`using System.Configuration;` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:7] that supports them; and the two committed credential keys
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17]. **Failure becomes observable** — a non-zero exit code and a
log record from a command someone ran, rather than silence inside a start-up path.

Provisioning moves out of the application and into an operator action, which is an **approved delta**
with **Security and operations** as its approval owners (section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)). The user-visible consequence is that a freshly deployed
environment has no administrator until the command is run, which the deployment runbook of
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) must include as a step.

## 11. The cutover decision

### 11.1 The decision

**A single cutover, not a strangler fig.** The ported application replaces the legacy application in
one switch, during a planned window, with a rollback plan.

This is a **decision**, not a comparison, and it is stated once. [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)
sequences around it. **A reappearance of this question as an unresolved comparison anywhere in the
deliverable set is a defect**, not a nuance — the incremental path appears below only as a conditional
alternative with named trigger conditions.

### 11.2 Why

MvcMusicStore is **one deployable unit** with six controllers and roughly **2,097 non-blank lines** of
C# in the migration source — the **sizing metric** of [08 §2.1](08-technical-debt-register.md), non-blank
lines excluding assembly metadata, which is the method [08 §4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) uses
for that figure and the only method under which it should be read. It has:

- **no independently deployable module** — one project, no `ProjectReference`, no areas, and one
  conventional route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:16-20] serving the whole URL
  surface;
- **no route family migratable in isolation.** The layout renders the cart summary and the genre menu
  on **every** page [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:25-26], and the cart identity
  lives in session [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180], so migrating any route
  drags session and identity across the boundary with it;
- **no traffic profile that makes a partial cutover safer** than a whole one — there is no measured
  load, no SLA and no observability to measure one with ([11 §3.8](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)).

The strangler path would require a second host, adapters on both sides, shared session across the
boundary and authentication continuity across it — real, permanent-feeling complexity, built and then
discarded, in exchange for a granularity this application cannot use.

### 11.3 What single cutover does not buy

It does not remove the need for the pre-port test suite; it increases it, because there is no
route-by-route soak period in which a regression surfaces on a fraction of traffic. Section
[12](#12-the-test-suite-architecture-and-coverage) is the compensating control, and it is why tests
precede the port rather than accompanying it.

### 11.4 Two accepted costs

Both follow from facts already established, and both are accepted **deliberately here** rather than
discovered on the day.

**Cost one — every signed-in user is signed out at cutover.**

Katana cookie authentication tickets are protected by the old application's key material, and the new
application has a different key ring; there is no shared key material in the repository to bridge them
(no `machineKey` in any edition — [11 §3.2](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md)). **The tickets are
unreadable by the new runtime.** The adapters' remote-authentication mechanism exists precisely to
avoid this and is not in play under a single cutover.

The response is **operational, not technical**:

- **Expire the legacy authentication cookie at the new application's first request**, so no browser
  retries an undecryptable ticket and then presents an ambiguous state. The mechanism — the cookie name,
  its attributes, the pipeline position, the idempotence guarantee, the record and the removal date — is
  section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 2 item 3 and is not restated here. What this
  cost records is that the expiry is a **deliberate deletion** rather than a reliance on the new runtime
  ignoring a cookie it cannot read.
- **Notify users ahead of the window.**
- **Accept re-authentication as the cost.** [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states it in the
  cutover runbook.

**Cost two — anonymous carts do not survive, even though their rows do.**

An anonymous cart's identity lives **only** in in-process session: a `Guid.NewGuid()` written to
session and never sent to the client as anything else
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:161-180], specifically [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:172] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:175]. When the old
process stops, **the browser-to-GUID link is lost**, so the `Cart` rows become **orphaned regardless of
whether they are migrated** — nothing can ever look them up again.

**Signed-in carts are unaffected**, because their key is the login name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:167], which the Identity data
migration preserves as its invariant (sections
[4.4](#44-what-the-cart-is-coupled-to--and-what-it-is-not) and
[5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)).

The response:

- **Schedule cutover in a low-traffic window** and **drain the legacy application** before switching, so
  the number of live anonymous sessions at the moment of the switch is as close to zero as scheduling
  can make it.
- **Migrate the `Cart` rows anyway.** No data is destroyed, and the orphaned rows can then be reported
  and cleaned up on a stated schedule afterwards rather than silently vanishing.
- **Building a session-bridging mechanism is explicitly rejected as disproportionate** — it would mean
  standing up shared session state between two frameworks in order to preserve anonymous shopping
  carts on a store whose checkout requires authentication anyway
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:8].

**Both costs, plus the maintenance window and the drain step, belong in the rollback plan — because a
cutover that must be reversed produces the same two effects in the other direction.** Reverting signs
everyone out again, and anonymous carts created on the new application are lost on the way back. The
rollback plan must therefore state: the window, the drain, the legacy redeployment, the **frozen** source
database — stage `M2` of the source-disposition lifecycle of section
[5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover) — as
the data position, and the post-`M1` backup of step 4 of section
[5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) as its copy, the second forced
re-authentication,
and the second anonymous-cart loss. **"Unmodified" was an earlier form's word here and is withdrawn**:
the rollback position is a store that received the two named mutations, so the published credential does
not come back with it. A rollback that is written as if it were free is a rollback nobody
will be willing to execute at 2am.

### 11.5 The full set of approved deltas

Behaviour preservation is the baseline: a visitor can browse genres and albums, view album detail, add
to and remove from a cart, see a cart count and summary, register, sign in and out, place an order with
promo-code handling, view their own orders, and — as an administrator — create, edit and delete albums.
Every one of those outcomes is preserved.

**The table below is everything that deliberately changes — forty-seven rows, each with its own approval owner.** Its purpose is to let validation
distinguish **a preserved contract from an approved change**, rather than treating every difference as
a regression — and equally to stop an approved change being used to excuse a real one.

**Forty-nine rows and forty-seven approved deltas, because two rows are retired identifiers.** The ids run
`D-01` to `D-49` with no gap, and two of them assert **no difference**. **`D-22`** records the withdrawal
of the duplicate-genre disambiguation listing, which section
[4.14](#414-the-duplicate-genre-browse-contract) withdrew as an unauthorized new capability. **`D-43`** is
the second, retired by this revision: it claimed the source persists a checkout submission that violates
its own annotations, and row 67 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts **zero** rows written on
**both** fixtures for exactly that submission shape, so the row was asserting a change that does not
exist. So the count of *rows* is forty-nine and the count of *approved deltas* is **forty-seven** —
`49 − 2 = 47` — and both figures are stated because a reader counting rows and a reader counting changes
get different answers, the difference being exactly those two ids. **Every citation of a delta anywhere in this document or in a sibling deliverable is by
id, never by position** — a positional citation breaks the moment a row is added, and this register
has been renumbered before. An id is **never reused**: a change that is withdrawn keeps its id retired
rather than passing it to a successor, which is why `D-22` and `D-43` each occupy a row rather than
vanishing and leaving `D-23` to be misread as the twenty-second delta. Where a single entry would carry two changes it is **split**,
because the two halves have different owners or different failure modes: `D-14`/`D-28` (the HTTPS
redirect versus the response header set), `D-17`/`D-29` (paging versus the tooltip cap) and
`D-18`/`D-30` (the character set versus the normalized-name semantics) are those splits.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Five entries follow: three classes of change this section is specifically asked about and deliberately
does *not* record as deltas — cart-mutation retry, the `NotFound()` conversions and checkout submission
idempotence — and two corrections, one promoting a difference to `D-49` and one naming a site that
appeared in the wrong list.** `3 + 2 = 5`, and the figure is stated because an earlier form of this
sentence said **four** while five bullets followed it: the `D-49` promotion was added without the count
moving with it. The reasoning is stated rather than left as an omission, because the table claims
completeness and a reader must be able to tell an item that was considered and excluded from one that
was forgotten.

- **Cart-mutation retry and idempotence is a *preserved* contract, not a delta.** Section
  [4.13](#413-the-cart-is-one-concurrency-domain-keyed-by-cart-identity) requirement 4 withdraws the
  earlier accepted over-count exposure and replaces it with a durable operation ledger. With that ledger a
  replayed mutation is a **no-op returning the committed result**, so the committed effect of one
  submission is **exactly one application** — which is precisely what the source does when no fault occurs
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:34-58]. The behaviour a visitor can observe is therefore
  unchanged, and promoting it to a delta row would misreport a defect *closed* as a contract *altered*.
  What **is** recorded is `D-20`, which covers the different case: the mutation that cannot be applied at
  all.
- **The three `NotFound()` conversions are not a delta, because they are not a difference at all.** The
  conversions of section [13](#13-resolution-register--all-23-blockers-of-deliverable-12) replace
  `HttpNotFound()` with `NotFound()` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:35],
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:76] and [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/StoreManagerController.cs:108] — the **same 404** from a renamed helper, on three branches the source already
  null-checks. There is nothing for an approver to decide and nothing for the suite to admit, which is
  why row 17 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts them as a **preserved** contract.
  **The authorization on those actions is preserved, not changed**: the
  administration attributes are the source's own.
- **An unhandled exception becoming a 404 *is* a numbered delta — `D-49` — and an earlier form of this
  section wrongly excluded it.** The four request-issued branches of section
  [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census)'s census where a **client-supplied
  identifier** resolves to 404 instead of throwing — the unknown genre name, the absent album on the cart
  *write* path, the absent cart record on removal, and the unknown public album id — together with the
  genre zero-match 404 of section [4.14](#414-the-duplicate-genre-browse-contract), which is the first of
  those four, are all one difference on four sites and are recorded as **`D-49`** in the table above.
  The *reason* is unchanged and is still a defect resolution: nothing documented ever said the
  application returns a 500 for an unknown
  album id or an unknown genre name, and [08 §5.4.1](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns those as recorded
  debt. **What changed is the recognition that a reason is not an approval.** The earlier text had the
  coverage assertions record these branches as
  **named baseline differences** citing only the debt owner — rows 38, 39 and 66 of section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage), and case `1c` — which section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s single admission rule would have reported
  as a **failure** on every one of them, because that rule accepts `EXPECTED-DIFFERENCE` **only** against
  a ledger id. Those rows now cite `D-49`. **Branch (a) of the Genre contract still carries no delta row
  of its own** — its 404 is `D-49`'s first site, and its unique index is a schema property with no
  caller-visible difference.
- **The missing id on confirmed delete is *not* in that class, and it was: it is a preserved 500.** An
  earlier form of the bullet above listed **five** branches and counted the confirmed-delete POST among
  them, which conflicted with section
  [4.15](#415-query-failure-contracts--the-complete-branch-census)'s own summary and would have made the
  404 an unnumbered delta. Census site **F5** now preserves the source's 500 exactly and adds only a log
  record, so the site appears in **neither** list: it is not a status correction and it is not an approved
  delta. Row 41 of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts the preserved 500 and the single
  `ADMIN-4003` record at outcome `AbsentRow`, and the underlying inconsistency — a GET that 404s and a
  POST that 500s for the same absent id — stays with [08 §5.4](08-technical-debt-register.md) as debt for
  a separately approved change.
- **Checkout submission idempotence is a preserved *outcome*, not a delta.** The submission key of section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) exists so that one submission produces
  **exactly one order**, which is what the source already does whenever no fault occurs
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:44-51]; the reconciled replay returns the order
  the lost acknowledgement was owed rather than creating a second one. Recording the mechanism as a delta
  would again misreport a defect *closed* as a contract *altered*. What **is** recorded is its two
  observable halves: `D-21` for the zero-line order a resubmission used to create, and `D-42` for the
  message a rejected or expired submission now carries.

### 11.6 The incremental path — a conditional alternative

The incremental path is **available and not selected**. It becomes the right answer only if one of the
following holds — stated as **operational conditions**, not as durations, because a duration is
[07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s to state:

- **The application must remain continuously available throughout the port, with no maintenance window
  available at any point.** Single cutover requires a window; if none can be obtained, the decision
  changes.
- **The Identity migration must be proven against live production traffic before it is committed.** The
  incremental path lets one host remain the authentication authority while the other is exercised.
- **A risk policy requires route-by-route isolation with independent rollback per route.**

Two facts make it genuinely available rather than theoretical: **MVC 5 targets the framework version
recorded at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj:16]**, which
clears the System.Web adapters' framework floor, and the reverse proxy supports the target framework.
[04 §7.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the conditional package pins for both, and this
document names no version.

**If it is selected, sign-in continuity is provided by the adapters' remote authentication** —
delegating authentication to the .NET Framework application so that **one host remains the single
authority** for the duration of the port. That is chosen over cookie-format interoperability, which
would require matching cookie names, authentication schemes, application names and key rings across two
frameworks and would fail silently and intermittently when any one of the four drifted. Remote
authentication has one authority and one failure mode.

Selecting it also **removes cost one and cost two of section [11.4](#114-two-accepted-costs)** and adds
its own: two hosts to operate, two deployment pipelines, an adapter surface on both sides, and a
proxy hop on every request for the duration. That trade is the reason it is the alternative rather than
the plan.

### 11.7 Approval-owned additions

**Why this register exists as well as section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas).** That table
records deliberate **changes to an existing** user-perceptible behaviour or interface. It is not the whole
approval surface, because the port also **adds** behaviour that no source behaviour corresponds to — a
validation summary where there is none, a pending state where there is none, a failure path where there is
none — and an addition cannot be recorded as a change to something that does not exist. Calling those
"improvements" and leaving them out of the approval accounting is the defect this section closes: an
improvement is still a decision, it is still visible to a user or to assistive technology, and somebody
still has to own it.

**This table is exhaustive for its category — sixteen rows, each with its owner.** Every deliberate net-new user-perceptible or
assistive-technology behaviour the port introduces is a row here. The rows carry their specifying section
rather than restating its design, so the requirement has one owner and this register stays a register.

| # | Addition | Why it exists | Specified in | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | **A validation summary on the checkout form** | The form has no summary today — `git grep -n ValidationSummary -- 'src/MVC5/*.cshtml'` matches seven views and not this one — so the model-level message the replaced bare `catch` adds renders **nowhere at all** on the page. **An earlier form of this cell also named the promo-code rejection as a message this summary renders; that is withdrawn**, because the source's rejection branch adds no model error [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:33-36], the target adds none, and no entry on either register authorizes one. **Oracle — discriminating in both directions.** Positive: section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) **row 31**, whose persistence-failure redisplay requires the model error rendered *in the validation summary* and which names this addition in terms. Negative control: **row 11**, which requires **no** `.validation-summary-errors` element on the promo-code redisplay. Visible text rather than a visually hidden label, because a sighted user has the same question | item **a5b** of [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements), asserted by row **89** of [12.4](#124-required-coverage) | **Product** |

**Where the boundary between the two registers falls, stated so the pair is closed.** A deliberate
difference in an **existing** user-perceptible behaviour belongs in section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas); a deliberate **net-new** user-perceptible or
assistive-technology behaviour belongs here. A difference in an existing behaviour that appears in neither
register is a **regression**. Changes with no user-perceptible surface at all — a namespace substitution, a
registration moving into `Program.cs`, the cart handler moving from an inline block into a served file — are
in neither register by design, and they are owned by the sections that specify them rather than by an
approver.

**Both registers are consumed together, and neither is a subset of the other.** [07 §7.1](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s
visual review takes the visible rows of both; [07 §7.2](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s sign-off counts
both and states the two counts **separately**; [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)'s accessibility
review takes the assistive-technology rows of this one. [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) W1's approval
gate covers both, because approving one and not the other would leave half the deliberate difference
unapproved.
