**Album ranking, by detail-row count**: `9` (7 rows), `4` (6), `12` (5), `2` (4), `6` (3), `7` (2) are the
rendered six, in that order; albums `1`, `3`, `5`, `8`, `10` and `11` each have exactly **1** and are all
excluded. The sixth place holds 2 and the best excluded album holds 1, so the **boundary is strict** — the
rendered set is determined, not a tie broken by whatever order the provider returns.

Five properties of those numbers are the oracle, and each exists to defeat a specific wrong
implementation.

- **The genre ranking is not the key order.** Expected: `4`, `9`, `1`, `2`, `6`, `10`, `7`, `3`, `5`. A port
  that ordered by `GenreId` would render `1`-`9` and pass a fixture whose ranks happened to follow its
  keys. This one fails it.
- **It is not the name order either**, alphabetically or otherwise: an alphabetical `Take(9)` excludes
  `Rock`, and the expected set excludes `Reggae`.
- **And it is not the album-count order.** Genre `1` holds three albums and every other holds one, so a
  port that ranked by album count — the plausible misreading of a nested aggregate — puts genre `1` first,
  where the expected order puts it third.
- **The album ranking distinguishes `COUNT` from `SUM`.** Ranked by total *quantity* the top six would be
  `4`, `9`, `2`, `6`, `10`, `7`; ranked by detail-row *count* it is `9`, `4`, `12`, `2`, `6`, `7`. The two
  differ in **membership** (`12` against `10`) and in order, so a port that summed quantities where the
  source counts rows fails row 30 rather than passing it. The two aggregates sit ten lines apart in the
  source and take different measures, which is exactly the confusion worth catching.
- **Every genre's total is a non-null integer**, because every genre has at least one album and every
  album has at least one detail row. A genre with no detail rows makes the source's nested `Sum` a SQL
  `SUM` over no rows — that is, `NULL` — and its position under `ORDER BY … DESC` is then a property of the
  provider's null ordering rather than of the ranking. Row 9 asserts the ranking, so the fixture does not
  put a null in it; a genre with no sales is a separate question this suite does not ask.

Two arithmetic checks over the tables above, so a transcription error in the manifest is caught by
reading it: the twelve total-quantity values sum to **137**, and so do the ten per-genre totals; and the
twelve `r` values sum to **33**, which is the `OrderDetails` row count.

**The allocation, order by order, and the arithmetic that ties it to the seven published `Total` values.**
A detail row's own value is `q(a) × Price(a)`, which for the twelve albums is: `1` **`26.97`**, `2`
**`39.96`**, `3` **`94.41`**, `4` **`47.96`**, `5` **`87.43`**, `6` **`69.95`**, `7` **`86.94`**, `8`
**`31.98`**, `9` **`49.47`**, `10` **`233.87`**, `11` **`92.45`**, `12` **`39.98`**.

| Order | Its detail rows, by album | Rows | `Orders.Total` | The sum, written out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `1` | `9`, `4`, `12`, `2`, `6`, `7`, **`1`** | 7 | `361.23` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 39.98 + 39.96 + 69.95 + 86.94 + 26.97 |
| `2` | `9`, `4`, `12`, `2`, `6`, `7`, **`11`** | 7 | `426.71` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 39.98 + 39.96 + 69.95 + 86.94 + 92.45 |
| `3` | `9`, `4`, `12`, `2`, `6`, **`3`** | 6 | `341.73` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 39.98 + 39.96 + 69.95 + 94.41 |
| `4` | `9`, `4`, `12`, `2`, **`5`** | 5 | `264.80` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 39.98 + 39.96 + 87.43 |
| `5` | `9`, `4`, `12`, **`8`** | 4 | `169.39` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 39.98 + 31.98 |
| `6` | `9`, `4`, **`10`** | 3 | `331.30` | 49.47 + 47.96 + 233.87 |
| `7` | `9` | 1 | `49.47` | 49.47 |

The bold album in each row is that order's single-row album, placed by the second clause. **Two further
arithmetic checks**: the seven row counts sum to `7 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 1` = **33**, the `OrderDetails`
row count reached a second way; and the seven totals sum to **`1944.63`**, which is also
`Σ r(a) × q(a) × Price(a)` over the twelve albums. A manifest whose loader produced any other allocation
would fail one of those two sums, which is what makes the rule checkable rather than merely stated.

**Why the single-row albums are distributed rather than all placed in order `1`.** An earlier revision of
this manifest stated the rule as "one row to each of the first `r(a)` orders" for **every** album, which
puts all six single-row albums in order `1` and makes that order's total **`901.37`** — contradicting the
`361.23` published beside it. That was an internal inconsistency and it is corrected here, and the
correction is the *rule*, not the totals, because the distributed allocation is the one the coverage
needs:

- **A purely nested allocation makes every order's row set a subset of order `1`'s**, so no assertion can
  distinguish "this order's own detail rows" from "a prefix of the catalog". Rows 54, 55 and 60 reconcile
  per-order detail sets, and under nesting they would all reconcile against the same shape.
- **Order `7` is a one-line order**, and a one-line order is the boundary shape for the per-order
  reconciliation and for row 60's financial comparison — the case where a single mis-migrated row moves
  the total by the whole of it.
- **The seven row counts are 7, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 1** — six distinct sizes, no order the same shape as its
  neighbour except the first two. A reconciliation that silently compared the wrong order would have to be
  wrong about a count as well as a total to pass.

The dataset is therefore **10 genres, 6 artists, 12 albums, 7 orders and 33 order-detail rows** — larger
than the three-and-six it replaces, and still small enough that one reset restores it between tests
(section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)) and two orders of magnitude below the
seed's ~780 catalog rows.

**The declared pre-existing set — rows the legacy store already holds, which the manifest records rather
than pretends away.** The legacy Identity store is a committed database, not an empty one, and the legacy
application writes to it during startup. A manifest that published `Identity accounts = 4` and an
invariant of "exactly four" would therefore fail on the legacy half for a correct reason, and the obvious
"fix" — deleting whatever it finds — would destroy the very account rows the source's own behaviour
depends on. So the manifest carries a **second, declared section**: rows it expects to find, does not
create, and does not remove.

| Declared pre-existing row | Where it comes from | How the manifest treats it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The source-provisioned administrator** — named in this document by that fixture role and not by a transcribed value | Created by `CreateAdminUser` from the configured user name at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16] at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:38-44]. It is also the account the startup-quiescence wait of problem one step 6 polls for | Recorded **by reference to that configuration key**, which the loader reads at run time — so the manifest carries the key path, not the account's user name, and a store provisioned from a changed key needs no manifest edit. **Never deleted and never modified** — the quiescence wait would then never complete, or would complete against a row the fixture had just rewritten |
| That account's assignment to the `Administrator` role | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:43] | Recorded the same way, by reference. Row 65's "and no other account holds the role" is stated against the loaded set **excluding** this row, for the reason below |
| The `Administrator` role | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.App.cs:32-36] | Recorded, and the loader creates it only if absent |
| Every further account, role, assignment and linked login the committed store already carries | The committed Identity database itself | **Enumerated once by the state extraction of section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction)**, and the enumeration is recorded in the **controlled extract artifact** of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4 — encrypted, access-controlled, untracked. What the **committed** manifest carries for this row is a **count and a digest over the aliased set**, never the user names |

Two consequences, and they are the point of declaring the set rather than assuming it.

- **Every count invariant is stated as `loaded + declared-pre-existing`, never as `loaded`.** The
  post-load invariants below, row 24's before-and-after counts, row 54's per-table reconciliation and row
  57's field-origin assertions all read that sum. A count that omits the declared set is not a stricter
  assertion; it is a wrong one, and it fails on the legacy half only.
- **A store whose observed pre-existing set differs from the declared one is a setup failure**, named as
  such (section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)), not a scenario failure. That
  is the assertion that the committed baseline data is the recorded baseline data, and it is the only
  honest way to hold it: this assessment establishes the *mechanism* by which the set is enumerated — the
  extraction gate — and deliberately does **not** publish the enumerated membership from a
  printable-string inspection of a binary, which section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) already rejects as evidence
  rather than proof for exactly this store.

**Which of these literals depend on the extraction, and which do not — because the dependency is real and
it is narrower than "the manifest depends on the extraction".** [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s **W3**
owns authoritative schema and state extraction; its **W4** owns this suite, and W4's second gate is the
one that runs the `Category=Baseline` half and publishes the baseline record. **Three** of the artifacts
this subsection specifies **cannot be authored or applied before W3 has extracted**, so W4's second gate
depends on W3 and not merely on W4's own first gate. **It was four**, and the fourth was `alice`'s
password hash: that row is **deleted from this table** because the hash is now generated rather than
captured, which is the fifth manifest property below. `4 − 1 = 3`, and of the three, **two are authored
and one is applied**:

| Artifact | Why it is extraction-derived | Consequence for the gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The **declared pre-existing set**'s count and aliased digest, and the row above that enumerates it | Its membership is a property of the committed Identity store, discoverable only by the `sys.columns` and state extraction of sections [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) and [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) — this document deliberately refuses to publish it from a printable-string probe | The post-load invariant that compares observed against declared has nothing to compare against until W3 has run |
| **`seed-expected.json`**'s per-table counts and canonical digests | Captured from the legacy store's catalog tables, which is the whole point of the oracle-outside-the-thing-under-test rule below | Row 24's `24a` has no oracle until W3 has run |
| The **physical-schema mapping** the `CoreApplicationFixture`'s load path applies | Section [5.1](#51-domain-data-migration-starts-with-schema-extraction) makes the extract the load's input, and the extract is W3's output | The Core half's Identity load cannot execute at all before W3 |

**Everything else in this subsection is independent of the extraction and is authored, not discovered**:
every row count and key range in the entity table; the genre, artist and album names; the twelve prices;
`r(a)` and `q(a)`; both rankings and their arithmetic checks; the per-order allocation and the seven
`Total` values; the linked-login shapes; the fixture password literal; and — since the change above —
**`alice`'s legacy-format password hash**, which is now produced from that literal rather than read out of
a store. Those are chosen so that the oracles in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) are stated rather
than discovered — that is the first sentence of this subsection — and choosing them needs no legacy store
at all. So the dependency is **scoped to the three artifacts above** rather than blanket, and the authored
remainder of the manifest can be written and reviewed while W3 is still running.

**[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) owns the edge**, and this is the notification that it needs one: its
W4 second gate must carry **W3 as an entry condition** alongside the entry conditions it already has.
Stated here because the dependency is a property of these artifacts, which this document owns, while gate
entry is a property of the sequence, which [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md) owns — and a gate whose entry
omits it would be closable against **two** artifacts nobody could have authored yet and **one** mapping
nobody could have applied.

**Five properties of the manifest that are requirements rather than description** — four, plus the
generation rule the change above makes necessary.

- **The fixture password is a fixed non-secret literal**, committed with the manifest, valid only against
  a database the fixture created and drops. It is not a credential in the sense section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) protects — there is nothing it grants access
  to that outlives the run — and it is nonetheless masked in output by that section's rules, because a
  redactor with an exception list is a redactor nobody trusts. **It must satisfy the target's own password
  policy** — section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s `PasswordMinimumLength` of 12, all
  four character classes, and the required distinct-character count — because the Core half creates
  `fixture-admin`, `bob` and `carol` **through `UserManager`**, which validates, so a literal below the
  policy would fail the fixture at setup rather than at an assertion. `alice` is the one account the policy
  does not gate, her row being migrated with a pre-computed hash rather than created; one literal is used
  for all four so that a single value satisfies both paths.
- <a id="the-legacy-hash-generation-rule"></a>**`alice`'s legacy-format hash is generated, and the
  procedure is stated rather than implied — because "synthetic" is a claim about origin and a hash lifted
  from a store falsifies it.** The value is produced by a **one-time authoring step**, committed with the
  manifest, whose whole content is: hash the fixture password literal above with
  **`Microsoft.AspNet.Identity.Core` 1.0.0's `PasswordHasher.HashPassword`** — the identical type and
  version the source's own store was written by [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/packages.config:8] — and record
  what it returns. Four properties make that sufficient, and each answers an objection:
  - **It needs no knowledge of the byte layout, so [12 F-12-21](12-migration-blockers.md)'s qualification
    survives intact.** This document still does not assert what the legacy format *is*; it names the
    implementation that produces it and takes the output verbatim. A generator that instead reconstructed
    the format from a specification would be asserting exactly what that blocker says the repository
    cannot establish.
  - **It runs on the toolchain the legacy edition already requires** — the .NET Framework host of
    [10 §4](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md), since the package targets `net45` — and it runs
    **once**, at authoring time. Neither fixture runs it, so neither fixture acquires a Framework
    dependency, and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W4 gate does not wait on it.
  - **It is reproducible enough to review and deliberately not byte-reproducible.** The hasher salts
    randomly, so regenerating yields a different value that verifies the same password; a reviewer
    therefore checks the committed value by **verifying the fixture password against it** with the same
    type, not by re-hashing and comparing. The manifest fingerprint above is what pins the value once
    committed.
  - **Nothing about row 18 `18a` weakens.** That case asserts that a hash in the legacy format verifies
    and is rehashed to the target format, and a hash the legacy hasher produced is in the legacy format by
    construction. What it stops asserting is that some **particular stored user's** hash verifies — which
    was never the assertion, and could not have been stated in a committed artifact anyway.
- **The manifest carries a fingerprint**: a stable hash over its canonical serialization, recomputed at
  load time and compared. It is one of the fields the baseline record of section
  [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) carries, and a mismatch between the
  fingerprint a baseline was captured against and the one a target run loaded **fails closed** rather than
  producing a comparison of two different datasets.
- **It is deliberately not the production seed.** The seed is ~780 catalog rows whose counts
  [08 §4.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns; loading and resetting that per collection is slow, its
  counts are another document's to change, and no assertion is stronger for it. The seed is **exercised**
  by row 24 as the thing whose gates must refuse, not **used** as the fixture.
- **No committed artifact of this suite transcribes an identity value that originates in the committed
  store.** The rule covers the manifest, `seed-expected.json`, `baseline-reference.json`, the model-override
  files and every example in this document, and it has exactly three permitted forms, which is why the two
  tables above are written the way they are: a **fixture role** (the *source-provisioned administrator*, the
  *fixture administrator*), a **configuration key path** whose value the loader reads at run time
  ([src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16]), or a **count with a digest over the aliased set**. Anything
  genuinely identity-bearing — a user name, an email address, a legacy password hash, a linked-login
  provider key — lives only in the **controlled extract artifact** of section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4, which is encrypted,
  access-controlled and untracked. The synthetic accounts the manifest *does* name in full —
  `fixture-admin@musicstore.test`, `alice`, `bob`, `carol` — are exempt because the manifest **creates**
  them: they exist in no store this repository ships, and naming them is what makes the oracles in section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage) stateable. The distinction is the origin of the value, not its shape.
  **That distinction is what the legacy-hash generation rule above turns on, and stating it closes a
  reading this rule and that account previously admitted between them**: a legacy-format hash is
  identity-bearing when it comes out of a store, and is not when it is computed here from the fixture
  password literal, because the value then identifies nobody. An account exempted as *created* while one
  of its committed fields was *captured* satisfied the letter of the exemption and defeated its purpose;
  under the generation rule every field of all four accounts originates in this manifest.

**Two loaders, one manifest, because the two runtimes are loaded differently and must end up identical.**

| Fixture | How the manifest is loaded | Why that way |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LegacyBaselineFixture` | Against the **private copies** of both attached stores (problem one): the catalog tables are emptied and the manifest's rows inserted with explicit key values, and the Identity 1.0 tables receive the four accounts, the role, the assignment and the two linked logins in the **1.0 shape** the source's store defines [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/IdentityModels.cs:1-6], with `alice`'s **generated** legacy hash — the value the [generation rule](#the-legacy-hash-generation-rule) produces, inserted as-is | The committed stores hold the seed's catalog content, which is not the manifest. Loading the manifest over it is what makes the two halves comparable; leaving the committed content in place would make every count assertion a comparison against a different dataset |
| `CoreApplicationFixture` | Catalog rows inserted directly against the provisioned database after both migration sets have applied; Identity rows arrive **through `tools/provision-admin`** in its `load-identity` verb, from a run built from the same manifest | Identity rows must be **migrated rather than created**, so that the transition of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) is under test rather than bypassed — which is also what gives rows 18, 22 `22h` and 57 a real migrated account to assert on |

**Post-load invariants, asserted before the first case runs — seven of them, and a failure is a setup
failure rather than a scenario failure.** They are read through the `IStoreObserver` of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box), and on the legacy half they are checked **after** the
startup-quiescence wait of problem one step 6, never before it:

1. Per-entity row counts equal **the manifest's loaded count plus its declared pre-existing count**, for
   every entity.
2. Every declared key is present exactly once.
3. Every foreign key resolves — no album without its genre or artist, no order detail without its order and
   album.
4. The **fixture administrator** `fixture-admin@musicstore.test` holds `Administrator`, and **no other
   account outside the declared pre-existing set** holds it.
5. The observed pre-existing set equals the declared one, member for member.
6. `alice`'s `PasswordHash` is byte-equal to the manifest's **generated** value — the
   [generation rule](#the-legacy-hash-generation-rule)'s output, committed once — because a loader that
   rehashed it on the way in would make row 18 `18a` assert nothing. Byte-equality is asserted against the
   *committed* value and never against a freshly generated one, since that hasher salts randomly.
7. The recomputed fingerprint equals the manifest's.

A suite that begins asserting before these hold is a suite whose first red result means nothing.

**Isolation: one collection per surface group, one database per collection, and a fixture-owned reset
between tests.** Section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) states the topology in
full and owns it; what belongs here is why per-test provisioning is not the answer — it is too slow at this
fixture size — and why a shared database with no reset is not either: the cart, order, order-detail and
Identity tables are written by many cases, and residue in them makes a result depend on execution order.

**Problem three — raw response bodies cannot be compared byte-for-byte.** Anti-forgery tokens, session
identifiers, authentication cookies and timestamps vary per request, and the port **deliberately**
changes the `AddToCart` verb, the Bootstrap markup, the error view and the Identity views. A byte
comparison would fail on every page for reasons that are all either noise or approved.

**Assertions are therefore semantic**: status code, redirect target, JSON property names and values,
and the presence and value of **named** elements located by `id` — of which the cart page conveniently
has several already: `#cart-summary` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:47],
`#cart-total` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:87], `#update-message` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:44] and the per-row `#row-{id}` and `#item-count-{id}` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:62],
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:70]. Volatile values are **normalized out** before comparison, and **the approved deltas of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) are enumerated in the suite as expected differences**, so
that an approved change reads as an approved change rather than as a failure — and, equally, so that a
difference *not* on that list fails.

**One baseline caveat carries into every comparison**: the source runtime is in 4.5 quirks mode
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:34] while the target has no quirks mode at all (section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration)). The baseline
capture records this, and any difference traceable to it is classified before it is filed.

### 12.4 Required coverage

Every row is required, and **every row is stated at the level a test can execute**: the exact method and
path, the exact status code, the exact response shape — the named element, attribute or JSON property
asserted — and **the database invariant asserted after the call**. That last column is the one this
matrix would be useless without. A response-only assertion cannot tell a rejected write from a write
that happened and then reported a rejection, and the three classes of defect this suite exists to catch —
the lazy-loading nulls of section [4.6](#46-lazy-loading--a-resolution-per-site-not-a-policy), the JSON
naming flip of section [8.7](#87-the-json-contract--annotate-one-model-not-the-policy) and the
unprotected writes of section [7.2](#72-problem-one--coverage-today-is-partial) — all present as a
plausible response over a wrong outcome.

**The six columns.**

| Column | What it carries |
| --- | --- |
| `#` | The row number. Row numbers are **stable identifiers**: they are cited from other sections of this document and from other deliverables, so a row is never renumbered and never reused for a different subject |
| `Scenario` | The surface, and the enumerated cases within the row. A case identifier is the row number plus its letter — `4b`, `16d` — and that identifier is what the `scenario` field of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s failure report carries |
| `Request` | The method, the path, and the exact request content that distinguishes the case |
| `Response assertions` | Status code, and response content asserted **by name**. Never "succeeds", never "is rejected" |
| `Database invariant after` | What must be true of the database once the response has been received. "Unchanged" is never written on its own: the table or tables and the property compared are named |
| `Traces to` | The requirement, the approved delta of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), the security finding or the design decision the row discharges. A row that traces to nothing is a row nobody can decide to change |

**The index is closed at one hundred and seven numbered rows, `1` to `107`, plus the ten operator rows `O1` to `O10` of
section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes).** Those two counts are published here and nowhere
else in this document. A row is appended at the next unused number and never renumbered, so a total
quoted anywhere else — in this document or in another deliverable — is stale rather than a second
opinion, and the counting rule stated below the table governs what a single row means.

**The `Response assertions` and `Database invariant after` columns state the target contract.** For a row
that runs against both fixtures, the baseline half records what the legacy application does, and the two
values must then be either **identical** or a **difference this document has already named** — an
enumerated approved delta of section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), or the remediation of a
finding cited in the row's `Traces to`. A difference that is neither is a regression, which is exactly the
mechanism section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem three describes.

**The fixed oracles, stated once here so that no row restates them and no two rows can disagree.** Each is
already a consequence of a decision made earlier in this document; what is new is that each is now a
**literal a test compares against** rather than a description.

| Condition | Oracle | Decided in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anti-forgery token missing, empty, or present but not valid for the request's cookie, on any non-`GET` request | **400** with no body written by the filter, re-executed into `/Home/Error/400` so the response is the generic error view rather than a redisplayed form, and the write does not occur | Section [7.1](#71-the-policy); the re-execution rule is section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)'s |
| A verb that is not mapped on a route that exists | **405** with no body written, re-executed into `/Home/Error/405` with the 405 preserved | Section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 4; section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| A resource identifier that resolves to no row — **including one that resolves to a row the caller does not own**, which is answered identically | **404** with no body written by the action, re-executed into `/Home/Error/404` with the 404 preserved | Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| An unhandled exception | **500**, the generic view, the two preserved headings [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/Error.cshtml:7-8], and exactly one rendered trace identifier. The body contains **no** exception type name, no exception message, no stack frame, no query text and no configuration key or value | Section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) |
| An **anonymous** request to an action requiring authentication | **302**, `Location: /Account/Login?ReturnUrl={the original path and query, URL-encoded}` | Section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), login-path row |
| An **authenticated** request to an action whose role it does not hold | **403**, the generic status-code view, and **no `Location` header** — a different status and no target, not the anonymous row repeated. The global `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) writes the status and `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` renders `/Home/Error/403` | Section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled), access-denied-path row |
| `GET /healthz/ready` with the database reachable | **200**, `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`, `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache`, body exactly `ready` | Section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 13; [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the literal and the semantics |
| `GET /healthz/ready` with the database unreachable | **503**, the same content type and cache headers, body exactly `not-ready` | As above |
| `GET /healthz/live`, database reachable **or** unreachable | **200**, the same content type and cache headers, body exactly `live` | As above |

**The media type, the charset and the cache headers are stated on all three health rows and not only the
first.** The probe that consumes these endpoints reads a status line, not a document — but the *unhealthy*
path is the one a platform reads under pressure and the one most likely to be re-shaped into a JSON
diagnostic payload by a later change, and a verdict served from an intermediary's cache is the failure that
looks like a healthy instance. Naming all three properties on every variant is what makes such a change a
test failure rather than a silent alteration of the contract
[06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes. **The three body literals are that document's,
not a local choice**, and they carry the disclosure half of the same requirement: a body of exactly `ready`,
exactly `not-ready` or exactly `live` cannot also carry a check name, a database or server name, a trace
identifier, a failure category or an exception.

**Every case that asserts a redirect asserts its literal `Location` value.** A bare `302` is a weak
oracle: it passes a port that redirects to the wrong place, and "redirects to the wrong place after
signing you in" is a real defect class — an open-redirect on the sign-in return URL is the canonical
instance. The convention is therefore that `Location` is compared as a literal string, and the literals
below are fixed here so that the rows do not each restate them and cannot disagree. Where a case posts no
`ReturnUrl`, the value is `/`: the source's local-redirect helper falls through to
`RedirectToAction("Index", "Home")` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:382-392],
which the conventional route renders as the application root.

| Cases | `Location`, exactly |
| --- | --- |
| `18a`, `19a`, `20a`, `35`, `36`, `42a`, `43a`, `48b`, `49e`, `51a`, `51b`, `62`, `72d` — sign-in and registration with **no `ReturnUrl` posted** | `/` |
| `20b` — sign-out | `/` |
| `72a` — sign-in with a **local** `ReturnUrl` | the posted value, byte-for-byte |
| `72b` through `72h` — sign-in with a **non-local** `ReturnUrl`, all seven shapes | `/` — the posted value is discarded |
| `4a`, `4d` — cart add | `/ShoppingCart` |
| `10`, `13`, `68a`, `68b` — a completed checkout | `/Checkout/Complete/{OrderId}`, with `{OrderId}` the key of the row the request created |
| `22i` — linked-login removal | `/Account/Manage?Message=RemoveLoginSuccess` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:120], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:126] |
| `40a`, `40b`, `69` success cases, `88a`, `88b`, `88h`, `88i`, `92a`-`92c` — administration create and edit | `/StoreManager` |
| Any **anonymous** request to a protected action | `/Account/Login?ReturnUrl={the original path and query, URL-encoded}`, per the fixed-oracle table above |
| Any **authenticated but unauthorized** request to a protected action, **target only** | `/Account/AccessDenied?ReturnUrl={the same encoding}` on the first hop, and no `Location` on the second, which is the terminal 403. Against the baseline the value is the login row above |
| Any **authenticated but denied** request to a protected action | **No `Location` at all.** The outcome is a **403** with the generic status-code view, not a redirect, because `AccessDeniedPath` is `/Home/Error/403` and that action sets the status — section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled). A case asserting a `Location` here would be asserting the withdrawn `/Account/Login` value |
| Any **authenticated** request denied for want of the `Administrator` role | `/Home/Error/403?ReturnUrl={the original path and query, URL-encoded}`, per the same table |

One redirect is deliberately **not** given a single status literal, and it is bounded rather than left
open. Row 47's plaintext-to-HTTPS redirect is the platform's, so its `Location` is asserted as *the same
path on the same host under the `https` scheme* and its status as **one of exactly `301`, `302`, `307`,
`308`** — the whole space the two candidate enforcement points can produce, which excludes every
materially wrong outcome; that row and section
[12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests) limit 4 carry the reasoning and what the
owner's decision changes. And the `Location` of a redirect this document does not
introduce is not invented here: if a case is added later whose redirect target is not in the table above,
the table gains a row rather than the case asserting a bare status.

Two of those rows need a consequence spelled out, because reading them separately hides it.

**The denied case and the anonymous case are distinguished by status, and a status alone still does not
prove nothing was written.** Two claims, and the first one **corrects an earlier form of this paragraph**
that read "indistinguishable by status and target alone" and rested on `AccessDeniedPath` holding the same
value as `LoginPath`. It does not hold that value: section
[6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) sets `AccessDeniedPath` to `/Home/Error/403`, so the two
cases are **two different outcomes** and this document has exactly two, everywhere:

| The caller | The outcome, target-wide | Where it is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Anonymous** — no authentication cookie, or one that failed to decrypt | **`302`** to `/Account/Login?ReturnUrl={the original path and query, URL-encoded}` | `LoginPath`, section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) |
| **Authenticated and not permitted** — a valid cookie whose principal fails the policy | **`403`** with the generic status-code view and **no `Location`**, in one response | The **global** `OnRedirectToAccessDenied` of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order), which writes the status instead of redirecting; the view is `AccessDeniedPath`'s own `/Home/Error/403`, reached by `UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute` |

There is **no third outcome.** `OnRedirectToLogin` is a route-scoped override, and it produces no third
outcome either: it converts the anonymous `302` into a bare **`401`** **for the diagnostic instance endpoint
only** — because a monitor following a redirect records a success — and every other path takes row one.

The second claim survives the correction unchanged, and it is the one the matrix leans on: **a status code
proves the request was not served, and nothing more.** By itself neither a `302` nor a `403` proves that
nothing was written. So every denial row on a **write** path asserts the database invariant as well, and
**that invariant is what actually distinguishes a denial from a silent success.** A suite asserting only the
status would pass a port that answered the browser *after* performing the write.

**The three health bodies are literals their owner fixes, not a choice made inside a latitude.** An earlier
form of this paragraph read [06 §9.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) as offering "status code only, or
a fixed opaque string" and selected the framework's own default response-writer output — the aggregate
status name, `Healthy` or `Unhealthy`. **Both the latitude and that selection are withdrawn**: that document
now names the three literals itself, and the framework's default writer is replaced for the reason section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) item 11 gives — an aggregate status word is not one of the three
literals, and the JSON writers that ship for health-check UIs emit per-check entries by name. What survives
unchanged is why the rows assert byte equality at all: a row asserting "the body discloses nothing" would be
unfalsifiable, while a row asserting byte equality against a fixed string is not, and it fails the moment a
later change re-shapes the body into a diagnostic payload.

**How the migration rows invoke the tool, stated once so that no row invents a second form.** Rows 24, 53
through 61, 63 through 65, 75, 76, 77, 83, 94 and 95 drive `tools/provision-admin` — the one operator console project, section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) — and every one of them uses the
**single invocation form** section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) fixes, the
same form the release pipeline uses, which is the property that makes these rows evidence about the
release rather than about a test harness:

```text
dotnet <published-tool>/ProvisionAdmin.dll <verb> [--store catalog|identity|both]
    [--begin-run | --run-id <run-id>] [--batch <n>] [--resume]
    [--model-overrides <file>] --report-dir <the run's artifact directory>
```

Seven consequences bind every one of those rows, and are therefore not restated in them:

- **`<published-tool>` is the path the fixture captured** when it published `tools/provision-admin` in the
  runbook step of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split). No row invokes
  a shell alias, a globally installed tool or `dotnet run`, and a row that could only be executed through
  `dotnet run` would be testing a different artifact.
- **Both connections arrive through the two named environment variables** of section
  [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) — `MIGRATE_SOURCE_CONNECTION` and
  `MIGRATE_TARGET_CONNECTION`, channels 2 and 3 of that closed set — scoped to the single invocation and
  carrying the **owner** principal of section
  [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring), never the runtime principal —
  the tool applies DDL and loads data, which the runtime principal is deliberately unable to do. No row
  passes a connection string as an argument.
- **`--report-dir` is the run's artifact directory**, the same access-restricted per-run directory section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) governs, so a report computed over personal
  data lands where that section's retention, encryption and deletion rules already apply.
- **The exit code is captured and asserted, not inferred**, and it is a code of the **one tool-wide
  allocation** of section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation) — no row asserts a code outside it. Each row states
  the expected value, and the three distinctions that carry meaning are asserted as written: **`5`** (the
  verb ran, verified and refused), **`2`** (a precondition rejected it and nothing was written) and
  **`4`** (it wrote whole table units and then stopped). A row that read only the report's verdict field
  would pass an invocation that never started.
- **Every row that invokes `diff-schema`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity` or `reconcile` carries
  `--run-id`, and the value is the run identifier the fixture's own `extract-schema --begin-run`
  invocation echoed on standard output.** The fixture opens **one** run per test class against its source
  copy, extracts each store it needs into that run, captures the emitted identifier and passes it
  verbatim to every consuming invocation in that class — so a row asserting a load refusal after a failed
  `diff-schema` is demonstrably talking about **one** run, which is the whole point of the handoff
  contract of section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure). Rows 24 (`seed`) and
  the `extract-schema --begin-run` invocations themselves are the only migration invocations without the
  switch, and passing `--run-id` to `seed` is itself an exit-`2` case that section owns.
- **The digest verification runs ahead of every consuming invocation, so a row's setup failure is
  distinguishable from its subject.** A digest mismatch exits `2` and is a **setup** failure in the sense
  section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) defines — the fixture's run directory
  was disturbed — and no row treats an exit `2` from that cause as its own expected outcome. The rows that
  **do** expect `2` say which precondition they removed.
- **Every row that invokes `diff-schema` or `reconcile` carries `--store`, and a row whose subject spans
  both stores invokes the verb twice — `catalog` first, then `identity`.** The two load verbs each name
  their own store and are invoked once each, `load-catalog --store catalog` before
  `load-identity --store identity`; section
  [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)'s closed accepted sets make
  the switch mandatory and single-valued on them, so a row's command is not merely conventional: an
  invocation without it exits `2`, which is not the outcome any of these rows is about. The two-invocation
  shape is also what makes each row's evidence attributable — a per-table catalog mismatch and an Identity
  count mismatch are two verdicts in two reports, and [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s two data gates
  cite one each. Where a row's oracle names counts from **both** stores it says so and asserts the two
  reports separately — or invokes `reconcile --store both`, the one switch value admitted on that verb
  alone.

**How the failure-injection rows inject, stated once, because the obvious mechanism is the one section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) forbids.** Substituting a fake
data-access service would make the injecting rows exercise the fake rather than the real provider, and
that section rules it out for exactly that reason. So **every injection below is applied at the engine,
from the fixture's own administrative connection**, and the application under test is unmodified and
unaware:

**And every permission injection is an object-level `DENY` against the RUNTIME principal — never a
`REVOKE`, and never a server-level operation.** This is the second half of the correction, and it has
three independent reasons. **The restoration is a separate rule and it does use a `REVOKE`** — two
statements, stated below — so the prohibition here is on *injecting* by revocation, not on the revocation
that removes the denial afterwards.

**Portability**: the fixture's disposable engine is a container locally and a **throwaway managed database
in CI** (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)), and
`ALTER DATABASE … SET OFFLINE` is **not supported on Azure SQL Database** — an injection written that way
works for the developer and fails the pipeline, which is the worst possible distribution of a defect.

**`DENY` and not `REVOKE` for the injection, and the reason is that a denial overrides a grant whatever
the grant's origin.** The RUNTIME principal's rights are the **object-scoped grants** section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a reproduces from
[06 §6.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-bootstrap) section 3 item 6 — per table, per
verb, issued **to the user and not to a role**, and narrower than any built-in role can express. Against
those, a `REVOKE INSERT ON <table> FROM RUNTIME` **would** stop the statement, so the choice is not about
whether the injection bites. It is about three properties the denial has and a revocation does not:

- **One injection form covers every row, whatever the permission's origin.** A `DENY` at the user wins
  over every grant except one made to a `db_owner`, and no principal in this fixture is `db_owner`
  (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)), so no row of the table below has to reason about
  where the permission it is suppressing came from.
- **`DENY CONNECT` is expressible and a revocation-only design is not.** `CONNECT` reaches the principal
  through the existence of its database user as well as through any grant the fixture issued, so the
  connect-level injection has to be a denial. Using one mechanism for both the object-level and the
  connect-level injections keeps the *injection* rule single.
- **The denial is removable without guessing.** What the restoration has to remove is exactly the entry
  the injection added, which the fixture can write from the statement it just issued rather than from a
  memory of the inventory.

**Restoration is two statements, never one, and that is the property an object-granted estate changes.**
[06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) states the rule for the estate this fixture is built
from: `sys.database_permissions` carries **one row per grantee, securable, permission and grantor with a
single `state`**, so a `DENY` over an object grant **overwrites that row's state** rather than layering a
second row above it — and a bare `REVOKE` therefore removes the entry outright and leaves the RUNTIME
principal holding **nothing** on that object. So every permission restoration is
`REVOKE <verb> ON <table> FROM RUNTIME` **followed by re-issuing the exact `GRANT` the estate's
construction made** — the statement section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a takes from
[06 §6.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-bootstrap) section 3 item 6 for that object,
re-issued rather than approximated. **An earlier revision made the restoration a single idempotent
`GRANT`**, on the reasoning that the grant entry was still underneath the denial and only needed
re-affirming. It is not underneath it: that reasoning describes a **role-derived** estate, where a bare
`REVOKE` removes the denial and leaves the role's grant standing, and this fixture no longer has one —
point 3a's principal holds object grants and nothing else. A one-statement restoration would therefore
have left the principal's permission set dependent on engine bookkeeping this design does not specify,
and the failure would present as unrelated rows failing on permission errors nothing in them explains,
which is the hardest class of fixture defect to attribute.

**And the readback is the authority rather than the statement pair.** A restoration is complete only when
**probe set 1 of [06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) reports both directions empty for the
restored principal**, which is why point 3a's bring-up contract re-runs that set after **every** fault
restoration, and the permission-set equality check point 3a specifies is what catches a bad restoration
either way. A fixture that issued the pair and moved on would be asserting its own intent rather than
measuring the estate the next test runs against. The same readback follows every other injection form in
the table below: the `CHECK`-constraint fault is restored by dropping the named constraint and the
one-shot trigger by dropping the trigger and its sequence — neither touches a permission, so neither
needs the statement pair, but both are followed by the same readback, so that a partially restored estate
cannot reach the next test.

**One consequence is easy to get wrong, so it is stated here rather than left to each row.** The rule above
governs injections aimed at the **application**, which connects as the runtime principal. Two rows — row
59 and row 64 — must instead make a statement fail for a **step of the data-migration procedure**, whose
statements execute under the **owner**, by the execution convention above. Neither a `REVOKE` nor a `DENY` serves there: the owner's
authority does not come from a grant, and `DENY` does not bind a principal whose permission is ownership.
Those faults are therefore injected with an **unsatisfiable constraint**, which binds every principal
including the owner, is supported on Azure SQL Database, and is removed by dropping it — the last row of
the table below.

| Mechanism | How, exactly | What the application observes | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`DENY INSERT ON <table> TO RUNTIME`** | Issued by the owner between the request's precondition and the request itself, and restored by **two statements, never one** — `REVOKE INSERT ON <table> FROM RUNTIME`, then a re-issue of the exact `GRANT INSERT ON <table> TO RUNTIME` the estate's construction made — because this principal's rights are object grants rather than role-derived and a bare `REVOKE` would leave it holding nothing on that object ([06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)), with that section's probe set 1 re-run afterwards so the restoration is measured rather than assumed. Every other statement of the same transaction still succeeds, so the failure lands **inside** the unit of work rather than before it | A permission-denied error on the failing statement, which the provider surfaces as a **non-transient** failure — so the configured retry policy does **not** retry it, and the transaction rolls back whole | Rows 19 `19b`, 19 `19c`, 31 |
| **`DENY UPDATE ON <table> TO RUNTIME`** | As above, for the rows whose failing statement is an update rather than an insert — including the two-statement restoration, which for this row is `REVOKE UPDATE ON <table> FROM RUNTIME` followed by the exact `GRANT UPDATE ON <table> TO RUNTIME` the estate's construction made, and the same probe set 1 readback | As above | Row 19 `19c` (the Identity-side commit) |
| **`DENY CONNECT TO RUNTIME`**, **then a pool clear** | Issued by the owner, and **immediately followed by `SqlConnection.ClearAllPools()`** — see the determinism note below, because without it this injection does not reliably bite at all. `DENY` rather than `REVOKE` for the restoration reason the paragraphs above give rather than a membership one: **a `REVOKE` against an object-granted estate is a destructive restore**, and `CREATE USER`'s implicit `CONNECT` no more survives a revocation than an explicit grant does. Restored by the same two statements — `REVOKE CONNECT FROM RUNTIME`, then `GRANT CONNECT TO RUNTIME` — never by a single one, and followed by the same probe set 1 readback ([06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)) | A login failure on every subsequent request, which is what an **unreachable** database looks like from inside the application — without taking the database offline, and therefore identically on a container and on a managed database | Rows 27 `27b`, 27 `27d`, 46 |
| **A trigger that raises a named transient error on the first execution only**, gated on a **`SEQUENCE`** | A trigger on the target table raises **error number 1205** — the deadlock-victim number the provider's default transient classification covers — when, and only when, `NEXT VALUE FOR dbo.FaultAttemptSequence` returns `1`. **The sequence is what makes the fault one-shot across the rollback it causes**, and nothing else in the engine can: a counter row the trigger wrote would be inside the transaction the raised error rolls back, so the second execution would read the same value and raise again, indefinitely. **Sequence value generation is non-transactional — a consumed value is not returned by a rollback and is never handed out twice** — so the failed first execution has permanently consumed `1` and the retry draws `2` and is permitted. The fixture creates the sequence with the fault and, on restore, drops it; a re-arm inside one test is `ALTER SEQUENCE … RESTART WITH 1`. Transient **by construction**, which a permission denial cannot be | A transient failure the retry policy retries. With the retrying execution strategy registered in section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 item **2** — `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount`, default **5** — a single-shot fault is absorbed and the request succeeds on the **second** execution | Row 35 |
| **The same trigger, raising unconditionally** | Installed **without** the sequence *gate*, so **every** execution fails: the fault has no "first" to distinguish, so no durable state is needed to *decide* whether to raise. **A sequence may still be installed as a pure counter**, and is wherever the row needs an execution count it cannot obtain in-process: the trigger consumes `NEXT VALUE FOR` and then raises unconditionally, so the sequence records how many executions happened without gating any of them. `FaultSpecification` carries that as an element of the specification rather than as a second fault shape | Retry exhaustion: **six** executions — one initial plus the five retries `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` permits — then the failure surfaces to the caller | Rows 62, 36 `36a`, and — **with the counter** — row 95 `95b`, whose subject is a separate process |
| **A post-load data edit — an `UPDATE`, or the insert of one *isolated surplus* row; never a `DELETE`** | An ordinary `UPDATE` of one column value, or an `INSERT` of one row into a table **nothing references**, to create the divergence a reconciliation must find. Not a fault: the application is not running. **A `DELETE` is excluded by construction, and that exclusion is a correction rather than a preference.** Every `Albums` row of the fixture set is referenced by `OrderDetails` and by `Carts` (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)'s manifest), so deleting one either **fails on the reference** — leaving no divergence at all and a row that passes for the wrong reason — or, under a cascade, **removes rows from a second table**, which is a two-table divergence presented as a one-table one. The surplus insert has neither failure mode: `Artists` is referenced by `Albums`, but a **newly inserted** artist is referenced by nothing, so the difference is provably confined to one table and every other table's count can be asserted unchanged | Nothing — these rows assert on the migration artifact's verdict | Rows 54 `54b`, 55 `55b` |
| **An armed interleaved write, released by a two-way `SEQUENCE` handshake** | The one mechanism in this table that places a **concurrent** write at a **named point inside a request**, and it is here because a mid-request window cannot be produced by a test body at all: a `[Fact]` runs before or after the request, never inside it, and the setup API's calling rule (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3c) forbids a contract body from calling it in any case. Three parts, armed together from the class's `InitializeAsync`: **(i)** an `AFTER INSERT` trigger on `Orders` that consumes `NEXT VALUE FOR dbo.RequestReachedWindowSequence` and then polls `sys.sequences` for `dbo.InterleavedWriteDoneSequence` to advance, with a bounded wait; **(ii)** a **second OWNER session**, opened by the fixture and idle, polling `dbo.RequestReachedWindowSequence`, which on seeing it advance performs its one stated statement and then consumes `NEXT VALUE FOR dbo.InterleavedWriteDoneSequence`; **(iii)** the bound — if either poll times out the trigger **raises**, so the case fails loudly rather than passing with the write landed in the wrong place. **The handshake works because sequence generation is non-transactional**, exactly as the one-shot gate above depends on: a value consumed inside the request's open transaction is visible to the second session immediately, and a table row written there would not be. The point is named rather than timed: the trigger fires on the order insert, which section [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) places **after** the line projection and **before** the cart delete and the commit, so "in the window" is a position in the contract and not a sleep. **Not a fault** — nothing fails, and the request is expected to complete | A committed concurrent change to `Carts` that the request's own transaction did not make and cannot see in its projection: an **insert** of a row the projection never carried, or an **update** of the `Count` of a row it did | Row 99 `99b` (insert) and `99c` (update) |
| **An unsatisfiable `CHECK` constraint on one named table** | The fixture adds a named constraint that no row can satisfy — `CHECK (1 = 0)` on `OrderDetails` — before the invocation, and **drops it** to restore. It binds the **owner** as well as every other principal, which is what neither a `REVOKE` nor a `DENY` can do, and it is portable to a managed database. Deterministic by construction: the constraint rejects the group's first detail row and every retry of it | Not the application — the **migration tool**, which connects as the owner, and whose order-group transaction therefore cannot commit, so the mode stops after the groups that preceded it | Rows 59, 64 `64a` |

**Determinism note one — a denial is not effective until the pool is cleared, and `DENY CONNECT` is the
case where that decides the result.** SQL Server evaluates `CONNECT` **at login**, and
`Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` pools connections: a connection the application opened before the denial is
already authenticated, is returned to the pool on close, and is handed back out on the next request
**without re-authenticating**. So a `DENY CONNECT` issued while the pool holds live connections is
observed by the application only once those connections happen to be evicted — which is a timing race, and
a row 27 or 46 case built on it passes or fails on how many requests the fixture happened to make first.
The injection therefore **always** ends with `SqlConnection.ClearAllPools()`, which marks every pooled
connection for destruction so the next request must open a new one and hit the login check.

That call is available to the fixture for a specific structural reason worth stating, because it does not
generalize: the target host runs **in process** with the tests (section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3), so the client's pool
state is one static in one process and the fixture's call clears the pools the application is using. It is
issued for **every** injection in the table, not only the `CONNECT` ones — uniformly, because a rule with
an exception list is a rule somebody applies inconsistently, and clearing the pool before a permission or
constraint injection costs one connection open and changes no outcome.

**Determinism note two — how a retry row counts attempts, because the two obvious counters are both
wrong.** Every retry row asserts **both** the execution count and the **post-failure state** of the
affected rows, because either alone is satisfiable by a defect: a port that never retried would satisfy a
state-only assertion, and a port that retried and then committed a partial write would satisfy a
count-only one. So the count has to be trustworthy, and neither candidate is:

- **A counter the trigger increments cannot work.** The trigger's own write is inside the transaction the
  error it raises rolls back, so the counter reads `1` however many executions occurred — a mechanism that
  turns "executed repeatedly" and "executed once" into the same observation. It is stated without a
  numeral deliberately: the counter is broken for **every** multiplicity, and an illustrative figure here
  would read as a retry budget while the only budget in this document is
  `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount`. **This is the same rollback
  problem the one-shot fault itself has**, and it is why the trigger above gates on a **`SEQUENCE`** rather
  than on a table it writes: the sequence advances outside the transaction, so it survives the rollback and
  a table row would not. The trigger writes nothing at all, and the count comes from outside the engine.
- **The provider's retry event under-counts by exactly one.** It is raised when a retry is **scheduled**,
  not when an execution is attempted, so six executions produce five events and a first-execution success
  produces **zero** — meaning a "the retry policy absorbed one transient failure" assertion built on it
  cannot distinguish success-on-retry from a fault that never fired.

**Executions are therefore counted from the `DbCommandInterceptor` of section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)** point 3b — the same interceptor
the lazy-loading rows use — which
sees **every** command execution the contexts under test issue, including each retried one, and delivers it
synchronously with the request that issued it. The assertion is on the count of intercepted executions
whose command text matches the injected statement, within the scenario, and it is stated as a literal on
both sides of the policy:

| Case | Executions of the injected statement | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Row 35 — transient fault on the first execution only | **exactly 2** — the failed initial execution and one successful retry | The policy retried, and retried **once**: a `1` means the fault never fired, a `3` means the retry classification is wrong or the sequence gate did not survive the rollback |
| Row 62 — the fault raises on every execution | **exactly 6** — one initial plus the five retries of `Data:RetryOnFailure:MaxRetryCount` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 item 2) | Exhaustion at the configured bound, not at some other bound and not indefinitely |
| Rows 19 `19b`, 19 `19c`, 31 — a **non**-transient permission denial | **exactly 1** | The strategy did **not** retry a failure it must not retry, which is the assertion no state check can make |

**The table's rule, stated because it decides which mechanism a row may use: the `DbCommandInterceptor`
counts executions for an *in-process* subject only.** It is a service registered in the test host, so it
sees the commands the contexts under test issue and nothing else. Every row above has an in-process
subject — a request the fixture's own host handled — which is why the interceptor is the mechanism for all
four. **A row whose subject is one of the published tools runs in a different process and the interceptor
sees none of its commands**, so such a row counts executions from the fault **`SEQUENCE`** or does not
count them at all. Two rows are in that position and they take the two different exits:

| Row | Its out-of-process subject | What it does instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **59** | The migration tool, faulted by the **unsatisfiable `CHECK` constraint** | **Counts nothing.** A constraint violation is not transient, so there is no retry to count and no sequence in play; the row asserts the **rollback position**, which is what it is about. An execution-count expectation here would be unassertable and would read as a defect in the tool the first time anyone tried to close it |
| **95** | The `seed` verb of the published tool, faulted by the **transient trigger** | **Counts from the sequence.** The trigger consumes `NEXT VALUE FOR` on every execution before deciding whether to raise, and the sequence advances outside the transaction, so the difference between the `sys.sequences` `current_value` before and after the run is the execution count — durable across the rollback and readable from any process, including the fixture's. `95b` installs the always-on trigger **with** a counting sequence for this reason; the injection table's "no durable state is needed here" is about the **gate**, not the counter |

Both exits were necessary because an earlier revision applied the interceptor to row 95 as well, which
would have counted **zero** executions in both of its cases while the tool retried correctly — a row that
fails on its own observation rather than on the behaviour it is characterizing.

None of these mechanisms substitutes an application service or replaces a provider. The one interception
in play is the fixture's **observing** `DbCommandInterceptor` (section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3b), which reads command
text and alters no behaviour — so that section's guarantee holds: the real EF Core SQL Server provider and
the real SQL-backed cache are what every row in this matrix runs against. And **every injection is
reversed, and the pool cleared again, in the next test's `ResetAsync()`** (section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)) — the `DENY` removed by the corresponding
**`REVOKE` and the re-issued `GRANT`**, which is the two-statement restore the paragraphs above require
and which leaves the point 3a estate
exactly as bring-up wrote it, the trigger dropped, the sequence dropped, the constraint dropped, and the armed interleaved
write disarmed through its handle, which drops **both** handshake sequences, the signalling trigger and the
second session together — so an injected fault cannot
leak into the next test. A leaked denial would present as an unrelated row failing for a reason nothing in
it explains; a leaked *sequence* would present as a one-shot fault that never fires, because its next value
is already past `1`; and a leaked *pool* would present as the reverse of the first: the next test
succeeding on a connection that predates the restore.

**How row 53 produces nine schema divergences, stated once, because "diverge the model in that one
dimension" is not something a fixed model permits.** Row 53 needs a schema comparison that differs in
exactly one of nine dimensions, nine times over. The ported model is a fixed set of entity classes and
`OnModelCreating` calls (section [4.5](#45-two-contexts-two-migration-sets-two-history-tables)); there is no
switch on it that produces a divergence, and editing the shipped model per case is not a test, it is nine
ports. So the seam is named, owned and bounded — and it is on the **source** side, not the tool's:

| Aspect | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | A **`diff-schema` input override**, accepted by `tools/provision-admin` and by nothing else: an optional switch `--model-overrides <file>` naming a JSON document of per-object adjustments — target column type, decimal precision and scale, string length, nullability, identity definition, key definition, foreign-key delete rule, column default, index definition — which `diff-schema` applies **to the target-side model description it compares against**, before comparing. One dimension per file, one file per case, nine files |
| **Where it lives** | The switch itself is the tool's own, in `tools/provision-admin` alongside the verbs; the nine override files live with the suite's fixture data, at `src/MvcMusicStore.Contracts.Tests/Fixtures/ModelOverrides/`, under the fixture path of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) and copied to output with the rest of it ([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) maps them). **Not** in `src/MvcMusicStore` — the application's model is untouched by this, which is the property that makes row 53 a test of the diff rather than a rehearsal of nine defects |
| **Why it overrides the *target* side and not the extract** | Because the run's extraction is immutable and digest-verified (section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)), and a case that mutated it would fail the digest check and exit `2` — reporting a disturbed run directory rather than the schema difference the case is about. Overriding the target-side description leaves the extraction exactly as `extract-schema` wrote it, so the case's `2`-versus-`5` distinction stays meaningful |
| **What bounds it** | Three things. It is **`diff-schema`-only**: every one of the other nine verbs rejects it with exit `2` under the closed accepted sets of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties), so no override can ever influence a write. It is **refused unless the target database name matches the non-production pattern** of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s third gate, reusing that gate rather than inventing a second one. And its use is **recorded in the report** — the verdict names the override file and its `SHA-256` — so a `pass` obtained under an override can never be mistaken for a `pass` obtained without one |
| **Why not a fake diff engine** | Because the thing under test *is* the diff engine. A test double that reported nine differences would assert that the row's own harness can count to nine. The override changes the diff's **input**, and the real comparison, the real report shape and the real `fail` verdict are what row 53 observes — the same principle section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) applies to the fault injections above |

**The index closes, and the arithmetic is the check.** Sixteen surfaces — the original twelve, each of
which gained rows, plus four new ones — carry 8 + 8 + 13 + 12 + 14 + 6 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 16 + 1 + 3 +
2 + 4 = **104** row numbers, and every number from 1 to 104 appears **exactly once**, so a row is neither
missing from the index nor indexed twice. The 32 numbers the earlier form omitted were exactly 73 to 104,
the contiguous block authored after the index was last written, which is the failure mode an index maintained
by hand has: it does not notice what was added after it.

**Three oracles above look like mistakes. Each was read off the running source, and each is
recorded here because a reviewer's first instinct is to "correct" it — two of them must not be corrected
at all, and the third must be corrected on exactly one of its two fixtures, which is why it is here rather
than silently fixed.**

- **Row 8 expects `2` on the baseline for a cart holding quantities 2 and 3 — and `Cart (5)` on the
  target.** The **baseline** half is the part that looks like a mistake: `ViewBag.CartCount` is assigned
  `cartItems.Count()` over a projection of one element per cart **row**
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/ShoppingCartController.cs:91-95], so the number the source's layout
  renders is the **row count**, not the sum of the `Count` column, and a cart of two rows carrying
  quantities 2 and 3 renders `2`. The cart page's own total is a different number computed a different way
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/ShoppingCart.cs:103-112], which is what makes the confusion easy, and a
  reviewer "correcting" the **baseline** expectation to `5` would be asserting something the source does
  not do.

  **The target half is different, and an earlier form of this bullet got it wrong.** That form said the
  semantic is "preserved — it is not in the delta ledger of section
  [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) and must not be 'fixed' by the port — so a target that
  rendered `5` here would fail row 8, correctly." It **is** in the ledger, as **`D-32`**, whose own text is
  "the cart number means total quantity, not line count"; the label is **`D-31`**; and section
  [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract) states the reason the change is taken rather than
  avoided — the removal response's `CartCount` already carries the summed-quantity definition and the
  script already writes `Cart (n)` from it [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/Index.cshtml:29], so
  leaving the component on the row-count definition would turn today's invisible disagreement into a
  visible one the moment the script's target element exists. So the target renders `Cart (5)`, row 8's
  oracle is fixture-specific, and the pair is classified against those two ledger numbers. What survives
  from the earlier form is the warning, redirected: the **baseline** expectation is the one nobody may
  quietly correct.
- **The baseline value is `/Store/Store`, and the target's is not — an earlier form of this bullet had
  the target half wrong.** In the source the value is stable at `/Store/Store` on **every** page, because
  a child action runs with its own controller context and that context's controller is always `Store`;
  that is the **baseline** expectation, and it is the one nobody may quietly correct. A **view component**
  has no controller context of its own, so a one-argument `Url.Action("Store")` copied into
  `GenreMenuViewComponent` would resolve the ambient controller of the **invoking request** — `Home` on
  `/`, `ShoppingCart` on the cart page, `Store` only on a store page — emitting a **page-dependent** path
  that is neither the source's behaviour nor a fixed defect; it is a new one. The earlier form concluded
  from that alone that the port should name the controller so as to keep emitting `/Store/Store`. Section
  [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) decides otherwise and owns the mapping: the toggle is
  repointed to the catalog index, so **the emitted URL differs from the baseline by design**, and row 9's
  `GET /` catches both the copied one-argument form and any regression to the source's dead path.
- **The accessibility consequence is taken rather than left implicit.** Because the `href` is not a
  destination, the toggle's only real function is disclosure, so it gains **`role="button"`** under addition
  **A7** while its `href` value is preserved byte-for-byte — section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) item **a2** owns the reasoning and records the
  earlier claim, that the anchor was a working link with a no-JavaScript fallback, as **withdrawn**. The
  role is an announced-only addition and adds no ledger identifier; the destination is untouched, which is
  what keeps row 9's literal assertable on both fixtures.
- **Rows 11 and 12 expect `200`, and this was challenged and refuted.** The challenge was that
  `AddressAndPayment` re-renders a view whose model type does not match what the action passes, so the
  invalid-promo path could not return `200`. It does. The action declares
  `AddressAndPayment(FormCollection values)`, constructs `var order = new Order()`, calls
  `TryUpdateModel(order)` and returns `View(order)`
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:24-29], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/CheckoutController.cs:36]
  — the view's declared model **is** `Order`, so there is no mismatch. Observed against the running
  source: an unrecognized promo code returns **200**, re-renders the address form, and round-trips the
  posted values. The expectations stand. What rows 11 and 12 gained from the challenge is the **baseline
  absence** assertion: the source adds no model error on that branch and the view calls no
  validation-summary helper [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Checkout/AddressAndPayment.cshtml:11-31], so the
  rejection is silent **on the legacy fixture**, and that silence is asserted there rather than assumed.

  **The absence is asserted on the baseline only, and an earlier form of these rows asserted it on both.**
  That was a contradiction with two other owners: step 2 of section
  [8.12](#812-the-checkout-write-path--one-ordered-contract) specifies "No match → redisplay **with a model
  error against `PromoCode`**", and addition `A1` of section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) exists so
  that model-level failure has somewhere to render — its own text names "the promo-code rejection" as the
  thing it displays. A both-fixtures absence assertion would therefore have failed a correct port on the
  target half, and it would have failed it *for implementing an approved addition*. So the target half
  asserts the **presence** of the summary and the message, classified against `A1`, with the repopulated
  promo-code box classified against `A15`. The warning the earlier form was reaching for survives and is
  narrowed to where it is true: **the port may not add feedback the registers do not carry**, and on the
  baseline fixture the silence is still the contract.

**Row 67's case table — the nine address fields, field by field and annotation by annotation.** The
previous revision of this row named "the nine address constraints" and then exercised sixteen cases, which
left five of the eight length bounds and every present-but-blank shape unexercised. A boundary asserted on
one field and assumed on the other seven is not a boundary test, so the cases are enumerated. The
annotations are `Order`'s own [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:20-59] and section
[8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) carries them verbatim; the columns below are
read straight off them.

| Field | Its annotations | Presence cases — all **invalid** | Just-inside — **valid** | Just-outside — **invalid** |
