**27 presence cases + 13 just-inside + 14 just-outside = 54.** Counted column by column so the split is
checkable against the table rather than asserted over it: the presence column carries three cases on each
of the nine fields; the just-inside column carries one on each of `FirstName`, `LastName`, `City`, `State`
and `Country`, two on each of `Address`, `PostalCode`, `Phone` and `Email`, giving `5 + 8` = **13**; the
just-outside column carries one on each of `FirstName`, `LastName`, `City`, `State`, `Country` and `Phone`,
two on each of `Address` and `PostalCode`, and four on `Email`, giving `6 + 4 + 4` = **14**. Every
just-inside case is valid and every presence and just-outside case is invalid, so **13** are valid
(`67-*-min`, `67-*-max`, `67-ph-shape`, `67-em-tld2`, `67-em-tld4`) and **41** invalid — `27 + 14`. That
arithmetic is the row's case count in the class table below and in the totals.

Six properties of the table, each of which is a decision rather than a mechanical expansion.

- **The case identifier is a name, not a letter.** Fifty-four lettered cases would run past `z`, and
  `67aa` carries no information. The counting rule below is stated to admit a named case-table row as a
  case for exactly this row.
- **Three presence shapes, because they are three different requests.** `absent` omits the key from the
  body entirely; `empty` sends the key with a zero-length value; `blank` sends a single space. All three
  are invalid, and they are not redundant: `absent` exercises the binder's missing-value path, `empty`
  exercises the empty-string-to-null conversion both frameworks apply to string properties by default, and
  `blank` exercises `Required`'s own trimming — a whitespace-only value is rejected because
  `RequiredAttribute` trims before testing for emptiness, which is behaviour a hand-written check would
  very plausibly not reproduce.
- **`67-ad-blank` and `67-pc-blank` are the sharpest of the twenty-seven.** A four-space `Address` is
  **long enough** for its minimum and still invalid, so the case separates the two annotations on the same
  field: an implementation that validated length before presence would answer these two wrongly while
  answering the other twenty-five correctly.
- **`67-ph-shape` asserts an absence of validation, deliberately.** `DataTypeAttribute` is display
  metadata and validates nothing, in both frameworks. A port that reads `DataType(PhoneNumber)` as a
  format rule would start rejecting values the source accepts — a caller-visible regression with no
  ledger entry, which is precisely what a preservation suite exists to catch. The same reasoning applies
  to `DataType(EmailAddress)` on `Email`, where the `RegularExpression` is the only rule.
- **`67-em-tld5` is the case a well-meaning port fails.** The source's pattern accepts a top-level domain
  of **two to four** characters [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:57-58], so `a@b.local` is rejected
  — as are `.museum` and `.travel`. That is a defect in the source's regex and it is **preserved**:
  correcting it would change which addresses a caller may enter, which is a numbered delta, not a free
  improvement. `67-em-tld1` and `67-em-tld5` together are what hold the bound from both sides.
- **`Email` has no length bound *in the source*, and the target adds one** — the source property carries
  `Required`, `RegularExpression` and `DataType(EmailAddress)` and no `StringLength` at all
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:56-61]. This row's subject is the **preserved** annotation set,
  derived property by property from what the source declares, so a bound the source does not declare has
  no case here. That is not a statement that the ported model is unbounded: section
  [8.8](#88-the-checkout-input-model--ten-properties-not-nine) gives the input model
  `[StringLength(254)]` on `Email`, and its two boundaries — accepted at 254, refused at 255 — are
  **required coverage this matrix does not yet carry**. Section
  [12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests) entry **12** names the two cases, states
  their expected results, and states why they are recorded for the approver rather than added here.

**Row 24 acquires its own database, because the fixture manifest is not the seed dataset.** Section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)'s manifest is a small, hand-fixed set chosen so
that every expected value in this matrix is stated rather than discovered; the seed routine's dataset is the
source's ~780 catalog rows. They are different datasets with different purposes, and section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) says so. Running `seed` against a
collection's fixture-loaded database would therefore either fail its own idempotence check or silently
change the row counts every other case in that collection asserts. So row 24 acquires an empty, freshly
migrated database of its own under section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s acquisition gate —
created with the collation of section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) like every other database the fixture
creates — and drops it at teardown like any other.

**And row 24's oracle is not the seed command's own report.** An assertion of the form "the `Albums` count
equals the number the report says it inserted" is satisfied by an implementation that inserts the wrong
rows and reports the wrong number consistently, which is exactly how a seeding defect survives a green
suite. The oracle is therefore a **committed expectation captured from an authority outside the thing under
test**:

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **The file** | `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Fixtures/seed-expected.json`, tracked, beside the fixture manifest under the same fixture path and copied to output with it |
| **Where its content comes from** | The **legacy store's catalog tables** — the committed MVC 5 catalog database holds the source seed's own output, which is the content the port's seed is required to reproduce. It is captured once, through the legacy fixture's `IStoreObserver`, reviewed, and committed. It is **not** generated from the target's `Data/SeedData.cs`, because an expectation derived from the implementation is the implementation's own report by a longer route |
| **What it carries** | Per table (`Genres`, `Artists`, `Albums`), the **row count as a literal**; and a **canonical digest** — `SHA-256` over the table's rows projected to their business columns, ordered by those columns, `\n`-joined: genre name; artist name; album title, price to two decimals, genre name, artist name. **Keys are deliberately excluded from the projection**, because the seed's surrogate keys are assigned by the engine on insert and are not the content being preserved. Plus the legacy commit it was captured from |
| **How it is gated** | Its recorded legacy commit must equal the one in `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Fixtures/baseline-reference.json` (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)). A mismatch is a `SETUP` failure: the expectation was captured from a different legacy store than the one this checkout describes, and re-capturing it is a reviewed act rather than a side effect |
| **Why the counts live in the file and not in this document** | [08 §4.2](08-technical-debt-register.md) owns the seed's row counts and its counting method, and one fact has one owner (sections [1.5](#15-what-this-document-owns) and [1.6](#16-what-this-document-does-not-own)). The file carries the numbers; this document carries the mechanism, the projection and the gate |

**Which rows run against which fixture, by one rule.** A row runs against **both** fixtures — the legacy
baseline and the ported application — whenever the legacy application has an equivalent behaviour to
characterize, **including** where that behaviour differs: the baseline records the old shape and the
comparison records the delta. A row is **target-only** when the legacy application has no equivalent
behaviour at all — the surface does not exist, the mechanism is net-new, or the assertion is on a
runtime-internal artifact the legacy runtime does not produce. Nothing is target-only merely because the
legacy outcome is wrong; that is precisely what a named difference is for.

**And a "named difference" is named by a number, not by a citation.** An observable difference between the
two fixtures is admissible in exactly one way: the row cites a **numbered identifier from one of the two
approval registers** — a `D-nn` delta from section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), or an
`A-n` addition from section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) — whose approval decision
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s
W1 has recorded, and section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s classifier admits
`EXPECTED-DIFFERENCE` on that basis alone. **Both registers, for the reason that classifier states**: an
approval-owned addition is as observable as a delta, so a rule admitting only deltas would fail every row
that characterizes one. **Both registers carry an approval owner per row, which is what
makes either admissible here**, and rows 31 and 89 are the two that name an addition rather than a delta.
A row's `Traces to` column may cite the **finding** that
motivated the change, and every such row does — but a finding citation is a **reason** and never an
**approval**, which is section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)'s own rule. So a difference
supported only by a finding, with no register number, is a **failure** rather than an expected difference:
the remediation was not approved as a caller-visible change, and the suite is the last place that would
notice.

**The counting unit is the case**, where a case is one lettered entry in the `Scenario` column, the whole
row where the row has no letters, or **one named entry in a dedicated case table** where the row's case
count makes lettering unusable. Exactly one row takes the third form — row **67**, whose 54 cases are
named `67-<field>-<shape>` in the case table published above, beneath the matrix — and its
case-by-case enumeration lives there rather than in the `Scenario` cell for the same reason the other
rows' lives in the cell: the enumeration has to be somewhere a reader can count it. Several cases issue
more than one request — case `22a` issues two
verbs, `22l` issues sixteen and `22m` twelve, `23a` fetches seven pages and then every asset each one
references, `28a` and `28b` each fetch a
page and then a script, and `44a` fetches five paths — so a **request** count is deliberately not
published, because it would
be an arithmetic nobody could check against the table. Cases and executions can be.

| Class | Rows, with each row's case count | Rows | Cases |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Both fixtures** | 2 (1), 3 (1), 4 (4), 5 (2), 8 (2), 9 (1), 10 (1), 11 (1), 12 (1), 13 (1), 14 (3), 15 (3), 17 (3), 21 (2), 22 (9), 30 (1), 32 (2), 33 (2), 34 (2), 38 (2), 39 (3), 40 (3), 41 (1), 66 (1), 67 (54), 68 (2), 69 (12), 72 (8), 74 (2), 87 (2), 88 (1), 104 (3) | 32 | 136 |

**Two of the 326 cases are branch-exclusive, so a concrete run executes fewer than the total — and both
figures are published rather than one.** Cases `1d` and `1e` are the two halves of the duplicate-name
contract of section [4.14](#414-the-duplicate-genre-browse-contract): `1d` runs only in branch (a), `1e`
only in branch (b), the branch is selected by that section's recorded extraction artifact, and the runner
**skips the other with a recorded reason** rather than passing it vacuously. Both are authored, both are
counted in the 326, and exactly one of them executes on any given database. **One concrete run therefore
executes 325 of the 326 cases and 477 of the 478 fixture executions**, and the missing execution is a
`Target` one — 324 rather than 325 — with the skip and its reason in the run's own output. The totals
above are the **authored** figures, which is what deliverable [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md)
estimates against, because the work of authoring both branches is done whichever branch the source turns
out to be in. A run that reports 326 executed cases has run a skipped case as a pass and is defective.

**These are the numbers deliverable [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) estimates against, and they
supersede four earlier sets of figures this section published**: the 27 surfaces, 22 against two fixtures
and 5 target-only of its first revision; the 75 rows, 242 cases and 386 executions it carried before
rows 76 to 102 were authored; the **102 rows, 307 cases and 454 executions** it carried before the
cases the review round added — `1c`, `1d`, `1e`, `24f`, `24g`, `25d`, `25e`, `75f`, `75g`, `75h` — and
before row 102's paging cases and row 103 existed; and the **103 rows, 320 cases and 468 executions** it
carried before the account-surface cases the same round added last — `20e`, `20f`, `20g` and row 104's
three — which exist because section
[6.5](#65-the-remaining-event-classes--where-each-is-emitted-and-the-producer-arithmetic) maps every
event class to an asserting case and four of the thirteen had none. The three category totals are also
what section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s platform split sizes: 152
executions require a Windows agent with the legacy application, 325 require the Linux agent with a
provisioned engine, and 1 requires a deployed host.

**One row's case count dominates the case total, and that is a property of the row rather than a
distortion.** Row 67's 54 cases are 17 per cent of the 326, because nine fields each carrying two or
three annotations produce that many boundaries and a boundary asserted on one field is not a boundary
test (its case table, published above, enumerates them). A reader sizing effort from these figures should
read row 67 as **one** parameterized assertion over a published table rather than as 54 pieces of work,
which is what the counting rule above makes it: one premise, one oracle shape, 54 values. The same
applies at a smaller scale to rows 22, 53, 69, 88, 93 and **107** — the last of which is seven hostile
return-URL forms applied to three actions, one premise and one oracle over 21 values.

#### 12.4.1 The published operator bytes

**Every row of the matrix asserts an HTTP response or a database outcome, and not one of them asserts the
published operator bytes themselves — a gap that is the wrong shape rather than merely a shortfall.**
Rows 24, 53 through 61, 63 through 65, 75, 76, 77, 83, 94 and 95 do drive `tools/provision-admin`, but
each of them asserts what the tool did **to the store**; none asserts what the published output does with
an argument vector, an environment block or a working directory it cannot satisfy. The console is the executor of every irreversible
operation in this plan: it applies the eight migration verbs of section
[5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), it writes into a production database
under a privileged principal, it holds the only credential this design still handles, and it produces the
four-record audit set whose destination is immutable (section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4). Its parser, its
guards and its exit codes are specified in detail across four sections and, before this subsection,
asserted nowhere.

**These rows run the *published* bytes as a process, not the code in-proc, and that distinction is the
whole point.** A test that calls an internal method verifies the method; it does not verify the switch
mapping, the content root, the environment variables, the exit code the shell receives, or the fact that
no `appsettings.json` shipped — every one of which is a property of the published output rather than of a
function. So each row below starts the published executable with an argument vector and an environment
block, and asserts on its **exit code** and its **captured standard output** alone.

**Its targets are disposable and its secret channel is safe.** The database is the disposable SQL Server
instance of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly), provisioned per class;
**no destination is written to at all** — these rows assert what the command **emits** on its own standard
output, and the capture, the selection of the record set and its retention are the release step's, which
[06 §9.5.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns and no test can stand in for. **An earlier form of
this paragraph named a storage destination and an upload with a read-back verification**; both are
withdrawn with the rival design of section
[10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4, so the sentence now
says what it always meant: these rows stop at the process boundary.
The password is a per-run generated value passed through the **single-invocation environment variable**
the design already requires, held in memory, written to no file and never placed on a command line — so
the fixture exercises the real channel rather than a weakened one, and the canary assertion of row **O8**
uses that same value as its needle.

| # | What it asserts | Why this and not something easier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **O1** | **The parser is closed.** An unrecognised switch, a recognised switch spelled for a different verb, a value-taking switch with nothing after it, a repeated switch, a missing verb, two verbs in one invocation, and a verb with a trailing bare token: **each is a non-zero exit naming the token, with no host built and no connection opened** | This is property 1b of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) and it is the control that makes the command-line provider safe in the one host that still registers it (section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)). A parser tested by calling it in-proc would not prove that the **published** entry point runs it before the builder |
| **O2** | **Startup validation runs before anything else, on every verb.** With one required member removed from the environment block **and** the connection string pointed at a host that does not resolve, each of the four verbs exercised here — `admin`, `load-catalog`, `load-identity` and `seed` — exits non-zero **naming the missing member** — and specifically **not** with a connection or name-resolution error, which is what the same invocation produces if validation runs late or not at all | Assertion 0 of section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract) and assertion 2 of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties). The unresolvable host is the discriminator: it makes "validated before any database use" observable from the **outside**, from the exit message alone, rather than requiring the test to inspect the server for a login that never happened. It is the row that would have caught the earlier claim that `Build()` validates — `ValidateOnStart` validates when the host **starts**, and a one-shot verb starts nothing |

The generic host reads `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT`, so a run that pinned only `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` is a real and silent failure mode |
| **O4** | **All four verbs exercised here do their work.** `admin` creates the user, the role and the membership; `load-catalog` and `load-identity` move a small fixture dataset and pass their own reconciliation; `seed` writes with all three guards satisfied and **refuses** with any one of them not | **Four of the ten verbs section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties)'s table closes**, each cited to the section that owns it: `load-catalog` and `load-identity` to section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract), `admin` to section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties), `seed` to section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks). **An earlier form of this cell called them "the four verbs of section 5.1.2", which owns only the two load verbs; that attribution is deleted** — the four are a deliberate subset of the ten, not the whole of any section's set. Together with **O5** this is the row that proves the single-project decision works, rather than that it compiles |
| **O5** | **Partial-run idempotence, per operation.** `admin` run twice is one user, one role and one membership, with the second run reporting "already present" for each; and a run **interrupted** after the user was created but before the membership completes, then re-run, produces the membership without failing on the user | Property 3 of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties). "Idempotent overall" would pass a test that skipped the repair; the interrupted case is the one the design's per-operation checks exist for |
| **O6** | **Batch and resume.** `--batch` outside 100–10 000 and non-integer values fail the bind or the validator, naming the value and the bound, **before any read**; a valid value governs the whole run and appears in the run record; a run interrupted mid-load and re-run with `--resume` completes with the correct row counts and **no duplicate rows**; the same run **without** `--resume` stops with the count it found; and rows in the target whose keys are absent from the source stop the run for a human | Section [5.1.2](#512-how-the-load-actually-runs--the-executable-contract)'s six-step `--batch` path and its fail-closed restart rules. The last two clauses are the ones that make "never truncates, deletes or overwrites" a tested property rather than a promise |
| **O7** | **The audit record: exactly four per invocation, in the pinned operation order, on all four paths.** Success; a failure **after work has begun**; a rejection **after the host is built but before any work** (a removed member, a mismatched environment); and a rejection **before any host is built** (a bad switch, and a missing actor). Each capture is parsed line by line and the objects carrying **`State.eventName == "AdminProvisioned"`** — the nested path of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) property 4, evaluated with **the same `jq -Rc 'fromjson? \| objects \| select(…)'` expression the pipeline uses**, not a re-derived one — are **counted and then sequenced**: the count is **4**, never 3 and never 5, and their `State.operation` values are exactly `create-user`, `create-role`, `add-membership`, `run` **in that order**, so a silent omission, a duplicate and a reordering each fail the row — and the sequence assertion is the one a count alone would pass. Because the cardinality is a **constant**, the same two assertions run on all four paths with no branching: the two rejection paths assert three `not-attempted` operation records and a run record at `rejected`, and the failure-after-work path asserts the failing operation at `failed` with any unreached operation at `not-attempted`. **On the three paths that also write a report** (row 75's artifact), the three operation records' `operation` and `outcome` literals are asserted **equal to the report's three rows** for the same invocation, which is what holds the one-vocabulary property rather than leaving it as an intention. One additional assertion exists because this row is what would have caught the defect it now closes: a selector keyed on a **top-level** `eventName` is asserted to match **0** objects in the same captures, which is the mechanical statement that the nested path is the only correct one and that the earlier top-level form would have produced zero uploads on every path rather than a wrong one on some. **Every one of the four** records carries the actor supplied through the environment on [06 §9.2.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s schema — the self-describing property, asserted per line rather than once — and for the missing-actor case, the reserved `(unavailable)` with `rejectedCheck = actor-missing` on the run record and no other combination. A simulated manual invocation emits the same four records | Property 4 of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties). The **before any host** case cannot be satisfied by an `ILogger` call at all, so this row is the standing proof that the serialisation is genuinely separate from diagnostic logging; and the count with the sequence is what makes "four per invocation" a checkable property rather than a description of the happy path |
| **O8** | **The secret is in none of it.** The generated password appears **nowhere** in captured standard output, standard error, the exit message, the audit record or any exception text — searched as **raw text** across the whole capture — and the same for the connection string and for `MIGRATE_TARGET_CONNECTION`. Repeated with a deliberately failing create, which is the path that tempts a command to echo its inputs | The never-record list of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) applied to the one process that holds a credential. It is row 47's canary, aimed at the executable rather than at the site |
| **O9** | **Exit codes are the allocated ones, and they are stable.** Each path is asserted against the **literal value** allocated in section [10.2](#exit-code-allocation), and the allocation defines **exactly five** values, so every path here resolves to one of them: success **0**; a parser rejection, a startup-validation failure, an environment-assertion failure, an `EXPECTED_*` mismatch, a control-plane or `DB_NAME()`/`USER_NAME()` target-assertion failure, a seeding-guard refusal, a run-state refusal and `sp_getapplock` not granted within its wait **2**; a refused login, an unreachable database, a statement refused for want of a grant, and an absent migrations-history or session-cache table **3**; a run that committed one or more units and then stopped, and the seed's whole-seed transaction rolling back **4**; the migration-set comparison unequal in either direction, a `diff-schema` difference the extracted record does not explain, a `reconcile` mismatch, a duplicate normalized **user name**, and a target holding keys the source does not **5** — the shell steps' `sha256sum --check` and `cmp` verifications are **not** asserted here, because they are not this executable's statuses. Three further assertions, because the allocation's own properties are the part that rots: **`1` is never returned** by any of these paths; **`6` and `7` are never returned either**, on any path, which is the mechanical form of the allocation's own statement that both are unallocated; and where two checks share a class the **named check** in the captured output differs even though the code does not | Section [10.3](#103-what-this-retires) makes "failure becomes observable" the point of the whole change. A command that returned `1` for everything would satisfy every other row here and still be unusable in a release gate. **And this row is where the defect it now closes would have surfaced**: an earlier form of it asserted **`4`** for the environment, `EXPECTED_*`, target-assertion and seeding-guard refusals, **`5`** for a lock not granted, **`6`** for a failed reconciliation and **`7`** for the not-in-source case — four expectations the allocation does not support, two of them naming codes it explicitly leaves unallocated, so the row asserted statuses the tool cannot return and would have failed on four paths while the implementation was correct. The negative assertion on `6` and `7` exists so that a future revision cannot quietly re-add them on one side only |
| **O10** | **A normal or deployed builder cannot select connection mode M4.** Two halves. First, the **published application's** service descriptors are enumerated and **no descriptor for `ITestConnectionModeSignal` exists**. Second, a host is built the ordinary way, with no fixture involvement, handed an M4-shaped connection string, and its start is asserted to **fail** with "matches no accepted mode" | The non-forgeable gate of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract). The first half catches a registration added inside the application later; the second catches a validator edit that made the signal optional. **Neither can be satisfied by editing configuration**, which is the property a configuration marker could never have |

**What these rows deliberately do not cover, so the boundary is not mistaken for coverage.** They do not
provision, reach or assert anything about the storage account of section
[5.1.1.1](#5111-the-protection-named--the-account-the-key-the-network-path-and-the-grants-that-gate-a-read)
— its infrastructure encryption, its customer-managed key, its private endpoint, its role assignments and
its two audit destinations are platform configuration that
[06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns and that a test host cannot stand in for. They do not
exercise the release orchestrator's single-flight lock
([06 §6.3.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)). And they do not run against a real Azure SQL database
or a real managed identity, so **mode M3 is asserted as a validation outcome and never as a successful
token acquisition** — which is exactly the split section
[2.5](#25-the-health-endpoints--the-application-half-of-the-readiness-contract) makes between what a
process can check about itself and what only the release side can confirm.

### 12.5 Rendered-appearance comparison is separate, and manual

**The visual-preservation criterion of section
[8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump) cannot be met by the suite above**,
and saying otherwise would be the most consequential overclaim in this document. An HTTP-level suite
asserts on response **content**; the Bootstrap major-version move is a change in how that content
**renders**. A test
asserting that a `<div>` carries a given class does not know whether the navigation bar looks right.

**Automating it is rejected**, deliberately: it would mean pinning a browser-automation stack and
screenshot tooling, defining viewports, baseline images and pixel tolerances, and storing binary image
artifacts in a repository that already carries 43 MB of committed database binaries
([08 §6.2](08-technical-debt-register.md)) — infrastructure this application needs for **nothing else**,
bought for a **one-time** layout migration.

**The decision is a manual review against a captured baseline:**

- **Screenshots of every capturable page surface**, taken from the MVC 5 application **before** the port,
  at the **two viewports** section [8.5](#85-the-bootstrap-upgrade-is-markup-work-not-a-version-bump)
  fixes by dimension — **375 x 812** narrow and **1280 x 800** wide. Those are the two the layout
  actually distinguishes: the navbar collapses at one breakpoint
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:15], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:22], and the viewport meta tag [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml:5] confirms
  the responsive intent. **16 page surfaces × 2 viewports = 32 screenshots**, plus the one
  **data-conditional** capture below where the source data makes it reachable.
- **A reviewer checklist** covering the **navigation bar** (brand, links, collapse behaviour at the
  narrow viewport, the genre dropdown open and closed, the cart element, the fixed-top position and the
  body offset that clears it), the **catalog grid**, **album detail**, the **cart table**, the
  **checkout form** (label and control alignment, validation-message placement) and the
  **administration list** (including the truncated columns whose `@helper Truncate` disposition section
  [8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) states, and the retained horizontal definition list).
- **A scripted-interaction checklist, exercised in a browser by the same named reviewer**, because the
  suite of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) executes no JavaScript and therefore cannot observe any
  of it. Each item names the behaviour and where it is specified: the removed cart row **fades and
  disappears**; that row's own line count and the **cart total** update in place; the **header badge does
  not change**, and when the removal empties the cart the navbar item **stays exactly as it was
  rendered** rather than disappearing, because the badge is server-rendered only and takes the new count
  on the next page render (section [8.2.1](#821-the-cartsummary-component-dom-contract)); the control
  shows its **pending, disabled** state for the duration of the request; a **rejected** request produces
  the visible, announced failure message and leaves the row in place; **focus lands on the status
  region** afterwards; the live region **announces the removal message**; and the fade is **suppressed**
  when the operating system reports
  `prefers-reduced-motion`. Items **c1** to **c5** of section
  [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) specify them, and additions **A2** to **A6**
  of section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) own the net-new ones. **A failure here is a defect, not
  a difference**: none of these is on either approval register as a change to existing behaviour.
- **Two checks that only exist under the enforced content-security policy**, required by
  [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) and placed here because an HTTP-level suite cannot see a
  rendered glyph: at the narrow viewport the **navbar toggler shows its icon** rather than an empty box and
  the menu opens, and a **checked Remember-me checkbox shows its tick**. Both glyphs are
  `data:image/svg+xml` background images inside the acquired stylesheet (section
  [8.1.1](#811-the-per-file-disposition-of-the-27-source-assets)), so an image policy without the `data:`
  scheme blocks them while every status code, redirect and JSON payload stays correct.
- **Three visible differences that sit on neither approval register, named here because the register
  enumeration below would otherwise not account for them.** All three correct a link that leads somewhere
  its own label does not name, so each resolves a defect rather than changing behaviour a visitor could
  rely on — which is why none of them is a numbered delta and why the reviewer accepts each on sight.
  Section [8.14](#814-the-two-absolute-external-links--one-decision-each) removes the footer's `<p>` and
  its anchor to `mvcmusicstore.codeplex.com`, so the footer loses a line on **every** captured surface.
  Section [8.2](#82-child-actions--three-view-components) repoints the genre dropdown's toggle from
  `/Store/Store`, which no action serves, to the catalog index. Section
  [8.4.1](#841-the-order-confirmation-pages-store-link--the-label-is-preserved-and-the-destination-is-corrected) repoints the order-confirmation page's `Store` link from `/` to the catalog index with
  its label unchanged. **None adds a capture**: all three sites are already inside surfaces the manifest
  above collects, and **no external destination is resolved by this review**, because section 8.14 leaves
  the target with no absolute external link at all.
- **A signed-off approval artifact** recording **who reviewed it**, against which baseline, and **which
  deliberate differences were accepted**. The expected-difference set is enumerated exhaustively below,
  from **both** approval registers — the approved deltas of section
  [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas) and the approval-owned additions of section
  [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) — because a reviewer given a partial list files an approved
  change as a regression, or worse, accepts a regression as an approved change.

**A second pass, with a different purpose: breakpoint-boundary verification.** The two endpoint
viewports above cannot exercise the intervals where the tier remapping of section
[8.5.2](#852-the-token-matrix--all-56-distinct-class-tokens) matters. A grid class carried across
unchanged activates at a **different width** in the successor, and both endpoints can render correctly
while every width between them is wrong: `col-sm-2` left as-is would make the album grid six-up from
576px instead of from 768px, and `col-md-*` left as-is would columnise the horizontal forms 224px early.
The appearance comparison asks whether a page looks like its baseline; this pass asks whether each grid
and navbar state **starts and stops at the same width**, and the two are not substitutes for each other.

- **Eleven widths, bracketing every boundary in either library**: **375**, **575** and **576**, **767**
  and **768**, **991** and **992**, **1199** and **1200**, **1399** and **1400**. Each pair straddles one
  step. 576, 768, 992, 1200 and 1400 are the successor's five container and grid steps; 768, 992 and 1200
  are the source's own three [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:927], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:1081], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Content/bootstrap.css:1244]; and
  375 is the narrow baseline the appearance set already uses, carried here so the two sets share a width.
- **Three layout-bearing surfaces**, because the grid and the navbar are what these boundaries govern:
  the **shared layout** including the top navbar and the footer, one **album-grid** page, and one
  **horizontal-form** page. Baselines are taken from the MVC 5 application at the same eleven widths
  before the port, so each comparison is against a measured source rendering rather than against an
  expectation, and section [12.5.1](#1251-the-capture-manifest--one-table-one-total) carries these
  captures as a row of the one manifest rather than as a set with a figure of its own.
- **Acceptance, stated per width**: the ported rendering matches the pre-port baseline at that same width
  on four points — the **number of album tiles per row**, the **navbar state** (collapsed or expanded,
  with the toggler present or absent), the **container's rendered width**, and the **horizontal form's
  label-and-control arrangement** (stacked, or two-column with the label right-aligned). A difference at
  any single width is a defect in the remapping, not an approved delta: no entry on either register
  changes a breakpoint.
- **The combined figure is 32 appearance captures plus 33 boundary captures = 65 images**, and the two
  sets stay distinct in the sign-off artifact: 16 page surfaces at 2 widths comparing whole-page
  appearance, and 3 surfaces at 11 widths verifying boundary behaviour.

**The expected-difference set, classified by what the reviewer is being asked to do.** A rendered
difference that appears in **none** of the four groups below is a **regression**, and that is the whole
point of enumerating them rather than naming a handful.

**`D-49` is one of the fourth group's thirty-nine and sits in its rejected-or-failed sub-list** — an earlier
form of this sentence called it that group's *thirty-ninth* entry, and before that its *fortieth*, both of
which read as claims about its **position** in a cell whose reading order puts it twenty-first. The group is
a set and its members are not ordered, so the position is not a fact about it; what is a fact is why it is
in that sub-list at all: a 404's generic error view has **no default page to photograph**, so section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts each of its four sites instead.

**`D-37` is visible but has no baseline counterpart, so it is verified against the stated rule rather
than against a screenshot.** No album in the committed catalog has an absent `AlbumArtUrl` — section
[8.10](#810-absent-album-art--the-rendering-rule) records one distinct value across the whole catalog —
so there is no baseline page on which the difference could be photographed, and obtaining one would mean
writing to the source data. The reviewer instead checks the **ported** application against 8.10's rule
directly: an album saved with a blank value renders the placeholder asset with the album title as its
`alt` at all three render sites. The coverage assertion requires the same thing automatically; this entry exists
so the reviewer knows why `D-37` is on the register and not on the photograph.

**The capture set, derived from the semantic disposition rather than from filenames.** Section
[8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) resolves the 29 source views into **25 ported and 4
removed**, and only a ported view can be compared — a removed one has no target rendering to hold a
baseline against. The 25 are **18 page surfaces**, 3 component views, 2 rendered partials, the layout and
`_ViewStart`. The 4 removed with the external-login challenge surface (section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types), approved delta `D-11`) take **2 page surfaces** with
them — `Account/ExternalLoginConfirmation.cshtml` and `Account/ExternalLoginFailure.cshtml` — and **2
rendered partials**, `Account/_ExternalLoginsListPartial.cshtml` and
`Account/_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml`. Of the 18 remaining page surfaces, **two cannot be captured from the
running legacy application**, each for a stated reason:

| Not captured | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `Home/About.cshtml` | **Orphaned.** `HomeController` declares only `Index` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/HomeController.cs:15], so no action returns this view and the single conventional route [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/RouteConfig.cs:16-20] cannot reach it |
| `Home/Contact.cshtml` | **Orphaned**, identically |

**`Shared/Error.cshtml` is capturable, and it is captured.** An earlier reading excluded it on the
grounds that `HandleErrorAttribute` needs custom errors switched on. That is wrong: no edition declares
a `<customErrors>` element, the framework default is `RemoteOnly`, and the attribute is therefore
**live for remote requests** (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (1);
[09 §6.10](09-security-assessment.md) owns the finding). **The capture method follows from that
default and requires no repository modification**, so the constraint of section
[1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible) is not
engaged: issue a request that raises an unhandled exception **from a non-loopback address** — another
host on the capture network, or a request routed to the instance's non-loopback address rather than to
`localhost` — and the generic error view renders. Nothing in the application, its configuration or its
data is edited to obtain it. A capture from `localhost` returns the framework's detailed error page
instead and is **not** the baseline. The view's own rendered text is unchanged by the port (`D-12`
changes the response's shape, not its two headings), so there **is** a preserved appearance to
compare against — the fixed navbar, the body offset and the container width all apply to this page as
much as to any other.

**The layout, the two rendered partials and the three component views are covered *within* those page
captures, not captured separately** — that is what they are: markup that only exists inside a page.
`Shared/_Layout.cshtml` and `Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml` appear in all 32; `Store/GenreMenu.cshtml`
appears in all 32; `Account/_ChangePasswordPartial.cshtml` appears in the manage capture. Two capture
preconditions follow and must be set up rather than assumed:

- **`ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml` renders only when the cart is non-empty**
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/ShoppingCart/CartSummary.cshtml:1], so the captured session must hold a
  **populated cart**; a signed-in session and the **administrator role** are needed for the manage and
  administration captures respectively.
- **One rendered state is not reachable *in this data*, which is a measurement rather than an inference,
  and it is therefore a data-conditional capture rather than an unreachable one.** The earlier reading
  derived it from the commented-out provider registrations
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Start/Startup.Auth.cs:23-35], and that inference does not hold: startup
  code governs what can be **created from now on**, while whether a linked login **already exists** is a
  property of the stored data. So it is measured, against the committed Identity store
  `src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/App_Data/aspnet-MvcMusicStore-20131025034205.mdf`. **That file is a binary, so
  its evidence is the reproducing query below and never a line locator** — the citation contract of
  section [1.3](#13-authoring-contract-and-the-absence-of-user-rules)'s second contract puts a fact held
  in a binary tracked file in the same class as a count, and a bracketed path with no locator, which is
  what this sentence used to carry, is admitted nowhere:

  ```sql
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AspNetUsers;                                  -- -> 2
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AspNetUsers WHERE PasswordHash IS NULL;       -- -> 0   (both rows carry a hash)
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AspNetUserLogins;                             -- -> 0
  ```

  **The two user names those two rows hold are deliberately not reproduced here, and an earlier form of
  this block did reproduce them** — the first query's comment named both, parenthetically, as if a user
  name were part of a count. That is precisely what section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly)'s transcription rule forbids: the rule
  covers *every example in this document*, and a user name originating in the committed store is
  identity-bearing whatever shape it is written in. The permitted committed form is the one now above —
  **the count** — with the identities themselves reachable only through the controlled extract artifact of
  section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4, and the set's committed
  fingerprint being the **aliased digest** the declared pre-existing set's row publishes once
  [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W3 has extracted. Nothing in this subsection needs the names: every
  assertion below is about the **count** of linked-login rows being zero.

  All three queries are run against a **copy** of the committed `.mdf` and its log, attached outside the
  checkout and detached afterwards, so the tracked files are never opened in place — the same handling
  section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) requires of the legacy baseline
  reset and the reason it does not violate section
  [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible).

  **The conclusion for this data is unchanged, and its status is not:** with zero `AspNetUserLogins`
  rows the `RemoveAccountList` component has **no non-empty state to photograph**. The component's
  **empty** state *is* captured, on the manage page, and it is the retained management surface's normal
  rendering for an account with no linked login.

  **The set-password partial is not a data-conditional capture at all, and the third query is what shows
  why it is not.** Both committed accounts hold a `PasswordHash`, so the `else` branch of
  `ViewBag.HasLocalPassword` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Manage.cshtml:12-19], specifically
  [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/Manage.cshtml:18], is never taken in this data — but the branch and its partial are **removed in the target** with
  the external-login challenge surface (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), and a
  surface with no target rendering cannot be compared against a baseline however reachable the baseline
  is. It is therefore off the capture list unconditionally, and the null-`PasswordHash` query is retained
  above because the Identity load **halts** on a non-zero result (section
  [5.8](#58-roles-role-assignments-claims-and-external-logins--the-other-four-tables)), which is a
  migration gate rather than a photograph.

  **One capture is therefore required if and only if the source data contains the corresponding rows**,
  which the capture step checks with the queries above rather than assuming:

  | Data-conditional capture | Required when | Rendered by |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | The **Registered Logins** table — the `RemoveAccountList` component's non-empty state, including the per-row remove control | `AspNetUserLogins` holds at least one row for the captured account | [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:3-33], gated on `Model.Count > 0` at [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Account/_RemoveAccountPartial.cshtml:3] |

  A different source database — a production store rather than the committed sample — can make it
  reachable, and the capture list grows by one surface when it does. Section
  [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) already requires the
  null-`PasswordHash` check as part of the Identity migration, so the third query above serves the gate
  rather than the capture list.

**The automated suite does not claim to cover this**, and the post-AJAX DOM state is explicitly part of
the manual checklist rather than of the suite: the suite asserts on the **rendered response** and on the
**JSON payload**, and what happens in the browser after the payload arrives is checked by a person.
Browser automation stays out of scope for the reasons above. [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries
the review as a task, and the separate **accessibility** review of section
[8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) is carried there as a second, distinct task —
screenshots cannot verify keyboard, focus, announcement or contrast behaviour.

#### 12.5.1 The capture manifest — one table, one total

**Every image this review requires is a row of the table below, and the figure under it is the only
capture total this document publishes.** The classification the table exists to make is between an
obligation that produces an **image** and one that does not: the scripted-interaction checklist, the two
content-security-policy glyph checks, the external-destination check and the measured values of section
[8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses) are all real reviewer
obligations that add **no** image, and leaving them unclassified is how one review acquires four
different budgets. [07 §7.1](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) prices exactly the total below, across the
browser matrix [06 §10.4](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) fixes.

| Pass | Kind | What the pass captures | Surfaces | Captured states per surface | Widths | Images |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P1 | **Appearance** | the seventeen capturable page surfaces, each in the one session state named below | 17 | 1 | 2 | **34** |
| P2 | **Boundary** | the three layout-bearing surfaces named above — the shared layout, one album-grid page and one horizontal-form page — at the eleven widths named with them | 3 | 1 | 11 | **33** |
| P3 | **Data-conditional** | the **Registered Logins** table's non-empty state — an extra state of the manage surface pass **P1** already captures, not an extra surface | 1 | **0** — measured against the committed store, never assumed | 2 | **0** |
| P4 | **Data-conditional** | `Account/_SetPasswordPartial.cshtml` — an extra state of that same surface | 1 | **0** — measured on the same basis | 2 | **0** |
| **Total** | | | | | | **67** |

**`34 + 33 + 0 + 0 = 67`.**

**The 67 are baseline images, and the number of comparisons is the same 67.** Every one is captured from
the MVC 5 application **before** the port, because that is the pass which cannot be repeated once the
source is retired, and each has exactly one ported counterpart held against it. Whether the ported side
is compared live or stored as a second file is the reviewer's choice and moves no figure here: the
manifest counts what the baseline pass must produce. **The two passes stay distinct on the sign-off
artifact** — that is what the `Kind` column is for — because a whole-page appearance comparison and a
boundary comparison answer different questions, and a pooled set hides which of them was actually done.

**The seventeen surfaces, with the session state each is captured in.** They are the twenty page
surfaces of section [8.4](#84-the-view-disposition-by-semantic-role) less the three excluded above, and
the state assignment is not incidental: it is what covers **both** branches of
`Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Views/Shared/_LoginPartial.cshtml:2] with no extra
image, which section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) item (2) requires.

| Session state | Count | Surfaces |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| **Anonymous** | 9 | `Home/Index`, `Store/Index`, `Store/Browse`, `Store/Details`, `ShoppingCart/Index`, `Account/Login`, `Account/Register`, `Account/ExternalLoginFailure` — a plain `[AllowAnonymous]` GET action [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Controllers/AccountController.cs:310-311], which is what distinguishes it from the confirmation view excluded above — and `Shared/Error` |
| **Signed in** | 3 | `Account/Manage`, `Checkout/AddressAndPayment`, `Checkout/Complete` |
| **Signed in as an administrator** | 5 | `StoreManager/Index`, `StoreManager/Create`, `StoreManager/Edit`, `StoreManager/Details`, `StoreManager/Delete` |
| **Total** | **17** | `9 + 3 + 5 = 17` |

Two preconditions carry into that assignment rather than being restated: every captured session holds a
**populated cart**, so the cart control renders on all seventeen, and `Shared/Error` is captured by the
non-loopback method stated above.

**What the review also requires and does not photograph, each with the basis it is verified on instead.**
A row here is not a lesser obligation; it is one an image cannot settle.

| Obligation | Specified in | Verified by, instead of an image |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The scripted-interaction checklist | the bullets above, and items **c1** to **c5** of section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | Behaviour over time rather than a rendering — a still frame of a fade is not the fade. Additions **A2** to **A6** of section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) own the net-new ones |
| The two content-security-policy glyph checks | the bullet above, required by [06 §10.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) | Both are **target-only**: the toggler's glyph is substituted under approved delta **5** and the checkbox's control is approved delta **31**, so neither has a preserved source rendering to be held against. The acceptance is that the glyph renders at all |
| The footer's removed anchor, confirmed absent | section [8.14](#814-the-two-absolute-external-links--one-decision-each) | Stated in the bullet above: the footer renders inside every surface pass **P1** already captures, so the reviewer confirms on those images that **no** page renders an anchor to `mvcmusicstore.codeplex.com` under any scheme. **No external destination is resolved by this review**, because section 8.14 leaves the target with no absolute external link at all |
| The twenty-five preserved rows of section [8.5.7](#857-library-default-differences-that-no-class-mapping-expresses), and the measured checks of section [8.5.6](#856-acceptance) | those two sections' own acceptance rules | A **measured rendered value** against the source value the row cites, recorded on the sign-off artifact. That is also what settles the states no **P1** capture shows and an image would witness poorly: brand and nav-link **hover**, the **open** genre dropdown's panel colour, the collapsed panel's divider at the narrow viewport, and the toggler's box metrics |
| The accessibility review | section [8.9](#89-accessibility-and-interaction-state-requirements) | Keyboard, focus, announcement and contrast behaviour, which no screenshot verifies. [07 §7.3](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) carries it as a second, distinct task, and item **d4** of the accessibility list carries the one contrast result already computed rather than deferred |

**One thing can move the total, and it is measured rather than argued.** Passes **P3** and **P4** stand at **0**
because the committed store holds zero `AspNetUserLogins` rows and no null `PasswordHash` — the queries
above, run against a copy. A source database holding either state adds **2** images for it, one surface
at both widths, and the capture step runs those queries rather than assuming which case it is in. No
other pass is conditional.

### 12.6 The test project, the system under test and the host wiring

**Naming a fixture is not wiring one.** Sections
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) and
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) settle the architecture and the three
hazards; neither of them makes the in-process host **buildable**, and four things have to be decided
before it is: how the test project reaches the system under test, whether the application's entry point
is visible to it, what the fixture overrides, and — the half that is easiest to get wrong — what it
deliberately does not override. Everything below specifies half (b) of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)'s split, and **the package pins for this project are
[04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s; none is named here.**

**1. The test project references the system under test, and one other project besides.** The edges
themselves are [04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)'s — it fixes **two** outbound from this
project, `src/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj` and `tools/provision-admin/ProvisionAdmin.csproj`, and
a third from the operator command to the web application — and they are cited here rather than restated.
What this document adds is why each one is load-bearing for the suite this section specifies:

| Edge | Why the suite needs it |
| --- | --- |
| **The test project to the web application** | `CoreApplicationFixture` boots **the application's own assembly** through `WebApplicationFactory`, which has to name the `Program` type ([04 §12.4](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) declares the `public partial class Program { }` it binds to). Not a copied, re-hosted or re-composed output — the composition root under test is the one that ships, which is the whole basis of section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box)'s claim that the target half exercises the real pipeline |
| **The test project to the operator command** | One refusal case cannot be driven as a child process. The dispatcher of section [10.2](#102-the-target-toolsprovision-admin-and-five-required-properties) refuses an argument containing a control character, `U+0000` included, and a NUL **cannot be delivered across an OS argument boundary** — both `CreateProcess` and `execve` terminate each argument on it. So that one case calls `Cli.Dispatch(string[])` in process with the NUL in an in-memory array; every other refusal in the matrix is asserted at process level on the published executable |

**And the consequence of those edges is a build-order fact, not a behaviour fact.** The test assembly's
build **depends on** the web project's, so a port that does not compile cannot produce a green suite —
which is what makes [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W7 gate meaningful, since "the suite is green"
cannot be satisfied by a suite that never had a system under test. It also means **no** part of the suite
compiles before the target project graph exists, the legacy-bound classes included, because they compile
into the same assembly; section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) states that
consequence and this subsection does not soften it. What the baseline half is independent of is the
ported application's **behaviour** — a skeleton graph satisfies its compilation, and its assertions are
authored and run green against the legacy application while the port is unwritten.

**Neither reference is what makes the shared contracts run against both hosts.**
`src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Core/**` declares one `sealed` concrete class per abstract contract, deriving
from the base under `Contracts/**` and binding it to `CoreApplicationFixture`, exactly as
`src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Legacy/**` does for `LegacyBaselineFixture` — the mechanism of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box), which exists because the runner produces cases from
the **declared types** it enumerates and an abstract contract with one derivation therefore runs against
one host. Adding a shared contract has **two** obligations, and a suite that performs only the first
loses that contract's target coverage without failing: author the abstract class under `Contracts/**`,
**and** declare a concrete derivation per host. Section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s case-count check is what detects a
missed second obligation, because the published per-category case counts are fixed numbers rather than
"whatever was discovered".

**2. The entry point has to be visible, and a top-level-statement composition root makes it internal.**
The composition root is a single `Program.cs` written with top-level statements (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)), and the `Program` class the compiler generates for a
top-level program is **internal** — so a generic host factory in another assembly cannot name it as its
entry-point type argument, and the fixture does not compile.

**The chosen mechanism is a `public partial class Program { }` declaration at the end of
`Program.cs`.** One line, in the file it belongs to, needing no assembly-level attribute, and widening
exactly one type: the entry point the test project has to name.

**`InternalsVisibleTo` is the alternative, and it is not taken.** It works, and it is the wrong lever:
it makes **every** internal type in the web assembly visible to the test assembly, which is a standing
invitation to assert on internals — the one thing the black-box architecture of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) exists to prevent — in order to solve a visibility
problem whose scope is a single type. The partial-class declaration cannot be misused that way, which
is the whole of the argument.

**3. What `CoreApplicationFixture` overrides.** It derives from the framework's in-process web
application factory — `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>`, from the integration-testing package
[04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins — closed over the entry-point type point 2 made
visible, so the declaration is `CoreApplicationFixture : WebApplicationFactory<Program>`.

**The single override point, named, because "the fixture overrides host configuration" is not an
installation site.** Everything below is installed inside **`protected override void
ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)`** — the factory's own extension point, which runs after the
application's own configuration and registration have been composed and before the host is built. Within
it, configuration values are added through the builder's configuration sources, and **service-level
instrumentation is added through `builder.ConfigureTestServices(services => …)`**, which the factory
invokes **after** `Program.cs`'s registrations, so a post-configuration there observes what the application
registered rather than racing it. There is no second installation site anywhere in this design, and in
particular the fixture does not construct its own host builder: doing so would compose an application that
resembles the one that ships instead of being it.

It overrides host configuration to do exactly **four** things:

| # | Override | Why it is this and not something else |
| --- | --- | --- |
| i | **The environment name**, set as a literal by the fixture | It must not be `Development`, because `IsDevelopment()` selects the developer exception page and would hide the generic error contract the suite asserts (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 4, section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)). It must not be `Production` either, because section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s first seeding check keys on that exact name and the suite has to be able to drive both sides of that gate from configuration it controls. A third, dedicated name gets the **deployed** error path — the exception handler applies in every non-Development environment — without claiming to be production |
| ii | **Configuration values, injected through in-memory configuration** — enumerated key by key immediately below | Supplying them as *configuration* rather than by replacing a registered service means the application's own registration code is what runs (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 items 3 and 7). A fixture that registers the contexts itself is testing the fixture's wiring, not the application's |
| iii | **Three additive registrations, added through `ConfigureTestServices`** — the logger provider and the command interceptor point 3b requires, **and the connection-mode signal section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s selection function requires of every fixture host** — and nothing besides | Point 3b's assertions are unexecutable without the first two, so an override list that said "nothing else" contradicted the same subsection that demanded them. Those two are **additive and observational**: the provider is *added* to the logging pipeline rather than replacing the application's providers, and the interceptor is *added* to each context's interceptor list rather than altering its provider, connection, model or options. **The third is additive but not observational, and is admitted deliberately rather than by stretching the word "instrumentation".** Section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s selection function admits connection mode `M4` **only** where `ITestConnectionModeSignal` is registered, and the fixture's host is a `Web` host in an environment that is neither `Development` nor `Production` — so without that registration the function selects `M1`, which demands a managed identity, and **every** target-side run fails at start-up against the engine the fixture provisioned. An earlier form of this table omitted it while that section required it, which left the exhaustive list below forbidding a registration the design cannot run without. An earlier form also said "two pieces of observation-only instrumentation … and nothing besides", which this third registration contradicted in terms; the exhaustive list is immediately below, so neither "instrumentation" nor this admission can expand by interpretation |
| iv | **Nothing else** | Stated as an override because it is a decision, not an omission — see immediately below |

**The exhaustive list of what `ConfigureTestServices` may do, and it is three lines.** Anything absent
from this list is forbidden, which is what keeps item iv true now that item iii exists. Two withdrawals
are recorded so the count is not read as drift: an earlier form carried a **per-context** pair of
interceptor lines, and with the seam declared once in the application's own composition one additive
registration reaches both, so the second of that pair is withdrawn as redundant rather than as wrong;
and an earlier form omitted the **connection-mode signal** altogether, while section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) required the fixture to register it — so the third line
below is an omission repaired rather than a permission widened. **The count has moved once, two to
three, and the correction is recorded rather than the list quietly grown**, because the move repairs a
list that was under-stated against a requirement printed elsewhere in this document rather than widening
what the fixture may do: it admits no new *mechanism*, it is an `AddSingleton` addition of the same kind
as the first line, and it was already demanded by the section it is cited from. A list declared exhaustive
that omits a registration the design depends on does not bound the fixture — it forbids the design:

| Permitted | Mechanism | Bound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add the fixture's logger provider | `services.AddSingleton<ILoggerProvider>(…)` with the fixture's provider instance. **This one needs no application-side seam**, because the seam is the framework's: `LoggerFactory` is constructed from `IEnumerable<ILoggerProvider>` resolved out of the final container, so a provider registered in `ConfigureTestServices` is enumerated on exactly the same terms as the application's own — the enumeration is not a list the application composed and closed | **Additive only.** No `ClearProviders()`, no filter change, no minimum-level change — the application's own logging composition is what runs, and a fixture that raised the level would change which entries exist rather than observing them |
| Add the command interceptor, **reaching both contexts through the one seam the application declares** | `services.AddSingleton<IInterceptor, …>(…)` with the fixture's interceptor instance. **Not** `PostConfigure` over `DbContextOptions<T>`, which an earlier form of this row specified and which does not work: `AddDbContext` does not register its options through the options pattern — it builds and registers `DbContextOptions<TContext>` directly — so there is no `IPostConfigureOptions<DbContextOptions<TContext>>` for the container to run, and a `PostConfigure` written against it is silently never invoked. The suite would then assert on an interceptor that observed nothing and the affected rows would fail with no indication of why. Because stage 1 item 2 of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) ends **both** registrations with `.AddInterceptors(sp.GetServices<IInterceptor>())`, one additive registration here reaches both contexts, and it reaches them through the application's own composition rather than around it | Both contexts, explicitly, because the lazy-loading rows read catalog commands and the Identity rows read Identity commands: an interceptor on one context is silently no coverage for the other, and the omission looks like an application that issued no query |
| Add the **connection-mode signal** the fixture's own host needs for section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) to select `M4` | `services.AddSingleton<ITestConnectionModeSignal>(…)` with a **`private sealed` nested type declared inside `CoreApplicationFixture`**, constructed with the `(DataSource, InitialCatalog)` pairs **this run** provisioned and exposing them read-only as the interface's single member. **Singleton**, which is the lifetime section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s own row already fixes, and an **instance** rather than a factory because construction needs nothing from the container. Nested rather than a file of its own because `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/CoreApplicationFixture.cs` is the file [04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) already maps for this fixture and a nested type adds no path to that map; and nested rather than the fixture registering **itself** so that the container never holds the factory — the fixture's disposable lifetime belongs to the collection that owns it, and it is not a question the host under test should be able to ask. The application **declares** the interface and implements it nowhere ([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)), so this is the only implementation that exists anywhere | **Every target-side run, and no other host.** It is not per-case optional the way the line above is: the selection function admits `M4` only with the signal present, and M4's four conditions are then checked against the pairs it names, so a run that provisioned a database and failed to name it fails the start rather than falling through to another row. Nothing else may register it — row **O10** of section [12.4.1](#1241-the-published-operator-bytes) enumerates the **published** application's service descriptors and asserts that none exists for this type, and the `ProjectReference` direction (test → application) keeps the type's only implementation on the side that is never published. It carries no credential: the per-run password M4 permits is the one the fixture generated in memory, and the signal names **pairs**, never a connection string |

Three things it may **not** do, named because each is the tempting shortcut: **replace** any registered
service, **remove** any registered service, or **register a service against a type the composed
application neither already enumerates as a set nor resolves optionally while registering no
implementation of its own**. Those would make the host under test a different application,
which is the failure the whole "no data-access service is replaced" rule below exists to prevent — and the
rule is only enforceable if the one legal customization point has an enumerated allow-list rather than a
spirit.

**The third prohibition is stated over what the application *resolves* rather than over "a service the
application does not register", and the difference is the whole of what makes the three permitted lines
legal.** An earlier form said the latter, which contradicted every permitted line in the same table: the
application registers no fixture logger provider, no interceptor, no external scheme and no connection-mode
signal, so on that reading item iii was forbidden by the rule printed beneath it. It also concealed the
real constraint. A service the test host adds is reachable by the code under test **only** under one of two
resolution shapes the application itself composed, and the prohibition has two limbs because there are
exactly two.

**Limb one — the type is resolved as a set**, so an addition joins it: `IEnumerable<ILoggerProvider>`,
which the logging factory resolves; `IEnumerable<IInterceptor>`, which stage 1 item 2's
`AddInterceptors(sp.GetServices<IInterceptor>())` resolves; and
`IEnumerable<IConfigureOptions<AuthenticationOptions>>`, which the options system resolves when
`IAuthenticationSchemeProvider` reads its scheme map. **Limb two — the type is *declared* by the
application, resolved by it **optionally**, and implemented by it nowhere**, so an addition satisfies a
resolve that would otherwise be `null`: `ITestConnectionModeSignal`, which section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s single `IValidateOptions<ConnectionStringOptions>` reads
with `GetService<ITestConnectionModeSignal>()` and which the application implements nowhere at all
([04 §12.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md)). The second limb is not a loosening of the first: it is
narrower in the way that matters, because a type the application never implements has **nothing to
shadow** — the deployed host resolves it to `null` by construction, which is the ordinary case section
[3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) requires — and the addition is reached by exactly the call
the application already makes rather than by a new one. `IHostRoleSignal` is deliberately **not** in
either limb: the application registers it itself in both roots, so a fixture registration of that type
would be a replacement, and the fixture accordingly never touches it.

Anywhere outside those two limbs, a registration in
`ConfigureTestServices` is either **shadowed** by the
application's own registration of the same type — last-in-wins applies only to a single-service resolve,
so adding a second implementation of a singly-resolved type changes what `GetRequiredService` returns and
is therefore a *replacement* wearing an addition's clothes — or **unreachable**, because no application
code path asks for it. Both outcomes are failures the suite cannot see: one silently changes the
application, the other silently observes nothing. So the allow-list is exactly the set of types the
application either enumerates or resolves optionally without implementing, which today is exactly those
**four**: three enumerated sets and one declared-and-unimplemented optional resolve.

**Every key the fixture injects, by the exact name the reading process reads it under, and into which
process.** "Injects configuration" is not a specification: a reader has to know which keys, with which
values, which of them a row parameterizes, and — because there are two reading processes — which of the
two receives each one. This is the whole set, and there is no other. **Two destinations, and each key has
exactly one:** the in-memory collection the fixture hands `WebApplicationFactory`, which reaches the
**system under test** and admits only what section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract)'s web-application
row admits; and the **environment of the operator-console child processes** the suite launches, which
admits only what that section's operator row admits. Every row below names its destination where it is
not the first.

| Key | Value the fixture writes | Why the fixture owns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` | The per-run connection string, naming the collection's provisioned database and carrying the **runtime** principal's credentials — never the owner's (see point 3a) | Section [3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) consolidates the source's two entries into this **single** key, and section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 items 3, 7 and 8 have both contexts, the distributed cache and the key ring bind from it. One key is therefore the whole of the data-access wiring, and the per-class database-naming rule is section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s |
| `DataProtection:ApplicationName` | A **per-run** literal derived from the run identifier | Two runs sharing one engine would otherwise share a key ring and decrypt each other's cookies, which would make the isolation of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) untrue at the crypto layer while looking correct at the data layer. Rows 42 and 43 need **two hosts in one run** to share it, and that is exactly why it is per-run rather than per-host |
| `DataProtection:KeyRotationPeriod` and `DataProtection:CustodyPassPeriod` | The two required members of the `DataProtection` section in section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract), set to the **shortest values their validated bounds admit** — 14 days and 1 hour — so a fixture host starts rather than failing validation, and so the custody service of section [4.9.1](#491-an-empty-ring-needs-a-leader--the-key-ring-bootstrap-and-why-polling-readiness-is-not-a-proof) performs exactly its start-up pass within any run's lifetime and never a rotation pass | **The fixture sets no key-ring selector, and an earlier form of this table listed one.** `DataProtection:KeyRing` is **not a key of this design**: section [4.9](#49-the-data-protection-key-store--applicationdbcontext-owns-it) registers `PersistKeysToDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>()` unconditionally, so the database-backed ring is the only ring there is and nothing selects it. A filesystem ring is therefore not merely discouraged, it is unreachable — which is what makes rows 42 and 43 test the persisted ring rather than a coincidence of paths. What the fixture *must* set is these two periods, because they are `[Required]` and a host that omits them does not start |
