| `Seeding:Enabled` — **written into the operator console's child-process environment as `Seeding__Enabled`, never into the system under test's configuration** | **`false`** by default, and set to `true` **only** by the row 24 cases that require it | This is check 2 of section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s three, and the default must be off for the same reason the deployed default is: a fixture that left it on would seed ~780 rows over the manifest and invalidate every count assertion. **The destination matters and is stated because the two are not interchangeable**: the guard executes in `tools/provision-admin`, whose admission row in section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) admits `Seeding__Enabled`, while the web application's row **excludes** it by name — so a fixture that added this key to the `WebApplicationFactory` collection would fail the system under test's unknown-member validation and prove nothing about the guard |
| `Seeding:AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` — **also written as `Seeding__AllowedDatabaseNamePattern` into the operator console's child-process environment, for the reason the row above gives** | The pattern matching the fixture's own generated database names, **in the exact case the fixture generates them in** — because check 3 is ordinal and case-sensitive (section [5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)), a pattern differing from the generated name by one letter's case would fail `24a` rather than `24d` | Check 3 of the same three. It is written rather than defaulted, so that row 24 can fail this gate **alone** — with the environment and the flag both permitting — which is the only way to prove the gate the other two miss. Rows `24f` and `24g` override it per probe with the literal patterns those cases name |
| `Security:ContentSecurityPolicy:Mode` | `ReportOnly` or `Enforce`, per the case | Row 45 is parameterized by it (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 5), and the key has no default, so the fixture must supply one or the host fails to start |
| `Site:Hosts` | The in-process client's host value | Host filtering runs in the pipeline (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)); an unset value combined with a client host the application rejects produces a 400 on every row, which reads as a total port failure and is a fixture defect. **The key is `Site:Hosts` and not `AllowedHosts`**, because section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) leaves the framework's own `AllowedHosts` key unset in every file and every environment and fills `HostFilteringOptions.AllowedHosts` from this member instead — a fixture that set `AllowedHosts` would be configuring a key the application does not admit, and its value would be overwritten by the empty `Site` list at startup |
| `Paging:GenrePageSize` and `Paging:AdminAlbumPageSize` | **Left unset — the published default of 25 — for every row except section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 102, which sets each to `4`** | The manifest holds 10 genres and 12 albums, both below the default page size, so at the default every list fits on one page and the paging mechanism of section [4.11](#411-result-set-bounds-and-per-request-query-cost) is never exercised. Row 102 lowers the size rather than enlarging the manifest, because enlarging it would move the counts every other row asserts. The keys are members of the `Paging` section of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) and are admitted by the system under test; a value of `0` or less would fail that section's startup validation, which is itself why `4` and not `0` is how the row makes pages small |
| `Localization:DefaultCulture` | **`en-US`**, the literal section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) pins | Section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) stage 1 item 18 reads it and pins the process culture, so the fixture and the deployment pin the culture by the same key rather than the fixture doing it a private way. Every exact-text currency and date assertion in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) depends on it |

**Three values the fixture fixes that are *not* configuration keys**, listed here so the set above is not
mistaken for everything the fixture controls: the **time zone**, set as the `TZ=UTC` process environment
variable rather than through `IConfiguration`, because the runtime reads it from the environment and not
from configuration; the **collation** of every database the fixture creates, fixed in the
`CREATE DATABASE … COLLATE` statement that section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) makes literal; and the **base address**,
below. The culture is a configuration key and is therefore in the table above rather than here.

**3a. Three SQL principals, two of them created per run, and only one of them ever reaches the
application.** A single fixture-wide login that both creates databases and serves the application under
test is the mechanism by which a suite proves nothing about least privilege — and worse, it lets an
application defect that issues DDL succeed silently, because the credential it holds is allowed to. So the
run uses **two run-scoped logins**, both named from the run identifier and both dropped at teardown — and a
**third, externally provisioned** identity that brings them into existence, because a login cannot create
itself:

| Principal | Held by | May do | May not do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **BOOTSTRAP** | The **fixture only**, supplied as configuration from the pipeline's secret store or an operator session. **The only externally provisioned credential in this design** | Create and drop **databases** and **logins** on the allow-listed test server (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)) — and nothing else. Its whole purpose is to bring OWNER and RUNTIME into being and to remove them | **No DML and no `SELECT` on any application table.** Never written to a configuration key the application reads, never used to apply a migration, never used by the migration tool, never used to run a test |
| **OWNER** | The **fixture only**, created by BOOTSTRAP. Its connection string is never written to any configuration key the application reads | Own the run's databases; apply **both** migration sets; create the session cache table; run `tools/provision-admin` in every verb (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s invocation convention); load the fixture-data manifest; read and reset rows between tests; issue the fault injections | **No rights on any database it did not create**, and **no ability to create or drop a login** — which is why BOOTSTRAP, not OWNER, removes the run's logins at teardown. Its **blast radius** is bounded by the allow-list, the acquisition gate and its lack of cross-database rights rather than by per-table grants |
| **RUNTIME** | The **application under test**, through `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection` above. It is the only credential the host ever sees | **`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` exactly as [06 §6.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-bootstrap) section 3 item 6 grants them, one statement per object, to the user and not to a role** — so the verbs differ by table exactly as production's do — and **`EXECUTE` on nothing**, because the design has no stored procedures. Those statements are reproduced rather than approximated, and four of the objects they name are narrower than the rest, which is the reason for reproducing them literally: `AspNetUserLogins` carries `SELECT` and `DELETE` and **no `INSERT`**, which is the grant section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) derives from the retained management half; `AspNetUserClaims` and `AspNetRoleClaims` carry `SELECT` only; and `AspNetUserTokens` carries **no grant at all, with all four verbs explicitly denied**, since no flow in this application reaches it | **No DDL of any kind**: no `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, no `TRUNCATE` (which is a DDL-privileged operation and would otherwise let the application empty a table it may only delete from), and no schema ownership. **No membership in `db_datareader`, `db_datawriter`, `db_owner` or any other fixed database role, in any state of the run**: its data rights come from object grants and from nothing else, which is what makes [06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s probe set 1 a meaningful assertion rather than a failing one — a role-derived estate reports an `unexpected` row for every table-wide permission the role confers and a `missing` row for every object grant nobody issued. That is a correction rather than a detail. An earlier form of this row gave the principal blanket `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` on "the Identity tables" and derived it from "the two fixed data roles", which was wrong in two directions at once: the two built-in roles are **database-wide** and cannot express any of the four narrowings above, so a suite wired that way would run the application at **wider privilege than production** and could not detect a statement production refuses — the `INSERT` into `AspNetUserLogins` and every write to `AspNetUserTokens` would have succeeded here and failed on deployment, which is the worst place to find out. [06 §6.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-bootstrap) creates no role for this identity, and neither does the fixture. **No permission at all on either migration-history table and none on `dbo.AspNetUserTokens`** — [06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `DENY` block denies all four verbs on each — so a startup that tried to apply a migration **fails** rather than succeeding quietly, which is the assertion that section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)'s "no migration call in `Program.cs`" is actually true rather than merely intended, and so that probe set 2's `can_read_history` and `can_read_tokens` columns return the `0` that section requires |

Section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) owns the bring-up and teardown **order** — who creates
whom and who drops whom — and states it once; it is not restated here. Two consequences of the split are
used elsewhere. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s permission faults are expressed as **object-level
`DENY` statements against the runtime principal** — `DENY` and not `REVOKE`, for the reason that subsection
states, which is that **a `REVOKE` against an object-granted estate is a destructive restore**: this
principal's rights are object grants rather than role-derived, so a bare `REVOKE` removes the permission
entry outright and leaves it holding nothing on that object. That is why the restoration of a permission
fault is **two statements and never one** — `REVOKE <verb> ON <table> FROM RUNTIME` followed by a re-issue
of the exact `GRANT` the estate's construction made — and why
[06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s probe set 1 is re-run after every restoration rather
than the statement pair being taken on trust; that subsection states the precedence rule and the restore.
The same subsection also states why a permission fault cannot serve for the **migration tool**, which
connects as OWNER. And a row that needs the database to be *unreachable* rather than *unwritable* issues
`DENY CONNECT` against the runtime principal, which is reachable from the fixture precisely because the
identities are distinct.

**Bring-up provisions the whole of [06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s fixture estate and
then measures it, and both halves happen before the collection's first test.** The three connecting
principals above are what the *suite* uses; they are not the whole of what the database must contain for
the permission assertions to have subjects. So bring-up constructs that section's estate **`F1` through
`F7`, statement for statement**: the runtime principal's per-object grants with no fixed-role membership
(`F1`); the monitoring and jobs principals, created even though no test connects as either (`F2`); the
schema-extraction, data-load and break-glass principals as `CREATE USER … WITHOUT LOGIN`, which is a valid
`EXECUTE AS USER` subject (`F3`); and **the whole `DENY` block as the closing act of construction** rather
than as a separate later occasion (`F4`). It then runs that section's probes before any test executes:
**probe set 1 and probe set 3 unchanged, requiring both directions of set 1 empty, every column of set 3
zero and zero role-membership rows** (`F5`), and **probe set 2's six applicable blocks — runtime, jobs,
monitoring, schema extraction, data load and break-glass — executed by the OWNER principal in place of a
logical server's administrator group, with its deployment-identity block declared inapplicable by name
rather than run** (`F6`), because the OWNER of this run unites production's deployment and operator roles
continuously and section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s allow-list and acquisition gate are
what bound it instead. **Probe set 1 runs again after every fault restoration**, which is what makes a
restoration verified rather than assumed and is the check that catches the destructive-restore defect
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s two-statement rule prevents. A failure in any of these is a
**bring-up failure**, reported as the estate defect it is and not as a test failure, because no functional
row means anything measured against the wrong estate. And `F7` is the precondition for all of it, already
required above and restated because it is the one that makes the rest meaningful: **the application under
test connects only as RUNTIME**, and the OWNER and BOOTSTRAP connections — which provision the estate,
inject each fault and restore it — are never written to a configuration key the host reads.

**Standing denials and injected denials are two different things, and the fixture is required to tell them
apart.** The inventory above contains `DENY` entries of its own — `AspNetUserTokens`' four verbs, both
migration-history tables' four verbs each, and the rest of the block
[06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) publishes — installed at bring-up and meant to
stay. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injections add `DENY` entries meant to be gone by the next
test. Without a way to distinguish them, the leak check would either ignore real leaks or condemn the
standing set. So the fixture **records the runtime principal's complete permission set immediately after
bring-up**, from `sys.database_permissions` joined to `sys.objects`, and `ResetAsync()` re-reads it and
asserts **set equality** with the recorded baseline. A leaked injected `DENY` fails there, by name, in the
run that leaked it; a standing `DENY` is in the baseline and is never a finding. The comparison is on the
whole set rather than on the injected entries, so a *missing* standing denial — an over-eager restore that
`GRANT`ed something the inventory denies — fails the same check, which is the direction a
leak-only check would miss entirely.

**3b. What the fixture captures, and how, because "assert exactly one log entry at `Error`" is otherwise
not executable.** Rows 46 and 27 assert on the application's **structured log**, and rows in the
lazy-loading group assert on the **SQL the application issued**. Neither is observable without wiring, and
the wiring is specified rather than assumed:

- **A fixture-owned logger provider is added to the host's logging pipeline** — added, not replacing the
  existing providers, so the application's own logging composition is still what runs — and it records
  every entry with its **category**, **event id**, **level**, **scope values**, **state** and — the field
  an earlier version of this contract omitted — the entry's **exception**, in order, into a per-scenario
  buffer the assertions read. The trace identifier rows 46 and 17 correlate on is read from the entry's
  scope, which is where the framework places it.
- **The exception is recorded as the sanitized projection of section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1c, at the moment of capture**, never as
  the exception object and never as its formatted text. This matters because the application's error policy
  logs an exception by design (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) and rows 27 and 46
  assert on that entry: without the field there is nothing to assert against, and with the raw field the
  buffer holds an unbounded string that the first artifact write would publish. Projecting **at capture**
  rather than at emit is deliberate — it means no code path anywhere in the suite holds the raw text long
  enough to log it by accident. **It is a second line and not the control**: the application already emits
  its exception entries as a projection built before any provider is invoked (section
  [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), so this provider observes an entry that is already
  reduced, and the capture-time projection exists so that the property does not depend on the application
  half being correct — which is exactly what these rows are testing.
- **"Exactly one entry at `Error`" is scoped to the application's own categories and event ids**, and this
  is the ambiguity the finding is about: a bare count over every provider's output also counts
  framework-origin diagnostics — a connection-resiliency warning promoted to error, a hosting-layer entry
  during shutdown — and a suite whose oracle moves with a framework patch is not an oracle. So the
  assertion is: **exactly one entry whose category is the application's own** (the type that logged it,
  under the application's root namespace) **and whose event id is the one the composition assigns to that
  path**, and **zero** entries at `Critical` in any category. Framework-origin entries at `Error` are
  **recorded and reported in the failure diagnostic** but do not satisfy or violate the count — with one
  exception, stated so the leniency cannot hide a regression: a framework-origin `Error` whose category is
  the data provider's is a **setup** signal (the database is not in the state the case requires) and fails
  the case as a setup failure rather than passing it.
- **EF Core command capture is by interceptor**, registered by the fixture on the context options it does
  not otherwise alter — `DbCommandInterceptor`, which sees the command text and parameters — rather than by
  subscribing to the diagnostic-listener stream. The interceptor is chosen because it is **scoped to the
  contexts under test** and delivers commands synchronously with the request that issued them, whereas the
  process-wide listener stream interleaves every context in the process, which under a fixture that holds
  two hosts (rows 42, 43) cannot be attributed to a scenario. Captured command text is subject to section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s redaction before it reaches any artifact,
  because parameter values are the fixture's personal data.
- **The event-id contract is the application's, not the suite's.** The composition assigns a stable event
  id to each logged path the suite asserts on — the unhandled-exception entry, the cart-migration failure
  notice of row 37, the provisioning audit of section
  [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) — and those ids are part of the
  application's observable contract for the same reason a status code is. A suite asserting on message
  **text** would break on a wording change that no caller can observe; asserting on category and event id
  does not.

**3c. `IStoreObserver` reads; a second, distinct interface writes — and the split is enforced by where
each one is reachable from.** Section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) declares
`IStoreObserver` a **read-only** projection, and it is: every member returns state and none mutates. But
the suite plainly needs writes that are not the application's — a pre-state to provision, a fault to
inject, a reset to perform — and an earlier revision of this design attributed some of them to the
observer, which made the read-only claim false and put a mutation on the one surface a contract assertion
holds. So the writes have their own interface:

| Property | `IStoreObserver` | `IStoreSetup` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Connection** | The **OWNER** principal of point 3a, read-only statements only | The **OWNER** principal, the only one with the rights these operations need. **Never RUNTIME**, so a setup step cannot accidentally prove that the application's own credential could have done it |
| **Where it is reachable from** | The **injected context** of section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) part 3, so every contract and every derivation has it | A **member of the fixture only**. It is deliberately **not** on the injected context, so a contract body cannot name it — the boundary is a compile-time fact rather than a review convention |
| **Who may call it** | Any assertion, in any contract | **Fixtures and setup steps only**: the collection fixture's `ResetAsync()` and data load, and a concrete class's `InitializeAsync` where its row declares a pre-state. **No `[Fact]` body calls it**, and no assertion is expressed in terms of its return value |
| **What a call proves** | Something about the application under test | Nothing. It is arrangement. Every oracle remains an `IStoreObserver` read or an HTTP response, which is what stops a row from asserting that its own setup worked |

**Every write the suite performs, on `IStoreSetup`, with the caller that performs it.** This is the whole
surface; a write not listed here does not exist:

| Member | What it does | Called by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LoadManifestAsync()` | Inserts the fixture-data manifest of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) with explicit key values, in dependency order, and re-asserts that section's post-load invariants | The collection fixture, once, at collection start |
| `ResetMutableStateAsync(ResetOptions)` | The deterministic restore section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) specifies — reverse-order deletion and dependency-order insertion of the mutable set, the conditional catalog reload, and the cache-and-key-table emptying with the row 25, 42 and 43 exemption carried in the options | The collection fixture's `ResetAsync()`, which each concrete class's `InitializeAsync` calls |
| `EnsureAccountAbsentAsync(userName)` and `EnsureRoleAbsentAsync(roleName)` | Removes an account, a role, or a role assignment if present, independently of each other | Row 75's three pre-states — nothing present, the role present without the account, the account present without the membership — which is what makes each of its cases a statement about the tool rather than about the previous case |
| `EmptyAllApplicationTablesAsync()` | Deletes every row from the application's own tables in reverse dependency order, leaving the schema and the migration history intact | Row 24's own collection, to reach the **empty, freshly migrated** database its cases require |
| `SetIdentityStateAsync(userName, IdentityStateOverride)` | Sets `AccessFailedCount`, `LockoutEnd`, `PasswordHash`, `SecurityStamp` or `ConcurrencyStamp` to stated values | Row 71's constructed lockout-expiry state, the rows that need a specific hash format present, and row 75 `75f`, whose pre-state is the **neutralized** hash of section [5.5.1](#551-published-credential-accounts-are-neutralized-before-the-load-not-after-the-cutover) — computed by the fixture with the target's own `IPasswordHasher<ApplicationUser>` over a random value it discards, so the pre-state is produced by the mechanism under discussion rather than by a transcribed constant |
| `InsertSurplusRowAsync(LogicalTable, values)` and `DeleteRowAsync(LogicalTable, key)` | Adds or removes exactly one row by logical name and explicit values | The reconciliation-divergence rows, which need a **stated** one-row difference rather than a side effect |
| `ApplyFaultAsync(FaultSpecification)` and `RemoveFaultAsync(FaultHandle)` | Installs and removes one of the enumerated fault mechanisms of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injection table — the object-level denial, the unsatisfiable constraint, and the one-shot and always-on triggers, the one-shot together with the `SEQUENCE` that is what carries its state across the rollback it causes — returning a handle so removal is exact rather than a guess at what was installed, and so removal drops the sequence with the trigger rather than leaving a gate whose next value is already past `1` | The concrete class's `InitializeAsync` for a fault-injecting row, and its `DisposeAsync` for removal, so a fault never outlives the case that wanted it **even when the case fails** |
| `EnsureIdentitySchemaAbsentAsync()` | Provisions a database with the **catalog** migration set applied and the **Identity** set deliberately not applied | Row 25 `25c` alone, and see the lifecycle note below |
| `ArmInterleavedWriteAsync(InterleavedWriteSpecification)` and `DisarmInterleavedWriteAsync(InterleavedWriteHandle)` | Installs the three parts of the armed interleaved write of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injection table — the signalling `AFTER INSERT` trigger, the two handshake sequences, and the idle second OWNER session holding the one stated statement — and tears all three down. The specification names the statement, the table it targets and the bound on each poll; the handle is what the teardown uses. **Arming is a write, which is why it is on this interface and not on the observer**, and it is called from a concrete class's `InitializeAsync` — never from a case body, which is what keeps the interleaving out of the contract's own reach | Row 99 `99b` and `99c`, the only rows that need a write to land **inside** a request rather than before or after it |

**Row 25 `25c` gets its own database and its own host, not the collection's.** Its premise is a database
whose Identity schema is missing, and the collection's database has that schema applied before the
collection's first test — so the case cannot be expressed inside the collection at all without breaking
every other case in it, and dropping the Identity tables from a shared database would leave the collection
unusable for whatever ran next. So `25c` is its own collection (section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) part 5's rule), and within it: `EnsureIdentitySchemaAbsentAsync()`
provisions the half-migrated database; a host is started against it and the first request asserted; the
Identity set is then applied through the fixture's own migration path (the same one point 3 uses, under
OWNER); **a second host is started** and the second request asserted against that. Two hosts rather than
one, because the schema changed underneath and a host that had already resolved its services would be an
unreliable subject — and both hosts, plus the database, are disposed in the fixture's teardown whether
the case passed or failed.

**And `IStoreObserver`'s read surface is completed here, so that every oracle in section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) is expressible without a write.** Section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) lists the members the earlier revision named; these are
the additional read projections the matrix requires, and with them no row needs anything the observer does
not offer:

| Additional member | Returns | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GetTableDigestsAsync(IEnumerable<LogicalTable>)` | The canonical digest of each named table's contents, computed by the column order and normalization rule the seed expectation fixes | Row 24's digest comparison against `seed-expected.json`, and the idempotence re-check its second invocation makes |
| `GetAlbumAsync(int albumId)` | A DTO of that album's stored column values, including its genre and artist keys | The administration create, edit and delete rows, whose oracle is the stored row rather than the rendered page |
| `GetLinkedLoginCountsAsync()` | Linked-login counts **per provider** | Rows 54 and 65, whose reconcile assertions are per-provider |
| `GetMigrationCheckpointsAsync(string store)` | The `dbo.__DataMigrationCheckpoint` rows of section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) for that store, in commit order: table unit, row count, run id and per-store source fingerprint | The crash cases, whose subject **is** the checkpoint bookkeeping, and which cannot be expressed by reading the local evidence file |
| `TableExistsAsync(LogicalTable)` | Whether the table exists at all, distinct from holding no rows | Row 25 `25c` before and after the Identity set is applied, where "absent" and "empty" are different claims |

**No data-access service is replaced, and that is the point of the fixture.** No in-memory provider is
substituted for the SQL Server provider; no fake distributed cache is substituted for the SQL-backed
one; no user manager, sign-in manager or data-protection key repository is stubbed. Section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two gives the reason for the first
two — migrations and the session cache both require a real engine — and the key repository is the third
instance of the same reason: the persisted key ring is what the cross-host and restart rows of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) exercise, and a substituted repository would make them pass against an
application that could not share a cookie between two replicas. A suite whose cart identity is backed by
a fake cache cannot detect the failure mode section [6.3](#63-session-and-cart-identity) exists to
prevent: a cart that empties itself unpredictably.

**Nor does the fixture apply migrations from inside the host.** It applies them itself, as part of
provisioning, using the **same** migration sets in the **same order** as section
[5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order) — which is what the four steps of section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two describe. This keeps the
fixture consistent with the decision that no migration call appears in `Program.cs` (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order)); a fixture that migrated at startup would be exercising a
composition the target does not have.

**4. Two clients, both on an `https://localhost` base address — and that address is a URI convention, not
a transport.**

**What the client actually is, stated first, because the rest of this point is misread without it.** A
client the factory creates does **not** open a socket. Its message handler is the in-memory test server's,
so the request is handed to the application's pipeline directly: **there is no network listener, no port,
no certificate and no TLS handshake anywhere in this fixture.** "The base address is `https`" therefore
claims nothing about transport security and must not be read as claiming it — what it does is set the
**scheme on every request URI**, which is the only input the scheme-sensitive parts of the pipeline have.

**Why the scheme still has to be `https`, given that there is no TLS.** Three of the pipeline's decisions
read `HttpRequest.Scheme`, and the in-memory server populates it from the request URI exactly as a
TLS-terminating proxy would populate it from a forwarded header: HTTPS redirection (section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 6) turns a request whose scheme is `http` into a
redirect, so **every** row that asserts a status code would assert the redirect instead; scheme-sensitive
**URL generation** — absolute links, the `Location` values rows 4, 10, 51 and 72 assert — emits the
request's scheme, so a plaintext base address would produce `http` targets and the assertions would be
comparing the fixture's convention rather than the application's behaviour; and the `Secure` cookie
attribute under a `SameAsRequest` policy is decided from that same value. So the convention is `https`,
and **the plaintext path is exercised by the rows that are about the plaintext path** — row 47 at the
deployed edge, where there really is a listener and a certificate — never as an accident of a client
default.

**One consequence that follows from having no listener, and it is stated as a bound rather than left to be
discovered.** A handler-based client is reachable only from inside this process, so **nothing external can
address it**: a browser engine, a load generator or a `curl` invocation has no URL to open. **No case in
this suite requires one**, and that is a property of the coverage rather than a gap papered over here —
the one activity that would need an externally addressable listener is browser-executed behaviour, which
section [12.11](#1211-coverage-limits-and-the-scope-change-requests) records as an open limit and section
[12.5](#125-rendered-appearance-comparison-is-separate-and-manual) covers manually against a captured
baseline. So this fixture starts **no** network listener, and no row is permitted to introduce one.

**One consequence for cookie attributes, corrected here rather than left as a trap.** A cookie attribute
cannot be observed on a plaintext request at all: the request is redirected **before** any handler runs, so
no `Set-Cookie` is produced to inspect. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 52 therefore observes
the three cookies' attributes over **HTTPS**, and the `Always`-versus-`SameAsRequest` distinction — which a
plaintext observation was meant to establish and cannot — is asserted **on the resolved options**: the
fixture resolves the cookie, session and anti-forgery options from the host's service provider and asserts
that each one's secure policy is the literal section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled) fixes.
That is the one place the suite deliberately reads an application internal rather than an HTTP response,
and it is justified narrowly: the difference between the two policies is **unobservable over HTTP** in a
correctly configured application, so an HTTP-only assertion would be vacuous.

- **The default client follows no redirects and keeps cookies.** Automatic redirect following is
  **disabled**, because a followed redirect turns a 302 into its target's 200 and every redirect
  assertion in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) — the `AddToCart` redirect to the cart, the
  checkout redirect to completion, the `/Account/Login?ReturnUrl=…` anonymous and `/Home/Error/403?ReturnUrl=…` denial targets and the
  `/Account/AccessDenied?ReturnUrl=…` first hop of an authorized-but-denied one — would then be
  asserting the wrong response, and asserting it *successfully*. Cookie handling is **enabled**, because
  authentication, session and anti-forgery all depend on a cookie jar that survives across the requests
  of one scenario: sign in, then post a form.
- **A second client keeps no cookies**, and exists for the token-transport rows. The anti-forgery
  contract is a **pair** — a cookie and a field or header value (section
  [7.4](#74-problem-three--cart-removal-posts-without-a-form)) — so "no valid token" has two distinct
  shapes: the header absent with the cookie present, and the cookie absent with the header present. A
  client that silently replays its cookie jar cannot construct the second, and would quietly repair the
  request a negative row is trying to make. Both shapes are required rows in section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage), which is why both clients are required here.

**4a. Row 28 `28b` runs against a real Kestrel listener on a loopback port, because a browser cannot reach
the in-memory server.** This is the **only** case in the suite that needs one, and the exception is scoped
to it rather than being generalized into "the target fixture serves over the network":

| Element | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **Why it is required** | `28b` drives Chromium through the driver [04 §7.7](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins. The browser is a **separate process**; it navigates to a URL and opens a socket. Point 4's client has no socket to open, so the case is not merely awkward against the in-memory server — it is impossible, and a plan that named the driver without naming a listener would fail at the first navigation |
| **What starts it** | A **separate** fixture host, built from the same `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` configuration as point 3 — the same environment name, the same injected keys, the same instrumentation — but **started as a host with a Kestrel endpoint** rather than consumed through its handler. Same composition, different server, so the application under test is the same one every other row exercises |
| **The port** | **Acquired, not chosen.** Kestrel is bound to `127.0.0.1:0`, the operating system assigns a free port, and the fixture **reads the assigned port back from the server's resolved addresses** after start. A literal port and a scan-for-a-free-port loop are both rejected: the first collides with a sibling run on the same agent, the second has a race between the probe and the bind that produces an intermittent failure indistinguishable from a regression |
| **The scheme** | **`http` on loopback**, deliberately, and it is the one place in the target half where the scheme is not `https`. A listener would otherwise need a certificate the browser trusts, which means provisioning and trusting one on every agent — a setup dependency with its own failure mode for a case that asserts nothing about transport. HTTPS redirection is therefore **disabled by configuration for this host alone**, through the same key section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 2 item 4 reads, so the browser is not redirected away from the page it is asserting on. `28b` asserts nothing scheme-sensitive; rows 45, 47 and 52 own the transport and header assertions and none of them uses this host |
| **Readiness** | A **bounded poll** on `/healthz/ready` (section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) Stage 1 item 11 and Stage 2 item 13) over loopback — fixed interval, fixed maximum attempts, both literal — before the browser is launched. Exceeding the maximum is a **`SETUP`** failure naming the port and the last response, per section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction), so "the host did not come up" is never reported as "the page did not work" |
| **Teardown** | The host is stopped and disposed, and the browser context and browser are closed, in the fixture's disposal path — which runs **whether the case passed or failed**, on the same basis as section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)'s teardown rule. A leaked listener holds a port and a leaked browser holds memory on a shared agent, so neither is left to process exit |
| **Its isolation** | It is its **own collection** with its own fixture instance and its own provisioned database, per section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) part 5's rule for a row that needs its own host. It does not share the catalog or cart collection's database, so the browser's clicks cannot perturb another row's counts |
| **What it does not change** | Every other row in the target half continues to run through point 4's handler-based client. This host is not a second general-purpose transport, and no row other than `28b` is permitted to use it — stated as a bound because a network-addressable host is exactly the kind of convenience that spreads |

**5. `LegacyBaselineFixture` is not an in-process host factory, and it cannot be.** It **deploys, starts
and drives the MVC 5 application out-of-process, over HTTP, at a base address it produced itself.** The
reason it cannot be in-process is structural rather than stylistic: the legacy application's application
class derives from `System.Web.HttpApplication` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11] and is declared
to the ASP.NET pipeline by a markup file, so it is started by a Windows web server rather than by a test
process — [10](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) owns that toolchain and topology.

**The reason it produces the base address rather than reading one** is section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one's seven-step lifecycle, which this
fixture owns in full: the private per-run deployment outside the checkout, the copies of both store pairs
with the deployed copy's connection strings rewritten, the host process it **started and whose process id
it captured**, the bounded readiness poll, the startup-quiescence wait, and the teardown that stops
**that** process, detaches both databases and deletes the directory. **The tracked `.mdf`/`.ldf` files are
never attached**, and the base address is therefore always an output of step 4.

**There is no configuration key that supplies a base address instead, and the earlier one is removed.** A
previous revision of this design carried an optional `Tests:Baseline:BaseAddress` for the case where an
operator had an instance already serving. It is **deleted**, and the two reasons are not stylistic. It
reinstates precisely the failure the fixture exists to eliminate: a baseline that is whatever an unowned
process happens to be serving, resetting neither store between runs, so the sign-in and count assertions
pass or fail on run order — the fixture would then be a prerequisite dressed as one, which section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one already rejects. And it destroys
the **provenance** the baseline record of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) is required to carry: a cross-runtime
comparison means something only if the legacy binary and the legacy data are the recorded ones, and an
externally served instance can attest to neither. Every legacy execution therefore runs against a
deployment this fixture made, from inputs it can name.

Its remaining responsibility is the one that makes comparison valid: it hands out an `HttpClient`
configured with the **same** redirect and cookie policy as the target-side default client above — no
automatic redirect following, cookies kept — and, for the token-transport rows, a second cookie-less
client on the same terms, because a difference between the two runs has to be a difference in the
application and not in the client.

**The one property it cannot match, and the reconciliation it forces: the legacy base address is
`http`.** The legacy host is IIS Express as the project configures it — a plaintext debug URL and an
**empty** SSL port [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj:19], [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/MvcMusicStore.csproj:285],
with no certificate to present ([11 §3.6](11-cloud-readiness-assessment.md) owns the plaintext finding) — so
this fixture serves `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` and **cannot** serve `https`. Provisioning and trusting a
certificate for a baseline whose entire purpose is to characterize the application as it exists today would
be changing the subject. The consequences are three, and each is a bound rather than a caveat:

- **No shared contract may assert a scheme, a scheme-derived absolute URL, or a transport header.** The two
  base addresses differ in scheme by construction, so such an assertion would report the fixtures'
  configuration as an application difference on every run. Redirect assertions in shared contracts are
  therefore on the **`Location` path and query**, compared after the normalization of section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem three strips scheme and authority —
  which is what makes them comparable at all.
- **Every scheme-sensitive assertion in section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) is `Target`-only, deployed,
  or made on resolved options rather than over HTTP** — and the matrix already satisfies this, which is
  why the rule is a reconciliation rather than a change: row 45's header set and row 52 `52a`'s cookie
  attributes are Target-only, row 52 `52b` reads the resolved options, and row 47 is the sole
  `Category=Deployed` case, at the one edge where a listener and a certificate genuinely exist.
- **The plaintext baseline is itself a finding, not a defect in the fixture.** That the reference
  implementation cannot be driven over HTTPS is one of the transport findings the port exists to remedy, so
  the asymmetry is recorded here and asserted at the deployed edge rather than papered over inside the
  baseline.

**So the two fixtures share the `Contracts/**` abstract classes and nothing else**, and neither is a mock
or a subclass of the other. What the contracts receive is the fixture-owned context of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) — base address, the two clients, an `IStoreObserver`
and the delta ledger; what supplies it is either a Windows-hosted legacy application or an in-process
target host, which is exactly the platform split section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) specifies. `LegacyBaselineFixture`
supplies `LegacyStoreObserver` over the copied attached stores; `CoreApplicationFixture` supplies
`TargetStoreObserver` over the provisioned database under the owner principal.

### 12.7 Fixture lifecycle, isolation and parallelism

**The test runner's default is the hazard here, so the policy is stated rather than left to it.** The
selected framework runs **test collections in parallel by default** — a test class with no explicit
collection is its own collection, so a suite that says nothing about parallelism gets as many
concurrent collections as the runner's thread count. Combined with a topology in which each collection
provisions a database, that default means N collections provisioning N databases inside one engine
simultaneously, each running DDL and a data load — and, on the legacy side, N hosts competing for a port
and a LocalDB instance. That is the arrangement in which a shared engine runs out of capacity, a reset
races an attach, and a failure is not reproducible.

**Collection parallelization is disabled at the assembly level, in the one committed file that governs
the one test assembly.** The mechanism is a runner configuration file shipped with the future test
project — `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/xunit.runner.json`, marked as content copied to the output directory
and carrying **`parallelizeTestCollections: false`**. **One file is sufficient *because* the setting is
per test assembly and section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) puts both halves in one
assembly** — the arrangement that would need two files, and would silently leave one half parallel if it
got only one, is the two-project split that subsection declines. It is named here so the plan is
executable; **it is part of the future test project and nothing in this repository is changed to create
it** (section
[1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible)), and it sits
inside a project [04 §12](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) already maps, so no plan amendment is asked
for. Two notes on the choice:

- **It is a file, not an attribute, deliberately.** The switch can be expressed either way; in a file it
  is visible in a directory listing, reviewable in a diff, and cannot be lost when the assembly-level
  attribute file is refactored.
- **What is disabled is *collection* parallelism, not the fixture's own concurrency.** Tests within one
  collection still run sequentially — they always did — and asynchronous provisioning inside a fixture
  is unaffected. Nothing in this policy makes the suite synchronous; it makes the **engine's** workload
  serial.

**One collection fixture per surface group, and each owns its own database.** The groups are the ones
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) organizes its rows into — catalog, cart, checkout,
administration, account and Identity, seeding, continuity, operational, data migration — and the
**declaration** that makes each group a collection is section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) part 5's per-fixture `[CollectionDefinition]` class
with its `ICollectionFixture<TFixture>`, which is what causes the runner to construct exactly one fixture
instance per group. Two rows need their own group rather than a place in one of these — row 24 and row 25
`25c` — for the reasons those rows and section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) give. Each group's
collection fixture provisions **its own freshly created database** at the start of the collection and
drops it at the end. The consequences are the isolation guarantees, and each is stated as a rule the
suite is held to rather than as an aspiration:

| Rule | What it forbids | Why the alternative fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No test depends on another test's state** | Ordering assumptions of any kind, including "the sign-in test runs before the cart test" | The runner gives no ordering guarantee within a collection and is free to change it; a suite that depends on one is a suite that fails on a runner upgrade rather than on a regression |
| **No shared mutable static state** | Static fields holding a client, a connection string, a cached token, a captured baseline record or a row count | Two collections would then interfere through process state that no database reset can undo, and the failure would move when the collection count changed |
| **Each row's preconditions are established by the row itself, or by its collection fixture's data load** | "The album added by row 4 is still there" | The cart and order tables are written by several rows; a precondition that is another row's side effect is the leak section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) rejected shared-database isolation over |
| **A row that mutates asserts its own database invariant** | Passing on a status code alone where a write was involved | Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires this per row; it is repeated here because it is also an isolation property — a row that does not check what it wrote cannot tell its own write from a neighbour's |

**Determinism inside a collection comes from a reset between tests, not from a database between tests.**
One database per collection is the provisioning unit; it is **not** the isolation unit, and conflating the
two is how a suite ends up either intolerably slow (a database per test) or order-dependent (a database
per collection with no reset).

**But the reset cannot be hung on the collection fixture's own lifecycle, and that is the mechanism this
rule turns on.** A collection fixture is constructed **once per collection** and disposed **once per
collection**: its asynchronous initialization runs before the collection's first test and its disposal
after the collection's last, and the runner gives it **no before-each-test callback of any kind**. "The
collection fixture resets before every test" is therefore not a sentence the collection fixture can
implement — a design that stopped there would reset exactly once per collection and leave in place the
order dependence it claims to remove, silently, because nothing about it errors. The mechanism is
therefore split in two:

| Piece | Where it is declared | When it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`ResetAsync()`** — the deterministic restore itself | On the **collection fixture**, which is the thing that owns the database, its connection and the loaded manifest. It performs the restore through **`IStoreSetup`** (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3c) under the OWNER principal, never through `IStoreObserver`, which has no write member | Only when it is called. It is not wired to any runner callback |
| **`InitializeAsync()` and `DisposeAsync()`**, from the runner's **`IAsyncLifetime`** | On **every concrete test class** — the `Legacy*Tests` and `Core*Tests` derivations of section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box), which is why they are the place the binding lives | The runner constructs a **new instance of the test class for each test method** and awaits `InitializeAsync` before the method body and `DisposeAsync` after it, **whether the method passed, failed or threw**. That is the per-test hook the collection fixture does not have, and it is the only one the runner offers |

So each concrete class's `InitializeAsync` does exactly two things — **call the collection fixture's
`ResetAsync()`**, and construct the per-test client set below — and its `DisposeAsync` releases what it
constructed. Two consequences are worth naming: a test that throws mid-way still leaves the next one a
clean dataset, because the reset is the *next* instance's initialization rather than this one's cleanup;
and a shared contract needs no per-test plumbing of its own, because the derivation it runs under supplies
it. A test-authored cleanup at the end of the test body would be skipped on exactly the failures where
residue matters most, which is why it is not the shape chosen.

**What `ResetAsync()` restores, exactly.**

- **The mutable set, deterministically**: every `Carts` row, every `Orders` and `OrderDetails` row, and
  every Identity row a case can alter — accounts created by a registration case, role assignments, linked
  logins, and the `AccessFailedCount`, `LockoutEnd`, `PasswordHash`, `SecurityStamp` and
  `ConcurrencyStamp` columns of the manifest's accounts. Deletion is in reverse dependency order and
  insertion in dependency order, with explicit key values, so the restored state is byte-identical to the
  manifest's rather than merely equivalent to it. The **declared pre-existing rows** of section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) are **not** touched: they are not the
  fixture's to create and not the fixture's to remove.
- **Catalog reference data only when a case mutated it.** The administration rows write `Albums`; nothing
  else touches `Genres`, `Artists` or `Albums`. Reloading the catalog before every test would be harmless
  but dishonest about what the suite depends on, so the reload is conditional on the case having declared
  itself a catalog-mutating case, and the manifest's post-load invariants are re-asserted after any such
  reload.
- **The session cache table and the key table are emptied**, because a stale session row is a stale cart
  identity and a stale key row would let one test's cookie decrypt in the next — except in rows 25, 42 and
  43, which are *about* key-ring persistence and declare themselves exempt so that the reset does not
  delete the thing they assert.

**A fresh cookie jar and client per test, and this is the other half of isolation.** A database reset
undoes nothing that lives in a client: an authentication cookie, a session cookie, an anti-forgery cookie
and the cart identity keyed by it all survive in the handler's cookie container, so a client shared across
tests carries an identity from one test into the next and a "signed out" assertion can pass because a
neighbour signed in. So:

- **Each test constructs its own `CookieContainer`, its own `HttpClientHandler` over that container, and
  its own `HttpClient` over that handler**, in `InitializeAsync`, and **disposes all three** in
  `DisposeAsync`. Nothing is static, nothing is cached on the collection fixture, and no client outlives
  the test that made it — which is also the rule that makes the "no shared mutable static state" row in
  the table above enforceable rather than aspirational.
- **The redirect and cookie policy is the fixture's, identical on both sides** (section
  [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 4), so the per-test
  construction changes who holds the jar and never how the client behaves.
- **Several requests on one client inside one test is the scenario, not leakage**, and the distinction is
  the client's *lifetime* rather than its request count. The multi-step cases depend on it: rows 4, 5, 10,
  16, 19, 20, 35, 36, 37, 50, 51, 65, 67, 70 and 71 each fetch a page, read its token or cookie and then
  post — sign in, then post a form — which is precisely the sequence a browser performs and cannot be
  expressed with a client that forgets between requests.
- **Where a test deliberately holds more than one client, it is because the scenario has more than one
  caller**, and each is constructed and disposed by that same test: the **cookie-less** client of section
  [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 4 for the token negatives
  in rows 6, 7, 16 and the checkout token cases; **one client per host** in rows 42 and 43, which is what
  makes "the cookie H1 issued is accepted by H2" a real assertion; and **two distinct caller clients** in
  row 38, whose entire subject is that one caller cannot see the other's cart.
- **No case may depend on a prior case's residue, even within its own collection.** A case that needs a
  cart, an order or a signed-in account **performs that operation itself, inside the same test**, through
  the same HTTP surface a caller would use. This is what makes a single failing test diagnosable: its
  entire precondition is visible in its own body, and re-running it alone reproduces it.

**Provisioning and disposal are asynchronous, and disposal runs on failure as well as success.** Both
fixtures implement the runner's **asynchronous lifetime interface** — an async initialization method for
provisioning and an async disposal method for teardown — because every step involved is I/O:
provisioning an engine or a database, applying migrations, loading fixture data, copying and attaching
the legacy store pairs. Two properties are required of the teardown side specifically:

- **It runs whether the collection passed or failed.** Teardown lives in the fixture's disposal path,
  which the runner invokes after the collection completes **in either outcome**, and every destructive
  step inside it is written so that a step's failure does not skip the steps after it — the resources are
  released in reverse order of acquisition, each in its own guarded step, with the first failure recorded
  and re-raised after the rest have been attempted. A teardown that abandons the remaining resources on
  its first error is how an orphan is created.
- **It does not depend on the assertions having run.** A collection that fails during
  **initialization** — an engine that never became reachable, a migration that would not apply — still
  disposes whatever it did acquire, which is why the fixture records each resource identifier **at the
  moment of acquisition** rather than reconstructing it at teardown.

**Every resource name derives from a per-run identifier — and the identifier is generated by the
**caller**, not composed by the process.** It arrives as one configuration value, **`Tests:Run:Id`**
(environment form `Tests__Run__Id`), generated **once** by whatever invokes the run — the pipeline, or a
developer's script — and handed to **every job of that run**: the test job and the always-run sweep job of
section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) alike.

**A process that finds no value refuses to acquire anything**, reporting a `SETUP` failure, and
specifically does **not** compose one of its own. That is the correction, and the reason is mechanical
rather than tidy: the sweep partitions candidates by `runId` (section
[12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)), so a self-composed identifier makes the two jobs of one run
strangers — the sweep would see the killed test job's database as *another* run's, defer it behind the
24-hour gate, and leave the exact leak layer 3 exists to close.

**Its shape is fixed, so a caller has a rule rather than a preference — and the rule is the one closed
grammar of section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure),
`^[0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6}Z-[0-9a-f]{8}$`, cited here rather than described again.** This paragraph previously
carried its own description of a shape — a sortable, punctuation-free UTC timestamp plus a short random
component — and that description is **deleted**, not reconciled: it admits values the grammar rejects, and
a caller reading one rule while the consumers enforce another produces exactly the identifier that passes
here and fails there. The grammar's two halves serve this section's two needs, which is why it has them:
the fixed-width stamp is what a human scanning a server's database list sorts by, and the 32-bit nonce is
what makes two runs started in the same second — two agents, or a developer and a pipeline against one
engine — distinct, which a stamp alone does not guarantee. It is the same grammar as the migration run
identifier and **never the same value**: that one is generated by the tool, this one by the caller.

**Because this value arrives from configuration, it is matched against that grammar before the run
acquires anything — non-emptiness is not the check.** It becomes a container name, a directory name and a
JSON string in the ownership record of section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety), and a configured
value carrying a quote, a backslash or a newline would produce a record that does not parse — which, under
that section's rules, is a resource **nothing may authorize a deletion of**, and so the precise leak layer
3 exists to close. The check is the first thing Stage B of section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) does after binding the value, and its
failure is a `SETUP` refusal before any resource exists.

**The age input is never parsed out of a name**: it is
the `createdUtc` field of the ownership record, per section
[12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety). The per-collection database-naming rule that builds on this
identifier is in section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split), and section
[12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) makes the identifier part of a **safety** gate rather than only
a naming convention.

**A cleanup failure is reported, not swallowed.** A teardown that could not drop a database, delete a
copied store file or release an engine **fails the run at run level** — reported distinctly from an
assertion failure, per the classification in section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) — carrying the `resource` identifier, the
`operation` attempted as one of that shape's allow-listed operation codes, a **sanitized outcome code** and
the sanitized exception projection, in the SETUP record shape section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) defines. The reason is that the alternative is invisible: a
swallowed cleanup error leaves an orphaned resource and a green run, and the accumulation is discovered
later as an engine that is full or a bill that is larger than expected, with no record of which run
caused it.

**And because a cleanup failure is possible, an orphan sweep is part of the suite rather than an
operational afterthought.** It runs **before** provisioning at the start of a run, and it also runs as the
standalone invocation of section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) — a **concrete traited class in the one
test project**, driven by an **always-run pipeline job separate from the job the watchdog kills**,
which is the shape that matters: it is what makes the sweep a **post-process** guarantee rather than an
in-process one (see the run-timeout rule below), and a sweep placed as a final step of the test job would be
prevented from running by the very failure it exists to clean up after.

**Each candidate is authorized on its own registry row, never on the current run's identity.** A sweep
that required a candidate to match *this* run's identifier would authorize nothing, since by definition an
orphan belongs to a **previous** run — and a sweep that skipped the check because of that would authorize
everything. So the sweep evaluates, per candidate, exactly the two conditions section
[12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) defines for deletion of a resource this run did not create:
**the candidate's own ownership record names this suite as creator**, and **the creation time that record
carries** — read from the record, never inferred from the name — is **older than 24 hours**. A candidate the
sweep **cannot positively attribute** — no ownership record, an unreadable one, or one naming a different
creator — is **skipped and reported**, never deleted. Both conditions are required: the record is what
proves the resource is the suite's to remove, and the age bound is what stops a sweep from deleting the
resources of a run executing concurrently on the same engine.

**What happens when the sweep itself fails is stated, because "it sweeps" is not a policy.** The sweep
**does not fail the run**, and it is the one operation in this section that does not: it is a hygiene
step for previous runs' residue, and failing the current run because a previous run's orphan could not
be removed would make an unrelated run red. Instead:

- Each unremovable resource is **reported individually** at warning level with its identifier, its age
  and the error, through the same allow-listed diagnostic channel as everything else (section
  [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)).
- The run **continues**, because its own provisioning is unaffected by an orphan it did not create.
- A sweep that finds **more than a stated threshold** of unremovable orphans — ten — **fails the run at
  run level**, on the ground that ten is no longer residue: it is evidence that teardown is broken or
  that the fixture principal has lost the rights section
  [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) requires, and both are conditions the suite
  should stop on rather than accumulate against.
- The sweep is **never a substitute for teardown.** Teardown remains mandatory and its failure remains a
  run-level error; the sweep exists because a process can be killed between acquisition and disposal, not
  because disposal is optional.

**What happens when the run is killed, stated honestly, because the tempting sentence is false.** A
fixture's disposal path is code inside the test host process. If that process is **forcibly terminated** —
an external timeout, an agent cancellation, an operator, a machine restart — the runner used here **cannot
deliver** the asynchronous disposal callback, and a document claiming teardown still runs in that case is
describing something that will not happen. What is specified instead is three layers, so that the
guarantee stated is a real one:

| Layer | Mechanism | What it actually guarantees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Cooperative cancellation, bounded everywhere** | A cancellation token, created per run and per scenario, is passed to **every** HTTP call, **every** SQL command and **every** child process the fixture starts — the migration tool, the engine command, the legacy host. Each carries its own bound: the per-scenario ceiling for requests, an explicit command timeout for SQL, and a bounded wait followed by a kill for child processes | That a hang **inside** the fixture becomes a failure in-process, with disposal still reachable — which covers the overwhelming majority of hangs |
| **2. An external per-stage watchdog** | Each runbook stage of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) runs under a **stage timeout owned by the caller** — the pipeline stage, or the operator's wrapper — set above the run ceiling by a stated **grace period**, so layer 1 gets its chance to fail cleanly first. When the grace period expires the watchdog **kills** the run | That an agent is never occupied indefinitely. It explicitly does **not** guarantee teardown: it is the thing that prevents teardown from running |
| **3. A guaranteed post-process orphan sweep** | The sweep above, run as its own **always-run pipeline job, separate from the job the watchdog kills** — never as a step inside it, since a step in a killed job does not run. Section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) fixes the job, the concrete class it invokes, and its grace period and deadline | That the run's resources are released **even when disposal never ran**. This is the actual cleanup guarantee, and it is why the sweep authorizes each candidate from its own ownership record rather than from a live process's word: the process that created those resources no longer exists to vouch for them. Its own run's records carry the `runId` the job was handed and are therefore ungated by age (section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)); every other `runId` takes the 24-hour bound |

### 12.8 Destructive-operation safety

**This suite creates and drops databases, and it restores database files over each other. Those are the
same operations an accident is made of, so they are gated rather than merely intended.** The
requirement is not "point the fixture at a test server". It is that **a fixture pointed at the wrong
server by a mistyped configuration value, an inherited environment variable or a copied connection
string must refuse to run** — and refuse before it writes, not after. Three gates, evaluated **in this
order**, cover **every** destructive operation: creating a database, dropping one, attaching or
overwriting a store file, removing a container-hosted engine, and invoking the seeding mode of section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks).

**Gate 1 applies to all of them; gates 2 and 3 divide by direction, and that division is the correction
this subsection turns on.** An **acquisition** — creating a database, starting an engine, copying and
attaching a store pair — passes gates 1 and **2**. A **deletion** — dropping a database, removing a
container, deleting a copied store directory — passes gates 1 and **3**. They cannot be one gate, because
the evidence each rests on does not exist at the other's moment: at acquisition there is nothing yet to
own, so the only honest check is on the name and the allow-list; at deletion the name is the **weakest**
available evidence and the ownership record captured at acquisition is the strongest. A single combined
gate has to weaken one of the two halves to be satisfiable at both moments, and the half it weakens is
always deletion.

| # | Gate | What it checks, concretely | The mistake it stops |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The target server is on a test-only allow-list** | The server or instance the connection string names is compared against an **allow-list supplied by configuration** — an explicit list of servers the suite is permitted to touch, with **no default and no wildcard entry**, so an unset value is a refusal rather than a permission. A connection string naming any server **not** on that list is refused outright, and so is one carrying a hostname, database name or credential shape that matches a **production** target under the pattern the same configuration declares | The inherited value: a developer's user-level environment variable, a pipeline variable scoped more broadly than intended, or a connection string pasted from a runbook. None of them is caught by "the fixture is only run against test servers", because that is a statement about intent |
| 2 | **Acquisition: the name is generated by the fixture and matches the non-production allow-list** | Evaluated **before** creation, and it is a **name-and-allow-list** check only: the name is **generated** by the fixture from the run-identifier-derived rule of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) plus the collection's suffix, and it must match the allow-listed non-production pattern the same configuration declares. No ownership marker is required or consulted here, for the plain reason that **no marker can exist before the resource does** — a gate demanding one before creation could never pass, and a gate that pretended to check one would be theatre | Creating a resource on a permitted server under a name that is not distinguishable as this suite's, which is what makes every later authorization decision guesswork |
| 3 | **Deletion: the target is authorized from its ownership record, and the record is re-verified against the live engine immediately before the statement** | Evaluated before **every** destructive statement, and it is the gate acquisition's is deliberately not. Its mechanism is stated in full immediately below, because it does not fit a cell and because the obvious short version of it — "drop by immutable identifier" — is **not executable** against SQL Server. In outline: ownership is recorded **durably in two places** at acquisition; deletion **re-resolves** the recorded name to the engine's own identifiers and requires them to equal the captured pair; the statement is then issued against the **safely quoted name**; and a disagreement is a refusal, never a retry with looser criteria | Three distinct accidents. Name reuse: dropping somebody else's database that happens to match a test pattern, including a previous incarnation of one a person has since repurposed. The wildcard teardown: a cleanup written as "drop everything matching the test pattern" is one truncated pattern variable away from dropping everything. And the reused container name: `docker rm -f` against a name is a command whose target depends on what else is running |

#### Gate 3 in full — the ownership record, the re-verification, and the statement

**"Drop by immutable identifier" is not a statement SQL Server accepts, and the previous phrasing of this
gate was therefore not executable.** `DROP DATABASE` takes a **name**. There is no form of it that takes
a `database_id`, and `database_id` is not immutable in the sense the gate needs anyway: it is an
engine-local value that is **reused** after a database is dropped, so a later database can legitimately
carry the id an earlier one had. Nothing about the identifier alone therefore proves the name still denotes
the resource the record describes. The gate is specified as the three steps that do prove it.

**(a) At acquisition, ownership is recorded durably in two places.** One record, written to both, before
any test runs:

| Field | Value | Why it is in the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `creator` | The fixed literal identifying this suite as creator | Gate 3 authorizes on "this suite created it", and a record with no creator field authorizes nothing |
| `runId` | The run identifier of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) | Distinguishes **this run's** resources from another run's, which is the whole basis of the own-versus-orphan split below |
| `agent` | The host or agent name the resource was created from | The first thing a human needs when an orphan is found, and the field that identifies a machine whose teardown is failing repeatedly |
| `createdUtc` | The **suite's** UTC creation timestamp | The age input for the orphan sweep. Read from the record, never parsed out of the resource's name |
| `databaseId` | The engine's `database_id` for the created database | Half of the re-verification pair in (b) |
| `createDate` | The engine's own `create_date` for the created database | The other half, and the one that makes the pair meaningful: `database_id` alone is reusable, and `create_date` distinguishes an id that was reused from an id that was retained |

**The `runId` field is the caller-generated value of section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism), read from configuration** — which is what lets
two jobs of one run agree about what "this run's" resources are, and is why a process with no configured
value acquires nothing rather than inventing one.

**One of the two places is the authority and the other is a convenience, and which is which depends on
where the resource lives — stated as one rule, because two rules is how a resource ends up authorized by
the weaker of them.**

| Resource class | Authoritative record | The other copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Everything **inside** the engine — the run's databases, the two run-scoped logins | **The registry row**, in a fixture-owned control database on the allow-listed server. It is transactional, reachable by any principal that can reach the server, and it survives the agent, the artifact-retention window and a wiped workspace — which is what matters, because the machine that created a database is frequently not the machine that discovers the orphan. **Cross-job discovery is therefore through the registry**: the standalone sweep of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) connects and reads it | The JSON sidecar, for a human reading a failed run's artifacts |
| The **engine itself**, and every **filesystem** resource — the copied store pair, the deployed legacy copy, the per-run artifact tree | **The filesystem marker**: one JSON file per owned resource, in the run's artifact directory for the engine and *inside* the directory for a copied tree. It is the authority here of necessity rather than preference — on the developer path the control database **lives inside the container**, so a container cannot be registered in a table it hosts; and a directory has no engine to re-resolve a pair against at all | The registry row, where one can be written |

**Authenticated, because a record that anything can write authorizes nothing.** The control database is
owned by **BOOTSTRAP** (the three principals are below), the registry table's `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`
and `DELETE` are granted to **BOOTSTRAP only**, and they are **`DENY`ed** to the OWNER and RUNTIME logins —
`DENY` and not merely "not granted", for the precedence reason section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injection table states. So neither a defect in the run nor the application
under test can forge a record, alter another run's, or delete one to make a resource unauthorizable.
**BOOTSTRAP is also the cleanup identity**: the always-run sweep job connects as BOOTSTRAP and as nothing
else, which is what lets it drop a database whose OWNER login it is also about to drop.

**Acquisition fails closed on the record, not on the resource.** The authoritative record is written
**immediately after creation and before any test runs**, and `CREATE DATABASE` cannot be enlisted in a user
transaction, so the two are not atomic and the window is real. If the record write fails, the invocation
**drops the resource it has just created, at once, while it still knows what it created**, and reports a
`SETUP` failure. The alternative is the orphan the record exists to prevent, created by the record's own
failure.

A resource whose **convenience** copy is missing is still authorized, and the absence is **reported as a
hygiene warning** — refusing to clean up because half a record is missing would manufacture that same
orphan. A resource whose **authoritative** record is missing is **never deleted**: it is skipped and
reported, and it becomes a candidate for a human rather than for a looser gate.

**(b) Immediately before the destructive statement, the recorded name is re-resolved and the pair must
match.** Not at teardown planning time and not once per run — immediately before, in the same connection,
with nothing between the resolution and the statement:

1. Query the engine for the `database_id` and `create_date` of the database with the **recorded name**.
2. Require **both** to equal the recorded `databaseId` and `createDate`. Equality of both is what
   establishes that the name still denotes the same database the record was written about.
3. **On any disagreement — a different id, a different creation date, or no row at all — refuse.** The
   refusal is reported as a setup failure naming the resource, both values and both expectations. A
