   different pair is precisely the case in which the name now denotes **a different database**, which is
   the accident this gate exists to prevent; "no row" means somebody else already removed it, which is not
   an error to fail the run on but is an error to report.
4. Only then issue `DROP DATABASE` against the recorded name **safely quoted** — `QUOTENAME` around the
   name, so that a name is a name and never a fragment of a larger statement. There is no `LIKE`, no
   wildcard and no enumeration anywhere in the deletion path.

**(c) A container-hosted engine is removed by the container id captured at creation**, never by a container
name, because a name can be reused by an unrelated container while an id cannot. **A legacy host process is
stopped by the process id captured when the fixture spawned it** (section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one step 4), never by image name, for
the same reason.

**(d) A copied store directory carries a marker file, and deletion verifies the marker rather than the
path.** The private per-run deployment of section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one is a directory tree the fixture
recursively deletes, which is the single most damaging operation in this suite if its target is wrong — and
a path is weak evidence, because a mistyped or inherited `Tests:Baseline:DeployRoot` produces a
confidently-constructed path to somebody's documents folder. So the fixture **writes a marker file inside
the directory at creation**, carrying the same `creator`, `runId`, `agent` and `createdUtc` fields as the
record above, and deletion **reads and validates that marker first**: a directory with no marker, an
unreadable marker, or a marker naming a different creator is **skipped and reported**, never deleted.
Ownership is never inferred from the directory's name or its position under a configured root. **This is
not a second marker rule** — it is the filesystem row of the one table in (a), applied: for a directory the
marker **is** the authoritative record, because there is no engine to re-resolve a `database_id` and
`create_date` pair against, which is exactly why (b) has no filesystem counterpart and why a missing marker
here is a refusal rather than the hygiene warning a missing *convenience* copy earns.

#### The two deletion paths, and only one of them has an age gate

**The current run's own resources and another run's orphans are authorized differently, and conflating them
breaks both.** An age condition applied to the current run's teardown would forbid it outright — its
resources are minutes old — and an age condition omitted from the sweep would let it delete the resources
of a run executing concurrently on the same engine. So gate 3 has two variants, and every deletion
declares which one it is under:

| | **Own-resource deletion** (teardown, and the current run's failure paths) | **Orphan deletion** (the sweep of section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Candidate set | Exactly the resources whose records carry **this run's** `runId` | Only records whose `runId` is **not** this run's. A record carrying this run's id is never a sweep candidate, in any circumstance |
| Authorization | Steps (a) to (d) above: the record, the re-resolved pair, the quoted name, the marker | The same steps (a) to (d), **plus** the age condition |
| Age condition | **None.** There is no minimum age, no delay and no quarantine period; the resource is deleted as soon as the run is finished with it, and the captured pair is what authorizes that | `createdUtc` **read from the record** must be more than **24 hours** in the past |
| Unattributable candidate | Cannot occur — the run wrote the record itself; a record it cannot find is a **reported** cleanup failure and the run fails at run level | **Skipped and reported**, never deleted |

The consequence worth stating plainly: **the age threshold exists only to protect concurrent runs from the
sweep**, and it therefore belongs only to the sweep. Teardown does not need it and must not have it.

**"This run's `runId`" means the identifier the invocation carries, not the process that created the
resource** — and the distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic. The always-run sweep job of section
[12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) is a **different process** from the test
run whose leftovers it removes, and in the watchdog case that process no longer exists. It is nonetheless
**given the same `runId`**, by the pipeline that owns both jobs. So:

- Records carrying that `runId` are **own-resource deletions** with **no age gate**, which is what makes
  layer 3 below a real guarantee: a killed run's databases and copied store directories are removed minutes
  later, not a day later.
- Records carrying **any other** `runId` are **orphan candidates** and take the 24-hour gate, which is what
  keeps the same invocation from touching a run executing concurrently.

Without this definition the two rules collide: layer 3 promises release "even when disposal never ran",
while an age gate read as "any resource this *process* did not create" would defer exactly those resources
for 24 hours. One invocation, two candidate sets, partitioned by the `runId` it was handed.

#### Three principals, not two — because a run cannot create the login it is using

**Least privilege, so that a gate failure is not the only thing standing in the way.** The gates are
application-level checks and a check can be defeated by a defect; the principals' rights are what bound
the damage when one is. There are **three** identities, and the third is not a refinement: without it the
design is circular, since the run-scoped principals have to be created by **something**, and a principal
cannot create itself.

| Principal | Provisioned by | Lifetime | May do | May not do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **BOOTSTRAP** | **Externally, by an operator or the pipeline's secret store**, and supplied to the fixture as configuration. It is the **only** credential in this design that is provisioned outside the run, and therefore the only one whose secret has to be managed | Long-lived, and the same across runs | **Create and drop databases** on the allow-listed test server, and **create and drop logins** on it. That is the whole of its authority, and it exists so it can bring the two run-scoped principals into being | **No DML and no `SELECT` on any application table.** It is never handed to the application, never used to apply a migration, never used by the migration tool, and never used to run a test. Its connection string is read once at start-up and is not written into any key the application reads |
| **OWNER** | **Created by BOOTSTRAP**, per run, named from the run identifier | The run | Own the databases created for the run; apply **both** migration sets; create the session cache table; run `tools/provision-admin` in every verb; load the fixture manifest; read and reset rows between tests; issue the fault injections of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) | **No rights on any database it did not create** — no server-level administration role, no membership conferring rights across databases, and specifically not the ability to read, alter or drop a database another principal owns. It also **cannot create or drop logins**, which is why the sequence below has BOOTSTRAP rather than OWNER remove the runtime login |
| **RUNTIME** | **Created by BOOTSTRAP**, per run, and **granted** its rights **by OWNER** inside the run's databases | The run | The **object-scoped grant inventory** section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a reproduces from [06 §6.6.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md#principal-bootstrap) section 3 item 6, **one statement per object and issued to the user rather than to a role**, verb by verb and table by table, including its four narrowed Identity tables and its standing denials | **No DDL of any kind**, and **no membership in any fixed database role** — not `db_owner`, and not `db_datareader` or `db_datawriter`, which are database-wide and would silently widen four of those tables (point 3a states the correction). It is the **only** credential the application under test ever receives |

**The order, stated so the circularity is visibly gone.** Bring-up: BOOTSTRAP connects and passes gate 1;
BOOTSTRAP creates the OWNER login and the RUNTIME login; BOOTSTRAP creates the run's databases (gate 2) and
records ownership (gate 3(a)); OWNER is made the owner of those databases; OWNER creates the users inside
them — RUNTIME's, and the five further probe subjects of
[06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s `F2` and `F3` — grants RUNTIME its data rights one
statement per object, and applies the whole `DENY` block as the closing act of that construction (`F4`);
OWNER applies the cache table and both migration sets and loads
the manifest; and OWNER runs that section's probe sets, which section
[12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring) point 3a requires **before the
collection's first test** and again after every fault restoration. Teardown, in reverse: OWNER releases nothing it holds inside a database it is about to lose;
**BOOTSTRAP** performs the own-resource deletion of the databases, under the re-verification of (b); and
**BOOTSTRAP** drops the RUNTIME login and then the OWNER login. BOOTSTRAP drops both because a login cannot
drop itself and OWNER cannot drop logins at all — which is exactly the gap the two-principal design left
unstated.

Two consequences of the split are the point of it. A fixture defect that constructed the wrong database
name **cannot** drop that database through OWNER, because OWNER has no rights on it; and BOOTSTRAP, which
could, is bound by gate 1's allow-list and gate 3's re-verification rather than by grants. And the
production database, on a server that is not on the allow-list and to which none of the three has any
grant, is protected by three independent mechanisms rather than by one.

The **runtime** principal's lack of DDL adds a further independent mechanism: an application defect that
attempted a destructive statement — a stray migration call, a `TRUNCATE`, a schema change — fails on a
permission error rather than succeeding against a database the fixture is about to assert on. That is also
what makes section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s fault injection portable, since the permission faults
are **object-level denials against the runtime principal** — and a denial is the form that overrides that
principal's object grant whatever the grant's origin, which is why that subsection injects with `DENY`
rather than `REVOKE`. Its **restoration** is that subsection's two statements and not one — the `REVOKE`
followed by a re-issue of the exact `GRANT` the estate's construction made — because against an
object-granted estate a bare `REVOKE` would leave the principal holding nothing on the object, and
[06 §6.6.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s probe set 1 is what confirms the restoration landed.

**A refusal is a setup failure, and it is loud.** Any gate refusing terminates the run at that point,
reported as a **setup** failure under the classification of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) — distinct from an assertion
failure, because a refused gate is a statement about the *environment*, and reporting it as a behaviour
difference sends the reader to the application. The report names which gate refused, what it compared,
and what it found, with the connection string **redacted** to its server and database identity (section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)). **A refusal never degrades to a warning and never continues.** There is no configuration value
that relaxes a gate, no override flag, and no "force" mode; the suite has one behaviour when it cannot
prove a resource is its own, and that behaviour is to stop.

**The same three gates apply to the seeding rows, which is where they matter most.** Section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks) specifies a seeding routine whose own guard
fails closed on three checks — environment, enable flag, and an allow-listed database-name pattern — and
section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires the suite to prove all four of its outcomes: one
success with every gate satisfied, and three **independent** gate failures. Proving a *negative* means
**attempting** a seed that must not write, which is the one place in this suite where a test's purpose is
to run a destructive command against a configuration deliberately shaped to look wrong. Two rules keep
that safe, and they are not the seeding guard's own three checks:

- **The seeding rows never point at a real database.** The "production-shaped configuration" a negative
  row supplies is production-**shaped**, not production: the environment name is the literal
  `Production` and the database name is outside the seeding allow-list, while the **server** is the
  allow-listed test server of gate 1 and the **database** is this run's own registry-recorded database
  from gate 3(a).
  What the row varies is the input the guard reads; what it never varies is the target.
- **The suite's gates are evaluated before the seeding command's own guard, not instead of it.** Gates 1
  to 3 decide whether the command may be invoked at all; the command's three checks then decide whether
  it writes. The row asserts the command's outcome — a non-zero exit and identical row counts before and
  after — and the gates are what guarantee that a defect in the command could not have damaged anything
  the suite does not own.

**None of this is a substitute for the production-side control**, which is section
[5.4](#54-seeding--the-guard-fails-closed-on-three-checks)'s guard and section
[5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)'s separation of the deployment principal from the runtime
identity ([06 §6.2](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns that principal). This section is about the
**test** infrastructure, whose distinguishing property is that it performs destructive operations
routinely and unattended, on a schedule, from a machine nobody is watching.

### 12.9 Sensitive test data, diagnostics and redaction

**Two obligations pull in opposite directions here, and one mechanism satisfies both.** A failure has to
be diagnosable — a comparison suite that reports "row 12 failed" has told the reader nothing and costs a
day of local reproduction — and the data this suite handles must not leak, because the legacy fixture
attaches copies of a **credential store** and an **order store holding personal information**, and the
target fixture signs accounts in and posts a nine-field address form. The naive resolutions are both
wrong: dumping request and response bodies into the log makes failures diagnosable and publishes
password material and PII, while suppressing everything makes the suite safe and useless.

**The mechanism is an allow-list, applied to the diagnostic record rather than to the log stream.** The
suite never captures free text and then filters it; it captures **a fixed set of named fields** and
nothing else. Redaction is therefore a property of the record's *shape* rather than a filter that has to
be right every time — a filter is a list of things somebody remembered, and the field that leaks is the
one nobody thought of.

**1. Two record shapes, not one, and both entirely inside the allow-list.** A single exhaustive field list
was the first version of this subsection and it was wrong in a way worth recording: **a setup failure
cannot supply most of those fields.** When the engine never became reachable there is no endpoint, no verb,
no expected value and no observed value — so a schema that requires them forces every setup failure to
emit either empty fields or, worse, invented ones, and an empty `actual` next to a populated `expected` is
exactly how a fixture failure gets read as a behavioural difference. The two shapes below are therefore
**disjoint in their fields and identical in their discipline**: every field of each is named here, and a
field named in neither does not exist in any record the suite emits.

**1a. The ASSERTION record.** Emitted when a named field's observed value differed from its expected value
with the fixture healthy:

| Field | What it carries | Why a reader needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `class` | The literal `ASSERTION` — the classification of point 2 below, carried **as a field** | Without it the classification lives only in prose, and a consumer of the report has to infer from which fields are populated which kind of failure it is reading. That inference is the defect the two shapes exist to remove |
| `runtime` | Which fixture produced the observation — the legacy baseline or the in-process target host (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)) | Every row runs twice in the general case; a report that omits this is ambiguous about which of two runtimes disagreed |
| `endpoint` | The route template **and** the resolved path, both | The template identifies the code; the path identifies the case, including which identifier was used |
| `verb` | The HTTP method | Half the approved deltas and every 405 row turn on the verb (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)) |
| `scenario` | A stable scenario identifier: the section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row number plus the case within it | The reader has to be able to find the row in this document without guessing |
| `traces-to` | The requirement, approved-delta number or security finding identifier the row discharges — the traceability column of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) | It answers "does this matter?" without a second document. A failure tracing to an approved delta is read very differently from one tracing to a security finding |
| `expected` and `actual`, **per named field** | One pair per asserted field: status code, redirect target, each JSON property name and value, each named element's identifier and value, each database invariant | This is the difference between "the response differed" and "`CartTotal` was `10.99` where `21.98` was expected" |
| `normalized` | The list of fields **excluded** from comparison for this row — anti-forgery token, session identifier, cookie values, timestamps, framework-generated markup (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem three) | A reader must be able to see what was *not* compared, or a passing row is unfalsifiable. This field is why "the suite normalizes volatile values" is auditable rather than asserted |
| `invariants` | Each database invariant checked, with the expected and observed values — row counts by table, the order total, the cart row count for the key under test | Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) requires a database assertion per mutating row; the report has to carry its result or the requirement is unverifiable from the output |
| `trace-id` | The trace identifier the application rendered and logged (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) | It is the join key between the test output and the application's own log entry, which is the whole reason section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types) renders it |

**1b. The SETUP record.** Emitted when the fixture, the environment or a gate — not the application —
ended the attempt. Seven fields, and **none of the four observation fields above**:

| Field | What it carries | Why a reader needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `class` | The literal `SETUP` | It is the first thing the reader must know, because it is what tells them **no behavioural conclusion follows** |
| `operation` | A **typed, allow-listed code naming the operation attempted**, from a closed set the suite owns: `create-database`, `drop-database`, `create-login`, `drop-login`, `grant`, `deny`, `revoke`, `apply-migrations`, `create-cache-table`, `load-manifest`, `reset-mutable-set`, `copy-store-pair`, `attach-store`, `detach-store`, `delete-store-directory`, `start-host`, `stop-host`, `start-engine`, `remove-engine`, `probe-readiness`, `await-quiescence`, `invoke-migration-tool`, `invoke-seed`, `evaluate-gate`, `sweep-orphan`, `read-baseline-record`, `write-baseline-record` | Section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) promises a cleanup failure that carries "the operation attempted", and section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s gate refusals and re-verification refusals promise the same — a promise the field set had no field to keep, so the record either dropped it or smuggled it into free text. It is **enumerated** rather than free text for the same reason `outcome-code` is: a code aggregates across runs, and a sentence describing an operation is a place a database name, a path or a principal name arrives in. `stage` says which phase, `operation` says which statement, `outcome-code` says what happened to it — three orthogonal fields, and a reader needs all three to route |
| `stage` | Which step of point 2's enumeration failed, by its letter — engine provisioning, migration application, fixture-data load, legacy store reset, runbook precondition, safety-gate refusal, teardown | It is what routes the reader: `(a)` is an agent problem, `(f)` is a configuration problem, `(g)` is a leak somebody must sweep |
| `resource` | The identifier of the resource involved, **in the reduced forms point 3 fixes** — a database by server identity and database name, a container by its captured identifier, a store copy by its per-run directory name, a host by its base address with no credential | A stage without a resource is unactionable, and a resource emitted unreduced is a credential in a log line |
| `error` | The **sanitized exception projection** of point 1c — an allow-listed exception type name, a stable classification code and the trace identifier, and nothing else. Absent when no exception was involved | Without it the only way to say *what went wrong* is free text, which is how a connection fragment, a path or an account name enters a record. Its shape is fixed in point 1c because both record shapes carry it |
| `outcome-code` | A **stable, enumerated, sanitized code** from a fixed set the suite owns — for example a readiness timeout, an authentication refusal, a migration-application failure, an allow-list refusal | It is what makes setup failures aggregable across runs and greppable in a pipeline, which free-form text is not |
| `scenario` | The section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row and case that was **about to** run, or the stage identifier where no case had yet started | It scopes the blast radius: the dependent rows are reported **not run**, and this field is what identifies them |

**1c. The sanitized exception projection — because "no record carries the underlying error" leaves the
exception channel neither inspectable nor sanitizable.** An exception message, a stack frame, a file path,
a tool's captured output and a provider's own diagnostic text are all **free text of unbounded content**,
and each routinely contains exactly what point 3 masks — a connection string in a login-failure message, a
file path naming a copied store, an account name in a constraint violation. So none of them is emitted.
But *omitting the whole exception* is not a resolution either, and the earlier version of this subsection
made it one: the application's own error policy (section
[8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) **logs an exception**, rows 27 and 46 assert on that log
entry, and a capture contract that records only category, event id, level, scope and state cannot see the
exception at all — so the one channel most likely to leak was the one channel no rule here covered. The
projection is what covers it. It has exactly three fields and is **derived, never quoted**:

| Field | Value | Bound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | The exception's type name, **only if that name is on a closed allow-list** the suite owns — the provider's SQL exception, the framework's operation-cancelled and timeout exceptions, the invalid-operation and argument families, and the suite's own gate-refusal type. **Anything else is emitted as the literal `Other`** | A type name is a compile-time constant of a known assembly, so an allow-listed one carries no run data. `Other` is what keeps a novel type — including one whose *name* embeds a value, which some generated types do — out of the record |
| `code` | A **stable classification code** the suite assigns from the type and, where the provider exposes one, its numeric error number — `sql-login-failed`, `sql-permission-denied`, `sql-transient`, `sql-constraint-violation`, `timeout`, `cancelled`, `gate-refused`, `unclassified` | It is what aggregates. A message cannot be counted across runs; a code can, and "eleven runs failed with `sql-login-failed` on `create-database`" is a diagnosis where eleven distinct messages are a pile |
| `traceId` | The trace identifier, where one exists — the same value the ASSERTION record's `trace-id` carries and the same value the application renders (section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)) | It is the join key to the application's own entry, which is where a human with access to that log can read the full detail under that log's controls rather than under this record's |

**What the projection never carries, stated as a prohibition rather than an omission**: the exception
message, the stack trace, any inner exception's message or stack, a file or directory path, a server,
database, principal or connection fragment, any account name, email address or other personal-data value,
and any captured tool output. A projection built by formatting an exception and then filtering the string
is **not** an implementation of this field; the field is assembled from the three derived values above and
from nothing else, which is the same allow-list discipline the record shapes themselves rest on.

**Every channel the application's policy writes is captured, and every one of them is asserted.** This is
the other half of the finding: the policy writes to more than one place, and a suite that captured one of
them would report a leak-free run while a different channel emitted the message. So the fixture captures,
and the redactor's corpus covers, **all** of them: the structured log entry the exception handler writes
(section [8.3](#83-the-five-views-that-name-legacy-types)), **including its exception argument**, projected
as above before it reaches any buffer an assertion or an artifact can read; the response body the error
view rendered, which rows 27 and 46 assert carries the trace identifier **and no exception detail**; the
migration tool's own report and its exit code (section
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)); and the process **stdout and stderr** of
every child process the fixture starts.

**Retained console output is an artifact, and the earlier text was wrong to exempt it.** The previous
version of this subsection said a provider's own message "is available in the run's live console output,
which is inside the run's own trust boundary and is never an artifact". That is true of a developer's
terminal and false of every pipeline: a hosted agent **captures, stores, indexes and retains** stdout and
stderr, serves them over a URL, and frequently forwards them to a log aggregator — which is precisely the
"new places where it is newly durable and newly readable" that point 5 says these controls exist to
prevent. So stdout and stderr are treated as artifacts: passed through the redactor before they are
written, and held under the **same encryption, access-boundary, redaction and retention controls** as every
other artifact below, whose mechanism is [06 §9.5](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s. The genuine
diagnostic escape hatch is narrower and is stated as such: on a developer machine, an **interactive** run
may print unredacted provider text to the terminal, because nothing retains it — and that mode is
unavailable to any non-interactive invocation, which is every pipeline invocation.

**What is deliberately absent from both shapes**: the raw response body, the raw request body, the request
and response header collections, the connection string, any cookie value, and — per point 1c — any
exception text, stack, path or captured tool output. Each is a thing a
reflexive "log everything on failure" would include, and each is a vehicle for exactly the material
point 3 masks. Where a body's *content* is what failed, the report carries the **named fields** that
were asserted against it, which is what the black-box assertion style of section
[12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) already reduces every comparison to.

**2. Failures are classified, because a setup failure and an assertion failure send the reader to
different places.** A missing engine reported as "the target does not preserve the cart" is a false
regression, and it is the same category of error that section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) prevents on the other axis by enumerating
the approved deltas. Two classes, and the class is a field of the report:

| Class | What produces it | How it is reported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SETUP** | **(a)** engine provisioning — the disposable instance was not created or never became reachable within the readiness timeout of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split); **(b)** migration application — either migration set failed to apply, or the cache table was not created (section [5.3](#53-who-applies-ddl-and-in-what-order)); **(c)** fixture data load — the load failed, or the post-load row-count and key-invariant assertions of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two failed; **(d)** the legacy two-database reset — a store pair could not be copied, renamed or attached (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one); **(e)** a runbook precondition — tool restore, locked package restore, or the legacy application not answering at its configured base address (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)); **(f)** a gate refusal from section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety); **(g)** a teardown or cleanup failure from section [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) | The **SETUP record** of point 1b — its `stage`, its reduced `resource` and its enumerated `outcome-code`, and **no** endpoint, verb, expected or actual field, because a setup failure has none to give. It states explicitly that **no behavioural conclusion follows** — the run proved nothing about the application, in either direction. Every dependent row is reported as **not run** rather than as failed, because a row that never executed has not disagreed with anything |
| **ASSERTION** | A named field's observed value differed from its expected value, with the fixture healthy | The **ASSERTION record** of point 1a. This is the only class that may be read as a statement about the application |

**A third state exists and is not a failure: `EXPECTED-DIFFERENCE`.** A row whose observed difference
matches an enumerated approved delta (section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)) reports the
delta number and passes. It uses the **ASSERTION record's** shape with `class` carrying this third value,
because it *is* an observation of a difference — it is the verdict on that observation that differs — and a
suite with only two states forces every approved change to be re-argued at every run.

**The classifier's one admission rule, stated as a rule the harness enforces rather than as guidance.**
A record may carry `class = EXPECTED-DIFFERENCE` **only** if it carries a **numbered identifier from one of
the two approval registers** — a `D-nn` delta from the ledger of section
[11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas), or an `A-n` addition from the register of section
[11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) — whose approval decision
[03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s **W1** has recorded. Four consequences, and the last two are the ones
earlier revisions of this document got wrong:

- **A record with this class and no register identifier is itself a failure** — reported as `ASSERTION`,
  naming the missing identifier — because an unnumbered expected difference is a difference somebody decided
  was acceptable at the moment they read the failure, which is the entire failure mode the registers exist
  to prevent.
- **An identifier neither register contains, or one W1 has not decided, is also a failure.** Both registers
  are closed and numbered; an identifier outside them names nothing, and an identifier inside one that is
  still awaiting decision is unresolved scope rather than an approval.
- **Both registers are admitted, not just the delta ledger, and that is a correction.** An earlier form of
  this rule admitted a `D-nn` alone. But section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) exists precisely
  because the port **adds** user-perceptible behaviour that corresponds to no source behaviour — and an
  addition is **observable**, so it produces a difference between the two fixtures exactly as a delta does.
  Under the narrower rule every such difference was classified `ASSERTION` and **failed**, so the suite
  would have rejected the additions this document approves: the checkout validation summary of `A1` and the
  repopulated promo-code box of `A15` are the two that surface in coverage today, on row 11. Admitting both
  registers is not a loosening — section [11.7](#117-approval-owned-additions) states that
  [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W1 gate covers both registers, because approving one and not the other
  would leave half the deliberate difference unapproved, so the standard the identifier has to meet is
  identical in either case.
- **A citation of a finding is not an admission.** Section [11.5](#115-the-full-set-of-approved-deltas)
  already states that a finding is a **reason** for a change and never an **approval** of one, and this
  classifier is where that rule is enforced: a record citing a finding identifier — an `F-12-*`, a
  `09 §*`, or any other — **without** a ledger delta number is classified `ASSERTION` and fails. Section
  [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s both-fixtures rule is written to the same standard, so the two cannot
  drift: a caller-observable difference is admissible in exactly one way, by number.

**3. Redaction is mandatory, enumerated, and tested.** Nothing outside point 1's field set reaches a log
line or an artifact, and within that set the following are masked unconditionally — in the report, in
any fixture log, and in any file the run writes:

| Material | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Anti-forgery tokens — both the cookie value and the request field or header value | **Never emitted.** Presence and length may be recorded; the value may not. The token is a live credential for the duration of the session that issued it |
| Cookie values, for every cookie — authentication, session, anti-forgery | **Never emitted.** Cookie **names** and **attributes** are emitted, because section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts on `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite`, and an attribute is not a secret |
| Passwords, including the fixture's own and the one supplied to a negative sign-in row | **Never emitted**, in any form, including as part of a request body or a validation message |
| Password hashes | **Never emitted.** The migrated-account row of section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) asserts that the stored hash was **rewritten in the target format**, which is a statement about format and change, not about value — it is asserted by comparing format markers and a before-and-after inequality, neither of which requires the hash to leave the database |
| Connection strings | **Reduced to server identity and database name.** Every other keyword — credentials above all, but also application name and any option — is dropped. Section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s gate-refusal report is written against this reduced form, which is the one place a connection string legitimately appears in output |
| PII — the nine personal-data fields of the order entity, `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Address`, `City`, `State`, `PostalCode`, `Country`, `Phone`, `Email` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Models/Order.cs:8] ([09 §3.11](09-security-assessment.md) owns the inventory) | **Masked to a shape indicator** — field present, length, and validation-relevant class — never to a value. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s checkout rows assert on the *order and order-detail writes* and on validation outcomes, not on the address values, so nothing is lost |
| Usernames **and email addresses** | **Replaced by a keyed, deterministic, non-reversible alias** — see the paragraph immediately below, because "stable for the life of the run" is not a strong enough property and an earlier version of this row said exactly that. Email addresses are in this row **as well as** in the PII row above, and the two treatments are not in conflict: an email appearing as **order data** is masked to a shape indicator, because nothing correlates on it; an email appearing as an **account identifier** — in the Identity assertions of rows 57 and 63, and in the migration tool's own reports — is **aliased**, because those comparisons need to know that two records concern the same account and cannot know it from a shape |

**The migration tool's reports are inside this rule, not adjacent to it.** Section
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)'s modes emit reports that name accounts by
construction — the username-collision refusal names **both colliding names** (row 56), the normalized-email
notice names the carried accounts (row 63), and the reconciliation report names the administrator's
membership (row 65). Those reports are **retained artifacts**, published from a pipeline, so **every user
name and email address they emit is emitted as its alias**, never as the raw value, and the assertions in
those rows are written against the alias for exactly that reason. Two consequences: the reports remain
fully diagnosable, because an alias is stable and comparable and a reader with access to the alias key can
resolve it; and a report that leaked a raw account identifier would fail the redactor's own corpus rather
than reaching a store. The tool computes aliases with the same function, the same key and the same
`aliasKeyId` as the suite, supplied through the same secret channel as its connection strings (section
[5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure)) — so a report and a test failure concerning
one account carry the **same** alias, which is the property that makes them joinable at all.

**The username and email alias must be stable across runs weeks apart, which rules out the obvious
implementations.** The comparison this alias has to survive is not within one run: the Windows
characterization run emits a baseline record retained **for the life of the port**, and Linux target runs
consume it repeatedly, long after the run that produced it exited. A per-run salt, a per-process hash seed,
or the .NET string hash — whose seed is randomized per process by design — all satisfy "stable for the life
of the run" and all make the handoff incomparable the moment the two halves are not the same process. The
requirement is therefore **cross-run determinism**, and the specification is:

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **Canonicalization first, and it is Identity's own normalizer rather than a description of it** | The source value is canonicalized before it is aliased, and the canonicalization is performed by **invoking the pinned `ILookupNormalizer`** — the abstraction Identity itself resolves when it computes `NormalizedUserName` and `NormalizedEmail` (section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration)). It is resolved from the Identity core package rather than reimplemented; [04 §7.2](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) owns the pin and this document names no version. Without any canonicalization, `User-A` in one record and `user-a` in another alias differently and the two halves disagree about an account that is the same account. **The correction here is specific and it matters**: an earlier version of this row said "trimmed, and upper-cased with the invariant culture", and that is **not** what .NET 8's default normalizer does — `UpperInvariantLookupNormalizer` performs `Normalize()` followed by `ToUpperInvariant()` and does **not** trim. Both halves of that discrepancy are real defects, in opposite directions: **trimming merges** two accounts Identity keeps distinct, so two source rows collapse to one alias and a per-account comparison silently compares the wrong pair; **omitting the Unicode normalization splits** two accounts Identity treats as one, so a name in composed form and the same name in decomposed form alias differently and a correct migration reads as a mismatch. Invoking the normalizer removes the possibility of either, and the normalizer's **type name and assembly version are recorded in the baseline metadata** (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)) so that a change to it fails the handoff closed rather than silently re-aliasing everything |
| **The alias format, in full, because a partial format is not reproducible** | **`HMAC-SHA256`** over the **UTF-8 bytes of the canonicalized value**, keyed as below; the 32-byte result rendered as **lowercase hexadecimal**; **truncated to the first 16 hexadecimal characters** (64 bits); and **prefixed** — `u_` for a user name, `e_` for an email address — so an alias is recognizable as one in a report and a user-name alias can never be confused with an email alias for the same account. Example shape, not a value: `u_1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b`. UTF-8 is stated because the byte encoding is part of the function: the same string under UTF-16 produces a different digest, and two implementations disagreeing about it is a silent handoff failure. Truncation to 64 bits is a deliberate bound — the alias space is a handful of fixture accounts plus the source store's own, so collision probability is negligible — and a **collision is detected rather than assumed away**: the alias table is built once per run, and a duplicate alias over distinct canonicalized inputs is a **setup** failure rather than a silently merged pair. Keyed, not bare: user names here are short, low-entropy strings, so an unkeyed digest is reversible by enumeration in seconds and would be pseudonymization in name only. One-way, not encrypted: nothing in this suite ever needs to recover the original from the alias |
| **A key identifier travels with every record that carries an alias** | The key has an **`aliasKeyId`**: the first 8 lowercase hexadecimal characters of `HMAC-SHA256` over the fixed ASCII label `mvcmusicstore-alias-key-id` under that same key. It identifies the key **without revealing it**, it is stable for the key's life, and it is carried in the baseline metadata of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split). A target run whose configured key produces a different `aliasKeyId` than the baseline record carries **refuses to run the comparison** and reports a setup failure. Without the identifier a rotated key produces a baseline whose aliases match nothing, and every per-account assertion fails as a behavioural difference — the exact false-regression class this section exists to prevent |
| **The key lives in the platform secret store, not in the repository and not in a fixture, and it has one name** | It is supplied to the run as a secret through the same mechanism [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) provides for every other pipeline secret, and it is never written to a report, a log, an artifact or a configuration file that is committed. A key committed alongside the records it protects protects nothing. **The name is `TESTS_ALIAS_KEY`**, an environment variable holding the key as base64, read **directly by name** by both the suite and the operator console and deliberately **not** a configuration key — the same treatment `MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD` gets and for the same reason. Naming it is what lets the per-process admission matrix of section [3.3](#33-the-target-configuration-contract) list it as a key rather than as a description of one |
| **Custody and readership are named** | The key is held by the team that owns the pipeline's secret store; it is readable by the pipeline identity that runs `Category=Baseline` and `Category=Target`, and by nobody else. A developer running the suite locally supplies **their own** key, which makes their records incomparable with the pipeline's baseline — which is correct: a local record is not a release artifact |
| **Rotation is defined, and rotation invalidates the baseline** | The key rotates when the port closes, when a holder leaves, or on suspected exposure. Because the alias is deterministic *in the key*, rotating it changes every alias — so a rotation **requires a baseline re-capture**, and the baseline record's metadata carries enough to detect the mismatch and fail closed rather than compare across a rotation (section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split)'s baseline-record metadata) |
| **Destruction at port close** | When the port completes and the baseline record is superseded for the last time, the key is destroyed with the record. Retaining a key whose only purpose was to link two sets of records that no longer exist is retaining a liability with no use |

**Artifacts have a location, a publication rule and a retention.** Every file the run writes — the
failure reports, the normalized baseline record of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split), any fixture log — goes to a **per-run
directory outside the checkout**, created with access restricted to the identity the run executes as.
It is **not published to a pipeline artifact store unless it has passed the redactor**, which is a
positive gate rather than a review step: publication takes the redactor's output, so an unredacted file
has no path to a store. Retention is **14 days** for a published redacted artifact and **the run's own
lifetime** for anything unpublished, which the teardown of section
[12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism) deletes.

**One artifact is deliberately exempt from that retention, and it is named rather than left as an
inconsistency**: the **normalized baseline record** of section [12.10](#1210-the-execution-runbook-and-the-two-platform-split) is an *input* to every later target
run, not a diagnostic output, so it is retained **for the life of the port** and superseded only by a
re-capture. The exemption is safe precisely because the record has passed the redactor — it carries
expected values for named fields, pseudonymized usernames and no masked material at all — and it is
required, because a 14-day window would expire the baseline long before the port it exists to judge.

**Everything at rest is encrypted at rest, with named custody.** Three classes of thing this suite writes
outlive the process that wrote it, and each of them carries either credential material or personal data:
the **copies of the two legacy store pairs** (point 4 below — a credential store and an order store), the
**retained redacted failure artifacts**, and the **normalized baseline record**, which is retained for the
life of the port. The requirements are the same for all three and are stated once here:

| Requirement | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **Encryption at rest, platform-provided** | The per-run directory and the artifact store both sit on **platform-encrypted storage**; [06](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the mechanism and this document does not restate it. Application-level encryption is deliberately **not** specified on top: it would introduce a key this suite would then have to manage, escrow and rotate, for material whose exposure window the platform control already closes |
| **Key custody** | The encryption keys are the platform's, held by whoever owns the storage account or agent image — **not** by the suite, and never in a fixture, a configuration file or a repository. The one key the suite itself holds is the alias key above, and its custody is stated there |
| **Rotation** | On the platform's own schedule for platform-managed keys. The suite's obligation is only that it never pins, caches or copies key material, so a rotation is transparent to it |
| **An access boundary, stated as an identity** | The per-run directory is created with access restricted to the identity the run executes as; the artifact store is readable by the pipeline identity and by the reviewers the pipeline's own access model names. **Not** anyone holding the build's URL, which is what an unqualified pipeline artifact means on most platforms and is why publication is a gate rather than a default |
| **Secure deletion at retention expiry** | Deletion at expiry is a **delete of the encrypted object**, and the platform's key lifecycle is what makes the residue unreadable — which is the property that matters, because overwriting a file on managed storage guarantees nothing about the underlying media. The retentions are the ones stated above: the run's lifetime for anything unpublished, 14 days for a published redacted artifact, the life of the port for the baseline record, and **at teardown, unconditionally, for the store copies** |

**The redactor is unit-tested, because a redactor with no test is an assumption.** It is exercised
against a corpus of **known secret shapes** — a `Set-Cookie` header carrying each of the four cookie
names, an anti-forgery form field and its header form, a connection string in each of the shapes this
repository actually contains, including the file-attached form with `Integrated Security=True`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13], an Identity password hash, and a populated nine-field address
payload — with a **negative** half asserting that the fields the suite legitimately needs survive
untouched: status codes, cookie names and attributes, JSON property names, element identifiers, row
counts and the trace identifier. A redactor that masks too much is the failure mode that makes people
turn it off.

**Its corpus includes both record shapes, and three cases that exist because they are the ones that leak.**
The redactor is exercised **on the records themselves**, not only on strings:

- **A populated ASSERTION record** — every field of point 1a — asserting that each field survives in the
  reduced form its row specifies and that no field outside the list appears.
- **A populated SETUP record** — every field of point 1b — asserting the same, and specifically that the
  record carries **no** `endpoint`, `verb`, `expected`, `actual`, `normalized`, `invariants` or `trace-id`
  key at all, present-but-empty included. A present-but-empty `expected` is the shape that gets misread as
  a behavioural difference, so its **absence** is asserted rather than its emptiness.
- **The `operation` field's closed set.** Every code in point 1b's enumeration round-trips unchanged, and a
  record constructed with a value **outside** the set — including one assembled from a database name or a
  path, which is exactly how a free-text operation description would arrive — is **rejected by the record
  constructor** rather than redacted, because a typed field whose invalid values are quietly masked is a
  free-text field with extra steps. This case and the schema case below are what make the field's
  allow-list real.
- **The exception projection's three fields, positively and negatively.** Positively: an exception of each
  allow-listed type yields its type name, the classification code point 1c assigns it, and the trace
  identifier. Negatively: an exception whose type is **not** allow-listed yields the literal `Other`; and an
  exception whose message embeds a connection string, a file path under the per-run deploy root, an account
  name and an email address yields a projection in which **none of the four appears** — asserted by
  searching the serialized projection for each of the four literals, not by inspecting the fields the
  implementation chose to populate.
- **An attempt to emit an underlying error.** A record constructed with an exception's raw text, a file
  path, and a captured tool output is passed to the redactor, and the assertion is that **none of the three
  reaches the output** — the emitted record carries the enumerated `outcome-code`, the point 1c projection
  and nothing else. This is the case that fails first when somebody adds a field "just for diagnostics",
  which is exactly why it is in the corpus.
- **The record schema itself, as its own test.** Serialize a fully populated record of each shape and
  assert that the **set of keys is exactly** point 1a's or point 1b's — no extra key, no missing key. An
  extra key is how every leak in this design would arrive: not by defeating the redactor, but by adding a
  field the redactor has no rule for, which a schema equality test catches and a value-level test does not.
- **Captured stdout and stderr.** A child process's output containing a connection string, a password, a
  bearer-shaped token, an account name and an address payload is passed through the redactor, and the
  assertion is that each is masked to the reduced form its point 3 row specifies while the surrounding
  progress text survives. This case exists because point 1c stops exempting console output, and an
  exemption removed in prose but not in the corpus is an exemption still in force.
- **The alias function's cross-run determinism, and its distinctness — which are two assertions and not
  one.** The same canonicalized user name, aliased in two separate processes with the same key, yields the
  same alias; with a different key, a different one. **Two names differing only in case yield the same
  alias**, because the canonicalizer upper-cases. **Two names differing only in surrounding whitespace
  yield *different* aliases**, because the canonicalizer is `UpperInvariantLookupNormalizer` and it does
  **not** trim — so those are two distinct `NormalizedUserName` values, two distinct accounts to Identity,
  and aliasing them to one value would merge two accounts a per-account comparison must keep apart. **This
  corrects an earlier form of this case**, which asserted that case-differing *and* whitespace-differing
  names alias identically: that assertion contradicted the canonicalization row above, which already
  states that trimming merges accounts Identity keeps distinct, and it would have been satisfiable only by
  a trimming canonicalizer this specification refuses. **The test was changed rather than the
  canonicalization**, for three reasons: the alias exists to be a faithful projection of Identity's own
  identity semantics, and a projection that merges what Identity separates is not a projection; the
  collision reports of section [5.6](#56-the-data-migration-executor) key a collision **group** on the
  shared alias and rely on the alias being computed over exactly the normalized value, so a trimming alias
  would report a group Identity does not consider colliding and would hide one of its members; and the
  target's own user-name character set (section [6.1](#61-the-policy-table-every-row-labelled)) admits no
  whitespace at all, so a whitespace-bearing name can only arrive from the legacy source, where treating
  it as distinct is the conservative reading. Without both halves of this case the handoff's comparability
  is an assumption in one direction and a silent merge in the other.

**4. The copied legacy store files are the most sensitive artifact this suite handles.** The legacy
fixture's reset operates on **copies** of both committed store pairs (section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem one) — and those two pairs are not
sample fixtures. One is the application's **credential store**, with its password material intact; the
other is the **catalog and order store**, whose `Orders` table carries the nine personal-data fields
above, persisted with no encryption, hashing or tokenization
([09 §3.11](09-security-assessment.md)). Their
handling is therefore the same handling section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) gives a
database, expressed in files:

- **A private per-run location outside the checkout**, with access restricted to the run identity —
  never a shared temporary directory, because a shared directory is readable by whatever else runs on
  that agent. The location is outside the checkout for the reason section
  [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) already gives: attaching a tracked file
  causes the engine to write to it and dirties the working tree, which section
  [1.4](#14-the-no-modification-constraint-and-the-boundary-that-makes-this-document-possible) forbids.
- **Never published as an artifact**, under any condition, including a failed run. There is no
  diagnostic value in the file that the reduced report of point 1 does not carry, and the natural
  instinct after a hard-to-reproduce fixture failure — attach the database — is precisely what this rule
  forbids.
- **Deleted at teardown, including on failure**, by the failure-tolerant teardown of section
  [12.7](#127-fixture-lifecycle-isolation-and-parallelism), and swept by the same orphan sweep on the
  same ownership-marker-and-age basis as section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety) — the marker
  for a file being its containing per-run directory's name, which encodes the run identifier and its
  creation time.
- **Target-side fixture data is synthetic or pseudonymized.** The users, roles, carts and orders the
  target fixture loads carry generated names, generated addresses and generated credentials. The one
  thing they must not be is *arbitrary*: they are **migrated** rows, so that the Identity data migration
  of section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) is under test
  (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two, step 2). Synthetic
  and realistic are compatible; synthetic and *absent* are not.

**5. What is already public, stated honestly, because overstating the control would misdescribe it.**
The administrator credential this suite signs in with is **already committed in plain text in this
repository** — `DefaultAdminUsername` and `DefaultAdminPassword`
[src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:16-17], with the identical pair in MVC 4
[src/MVC4/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:25-26] ([09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) owns it as finding
F-09-05, and section [10](#10-administrator-provisioning-becomes-an-operator-command) retires it).
Nothing this section does makes that credential secret again, and no control described here should be
read as protecting it. **The values are not reproduced here**, for the same reason
[09 §3.5](09-security-assessment.md) redacts them: this document is circulated for approval and is not
the place to widen an existing exposure.

**So the control is about not propagating, and that is a real objective rather than a consolation.** The
store files hold **whatever else** was written to them, and the repository cannot establish what that is
— section [5.5](#55-the-identity-transition--a-schema-decision-plus-a-data-migration) makes exactly this
point about the credential store's contents, which is why it requires an authoritative extraction rather
than inferring them. An account count, an order count, a set of addresses, a set of hashes: each is
unknown from the repository, and a control that assumed "it is only sample data" would be assuming the
thing that has not been established. What the rules above prevent is the material moving from a
committed binary into **new** places where it is newly durable and newly readable — a pipeline log, a
retained artifact store, a shared agent directory, a developer's temporary folder, a downstream system
that indexes build output. That propagation is the part still under anyone's control, and it is the part
this section controls.

### 12.10 The execution runbook and the two-platform split

**The suite cannot run on one machine, and that is a structural consequence of what it characterizes
rather than a limitation to work around.** The legacy half drives an application whose application class
derives from `System.Web.HttpApplication` [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Global.asax.cs:11] against two
file-attached LocalDB databases [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13] — that is Windows. The target
half runs on the **Linux** agent [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) mandates, and mandates
for a reason this suite depends on: a Windows agent reproduces the case-insensitivity that hides the
path-casing defect, so the case-sensitive static-asset assertion of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) only means anything on Linux. **Both constraints are real and they are
incompatible on one agent**, so the split is specified here, with the handoff between the halves named
explicitly — an unstated handoff is how a suite ends up quietly comparing the port against nothing.

**Ownership boundary, stated once.** [06 §12.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the **pipeline
stages** and does not name a provider; [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) owns the **agent
and base image**. This subsection owns the **commands, prerequisites and configuration** those stages
invoke, and names no provider, no pipeline file and no stage of its own.

**1. Three coverage categories, applied as a trait on every test — and one maintenance trait that is not a
category.**

| Category | What it runs | Hard prerequisites | Where it runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Category=Baseline` | The shared `Contracts/**` assertions driven through `LegacyBaselineFixture` against the **running MVC 5 application** | **Windows**; the legacy application built and served; **LocalDB** with the instance the connection strings name [src/MVC5/MvcMusicStore/Web.config:12-13]; write access to the private per-run copy location of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) holding **both** store pairs | A **Windows** agent or developer machine. This is the only category that requires Windows, and it requires it for the *legacy* application's sake — nothing about the **target** build needs it, which is [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s position and is not contradicted here |
| `Category=Target` | The same assertions driven through `CoreApplicationFixture` against the **ported** application in-process (section [12.6](#126-the-test-project-the-system-under-test-and-the-host-wiring)), plus every target-only row | A **SQL Server-compatible engine** the fixture may create and drop databases on (section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) problem two), reachable from the agent; the .NET SDK at the band [04 §3](04-dotnet8-migration-strategy.md) pins | The **Linux** agent of [06 §12.3](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md), for the casing reason above |
| `Category=Deployed` | **Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) row 47, and nothing else** — the transport and HSTS observation at the deployed edge, held by the deployed-only class of section [12.2](#122-the-architecture-http-level-black-box) | A deployed non-traffic target and its base address. **No database, no engine and no in-process host**, which is why this category is the only one with no infrastructure prerequisite at all | Wherever the release runs, and **out of the `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests` assembly**, because that is where the deployed-only fixture and class are declared and a runner discovers only the assembly it is asked to run. This is the category [06 §12.1](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md)'s **Verify** stage consumes |

**`Category=Deployed` is narrow, and its boundary is stated because it is easy to widen by accident.**
It covers **row 47 alone** — a single case, which is why the execution totals of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) show `Deployed` as `1`. **The health rows are not in it**, and the reason is
worth stating because "health checks are what you run against a deployment" is the obvious assumption:
row 27's six cases include the **unreachable-database** cases, whose fault is a `DENY CONNECT` the fixture
issues against its own disposable engine (section [12.4](#124-required-coverage)'s injection table).
Neither half of that is available against a deployed host — the suite owns no principal there and must not
break one — so row 27 is `Target` alone, and re-pointing it at a deployment would silently reduce it to
its two reachable cases while still reporting as the same row. It specifically does **not** cover the
**three deployment verifications** of section [2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order): those are
boundary observations rather than application assertions, section
[2.4](#24-what-programcs-contains-in-order) already states that none is run by this suite, and
[06 §10.6](06-azure-hosting-recommendations.md) carries the two forwarding-dependent ones in its own
gate. Adding them here would give one fact two owners.

**Category assignment is a rule, not a per-row decision.** Every row of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage) with a legacy counterpart carries **both** `Baseline` and `Target`; every
row whose behaviour is target-only carries `Target` alone; and **exactly one row, row 47, carries
`Deployed`** — in the singular, and instead of `Target` rather than in addition to it, because its
assertion is on the deployed edge's transport behaviour and there is no in-process equivalent to run. A
mixed row carries `Baseline` and `Target` at the row level and its target-only cases carry `Target`
alone. Section [12.4](#124-required-coverage) states which rows are which, and its counts are
derived from exactly that rule: 152 `Baseline`, 325 `Target`, 1 `Deployed`, summing to the 478 executions
that section publishes.

**`Category=Sweep` is a fourth trait value and deliberately not a fourth category.** It is carried by
exactly one type — `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Maintenance/OrphanSweepTests.cs`, the concrete
runnable class the always-run cleanup job of point 3 invokes — and by no row of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage). It asserts nothing about either application: it removes leaked resources
under section [12.8](#128-destructive-operation-safety)'s authorization, and it exists as a test class only
because that is the runner the pipeline already has on both agents. It is therefore **excluded from every
count in this document** — the row, case and execution totals of section
[12.4](#124-required-coverage), and the three category figures above — and a reader reconciling those
numbers against a runner's own output should expect the sweep class's cases to appear there and nowhere
here. Stating the exclusion in both places is deliberate: a maintenance trait silently folded into a
coverage figure inflates it with work that proves nothing.

**2. The handoff — what crosses from the Windows run to the Linux run.**

**The Windows characterization run's output is an artifact, and the Linux target run consumes that
artifact instead of driving the legacy application itself.** Concretely: a `Category=Baseline` run emits
a **normalized baseline record** — one entry per scenario identifier, carrying the expected value of each
named field in the schema of section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1, the `normalized` exclusion list for
that scenario, and the 4.5-quirks-mode note that section
[3.1](#31-configuration-webconfig-becomes-appsettingsjson-read-through-iconfiguration) requires the
capture to record. It passes the redactor before it is written, so it carries pseudonymized usernames and
no masked material, and it is retained for the life of the port under the exemption section
[12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) names. A `Category=Target` run reads it and
compares against it.

| | **Recommended: the redacted artifact** | **Alternative: a hosted Windows baseline service the target run queries** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mechanism** | The Windows run writes the record; the Linux run reads it as an input | A Windows host keeps the legacy application and its LocalDB copies running; the target run calls it per scenario |
| **What the baseline is** | **Immutable and versioned.** A target run six weeks into the port compares against the same characterization, which is exactly the frozen-reference property [03](03-modernization-roadmap.md)'s W4 exists to establish | **Live and mutable.** Whatever the legacy application is at the moment of the query, including any change somebody made to it since |
| **Standing commitment** | None. The Windows machine is needed for the capture and for a re-capture, and at no other time | A Windows host, LocalDB and a served legacy application available for the **whole** duration of the port |
| **Exposure** | The record is redacted; the store copies never leave the Windows machine | A network path from the target pipeline to a machine holding an attached **credential store** (section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 4), live for months |
| **Failure mode** | A missing or stale record is a **setup** failure naming the record (section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)) — unambiguous | The service being down, slow or mid-restart fails target rows for a reason that is not the port, which is the false-regression class this document keeps eliminating |
| **Its one advantage** | Adding an assertion late requires a re-capture run | Adding an assertion late captures on the next query |
| **Verdict** | **Selected.** Its one cost is a re-capture run, and that cost is largely notional: adding an assertion means learning the legacy application's value for it, which requires exercising the legacy application either way | Rejected on the standing commitment and the exposure, neither of which buys anything the re-capture does not |

**The record carries metadata in two separate namespaces, and only one of them gates.** An immutable
versioned baseline is only worth its immutability if a consumer can tell whether it is the right baseline;
without that, "immutable" degrades into "old", and a target run six weeks into the port compares against a
characterization of something else and reports the discrepancy as a behavioural difference. But the record
also has to carry things a consumer must **not** compare for equality — the agent that captured it, its SDK
patch, its engine image — because those legitimately differ between the Windows capture and the Linux
consumption and gating on them would refuse every run. Conflating the two is what makes a provenance block
either toothless or unusable, so they are two named objects in the record:

**`baselineSource` — immutable provenance of what was characterized. Eleven items, and every one of them
gates.** The count is published because [07](07-effort-risks-sequencing.md) sizes against it and a
namespace whose membership is only enumerated is a namespace two documents can disagree about the size
of: the table below carries **eleven gating items** — `legacyCommit`, `legacyBinarySha256`,
`legacyConfigurationFingerprint`, `suiteSchemaVersion`, `fixtureDatasetFingerprint`, `culture`,
`uiCulture`, `timeZone`, `databaseCollation`, `aliasKeyId` and `lookupNormalizer` — in ten rows, because
`culture` and `uiCulture` share one row and are two items. A
`Category=Target` run **refuses to consume the record** — a `SETUP` failure naming the mismatched item, per
section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1b — when any item disagrees with
the value the current run establishes for it:

| Item | What it pins | How the consuming run establishes its own value | Why a mismatch invalidates the comparison |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `legacyCommit` | The commit of this repository the characterized application was built from | From the committed baseline reference below — **not** from the consuming checkout's own `HEAD`, which has moved because the port is what moved it | The baseline is a statement about a specific source state. Comparing against a record captured from a different commit is comparing against a different application |
| `legacyBinarySha256` | The `SHA-256` of the built legacy assembly that was served | The same committed baseline reference | The commit is not sufficient: a build from the same commit with a different toolchain, configuration or restored package set is a different binary, and [10 §3.2](10-build-and-deployment-requirements.md) records that the legacy build is not yet verified on a supported toolchain — so the binary that eventually gets built is precisely the thing that must be identified rather than assumed |
| `legacyConfigurationFingerprint` | A digest over the configuration the characterized host ran with, including the 4.5-quirks-mode note above | The same committed baseline reference | Two runs of the same binary under different configuration are two behaviours, and the quirks-mode note is the case this document already knows about |
| `suiteSchemaVersion` | The version of the record format and the field set of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction) point 1a | The constant the running suite implements | A record written before a field was added has no value for it. Absent this, that field silently compares as absent-versus-absent and the new assertion is vacuous |
| `fixtureDatasetFingerprint` | The `SHA-256` of the fixture manifest of section [12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) | Recomputed over the manifest file in the consuming checkout | Every expected value in the record is a value *for that dataset*. A record captured against a different dataset is expected values for different rows |
| `culture`, `uiCulture` | The two locale literals pinned below | Read from the consuming process's own effective culture, after the pinning mechanism below has run | They decide currency rendering, decimal separators and date formatting in every exact-text assertion, and the two halves of the handoff run on different operating systems |
| `timeZone` | The literal pinned below | Read from `TimeZoneInfo.Local` in the consuming process | Row 10's `OrderDate` window, row 50 `50b`'s lockout arithmetic, row 51 `51b`'s cookie expiry and row 70's minted timestamps are all time comparisons |
| `databaseCollation` | The literal pinned below | Read from the consuming run's own provisioned database | String ordering and comparison **inside the engine**, which rows 1, 8 and 9 assert an order over |
| `aliasKeyId` | The key identifier of section [12.9](#129-sensitive-test-data-diagnostics-and-redaction)'s alias rule | Derived from the consuming run's configured alias key, by that section's fixed-label construction | A rotated key produces a baseline whose aliases match nothing, so **every** per-account assertion fails as a behavioural difference. This is the item whose absence would produce the largest number of confidently wrong answers |
| `lookupNormalizer` | The **type name and assembly version** of the `ILookupNormalizer` the aliases were canonicalized with | Read from the normalizer the consuming run resolves | A different normalizer merges or splits accounts relative to the baseline, per that section's merge-and-split correction — the failure would present as a per-account mismatch and belong to neither runtime |

**`targetRun` — provenance of the consuming run. No item gates.** Recorded so that a failure can be
diagnosed and never compared for equality: the run identifier; the agent's operating system and version;
the SDK version; the engine's resolved image digest or the managed instance's identifier; the provisioned
database name; the UTC start time; and the resolved `tools/provision-admin` output path. A record consumed on
a different agent than it was captured on is the **normal** case — that is the whole point of the two-stage
split — so an equality check here would fail every run for a reason that is not a difference in behaviour.

**The gating values for the three legacy items come from a committed baseline reference, because a
consuming run cannot compute them.** `src/MvcMusicStore.Tests/Fixtures/baseline-reference.json`,
tracked in the repository beside the fixture manifest and copied to output with it (section
[12.3](#123-three-problems-that-must-be-handled-explicitly) states the path rule once), carries
the `legacyCommit`, `legacyBinarySha256` and `legacyConfigurationFingerprint` the port has **accepted** as
its baseline. It is updated in the same change that accepts a re-capture, by the reviewer who accepts it,
which makes accepting a new baseline a reviewable act rather than a side effect of somebody re-running a
job. Without it there is nothing to compare those three items against, and a swapped or silently
re-captured record would be consumed without complaint — the record would be internally consistent and
about the wrong application.

**Fails closed, not warns.** A mismatch in **any** `baselineSource` item is a `SETUP` failure and every
dependent row reports **not run** — it is emphatically **not** a warning next to a comparison that
proceeded anyway, because a proceeding comparison against the wrong baseline produces confident, specific,
wrong answers, and those are worse than no answer. The remedy is always the same and is always available:
re-capture, and update the committed reference in the same change.

**A re-capture is a normal operation, not an incident**, and the runbook below is what makes it cheap:
it is the same command with the same category filter, run on the Windows machine, replacing the record.

**And the record has to actually travel between two machines, which is a mechanism rather than an
assumption.** Stage A runs on a Windows agent and Stage B on a Linux agent; they share no filesystem, so
"Stage B reads it" needs the transfer stated, and a transfer that is not verified is a silent corruption
path — a truncated record consumed as authoritative produces missing expected values, which read as
behavioural differences:

| Step | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| **Stage A writes both files** | `<artifacts>/baseline/baseline-record.json`, and beside it `<artifacts>/baseline/baseline-record.json.sha256` containing that file's `SHA-256` as lowercase hexadecimal. The record is written first and the digest second, so a digest that exists describes a complete record — the same ordering rule the extract manifest of section [5.7](#57-the-data-migration-is-an-artifact-not-a-procedure) uses, and for the same reason |
| **Stage A publishes them as one named artifact — and only on a complete, wholly passing capture** | Published as the pipeline artifact **`baseline-record`**, containing both files and nothing else, **if and only if** the capture ran every `Category=Baseline` case and every one of them passed. A capture that failed a case, or that did not reach every case, publishes the **diagnostic** artifact of the row below instead and publishes **no** baseline record — it neither creates one nor replaces an existing one.
